Oh my god guys I just finished the game literally just ten minutes ago and had to share my thoughts on it to anyone considering buying this game. It has been out a while and it's likely everyone already knows all about it but if not this is your wakeup call.
The story is solid and you get to feel for the character Amanda Ripley as she desperately tries to find out what happened to her mother. The lighting and music has been beautifully presented in this dark foreboding claustrophobic station and you tend to get real paranoid as you hear all the tiny little noises from vents above, below and all around you. It's sure to make you quake in your boots if you don’t save regularly. See it has next to no auto save feature which is understandable given the survival horror genre.
While a lot of time and effort was put into the characters there’s only ever two that stand out as memorable, otherwise they’re only there to give you tasks to complete or to be killed off in gruesome fashion to heighten the tension. The atmosphere is perfect and you get surprisingly quite a bit of freedom to explore provided to have the tools to do so which is appreciated as it pays to take a break from the intense environment.
The alien AI is to this day the best I’ve seen but saying that it does have slight flaws in places. But for the most part it's so terrifying early in the game as your being stalked relentlessly while having no other defence but to run and hide. Thankfully your given crafting and scavenging to help you survive by distracting enemies with noisemaker bombs and the like. Personally I enjoyed traversing a section filled with human survivors and summoning the alien to watch it brutally murder these poor people but it's oh so satisfying to see the guys who are shooting at you just be torn to shreds by your minion Xeno.
The game in my opinion is triple A and I rank it among the greats at a spectacular 9/10.

Although I've sailed a little in a Hobie Cat in San Diego bay I'm not a sailor.  I'd like to be but that takes money.  So, when I found this I was intrigued.
I like realism in simulations.  After all that is what a simulator is for: to simulate a real activity; as opposed to a game with points and earnings and goals and winning and losing.  It's all good, just not simulation.
This is a simulator.  Here one needs to be ready for at least some of the challenges and experiences of sailing: working the boat to get the most performance, reading the weather when laying out a course, even dealing with the tedium of long voyages over quiet water.  For those who want game-style action or challenges this title may not be for you.  But for those who want to experience sailing without getting wet this title delivers, in my opinion.
First, handling the boat is of primary importance.  When I started I could get the boat moving and roughly where I wanted it to go by following the tutorials and learning from the on-board help system.  One thing I really appreciate about this title is the levels of experience one can choose between.  On the simplest level you just point the boat where you wish to go and the sim handles the rest (provided you are not in irons).  on the most advanced level you must make all the decisions and all the adjustments to the various parameters - there's quite a bit to learn.  And there are several in-between levels with varying degrees of assistance.  These levels are nice to work through since the system tells you what it is doing and why thereby instructing you as if a seasoned captain was explaining his thinking while working the boat.
The weather and environment system is great.  I'm on a long voyage now between San Diego and Hawaii and I've been tracking the weather with real life resources.  The weather I'm experiencing in game is what is being reported in the real world.  The graphics are nice and I'm sure will improve over time.
There is a great community of sailors that are in world often and they are friendly and helpful.  It's fun to hear their experiences and with the teleport system you can plop your boat down next to them and sail along or, if they agree, you can join them on their boat or have them join you.  I've not done this yet but it sounds fun.
One thing I've picked up on and I really like: the dev team seem eager to listen and consider suggestions.
I should wait until I've played more before writing a review but I like this one so much I wanted to let others know.  The main thing I would suggest to prospective buyers is to consider that this is not a game.  It is a simulator and, hopefully, will remain so.  I've seen some complain because they can't create scenarios with time of day, weather, etc., and sail those.  Well, that's because it is a simulator using the real world as it's base.  That might be available later but for me it is not an important consideration.
Watch the videos and read the comments before buying.  It's not for everyone, but for those of us who love to sail and really want the experience to be as close to real as possible this is a great title.

Excellent way to learn sailing. Unlike some other simulators, this actually teaches you how to sail in real life (to a certain extent). Very informative tutorial and plenty of tips during gameplay, basically all you need to optimize the sails and your speed.
The game is early access, but I have not encountered any game breaking bugs.

I live in Boston and sailing is a hobby of mine (in real life). This simulator is pretty much unplayable to me. While you are in the boat, your point of view is rigidly attached to the boat, meaning that when the boat heels, the horizon gets tilted. This is extremely unnatural, and after a while it actually made me kinda nauseous. In real life, you have the feeling of gravity to keep your head upright - it is instinctual in real life that the horizon will be level to your eyes no matter how much the boat heels.
Someone in the forums said that the creators intend you to tilt your head in real life to keep the simulated horizon level as the boat heels, but I really hope they aren't serious. It is very uncomfortable to keep level a simulated horizon when it disagrees with the gravity that you feel in real life. Furthermore, by tilting the horizon on screen, you lose a lot of space that could otherwise hold more visual information.
The view angles overall feel very wonky. I find it slightly frustrating that the tell tales are completely out of view when I am adjusting the sail trim.
I am considering trying to get a refund for this game, but I am conflicted. The effect of sail trim seems really accurate and the waves are really well done. I desperately want them to succeed in making this a great sailing simulator, and I see great potential here. But right now the horizon problem undermines the whole experience.

Simulators are designed by adults who don't remember what fun was. Its been hammered into them that learning is fun so they think they're giving people a great time when they make a game that requires study and the learning of arcane terminology as in sailing.  I am not against learning, but I like fun too. Sometimes I'll find it in a simulator even though the designers have done their best to keep that childish thing out of their simulation. Unfortunately, Sailaway is not one of those sims.
Okay, I watched the tutorials a couple of times and I struggled through the stuff about lines and sails. It was somewhat informative. I got my boat moving along and my telltails sometimes have their tails horizantal on both sides of the sail and at the top and the bottom. I can see where it might be something to know which sail to use and which rope, I mean line to tighten or loosen, but I can just leave things where they are for many hours. There isn't much of anything to do.
The waves are different everywhere, but they're not that amazing. Surprisingly, I can't crank up a huge storm and test my boat out. I have to find real weather. If there are no Irma's or Jose's in the world at the time, I'm stuck with whatever there is. Isn't it obvious that I might want to crank things up and smash up my boat in a horrible storm? Isn't that what games and computers are for, to do things we can't do in real life? Sure, have the real weather, but also offer the option of creating the weather. Its not like bigger waves and high winds cost more money. Its not like I can't just restart with a brand new, even more expensive boat.
When I play a game like GTA Vice City, I enjoy the waves and I always think, it'd be great to sail these boats the way real sailboats work.  I'd like the weather to change, but there needs to be more. Shouldn't there be tons of quick races available through those magic hoops that all kinds of games use. That'd be nice, expected even. (maybe I just haven't found them). It would be nice if we had to find something, maybe some sailors with a broken mast or find a missing airliner by it's transponder. There's nothing like that.
In Sailaway, for the most part you can't see your sails going up and down and having this or that tightened while looking at the thing your working on. Your view is mostly restricted to the line you're pulling on and that's annoying. It also ramps up the frustration level. You think if I weree on the boat, I'd grab the rope and look at the sail as it went up and down or the tail pulled in closer or whatever. I wouldn't look at the damn rope. You just know you're in the early years of gaming when you see something like that. The tip boxes blink on and off as the boat rocks. The bars on the various info screens are exceedingly thin and hard to grab hold of when you want to scroll a screen and the middle mouse scroll is so slow even when its cranked all the way up. The tutorial doesn't draw your attention to things expertly and there isn't a way to go over something again without watching a bunch of long, boring videos.
You'll be impressed though with the lines. The controls on the boats are, as far as I know, all there. Its more sophisticated than anything else I've seen. There are all kinds of settings for putting your boat under auto pilot but I'm never sure if they're working and neither is the game from what I've seen.
I was going to get a refund, but I used up my two hours on the tutorial vids which I should have watched on youtube. I had to play a few more minutes to find some weather and so now I own the game. Bottom line is the game is amazing, but tedious to learn and boring after a couple of hours. There's nothing to do but race or go in a straight line.  As far as chatting goes, people are nice but there aren't that many people in there right now. There will probably be even fewer as time goes on and people go looking for something that's fun and engaging.
Make your sims fun and engaging, gamemakers. People should be thinking, wow, I love the way I can steer with one hand and grab the halyard and pull while looking at the sail and then the sunset. Its like I'm there. (Sometimes it can be satisfying to reach a level of skill in a clunky game where it feels like you are doing that)

Perhaps the one thing that distinguishes Homeworld from other RTSs is that it doesn’t feel primarily designed around its multiplayer/skirmish mode. This isn’t to say the multiplayer has no merits; however, it sets this game in its own league compared to old and modern RTSs. It’s often the role of botmatches/players to add long-term value whereas the single player is either an afterthought or a tutorial. Homeworld, old and new, dares to defy its contemporaries as it did back in the ‘90s by making the campaign as vital to the core experience as well as incorporating its revolutionary 3D space combat that has yet to be outmatched.
Before we continue, it’s first important for me to clear the air with its newly acquired publishers. It’s no secret that when it comes to Gearbox they are not on my best list of developers; however, if they showed as much as a modicum of the respect and the effort as they did with hiring the original developers to remaster Homeworld, then they would be one of my favorite publishers. Despite the subtlest of changes that may annoy diehards, the attention to detail to bring back this leviathan from its slumber amongst the stars should be the standard they set for all their future projects.
When it comes to revitalizing the original games, Homeworld Remastered strikes an interesting blend of old-and-new in its attempt to modernize the classics that might have made many irate fans who did not enjoy Homeworld 2’s numerous changes. These changes are not simply nitpicks as it undermines many fundamental gameplay aspects of the original Homeworld as the result of its source-code being lost. (I’m not sure I understand the problem if they are also selling the original games with the remastered versions—it sounds like they could reverse-engineer the code or make it more approximate to the original.) To newcomers, these changes are largely easy to overlook—and they will be far more agreeable—unless you intend to compare the classic games with their remastered counterparts.
The first of many changes, which is only apparent in HW1 classic versus HW1 remastered, is that damage is calculated as RNG rather than projectile based. To describe the math more simply, the classic games had its attacks calculated with “bullets” that were determined by the speed, formation, angles, etc. of vessels. HW2, the original, did away with this to render more ships in formation units and supplanted the damage system with RNG bullets on the same factors. The result is while HW2 is largely the same but improved with modern updates to the UI, graphics, etc, HW1 is not really the same as its original on its fundamental gameplay, which isn’t as bad as the other major change.
Adaptive difficulty gets a bad rep in games when it’s handled poorly like Max Payne 1 and, to original Homeworld fans, Homeworld 2. This was most likely done after the original because of the general tactic of salvaging (stealing) enemy ships to build your own army as your army is a persistent force across the games. Many fans did not like HW2 for this one reason because they viewed the game punishing them for smartly capturing ships by raising the difficulty if they went above the population limits. The original Homeworld game, however, could easily lose its bite for its underdog narrative if players simply stole an entire armada with nothing to balance it. As a result, the added adaptive difficulty across HW1 and HW2 is something I’ve come to admire about the remasters as the game always feels tailored to my level of skill when I am failing or succeeding, and I never had to restart a previous mission to keep my fleet—unless I botched an encounter horribly.
These changes, as well as auto collecting resources at the end of every mission to remove excess waiting, ultimately make Homeworld more palatable to new audiences than old. Some may rightfully argue this was done for the sake of multiplayer to make balancing more polished/unified, but I would argue the single-player also benefits from this unified system. The fact that most mechanics/tactics transfer over between HW1 and HW1 more smoothly, save for how HW1 builds smaller units individually versus HW2 builds them in squads of 4/5, makes the gameplay have a greater, shared foundation than having two different games play their own separate ways. This is ultimately why I love HWR as a whole in spite of the sequel not living up in its narrative, though it is as mechanically solid, as the original.
Aside from Cataclysm (now called Emergence on GOG), the sequel has always lived in the shadow of its original, and it’s easy to see why, narratively, the first Homeworld seems more memorable. It’s also apparent to see why the sequel struggles to capture the same wonder and emotional attachment as the original when it explores largely the same regions, threats, etc. gussied up with a “chosen one” narrative with the same highs and lows of gameplay.
HW1 is an example of a story that is not praised for being innovative in its plot but being highly regarded for its execution of a great story. The story itself is one about a group of exiles trying to find their home whom we never see and whom we only hear/experience through ship-models their emotional journey that reveals their history in the galaxy. In a tale that features planet-wide genocide, purging of history on a galactic scale, and the morose sadness of an exiled group of wanders removed from their former glory, there is a great sense of wonder, exploration and mystery about the universe of Homeworld that reminds one of the original Star Trek. Missions themselves do not feel scripted into encounters or loosely threaded arcs; instead, missions are often the result of wandering into a new section of a galaxy previous unexplored and coming across a new threat/friend with a new challenge to overcome. The tasteful execution of its storytelling as well as its style to convey it makes it one of the more mature, tasteful stories told in any videogame.
The sequel, however, never captures that sense of newfound wonder, yet its storytelling is still on par with the original, even with the same underdog narrative given more prophetical importance. HW2 still retains the majesty of every mission linking together into a series of conflicts, though the mission structure is more combat-focused with little time to pause and refit the fleet compared to most missions in the original. Even with a more “disposable,” some might argue, fleet, the bonds made between your persistent army still retains the Homeworld vibe as you accumulate more and more ships and mourn any losses. The only damnable offense is that, unlike Cataclysm, Homeworld 2 is more of the same—on the positive side, it’s more Homeworld and it’s another reason to stay enamored in its region of space.

How an IP like Homeworld ever interested Gearbox will always baffle me. Known for their meme-filled lands and that-other-game-I-forget-what-it-was-called, Homeworld feels out of place in their line-up grounded in as much seriousness as its subtlety for storytelling. Then again, Gearbox was also responsible for the Brothers in Arms games, so perhaps there is some reason why Gearbox would be interested.
Regardless of their intentions behind acquiring the license, HWR achieves what all great remasters attempt to do: Make great games worthwhile and as faithful for modern audiences to stand the test of time. HWR still retains its sense of challenge, its spectacle of 3D space combat that never is mandatory but always an optional tactical opportunity, the necessity of control-grouping units, and everything else that makes Homeworld what it is. As a strategy/RTS game, it’s probably not the most in-depth to master; however, its sense of victory and the satisfaction of reclaiming Higara and enacting vengeance makes it a legend.

The god game genre isn't a particularly large one, and for ones that support multiplayer it's even smaller. For Gods and Idols to be not only both of these things but also free, they pretty much had me slamming on the download button before I'd even read the details.
Gameplay involves you finding a star system within a huge galaxy where every player has their own system and planet(s), you then build up your people through placing down what buildings are needed to produce or construct materials for newer and better buildings. After you’ve got down all the basics you then finally make your way into space.
I've only been playing two days so far, and the best comparison I could put Gods and Idols to would be a browser based game that's been polished a bit.
Now, this could be seen as a bad or a good thing, depending on what types of games you like. As everything continues to move forward even if you don't have the game open, coming back to check each day, build a few more buildings or ships before finding something else to do reminds me of the usual 'dailies' that most browser games work on. I don’t mind this, but for people expecting more to do each time they boot up the game, they may get a bit bored.
The graphics aren’t exactly jaw dropping, but they’re nice enough. Though there are a few images still missing from the building menu, and a few things that require a restart to set the graphics higher when it doesn’t inform you of such. There’s quite a lot of things that are obviously going to be added into the game at a later point, with a lot of buttons seemingly unable to do anything yet.
If they’re all completed however, I think it’d help add a lot more interest to the game, and there could be a pretty nice small game here.
This isn’t a deeply fleshed out game that will keep you hooked for hours, but it is nice to come back to and play around with when you feel like checking up on how your followers are doing. For a free game, it’s worth at least checking out.

OK, First thing is first --- This is a pre alpha title and review
That said,  from what I have seen and played of this game, it will end up becoming a good title. Right now it is a little difficult to get through, but from what I have seen and read, the potential is there.
To begin, you are an acendent being floating in a vast nebula of stars. Travel, Explore, and when you are ready to settle in, begin acreteing an asteroid field into a world. Guide its development by deciding which asteroids will benifit your world and destroy those that are baneful to your plans.
Once your planet had formed, begin to guide the life that has formed upon it into a civilization that will be your worshipers. (No mechanic for this currently) Guide your population in the production of food, healthcare, military, and production. Watch as your world grows from a few desperate nomads into a thriving civilization.
Currently, that is it. That is the game. Almost an uncontested game of Civilization. But wait, did I mention this is Pre-Alpha. Plans are being lain for space exploration, magic, the effects of your worshipers...
In the end I see this game becoming an amalgum of Spore, Black and White (sans Creature), Civilization, and Stelaris with an open sandbox mmo kicker.
The Development team seems to be hammering away to get more content in the game, and as I have played for less than a week, there is already the announcement of a second update/patch coming in about a week that will introduce a player market for resources.
I give the game a thumbs up. I only see a positive potential for where this game is heading and hope that it reaches it's pre alpha goals post haste.

As a hardcore Alien fan i was excited to play a game like Isolation, which is loosely based on the original Alien (1979), and i was not disappointed. Isolation offers a great survival experience, as you step into a Nostromo-like vessel against different kinds of enemies. Unlike previous Alien (or AVP) titles, the developers did their best and delivered us a well designed game. Personally, i think it's the best entry of the entire Alien franchise.
The flight recorder of the Nostromo was discovered, 15 years after the disappearance of the vessel. It is located on a ship called Anesidora, on the Sevastopol remote space station. Amanda Ripley, daughter of Ellen Ripley, hoping to gain knowledge about her mother's fate, follows 2 Weyland - Yutani members in the station, which is not inhabited only by humans.
Took me about 18 hours to finish the Campaign. The time someone needs to complete Survival Mode missions can't be calculated
An atmospheric stealth - suvrival horror game that gives you the Alien experience better than any Alien game / movie. The atmospheric and realistic gameplay make you feel like a crew member. The first horror title of the entire Alien franchise leaves a very positive opinion, despite the existence of some not-so-minor drawbacks.
+ Graphics are as good as they get, and the game's requirements are not high at all.
+ The sound effects are the crown jewel. A masterpiece. Sound is essential in a horror game's design, and Isolation designers nailed it. Not only the main sounds are great, but also the random vents / steps are so realistic that can give you a heart attack. The voice acting was not equally great, though.
+ The environment of the Sevastopol was also good. Well designed interiors that remind us of the Nostromo, detailed enough to assist the other parts of the game give it a totally realistic look. Everything in the game are inspired by the original movie, and this is obvious with a closer look at the items in the game like the save devices, the computers, the motion sensor. Isolation even has the dusty look of the movie.
+ The gameplay was satisfying. Mostly hide & seek with some action parts, but generally, you can choose your approach and the enemies will repsond accordingly. There are also some minigames you complete via hacking PDA / cutting tools.
+ A variety of weapons and stuff to use, but with barely enough ammo to make you feel safe, and they are to be used with caution.
+ The AI is good(ish). There are many ways off a difficult situation, most of them via your inventory, and the enemies will respond accordingly.
+ Survival Mode. Kinda compensates the absent multiplayer. You start of with some equipment / weapons, with a time limit and some objectives. It is fast paced.

- The story is poor. A side story which as nothing to the franchise. Also, the plot is totally predictable, with some exceptions. This does not make the game less scary, but some horror games have more interesting plots
- The AI is not functioning correctly at some points. Sometimes enemies can spot you even if you hide in the darkest corner of the room and at the same time cant hear your steps 1 meter behind them. At some other points, the Alien will walk around your exact location even if it doesnt know you are there, won't give a damn about the flare you threw as a distraction while at other points will spot a flare 3 rooms away with a huge delay. This AI mulfunction can provoke the following.
- Boring gameplay from time to time. The AI problems might make you end up hiding in a closet or under a desk for several minutes, only to die by the time the enemy finally spots you. Also, the ammount of deaths you will experience is too damn high. Possibly the major problem of the game. Barely 20 hours of gameplay cant normally make you feel bored. That's the only reason the vast majority of people didnt even complete the game (The achievement you get for completing the story is owned only by 5% of the owners of the game).
- The price, especially for DLCs. Absent multiplayer, with only one survival mission, 50 euros (and another 50 for the DLCs which double the game time) are probably a lot. But it's still worth it.
Concluding, this game is worth buying, if you can afford it. If you cant, grab it on sale

No Ports ?
Many things are planned for this game, though the implimentations of ports are still up in the air. As an avid simmer since the mid 1980s, I cannot stress enough how important it is to have an actual arrival and destination point in the scenery. Arrival at such a point gives a real a sense of achievement , even if its crudely implemented -  like a buoy with a name pinned to it.  Right now it really feels somewhat pointless having an entire globe worth of oceans to sail on, and no actual ports. Having them will greatly enhance immersion.
This is my only gripe to an otherwise GEM of a simulation!

Great to learn sailing, probably, but not very exciting.  Doesn't seem like it's possible to capsize or damage the boat (the tutorial mentions that "gybing" can snap off the mast in fast enough wind but I tried it in the strongest winds on earth right now and nothing happened).  Not very exciting visually, couldn't find any crazy storms or anything, even the worst storm still had sunlight and was pretty meh-worthy, especially given the aforementioned inability to capsize.  Running aground is not exciting either, you just get a popup saying "help me" and your boat resets off the coast.  No human constructions (cities, NPC traffic) or other landmarks (like the Golden Gate Bridge).
That said, the sailing AI is pretty cool, it's neat to put it in auto-trim and watch it move the ropes around.  It explains why it's doing this, to a degree ("raising jib line to 40% to open top sail" or whatever).  However I wanted to watch this from an angle where I could actually see the sail moving, and that didn't seem to be possible: I couldn't find a good vantage point on the boat, and if you position the camera in an off-the-boat "3rd person" angle that shows the sails then the auto-trim button no longer works.  So all I really got to see most of the time was the rope ("line") moving in or out as the AI made their adjustments.
In conclusion, this is the best and onlyest sailing simulator I've played, and if you enjoy playing flight simulators for long-haul flights over the ocean in realtime then you may enjoy this game also.  If you have the patience it will doubtless teach you a lot about sailing, and the tutorials are somewhat helpful in that sense as well.  But it's not so much a game as it is a simulator, and I suspect it's not something the average consumer will enjoy.  The addition of real hazards or goals (e.g. transporting passengers to raise money to purchase better boats) could possibly change this in the future, but as it stands I would not recommend this to anyone who is not specifically seeking a sailing simulation program for educational purposes.

It would be very nice to have an online tracker (outside the game - like a mini app map) where you could set up the route and checkpoints and see where your boat is on the map.
You could enter for 5 minutes and check up on your boat.
Other than that great sim game!

I pull the trigger, a loud thud is heard as the bullet hits the crosseye of the target infront of me. I feel ready to go on my first hunting trip. I check my ammo, my rifle, my equipment and i set off on my journey. I admire the breath-taking scenery before me as i scan the horizon for any signs of movement. It's a beautiful day, an occasional rain shower makes the experience even more immersive. I've been grazing the plains for about an hour now when i hear a distinctive sound from the distance. My predatory insticts kick in as i silently creep up to a small hill to try and get a better look. Thats when i spot it, a beautiful white tail buck grazing and eating, it hasn't spotted me yet and must not have smelled me, i move in for the kill. I find a perfect cover spot and get my scope dialed in, i have lined up the perfect kill shot, this deer will be a story piece above my fireplace for generations to come. I'm ready. I take a deep breath before holding my breath and i pull the trigger, ready to reap the rewards for my patience and skill in tracking this majestic animal. My heart stops as i wait for the near-instantaneous results of my action, a message pops up. It explains to me how you have to have a membership and the proper license to hunt this animal. I'm shattered. The download for this game is free, the ability to walk around and shoot guns in breath-taking sceneries with good graphics, is free. The game looks like it would be worth paying for, but it's more or less World of Huntingcraft, you have to renew your membership wether it be ever Three or up to Twelve months. If you know you're going to, or are willing to spend money on this, then go ahead, it seems like it's fun and would be worth it. Don't waste your time if think it's truly a free game. Not your typical run'n'shoot zombie game you find these days
Either pop the zeds from a range with guns or save those bullets and get in melee. Thing is, a walker can endure two or three small firearms headshot before dying, unless you stay still while aiming with iron sights in which you enter "focus mode" after a while that increases the damage done. Ammos are extremely rare and there will always be more heads to pop than bullets to fire. Melee combat is also dangerous. Unless you charge your strike, most melee weapons cannot crack a skull in one hit. If you're careless, a zombie can grab and damage (sometimes infecting) you right after you take a swing. There is also a hidden stamina bar/meter/thing that depletes after every melee attack, meaning you can't go on a murderous melee rampage for more than 2 minutes.
Unlike in Left 4 Dead where zombies are made of papers (are those even "zombies"?), zombies in this game are bullet sponges from the neck down. This combined with their numbers and a risk to get infected when they damage you will make you fear them if you have no friends watching your back. Fortunately they walk slower than old people (sometimes they can sprint) and you can just run past them most of the time.
Axes, Hammers, Knives, Assault Rifles, Shotguns. There are many choices to bash zombies' heads in or to shoot yourself with.
This game pretty much DEMANDS good teamwork. If you have friends to play this with, you'll have fun working ways to get past a horde, mercy killing an infected friend, killing a friend to steal their stuff or just trying to beat a level seriously until that disastrous yet hilarious incident happen. It's also amusing to voice chat with complete strangers to try and survive together (though most of the time they won't bother and just try to solo the whole thing leaving you behind).

I've been following Sonic since his first game and having gone through the journey that has been this roller coaster of emotions, I would hope they would learn their lesson on the several mistakes made on the franchise.
Sonic Mania is a superior Sonic game hands down. This doesn't compare, although storywise it is linked. Sonic Forces releases with a price tag, double that of Sonic Mania and has less real content than Sonic Mania. I completed Sonic Forces in a single sitting of 4 hours. The only aspect of this game that is going to drive my time up will be the massively annoying collectables which force no less than three replays of every single stage.
The collectibles start at red rings. Then once you collect them all, numbered rings appear to collect in the next run. Finally after you collect those, Moon rings appear and you can do the separate run for that. They don't allow you to attempt for these all in one try and having to find them could require several runs ontop of that. It's just a false extension of the game to bump up that abysmally low playtime. I beat the game in under 4 hours including screwing around with costumes and taking the game slowly for collectibles.
Sonic Forces also doesn't help the very annoying cast of characters it didn't need. Constantly talking to you through a radio they like to chat you through your "mission" which is just complete the level. You can thankfully turn that off but still it is a massive annoyance. For comparison, spoilers in the next few sentences, Sonic Generations had a Super Sonic Final fight that had the supporting characters contantly talking to you. It drove me up the wall that they wouldn't shut up and this is worse then that. Like I said however it can turn off making it tolerable.
Character customization is actually more fun that I was willing to give it credit for. Mainly due to how silly the costume pieces get and the combinations you can use, it really takes you away from everything else. I enjoyed making various customizations that caused me to laugh as you can get some pretty awkward things rolling. Characters come in an assortment of races that each have a passive ability. Your character will also use a gun called a Wispon which has different styles of combat.
However it seems that Sonic Team just continues to ♥♥♥♥ up and fail to learn from mistakes. Had they focused in any one of the styles of play this game could have been tolerable but it was just a mess of mechanics from other sonic titles that did not work well. Modern Sonic, which has worked before, has become more stiff in his 2-D style play. You feel like you have less control on turns and there are several unfair deaths you'll take since a lot of transitions don't seem to work properly. Classic Sonic losses his quick spin dash command in exchange for the Drop Dash from Mania. However the platforming in the 2-D sections here is also abysmal since its floaty and hard to control in comparison to Sonic Generations. Finally the Customizable Character is just flawed and pointless. It seems they just put a ton of enemies out there for you to shoot but it takes no real effort nor skill. Just hold the button and they die.
The level design does not compliment the mechanics and the levels are far too short. They give you a total of 30 stages, including bosses, and you will breeze through them so fast you won't be able to enjoy them. Though yes you normally can complete a Sonic level quickly, these are shorter than you would expect. Just as you're beginning to enjoy the Aesthetic it just ends. You don't expect it. Sonic Generations did it so much better and it has half the levels!
Overall this is just an overpriced failure of another Sonic game. I'd honestly suggest picking up Sonic Generations as it does this game better as well as Sonic Mania as that is a glorious that puts Sonic Forces to Shame.

I've been out of the Sonic loop for a pretty long time, and Generations was the only game I've fully played since Sonic Adventure 2, so I admittedly am not the best person to speak on this subject. I had no idea that the series had switched gears almost entirely by switching to the "boost formula", which from what I've gathered from Forces means that the 3D levels are essentially roller coasters where you just hold the "gotta go fast" button until you win and occasionally choose left or right if you want to super win. Even if you wanted to turn right or left you can't do much beyond using the sidestep buttons that usually overshoot whatever you were trying to hit, because once you reach more than like 5 miles (or kilometers if you so desire) per hour the game might as well just disable the left and right movement controls for how much good they do in controlling Sonic.
I admittedly wasn't expecting miracles from the patented DeviantArt™ Sonic OC Creator, but they somehow disappointed me anyways. The character customization in the beginning is as barebones as it gets, and it's nearly impossible to make someone that actually looks good without copying an existing character. You do get clothing options that let you flesh them out, but the game seems to randomly allocate them after each mission, and even if you get the piece you want there's no guarantee that you'll get the color you want, since that's random too, and some of the parts are things that should've been in the creator from the start, like hair styles.
Port-wise, it ranges from adequate to not so great. There are no mouse controls, but that's mostly fine because there aren't any camera controls in the first place, even in the 3D sections. The game's full of surprises, and you never know exactly which bugs you're going to get in this grab bag. You may find that uncapping the framerate makes all the environmental effects run in turbo mode, or you may have the opposite problem and have the game only run at 30 FPS when set to 60 FPS and won't run at 60 FPs unless it's set to uncapped. Some people have jittery cutscenes, some don't, some people crash, others run it fine. Will you? Find out!
To top it all off, the game is fairly short, clocking in at 30 main missions that last about 2-3 minutes each plus a handful of bonus stages that are usually even shorter. You can fill the rest of the time with replaying them for better times or collecting medals, but if you're just in it for the story there's not much here. Admittedly the game does only cost $40 compared to the usual $60, but considering Mania was $20 it still feels like you're not really getting a value here. I wanted to believe that there's some kind of secret ending or something, because one of the classic Sonic bosses they show in the cutscenes doesn't even have a fight and the game just abruptly ends without even giving you a hype moment where they play the game's theme (they do finally play it in the credits, but the credits aren't long enough to actually finish it because they spend most of it playing some lame pop song).
If you just really like the Sonic boost games, or if you just really like the modern 2D segments and are okay with the knowledge that you're not getting a whole lot of it here, or even if you're just a masochist who really loves Sonic despite his near-constant blunders it might be worth picking up, but if you're a new (or long-returning, like me) player there's not really enough here to sell you on it. It's just an all around "okay but not great" game, which is hard for me to recommend for $40. The 2D sections are still fun, and even the 3D sections aren't necessarily bad, but there are better options out there.

I have played steam games for roughly 1,154 hours. Although this is not nearly close to others, this amount of time has collected vast amounts of memories both hilarious and frustrating (thanks CSGO). In those 1,154 hours, the 30 that I dedicated to this "early access game" are the most unique, interesting, and addicitve hands down.
-Science
Factorio is a sandbox game that proves to constantly introduce new goals to its audience. This is accomplished by its diverse and intuitive research dynamic. By progressing in the game, new items and structures are introduced allowing the player to further expand his/her creation through automation. Not only is this aspect of the game balanced, but it progesses the game at a pace which keeps you glued to the screen needing one more minute. I don't want to go into detaill about how science is made and such since this is only a review, but the main point I want to make is that this base gameplay experience is extremely addictive and makes the game aweome as a whole.
-Combat
Not only is combat relatively rare in these types of games, but if it is implemented, it is not oftenly made well. Let me tell you, Factorio is different. The fighting in this game is extremely balanced with the player not too weak or too strong in comparison to enemies. Instead, Factorio allows the player to research new military technologies to combat evolving natives that threaten their factory. Due to the constant growth rate of enemies and military strength, the game provides the player with a relatively constant need to stay alert and defend their base. By doing this, Factorio seperates from other automation and resource managing games by including two objectives: Automation and killing angry natives.
-Automation
Put simply, Factorio presents automation as one of the most fluid concepts the player has to learn. In Factorio, the player is forced to use their own imaginitive ideas in combination with the game-built designs in order to create an efficient factory. Although this may take a few tries and possibly a quick search on youtube, the feeling of accomplishment after automating a certain process is extremely rewarding unlike any other game I have played.
-Tutorial/Learning curve
An essential part of any game is teaching the audience how to play. Although the built-in tutorial teaches basic aspects of the game, I feel that in order to make a late-game factory, a player is forced to consult other resources for advice. This small, but critical characteristic is immensely important for casual gamers, but will most certainly be addressed during the full release of the game.
-End Goal
Like other reviewers, I feel the need for a greater end goal for Facotrio. I will keep this negative short though since the develpoers are working on this issue for the full release.
-Conclusion
In conclusion, Facotorio is most definitely an immensely polished game that deserves 100% positive reviews. The moddability and interaction with the community simply adds onto the already amazing game making it a masterpiece. Please do yourself a facor and play the free demo so that you can experience this fluid-like gameplay like the rest of us.

Borderlands 2 is an awesome game. It has an interesting story, great characters (especially the main villain Handsome Jack and your companion CL4P-TP aka Claptrap the mini robot) and some of the best gameplay I've ever experienced.
In a nutshell, you are a vault hunter and you are enlisted by a hyperactive CL4P-TP robot who calls himself Claptrap and refers to you as his minion. He wants you to help him bring down the villain Handsome Jack who is apparently responsible for shutting down the CL4P-TP production line.
You can play it single player, but at the same time open your game for up to three others so it becomes a co-op game, and it is at co-op that the game absolutely excels. The creatures on Pandora (where the game takes place) become stronger or weaker depending on how many players there are in a game.
As you progress through the story, you level up. Every mission you play, whether main or side mission has a certain preset level that would be nice for you to have making it clear in advance which missions are easier and harder. Expect more higher level missions as you progress. I think this system works very well indeed for this game. I had a ton of fun playing it, the dialogue is fantastic, the voice acting excellent, the diversity of characters and creatures is astoundingly large.
If you like FPS, humor, great story, great characters and excellently finetuned gameplay, this game is for you. If you liked Borderlands, you're gonna love Borderlands 2.

This title was released about 18 months too early.  The unfinished state in which it was released is main reason for the plethora of negative reviews it has received.
To be sure, even had the game been released in an aceptable state of completion, it would still have received some negative reveiws.  It is a marked change from the classic Total War titles released to date that I have played.  This caused me to stumble around trying to learn the ins and outs of the new way the game ran.  This, coupled with all the bugs and the fact that the game itself wasn't even complete, made me "not so much of a fan".  I left off playing it, for the most part, until a couple of months ago.
After two years and several patches, it has grown into a really good game.
The documentation it comes with (the built in "encyclopedia") is very combersome to use, doesn't present the infromation in an easy to relate fashion, and it isn't even completely current with the game as it is now.  There is information that is missing and some that isn't correct anymore.  This makes trying to learn the game (which is rather complex) a little harder and does require that you do some searching on-line for hints and tips.
Bottom line is, this is a very fun game to play and, finally after all the patches, it is actually  very well done.  You won't be sorry you spent the money.  Just know that there is a bit of a learning curve to get the most enjoyment out of it.

While the story doesn't seem as deep and slowly yet deliciously revealed as the first Dark Souls, and some of the graphics and textures reinforce that this was a game developed for previous gen systems like Xbox 360 and PS3, the game lured me in with it's unforgiving nature.  It's difficult.  It will punish you for being greedy.  I will make you feel like an idiot at times.  You may scream at the screen and want to throw things when you make a mistake, or when some disciple of the Brotherhood of Blood interrupts your 'good run' and murders you while trying to make it through the PVE portion of the game.
It's all part of it, and very few (if any other) games make you feel the sheer sense of reward when you do succeed against an enemy or boss that stands in your way.
It makes most games seem very easy in comparison, and that's why I keep going back to it.  It takes practise and patience.  It translates to the disappointments and difficulties of life, in a minor way.  The challenge is real.
ONE BIG HOWEVER - The PVP portion of the game is kinda broken, and while From Software keep 'balancing' things, the major problem is the usage of Peer to Peer matchmaking.  It seemingly creates a severe advantage to those with poor internet connections by giving their on-screen actions predominance, making a simple exchange of blows either do no damage, or in the worst situations 'teleporting' your character back into a backstab animation that is a critical hit.  You either need to keep the region lock on for matchmaking, or prepare for some dude in Australia with 2MB per second to make you his ♥♥♥♥♥ just because you have a better connection.  It's absolutely ♥♥♥♥ing ridiculous.

Not as good as Generations, and certainly not as good as Mania, but Forces manages to end up being a solid entry in the franchise. If you enjoyed Generations, you'll probably enjoy Forces. The level design was somewhat lacking, most of the levels being short and offering little-to-no challenge. Also, with Forces being more narrative driven than previous entries, the characters in the game talk...a lot, and more than they should. In many of the stages, they are redundantly jabbering on about useless crap that isn't needed to progress the story and fails to offer any significance to the game. The avatar creation system is fairly underwhelming, and the avatar you create I find to be forgettable at best. Honestly, the whole avatar system and avatar role seems to have been added last minute into the game, and feels more like an afterthought than a core concept to Forces.
Aside from those flaws, the game is quite responsive, and speeding through stages while smashing badniks is as rewarding as ever. $40 is more than reasonable of an asking price for this game, as it took me about 4.5 hours to beat the story, while I have yet to begin to hunt down the red rings or complete the healthy amount of challenges in the game.

This game is still the best space RTS ever made.  Others have come and gone, but none capture the epic gameplay, 3D map space mechanics, and beauty of naval sci-fi combat.  If you haven't tried it, play the Complex mod available in the workshop.  I still remember playing the original Homeworld when it was released in 1999.  That single player campaign was one of the most memorable and awe inspiring experiences I have had in gaming.  I played the original on a 19in CRT monitor with a GeForce 2 MX gfx card.  The Remaster was a labor of love.  I replayed this game in 4K on my 65 inch LED TV with a GTX 1080.  I am not trying to brag, just point out how beautiful this game looks on the highest settings. - Sonic Forces introduces us to a darker story than what past and/or recent Sonic titles got us used to. It's no longer only about kicking some evil scientist's butt for the fiftieth time. It's about taking back a world from an evil scientist actively hunting anyone who wouldn't submit to his rule.
- Played on the High graphics preset, the environments look amazing. Not sure what else to say about that, so rip.
- As always, Sonic offers an amazing soundtrack, and just like in Sonic Adventure 2, each playable character gets their own kind of music for their stages, with modern/electronic/synth songs for Sonic, more classic-themed songs for Classic and the return of vocals for the Avatar. And for once, we didn't get yet another remix of Green Hill.
- For the first time in the entire series, you get to create your own
custom character, or as they call it, Avatar. With enough options to make a truly terrifying cheap Sonic, if you're into that. Your Avatar is also a full important part of the story, even appearing in cutscenes! As an added bonus, and if connected to the internet, you can choose to have a second Avatar, with you on the next stage, created by another fellow player, allowing you to switch between yours and theirs with the simple press of a button!
- Shadow the Hedgehog returns as a playable character in his own free DLC, with three exclusive stages explaining Infinite's origins. He is also playable on a few Sonic stages in the main story! (Only after completing said stages once as Sonic.)
- I see all these people talking about crashes, though my game has only crashed once from start to finish, and an update was quickly released to fix these issues. Weird.
- Vector the Crocodile is still looking for the computer room.
- The main story is rather short, and can be completed in roughly two or three hours, excluding the bonus levels and Episode Shadow.
- Just like the story, most stages are really short, lasting one to two minutes for a decent player. The wispons also make the Avatar stages really easy due to how powerful they can be. (CUBE)
- The gameplay can seem really rough and unfinished at times, mostly in the Mystic Jungle stages where the character will just ignore a set of springs covering an entire waterpipe and just fall straight to their death, or on some Sonic stages where the boost doesn't seem to follow the intended path it wants you to take, sending you flying off the stage.
- Similar to Generations, most characters from the cast make their return, but only as side characters, restricting the playable cast to Sonic, Classic, Avatar and Shadow.
- SOS Missions feel really intrusive. What if I simply want to replay a stage, without being bothered by a mission where I have to help someone else's Avatar? Nope. If a SOS Mission spawns on a stage you wish to replay, you'll have to go through said mission first, even if you ragequit straight out of it.
- The Hero Rental system only offers up to nine Avatars from other random players, and there doesn't seem to be an option to play as your Steam friends' Avatars.
- This might just be me, but the keyboard controls are rather difficult to get used to. Thankfully, they're rebindable!
Sonic Forces doesn't quite live up to previous titles like Unleashed or Generations, but it remains as a decent game with unused potential. Hopefully the remaining issues will be fixed at some point.

Only Sonic Team could have the talent of taking an existing and proven formula and run it into the ground which can be seen blatantly in their latest effort Sonic Forces.
The game features 3 distinct gameplay styles of Classic and Modern Sonic as well as the new addition of the Custom Character.
The Custom Character in my experience was the most enjoyable. The levels felt large and the wispons were a nice addition to help with the average platforming found in these areas. The OC controls like a gimped modern sonic without boost but has more of a focus on combat with flamethrowers, whips, hammers, etc. These don't matter for the most part as enemies are destroyed in 1 hit. The Character Creation is simple but allows for some hilarious character models and some nice homages via the clothing items available.
Modern Sonic hit a revival with the boost era of games and Sonic Team have somehow took a successful formula almost 10 years old and destroyed it. There's much more momentum in his movement but it's much harder to control. The biggest example of this is when you need to go around corners that would normally use drifitng but since Sonic team removed drifting if you try to speed into the corner you will either bump into the wall present or fall of a ledge into your death (This is especially prevalent in Modern Sonic's Metropolis level). There is no reason to remove abilities such as light speed dash and wall jump if they have been present in the boost gameplay since Sonic Unleashed as it removes oppurtunities to create interesting levels. Levels are basically hold boost to finish as most of these levels can take 1 or 2 minutes to complete if you don't fall off into bottom less pits due to trash sense of controls. It wouldn't even matter since the game takes control away from you for half the duration of the level anyway to throw in some rubbish quick time events for some "set piece".
Classic Sonic's gameplay is what you expect from Sonic Generations. For the most part his level design is better than Modern Sonic and does use multiple routes to discover the best areas to speed past but is nowhere close to the complexity of Sonic Mania. Classic Sonic's physics are also notably worse than in Generations. The biggest example is his nerf of max speed, unless you are drop dashing every 2 seconds it can be a chore to try and speed through the levels. Another problem is his spin jump, often I would misjudge if Sonic would be able to hit an enemy or jump to another platform and as a result get hit or die in a bottomless pit. The physics haven't felt this 'wrong' to me since playing Sonic 4 Episode 1.
The game does look nice and runs really well however the game does lack zone variety with there being 7 different environments and 3 out of the 7 areas are just areas from the genesis era whilst the remaining 4 are just generic city or jungle environments.
Soundtrack is great but that's expected from a Sonic game at this point.
Sonic Forces is probably the most baffling game I've played in a long time. I don't even know what Sonic Team was doing for 4 years since Lost World. It took me 3.5 hours to beat the game along with the episode Shadow DLC. If Sonic Team think that releasing a game of this quality with that length of playtime they should realise that this isn't 1992 anymore. This should be a wake up call for Sega to find a different development team that is willing to try different ideas for Sonic because if Sonic Mania can prove that the hedgehog can have a great game from a Western Developer it would be time to invest elsewhere.
If not Sonic Team needs to know, just because a game looks nice, sounds nice and incorporates elements from fan favourite games doesn't excuse a game that plays like complete garbage especially compared to  Sonic Generations.

Reign of Kings turned Reign of Kids....
So I bought this game around a week after it was released, and was already throughly impressed by how many updates they had made in such a small time frame.
In the game, I enjoyed the graphics, even more so when they released Alpha 5 which improved my framerate.
My first encounter was slavery, and I was dragged around my two guys, who turned out to be really cool. We raided the kings castle as no one was their, and held the throne for a good 10 minutes.
When I died protecting my "leige", I decided it was time to do something I always wanted to do in a Medieval game, build a fortified keep for my people and conquer!
I met up with several guys who volunteered to help.
Before long we had 10 people as these guys began to recruit, and we all were working hard getting stone and sleeping in the keep's cellar. It was glorious looking, like a real medieval keep.
I really began to love how long it took just to make a few stone blocks and gather enough supplies, because easy would of been boring.
We got two floors done before it was the end of the day, and I was quite confident in saying this "is the best game ever". It was the biggest regret of words I've made.
Wake up the next day to find one my close second-in-charge had reported that our keep was destroyed by a "hacker bomb". It frustrated me a bit but I thought "hell, it's not something new to survival games", but something else was.
After Alpha 6, for some pecular reason a hoard of ego-testical male incapable humans had stormed into all the servers, bringing nothing but high taxes, swearing excessivally, abusing everyone for no good reason, and of cause the KOS.
This is something that completely ruined the game for me. Whilst the mechanics and scenery is great, this kind of community that I can only disgustingly compare to COD kids, is so new to me and I have never before seen it so bad in a survival game.
I have been roped and killed as a freshy 27 times, had 10k stone stolen from me, had my base destroyed several times, and have been abused to the point where everytime I log off I only feel angry and weak.
It has been a complete community shift in a WEEK! I have spoken to 4 people who completely agree with this, and felt the need to express it, and are left feeling absolutely devastated that this game that had a great community within it's first week is now full of nothing but "jackasses", for lack of a better term.
Until some server monitoring can be done on the official servers, I can no longer recommend this game that I had high hopes for.
5/10.

I personaly think it adds depth to the gameplay and immersion to the story, but it's something you should keep in mind before you buy the game.

Edit: now that I beat the game, 100% with all achievements, I can give a better review.
Sonic Forces in my opinion is the best sonic game since Unleashed. Sonic Generations did have better level design then this game, however Sonic Forces makes up for it by having waaaaay more replayability. The ranking System is heavily improved and some stages are very difficult to get an S rank (Episode Shadow stage 3). There's also red rings, numbered rings, and moon rings. So when it comes to gameplay mechanics, Sonic Forces in my opinion is just slightly worse than Generations.
I'll sum up how each characters gameplay styles for those interested.
Modern Sonic: In Forces, Modern Sonic is slower however this is a good thing as it allows the player to be able to interact and look at the environment more easily. Modern Sonic has more momentum then previous games, and this makes the 2d sections of modern sonic more fun to play then ever before. However, the 3d sections of modern sonic is worse then Generations or Unleashed. Sonic can't drift so you have to manually turn Sonic. The level design is brought down by this, and thats why modern sonic 3d sections are so linear with different paths to jump to.
Classic Sonic: Now IK why people are bashing on classic sonic, and i'm not the largest fan of him either, however I feel Classic Sonic is much better in Forces then Generations. I think people are saying his physics is worse then generations just because they got done playing Sonic Mania. In Sonic Forces, Classic Sonic has way more momentum. (only when your in a ball though which is bad. ) The drop dash is alot of fun and allows you to use skill to go through the levels faster. Also the level design is good with classic sonic stages. Classic Sonic is better than what he was in Generations, also Sega please don't bring back classic sonic in modern games anymore.
Avatar: is basically a slower version of sonic that can't boost, but can use wisp powerups. The levels were more open then Modern Sonic, and i found it to be surprisenly fun to play as. It has alot of costumes but could use more body editing. (Sega don't bring back ocs though its fine as a one time thing).
Now Let's get to the Story. Hands down this goes to Sonic Forces. There is alot of cliche friendship moments, however the characters do feel like themselves in the story so it makes it pretty interesting to watch. The ending is a little lackluster but ok. This is a good stepping stone, but Sega needs a slower paced and more thought out Story next game. Story is about 6/10 for me, infinite is great though. Sonic Forces also has the best graphics in any sonic game (2017 life). The music is also great and really can get you immersed in the game. This game took 27 hours to 100% compared to 100%ing Generations in about 5 hours. If You care about replayability, tone, and being immersed in a Sonic Game. This is definitely for you. If sega put more love into this game, with an epic ending, longer main campaign, and better level design. This game could have been a 9/10 Sonic game, however for the 4 years of work that Sega put into this game I would give it a 7/10.
Overall, mediocre gameplay, good graphics, fantastic replayability, short campaign, an ok story not put to the best use, great music, good tone, characters acting like themselves(besides tails).  Sonic Forces gets a 7/10.

Rome II Total War is a great war game. It has a lot of empire building features. Each province has 2 to 4 cities in them. Each of these cities can build improvements to increase the economy. Money is important, and improvements cost money to build but not to upkeep. Instead, improvement upkeep has two factors for the cost: first is food. As each improvement is levelled up it will cost more food as upkeep. If you run out of food the public happiness drops. The second thing is publec happiness. Some improvements increase food, public happiness and money. Also, improvements unlock new military units. There are a few other things improvements do but those are the main issues. This game has great depth for the improvments as there are multiple buildings that do similar things.
Military might is crucial to winning and expanding. Units have a money upkeep so to build a big army you need more funds. Each army starts with a General (fleets have Admirals) and, depending on how large your Empire is, there is a limit to the number of Armies and Fleets you may have at one time. New military units are unlocked with technology and city improvements. What I like about the unit upgrade system is that you can upgrade units for a cost even outside the province that has the military unit building capability.
Technology is great. There are two areas, military and civil. Military will unlock or improve the units. Civil, of course, gives economic bonuses. Both tech trees are really good.
Of course, Total War has full control of the units in battle. I usually avoid the city engagements and opt to auto fight those due to the crampt city streets, but all of the battles, including sieges, are really cool. Having many high tech legions is great! If you can afford them ...
The diplomacy options are wonderful. Other factions will usually approach you for trade, once you are powerful and have a decent sized empire. Early on trade is hard to acquire because the other kingdoms do not have much to trade, but it can still happen. The game has many small kingdoms at the start, Oh, if you trade with a small kingdom that has only one province that kingdom will have enough forces to start gobbling up its neighbors and become an Empire.
Anyway, Rome II is a great game. Some Total War games have serious design problems. Rome II is one of the better entries for the Total War series. I highly recommend this game.

The first Total War title I ever played was Total War Rome, and I loved it. So, of course when I decided to get Rome 2, I had extremely high expectations. It did not disappoint, although it was different. Luckily I avoided the myraid of glitches that were inherited with the game when it first came out, I bought it a year later for $20. And let me say, they have more than fixed the glitches.
THE GOOD
This game looks beautiful on any decent machine, and is runnable and still looks good on underpowered computers (I have seen it run on lackluster laptops). The gameplay is immersive and very in depth. I find myself spending hours into this game at a time, trying to negotiate traties with factions I wish to destroy at some point, but for now provide a good border that I wish to use as the backbone of my empire. Yet at the time, I am building up my cities to provide better units, rake in money, and most importantly, keep my people happy.
Also, the battles are better than ever. For those who don't know, the overall game is a turn based strategy, and then when you fight battles you can choose to auto resolve (for quick results, but higher losses and lower chances of winning), or to fight the battle on the battle map. Here, you can control each unit (up to 20 per army) and choose different strategies yourself. This is very engaging and dynamic, although I do like to set a time limit of 40 minutes or else you may find yourself in a situation where there is one hidden unit that you cannot find and it takes 50 minutes to end the battle! Anyway, the battles are the best aspect of the game and are very engaging.
And I can't forget to mention online campaigns, they are just extremely fun. If you have friends with this game, you will love the online coop campaign or the head to head!
Last but not least, this game has a great replay value. I have loved playing every faction I have tried (except Parthia, they literally have no good infantry). Each faction offers its own great units, buildings, locations, and strategies. I do recommned buying DLC however, because some of the more fun factions (such as any Greek faction, which I adimit, is annoying) is a faction you must buy. Also when you replay, trying different difficulites is fun. Playing this game on easy is a good challenge for someone new to the game, but way too easy for someone experienced. I find that the way to have the most fun is to challenge yourself!
THE BAD
The cost of the dlc. Plain and simple, this game is not cheap and the dlc is no cheaper. I DEFINITELY reccommend waiting for a sale to buy this game and its dlc; every dlc I have bought (which is everyone except 4 smaller ones) has been on sale. And I can say, on sale the dlc is fairly priced. And although the game is probably worth 60 dollars, if you wait long enough you can probably get it cheaper.
There are still some glitches, although only two major ones I have seen. One is that the function to move around the map will suddenly stop, for the rest of your campaign. This is very annoying, because now you have to double click the map to move anywhere, and sometimes your viewing angle will change, which you also cant change back. So you're looking at the map upside down and can barely move the camera around. It sucks. In my experience this happens more in online campagins. The other glitch is that sometimes during coop campaigns one player will just be dropped. Although this is annoying, it is a normal bug for all games and will likely be there forever. Also, since the game saves at the end of every turn automatically, it is not a big deal with losing save data.
THE CONCLUSION
Buy the game! On sale! WIth friends! It is definitely worth it. I love this game and do not listen to the reviews about the game breaking glitches, they have been fixed!

DISCLAIMER: I am reviewing the completely vanilla, unmodded version of this game. I have heard there are many great mods, but my first playthrough was without any.
This game really was a joy to play. From the awesome world and the terrifying encounters,  to the unintentionally hilarious vodka overdoses and the cheeki breeki-ing, I really ♥♥♥♥ing liked it. The game has been compared to Fallout and other RPG post-apocalyptic survival games, but I like to classify it as it's own type of game. A game where the unknown frightens you and you are left fighting for survival where it seems everything is out to get you. The specifics of what I liked and disliked are recorded in the following paragraphs.
THINGS I LIKED:
1.First of all, this game has something really special, and equally hard to describe. To put it simply, the world seems to be alive in a way I haven't felt in many other games. Let me paint a picture: You come back to an outpost after a hard day of fighting bizzare mutations and equally bizzare bandits and sit down the fire by a complete stranger playing the guitar. As night falls, you enjoy a diet sausage and a bottle of vodka around the open fire in silence, treasuring these moments of peace. This is what I really love about this game. That is about the only way I can describe it. The feel of the world is Just sublme.
2. The core gameplay feels very solid. Guns kill suprisingly quickly and gunfights feel very tense, as if you are actually fighting for your life.
3. The story is presented in a unique and fascinating way.  You must learn about your world and what is happening through the PDAs of dead stalkers and dialogue with living ones. The story is subtle and leaves a lot up to speculation, in a way similar to Dark Souls, which I absolutely love.
4. Lastly, the game runs like a pro. Kind of a big deal if your computer is utter♥♥♥♥♥♥ like mine.
That's what I liked, now here are the things that I kind of disliked (nit-picking ahead)
DISLIKES:
1. There are a few bugs, which can be expected from a game of this age, although I have read that the majority of them can be fixed with various mods.
2. Guns in the beginning are extremely inaccurate. This isn't necissarilly a con, but expect to be missing about 90% of your shots from anywhere over 20 meters until you find something that isn't a Kalashnikov variant.
3. The graphics aren't great. I say this, but the dull graphics kind of add to the game's gloomy mood. Again, if they aren't for you, there are a plethora of mods.
4. I like to pretend that the multiplayer doesn't exist.
CONSENSUS: I love this game. It is one of the most unique experiences that I have been a part of in a while. Whilethere are a few problems, I plan on playing through again with one of the many overhaul mods, which I heard can provied an even better experience. Will definately be checking out Call of Pripyat and Clear Sky.
NOTE: Helps if you speak Russian. Not a must, but adds to the immersion and authenticity.

+ Functional, user-friendly navigation and quest-mapping device
+ Artifacts add slight RPG-like stat combinations
+ Vast, detailed environments
+ Very, very strong sense of atmosphere pervading throughout
+ Boasts a large and active modding community (many mods do well to address some of the game's various pitfalls)
+ Equipment and weight limitations do much to force the optimization of one's gear, and make one choose what to discard and what to keep; this leaves the player feeling both challenged and rewarded as they acclimate to the concept
+ Ambient sounds are absolutely fantastic, and keep the player consistently unsettled
+ Weapon degredation adds to the challenge, and makes one keep an eye on their equipment
+ Manner of interaction with various game-world NPCs is largely determined by the player's actions throughout the adventure
+ The game's world and atmosphere compliments an intriguing plot; the story, itself, rewards inquisitiveness
+ Moderate variation in firearms
+ Absolute plethora of side-missions
- No fast-travel; this likely will not bother the realists out there, but I felt that there could have been a comfortable middle-ground implemented that would have kept everyone happy
- Lots and lots of bugs, some of which are quite problematic (again, most of these can be remedied via the modding community)
- Largely flat and uninspired voice-acting
- Malleable NPC relationships notwithstanding, the story is fairly (although not completely) linear
- No autosave function (except when entering new areas, but the environments are mostly sprawling areas, making this insufficient); massively frustrating when you die 45 minutes into a new area and forget to manually save, forcing you to take significant steps back in progress (although I believe there is a mod available to remedy this)

I enjoy Deus Ex and System Shock 2 as much as the next person, but for me S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernoybl towers over the first-person shooter genre.
It's that chilling feeling gotten by wondering across the bleak open landscape while hearing dogs howling in the distance (this being one of the very few games to be able to pull off outdoor daylight horror), It's that weird moment when you see some invisible monster for the first time and realise the game's surreal underbelly. It's the beautiful atmosphere created by the lightning. It's the tension built by running around trying to find that one last bit of radiation protection before you die of radiation poisoning. It's that feeling of satisfaction when you finally manage to fight your way through a group of clever AI enemies, or the stress built by panickingly trying to drink enough energy drink to simply run through them.
Or, more broadly - it's the perfect mixture of challenging difficulty, fantastic atmosphere and great survival mechanics which make it so special.
The game builds itself on creating tension through its inventory management system and creates such perfect results through it. Funnily enough, early in the game I found it annoying that managing your inventory doesn't pause the game and sometimes I stopped dead in the middle of combat because I was too heavy to move, but by the end I realised that was such an incredible way of building tension. S.T.A.L.K.E.R. is, after all, a game of scavenging and half the fun of the game is about deciding whether you can afford to go over to pillage a befallen enemy, work out what you need to take and if it's not too heavy to carry without getting killed.
But great survival mechanics and a really well balanced difficulty don't make a game on its own and the other main thing which really makes S.T.A.L.K.E.R. stand out is its gameworld. It's such a beautiful, desolate overworld and as much enjoyment as the challenge was just running over the baron plains with dogs howling and boars roaming around with some odd shots in the background. Even, the main homehub of Rostock has this incredibly eerie and desolate feel about it.
There's just this exquisite balance of challenge and ambience which make this the perfect FPS. Played alone, at night with headphones it is quite the experience.

Rome II Total War is a great war game. It has a lot of empire building features. Each province has 2 to 4 cities in them. Each of these cities can build improvements to increase the economy. Money is important, and improvements cost money to build but not to upkeep. Instead, improvement upkeep has two factors for the cost: first is food. As each improvement is levelled up it will cost more food as upkeep. If you run out of food the public happiness drops. The second thing is publec happiness. Some improvements increase food, public happiness and money. Also, improvements unlock new military units. There are a few other things improvements do but those are the main issues. This game has great depth for the improvments as there are multiple buildings that do similar things.
Military might is crucial to winning and expanding. Units have a money upkeep so to build a big army you need more funds. Each army starts with a General (fleets have Admirals) and, depending on how large your Empire is, there is a limit to the number of Armies and Fleets you may have at one time. New military units are unlocked with technology and city improvements. What I like about the unit upgrade system is that you can upgrade units for a cost even outside the province that has the military unit building capability.
Technology is great. There are two areas, military and civil. Military will unlock or improve the units. Civil, of course, gives economic bonuses. Both tech trees are really good.
Of course, Total War has full control of the units in battle. I usually avoid the city engagements and opt to auto fight those due to the crampt city streets, but all of the battles, including sieges, are really cool. Having many high tech legions is great! If you can afford them ...
The diplomacy options are wonderful. Other factions will usually approach you for trade, once you are powerful and have a decent sized empire. Early on trade is hard to acquire because the other kingdoms do not have much to trade, but it can still happen. The game has many small kingdoms at the start, Oh, if you trade with a small kingdom that has only one province that kingdom will have enough forces to start gobbling up its neighbors and become an Empire.
Anyway, Rome II is a great game. Some Total War games have serious design problems. Rome II is one of the better entries for the Total War series. I highly recommend this game.
