Sonic Forces is probably the most disappointing game of 2017 for me
You'd think after Unleashed, Colors, and Generations, that Sonic team would have something for the boost gameplay that works. I think the boost gameplay still has a lot of untapped potential that Sega and Sonic Team could capitalize on. But instead, what this game delivered was a watered-down version of Generations, with an edgier story. Let me break it down.
1: The Story
The story is probably the second strongest part of the game for me, and even then, it’s still just a mess. Infinite has nothing to his character other than "Oh I'm stronger then all you weaklings, look at my Phantom Ruby." His backstory is lazily explained, and chopped up to "Eggman created him using the Phantom Ruby". Not to mention, he's this unstoppable force in most cutscenes, but then when you fight him in the game he's either a joke, or just plain annoying. In addition, this game likes to try and take its story extremely seriously. Like, they imply Sonic's being tortured, there’s talk of death, suffering, fear all over the place. But it’s hard to take this game seriously, with the dialogue these characters say. Sonic still acts like he's in Colors, everyone else is just either super serious, or annoying. (Silver manages to be the worst of both). It's pacing is also very odd. The game would for example have you complete one level for say, a distraction. But then, the next level, they act like the other character is in the middle of the distraction, while you're taking advantage of it, even though you just saw them finish. True, you could say it's implied they're both happening at the same time, but the game doesn't exactly make this clear. In addition, a more specific example would be the inclusion of the Sonic Adventure 1 antagonist, Chaos. Or rather... the lack of said antagonist. For some baffling reason, he was teased as being one of the 4 villains you'd fight that were created by Infinite, and was shown not only in the trailers, but also in the opening cutscene. However, after that, you never see Chaos again. You maybe see him in the background of a cutscene near the end of the game, when there’s an army of them alone with the other 3, but there’s no Chaos boss, there’s no other mention of him. He just shows up in the beginning, and is never seen again. I don't understand how this could even happen. This is just kind of embarrassing to be honest.
2: The Gameplay
The Gameplay honestly is something that just baffles me to no end. I'm gonna list the issues I have with every character, and then each character individually
Overall: Every character has possibly the worst air-mobility I've ever seen. In 2D sections, it feels like my character is the heaviest thing in the world with how slowly they move when you hit jump. Plus, when you land on the ground from moving fast in the air from the few scripted times they let you, you don't keep any of the momentum at all, and it looks and feels so unnatural. In addition, I swear all the 3D characters have way too high of an acceleration. It feels like if you hold the control stick for more than half a second, they suddenly just sky-rocket in that direction. It made controlling them a pain in the butt during the more platform-heavy segments.
Classic Sonic: Dear god, what did they do to Classic Sonic? You know how in Generations How Classic Sonic felts very heavy and clunky? How he couldn't really do anything he could do in the classic games? They somehow made it worse. Now it feels like jumping is just a way to slow you down, the Drop Dash is barely utilized, and just a cheap way to connect this game to Mania, and for some reason they added a sort of speed cap to his running speed, comparable to the speed cap in the original Sonic the Hedgehog. Overall, Classic Sonic is by far the worst of this game's three gameplay styles. It’s just a pain to play, and it’s not fun. Not to mention, the music in his stages are mostly just eh. Because they went the same route as Sonic 4, and used the Genesis sound font for it. It doesn't sound great, except for maybe 1 or 2 stages.
Modern Sonic: Modern Sonic in contrast is probably the best gameplay style in my opinion, but it’s still not great. They got rid of the drift to start off, which is an incredibly confusing choice to me. The Drift allowed for more stuff to do during those "Hold X" straight-ways the boost games occasionally have. But it’s not like it matters anyway because Modern Sonic level design is just... not fun. There’s barely any 3D, and the parts that are 3D are usually always just a straight shot while you're holding boost. And the 2D segments make you feel like you don't need the boost at all. There’s rarely a moment you can really use it effectively. It drains super-fast, and only refills with enemies, and wisp capsules, rather than with rings like in Generations, or Unleased. And just like Classic sonic, your jumping in 2D is the worst thing ever. But its slightly better for Modern sonic, since he has a double jump, and the boost. The only thing I can say they've improved from Generations is that you can now boost in the air, and keep your speed. Rather than just being able to tap it once, and be helpless afterwards. Still, it’s still just a watered-down version of Generation's Modern sonic. Not even, it’s a watered-down version of Color's Modern Sonic.
Custom Character: The Custom Character overall was style I was the least disappointed in. Even though I still had more fun with Modern sonic then the Custom Character (Who henceforth will be referred to as "CC"), I was expecting it to be a lot worse. Still, it's not that great. It feels like just Modern Sonic, but you don't have a boost, a delayed homing attack that can swing off certain things since it’s also a grappling hook, and a weapon. The issue I have with the weapons though, is that they didn't feel very well thought out. All of them are basically OP, and destroy robots. The only one you should really be using if you want to go fast though, is the Flamethrower, since you can move while using it, and it still for some reasons one-shots every basic enemy if it barely touches it. The CC still has the same 2D issues as Classic sonic though, and unless you chose the bird, you don't have a double jump to help.
3. Final thoughts
Overall, I'd say the game is extremely mediocre. It had a lot of potential, and Sonic Team and Sega really should have tried to improve on what made Generations so great. Instead however, they just sloppily tried to copy it, and Sonic Forces is what we got. What Generations would look like if it was extremely lazily done/rushed/uninspired. If you want to get this game, wait for a price drop. It is not worth $40. It's worth $15-$20 at best.
There’s also some minor issues I have with the game too, like how the stomp sound effect plays the sound of you hitting the ground before you hit the ground a lot, or how the game crashed on me twice (And this was AFTER the patch before you point out how they patched the crashes), but most of that is nitpicking at this point.
The only positive things I can say about this game is there were atleast 2 levels I had fun with (Both were Modern sonic btw). Plus, the game graphics-wise looks great, and the art style is nice with the menus and such. And the music to me is kick♥♥♥♥♥Unfortunately, these positives are outweighed by all the negatives. Atleast we still have Mania and Generations to fall back on.
I give this game a 4/10

TL;DR: After a full playthrough, I enjoyed my first run more than my first run of Sonic Generations. Will it hold up over time? Can't say yet, but it has replay value. Gameplay 7/10, everything else 10/10.
This is a good Modern Sonic game. The only reason I can see to dislike this game is if you just don't like Modern Sonic games, in which case why are you buying a Sonic game? If you like Sonic, you will like this game.
Visuals: 10/10. Sonic Forces competes favorably against games with a similar style like Super Mario Odyssey and other modern 3D cartoons. It is an absolute visual delight, with a sense of speed that is overwhelming in the best of ways and backgrounds that are absolutely incredible. I'm certain that I will remember many of these stages as a gamer for years to come.
Music: 10/10. Sonic always has great music, and this is no exception. Compared to recent similar genre action games, Sonic Forces excels in its music. It also brings in some trance-like tracks in the Avatar stages, which we don't see too much of in the Sonic series, and ended up a fantastic inclusion.
Story: 10/10. This is everything that I want in a Sonic story. It is in-line with Sonic Adventure 1 and 2. It far surpasses games like Generations and Colors and delivers the first serious Sonic storyline in far too long. All dialouge--and there's a lot of it to enjoy for a Sonic fan--is voiced in the usual fun, campy, Sonic way. (Shoutouts to Shadow's VA Kirk Thornton, he is greatly improved from the actor's last outing with the character!)
Gameplay: 7/10. This is not among some of the ground-breaking, genre redefining games we've gotten in 2017 like SMO or Breath of the Wild, but it is a good Sonic game. It could be improved by removing some of the automation where it is in favor of bringing back Sonic Generation's drifting--In Sonic Forces, on nearly every  sharp turn, the game helps you turn so that you can minimize how much you need to touch your controller, preventing you from falling unless you *really* TRY to fall. But I cannot rate the gameplay any lower than 7/10, as that is approaching the territory of genuinely bad games, which this is not. The gameplay is fun, and although a bit frustratingly hard at times, if you take a step back and think about why you are dying, you'll clear whatever challenge you are facing.
Pros:
-First serious Sonic story in years! Modern Sonic games have a great world and cast of charcaters behind them and this game embraces it. Of course Infinite is edgy, haters!--the whole fun of a Sonic game's story is having edgy woodland critters who take everything too seriously! It is campy, and it is fun.
-Ridiculously amazing visuals and backgrounds.
-Absolutely fantastic soundtrack.
-Character creation is a cool feature!
-Lot's of missions and reasons to replay levels.
(Somewhat) Cons:
-Levels are short, but that makes them more replayable at the same time in many ways because they don't drag on. Still, they could stand to average about 30 seconds longer.
-Early levels are extremely automated; however, it gets better after like the first 4 (there are 30.)
-A single run of the game takes around 3-7 hours, greatly varying on how much side content you do like the SoS missions or how many times you replay levels as you progress through the story. But it is a Sonic game, you are meant to replay levels. It is arcade-style.
-Automation exists where it does not need to, and removes control from the player at times.

If you buy this game, you will be stuck with an obsolete version of "Dark Souls 2" that has no upgrade path to the new version that is coming in April 2015.  The newer version of the game will have an updated graphics engine (using DX11 vs DX9), support 6-player multiplayer, and it will include other changes to the game that won't be made available to owners of this "Dark Souls 2" game.  Savegames & achievements will not transfer from the old version to the new, and the online will be totally separate for the two versions. Dark Souls II is a distant cousin to Dark Souls. The stories are subtly related, but the Dark Souls II is noticeably inferior.
In Dark Souls II you find yourself thrown into a disconnected world with little guidance and no real purpose. This contrasts the elements of Dark Souls, in which the player found himself or herself immersed in a very connected world with a purpose but with little direction. The distinction may sound minute, but it drastically diminished the quality of the sequel. Without a true purpose, or at least without one you're able follow, the point of the game becomes "kill bosses, kill enemies, kill other players." Which is fun for a while, but the longevity of gameplay is significantly reduced by such monotony. In your purposeless wanderings in the course of the game, you will wholeheartedly feel like you are in a pieced together video game as opposed to a created world. You might ascend in an elevator at the top of an isolated tower only to suddenly find yourself... in a volcano... with other volcanoes as far as the eye can see.  With a world devoid of cohesion, the artistry that is existed is DS has been lost in its sequel.
Player vs. player interactions have been diminished in some ways and augmented in others. Connectivity is drastically improved, but the method the game used to connect players (soul memory) is undeniably flawed. You suddenly find yourself especially frustrated to die before reaching your bloodstain (which causes you to lose your acquired souls -- a faux currency for the game) because you now essentially have greater soul memory yet fewer souls. Additionally, players at soul level 200-300 can easily find themselves paired against a player at the maxed soul level of 838. The online gameplay itself has been altered in drastic ways as well. Shields have become essentially useless, more likely detrimental with the replacement of the kick attacked to a foreword stepping, shield swiping cartoonish attack. This is another change that, while seemingly small, drastically affects the game in a negative manner. Dark Souls was game, so by its nature it was outside the realms of reality. However, it carried a sense of realism in an alternate world, which is impressive because this realism was semi successfully merged with outlandishness (like using a massive two handed dragon tail sword the size of the person wielding it). Dark Souls II, however, tends to favor more the outlandish, fantastical side. Magic is stronger while physical damage is weaker (compared to DS); "quality builds" are a thing of the past regarding viability. In reality, a naked man wielding a pocket knife is not very likely to kill another man of equal size armored in chain mail and wielding a sword and a shield. Yet this is the ever present case in Dark Souls II player vs. player. Light armor is clearly favored over heavy armor by the developers, as is magic clearly favored over faith and dexterity is favored over strength (for PVP)
Overall, every change from DS to DS II seems to be an obvious attempt to expand the game's demographic by absconding features that made DS notoriously challenging. Reaching a new audience is fiscally savvy, but tends to alienate core fans. Personally, I doubt I will be purchasing another Souls franchise game (including Bloodborne).

Playing it, I'm waiting for it to become fun but it never does. It's dull as dishwater and I'm already bored to tears. I don't even know where to start, there's just too many things wrong with this one, but try this first, as I found this review to resonate well with my own impressions:
Seldom am I so lost for own words to describe something with, it's just that awful. I will instead try to explain how it made me FEEL when playing it, after having experienced that heavenly, spectacular title that came before it:
Imagine you're meeting someone you're incredibly fond of, someone you've experienced tons and tons of great moments with. Someone whom you love with all your heart. Imagine that person greeting you, and you're getting ready to embrace that person, and then, suddenly, you gasp as they shiv you through your guts with the nastiest, dirtiest passed-through-the-fecal-mattered-colons-of-a-rat screwdriver possible, time and time again. Shocked beyond belief, you can not help but stare helplessly as the same person continues the dope show by cutting off your junk with a pair of old, dull scissors.
Or imagine if some ethically sound and otherwise great personality, like Mahatma Ghandi or Dr. Oz, suddenly did a 180, and suddenly came to realize that becoming a murderous pedophile was better than their previous engagements.
How would that make you feel? How the everloving-gently-caress-my-butt would you react to something like that? What would your expression be like? Much like the expression you'd get from this games' worst offerings, of which there are copious amounts. All I know is that nothing - absolutely nothing in this world - could ever prepare you for it.
And that's what it feels like playing this.
It's not hard but fair, like Dark Souls.
It's not fun - at all.
It's ugly and atrocious, and I'm thoroughly disgusted by it. The graphics are a huge disappointment, both my character and the characters in the rest of the world look butt-ugly, even on the highest settings, rivaling even those atrocious faces in a modern, mediocre Bioware RPG.
But what's worse, the controls have become awful too. Gone are the great, crisp and clean controls from the first Dark Souls masterpiece, and what's left is some awfully clunky movements with some crappy sounds accompanying them:
In the Forest of the Tree Giants or whatever it's called, there are some wooden palisades/platforms with some enemy standing directly under me. Whereas I would kill him outright in the first Dark Souls, this time around I may lock onto the guy, walk carefully over the edge to plunge attack him, and my character will miss - even when I'm standing on a platform only one or maybe two meters above him. After dying to some other enemies later, I tried this again and the same thing happened, the lock-on is no longer a lock-on like it was in the first game. You should try it yourself, it's right outside of the bonfire in the tower with the old lady whom sells you stuff; go outside and down the wooden platform, get rid of the two first enemies, then run along the wooden palisade and jump over the little gap where there is a dead body with a soul. Right under you; that's the guy I'm talking about.
When backstabbing enemies, the audio can best be described like kicking a plastic bucket padded with leather rags or something; in no way is it reminiscent of the pure, sadistic pleasure one got from the sound when backstabbing enemies in the first Dark Souls. I actually had to check my speakers to make sure there wasn't something wrong with my sound system, but no, it turns out that the sounds, in all likeliness, were created during some From Software office party, with the sound designers randomly slamming buttons on their equipment while snorting coke from the nourishment endings of female street-night-workers in the sound lab, and the managers later telling them "this will unfortunately have to do, we're out of time and money before the release is due". Just terrible, terrible sound quality.
They did add more backstab animations, but these all have in common that they fail so epically at connecting the blade properly with the enemy body, that they just glitch past and through them, and it is terribly cringe-worthy to watch, for all the wrong reasons.
Oh yeah, I almost forgot:
In what seems like some random, esoteric, bad-taste prank, in the first village you enter, there are three small pigs/piglets attacking you when you go around a corner next to the cathedral, and some programmer thought it fitting or funny to infuse them with COPIOUS amount of energy/life. They're not necessarily hard, you just circle around them like you do with everything else in the game while stabbing them with your weapon, but it takes SO INCESSANTLY LONG, that I almost fell asleep right then and there. I would have laughed at this, was it not for it being so immensely out of place. It's something that would have fitted into, maybe, Saints Row 4's take on gaming, not Dark Souls'. Just imagine how movie enthusiasts would like it if there was a Schindler's List 2, but this one had some random Scooby-Doo shenanigans shoved into it. Probably fun while smoking jazz cigarettes, but no one could take the movie/franchise name seriously ever again.
From Software dropped the ball with Dark Souls 2. The magic is gone and has been replaced by a pestilence so foul it will make you hate gaming, and all the joy and happiness it SHOULD bring, forever. Let's just bury this one, deep in the darkest corners of our hearts, and suppress, suppress, suppress until we can - with inhuman effort and strength and with the uneasiest of smiles - pretend it doesn't exist at all.
The wreck of the Bandai Scamco Fitzgerald is sinking full speed - let it rest on the bottom of failure's ocean.

It's a bit difficult to review this game. It's not bad but it's far to be perfect. I've found really annoying the management of the provinces: you should own all the regions of a province to control it in a proper way, otherwise it's hard to extract all the value a province can give: this mechanic surely impacts on your game, alliances are more expensive to mantain because if you share the same province with your allies it will cost you a lot in terms of inefficiencies and low order.
If after a war you end up owning partially a province the game is like forcing you to begin another war to gain full control of it.
Once you take control of all the province it's easy to manage it and prosper (at normal and hard difficulty). In Rome I it was like impossible to mantain certain regions (carthago, cordoba...) always unhappy, so it's a good news for me to have more stability in your empire. You could find it too easy though.
Something I really don't understand are the sea battles. Maybe it's me but I find the battleground too narrow for so many ship. I mean that a 20vs20 sea battle will be a head-on collision because you just have nowhere else to go.
I have appreciated the battles and it's a nice game all considered. But I expect much more from a Total War game so I've felt disappointed.
Another issue: if you enter in war with some factions the only way to get rid of them will be total annihilation. For some reasons they will never make peace.
Finally the DLCs are a plague. You cannot use the greeks without additional cost, it's a cheap trick.
If you enjoy the Total war saga or just the Roman empire you'll have fun with this game nevertheless, but I think there are too many issues to endorse this game without making some points.

Okok hear me out here:
Yes, right now the only thing you can do is find a neutral system and create a single captial planet.
What you can't do right now is: Use God powers, colonize other planets or systems, make offical factions, PvP, store planets, scry for artifacts, get artifacts, Create/destroy stars, and a few more features. There is no main story line, no evil among us; everyone wants to builds up a nice happy relationship.
Looks bad, right?
But look at where this game is: Early-access Beta. This game is no where near finished and already there is a growing base of follows and backers who see the potential of this game. You see all those things that aren't implemented yet? Yeah, those things eventually WILL be implemented; PvP, colonization, empires among the stars. In a game named Gods and Idols, you will truely be a God with your massive fleets and civilizations. You will be able to destroy star systems in single sweeps of your mighty hand and create new life with but a thought.
So what can you do until then?
- The planet creation minigame is always fun, trying to get best stats for your new planet.
- Discover the Crux and find their lost artifacts around the cosmos
- There's more than 1 type of star; find unique stars that will provide special bonuses in the updates to come.
- Learn the basics of planet design so that when the game comes out in full swing, you will have an edge on one of the most unique real-time Multiplayer games out there.
In the end, you really won't know what you are missing until you try Gods and Idols for yourself. Come on -- become the deity you were always ment to be!

So far the only complaint is that the tutorial could be a little more descriptive. It took me several minutes on a few of the steps to even realize what they were talking about. It's very casual, the only interesting part for me is when I get to create a planet, as it's the most interactive it gets. Graphics are beautiful, music is great. I hope this game gets developed more so there are things to do other than just passing the time and waiting for resources to gather. It's definitely worth watching to see if anything else gets released from it's developers.

Gods and Idols is a space RTS with MMO elements.  Right now it's in very early alpha.  You can populate a planet, but not much else.  At the moment it just feels like a browser-based farming MMO.  Starports are not enabled yet, which means you can't actually do anything with a fully-populated and productive planet except populate another planet.
Perhaps this is the foundation of a good RTS/MMO, but it's waaaaaaay too soon to tell.  I'm disappointed that it was released on Steam so early that there's no player interaction beyond chat and viewing other planets, yet billed as an MMO.  However, I'm giving it a Yes recommendation because it's free and has no microtransactions (yet) so there's no appearance of a money grab or long con.
Given three or four months, this could turn into a fun game.

Rome II is a great game, i've played it alot. I made some cons and pros for this game.
Let's start with the Cons
- Lacking the amount of generals available for defending your strong points early on.
- The politics are a great new feature, but they could have more content.
- In Grand Campaign the 'computer' always perfectly know where the weakpoints are, It could use more variety.
- The 'computer' is always perfectly programmed to know the max range of your units, when your general uses 'dubble time'. They can never chase a opponent, and so they can always counter it with a 'ambush'.
- In the Rome I and Medieval Total War, you have many 'nature disasters'. In my opinion it was a very cool feature, but i don't really see it on Rome II.
- Minor bugs ingame, 'ships that keep stranding, and flying over the map'. It's really not that funny if you play a multiplayer game.
And now for the pros of the game.
- Amazing variety in units
- The graphics are amazing, and astonishing. Everything in the game gives so much atmosphere.
- The taunts in battle and on the battle map are really cool. And i still enjoy the general for battle speech.
- The character in the units and factions are really beautifull to see 'colours, units, generals, mounts etc'.
- Much variety everytime you start a Grand Campaign, faction never do the same and always amaze me.
- There are politics, and the city management is really well made.
- Researches are made very fair for every faction.
- Good diplomatics
- Fast loading screens, and smooth gameplay. (Not only due my PC) Optimalisation really well made.
- Many ways of playing the game, and much variety of choices. (Passive, offensive, alies etc.)
- Sea battles are really cool to see, and look amazing when u use 'cinnema mode'.
That was my review, i hope i've helped everyone to get a good look at the game.

This game isn't even remotely free to play. If I had to call the free content anything, it resembles a demo more than any F2P game I've ever seen. Oh sure, there's 2 in-game currencies, one bought with cash and the other earned through play which makes it look like a F2P until you realize you can't buy hardly any equipment using the earned currency. You can't even buy the most basic camouflage without spending cash. Oh, and the earned currency is a finite resource. Complete all missions, and that's it... unless you pay cash to reset your missions.
I can understand going the F2P route to fund the development. I can understand having a wide variety of gear and weapons available especially since you don't have to get everything to enjoy yourself. I can understand each new update largely focusing on something new to buy with cash. What I can't understand is breaking the F2P model in a way that even EA would be embarrassed to try. Yes I've put some money in because I really do enjoy this game. It plays great and it's scratched an itch I haven't had a game for in a long time. It can even be argued that dollar per hour of entertainment it's not too far off base with an MMO business model and for some people the expense can be worth it. It cannot be argued that this is even remotely a F2P title, and as long as it falsely calls itself one I unfortunately must leave a negative review.

I don't often write reviews, positive or negative. But Factorio deserves one. Do you like management games? Do you like engineering? Do you like factories or automation? If yes to any of these, there is NO better game than this. Sure, it's a little rough around the edges some time (it is still Early Access after all), but there just isn't another game quite like it, and the issues are really just minor inconveniences. Further, it has strong mod support and devs who know what their game vision is and what their players want, and usually do an impecable job at meeting both expectations. We NEED more games like this. Not necissarily this genre, but this kind; games made for niche and serious gamers. Games designed to satisfy those looking for more than something to kill time and enjoy the ride in. Games with substance over the superficial.
Is this game for everyone? No. Most certainly not. But it IS objectively the best game of it's kind. It's exactly what it looks like, and they have a demo. It's really hard to convey with words what makes this game interesting. On the surface, this game feels exactly as if you were doing real life work:
- You get a job.
- You are assigned your tasks.
- They feel like a chore.
- You screw up
- You get reprimanded
- Your responsibilities grow, while your salary stays the same
However, throw in the realities of having a 6 member family to provide for, and it starts getting complicated. Fail to bring home enough money and some family members may have to starve, or freeze. If one of them is sick, you may have to choose between medicine, food, or heating. Will you take bribes then to offset these costs? Will you cooperate with terrorists to get a pay cut? Will you try to get through that gate as many people as you can, since you get paid by the person?
At first it's really easy to make these desicions since you have no sense of what's really going on. After the first few hours go by, and you're grinding along day after day, you start to feel more like playing the character. You start to feel compassion for some of the pixelated people that desperately beg for entry. You start to make judgement calls based on how your family is doing. The game begins to develop into an extremely interesting experience where you're constantly being morally tested.
The game has about 20 or 30-something outcomes (can't remember off the top of my head). So far I've managed to see about 9 of them. Every time I finish I'm finding new paths and possibilities to explore in order to see where the story goes. This is one of the 10 best experiences I've had with video games this year, and I wholeheartedly recommend you give this one a chance.

I play over several different profiles and have quite a few hours outside of Steam. I would say that I have been playing this game for about a year now, and I must say it is very fun! However, due to recent patches and such, I am losing interest.
The unbalance desperately needs to be adressed, but Hi-Rez refuses to listen to players. The meta changes time and time again so drastically that you will often see the same character picked over and over and some characters never chosen in each patch. This is probably the biggest issue right now.
Another thing that bugs me is that, in this current patch, mid lane was made partially into a duo lane with the jungler, taking away the often dynamic gameplay elements seen before. This isn't the first patch like this. With every newer patch comes a more forced meta. Hi-Rez is trying to force players to play a certain way, otherwise you will always be unsuccessful. I prefer multiplayer games to allow creativity, choosing a playstyle that suits you and changing it to what's fun and unique. This is something Smite is now missing.
Another thing that goes without saying is that the community is terrible. It baffles me how, in beta, I met so little toxic players. The exact opposite, actually. People were willing to help others learn and become better at the game. Now, the community consists of either EXTREMELY toxic players or bad players who do not know how to play. I admit, with all the bad players on this game, it is excusable for people to get frusterated sometimes. However, when you're spewing death threats and other such hatred, that is very terrible behavior. The thing is, Hi-Rez seems to be alright with this behavior, because many people I've seen being just terrible, terrible people haven't yet been banned, even though I can imagine they have many reports under their belts. In my experience, even League of Legends was better with this, banning people in a just manner for spewing hatred unreasonably.
One of the last major issues I have is that, instead of focusing on balancing all of the current gods, Hi-Rez has been pumping out new characters, causing even MORE unbalance problems. To put it into perspective, this game has 80 gods right now. With so many characters, you'd figure the folks at Hi-Rez would be focusing on making each character well just right in terms of power. However, they'd rather be pumping time into the development of more characters, in what I can only assume to be a way to keep players interested in Smite, attracting "hype" if you will.
The last issues I have, and these are the minor ones, regard the prices of skins and other purchasables in Smite. I know, complaining about the price cosmetics in any game is looked down upon, but if you're anything like me, you enjoy making your character have a unique look, adding a bit of flare here and there. So, I will complain about it because I have the right to.
It doesn't end there. Most skins in the game, the "exclusive" skins, can only be purchased in chests. Many chests have around 50 items in them, making your chances of getting the skin near impossible on your first go. The chests cost 150-400 gems each, which is such a let down. Random chance chests have always been a bother of mine, especially when the only way to get the skin within them is to purchase it numerous times. Did I mention many of these chests are only available for a limited time? Awful.
The last itch about skins I have is the quest concept Hi-Rez has taken a liking to. The way quests work is that, in a limited amount of time, you must use real money in order to buy a large amount of items (skins, ward skins, avatars, etc.) in order to get a certain limited item/items. May I add, the reward(s) for completing quests is always amazing, whether it be a badass looking skin with a bunch of other goodies or something else really amazing. However, these "quests" are the only way you can get these items, for once the event is over, you can never purchase them again. This is quite a shady market practice, as, for example, the last events quest cost 3100 gems to complete. That is in the ballpark of $55.00. Needless to say, I haven't done any of the quests.
TL:DR
Not recommended due to:
Poor balance
Forced metas every patch
Overpriced skins

Smite continues to nerf the already useless gods and makes the broken ones even more powerful. This is a joke. Hi-Rez needs to stop investing time into shameless copies (Smite Rivals, Smite Tactics) and focus on balancing the game that people are actually interested in (Smite).

Ok first off I was a little sceptical of this release, especially with the premium asking price, however, after a few positive reviews decided to give it a chance, the fact this is a single developer who has worked tirelessly to release this, kudos to you, this is a very solid EA and so will give it my honest opinion.
Things I love so far;
- The weather is immersive.
- Boat customisation is a fantastic touch.
- The navigation of menu is easy to understand including little hint boxes for complete beginners to better get to grips with sailing mechanics.
- The sheer size of the map with real world time
- The multiplayer aspect, seeing other boats and knowing they are manned, including the option to race and sail together adds immensely to the gameplay.
It would be harsh to say I dislike anything, however, areas I can see that would benefit (or would look forward to being introduced) improvement are;
- Game resolution and more graphic tweak options (would love to see 2160p up there)
- Improved water, sky, and land texture (its good but could be better) let’s hope the Mac compatibility doesn’t hold this title back graphics wise.
- Random Marine life (Shark, Dolphin, Whale, Large fish, even Birds in the sky) this would seriously impact well on immersion, even some AI ships, or plane trails in the sky.
- Enterable detailed and operational cabin. (sleep, eat, log, charter, radio)
- An equipment store (the ability to purchase rations, supplies, spare ropes) for Transat crossings, to maintain a system of energy and morale.
- Some Major ports, with the ability to dock.
As I have seen by the road map some of these suggestions are already planned by the dev, this title has so much to offer, in both potential and scope.
It’s  a clear 7.5/10

I grew up with Homeworld. HW2 was a favorite of mine. I went back some more with Complex 8 and 9. The remastered collection was a no-thought purchase.
Looking back though, I'm seeing the only reason why is that the Homeworld series has been the only 3D space RTS in modern times produced by a AAA company, with it's only competition being O.R.B., long aged by the time Homeworld 2 came out, and 2.5D games, most notably ST:Armada and Sins of a Solar Empire, both not nearly as focused on fleet battles.
Before I talk about the singleplayer, let me speak first on the multiplayer balance. In a game about fleet compositions, there is simply no viable strategy for you to focus on anything other than frigates: it is what your opponents will be using; since frigates have counters to every other class of ships, counter themselves, and have the ability to capture themselves/capital ships, combined with their ability/cost being much lower than every other ship in game, there's no reason to use anything else.
Singleplayer: The difficulty in the first one isn't there, and that's partially because of enemy fleets choosing simply to ignore you in some missions. Otherwise, because of capturing being available to corvettes, you can scoop more than enough ships to cover any gaps forced upon you by fleet caps. In HW2, however, there is a massive difficulty cliff that is spawned around the seventh mission; by the ninth mission, enemy forces have quadrupled whilst your resource supply/mission has dwindled to nothing. I gave up after I was faced with ~20 missile corvette squadrons after my main force had been wiped and I had less than 1000RU because they had spawned an enemy strike force (after I had destroyed the gates which were supposedly responsible for the spawns) right behind the shipyard needed to repair the PS McGuffin.
So yeah. Pretty, but vapid. I can't recommend you spending 15 dollars on this, let alone 35.

One of the FPS genre's best games, hands down.  The base of the game still has a few persistent bugs, but fan patches have solved most of these.
Even for a game made in the mid 2000s, the atmospheric ambience holds up to modern standards and the shooter action continues to be solid.  There are a multitude of fan mods that focus on graphics, difficulty, gameplay tweaks, or even complete overhauls, such as the STALKER Complete set of mods.  You will be getting plenty of game for your money.
Pros (Based on the base game, not modded versions)
-Solid FPS action with survival elements
-The game is rife with ambience, from the creepy to the downright foreboding.
-Solid selection of weapons, all of which are balanced.
-The world is alive, NPCs will gather and talk smack, opposing NPCs will fight, and combat AI is fairly solid, though sometimes buggy.  People that die stay dead, others take their place if needbe.
-Your immediate choices affect your gameplay experience from the get-go
-Multiple fan mods and a dedicated community that LOVES this game for what it is and what it can be.
-Rare items and artifacts are abound for those that prefer to explore the game more thoroughly but aren't required to win.
Cons
-The switch between Russian and English during gameplay can get awkward.  English (in faux Russian accent) is used for important dialogue but NPCs will talk Russian for everything else.
-In the game's base form, ther are a few persistent bugs, some of them are game breaking, but fan mods and patches have fixed these.  It is very possible to complete the game with these glitches still in.
-Some parts of the game get faceroll easy when you acquire the right artifacts, which are plentiful.
Afterthoughts
-Left handed models are used for most of the weapons, despite shooting right handed, likely done for flair.  It may bother some more detail oriented players.
Overall, a game you don't want to miss.

I skimmed a review for this game before playing it. "Sad romance story" it said. Well then, we'll see how that works out, I thought.
Enter Emily. A girl who, off the bat, does nothing but vent to you, and shames you for trying to bang her when she was clearly in need of some comfort (or alternately gets really pissy with you if you refuse to have her over, given you have what's implied to be either a girlfriend or romantic interest named Emma). Emily is supposed to be your main romantic interest. To me, she came off as a ♥♥♥♥♥ who has no interest in or concern for you. I felt connected to noone in this game, though. Not even the protagonist. Let me tell you why.
One of the cardinal sins of Dungeons and Dragons style games is something called "railroading". It's when the game master puts his players on a railroad track in terms of storytelling, not allowing them to make meaningful choices that would alter the unraveling of the story that the game master had planned.
That's exactly what this game does. Without spoiling, you're forced to show sympathy for her in some places (why would I do that? she's awful), and in other places, what the protagonist actually says doesn't correspond with what you chose.
All in all it's not a terrible game. I had fun, but probably for all the wrong reasons. Being rude to someone with no concern for you in subtle ways was fun in a twisted kind of way. But I feel like this wasn't intentional, or even the intended route. The game certainly ends anticlimactically.

I play over several different profiles and have quite a few hours outside of Steam. I would say that I have been playing this game for about a year now, and I must say it is very fun! However, due to recent patches and such, I am losing interest.
The unbalance desperately needs to be adressed, but Hi-Rez refuses to listen to players. The meta changes time and time again so drastically that you will often see the same character picked over and over and some characters never chosen in each patch. This is probably the biggest issue right now.
Another thing that bugs me is that, in this current patch, mid lane was made partially into a duo lane with the jungler, taking away the often dynamic gameplay elements seen before. This isn't the first patch like this. With every newer patch comes a more forced meta. Hi-Rez is trying to force players to play a certain way, otherwise you will always be unsuccessful. I prefer multiplayer games to allow creativity, choosing a playstyle that suits you and changing it to what's fun and unique. This is something Smite is now missing.
Another thing that goes without saying is that the community is terrible. It baffles me how, in beta, I met so little toxic players. The exact opposite, actually. People were willing to help others learn and become better at the game. Now, the community consists of either EXTREMELY toxic players or bad players who do not know how to play. I admit, with all the bad players on this game, it is excusable for people to get frusterated sometimes. However, when you're spewing death threats and other such hatred, that is very terrible behavior. The thing is, Hi-Rez seems to be alright with this behavior, because many people I've seen being just terrible, terrible people haven't yet been banned, even though I can imagine they have many reports under their belts. In my experience, even League of Legends was better with this, banning people in a just manner for spewing hatred unreasonably.
One of the last major issues I have is that, instead of focusing on balancing all of the current gods, Hi-Rez has been pumping out new characters, causing even MORE unbalance problems. To put it into perspective, this game has 80 gods right now. With so many characters, you'd figure the folks at Hi-Rez would be focusing on making each character well just right in terms of power. However, they'd rather be pumping time into the development of more characters, in what I can only assume to be a way to keep players interested in Smite, attracting "hype" if you will.
The last issues I have, and these are the minor ones, regard the prices of skins and other purchasables in Smite. I know, complaining about the price cosmetics in any game is looked down upon, but if you're anything like me, you enjoy making your character have a unique look, adding a bit of flare here and there. So, I will complain about it because I have the right to.
It doesn't end there. Most skins in the game, the "exclusive" skins, can only be purchased in chests. Many chests have around 50 items in them, making your chances of getting the skin near impossible on your first go. The chests cost 150-400 gems each, which is such a let down. Random chance chests have always been a bother of mine, especially when the only way to get the skin within them is to purchase it numerous times. Did I mention many of these chests are only available for a limited time? Awful.
The last itch about skins I have is the quest concept Hi-Rez has taken a liking to. The way quests work is that, in a limited amount of time, you must use real money in order to buy a large amount of items (skins, ward skins, avatars, etc.) in order to get a certain limited item/items. May I add, the reward(s) for completing quests is always amazing, whether it be a badass looking skin with a bunch of other goodies or something else really amazing. However, these "quests" are the only way you can get these items, for once the event is over, you can never purchase them again. This is quite a shady market practice, as, for example, the last events quest cost 3100 gems to complete. That is in the ballpark of $55.00. Needless to say, I haven't done any of the quests.
TL:DR
Not recommended due to:
Poor balance
Forced metas every patch
Overpriced skins

Dark Souls II is a competently executed Zelda for grown-ups that is somewhat tainted by flaws stimming from an identity crisis and the occassional bout of plain old fashioned bad ideas. I should add that GFWL has prevented me from playing DS1, so this review will not compare the two games. Additionally, I cannot access multiplayer because I am playing this game on a potato. That said, let's begin the review, shall we?
The atmosphere is great and combat is for the most part visceral and satisfying, although I'd argue that the game in many ways shoots itself in the foot in the manner in which it deals with weight. You see, you can't just flail around spamming attacks in Dark Souls because blows have weight and force behind them. While a dagger or rapier will strike faster than a greatsword or maul, for comparison's sake, a light weapon in DS strikes about as fast as a two-handed weapon in Skyrim. (Incidentally, the ability to choose to wield one-handed weapons with both hands for extra damage is another nice touch in DS.) The problem is, at high levels, it is possible to dual wield Zweihanders roughly the size of the Incredible Hulk, a feat which quite frankly runs quite contrary to the quasi-realistic handling of weapons at lower levels and leaves the game looking a bit schizophrenic. Anything that manages to break suspension of disbelief in a game where a transgendered undead swordsman can buy spells from a demonic cat in a zombie shantytown can probably be considered to be an artistic failure. Additionally, while it is a good idea on paper to have armor negatively effect mobility, the way in which it is executed in practice can lead to some builds which can generously be described as batshit insane. For example, a good way to combine defense, mobility, and counteroffensive parrying capabilities is to have a sword-n'-boarder that runs around buck♥♥♥♥♥nude, allowing you to quick roll and run very fast while blocking the attacks of mooks, opening them to a counterstrike.
The controls are mostly solid and responsive with a few major puzzlers. For example, to jump, you must hold down B to sprint and then click the left stick, being careful not to accidentally nudge the stick slightly when doing so as this will cause you to veer off course and probably plunge into one of the game's many bottomless pits. I don't care if the game is supposed to be "Hardcore," not having a single jump button is not "challenging," it is just poor ergonomic design. The lack of an ability to pause is equally baffling. Sometimes you've got to answer the phone or go to the bathroom or whatever, and it'd be nice not to be splattered by the giant ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hippo monster when you put the controller down to do so. I suppose the argument could be made that PvP and Co-Op preclude the inclusion of a pause function, but I'd argue that all you'd have to do is disable it whenever you're being invaded, invading, summoning, or being summoned.
Another major flaw of the game is the way it handles death. When you die, you come back as an undead Hollowed and lose your souls, (the game's combination currency/XP) and a portion of your maximum health, (up to a maximum of half after a dozen or so deaths.) This makes the game progressively harder each time you die. Health can be restored by using a Human Effigy to restore your humanity, but there are a finite amount of them in the game. You can regain the souls you lost by touching the Bloodstain where you died, but because enemies respawn after you die or rest at a campfire until you kill them ten or so times, in a particularly challenging area, you'll probably just die again. As there can only be one Bloodstain active at a time, this means the souls in the previous Bloodstain are lost for good. And as enemies stop spawning after a point, there are a finite amount of souls in the game.The problem with this is not that it adds challenge, but that it discourages exploration and experimentation because a rational person is just going to grind in a relatively safe area until the monsters stop spawning, which frankly gets kind of dull after a point. It's also worth noting that the Artificial Intelligence isn't. Sometimes you can just stand there twelve feet in front of an enemy and he'll just stand there staring into space until you cross the arbitrary eleven foot eleven inch mark after which he will furiously charge you. Foes are challenging, but rely more on overpowered attacks than tactical expertise, and battles devolve into "figure out the unchanging pattern of the killer automaton." Granted, for a klutz like me who doesn't have quick reflexes, it's still quite the challenge, but for someone who's actually good at video games, I could actaully see the infamously difficult Dark Souls becoming too easy.
Overall, I would recommend this game for anyone looking for a good hack-and-slash dark fantasy adventure. However, I would add that the game's reputation as "OMFG HARDCORE" has created something of an Emperor's New Clothes type effect where people hesitate to point out the game's occassional spot of bad design out of fear of being labeled a "filthy casual" who needs to "git gud" since clearly the bad camera angle and poor lighting that caused you to die in that one dungeon was meant as a challenge to weed out♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥like you and was not a mistake, you ♥♥♥♥ing idiot. Of course, dismissing something because some of the fans are jerks will mean you'll have nothing left to like, so one obviously should not let this deter you from buying the game, and like most fandoms, most DS players are basically normal human beings, but one should be forewarned of the occassional toxic egotist in the community.
TL;DR: A solid and fun game that falls somewhat short of perfection. Challenging test of timing and reflexes, but relatively undynamic combat AI and the neccessity to grind can lead to tedium.

I played the first dark souls for a while but issues with the framerate eventually stopped me. I'm glad to say that there have been no such issues with dark souls 2. They did a superb job optimising the game this time around and I am loving it.
When you first glance at the game it looks like a run of the mill RPG with various character class / customisation options. That opinion only lasts a short while when you realise there is no difficulty level and death happens all too easy, This is a game that will brutally punish you for making mistakes. The end result always being death. You simply cannot charge into an enemy swinging wildly and hope to survive. In dark souls every move you make can be a difference between life and death. Your enemies are varied and often require different tactics in order to be the victor. This is especially the case with the bosses.
Fortunately you are not always alone. Dark souls has a brilliant co-operative play system merged with the game. This means that after a few levels you sometimes get the opportunity to invite other players in the form of a phantom. This is a great asset when it comes to dealing with difficult bosses. As helping players are rewarded you will often find them volunteering at certain areas of the game. There is a twist however in that just as some players can be invited to help, there are those who may drop in uninvited. These are players who appear as  dark phantoms and the last thing on their mind is to help you.
The graphics in the game are superb, atmospheric and at times dark. Unlike traditional RPG's dark souls offers you little assistance in terms of guidance. There is no go to point B and fetch this before returning to A. You literally have to find your own way and work things out. The game world is made up with a set of areas or zones which fortunately can be fast travelled to once you discover their bonfires. Some of these areas will contain foes who at first will seem impossible to beat and you will find yourself seeking out other less difficult paths before returning when you have levelled up enough.
The game has only once type of currency and that is souls which you claim from dead enemies. You will need these to level up and upgrade / buy / repair equipment. One consequence of dying is that you will lose all the souls you have obtained upon respawning. During the early stages of the game they can be reclaimed by returning to the scene of your previous death. There are other penalites to dying but I won't spoil it by revealing them.
The lure of various co-operative play styles and different character classes will most likely see you play the game through numerous times and thats without the various DLC's that have been added since release.
A dark, challenging and unique RPG that punishes you hard but also rewards in so many ways.

Pros:
1. Feels like you're actually in the movie Alien. The thing that this game does so well is the retro-futuristic atmosphere that the original movie had back in 1979. Uses the same sounds, models... everything. If you like the technology in Alien then this game will feel like tech-PORN to you :)
2.  AI is pretty damn smart. Very scary game. You eventually learn how to deal with it... or so you think. You won't be disappointed.
3. Sounds are amazing. Movie-accurate. Xenomorph's footsteps so bloody horrifying. Enough said.
4. Death animations are so awesome. First time I got pulled out of a locker by a xenomorph, I was like "HEEEYOOOO HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥WHAT IS THIS GAME ♥♥♥♥ YEAHEHEHEAHH"
5. Terminal hacking, blowtorching, lever pulling, button pushing, engine cranking, weapon crafting, core overloading... YOU NAME IT BUDDY
6. Game is addictive. Play time is around 20 hours. Long game. Lots of tasks. Lots of fun.
Cons:
1. Minor bugs. Doesn't affect gameplay. Pretty rare and requires you to look hard. But the game isn't 100% flawless. Saw a floating gun once. Alien tail clipped through the ceiling once too. Sounds seem to cut off in some small areas. Floating fluorescent lights in the transit areas and on a spacewalk elevator. Nothing too crazy.
2. Some parts towards the end seemed rushed. Especially experiencing a pre-rendered cutscene that was awkwardly placed during gameplay. Since I had film grain turned off, it was really noticeable seeing a pre-ren scene covered in film grain. The game's ending suffered as well, I believe. But that's just my opinion.
3. Plot is okay, but not totally unique. Could be better for fans of the franchise. They re-use a lot of the same elements from the Alien movie. For people new to the Alien franchise, you'd probably really love the plot. As for others, you might not be too suprised with some of the things that happen in the game. Especially about "the company". I'll just leave it there ;)
Final word:
Forget the cons, they don't spoil the game that much. Buy the game. Totally worth it. If you're not already a fan of Alien, you probably will be after this game.

Alien (1979) and Alien Isolation take place in a  alternative 1970s retro-vision of the future, so events that happened in our world from the 1980s onwards, probably did not happen in the Alien universe. Obviously there was no internet or computer or digital revolution as we know it, the cold war perhaps lasted longer than  the 1990s. Corporatism is the rule of thumb in the alien universe...And no Promethus does not exist  and did not  happen in the Alien Isolation universe, there are no engineers etc in this world, it's completly non-canon to this universe.

While Rome 2's now imfamous launch was attrocious, in its current state, the game is one of the best of the Total War series, and a shining example of a RTS.
1. Campaign: As always, Rome 2's campaign is a mix of turn based strategical management on the campaign map, and real time battles. For the most part, the AI does a good job managing their cities and armies. They don't make foolish mistakes, they defend their cities, and they attack any vulnerabilities left by the player. The UI is fine, but the lack of branching skill trees for generals can be annoying. The removal of family trees is another annoyance as you feel no attachment to your faction's characters. One place where Rome 2 shines, however, is its variety. There are dozens of faction to chose from, exact numbers based on DLC, all of which have interesting units, traits, and challenge levels.
2. Battles: Once again, we see the return of CA's battle AI. While it is not totally imcopetent, it consistently makes moronic mistakes. It will engage your pikemen head on, charge cavalry into the front of heavy infantry, and often attack with no real tact. However, the battles are still fun. Troops are easy to control and the battle UI is slick and customizable. Sure, when a cav unit inexplicably gets stuck on one lonely spearman it can♥♥♥♥♥♥you the hell off, but it never detracts from the overall expirience.
3. Multiplayer: Due to the variety of factions, Rome 2's multiplayer shines. Each faction is fun to play as and offers different stregnths and weaknesses. The added bonus of phasing out the battle AI is just the icing on the cake. However, technical issues still at times hinder the multiplayer, as you will often expirience severe lag and will occasionally be dropped from the game.
4. Graphics: As one of the best optimized PC games out there in its current state, Rome 2 has no issue delivering both stellar graphics (in-battles and on the campaign map) and smooth framerates.
5. DLC offerings: While the 'Wrath of Sparta' DLC fell short, and I still have yet to see the point of 'Blood and Gore,' Rome 2 still has some fine offerings for DLC. Some packs will add fun new factions, and others will offer new, full legnth historical camapign scenarios to be played out on customized maps. Without a doubt, 'Hannibal at the Gates' and Caesar in Gaul' stand out from the pack as superd additions to the game and engrosing windows into some of the most fascinating wars in antique history.
Without a doubt, Rome 2 stands out as one of the most extensive and deep offerings in the RTS genre. It is a stellar game and in its current condition, and it is the best Total War game to date.

I did a first review with mixed feelings for
when it first came out. I recently decided to give it another try. First off, it is important to state that this game is not Skyrim and will never be. Though, that doesn't make it bad or not part of the Elder Scrolls series. Following the colossal success of
made the hopes and aspirations for
an almost impossible to create experience. Zenimax Online Studios and Bethesda, had no margin of error and the multiple reviews were quick to criticize the project. A lot has changed since then.
Faithful to a very long Elder Scrolls tradition, everything begins behind bars. You don't really know why, except that you must have been crazy drunk, once again. The customization screen lets you create a character to your liking with a lot of different possibilities. You can't really process what is happening around you, but a great escape from this "jail" is on-going and you were "here". Reminding you of your escape from Helgen in Skyrim or the secret escape in Oblivion. This time on the other hand, you are escaping a Daedric prison. Not bad.
The Combat system is continuous and extremely dynamic, every action requiring either a mouse click or a button to press. Very similar to what
has always been. You can alternate between quick attack, strong attack, block, interruption and "exploit" (that will let you put a stunned enemy to the ground with a strong attack). Let's note that the dodge mechanic (a tumble in any direction) is now useable by all characters instead of being a skill to unlock.
The whole combat experience makes it for a very dynamic environment, you really feel a lot of satisfaction when you crush someone's face with a strong attack. I'm starting to think that only magic staffs could use a small enhancement in comparison to the good old steel.

Adding up to the fighting system is a skill bar, five plus an ultimate. Going from the gap closer to the poison. Nothing is really crazy or innovative but the fact that you can level up anything at anytime and use it will really have an impact on your gameplay, style and experience. You can then mix up any weapons, with any kind of armours and guilds you join will give you new skills that will add some spice or originality to your build. This freedom is greatly appreciated. It is also possible to become a werewolf or a vampire that will add up their entire perks of passive / active spells.
, will also let you acquire new skills by exploring, reading books, killing people in PvP etc.

In terms of questing, everything is quite linear and similar to other games. Go fetch X, go kill Y Z times. Every area opening the way for the other. On the other hand, you don't really get the feeling of always following the roadside. The extremely large size of the maps and the presence of content almost everywhere tries to give you the same feeling of freedom you could find in Skyrim while adventuring, tempted to do something else and exploring a new area at any moment's notice. Small dungeons and crypts or other instance are always present on every map for the curious adventurer. Making you forget the super important and time sensitive mission you were on because your attention deficit told you to go explore this instead.

Every character and quest is being voiced and that makes what could be a repetitive and broing experience more attractive.
is faithful to a long tradition of well built story and lore. Even though most quests are a bit weak on that part, some of the choices you will have to make are totally heartbreaking.
One of the big asset of the questing Zenimax did could also be its weakness. You feel like you are playing a Solo game; at all times. Except when you look around to see if someone's trying to kill a world boss or clear a public event.

Artistically, the game might be recycling the decors a bit too much. It becomes very obvious when entering a tower. But the fact that you won't lag when processing a ton of players fighting in PVP or big spells is quite a feat; even on some bad computers / connection. Otherwise, you will encounter beautiful landscapes and maps that will make for beautiful screenshot, but you won't find that Skyrim touch and taking screenshots in an MMO is more complicated sometimes !
Finally, the crafting system is rich, probably richer than most MMORPG without being completely unreasonable it seems being able to master the crafting arts is especially long. The interface is quite horrible, but nothing mods can't fix.

I grew up with Homeworld. HW2 was a favorite of mine. I went back some more with Complex 8 and 9. The remastered collection was a no-thought purchase.
Looking back though, I'm seeing the only reason why is that the Homeworld series has been the only 3D space RTS in modern times produced by a AAA company, with it's only competition being O.R.B., long aged by the time Homeworld 2 came out, and 2.5D games, most notably ST:Armada and Sins of a Solar Empire, both not nearly as focused on fleet battles.
Before I talk about the singleplayer, let me speak first on the multiplayer balance. In a game about fleet compositions, there is simply no viable strategy for you to focus on anything other than frigates: it is what your opponents will be using; since frigates have counters to every other class of ships, counter themselves, and have the ability to capture themselves/capital ships, combined with their ability/cost being much lower than every other ship in game, there's no reason to use anything else.
Singleplayer: The difficulty in the first one isn't there, and that's partially because of enemy fleets choosing simply to ignore you in some missions. Otherwise, because of capturing being available to corvettes, you can scoop more than enough ships to cover any gaps forced upon you by fleet caps. In HW2, however, there is a massive difficulty cliff that is spawned around the seventh mission; by the ninth mission, enemy forces have quadrupled whilst your resource supply/mission has dwindled to nothing. I gave up after I was faced with ~20 missile corvette squadrons after my main force had been wiped and I had less than 1000RU because they had spawned an enemy strike force (after I had destroyed the gates which were supposedly responsible for the spawns) right behind the shipyard needed to repair the PS McGuffin.
So yeah. Pretty, but vapid. I can't recommend you spending 15 dollars on this, let alone 35.

THE GOOD:
This game is AMAZING. Just simply, completely, utterly amazing. The stages are well done, the gameplay is usually fun (there are a couple of rough patches, but overall), the music -- as always -- is FANTASTIC, making me want the OST after just an hour in the game. The Avatar's gameplay is also very interesting, giving you a choice of various special abilities in place of homing attack and letting you decide which one that you like the best.
While stages do have a "favored" weapon type, ANY weapon can be used in any of the Avatar stages, you just can't take the short cuts. The game also makes sure to tell you every time you get a weapon, and on top of that, examining the weapons in your armory tells you EXACTLY what it does and what each bonus it has does (and there's a good number of bonuses). There's also a lot of parts for your Avatar -- you can even make them an unofficial robot or lizard with the parts! Their special abilities are also very interesting, and can change how you go through levels or the difficulty you might have.
The Classic and Modern Sonic stages are also very good, well put together and immensely enjoyable to go through, and all of the stages are beautiful. On top of that, the combined Modern Sonic/Avatar stages are really interesting, and the interaction between Avatar and Sonic is very cute.
Story-wise, it's pretty simple. Eggman has a powerful thing, he took over, stop him. There's nothing complicated or major here, but that doesn't make it bad at all, and I think a simple story in this case makes the game stronger. As well, Sonic's interactions with the Avatar and taking them under his wing is also very cute.
THE BAD:
The physics can be a little frustrating at times. The character you're playing as accelerates if you even breathe on the control stick, which can make precise movement very difficult. On top of that, it's not clear in a few spots if you can make jumps or need momentum to move them.
The optimization seems a little low as well. [NOTE: Sega has since fixed/patched the following complaints.] When loading into Modern Sonic or Dual Stages, the game slows down for a few seconds at the start. The cutscenes are mostly clean and smooth, but a bit of lag can sneak into them here and there. The lag itself won't affect gameplay except very little (if at all), but it is there. (I can't speak for if you have a lower-end computer, but that would be your lag issue there)
Like a lot of Sonic games, it's also a little short. You can finish all the story missions in about five hours. There's still plenty left to do after that, of course, from constantly-changing missions to getting high ranks to collecting Avatar pieces, but the story itself is done once you finish the 30th stage.
Classic Sonic's stages are awful. The controls are fairly bad, his hitbox is wonky, and most of your invincibility is wasted because he just falls on his butt and won't get up after you get hit. Classic really shouldn't have been in the game, or at the very least, it needed to be SIGNIFICANTLY tightened and tested.
OVERALL:
This game is worth buying, ESPECIALLY for fans. It's not at all flawless, but the flaws are fairly minor, and anyone who enjoys Sonic-style gameplay will love this. At the time of writing, there are apparently crash issues with some people (I say "apparently" because I didn't encounter even a single crash), so that may be something worth looking into, but the game itself is absolutely, positively worth playing. It's amazing, it's well done, and Sega knocked it out of the park.

I played the first dark souls for a while but issues with the framerate eventually stopped me. I'm glad to say that there have been no such issues with dark souls 2. They did a superb job optimising the game this time around and I am loving it.
When you first glance at the game it looks like a run of the mill RPG with various character class / customisation options. That opinion only lasts a short while when you realise there is no difficulty level and death happens all too easy, This is a game that will brutally punish you for making mistakes. The end result always being death. You simply cannot charge into an enemy swinging wildly and hope to survive. In dark souls every move you make can be a difference between life and death. Your enemies are varied and often require different tactics in order to be the victor. This is especially the case with the bosses.
Fortunately you are not always alone. Dark souls has a brilliant co-operative play system merged with the game. This means that after a few levels you sometimes get the opportunity to invite other players in the form of a phantom. This is a great asset when it comes to dealing with difficult bosses. As helping players are rewarded you will often find them volunteering at certain areas of the game. There is a twist however in that just as some players can be invited to help, there are those who may drop in uninvited. These are players who appear as  dark phantoms and the last thing on their mind is to help you.
The graphics in the game are superb, atmospheric and at times dark. Unlike traditional RPG's dark souls offers you little assistance in terms of guidance. There is no go to point B and fetch this before returning to A. You literally have to find your own way and work things out. The game world is made up with a set of areas or zones which fortunately can be fast travelled to once you discover their bonfires. Some of these areas will contain foes who at first will seem impossible to beat and you will find yourself seeking out other less difficult paths before returning when you have levelled up enough.
The game has only once type of currency and that is souls which you claim from dead enemies. You will need these to level up and upgrade / buy / repair equipment. One consequence of dying is that you will lose all the souls you have obtained upon respawning. During the early stages of the game they can be reclaimed by returning to the scene of your previous death. There are other penalites to dying but I won't spoil it by revealing them.
The lure of various co-operative play styles and different character classes will most likely see you play the game through numerous times and thats without the various DLC's that have been added since release.
A dark, challenging and unique RPG that punishes you hard but also rewards in so many ways.
