Immensely enjoyable sim/city builder game with a unique atmosphere and sense of humour. Its only significant weakness is the lack of more in-depth control over buildings and parametres, which can become a bit frustrating over time, as well as few missions that are genuinely challenging once you get a good hang of how the game works. This is the only thing stopping this game from becoming an addiction for hundreds of hours, but it's still incredibly fun, and since it's also easy to get into, it may be a great first choice if you've never played a game like this and want to give it a try.
GOOOOOOOOD EVENING TROPICOOOOOOO, I AM JUANITO- I mean, I am Lib and I bring you this glorious Presidente-approved review. In Tropico 3, you will learn how to build majestic sunlit cities, how to build an epic industry bringing you insane amounts of money while trying to stop the environmentalists from drowning you in broccoli, how to keep all the citizens and various groups on your island happy
, how to make the tiny insignificant countries called the US and USSR bend to your supreme might and give you money (called "foreign aid" for some reason but who cares about the name) and how to make tourists want to have Tropican flags over their beds. Oh, and how to not get assassinated or overthrown in a coup. And llamas.
So, what kind of presidente do you want to be? Do you want to build a socialdemocratic utopia where everyone is happy and fluffy unicorns walk around the streets? Of course you can, just make sure you build up a solid economy first. Or maybe you are a distant cousin of Satan and feel like the "arrange an accident" option should be the most fun in the game? You can do that as well, but you might want to make sure that your army likes you and the secret police is doing its job, or your iron fist rule may not last very long. And in either case, issuing edicts will help you along the way, with plenty of options ranging from social security to martial law.
But okay, this is getting dark, so JUANITO TIME, TROPICO NEWS TODAY. This game has a unique atmosphere unlike anything else
, with its heavily sarcastic (and yet pulled off with great taste) sense of humour and the constant combination of the "paradise island" setting with some fairly dark matters. The graphics are lovely (and I'm writing this in 2017), especially nature and the ocean, but the most interesting part of this game is... sound. I mean, it's a little bittersweet - it's totally unique, in the way the music is pretty much 24/7 Latin American party hard, and as a big bonus you get the already mentioned RADIO HOST JUANITO, TROPICO NEWS TODAY and whoever voiced that guy deserves a Nobel prize for voice acting (I don't care if there isn't one,
). Still... as fun as the music is, I feel it could use a bit more variety (I think there aren't even 10 songs altogether) and as much as Juanito's lines will probably crack you up, he has only
for every particular event. By the time you have 5 hours played, the "spiraling into debt" one will be burned into your mind.
But between all those things, comes my favourite thing about Tropico 3 - as simplified and "tongue in cheek" as it may be, it gives you a decent idea what ruling is like. There is
stuff to be done, nearly always someone unhappy (the results of which can vary from a small peaceful protest to an invasion) and always room for improvement. If you ever get a comfortable lead that lets you just sit back and relax, it's usually when you're near completing the mission anyway. As a result, this game does the "just 5 more minutes" syndrome probably better than anything I've ever played - you'll just want to complete that bunch of apartment blocks, oh wait the religious people are unhappy let's build a cathedral- OMGWTFBBQ REBELS I NEED AN ARMORY, okay that's done but the entertainment happiness is poor, let's build a cinema or something- ...♥♥♥♥ it's 5 AM. And the cool thing is that the game is generally very "newbie-friendly" and even though it all may sound very complex, it's quite easy to get the hang of.
However, this leads us also to my biggest issue with the game - once you're past that point and know the game well, you'll wish for some more in-depth manual control over various buildings to get things done even more efficiently... but there aren't really any - especially construction workers (though thankfully you can set building priority) and teamsters work in mysterious ways that I don't think even the greatest minds could explain, and farms having half the planet of fertile land around will sometimes pick the most nonsensical spot to plant crops. And in case of statistics and such, the almanac generally does its job very well, but could be a bit more intuitive and detailed, e.g. the various happiness levels - for instance, healthcare quality or liberty are relatively easy to understand, but I still have no clue what exactly affects environmental happiness, and there is no tab with all the "pluses" and "minuses" like with the happiness of each citizen group.
Speaking of which, that's one of the most fun and sometimes challenging parts - a big part of the game is balancing between the happiness of the various citizen groups, as of course they don't exactly all get along (such as capitalists and communists, for example...), as well as keeping good relations with the "superpowers" (US and USSR). The missions tend to expand that even further, as you'll encounter various events and your decisions will usually impact your relations with some of the groups or the foreign powers. The events are generally fun and cleverly designed, with the biggest plus being that your decisions usually
have an impact and further consequences, as you'll learn (you made a shady deal that seemed profitable? Well, someone found out about it). And the missions are generally quite fun and somewhat diverse (from "transform this boring island into a lovely tourist resort" to "screw everything, just get money in your Swiss bank acount"), although I really feel the later ones should be more challenging - only one leaves you with a limited choice of buildings at first forcing you to think out of the box, whereas for the rest you'll usually find out a reliable strategy at some point
and it may start to feel a little "rinse and repeat" over time.
There are two more minor issues with the game I need to mention though, just because of how... bizarre they are. The first one is that many workplaces require employees with a particular education and/or particularly men or women... and especially at the beginning when you have few citizens, the latter can be annoying. Now... it's not surprising priests need to be male or, um,
need to be female, but... only men can be doctors (the most consistently annoying one), only women can be high school teachers but only men can teach in colleges, only women can be journalists,
.
The second one... the cool thing in Tropico 3 is that you get to make your own "avatar" (i.e. your presidente persona) with a fairly nice variety of visual options, and you need to choose personal traits and flaws which have an effect on various factors in the game. Your avatar can be male or female, and being my troll self I of course picked female (I mean, is there something more boring than a male dictator, duh). And, well, in a little hilarious laziness on the developers' part, the traits are unchanged and all with descriptions written with a male character in mind... including the Womanizer flaw which remains completely unchanged. I mean, it's not impossible...
But did I enjoy those 40 hours? Of course I did.
And I miss Juanito already. ;_;

While Rome 2's now imfamous launch was attrocious, in its current state, the game is one of the best of the Total War series, and a shining example of a RTS.
1. Campaign: As always, Rome 2's campaign is a mix of turn based strategical management on the campaign map, and real time battles. For the most part, the AI does a good job managing their cities and armies. They don't make foolish mistakes, they defend their cities, and they attack any vulnerabilities left by the player. The UI is fine, but the lack of branching skill trees for generals can be annoying. The removal of family trees is another annoyance as you feel no attachment to your faction's characters. One place where Rome 2 shines, however, is its variety. There are dozens of faction to chose from, exact numbers based on DLC, all of which have interesting units, traits, and challenge levels.
2. Battles: Once again, we see the return of CA's battle AI. While it is not totally imcopetent, it consistently makes moronic mistakes. It will engage your pikemen head on, charge cavalry into the front of heavy infantry, and often attack with no real tact. However, the battles are still fun. Troops are easy to control and the battle UI is slick and customizable. Sure, when a cav unit inexplicably gets stuck on one lonely spearman it can♥♥♥♥♥♥you the hell off, but it never detracts from the overall expirience.
3. Multiplayer: Due to the variety of factions, Rome 2's multiplayer shines. Each faction is fun to play as and offers different stregnths and weaknesses. The added bonus of phasing out the battle AI is just the icing on the cake. However, technical issues still at times hinder the multiplayer, as you will often expirience severe lag and will occasionally be dropped from the game.
4. Graphics: As one of the best optimized PC games out there in its current state, Rome 2 has no issue delivering both stellar graphics (in-battles and on the campaign map) and smooth framerates.
5. DLC offerings: While the 'Wrath of Sparta' DLC fell short, and I still have yet to see the point of 'Blood and Gore,' Rome 2 still has some fine offerings for DLC. Some packs will add fun new factions, and others will offer new, full legnth historical camapign scenarios to be played out on customized maps. Without a doubt, 'Hannibal at the Gates' and Caesar in Gaul' stand out from the pack as superd additions to the game and engrosing windows into some of the most fascinating wars in antique history.
Without a doubt, Rome 2 stands out as one of the most extensive and deep offerings in the RTS genre. It is a stellar game and in its current condition, and it is the best Total War game to date.

I hated this game back when it was in beta and I was fully prepared to forget about it and wait for the Elder Scrolls 6. However I came back when the game went on sale and found the game has improved massively. It has one of the best pvp experiences of any MMO that I have played thus far.
The biggest question which most people want to know is, is this an Elder Scrolls game? Is it like Skyrim? The most common criticism is that ESO is not an Elder Scrolls game because it's not like Skyrim, this position rather bugs me considering that Skyrim is just one entry in the series and most people that hold this position haven't taken the time to experience other entries of the series which have major differences to Skyrim. In fact I would have agreed that ESO is not an Elder Scrolls game back when the game came out. On launch your character was restricted in a typical mmo fashion, Can't go to this zone until you reach this level, can't do this until you complete this, can't go here with X, can't do Y without Z. ESO used to be a typical on rails MMO experience until they overhauled the game, made everything scale to the player's level and opened up the game to allow the player to go wherever they want. This was one of the big features which made me come back to the game. Having an mmo where you can progress wherever and however you want is almost unheard of for an MMO. This is the freedom you'd expect from an Elder Scrolls  where you can pick a random spot on the map and explore. In fact unlike in most MMOs you DON'T need to quests to progress, in fact it's probably the only MMO that I'd recommend against questing which in my opinion is one of the most tedious, mind breakingly boring parts of mmos. You can level up at faster pace simply by exploring and doing the stuff you feel like doing instead of the stuff you're made to like a typical mmo.
Combat in ESO is a massive step up from the typical WoW clone formula. IE Tab target an enemy and press the number keys in a sequence over and over until the enemies are dead. In ESO you have to aim your weapon, block attacks and roll out of the way from incoming dangers. Unlike an MMO where you have about 150 abilities that you all bind to seperate keys and tap them one after another in a sequence, in this game you have 6 abilities which you combine with your weapon attacks to do damage to an enemy. You might for instance charge up a heavy attack and then throw a fireball right after for a massive burst of damage. Combat is not simply about doing your abilities in sequence but using the right abilility in right situation. You can hold two weapons with two sets of abilities for a total of 12, so switching between your weapons is an important part of combat. I would actually argue that the combat in ESO has more depth than any Elder Scrolls game to date. Even in Skyrim the combat boiled down to spamming the enemy with the same attack over and over until they died. In ESO you have to make much more tactical decisions while managing your stamina and magicka. None of the artificial difficulty of Skyrim, such as playing as a mage and getting one shotted by an iron arrow suddenly from 100 yards away because robes don't give any armour points.
On the topic of Combat ESO supports first person view and third person. However unlike in the main Elder Scrolls series where the game plays best in the first person view, this game pretty much requires you to play in third person as you need to be able to see everything around you at all times, especially in pvp. The fact that ESO is primarily a third person game will put many people off, but I personally enjoy the game in third person.
There ARE classes in this game. However unlike in a mmo where all your characters abilities come from your class and class skill trees, ESO has something quite different. In the game there are various skill lines. For example the two handed skil line, as you use your two handed weapon you will unlock new skills from that skill line. It's entirely possible to create a character build that doesn't use any class abilities at all, such as a vampire hunter build which is hilarious for trolling edgy werewolf and vampire characters in pvp. You essentially make a completely custom class from the various types of skills you can master. Your initial class choice is still important choice and you are locked into that class choice, also don't expect your warrior to be able to do massive damage with spells if you haven't specialized in magicka. The fact that you can encounter an enemy player with a completely custom array of abilities makes pvp encounters extremely interesting.
PVP is the biggest selling point of this game. Cyrodil isn't the peaceful woodland from Oblivion that you go around picking flowers in, there is a literal war going on there between players. Players fight for territory in Cyrodil by assaulting enemy resources such as farms and mines, but the main goal is to capture the enemy fortifications. Players fight for enemy keeps and outposts by assaulting them with siege weapons. Fights can break out between dozens and sometimes even hundreds of players at a single time. It's a truly epic moment when you see rows trebutchets and ballistas start destroying the enemies walls while masses of players clash together in a huge fight. It's brilliant chaos, particularly when you fire a flaming ballista into a group of 5 unsuspecting players and watch them panic. cyrodil isn't a simple 10 minute battleground but a massive zone dedicated to pvp. When one faction controls all of the keeps around the imperial city, the best player from that faction actually becomes the Emperor of Tamriel. When a player becomes emperor they essentially become Sauron in pvp. The emperor is like a world boss in cyrodil only a player in controlling them.
The best part about PVP and Cyrodil is that you can get massive amounts of xp from it as well as amazing gear as you level up. there are many guides out there that say you can't level up effictively in Cyrodil but this is completely false. You can get Xp from joining the large battles in Cyrodil and contributing, even as a low level. But there is also a place in Cyrodil dedicated to pve, the imperial city. The pve is a huge dungeon with many different zones, it is filled with monsters and bosses and there is also a sewer area ontop of the city. You can take on the Imperial city solo or join a group and go after the bosses too. Players from the enemy factions are also in this area looking for loot so pvp can break out at any moment you're in there. You can mug other players for their money (tel var stones) in this area so the stakes are high. Sometimes a group running a boss will unexpectedly run into another group and a massive fight will break out. You can pretty much level up exclusively in this area or in Cyrodil without having to do boring quests.
In conclusion. This game has an amazing pvp experience, the combat has much more depth and is far more satisfying than any typical MMO. However the skill floor for the game is somewhat high which may leave a casual Skyrim player overwhelmed. Questing in ESO is dull like pretty much any MMO (Although not nearly as dull as FFXIV), but the the game allows players to level up through exploration instead of tedious quests. This isn't a sequel to Skyrim but it is most definitely an Elder Scrolls game. Things such as stealing, murdering random people in towns and finding items in the enviroment are all in the game, but remember that this is an mmo with thousands of people playing at once so don't expect stuff like Radiant AI or a physics engine. Buy the game mainly for the pvp and social experience.

Hundreds of hours invested in this on the disc version purchased many moons ago. STALKER is a bleak, nightmareish vision brought to life even more so with the huge collection of community made mods available.
This was the first game in the trilogy of games the other two being Call of Pripyat and Clear Sky (a prequal). Both of which are also incredible, CoP more so.
When you leave the Cordon for the first time after speaking to Wolf, walking up that path towards the road, turning and seeing your brothers slowly disappear into the distance, hearing the wind howl around the barrel of your creaky old shotgun, suddenly hearing some sort of demonic cry far away to the east and a chill creeps down your back. The sun is low in the musty sky - but just up ahead there is an old abandoned mill to explore, just make use of the fading light.
For me this game creates an atmosphere I've never felt before (or since, other STALKER titles not including) of a world gone to hell - the Zone, a huge area of land around the defunct Chernobyl reactor, now infested with nightmareish creatures deformed by radiation, different collections of (human) mostly factions wanting to kill you on sight and rob your last tin of tuna. Secret underground labs where horrific experiments happened before everything went to hell. Deserted farm buildings where blood hungry things lurk in the dark. STALKER is all about tension and fear, but also survival.
There are mods you can get that improve just about every aspect of the original game, textures, weapons, music, audio, bugs ironed out, even previously unnavailble areas.
I love STALKER, it's tremendously satisfying to survive in the Zone, it's terrifying, compelling and full of detail (if you also read all of lore/diary entries that Marked One enters into your PDA throughout the game.
For anybody that likes FPS/open world survival shooters with strong RPG elements, for anybody that loves to become really immersed in their chosen universe, there is nothing quite like STALKER.
Just don't forget your anti rads, and take care of Nimble - he's worth it.

Just play this in combination with the "Complete Mode 1.4", you can find it by googling it on Modb. I never played STALKER when it was out, but the graphics tweaks, together with other pretty cool stuff, will do the trick and let you enjoy this pearl.

39 hours. That is like an eternity for me. And I loved every bit of it. The atmosphere is gorgeous. The story is quite all right, and the sense of increasing mystery as you progress is astounding.
Rather realistic (the more equipment you carry, the sooner you get tired, for instance) but not annoying. Many side-quests to explore the area, earn some money and upgrade your equipment, but never required to actually carry on with the story. (You will meet charismatic underdogs, the military, different and opposing paramilitary factions, bandits, dogs, and... other spooky stuff I will not go into.)
And you feel so FREE to explore, and play the game in the way and order that you wish (and kill or trust who you wish). That freedom is not as real as it feels, but that's exactly the point I guess.
If you like shooting bad guys in a rather realistic fashion, and if you like the mystery of Chernobyl, then this is a game you should absolutely buy.

Tropico 3 is two things: it's essentially an HD reskin of
except easier, and it's arguably a stripped down version of Tropico 4 that's more difficult.
The core game is still the same good Tropico experience, and there's two campaigns' worth of unique missions that are great fun. Ultimately though, Tropico 3 is probably more for series completionists, people who were turned off by the first game's age, and/or people who want to trade the more freeform experience of Tropico 4 and 5 for a challenge. The rest of this review is about how exactly Tropico 3 differs, and how it's more difficult for it.
Apart from the new buildings, edicts and other stuff in the
expansion (which is absolutely required if you're going to play this game), the inclusion of actual roads and cars, simplified construction, and new missions, it's a remake of the original from a time before remakes were cool. It introduces a couple of neat things like deficit spending up to $10,000, a tilt-shift effect when zoomed out and an isometric view.
Tropico 4 doesn't have those last two things for some reason, although it more than makes up for it since 4 really is kind of a Tropico 3.5. It runs on the same engine, the UI works pretty much the same, and it doesn't change up the gameplay much, but it simply has more content both in the base game and from its own expansion & DLCs.
It's more difficult than 4, since you don't have its convenience features or raft of DLC buildings to save you from tight spots. You must select two clearly defined character strengths and flaws for your Presidente, instead of 4's more even-keeled traits that usually ended up being good. Quick building doesn't exist, which forces you to plan ahead, and you can't do missions to patch up relations with factions, superpowers, or just to get yourself out of a tight spot. The missions are oriented more around long-term goals instead of more immediate objectives, which is a nice change of pace and allows for more leeway while also not handing you as many rewards simply for playing the mission.
On the flipside, the fact that construction workers no longer have to clear the foundations for new buildings and the mere existence of roads, cars and garages make the game easier than the first one. You still need to plan ahead with road and garage placement, and even then sometimes traffic will be bad, but honestly, even Tropico would have cars, wouldn't it? (The black humor is arguably more sharp than 4's humor as well, which relied a little more on references.)
Weirdly, if you own both the base game and the expansion pack, you can't even launch the base game without getting a prompt to play or install the expansion. You'd want to buy and use the expansion anyway if you ever play this, but it's still weird. It appears to overwrite the EXE of the base game while still appearing as a separate game in your library.
It's also weird how it actually runs
than Tropico 4. Even maxed out on my GTX 560, it stutters. Fortunately the game as a whole can still look good.
You also must make an account that is apparently separate from any existing Kalypso launcher accounts to access the online user challenges. I'm not sure if there's any life left in whatever 3 had for a community, but if you're stuck with this game for whatever reason, the user-made challenges are probably worth playing.
Tropico 3 definitely has a style of its own, a pretty good one that's worth pointing out in the face of otherwise little difference from 4's meat and bones, and something that might be worth experiencing for series fans. Some miscellaneous obervations about said style:
* The music is great, definitely more varied than Tropico 4 but not nearly as much as the original. It's mostly more upbeat than Tropico's, too.
* Unfortunately, the map generator is pretty generic: it usually makes flat discs as opposed to the more characterized islands of the first game. 4's map generation is better with this.
* It's interesting to note the difference between Presidente avatars in Tropico and Tropico 3. In Tropico, it stayed out of view because the player sitting at their computer was supposed to represent El Presidente. In 3, you can move your Presidente around on the map and micromanage them if you desire.
* There are immigrants from the USSR/USA that can come to Tropico in this version - I'm pretty sure you don't get American or Soviet immigrants in 4.
* 3's interface has a very pretty Cold War aesthetic, but is actually a little less ergonomic than 4's. I'll take 4's efficiency any day, but I'll always miss 3's look.
* The cover/banner art is the best in the series. Nothing quite matches El Presidente literally handling Tropico like his own little puppet.

One of the most immersive and atmospheric games I have ever played. Up there with the first Bioshock in terms of creepy atmosphere. This is especially a great game for any Alien/(s) fan, as it absolutely nails that look and feel.
As much as I liked this game, though, I did have a few complaints. The main one is that, while the alien AI is fantastic, the human AI was lackluster. Humans in general were implemented poorly into this game. They talk to each other as if they are complex, thoughtful human characters, but if you walk anywhere near them they turn into typical dumb FPS NPC characters that shoot on sight for no reason. It was almost jarring. But not *every* human is like that - some of them just run and hide, and killing them gives you a game over. So be sure to figure out which type of human character they are before killing any of them.
That aside, the gameplay in this game was great, especially when dealing with the alien. I don't feel there will be much replay value for me, but for the just over 20 hours it took me to complete this game, I got my money's worth. There are also some incredible visuals in this game. Especially towards the end, there was some stuff that I personally consider unparalleled in terms of sheer look and atmpsphere. This game looks insanely great and it runs really well even on medium gaming rigs.
I highly recommend this game to stealth fans, or people who liked Alien a lot.

The Dark Souls series has the reputation of being too hard for a normal hardcore game. This gem will kick you in the nutss and push you to the point of smashing the keyboard or throw your mouse (Yes, it does happen without you knowing it!).
But when you finally achieve victory over that♥♥♥♥♥♥of a boss or move past an impossible area, there is a great sense of accomplishment and a surging feeling of having the biggest balls in the planet. This is what makes these games VERY fun and addicting. You feel like you can conquer another map and kick another boss' ahsss.
Darksouls gameplay is extremely polished that every frames of animation - swinging a sword, rolling or casting magic, is very important. The hitboxes are so accurate that you have to master the distance of your swings, or the timing of your rolls, and if when to fire your projectiles. This is what separate this game from the usual hack and slash games out there. You need to be precise with your actions in order to succesfully defeat a monster or other players via pvp.
The world is very beautiful and well rendered, not a next gen graphics, but it runs perfectly smooth (teady 60fps) on my 3 years old gpu. The maps are detailed but it doesn't have that feeling that they are connected like on the previous Dark Souls. Maybe because you are allowed to fast travel at any lit bonfire and it makes backtracking less advisable.
The music and sound matches perfectly with the serene environment. The sword feels like a sword, the heavy gear you're wearing, feels like a heavy gear and casting magic, feels like you are casting magics. The voice acting is superb, it blends well with the lore of the game.
There's no doubt Dark Souls 2 is a great improvement on the previous one, but DS1 has its advantage over its predecessor too. I honestly feel DS2 a bit easy than DS1 (Maybe because I played DS1 before and it made me skilled enough). If you are looking for a hardcore hack and slash rpg game with a little pvp, then this game is for you. If you can't handle the challenge, I still recommend you to try and git gud at it;)
Graphics: 8 - Not a next gen graphics, but it runs perfectly smooth and no frame dropping that I know of. The animations are fluid and precise, and the world is rendered beautifully.
Gameplay: 9 - I gave it a much higher rating since the developers made sure to make the sword fights accurate and precise. The game is exceptionally hard for a new comer, but the feeling of accomplishment makes the gameplay enjoyable and addicting.
Music: The music is superb and blends well with the lore. The feeling of serenity and calm with a little touch of mystery and death around the corners. The sounds is excellent, it definitely makes it feel realistic when wielding weapons and armors.
Replay Value: 9 - Replayability in this game is a no brainer. Play the game and you'll know.
Overall Impression: 9 - DS2 is one of my favorite games in a long time. It's an improvement over DS1 and Demon Souls in gameplay and graphics, but it also misses some points it's predecessor has.

Don't get me wrong by this recommendation. I love Dark Souls 2 (and I think I'm one of the few that like it better than Dark Souls 1). But...
...If you are new to the Souls series, or don't yet own Dark Souls 2 for the PC, don't buy this game. Wait until Scholar of the First Sin comes out in 2015 (currently slated to be released in April). It is purported to be a vastly improved experience, with new enemies, NPCs, and quests - along with improved graphics. It will run in DX11, so make sure your computer will be able to handle it.
I DON'T like the fact that they will make the people who already own Dark Souls 2 re-purchase a game that is essentially an updated/patched version. It would be one thing if it were a DLC patch. But buying the entire game again and (most likely) losing all game progress? Not to mention the two games will be on differnt servers and thus unable to play with one another, thus splitting the already-limited community. What the hell, From Software? That's an incredibly unethical business practice if I've ever seen one. It makes EA, Ubisoft, and Activision look goddamned consumer-concious by comparison.
Sigh. Not sure if I'm actually going to buy the new game or not. I want the better version, but I don't want to support a blatant cash-grab that is clearly just aiming to milk our wallets. Purchase it, or don't. It's entirely up to you. I probably won't.

Wow, all I have to say is that this game is a blast to play. The presentation that it starts with is something we haven't seen since Unleashed, which is good. So, the gameplay for modern is similar to Generations and Colors, but it puts them together  with the best aspects of both. Classic is like Gens but with tighter control and a dropdash for smooth and fast gameplay (works well with Ghost Town, the first classic stage which has great level design) The avatar is a fun gameplay style utilizing the wispons for alternate routes and different ways of defeating enemies. Customizing your avatar is probably one of the best things about the game: getting parts and costumes for completing tasks is rewarding as it can be used to change your avatar throughout the game. The avatar control can be a little stiff at first, but over time you can get the hang of it, and with modern sonic it's very useful in the tag team stages. Overall, the story, gameplay, and music all make a great entry for what is to come in the Sonic franchise.
[P.S.- If anyone is having trouble with the performance of the game on pc shouldn't worry now as it is fixed]

THE quintessential survival crafting factory game.
Factorio will push your spatial management skills to their absolute limits as you start to formulate very complicated automated processes and how they string in with being able to incorporate additional inputs of resources and a continually progressing technology tree.

You know a game is amazing when you constantly think about it when you aren't playing it. Factorio is a very fun and addictive game. You mine for resources, using conveyer builts to then transport them to other areas where you will need them. Using inserters you can put them in boilders or other buildings to turn those resources into items. Using more conveyer belts you then transport those items elsewhere to be turned into something else.
As your factory grows you will produce more polution. This polution will make the native creatures angry and they will attack. You have a few different weapons, turrents and ammo types avaliable to help defend (or attack) the natives.
As you progress you will go from basic mining machines and boilers run by coal to better machines run on electricity. There are lots of things to research to help you progress through the game which allows you to choose which paths you want first. Do you want to get armored piecing rounds or risk being over powered by the natives and prioritize a different new technology.
As you expand and grow you will be able to use trains to transport everything longer distances faster. There are plenty of other fun things to play with which I won't mention so you have some nice suprises.
This game will feel confusing at first. Play the campaign missions which act like a tutorial and watch some youtube videos. Then jump into free play and you'll find you will pick everything up rather fast.
I highly recommend this great addictive game. For the price you will get a LOT of hours out of the game, which is still in early access and the developers have plans to add much more content. There are also plenty of mods to try out and being you can play single or multiplayer, you will put a lot of hours into this amazing game.

Reign of Kings, another Early Access survival game an individual may seem to think it is not worth the money and time.
As we all know, every survival game such as this is the same repetitive thing every time you play it.
But let me tell you, this game is unique. Its traits and characteristics such as its resource farming, looting, and combat system come from other survival games. Only using those certain traits even better and in a much more innovative way to capture the attention of fans of these types of games.
The combat system comes from Chivalry: Medieval Warfare, an amazing game which places you in a combat based, PVP map to fight other players. You have three different ways of swinging. You have the Overhead swing, the lunge, and the side swipe. And of course, the blocking, now this system takes a great amount of skill to master and understand, timing the correct blocks, the correct swing to damage and slay your opponent, etc. So, having all of that and placing that in an open world survival game is another way of thinking, but it's very interesting and extremely fun to use. It's personally one of my favorites in this game.
The resource collecting system comes from the indie game Rust, an open world survival where you are on a large island with radiation in some parts, allowing for radiated animals (ONCE ZOMBIES), etc. In Rust, you collect different types of metals such as sulfur, or stone, or iron. Also being able to collect wood, and different items from those radiated animals that you can kill. You then use those resources to put in a campfire, furnace, or whatever to give you new resources to create weapons to survive. Rust has guns, Reign of Kings has blades.
And of course, there are small things that may have been from other games related to this but the developers have added their own ideas in to this marvelous game. Such as the most anticipated and famous idea of the game... becoming the KING OF THE LAND! This feature adds the largest twist ever, players can by choice fight for the Ancient Throne allowing you to tax the land. The tax rate's max is 20%, and if you set it to that you are going to have some unhappy visitors if you know what I mean. After becoming the king, you are given the Ancient Sword and Crown symbolizing your royalty and giving you a powerful weapon.
Another feature is the guild feature, where you are able to create your own clan and invite friends, and make them family, etc. Whilst having a guild, you can place down a "Leather Crest" (Iron and steel are available) what the purposes of these crests are is what I will tell you. These crests claim a certain amount of land around where you put it, making sure only people from your guild can build in that certain area of land. The Leather Crest gives you the smallest amount of land, the iron crest, gives you the medium amount of land, and the steel gives you the largest amount of land. You can place down more than one crest, giving you more land, but you can only place down the amount of crests you have people in your guild.
This next part is what I like to call "The Prisoner/Slave System". This is a certain system that allows you to 'rope' a player and drag them around and either place them in a cage, pillory, guillotine, etc. You can upgrade your rope, and if you're being roped you can cut it by sharp stones if you conviently have any on you.
This is not even half of everything in the game that I just explained, but I am hoping I have interested you in buying this game. Trust me you will have an amazing experience  playing this game just like I have, and will continue. But for now, bye everyone :)

Around five years ago, Demon's Souls arrived in North America. That is when I started playing this series and have fond memories of the story, world setting, armor designs, and weapons. The entire package had me drawn in. The feeling of exploration and fantasy, victory and defeat, hanging out with the blacksmith when he fixes my sword, and meeting fellow explorers during difficult times. It was also one of the first games that crossed my fingertips where it could start all over in what was known as a new game mode.
Years have passed since then, and I almost wonder if my memories have faded. With no longer any access to a gaming console I thought the ability to play a Souls game would remain only a memory. Then I ran into Dark Souls 2, for PC. From a technical perspective the game runs fine. So far no crashes and the performance seems okay. Lost connection to the online component here and there, and the game is really made for a controller but this should not be a surprise given its roots.
As it stands however, this iteration of the game has not left any fond memories. The more I play it, the less I want to continue, not to mention revisit in another timeframe or as NG. The game deserves credit for getting me to take care of some items and chores long overdue on my todo list, as it was more appealing to do work then to play the game, oddly. This is not fun. And the thought of new game mode has me remembering that most of what I played was off, in a wrong kind of way. Not enjoyable at all, to put it simply. The line, whether it is believed to be a fine one or not, has been crossed in a big way.
Every step you take in this game has to be checked and then re-checked. You will learn to peek around every corner, and look down at every floor tile. You will learn to keep a stack of 999 arrows in your backpack when you reach the next writing on the floor that reads sniper spot/ranged attack. Then you will spend the next ten minutes chipping pixels of health off a few of the many enemies that exist in the next encounter. All of which can stunlock your character until you fall over. You will find archers/mages with homing arrows/spells placed all over the game world specifically to make melee based encounters massively frustrating. Often times these are in place in narrow areas with fall-to-your-death opportunites right at your side.
You will discover that you have a favorite weapon, and then a pile of non-favorites to use when yours breaks on the third enemy away from the bonfire. You will discover that you can be staggered very easily by enemies, and that you can take most of their health away while they do not stagger once. You will discover that enemies do not follow the same game world rules as you do. While your weapon bounces wildly off objects and walls, they can melee through objects and through entire corner sections of walls after you run around for cover. As a result, you'll learn that sipping estus flasks around corners is a massively bad idea. You will discover you have nearly no stamina, and that enemies appear to have unlimited stamina. You will find that no matter how far across the display your health bar reaches, two or three hits always seems to defeat you. The point has been made, I think.
These things I know by heart now, due to all the hours spent in this game world. For some reason, continuing on the hopeless journey to find fun. Maybe that was the entire point the game was trying to convey? What I remember to be fun in Demon's Souls does not exist here at all. Entire map sections are created specifically to be the most tedious and boring experiences I've spent in any game to date. You learn to solve every encounter based on 1s and 0s rather than by being immersed in the world and using strategy. My fault for not spending time reading reviews and instead being blinded by a previous experience. I'll try not to make the same mistake next time. Not recommended.

If you enjoyed Dark Souls...you're in for a bit of a dissapointment. Dark Souls 2 is not a bad game, but the world feels less interconnected and alive like the last one, and instead comes off as a bunch of random areas taped together. The deep, interesting and varied lore of the prior is gone, and though they attempt to replicate it, they ultimately fail to. The boss designs are generally poor, and except for one or two none of the bosses had designs I fell in love with. Some bosses are literal ripoffs of past bosses, and many abilities for pyromancy are straight ripped from Dark souls. Certain enemies and bosses will track you, making dodging feel significantly less fair than past games. The story is poor, and merely imitates Dark Souls story, without making the attempt to deepen and enhance it. If it sounds like I'm being overly harsh, its because I want you to go in with proper expectations and also because I want them to fix this stuff for the next game they make, which should not be Dark souls 3. There is stuff to like here-the graphics are much improved, PC performance is way better than the last game, and it runs at 60fps I believe, and it looks pretty good, though not really astheticlly as good as Dark Souls. It controls fine, and for the most part the game is pretty solid, but after beating it once, whenever I turn it back on, I can only play for a small amount of time before wanting to go back and play Dark Souls. I would still reccomend it, but not at full price. Its worth a playthrough, but just be aware that if you haven't played Dark Souls, its well worth the hassle to go play that instead.

Good game, however there are many things about this release that disappoint me coming from playing the original Dark Souls games.
First, the environment makes no sense. The level design is not consistent with other sections of the game. For example, you enter a large tower, go on an elevator that takes you to ascent, and arrive in an underground location consisting of lava beneath the areas your character can navigate through.
Some parts of the levels look incomplete, almost as if they were copy/paste'd there. Textures look downgraded and the lighting makes the game almost seem as it if were being played in grayscale.
NPCs are not interesting. Many of them are simply rehashes from the previous game that are reskinned, but none of them are memorable as other NPCs such as Seigmeyer and Solaire.
The graphics overall are downgraded from the E3 Demo and with the new Scholar of the First Sin version coming out, I recommend that you not buy this game and wait to see if FromSoft does anything to make the game as close to what was originally shown. Hell... Compare the screenshots from this page to gameplay footage on Youtube. Even the screenshots here look much better than the actual game running at max settings.
This game's difficulty is simply punishing and unfair whereas the original Dark Souls and Demon's Souls hit boxes were quite accurate. In the previous installments, you simply die from being reckless or doing something wrong. Whereas this game can kill you due to inaccurate hit boxes.
Multiplayer has been improved over the previous version, but the new Soul Memory mechanic adversely affects being able to play with other players after New Game Plus - it's almost impossible to join someone in coop or PVP.
The bosses are uninteresting and many of the battles are designed involving being ganked by a boss and its minions. Expect quite a bit of 2 vs 1 or even 5 vs 1 battles. In this game, you won't encounter boss battles that were as epic as fighting against Grey Wolf Sif, Artorias of the Abyss, Manus, and
O n' Smo. There is one boss in Dark Souls 2 that I consider to be interesting. However, that boss is only available in the DLC.
Wait until a "remastered" or "definitive" version is released with all the DLC rather than spend your hard-earned money on what I think is a stripped-down version of the game.

What became clear over time is that my fear wasn't of the Alien, or the environs containing him, but rather, the game itself had become the source of my fear. I was empty, as this game is rife with empty actions, scenes of blow torch cutting, scenes of lever pulling, scenes of console accessing, so many, many times over. I started to imagine Ripley in old age, with arthiritis in her fingers from hitting so many buttons during her time in Sevastopol Station. Her wrists twisted in agony from manipulating the cutting torches. A sadness came over me, I was sad for Ripley, what she endured, poor Ripley. I felt for her, I wasn't sure who to be mad at, the poorly constructed trope of the corporate bad guy, or the developers for their sadism. And in the end she cast herself into space, only to be discovered, and surely, only to find that a new nightmare awaits her. How unfair is that? So you've heard of Skyrim, right? You may have even played it, finished all DLC, modded the game until it was a mere shadow of it's former self and yet still wanted more. Well, get that out of your head, Elder Scrolls Online isn't Skyrim-Online or Skyrim-CoOp. Sadly. It IS a good MMO, though. (I'm covering base game as I've yet to touch DLC content or dungeons and pvp.)
Positive Aspects:
Great, massive lore covering every square inch of the world apparently.
Absurdly gigantic world.
Great combat.
Great talent/skill system.
Excellent quests.
Great voice acting.
Overall it's a very pretty game.
Negative Aspects:
Despite it being a rather attractive game, the actual animations for character models are pretty terrible and clunky.
No real auction-house, just guild merchant crap.
Player interaction is bare-minimal. (It's a MMO, that you play as if it were a single player game. Without mods. Argh.)
The GUI is fairly atrocious, even if it is nicely minimalistic.
Camera & mouse controls are a bit wonky because they had to design around sub-human console peasants.
The engine runs barely "ok" on great hardware.
It's not Skyrim Co-Op or Skyrim Online.
I loathe crafting and everything related to it.
All in all, I'd rather have had Skyrim-Online or another expansion or some such, regardless, this is a good game and I enjoy what I do here. The main storyline(s), quests, skill system and combat are exceptional. Yes, I consider it worth the price and will probably put several hundred hours+ into it before I get bored. (The world is LARGE.)
This is easily the most playable MMO released in the past well, decade and if you like the other E.S games you'll probably enjoy it.

I, personally, enjoyed the game most of the way through. Character customization, level details, story and voice acting are all suprisingly good.
But for the sake of getting a message across to Sonic team, I have to give this one a negative review. They just never learn their lesson, and can't let a good thing continue.
It seriously feels like they took one step forward, and three steps back on this one. The whole OC idea is actually really good, and the weapons and their movement abilities are the start of a really good idea, but one that is never fully fleshed out.
Controls were already really good in Unleashed, Colors, and Generations, but they somehow ♥♥♥♥ed it up here. Acceleration is way to high, and air control is stiff or slippery and uncontrollable depending on what speed you jump at.
Levels are linear and very automated, for the most part. Very poorly designed compared to the other titles.
If I was to rate this game compared to the other boost formula games, it would be; Generations > Colors > Daytime Unleashed > Forces.
It's not THAT bad, especially if you already enjoy the other games, but it's just baffling how Sonic Team can ♥♥♥♥ up something they already perfected.
TL:DR, worst of the boost games, but not THAT bad. Negative review because Sonic Team needs to learn from their mistakes and fire Iizuka.

A good survival-FPS I must say.Very much alike to the fallout series yet FPS becomes more dominant than RPG in this game.You can be a ninja and melee a group of super-mutants in fallout due to its rpg elements(perks,poweramor,etc),yet in STALKER you can only rely on your headshot skills and pray that the little bandit you are fighting won't throw a god-damn grenade right below your belt without even seeing where you are(And they hit the spot every time!).Current working on it and hope to beat it soon so I can get my hands on its sequel I've just bought.
Anyway here are some pros and cons to summarize:
Pros:
1.Realistic pack-limit.When you play an open-world rpg,I bet most of you have developed a habit of looting every foe you kill and take everything so you can sell to a merchant to make money.Yet in this game you will find out soon enough that you can only carry so LITTLE.Normally I carry a rifle,one elite rifle just in case and a side arm pistol,some ammo,and a few bandages,medkits,anti-rads,and some everyday stuff.And THAT's ALL YOU CAN CARRY,if you loot and take everything from your enemy's corpse you won't get tired really fast(exceeding your pack limit) or even become completely immobilized(10 kg above your pack limit).
2. Fantastic night sight and weather system.(Probably have some thing to do with the STALKER COMPLETE 2009 MOD)
When the sun sets.It'be better if you crawled into your sleeping bag and actually sleep like in real life.If you dare to venture out at night you will find it hard to survive as you will either:A.Turn on the flash light and become a easy target and die quickly.B Turn off the flash and you can's see♥♥♥♥♥♥And also he weather system will change your sensibility and the sensibility of your enemies.During a rainy night the sounds will cover your footsteps for a sneak-in slit throat and you may be able to detect your enemy via the moonlight on a clear night.
3.Atmosphere and sound effects are captivating.You can sometimes here the howl of a monster or some distant gunshots in a vast plain,as where as strange the cry of babies when you ventured in some underground tunnels.They really creates a horrifying atmosphere as if you are really in a apocalypse.And when you finally make it to a camp and take a deep breath,you will find it extremely comforting to see one of the fellow stalkers take out a guitar and slowly plays some gentle Russian folk tunes.
Cons:
1.Just like fallout ,the survival element aren't emphasized enough.The game time elapse the same speed in real world so you won't get hungry normally in one gameplay experience (say 2hours).You can manually speed up the time though and you will find soon enough when it gets dark and you can't see anything and regret changing that!(Sight at night is a pro BTW).
2.Weapons feels really strange to handle.It feels like neither the normal FPS type(COD,Metro,Farcry,etc) nor the shooting simulator type(ARMA,Red Orchestra,etc).It just feels so strange,can't really tell what's wrong.
3.No quick-save option.Even if you can do it via the COMPLETE MOD,you will generate a save file every time you quick save and I JUST DELETE 1GB of saves after about 5 hours of gameplay. And there's no quick travel mechanics as well.(The Mod add a teleport option and that literally means TELEPORT(1000 miles in 0 seconds and you can teleport to somewhere you haven't even been to)
To conclude,as a fallout and survival game fan I STRONGLY RECOMMEND THIS GAME

The greatest game to ever exist.
Homeworld 1, albeit different from the original 1999 Homeworld, combines the bug-fixes and graphics of modern-day gaming with the gameplay of then. The story, although this is a RTS game, interjects at the most appropriate times so that gameplay doesn't throttle you. Out of every game, movie, and book that I have witnessed, the Homeworld story is one of the few that have actually managed to make me sob.
The gameplay makes it all the more better. In the campaign, you start off with almost nothing, and with gradually implemented research and resource development, you get newer and better ships, especially at the most appropriate of times. And let's not forget almost every Homeworld player's favourite ship: the Salvage Corvette. Nothing is more satisfying than breaking standard limits of the game by stealing all of the enemy Capital Ships. And when the missions are all said and done, there is multiplayer to keep one satisfied.
And don't get me started on the wonderful, smooth ambiance of the music and scenery.
All in all, a 100% S-Rank game. Would honestly beg people to play, if it werent socially unacceptable.

Slight bias: I grew up with Homeworld Classic
I generally recommend this. The new graphics are beautiful, and the gameplay for HW2 is great in the remaster. The HW1 remaster, however, is clunky to the point of unplayability.
HW1 should never have been ported into the HW2 engine, it's fundamentally a different game, with different mechanics. The attempt to overhaul them has fallen short of the mark, by a long shot. To me, it feels as though I have to fight the game to get fleets to behave as expected.
However, HW1c plays as smoothly and beautifully as I remember, and is still worth playing from a strategy perspective.
HW2r is more beautiful, more smooth, and all-round better than its classic counterpart. HW2r is the game as if it were made today.
Overall, I think in order to properly remaster HW1, it should simply be re-built with better graphics in mind, the movement and combat code can likely be copied and pasted direct from source. The HW2 remaster is, without a doubt, better in every way than the original.
TL;DR: Play Homeworld Classic and Homeworld 2 Remastered.

Good game, however there are many things about this release that disappoint me coming from playing the original Dark Souls games.
First, the environment makes no sense. The level design is not consistent with other sections of the game. For example, you enter a large tower, go on an elevator that takes you to ascent, and arrive in an underground location consisting of lava beneath the areas your character can navigate through.
Some parts of the levels look incomplete, almost as if they were copy/paste'd there. Textures look downgraded and the lighting makes the game almost seem as it if were being played in grayscale.
NPCs are not interesting. Many of them are simply rehashes from the previous game that are reskinned, but none of them are memorable as other NPCs such as Seigmeyer and Solaire.
The graphics overall are downgraded from the E3 Demo and with the new Scholar of the First Sin version coming out, I recommend that you not buy this game and wait to see if FromSoft does anything to make the game as close to what was originally shown. Hell... Compare the screenshots from this page to gameplay footage on Youtube. Even the screenshots here look much better than the actual game running at max settings.
This game's difficulty is simply punishing and unfair whereas the original Dark Souls and Demon's Souls hit boxes were quite accurate. In the previous installments, you simply die from being reckless or doing something wrong. Whereas this game can kill you due to inaccurate hit boxes.
Multiplayer has been improved over the previous version, but the new Soul Memory mechanic adversely affects being able to play with other players after New Game Plus - it's almost impossible to join someone in coop or PVP.
The bosses are uninteresting and many of the battles are designed involving being ganked by a boss and its minions. Expect quite a bit of 2 vs 1 or even 5 vs 1 battles. In this game, you won't encounter boss battles that were as epic as fighting against Grey Wolf Sif, Artorias of the Abyss, Manus, and
O n' Smo. There is one boss in Dark Souls 2 that I consider to be interesting. However, that boss is only available in the DLC.
Wait until a "remastered" or "definitive" version is released with all the DLC rather than spend your hard-earned money on what I think is a stripped-down version of the game.

After an extremely controverisal release, I can honestly say that the final patched version of Rome II is a very good game. The huge faction diversity allows for complex gameplay, with improved combat AI. Siege AI is still problematic but mounted wall artillery makes siege battle a much different experience that previous TW's.
The complex economy system introduced in Shogun 2 continues but with the introduction of provinces indiviudal cities can get complementary bonuses based on specialization. This is a interesting addition. Fleets can now be set to patrol mode, so the constant raiding and pillaging of coastal towns can finally be stopped (whereas before the turn-based game garunteed that fleets could sneak around and wreck havoc).
Game combat is complex compared to some other TW titles due to the unit variety. Excellent past games (Shogun 2, Napoleon) lacked this amount of unit variety and mastering one faction meant mastering all of the others (more or less). This isn't true for Rome II: factions vary in the usefulness of cavalry, infantry, and ranged units, meaning that factions can require many different playing styles.
The agent system introduced in Shogun 2 continues under a different format. Differentiating between the different skills sets can sometimes be annoying, and upgrading agents and generals sometimes seems like a chore. Agents are essential to gameplay and neglecting their use won't go over very well.
Graphics look great but sometimes when advisors or units open their mouths to speak things look a little weird. Doesn't really bother me all that much but some people are still up in arms about it.
People still have valid complains about this game, but I think if the game was realeased as it is now it would've gone over swimmingly. Depending on the faction and campaign difficulty, the game can remain challenging even to regular players of the game franchaise. I would reccomend this game.

No more room in hell is a game about surviving the zombie apocalypse, but before you all sigh from boredom as you contemplate the ever growing mountain of zombie games cluttering up your steam library, let me finish. This is one of the only zombie games in which you play as a fat guy fending off the undead. At laest that's the only reason that i can come up with as to why your character's movement speed is so appallingly slow. It also makes more attempts at realism by giving you a limited inventory with smaller and bigger items taking up a certain amount of space. In attition, there is quite a detailed level of item tweeking you can do. So you've heard of Skyrim, right? You may have even played it, finished all DLC, modded the game until it was a mere shadow of it's former self and yet still wanted more. Positive Aspects:
Great, massive lore covering every square inch of the world apparently.
Absurdly gigantic world.
Great combat.
Great talent/skill system.
Excellent quests.
Great voice acting.
Overall it's a very pretty game.
Negative Aspects:
Despite it being a rather attractive game, the actual animations for character models are pretty terrible and clunky.
No real auction-house, just guild merchant crap.
Player interaction is bare-minimal. (It's a MMO, that you play as if it were a single player game. Without mods. Argh.)
The GUI is fairly atrocious, even if it is nicely minimalistic.
Camera & mouse controls are a bit wonky because they had to design around sub-human console peasants.
The engine runs barely "ok" on great hardware.
It's not Skyrim Co-Op or Skyrim Online.
I loathe crafting and everything related to it.
All in all, I'd rather have had Skyrim-Online or another expansion or some such, regardless, this is a good game and I enjoy what I do here. The main storyline(s), quests, skill system and combat are exceptional. Yes, I consider it worth the price and will probably put several hundred hours+ into it before I get bored. Played this during the NA betas.
++Very pretty aesthetic.
++Sound track is 10/10
+Class system is nice. Lots of variety,
+Can be played with keyboard, mouse, gamepad, or any combination of those
+Runs on anything with a good CPU. Barely needs GPU due to the low-poly, low res, but very effective graphic style.
+Lore and theme based on Lithuanian mythology. A nice change of pace from the usual nordic gods or all encompassing black evil corruption mist tentacles from the abyss tripe. Klaipedia is just a city in Lithuania. (THE MORE YOU KNOW)
=Everybody can craft so long as they have the recipe and the materials. Considering the game's unusual number of support classes I feel this was a wasted opportunity.
-Godawful quests. Perhaps the worst I have ever seen. Kill ten bears to acquire bear asses, turn in to bear♥♥♥♥♥monger. Repeat. Completely linear straight to level 180, which was as far as I got.
-Said quest content is also completely soloable if you have two brain cells to rub together and didn't choose a support class.
-Zones built around said awful quests. Also completely linear. Each area is a collection of islands and bridges or narrow corridors. World design is horrid, once your level has outgrown a zone you will never return. This will ultimately result in the early zones becoming completely abandoned as the game ages. No sight of a proper dungeon after 180 levels. Everything is a questing zone.
-Monsters spawn in the exact same locations. This will cause botting problems.
-Group questing is a cluster♥♥♥♥ because all the quests are single-player centric. Also, any time somone encounters their quest boss, which is visible only to them and their party, it teleports your entire party to you. This is really annoyign if for some reason you wanted to split up. Heaven forbid players just coordinate on their own.
--Restricted player trading. Every time equipment is traded its enhancement potential diminishes. Consumables and ingredients can be traded exactly once. This is supposed to stop commodities trading in the marketplace.
--------XP PENALTIES FOR KILLING THINGS ABOVE YOUR LEVEL. Say you are level 50. A level 50 mob gives you 100XP. A level 1 mob give you 1XP. A level 40 mob gives you 80XP. A level 60 mob gives you 80 XP, and a level 70 mob gives you 5XP. Make sense yet? This is supposedly to stop power leveling. What it really means is that you and your entire party are perfectly synced while leveling or someone is going to be wasting their time grinding with you. This is also a method developers use when they are too lazy to make a proper XP table for all their monsters and coordinate it with the quest/level progression. Why do all that work when you can write an equation?

Homemade Tortilla (for 8 servings)
Prep : 30 mins
Cook : 25 mins
Ingredients :
- 1 3/4 cups all-purpose flour
- 3/4 teaspoon salt
- 1/4 teaspoon baking powder
- 1/4 cup vegetable shortening
- 1/2 cup hot water
Directions :
1. Whisk flour, salt, and baking powder together in a large bowl. Add vegetable shortening and work into flour mixture using a pastry cutter until it resembles coarse crumbs.
2. Form a well in the middle of flour mixture and mix in hot water. Work flour and water mixture together with a fork and transfer to a cutting board.
3. Knead until a smooth, soft dough is formed, about 3 minutes. Add more flour if dough is too sticky.
4. Place more flour on cutting board, cover dough with bowl, and let rest for 15 minutes.
5. Cut ball of dough into eight equal parts and cover until needed.
6. Roll out balls of dough either by hand or with a tortilla press.
7. Heat a large skillet over medium-high heat. Place flattened tortilla in skillet and cook until it begins to bubble, about 1 minute. Flip tortilla over and cook for an additional minute. Flip again and cook for 1 more minute. Repeat with remaining dough.Homemade Tortilla (for 8 servings)

I wrote up a review a few hours after I played & finished the game for the first time, but now I'd like to write one now that I'm very close to 100%ing the game.
The story in this game is weak overall, atleast in my opinion. There ARE some good moments in here, but overall the plot of this game feels weak and rushed.
Sonic starts off in Green Hill Zone, which is now flooded with sand (it's never explained why), after rushing through the stage and making his way to the city, Sonic destroys a group of badniks attacking Tails & some miscellaneous citizens. This is when Eggman reveals his new super squad of badguys, the head of which is the new character Infinite. The group of villains proceed to beat the ever-loving crap out of Sonic, who succumbs to his injuries, faints, and is taken away by Eggman and his group.
This intro is perfectly fine, it sets up the plot very quickly and we meet the new 'big bad' for the first time. What isn't fine however is how the game suddenly skips months of time (via text, and it does this A LOT) and throws us into a random Resistance HQ full of past Sonic characters: Amy, Knuckles, Silver (no Blaze for some reason?) Vector, Espio, Charmy and their newest recruit, you!
My problem with this transition is that we get 0 time to see the turmoil the group has to face after losing Sonic. Knuckles says that Tails has apparantly 'lost it', but in the next cutscene we see Tails in he seems perfectly fine and happy. This is the first of many plot elements that are rushed, and ultimately the entire intro falls flat because of it.
I won't bother typing out the entire game, but I do want to touch on what is supposedly a major plot element: 'Null Space'. Null Space is a dimension that Infinite can create by using the power of the Phantom Ruby,  and is quickly forgotten about until the final boss because once Infinite sends you to Null Space, your OC and Sonic team up to do a double boost (which they've done a few times before this) and manage to escape Null Space in the span of 15 seconds. SEGA/Sonic Team really wanted to push this as the turning point of the game, where Sonic and his 'Forces' begin their push back against the Eggman empire and Infinite. But it falls flat, because if Sonic and co can just team up, boost out and be fine and dandy in 15 seconds then Infinite really has no power over anyone. This is a major issue, because they try to set up Infinite as some all-powerful bad guy, but everything he throws at Sonic & co is quickly defeated in a matter of seconds.

Sonic Forces is a Generations styled game; you have Modern Sonic, Classic Sonic & the OC (Your character, who I'll just refer to as OC from now on.).
Modern Sonic plays just like he did in Generations / Unleashed, except for some reason they decided to remove his drift ability (which makes some tight turns incredibly difficult to pull off in your first attempts at this game) and they also removed his Light Dash which he has had since Sonic Adventure 1 & 2. The light dash was probably removed in favor of the Lightning Wispon, which I'll cover later.
Classic Sonic plays pretty similarly to Generations, except now he has the added drop-dash mechanic from Sonic Mania. I'm not going to lie, Classic Sonic in this game is really janky; he has no momentum whatsoever. For example, in Chemical Plant Classic, you run down the hill at the beginning of the level and instead of gaining speed, you somehow LOSE speed and then can't make your way up the small ramp at the end of the hill. On-foot, Classic Sonic is at his worst, the only way you'll gain any speed is by spamming the drop dash/spin dash at all times.
The OC plays similarly to Modern Sonic, except with the new addition of 'Wispons'. Wispons are new weapons created by the Resistance to take on the power of a chosen Wisp. Each Wisp gets one (and ONLY one) wisp power-up depending on the type of Wispon you choose. For example, the Lightning Wispon gains the power-up of Sonic's light-dash. As a concept these Wispons aren't so bad; they create a decent level of diversity and different ways to clear each OC level. My problem with them is that in turn, the Wispons have dumbed down Modern Sonic's gameplay to running, jumping and sliding, which makes his gameplay a lot less fluid.
My MAIN problem with every single gameplay type in this game is aerial control. Once you jump, you are going exactly where you aimed with little-to-no means of adjusting your position whilst mid-air. This is especially frustrating during the OC levels in 2D sections, since you only have one jump. (Modern Sonic has a small double-jump, which isn't too helpful but atleast gets the job done, sometimes. And Classic Sonic probably controls the best in the air out of all three, but is still pretty stiff.).
I have to hand it to Sonic Team, this truly is a next generation Sonic game. The character models are crisp and well-textured, the stages look gorgeous (even if the level design is sub-par) and the lighting and shading in this game is beautiful.
Some of the animations do look a little strange/stiff, like when you're jumping around using your weapon as the OC, but overall this game looks incredible.
I think my only issues with the presentation are the colours used for Classic Sonic. His shoes are a weirdly-dark shade of red, whilst the rest of his body is bright and highly contrasted, especially his skin which looks more yellow than the peachy-brown we're used to.
Modern Sonic: Wonderfully up-beat instrumental tracks, most of which are incredibly memorable. Especially Lost Valley and Egg Gate.
Classic Sonic: Interestingly, they decided to go with what sounds like a Genesis soundfont for Classic's music. Sometimes it works, sometimes it sounds horrible. Ghost Town is probably my favorite track out of all, with Classic Green Hill being my least favorite. (Go listen to it, it sounds like something out of Sonic 4).
OC: The OC has a mediocre set of songs overall, atleast in my opinion. The OC songs are hit or miss, with no real inbetween. They brought back tracks with lyrics in them just like in Adventure 1 & 2, and this really works to the games' advantage with overall immersion in levels when the lyrics mix well with the instrumental. Aqua Road is my favorite OC song (and favorite song in this game overall), it really gives me Adventure 2 vibes, it's like if they gave White Jungle/Green Forest lyrics. I
say that if you're not a fan of electronica/light-dubstep then you probably won't like what the OC has to offer in terms of music.
Main Theme: Fist Bump is an incredible main theme, on par with the likes of Open Your Heart and Reach for the Stars. Live and Learn still remains my favorite main theme of any Sonic game, though.
Overall, I'd say that Sonic Forces just about beats average for a Sonic game, it's certainly not comparable with the likes of 06, but it also isn't good enough to be on the level of Generations/Adventure/Colours. I think it sits perfectly in the middle with Sonic Unleashed (if you include the night stages too.).
Story wise, this game is incredibly weak. The plot moves too quickly, nothing is explored further than a couple of text boxes and the big bad Infinite just falls flat on his face in terms of motives and the things he does within the story. It starts off decently but then slowly meanders the rest of the way through.
Gameplay wise, the game is a mixed bag. I REALLY wish they'd have just focused on OC & Modern Sonic, and left Classic out alltogether, they really didn't need to shoehorn him in.
My score for this game is a 6.5/10. Just above average, but it doesn't do enough
to justify a higher score.

________________________________________________________________________________

You won't notice until new game plus 3 or something like that and if you know earlier it won't bother you and you'll just adapt, but it really gets annoying when you're doing a no bonfire run.
Overall this game is worth the money. The story is good, the graphics are great, and there is a lot of content that will leave you in the world of DS2 for at least a couple of months. Negatives are that durabilility bug, and sometimes some connection problems in critical moments when you need to summon a player to help you.

The one word I would use to describe this game is "mindblowing!"
This game is simply amazing, It is far and away one of the most thrilling experiences I have ever had. Being a life long fan of Alien, the thrill was even better.
Things I loved about it:
The environment is astonishing! The quality of the graphics is as good as it gets, on top of being optimized very well. Sometimes it feels so real you could swear you can reach out and touch the wall. There are some tweaks you can use to improve them just a bit more too.
The sounds build an environment of their own. The ambiance is perfect, just enough silence and just enough creepy sounds in the distance (often giving clues if you pay attention). Much of the time you must rely on sound to know where threats are. Headphones or surround sound will increase your experience with this game A LOT!
The music is great too, all right from the movie and put together so that it changes very smoothly, not always just as a direct indication of whats happening around you. Sometimes it picks up when you cannot be sure if there is something nearby, or it will remain quiet when the alien is near. No jarring music changes, it is very organic sounding.
Great characters and voice acting, sometimes the lip syncing is a little off, but all in all about as good as you would expect of a game. I instantly liked the main character, and had different feelings about everyone I met. They are varied and all have something about them that makes them stand out.
The AI is pretty good (I played the game on hard) The only real complaint I had about it was fixed with a simple mod. The Alien by default was "leashed" to you, meaning it was always nearby, and would almost always return from the direction he left. The mod I got removes this leash, meaning the Alien can wander more freely surprising you from any direction and hunting more based on its senses rather than a magic leash that keeps it by you. Even without the mod the Alien does not simply patrol the same way at any time, so there is always just enough risk when trying to move around of the Alien happening in your direction. Also worth noting with the AI is it learns from you, if you blast it with the flame thrower too much it will start to just stand there and watch you, waiting to see if you will keep doing it getting more bold. If you hide a lot it will stay very near the last place it heard you, if you move fast, it will start to drop into rooms at random hoping to surprise you (sometimes it succeeds O_O) just some examples.
The crafting system is decent, nothing special really but adds a little depth. The items you can make are all useful too, some are better for some threats than others, but they can reward creativity.
The level design is really good, with VERY thoughtful placement of objects in the world for hiding. Some crafting items and ammo seemed to spawn randomly in containers and just out in the world (when I reloaded a game, items I had looted since the last save would be different). Some items seemed to always been the same ie. find a new gun and some ammo for it would often be nearby to give you a good start in using it. You sometimes visited areas more than once or backtracked, not too often, but just enough to remind you that you are on a space station and that your parth is not just from A to B, but rather to navigate one big environment.
And of course, the story. As a whole it had just enough to keep it interesting even if it was sometimes very predictible if you knew Alien very well. The predictible points aside, it was well put together, quite long and interesting, and I often felt invested in it. It made me, sad, angry, happy and of course scared among other things. It would play very well for a person who knows nothing about Alien too, it has a great deal of story to put together.
At the writing of this review (37 hours played) I have not encountered a single bug, just a few physics glitches.
Things that could be better:
The only 1 thing that really annoyed me about the game was at the beginning, there is an item which you could want very badly. Even if you manage to subdue a person with said item, and saw it laying right on the floor you could not pick it up!! It forced you to find this item by storyline. You get it very quickly so its not the worst thing ever, just annoying and frankly immersion breaking.
Another possible gripe is how you are led around sometimes feels a *little* too forced. Making me think "oh yes I must have to go this way" just based on how things were put together. This might just be because I have played a ton of games and might not really be noticable to other people.
Occasionally the physics got a little whacky and made bodies fall into the floor, or my flamethrower would seem to rattle a lot until I pulled it out, enemies didnt take notice to these things though.
On occasion the anti aliasing leaves more jaggy edges than it should.
I definately recommend this game, its a good solid stealth game set in a world with a rich story and the best in art design.
