Homeworld 1 (not reviewing 2, since I haven't finished it) is a mixed bag, but the pure joy I had when I was young(er) when I first played it makes it impossible for me not to recommend it unless you really hate real-time strategy games.  Even then, I'd still argue it's worth the experience even if you can't stand micromanagement, hot keys, and the stuff that makes a RTS a RTS.
The fact is it's not always going to be pretty for the novice.  Battle plans tend to fall apart into chaos if you're not keen on grouping or micromanagement.  You certainly cannot take certain ships or your orders or lackthereof for granted in Homeworld!   With a bit of practice, you will coordinate an attack (or defense) with a bit of finesse, and you will fill the void with an array of colorful explosions.  Nothing quit as satisfying as taking apart a heavy battle cruiser and harvesting its left-overs.  (Harvesting resources in this game is probably one of my favorite features - it's just so cool to watch the ships go about their business!  Homeworld: Space Miner!?)  The first play-through (especially without a guide) might get downright ugly, but Homeworld is overflowing with charm and the passion of its developers both past and present.  It's a beautiful game, to say the least.  (If you have a nice 4K monitor, I believe you might need to wear protective eye gear.  It looks good on my little ol' LCD.  It's hard to not be impressed with the work they put into the textures and fx.  This game wasn't ugly by any stretch of the imagination, but to have a game from 99' look competitive?  Nice work.)
It's a tootin' shame there's no replay function - that I'm aware of - built into the game?  (Maybe multiplayer has it?   Zooming in on the individual ships and formations is where it's at!) It's one of those games, like most RTS, where you're tasked to do a lot of stuff at once.  Positioning in a three-dimensional space in the void of space is awkward, and the grouping and fleet formation design is better/more polished than the original.  But, IMHO, it's still a bit confusing and difficult in the heat of battle.  I know what I want to do with my ships and how I want my strategy and attack to develop, but excuting it with a keyboard and mouse is what it is.  I would say it's part of the inherent challenge in all popular RTS, so it's hard to fault the game for asking you to anticipate and plan a few moves ahead.  Know thy hotkeys.  Some are better at this keyboard magic/micro than others.  I find keeping the ships moving helps as it's surprisingly easy to lose a ship or forget to designate the proper orders.  (I can't tell you how many of my salvage corvettes (boarding ships, basically) took a leave of absence during a mission.  C'mon, seriously guys?  Get to work!)  I also found myself frustrated during a couple of the more difficult missions, but thankful for the challenge.
I think the biggest key to this game -  at least my enjoyment - was the story, music and sound direction. (I believe they actually brought back some of the original voice actors for the re-master.) This game just reeks of a space opera waiting to be made again and again.  Is there every a shortage of sci-fi?  I hope not!
Hope you enjoy it as much as I did when I was a kid.
As a side note:  If you make a mistake with your resources or the type of strategy you employ it will mean starting over or replaying an older save game.  Worst case?  Strategy guides are plentiful.  (Luckily, it's not a horribly long campaign, so not a big deal if you decide to go in blind and DIY.)  So, be prepared, and always save, save, save!

Review Change: 11/24/2017
The previous version of this review, written the day after release, described a horrid amount of crashes that would often happen during gameplay and cutscenes. I'm happy to say that these crashes are no longer an issue, thanks to an update released very recently; and thusly I've decided to update this review.
Sonic Forces is a good, though flawed game. Portions of some early levels can be beaten without even holding the controller, although thankfully such segments are very, very few and far between; and are no longer present by the time you're even a third of the way through. Most of the time, the gameplay is very fun and fluid; although Classic Sonic levels are somewhat annoying due to bad momentum- make sure to spindash a lot, otherwise you'll constantly be just barely falling short of a ramp that you totally should have made.
The length of the game has reached meme status by this point- 3 hours. Needless to say, not very long. However, the bulk of the enjoyment for this game comes from attempting 100% completion- this easily added an extra 30 hours onto my end gameplay time. If you're going for completion, then Sonic Forces is definitely worth the current price tag.
The character creator, something I was incredibly skeptical about, turned out to be one of the few areas the game truly shines. While body and facial options certainly could have been more varied, the many pieces of apparel you unlock throughout the game provide more than enough variety for your custom characters. If there is DLC planned to expand upon this feature of Sonic Forces, then I'll more than happily recommend it.
In short: Sonic Forces is a comparatively decent entry into the modern Sonic the Hedgehog library. Much better than Lost World, I'd even say about as good as Generations.  If you're just playing for the main storyline, you won't be kept long, you'll most likely even be a little disappointed. However, if you're playing for completion's sake, I can guarantee you'll be held for a while; certainly long enough to get your money's worth.

Once you get past (or, in other works, vote kick) the occasional troll, it really is an enjoyable experience.
I give it a solid 9/10.

Not a bad game by any stretch but definitly a step-down from Total War : Shogun 2 and the Fall of the Samurai. There is a huge map with large number of opponents but it all feels more oppressive than grand. If you're willing to put a hundred or so hours into the game it will most probably be rewarding but as there is no short-campaign option, more time-challenged gamers will find this too slow paced. The need for large investments of time in each game you play means that it can be almost impossible to see why one faction differs from another (apart from starting position) as the bonuses don't add up to large gains very quickly.The unit cards used as displays for what is in your army don't differ enough and the user interface is unusually cluttered without actually revealing any more information than the previous games in the series did. All in all it means the user will have to have a very long look at the game's encyclopedia before any action takes place.
The parent company, Creative Assembly, have continued to release patches for this game but have also continued charging a high price ($80 AUSD base game + $7 AUSD for factions/unit packs +  $14+AUSD for campaigns) coupled with core-game features needlessly hidden behind DLC (Blood and Gore, All the faction packs for the grand campaign). Imperetor Augustus campaign is a good free DLC and there should have been more for free up to the point of writing this.
Overall 2.5/5 - The tighter combat and map design in Shogun 2 was more to my liking. I live in a place in Australia were online play is unstable so I can't comment on this game's multiplayer.

Engrossing. Engaging. Atmospheric. Terrifying.
These are just some of the words to describe this fantastic game. If you are a fan of the Alien films you owe it to yourself to play......no, EXPERIENCE this game. That's right, you don't just merely play this game, you experience it. Right from the onset, you can feel the love and dedication that was put into this game by the people at Creative Assembly. They are huge fans of the Alien franchise, and it shows. As I played through it, there were times I actually teared up a bit because this is the Alien game I've always wanted since I was a kid. I had always dreamed about a game like the first Alien movie where you get to feel what Ellen Ripley felt and the fear that she experienced in the Nostromo. Well this game IS that game. (Hell, if you buy the DLC "Last Survivor" you actually get to be Ellen Ripley and replay the first movie's climax! It's well worth the $3.99, believe me.)
I gotta warn you though, this game will terrify you. It is a genuinely scary game. Not just because of the alien itself, but also because of the androids (which have gone crazy) that are scattered about the space station you are on. Some people I've talked to have even said that the androids scared them more than the alien, and I can definitely see why.
So thank you Creative Assembly for making this game. It was a pleasure to play. Never in my life had I ever had so much fun being so scared. For me, this was the game of the year for 2014. If this game was an apology for the travesty that was "Aliens: Colonial Marines" then it is one hell of an apology!
I should also mention that this game is amazingly optimized for the PC. My computer is ancient (i3-2100, GTX 650 Ti Boost, 6 gigs of RAM, 1440 x 900 monitor) and this game ran perfectly on it on mostly all the highest graphical settings with a solid 60 FPS all the way through. Well done guys!
And oh yeah, just as a suggestion, you may wanna buy some extra pairs of underwear while playing this.

Do you like Alien of 1979 before Ridley Scott butchered the Alien universe with Prometheus? Then you should get this game and try it out. This is the definitive Alien game of all time and is easily the best in terms of storytelling, graphics, production values, sound, atmosphere etc. Now as all creations have their issues, so does this. However this is by far the best out there and the issues that are there will not ruin your game for you in terms of the overall experience. This game is in fact one of the most atmospheric and suspenceful games ever created! It is a gem in it's own little world. The other good thing about this game is that Creative Assembly understood to avoid the problems other movie franchise games often fail at. They deliberately designed the game to be similar in aspects to film but keep free of meddling with the lore or tangle themselves in to the movies plots which is often fatal as seen in the infamous Colonial Marines of 2013. This game follows Ripley's daughter and that besides the creature alien is all that ties the writers of this game down. Therefore they don't have to worry about butchering the story of the films or ruining peoples fond nostalgic memories of the iconic films. They are free to explore ideas and gameplay story wise without having to break the original concept.
This shows brains behind whoever went into thinking how this game should approach things. Eerily this game shares a lot with it's utterly failed predecessor Colonial Marines. Colonial Marines got patching after patching and after extensively playing that one, I was shocked to find eerily similar Nostromo map here + other similarities as if the makers of Isolation had actually went in and studied what was a failure in Marines and what worked (hardly anything with exception to maps) And pick and choose what to do properly in this game. There are a lot of things that I've found similar with this game with the obvious exception that Marines did them without soul and implemented poorly and this game took the idea and put serious effort and understanding into what they were making and why. ACM has a Stasis Interrupted DLC and in it are similarities with this (Blowing up the ship sequence) Obviously this one does not have the action based dynamics of ACM but it isn't purely Ridely Scotts Alien either. It feels like an amalgamation between the two with heavy leaning towards the mechanics of the original Alien film. Suspence rather than action, yet it's not Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell with aliens either. This game is faster in terms of pacing than Mr.Scott's original classic, and that's where you feel the amalgamation with other alien films. The faster pacing does not mean the game is short, by all means this game will give your money's worth. Maybe even too much depending on the gamers preference. As to my guessing of whether the similarities I find in ACM and this one (not gameplay wise) Are in fact real or not, I do however think no one in the gaming world could escape the abysmal sensation of ACM and it's aftermath. So in that sense I would consider a possibility of makers of Isolation to actually compare and try and figure out WHAT NOT TO DO here.
All in all it will be interesting to see whether CA can succesfully go forward with a good start and make this even better for DLC or even sequel. If they listen what people found frustrating with this yet understanding the good, they should at least be able to streamline the experience even more. Now if the next step would be similar to James Cameron's version but again with the understanding of not jumping in and trying to replicate the exact experience and end up spoiling it, but rather have the mood, atmosphere, ideas but not necessarily same people, locations etc. So that it stays fresh and free from breaking the past. That would be COOL in my books! Now we have the thriller version of Alien in videogame form, next step would logically be the suspence action ride of Aliens! Here's hoping!

Papers, Please is a punishing puzzle with an inventive story, told in a unique manner.
Hopefully that didn't scare you off. It's clear that this is an indie game; most big publishers
be scared off by the game's punishing yet fundamentally repetitive gameplay. However, anyone who enjoys brainteasers and an excellent story will be impressed with Papers, Please.
The game, which takes place in an Arstotzkan border checkpoint at East Grestin, is based on sorting through papers. Does this person have all required papers? Are the papers valid? Does anything about the documents conflict with something else? These, and other new complexities, are difficult to understand at a glance, so game difficulty is no problem (though I haven't tried the Easy Mode yet). New twists, often caused by events at your own checkpoint (Kolechians are temporarily forbidden from entering Arstotzka following a Kolechian terrorist attack), are introduced, and often moral dilemmas arise, as bribes, anti-government rebel agents, and star-crossed lovers (Ooh-la-la) are frequent occurences on this border. Money troubles also appear, as you must maintain your family of four (fun things like "Your wife, uncle, and son died" are treated with little fanfare).
The depth of the story (which has 20 endings) is (quite) deep. The unique method of storytelling, where you see just a snapshot of the lives of travelers, is enough to recommend the game on. The gameplay is interesting, but loses much of its appeal early on. For one to look at this as an incredibly difficult and intense virtual novel would be a good summary, and if you enjoy those types of things, then this could be one of your favorite new indie titles. For gameplay first, story second players, the game is likely to bore you, as the story is the real selling point here.

Sonic Forces, a game I was very excited for, turned out to be a mixed bag in terms of how "good" it really is. I've always enjoyed playing the Sonic series, even games such as the infamous Sonic 06. The only game in the series I have not enjoyed was Sonic Boom Rise of Lyric. However Sonic Forces honestly is the first game in a long time that has truly disappointed me with it's level of unpolish. It seems from the time the game was revealed to now there has been very little done in the realm of polish leading to some very glaring issues. The physics come to mind as one thing that really throw me off (Litterally). Moments where boost sections lead into me being shot in an opposite direction for no reason, trying to do the ever so extremely repetitive 2D platforming with controls almost as slipery as though I was on ice at all times, and also just the Classic Sonic stages in general. Basically, it's no Sonic Mania (Clarification: I do not own Sonic Mania on Steam, I own it on the Switch because I enjoy taking games like that on the go). The legnth of the game is also almost mind boggolingly short. Like I know there's bonus challenges, but those really don't add much to the overall legnth of the game since all they do is focus around a single quick gimick. The only long lasting life (and the reason why I'll be keeping this game) is from the hopeful modding support.
However you may notice that I reccomend this game? Yes, I do indeed. Addressing the negatives first is just something I personally do. Anyways, the game however offers the return of the boost gameplay style. For many, including myself, this is the best style of gameplay that suits the Sonic series. Regardless of the poor handling of the style in this new title, I still found a lot of enjoyment out of the few times I got to go the speed of sound. Another thing I found myself enjoying was actually the AVATAR stages. Oh yes the DeviantArt The Fan Character itself is one thing I haven't mentioned in the negatives for a good reason. Honestly the Avatar stages are some of the better ones in the game, they offer a good mix of platforming and speed all in a equal manner. The wisp gimick has honestly never been fun to me, but you can pretty much ignore it for the most part. However the "Wispins" are a really interesting addition to combat, and make it pretty fun. Probably the best part about this game was the music however, I really enjoyed the trance like tracks in the Avatar stages, the music of the Modern Sonic stages, and even the Genisis Sound Font of the Classic Sonic stages. All of the compositions sound nice, and are something I will probably listen to occasionally on their own. The overall sound design of the game is very well done, and the voice acting of course is spot on. Especially Mike Pollock's Eggman.
Final thoughts, I'm probably going to keep this game for future modding support if any. I overall had a mixed experience, but if you're a Sonic fan I'd say go ahead and grab it. It's a decent game for a Sonic fan, but for the general audiance it'll probably have no lasting appeal at all. If you're a non Sonic fan then grab Sonic Mania instead, it's a much better game for anyone who is a general fan of platformers. Anyways, that is all. Thanks for reading!

They do get more diffacult as you progress through the game but still it felt like there was always just sorta of one way to go for the most part. So let's deal with the Elephant in the room first; the lore.  To be blunt those who argue that ESO's Lore is bad know nothing of the lore.  TES itself plays big on the "Unreliable Narrator" trope.
With each new TES installment Bethesda butchers and does massive retcons of the lore, ESO is the only game where they keep things consistent with each update.
You know the Island of Solstheim? Didn't exist until the Bloodmoon Expansion for Morrowind. The Dragon Fires? Never once mentioned until Oblivion. Dragon Cults? Didn't exist until Skyrim.
That and the Lore is amazing, we finally see things from the day to day life perspective on the folks living in Tamriel and experience their actual culture instead of everything being Imperialized  like in Skyrim.
Now for the actual gameplay;
I will admit, ESO started off in a bad way, but that was when it was released, now we are several massive updates in, as well as having a almost free form housing update coming soon! They improved a lot, just like in the main games you can easily ignore the main quest and go do what you want to do, with One Tamriel now you're not restricted by level or faction.
I haven't touched the main TES games in a while; ESO's story and characters beat the main series by a long shot. I actually found myself caring for these characters, I want to know what happens and when presented with a choice most of the time I have to sit down and think! Most choices in game are grey in morality, which I love.
My only real complain is not enough weapon types or classes. The more options the better and I did hear that they datamined the Warden class from the new PTR. But I would love to see weapon types like Spears, Throwing Weapons, Unarmed.
I give this game a firm 8/10, it might raise in the future depending on how the housing system goes.

Homemade Tortilla (for 8 servings)
Prep : 30 mins
Cook : 25 mins
Ingredients :
- 1 3/4 cups all-purpose flour
- 3/4 teaspoon salt
- 1/4 teaspoon baking powder
- 1/4 cup vegetable shortening
- 1/2 cup hot water
Directions :
1. Whisk flour, salt, and baking powder together in a large bowl. Add vegetable shortening and work into flour mixture using a pastry cutter until it resembles coarse crumbs.
2. Form a well in the middle of flour mixture and mix in hot water. Work flour and water mixture together with a fork and transfer to a cutting board.
3. Knead until a smooth, soft dough is formed, about 3 minutes. Add more flour if dough is too sticky.
4. Place more flour on cutting board, cover dough with bowl, and let rest for 15 minutes.
5. Cut ball of dough into eight equal parts and cover until needed.
6. Roll out balls of dough either by hand or with a tortilla press.
7. Heat a large skillet over medium-high heat. Place flattened tortilla in skillet and cook until it begins to bubble, about 1 minute. Flip tortilla over and cook for an additional minute. Flip again and cook for 1 more minute. Repeat with remaining dough.Homemade Tortilla (for 8 servings)

Smite is a third-person MOBA, which was developed and created by HiRez Studios (the ones who brought you Tribes: Ascend and Global Agenda).
Pros:
• A very noobish-friendly MOBA, with a good varity of competitive play
• Decent Graphics
• On consoles (for those people...)
• Everything is based on gods (Roman, Greek, Chinese, ect)
• Updated VERY frequently
• New "gods" are added almost all of the time
• The best 3v3 MOBA gamemode ever
• Many, MANY events
Cons:
• Takes a ton of time to get real into (like any MOBA really)
• There is a lot of things you can buy with gems (HiRez's money currency) [however most are just skins]
• Most of the events actually take a good amount of effort to complete
• If you are someone who wants to get all of the gods mastered, it is more challenging when there are many gods getting released at once
• You have to buy all of the gods, whether you buy the god pack or not (which is 30$) otherwise you spend favor (the free in-game currency) or gems to buy them
• The community can be kind of "cancer" or "toxic" at sometimes, but as someone who plays a lot of MOBAs that was just normal for me
Overall, this is probrobly one of the best MOBAs I have ever played, I would recommend even trying this game, after all it is free to play.

Graphics: 2/3
Story: 1.5/3
Game Play: 2.5/3
Re-playable: 1/1
Sale Rate: 10% At Most
Total: 7/10
Graphics: 2/3
The game focuses on making you the player feel as isolated as possible. The music is barely audible and only starts up when you are fighting a boss. As you wonder around the world, you start to notice places that you were before. Majola, the hub town, can be seen from Hieds Tower of Flame. The distance that you walked in no stretch of the imagination equal to the distance that you see. No big deal right? Wrong, if you played the original Dark Souls, otherwise, correct. This is a pattern throughout the game, when you can see the other areas in the background, they are disproportional compared to the actual distance. Some places just don’t make sense in their placement, like a giant lake of lava taken directly from Shrek is on the top of a windmill? This gives the illusion that the game had cut content that was hastily removed and patched the remaining content together. It takes a little from the game, but not much.
Story: 1.5/3
The game hides its story to the best of its ability, giving you a chance to give your hero a purpose and backstory. It is very similar to the first Dark Souls in this regard, but is heavier on dialog than the first. What is nice about this is that the vast majority of dialog is optional and the casual player will miss most of it. This does not really add anything to the game, but is left open enough that it doesn’t take anything from the game.
Game Play: 2.5/3
The game uses the same combat from the first Dark Souls with a few tweaks to improve it. If you are not familiar with Dark Souls, the basic combat is stamina management while choosing block, dodge, or attack. The range attacks in the first game took less stamina to shoot than was regened in the recovery time. Dark Souls 2 introduced wielding 2 swords at once in a feasible way. It also increases the stamina recharge time, making the fighting tenser. The combat is not as tight as in the first game, mainly because they introduced a state that increase the I-frames for rolls. Since this is now variable, it is not nearly as well displayed why one was a dodge and another is a hit. It is a good brawler that has solid game play and good feedback.
Re-Playability: 1/1
If you take the daunting task and hope to complete the game, you will not be satisfied with its conclusion. You will be stuck in the never ending struggle for a greater challenge. You will play again and again with different builds. The endless struggle that this game creates will haunt you for years to come. Or, you could just play Dynasty Warriors and be done.
Should you buy it?
An unforgiving brawler that punishes you for your ignorance and mistakes until you dig yourself into a hole so deep that every ray of hope has been consumed by darkness. That is what Dark Souls is, and I love it.
Every enemy has the ability to kill you at nearly every stage of the game. Level 1 enemies have killed my end game character more times than I would like to admit, but they were not cheap. I messed up and the game punished me for it. The game wants you to die, not to defeat you, but to teach you, so every death can be avoid with enough skill and victory is all the sweeter for it.

Not only is it still playable in its vanilla state, but any real S.T.A.L.K.E.R. will tell you that what really makes or breaks any game in the series are the mods that you choose to play it with. After your first vanilla playthrough, or even before your first vanilla playthrough (as there are many mods that don't change much about the story or vanilla gameplay and only fix broken mechanics, bugs, and improve/optimize graphics), you'll have a plethora of mods to choose from installing, all of them relatively unique. Some of them will turn the game into a hardcore survival simulator, where you die everytime you come in contact with a single bullet or a single radioative particle, for that matter, while others will bring the game back to its alpha state allowing you to experience parts of the game that were cut before release.
Can't go wrong with this series; excellent story, excellent gameplay, excellent mod selection allows for a ton of replayability and variety.

The game itself is really good, it has amazing atmosphere, the gunplay might feel a bit rough around the edges but once you get used to it it's really satysfying to kill an enemy. The game really has a survival feel. You have to eat every so often, there is limited amount that you can carry and you are not a rambo like in many other games.
One of the things that i didn't like about the game was the limited amount of time for side quests (if you don't complete them, the taks will fail, which is kind of annoying especially when you didn't pay much attention to the side missions). Another annoying thing is that there is no sleeping bad in the vanilla game* and you can't see anything during the night so you can't really do anything unless you get a night vision which is really hard to get for the first days of the game. Also, I would have prefered if the map would be just a whole map not a bunch of sections joined together by loading screens. I guess that was due to the hardware limits in 2007.
Overall the game is worth playing and in my opinion the only mods you need to get that will not alter the atmosphere and experience of the game are:
1) Zone Reclamation Project (ZRP) - this is a patch which will fix the buggs which are common in the vanilla game.
2) Absolute Nature - improves the nature in the game.
3) Absolute Textures - improves the appearance of the structures in the game.
4) Weather Overhaul -  adds different types of weather such as heavy rain,  storm, etc.
5) Shaders Max - improves shadows in the game.
Last 4 mods just improve the game's slightly outdated and blocky graphics.
*The sleeping bag now comes with ZRP (it can be enabled in the modifier in the gamedata).
The game at the beginning is difficult, but after a few hours I guarantee you will get a decent equipment and you will be fine then.
I recommend playing on Veteran difficulty (it's not like COD's veteran in campaign) to feel the hardcore of Chernobyl. The highest difficulty, Master, might be a little too much for some people.

THE quintessential survival crafting factory game.
Factorio will push your spatial management skills to their absolute limits as you start to formulate very complicated automated processes and how they string in with being able to incorporate additional inputs of resources and a continually progressing technology tree.
There are some people who play Factorio for 10 hours straight, and there are some who are mentally exhausted after 3-4 hours and can no longer push themselves further. This is an indicator of a game with plenty of depth to offer.
As for the early access part of it - Factorio is mostly feature complete, the only bugs that really hinder gameplay are all present in the multiplayer netcode and currently being worked on. The development philosophy of the creators has been spot on for the past few years.
Unless you aren't seeking a game that will deeply mentally stimulate you, I highly recommend Factorio, even at full price.

You know a game is amazing when you constantly think about it when you aren't playing it. Factorio is a very fun and addictive game. You mine for resources, using conveyer builts to then transport them to other areas where you will need them. Using inserters you can put them in boilders or other buildings to turn those resources into items. Using more conveyer belts you then transport those items elsewhere to be turned into something else.
As your factory grows you will produce more polution. This polution will make the native creatures angry and they will attack. You have a few different weapons, turrents and ammo types avaliable to help defend (or attack) the natives.
As you progress you will go from basic mining machines and boilers run by coal to better machines run on electricity. There are lots of things to research to help you progress through the game which allows you to choose which paths you want first. Do you want to get armored piecing rounds or risk being over powered by the natives and prioritize a different new technology.
As you expand and grow you will be able to use trains to transport everything longer distances faster. There are plenty of other fun things to play with which I won't mention so you have some nice suprises.
This game will feel confusing at first. Play the campaign missions which act like a tutorial and watch some youtube videos. Then jump into free play and you'll find you will pick everything up rather fast.
I highly recommend this great addictive game. For the price you will get a LOT of hours out of the game, which is still in early access and the developers have plans to add much more content. There are also plenty of mods to try out and being you can play single or multiplayer, you will put a lot of hours into this amazing game.

The one word I would use to describe this game is "mindblowing!"
This game is simply amazing, It is far and away one of the most thrilling experiences I have ever had. Being a life long fan of Alien, the thrill was even better.
Things I loved about it:
The environment is astonishing! The quality of the graphics is as good as it gets, on top of being optimized very well. Sometimes it feels so real you could swear you can reach out and touch the wall. There are some tweaks you can use to improve them just a bit more too.
The sounds build an environment of their own. The ambiance is perfect, just enough silence and just enough creepy sounds in the distance (often giving clues if you pay attention). Much of the time you must rely on sound to know where threats are. Headphones or surround sound will increase your experience with this game A LOT!
The music is great too, all right from the movie and put together so that it changes very smoothly, not always just as a direct indication of whats happening around you. Sometimes it picks up when you cannot be sure if there is something nearby, or it will remain quiet when the alien is near. No jarring music changes, it is very organic sounding.
Great characters and voice acting, sometimes the lip syncing is a little off, but all in all about as good as you would expect of a game. I instantly liked the main character, and had different feelings about everyone I met. They are varied and all have something about them that makes them stand out.
The AI is pretty good (I played the game on hard) The only real complaint I had about it was fixed with a simple mod. The Alien by default was "leashed" to you, meaning it was always nearby, and would almost always return from the direction he left. The mod I got removes this leash, meaning the Alien can wander more freely surprising you from any direction and hunting more based on its senses rather than a magic leash that keeps it by you. Even without the mod the Alien does not simply patrol the same way at any time, so there is always just enough risk when trying to move around of the Alien happening in your direction. Also worth noting with the AI is it learns from you, if you blast it with the flame thrower too much it will start to just stand there and watch you, waiting to see if you will keep doing it getting more bold. If you hide a lot it will stay very near the last place it heard you, if you move fast, it will start to drop into rooms at random hoping to surprise you (sometimes it succeeds O_O) just some examples.
The crafting system is decent, nothing special really but adds a little depth. The items you can make are all useful too, some are better for some threats than others, but they can reward creativity.
The level design is really good, with VERY thoughtful placement of objects in the world for hiding. Some crafting items and ammo seemed to spawn randomly in containers and just out in the world (when I reloaded a game, items I had looted since the last save would be different). Some items seemed to always been the same ie. find a new gun and some ammo for it would often be nearby to give you a good start in using it. You sometimes visited areas more than once or backtracked, not too often, but just enough to remind you that you are on a space station and that your parth is not just from A to B, but rather to navigate one big environment.
And of course, the story. As a whole it had just enough to keep it interesting even if it was sometimes very predictible if you knew Alien very well. The predictible points aside, it was well put together, quite long and interesting, and I often felt invested in it. It made me, sad, angry, happy and of course scared among other things. It would play very well for a person who knows nothing about Alien too, it has a great deal of story to put together.
At the writing of this review (37 hours played) I have not encountered a single bug, just a few physics glitches.
Things that could be better:
The only 1 thing that really annoyed me about the game was at the beginning, there is an item which you could want very badly. Even if you manage to subdue a person with said item, and saw it laying right on the floor you could not pick it up!! It forced you to find this item by storyline. You get it very quickly so its not the worst thing ever, just annoying and frankly immersion breaking.
Another possible gripe is how you are led around sometimes feels a *little* too forced. Making me think "oh yes I must have to go this way" just based on how things were put together. This might just be because I have played a ton of games and might not really be noticable to other people.
Occasionally the physics got a little whacky and made bodies fall into the floor, or my flamethrower would seem to rattle a lot until I pulled it out, enemies didnt take notice to these things though.
On occasion the anti aliasing leaves more jaggy edges than it should.
I definately recommend this game, its a good solid stealth game set in a world with a rich story and the best in art design.

Engrossing. Engaging. Atmospheric. Terrifying.
These are just some of the words to describe this fantastic game. If you are a fan of the Alien films you owe it to yourself to play......no, EXPERIENCE this game. That's right, you don't just merely play this game, you experience it. Right from the onset, you can feel the love and dedication that was put into this game by the people at Creative Assembly. They are huge fans of the Alien franchise, and it shows. As I played through it, there were times I actually teared up a bit because this is the Alien game I've always wanted since I was a kid. I had always dreamed about a game like the first Alien movie where you get to feel what Ellen Ripley felt and the fear that she experienced in the Nostromo. Well this game IS that game. (Hell, if you buy the DLC "Last Survivor" you actually get to be Ellen Ripley and replay the first movie's climax! It's well worth the $3.99, believe me.)
I gotta warn you though, this game will terrify you. It is a genuinely scary game. Not just because of the alien itself, but also because of the androids (which have gone crazy) that are scattered about the space station you are on. Some people I've talked to have even said that the androids scared them more than the alien, and I can definitely see why.
So thank you Creative Assembly for making this game. It was a pleasure to play. Never in my life had I ever had so much fun being so scared. For me, this was the game of the year for 2014. If this game was an apology for the travesty that was "Aliens: Colonial Marines" then it is one hell of an apology!
I should also mention that this game is amazingly optimized for the PC. My computer is ancient (i3-2100, GTX 650 Ti Boost, 6 gigs of RAM, 1440 x 900 monitor) and this game ran perfectly on it on mostly all the highest graphical settings with a solid 60 FPS all the way through. Well done guys!
And oh yeah, just as a suggestion, you may wanna buy some extra pairs of underwear while playing this.

Aiming in vehicles feels floaty and awkward, making otherwise enjoyable sections a bothersome chore to slog through.
The constant requirement to complete challenges for gears to upgrade things is a headache. The challenges are not fun, they're a roll of the dice against which ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t thing is going to happen to you on that run. Well got the game earlier today, and first time I tried to run it I got through the first level and the game crashed. Then it continued to crash as soon as I hit continue every time from there. So... The game was broken at first. Great release Sega! =D To their credit, they did release a patch within hours that fixed the problem so I was able to get into the game.
So Sonic Forces. It's not a bad game. It's certainly not a great game either. It's average. The short of it is, if you like the Sonic franchise, you'll probably be wiling to overlook some of the game's flaws. If you're not a fan of the Sonic series, this isn't going to be the game that wins you over.
Let's talk about a few things about the game. First, the thing that got many people including myself interested, the customizible charactrers. They're pretty nifty. I was concerned at first when I saw they were going to be a gadget and gun user and was afraid this was going to be a return to Shadow the Hedgehog gun style gameplay. Luckily, these fears were misplacaed. For the most part the avatar plays pretty well. The jump line and the wisp guns are intergrated into the running pretty well. As for customizing the characters. There's some decent options but I do feel a bit limited. With only one base body and just matching heads and tails the avatars don't quite feel different enough from each other. Would be nicec if I could adjust their proportions a bit. I wanted to make my avatar proportioned similiar to the pot bellied Classic Sonic as opposed to the newer versions. Ah well. I can dream. Anyway, when you start out there's not much to customize your outfit with, but you do unlock a pretty extensive combination of outfits as you go on. This is nice, though parts of it leave something to be desired. I couldn't find anyway to customize the color of each outfit piece. This was... Rather frustrating as it  meant if you liked the specific look of an item but wanted it in a different color then you have to keep unlocking things and hope it pops up. I think the worst offender is the bit of chest fluff. Had to change my fur color completely to make it work. I honestly would have rather had less unlockables over all and instead just gotten a way to change the color of existing costume pieces.
Anyway, the six species themselves don't play substantially different. They have a few minor differences, with the bird being the most drastic difference having a double jump. The lack of difference between them will make it a bit dull for anyone who's trying to rank up all six species for the purpose of achievements and unlocking more clothing.
Now, as for the story. I've heard complaints that the story feels a bit like it's way to much of a try hard fanfic about an Edgelord villain and to that I say... Welcome to Sonic games. Having Sonic get defeated by a new villain to prove how much of a threat they are is... nothing new. I mean heck in Unleashed he got curb stomped while Super sonic, turned into a monster then thrown out of a moving carrier and left for dead. Beaten up and thrown into a prison? Not that different. I'd say Sonic was edgier back in Adventure 2 when we were led to believe Sonic was actually blown up by Eggman. Anyway, the story is... Not exceptionally novel  but it does have some improvements over previous Sonic games. That's not much of an improvement! I hear some of you say. But in this case it kinda is. A lot of Sonic's friends are less annoying. Knuckles is far less stupid and Amy much less obsessive than in other games. It began to make me realize that I'm not actually compleltely against some of Sonic's friends showing up when they don't have to be a punchline every 5 seconds.  Having said that... One character's role in the story I do take major issue with though would have to be Tails. Hey, remember in the Adventure Era when he came into his own and learned not to be codependent on Sonic? Remember how he grew into a gadgeteer genius who could survive on his own without Sonic's protection? Sega sure doesn't! Sorry Tails fans, but Tails is rather pathetic in this game, depicted as being almost entirely codependent on Sonic to the point he breaks completely upon thinking Sonic parished in the opening. Again I am forced to recall Adventure's version... who upon seeing Sonic 'die' became a determintor that would stop at nothing to take on Eggman. I really feel they could have handled him better.
Anyway, let's talk about the villains for a bit. So we get a big villain team up between our new original generation villain Infinite, and some returning villains Eggman, Shadow, Chaos, Metal Sonic and Zavok. So... Going to give a sort of minor spoiler real quick. Two of these villains are never fought in the game. Despite this team up being heavily advertised it seems Shadow and Chaos couldn't be bothered to show up for actual boss fights. Instead, they'll simply be dealt with rather quickly in a cutscene. Not even a cutscene with QTEs. This greatly bothers me, especially since the game had time to include and give Zavok a boss fight. Seriously, Zavok. Don't know who he is? Exactly. He's one of the Deadly Six from Sonic Lost World, and considering that game's reception, and the fact the Deadly Six bareley had one personality between the six of them it's very jarring Zavok got included in the roster. I really wouldn't mind this, except while he had time to spend on him we couldn't be bothered with fights for Chaos or Shadow. It's just... Really really annoying. Granted, other than Infinite and Eggman they don't actually do much with any of the villains... And there's actually a decent plot reason for that so I won't say more. Just. Seriously? Zavok? Really?
So right. The story, it's not anything to write home about, but neither is it offensively bad. It's about what I expect of a Sonic storyline. It has its moments... and seems to be working to try to make Eggman a credible villain again which is nice. The game does do a good job of escalating and making the situation feel more dire. It does a pretty decent job building to a climax. Overall though the story here is taking a back seat to the gameplay... and honestly for a Sonic game... I'm okay with that.
But now let's talk about the gameplay
I touched on the Avatar a bit. He runs slower than Sonic, but makes use of a grappling hook for his own version of a homing attack and to grab onto various parts of the stage. He's also armed with a  wisp powered weapon you can change. You'll also probably stick to the basic flame thrower because it gets the job done. Overall, not to many complaints about how the avatar works that don't apply to everyone. Will touch on those in a minute.
Modern Sonic is well... Modern Sonic. Do homing attacks, hit boost, run fast. Though he seems to have lost the ability to drift which can make going around corners at high speed a tad annoying. His gameplay tends to work when you're going fast. It doesn't feel as great when you have to slow down for precission jumping.
Classic Sonic... So... I think Sonic Mania spoiled me... Because I felt like Classic Sonic just didn't control great in this game. Maybe it's just my imagination but he felt very stiff to control compared to in Mania or Generations. Though some of this may be that he's forced to slow down more.. So let's touch on that.
I mentioned there's some problems that apply to all of them. The game just falls apart when it forces you to slow down and do precission platforming. You're going to find that control of your jump leaves much to be desired and a lot of things can just cause you to compleltely lose momentum on your jump. It also doesn't help when the camera suddenly swerves mid jump sometimes.
So overall, if you like Sonic get the game. It's fun, and feels unfished at times but is a decent play. I wouldn't mind seeing a continuation of the Forces style in the future just fine tuned a bit and with more than 5 hours content.

GOTY 2013, Hands Down
Papers Please is advertised as an Adventure title but I feel that it leans more towards Border Patrol Simulator. Although I imagine that it would have been easier to market the game as an Adventure title, but I digress.
The premise is simple enough, you are a border patrol officer working in a fictional Dystopian country whose main driving point is to simply get enough money to keep your family alive. Very straightforward, but the game shines by doing something that is rarely seen in video games; tackling ethical issues such as whether or not to let a woman in to reunite with a long lost relative or letting a man take revenge on the man who killed his child. Money issues are a part of the gameplay too, if you don't have enough money then you won't be able to pay for food or warmth possibly resulting in a family members death. Far more successful than something such as Bioshock Infinite I would say, being the complexity in that game just involved shooting everyone but the fate of people in this game are literally in your hands and can be turned away at the press of a stamp.
As the game goes on, laws become more strict and more paperwork is introduced making the game a chore as it goes on, but yet the game still manages to immerse you in the universe created and never seems to become dulldue to memorable moments where you have to defuse a bomb, or the memorable characters such as the comical drug dealer who attempts to enter the country with a crayon passport.
The art design makes the game instantly recognisable as opposed to 'SUPAH HYPA REALISM 3D OMG' instead choosing personalised sprite work. The game ultimately has a true identity of it's own.
If you let someone in or deny someone you weren't supposed to then the game will issue you with a penalty warning but you don't lose money until the third strike, this is a great mechanic because not only does it allow you to see where you went wrong with that person but it also prompts you to take bribes and you can get rewarded for bending the rules for your favour.
Overall Papers Please is not only the best game of 2013 but also easily one of my favourite games of all time.
FINAL VERDICT: MUST PLAY! GLORY TO ARSTOTSKA!

I played this game in beta and was disappointed. After it launched, the feedback I got from friends and community sites confirmed everything I wasn't liking in beta, so I didn't jump in. Recently, I started reading about the One Tamriel update and the expansions. It looked like they might have addressed many of my concerns, so I decided to give it another shot.
This game is now a solid Elder Scrolls game. When I play, I really get the feeling that I'm playing a Skyrim-like game (minus the ability to pause or reload). The graphics are great even on low (I'm playing on a machine purchased for battery life and office performance, not gaming). The mechanics offer enough complexity to require paying attention, but they aren't so complicated that they distract you from what is going on.
In particular, the Dark Brotherhood expansion is great. I really wondered how they would pull off that kind of gameplay in a multiplayer world, but what they did works quite well. The game is largely soloable at early levels, but occassionally you are thrown a quest that requires help. Sometimes you get an NPC to help, other times you have to grab one or more players to help out. The removal of level barriers makes it so that you can group with anyone you find.
Much of the world is open and seamless, which is fantastic. Sure, there are dungeons and such that require load times, but even most large cities can be entered without hitting a door or load screen. It seems like I spend less time loading in this game than I did in Skyrim, which is pretty impressive considering how seamless Skyrim was and that ESO is an MMO.
All things considered, I like the game so far on this go-around.

Very fun game. I am not really into online games let along MMO's, but I am an avid Elder Scrolls fan. My friend (who is not really an Elder Scrolls fan but a player of MMO's) told me ESO is surprisingly fun and relaxing to play, so I thought I'd try it out. Others have emphasized how this game is not Skyrim online, so I got into the game blindly and not really expecting anything. To my surprise, the game is not entirely unlike Skyrim in terms of UI and other familiar elements such as theiving (don't expect anything beyond that, however.). Despite my general disinterest in MMO's this game is pretty fun to play.
Gameplay wise, it kind of plays like Diablo/Grim Dawn, or any similar arpg, except you play in 3rd or 1st person. The "core" consists of theory buliding (numbers and stats) and grinding mobs and bosses for loot. There are a lot of other activities aside of that, however.
Pros:
+ Lots of activities (leveling up, quests, crafting, collecting, skills, PvE, PvP, guilds, exploring, roleplaying, achievements(with rewards such as paint color and items))
+ Decent graphics/visuals
+ Good (although limited) soundtrack
+ True to Elder Scrolls lore
+ Travel to different areas of Tamriel
+ Beginner friendly
+ Everything is fully voiced.
+ Can be played solo
+ Fun interacting with other players
+ Crafting is fun
+ Can download user created addons to improve UI and provide utilities
+ Added content and events through time
+ Friendly, mostly mature/older community (does not mean it is entirely free of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, however)
Cons:
-Quests are boring because 99% of npc's are generic/uninteresting (meaning I don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about what they want and what they have to say, unless you are a 300% loremonger), but this is expected from an mmo. The main story is the typical YOU ARE THE CHOSEN ONE TO SAVE THE WORLD. Zzz. So are the 100's of people around you running around.
- PvP performance is very bad. You WILL get extrememly long and sometimes infinite loading screens at some point. Even Zenimax themselves don't exactly know what causes this and therefore cannot fix it. The loading screen bug just destroys your pvp gaming experinece.
- You will be severly handicapped if you don't have the monthly subscription, especially towards inventory management (affects crafting and ability to make a lot of gold).
- Cosmetic pets and some of the mounts are loud af and therefore annoying af, and there is no way to turn the volume down without also turning down other sound effects you don't want to turn down.
- There might be a lot of lag in dungeons and trials. All the lag and loading screen bug in this game has nothing to do with your beast pc.
- Do not ever expect any "immersion" out of this game. It may be an Elder Scrolls, but it's an MMO. You cannot have both immersion and MMO.
-You can buy and decorate your own home. However it serves zero purpose and gives no "homey" feel you get in single player Elder Scrolls because: you can't store anything in your home, your pets stand there like statues. Unless you are a guild leader where your house is a guild hall, your home will feel dead because it is.
- You might frequently encounter trains of bots running around farming nodes and dolmen. Zennimax does not give a damn because reporting them does absolutely nothing.
Interesting Points:
* Yes there is grinding because RNG is strong. They did implement retrait system very recently which got rid of about 80% of the grind. It is still difficult to get a right weapon set piece to drop, however.
*You can play solo, yes, but if you want to be an above average player and get good gear and such, you willl definitely have to socialize/ group up with people in chat or through a guild/community.
* Even though it's Buy to Play, the business model with the subscription and the loot boxes, crown store feels very much like Free to Play..
* If you expect multiplayer Skyrim, you will have a bad time. This is an MMO first.
* There is little to no median difficulty. Overworld content is laughably easy. Veteran and Veteran hardmode raids can only be completed by top teir players in organized guilds.
* Because this is an MMO, expect the typical Skinner box mechanic and daily incentives to "force" you to login every day.

Not a bad game by any stretch but definitly a step-down from Total War : Shogun 2 and the Fall of the Samurai. There is a huge map with large number of opponents but it all feels more oppressive than grand. If you're willing to put a hundred or so hours into the game it will most probably be rewarding but as there is no short-campaign option, more time-challenged gamers will find this too slow paced. The need for large investments of time in each game you play means that it can be almost impossible to see why one faction differs from another (apart from starting position) as the bonuses don't add up to large gains very quickly.The unit cards used as displays for what is in your army don't differ enough and the user interface is unusually cluttered without actually revealing any more information than the previous games in the series did. All in all it means the user will have to have a very long look at the game's encyclopedia before any action takes place.
The parent company, Creative Assembly, have continued to release patches for this game but have also continued charging a high price ($80 AUSD base game + $7 AUSD for factions/unit packs +  $14+AUSD for campaigns) coupled with core-game features needlessly hidden behind DLC (Blood and Gore, All the faction packs for the grand campaign). Imperetor Augustus campaign is a good free DLC and there should have been more for free up to the point of writing this.
Overall 2.5/5 - The tighter combat and map design in Shogun 2 was more to my liking. I live in a place in Australia were online play is unstable so I can't comment on this game's multiplayer.

A Rust Clone that stands as its own game. Quirky and hilarious, and probably the most enjoyable alpha experience I have ever had. Bring your friends along for a wild ride of strangely ironic forced roleplay, such as♥♥♥♥♥♥talking the king or being him, and playing a giant game of king of the hill. (Literally.)
Pros:
(+) Unique twist of the survival genre, engaging players in a battle to be the King, or just dethrone him.
(+) Kingship comes with rewards, such as free materials stolen directly from hard working others due to magical taxation, however it is important to remember what you are dealing with; other angry players.
(+) Easy to meet up with buddies, even BEFORE you build beds (respawn points) or a base to call your own. Once you find each other once (trust me it is not hard) you can join a guild and standard respawns will put you near each other.
(+) Hilarious characters. Trust me, I've never enjoyed a character creator so much in any game I have ever played. Meet racist sterotypes, aliens, and possibly normal humans along your adventure with friends. Make a new character every new server you join, including a different name/banner/inhuman design.
(+) Durable bases, allowing you to sleep easily with a good chance of returning alive tomorrow.
Cons:
(-) The durability of bases can be troublesome when a powerful group holds the keys to the kingdom. This can lead to a quite literal powerhouse group permanently controlling the kingdom. Siege weaponry does exist, but are ineffective due to the strange layout of the throne room.
(-) While quite hilarious in appearance and effect, there are serious issues with jumping and block clipping. Your character can jump two blocks up from a flat surface, but as it stands you can quite easily jump around three-four blocks up by holding space and your body to the wall. As well as that, you can jump on your friends heads... you get the idea.
(-) Hitboxes are goofy due to the hilarious characters, it is not game breaking but it is definately worth listing.
(-) It is sometimes frustrating when you require a certain crafting table (or its upgrade) to view a recipe. It would be nice to be able to look back and see exactly what I need from my standard inventory.
(-) The hogtie mechanic is awesome in every single way... except that it can be VERY easily abused in combat. I have had several instances where my friends will be battling a man and I will just walk up behind him and rope him up. At that point my friends just usually stab his defenseless body. I wish I could think of a workaround for this issue, but I really do not want to hinder the fun of player capture at all.
The Little Things:
(+) People are usually pretty nice, don't seem to have the mindset of DayZ or Rust, and enjoy to chitchat with you on roads or tie you up and drag you around for a bit. There are of course people who attack on sight, but usually it is not a band of dudes and just some naked man who very likely won't kill you if you have any gear.
(+) Slightly forced roleplay, while people will have servers dedicated to this concept, it is fun to be able to talk down upon the king for his taxation in a jokingly medieval vibe.
(-) ...but there are those who need to take their roleplay to the servers designed for it.
(+) You can shove sharp rocks in your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to allow you to break out of player traps or just to bash your head in. The suicide option as stated describes you as "bashing your head" but I would like to stress it is more of a "bonk".
(+) Directed by Quentin Tarantino, there will be blood EVERYWHERE.
(=) Resource nodes respawn, in the same spots, but the danger of this is apparent when people will build around them in order to claim them forever.
(=) Crazy monsters, such as the werewolf and the plague villagers. While they are interesting and drop cool things, the issue is that they are practically battled only with ranged weapons even in the best armor.
Overall, this game is a riot. It knows what it is and I appreciate that. This is one hell of an alpha game, I do not believe I have enjoyed an EAG on steam this much... ever.

Sonic is like marmite, you either love him or you hate him.  Being a kid that grew up in the 90's, Sega and Sonic were at the forefront of consoles and video games and whilst the years have gone by some games have been mediocre or pretty bad, I've always had faith that all the experimentation Sega were doing with Sonic as a franchise would pay off with some really good games.
Sonic Forces is one of those games.
Right from the get-go, it has some very familier gameplay elements.  Since it runs on the Hedgehog Engine that was introduced to us in Sonic Unleashed, you can expect very fast paced action and platforming, with pretty visuals and the game rewarding you for quick reflexes.
But that's just the tip of the iceburg.  Deeper down we have some really fleshed out characters.  All of Sonic's pals, and Sonic himself, have been given more personality and character than any previous 3D Sonic game.  They don't seem like such flat 'good guy' characters anymore, they each have different ways of acting around one another and the English voice cast did a really good job of bringing each character to life.  Even Roger Craig Smith (who we originally know as the voice of Chris Redfield from Resident Evil) seems to have gotten the hang of giving Sonic the personality he's meant to have, brash, impulsive, over-confident, but determined to do what is right.
Next is the avatar creation system.  At first there is a very limited supply of clothing and outfits for your custom character, but as you progress through the game, earning medals and getting S ranks in missions you'll unlock a bountifull menagerie of things from hats, glasses, backpacks and gloves to shoes, t-shirts, bodysuits and visual designs to really make the character feel like your own.  It's really well thought out and makes your character blend in nicely with the usual Sonic cast without feeling misplaced.  Also since the game is set on Mobius (Let's get geeky here), the majority of the population of the planet look 'sonic-like', so it makes sense for your avatar, a resistence fighter that's just joined to battle Dr. Robotnik, looks the way that they do.  It's not so much a case of 'appeasing the Sonic OC fan-art creators' as simply bringing you in to the world in a persona that fits the theme.
The soundtrack, like pretty much every Sonic game since the franchise first began, is superb.  There's a lot of audio variety from drum and bass, techno and chiptunes all the way to the familiar heavy rock and industrial metal that more modern Sonic games have taken to using.
Performance, at least from my experience so far, has not been an issue at all.  Whilst I did notice that when the game first loaded up the framerate tanked into the single digits, I quickly realised this was simply because the game had not finished loading all the necessary data it needed, and was causing the game to lag whilst it finished processing everything.  In all it took about a minute for everything to smooth out at the main menu, but after that the game ran smooth as silk.  Given the nice visuals and the speed that a lot of the stages pass by, it's pretty impressive to see it keep a stable 60fps even on my computer, which is getting on a bit now (though it's still able to run The Evil Within 2 perfectly fine so it isn't a huge surprise I guess).
Gameplay.  This was what surprised me the most about the game.  The Modern Sonic stages play like they have before in Sonic Unleashed, Sonic Colours and Sonic Generations.  Fast-paced with lots of badniks to destroy, platforming sections and plenty of boosts to make the world fly by at the speed of sound, nothing much here has changed but that's a good thing, because these kinds of 3D Sonic stages have always been good and really lend to giving the player the experience of being Sonic.
Original Sonic stages also return, though they feel more token.  Honestly I kind of feel like the game could have gotten by without them, as they feel almost unnatural in this case, but they're still enjoyable for a change of pace once in a while, so not really a bad thing.
The Avatar stages are where the game gets really interesting.  Your character doesn't possess the speed or power of Sonic, and so relies on a weapon called a Wispon that allows them to grapple and swing on nearby hooks or smash into enemies, along with unleash attacks like flamethrowers or lightning whips.  They also offer abilities such as the light speed dash seen in Sonic Adventure games that allow you to follow trails of rings and many other things.  Some also have unique bonuses that allow you to gain a better score at the end of the stage, making it that little bit easier to get an S rank and earn some unlockable cosmetics, or even a new Wispon with new abilities.
Along with this there is also a 'duo-stage', where your character and Sonic run alongside each other, a little bit like Sonic Heroes, and it allows you to utilise both characters abilities.  If you need to homing attack enemies, Sonic will take over and do that, but if you need to use a grappling point, your character will seamlessly take over and use their Wispon without any character switching button input.  These stages also have some really unique powerups that are both cool to look at and exciting to use, which really amps up the fun factor.
All in all, I have no complaints.  It's a really fun 3D Sonic game that takes what Sonic Team learned in previous games, added some new and fun things in to the mix, then polished it to a shine.  It isn't going to suit everyone's palette, but that's because people always want different things from Sonic games, and a single game cannot give everyone what they want.  However, if you enjoyed the previous 3D Sonic games like Sonic Generations and Sonic Colours, then I highly recommend this to you.

I'll try to summarize all my angst for this game in a few points.
* With the exception of maybe 1 or 2 levels as Modern Sonic, this game is pretty bland in terms of level design. When level design isn't too busy being bland and unimaginative, its unfairly brutal in terms of platform placement.
* Good physics are not a thing to be found in this game. Seriously, how did Sega screw this one up after making solid games in the Hedgehog engine?

At this point, supporting Sega by buying into every Sonic game hoping for an extended comeback is just fueling the dumpster fire that is modern Sonic. There I said it. Happy Sega? Oh well, maybe if someone can mod Super Mario Odyssey and replace Mario's model with Sonic, we can get a semi-legitimate 3D Sonic game again. Because in Odyssey, Mario just beat Sonic at his own game.

I played this game in beta and was disappointed. After it launched, the feedback I got from friends and community sites confirmed everything I wasn't liking in beta, so I didn't jump in. Recently, I started reading about the One Tamriel update and the expansions. It looked like they might have addressed many of my concerns, so I decided to give it another shot.
This game is now a solid Elder Scrolls game. When I play, I really get the feeling that I'm playing a Skyrim-like game (minus the ability to pause or reload). The graphics are great even on low (I'm playing on a machine purchased for battery life and office performance, not gaming). The mechanics offer enough complexity to require paying attention, but they aren't so complicated that they distract you from what is going on.
In particular, the Dark Brotherhood expansion is great. I really wondered how they would pull off that kind of gameplay in a multiplayer world, but what they did works quite well. The game is largely soloable at early levels, but occassionally you are thrown a quest that requires help. Sometimes you get an NPC to help, other times you have to grab one or more players to help out. The removal of level barriers makes it so that you can group with anyone you find.
Much of the world is open and seamless, which is fantastic. Sure, there are dungeons and such that require load times, but even most large cities can be entered without hitting a door or load screen. It seems like I spend less time loading in this game than I did in Skyrim, which is pretty impressive considering how seamless Skyrim was and that ESO is an MMO.
All things considered, I like the game so far on this go-around.

Very fun game. I am not really into online games let along MMO's, but I am an avid Elder Scrolls fan. My friend (who is not really an Elder Scrolls fan but a player of MMO's) told me ESO is surprisingly fun and relaxing to play, so I thought I'd try it out. Others have emphasized how this game is not Skyrim online, so I got into the game blindly and not really expecting anything. To my surprise, the game is not entirely unlike Skyrim in terms of UI and other familiar elements such as theiving (don't expect anything beyond that, however.). Despite my general disinterest in MMO's this game is pretty fun to play.
Gameplay wise, it kind of plays like Diablo/Grim Dawn, or any similar arpg, except you play in 3rd or 1st person. The "core" consists of theory buliding (numbers and stats) and grinding mobs and bosses for loot. There are a lot of other activities aside of that, however.
Pros:
+ Lots of activities (leveling up, quests, crafting, collecting, skills, PvE, PvP, guilds, exploring, roleplaying, achievements(with rewards such as paint color and items))
+ Decent graphics/visuals
+ Good (although limited) soundtrack
+ True to Elder Scrolls lore
+ Travel to different areas of Tamriel
+ Beginner friendly
+ Everything is fully voiced.
+ Can be played solo
+ Fun interacting with other players
+ Crafting is fun
+ Can download user created addons to improve UI and provide utilities
+ Added content and events through time
+ Friendly, mostly mature/older community (does not mean it is entirely free of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, however)
Cons:
-Quests are boring because 99% of npc's are generic/uninteresting (meaning I don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about what they want and what they have to say, unless you are a 300% loremonger), but this is expected from an mmo. The main story is the typical YOU ARE THE CHOSEN ONE TO SAVE THE WORLD. Zzz. So are the 100's of people around you running around.
- PvP performance is very bad. You WILL get extrememly long and sometimes infinite loading screens at some point. Even Zenimax themselves don't exactly know what causes this and therefore cannot fix it. The loading screen bug just destroys your pvp gaming experinece.
- You will be severly handicapped if you don't have the monthly subscription, especially towards inventory management (affects crafting and ability to make a lot of gold).
- Cosmetic pets and some of the mounts are loud af and therefore annoying af, and there is no way to turn the volume down without also turning down other sound effects you don't want to turn down.
- There might be a lot of lag in dungeons and trials. All the lag and loading screen bug in this game has nothing to do with your beast pc.
- Do not ever expect any "immersion" out of this game. It may be an Elder Scrolls, but it's an MMO. You cannot have both immersion and MMO.
-You can buy and decorate your own home. However it serves zero purpose and gives no "homey" feel you get in single player Elder Scrolls because: you can't store anything in your home, your pets stand there like statues. Unless you are a guild leader where your house is a guild hall, your home will feel dead because it is.
- You might frequently encounter trains of bots running around farming nodes and dolmen. Zennimax does not give a damn because reporting them does absolutely nothing.
Interesting Points:
* Yes there is grinding because RNG is strong. They did implement retrait system very recently which got rid of about 80% of the grind. It is still difficult to get a right weapon set piece to drop, however.
*You can play solo, yes, but if you want to be an above average player and get good gear and such, you willl definitely have to socialize/ group up with people in chat or through a guild/community.
* Even though it's Buy to Play, the business model with the subscription and the loot boxes, crown store feels very much like Free to Play..
* If you expect multiplayer Skyrim, you will have a bad time. This is an MMO first.
* There is little to no median difficulty. Overworld content is laughably easy. Veteran and Veteran hardmode raids can only be completed by top teir players in organized guilds.
* Because this is an MMO, expect the typical Skinner box mechanic and daily incentives to "force" you to login every day.

GOTY 2013, Hands Down
Papers Please is advertised as an Adventure title but I feel that it leans more towards Border Patrol Simulator. Although I imagine that it would have been easier to market the game as an Adventure title, but I digress.
The premise is simple enough, you are a border patrol officer working in a fictional Dystopian country whose main driving point is to simply get enough money to keep your family alive. Very straightforward, but the game shines by doing something that is rarely seen in video games; tackling ethical issues such as whether or not to let a woman in to reunite with a long lost relative or letting a man take revenge on the man who killed his child. Money issues are a part of the gameplay too, if you don't have enough money then you won't be able to pay for food or warmth possibly resulting in a family members death. Far more successful than something such as Bioshock Infinite I would say, being the complexity in that game just involved shooting everyone but the fate of people in this game are literally in your hands and can be turned away at the press of a stamp.
As the game goes on, laws become more strict and more paperwork is introduced making the game a chore as it goes on, but yet the game still manages to immerse you in the universe created and never seems to become dulldue to memorable moments where you have to defuse a bomb, or the memorable characters such as the comical drug dealer who attempts to enter the country with a crayon passport.
The art design makes the game instantly recognisable as opposed to 'SUPAH HYPA REALISM 3D OMG' instead choosing personalised sprite work. The game ultimately has a true identity of it's own.
If you let someone in or deny someone you weren't supposed to then the game will issue you with a penalty warning but you don't lose money until the third strike, this is a great mechanic because not only does it allow you to see where you went wrong with that person but it also prompts you to take bribes and you can get rewarded for bending the rules for your favour.
Overall Papers Please is not only the best game of 2013 but also easily one of my favourite games of all time.
FINAL VERDICT: MUST PLAY! GLORY TO ARSTOTSKA!

I am so disappointed with this drab, drawn-out sequel that it has exhausted me.  Titanite is limited, so you have to get used to a limited equipment set (forget the joy of experimentation, in other words).  Enemies disappear after a few kills, so you are dependent on co-op for leveling -- but co-op is difficult to initiate later in the game, when leveling is needed the most.  The stages get more boxy and uninspired as you proceed, with "spam hordes of generic, super-powered humanoid enemies" serving as a central design principle.  Parrying is glitchy.  There are other terrible design decisions, like your health bar shortening every time you die -- and the human effigies that reverse hollowing and re-extend the bar are far more rare than humanity sprites in Dark Souls I.   Lore is virtually non-existent, and what is there is nothing more than a shallow call-back to DS1.
This game should have been a prettier, smoother, deeper and more lore-filled Dark Souls, but it just turned out to be a cheap cash-grab with none of its predecessor's inspiration and some terrible new mechanics.
Quite a bit of lag/hacker issues, but other than that, generally a good game.

I'll just start off by saying that I caught Tropico 3 on sale, about 3 or 4 bucks.
And a price like that is literally a STEAL for a game like this.
One thing I'd like to say is that it's a good solid game. With plenty of challenges and acheivements to acheive (Sadly though, they aren't Steam Acheivements) So you can get a good amount of hours from this game depending what you do, it's also a good time killer, if you're into those.
Another thing I would like to say about this, is that it follows up on history pretty well. Game starting about late/after WWII and taking place mostly during the Cold War. Meaning you will take sides with the USSR or the US, or if you want, juggle relations with both of them.
There are also plenty of some real life problems that you can deal with in the game as you dictate your Tropico Island Paradise.
I would also like to point out that this game runs well on even weak machines. I'll have you know that at the time I made this review, my Desktop sucks and runs Cities Skylines at 7 FPS average. That's actually one of the main reasons I bought Tropico 3 so I have a City Builder to play until I get an actual Gaming Computer.
I think in my opinion that it's fantastic for a game to run on weak machines, so EVERYONE can play, regardless of Computer specs. (Well, unless you play on a computer made in the 1990's, there's no hope for you) Also, Tropico 3 looks VERY GOOD with some lower graphics, so that's also a plus.
The only problem I really have with this game is the lack of variety in Buildings. Sure there's plenty of buildings you can place, but they almost always look the same, making kinda of look un-realistic. Not to mention, you don't want to put a Clinic next to a Hospital, because there's already health care in that area.
That's mostly just me, what you'll think is up to you, really.
So I'm going to end it with me asking myself...:
Do I recommend this game? Yes
I also recommend you should find a day to catch this on sale, because it's like, super cheap by then.
