I don't know why I never wrote a review for S.T.A.L.K.E.R., I've been playing it since 2007 and it is probably my favorite game. That is not to say I don't recognize the faults it has, especially in unmodded form, but once you get a hang of the game, it plays really well and is very memorable. I've replayed it a few times, replayed the sequals, installed a few different mods, and I have more mods to install and try out. The modding community is amazing and will keep this game and it's sequals alive for at least another 7 years.
So first off, I recommend doing some research on these mods. Complete Mod is a popular mod that doesn't change any story or gameplay elements, just updates the graphics and fixes some remaining bugs, I suggest Complete for a first or second time play through, it should fix some of the issues people have mentioned, and will give the graphics a boost.
Don't try to play it on a junk computer, this shouldn't be a problem by now, but keep in mind that when this game came out it required a decent computer, you can't really play it on a 5 year old entry level computer. Any modern computer with a halfway decent card can play the original game just fine, might need a bit more performance for the Complete mod, and some mods actually require quite a bit because of their high res textures and added material.
I recommend some patience because this game is certainly from Ukraine and therefore things are a bit different from most FPS/RPG games from American studios, I'm not even sure how to explain it, there are some flaws and unpolished things everywhere you look, but when you focus on the gameplay it really becomes immersive and captivating.
Anyways, onto the gameplay itself. You start with a cutscene, a bit creepy, you find out that something unknown has happened to you, and now you're essentially a newbie in The Zone. You have to find out who you are, and you have a task that you know nothing about. Sidrovich pretty much owns you at this point, so you gotta do some work for him in return for his help. And off you go into the zone with little more than a Makarov handgun, binoculars, PDA (this will contain your map, locations and tasts, messages, and some Zone info), and some completely unprotective clothes. Guns are very cool in this game, in my opinion. You can snap shoot guns, and get pretty poor accuracy, or use the sights, and get slightly better accuracy. Some people have complained about the guns, but I personally found them to feel fairly realistic (looks and sounds not so much, but handling, firing, and accuracy, yes). Cheap handguns are not very accurate, don't expect to be picking off mutant dogs easily, in fact a dog running around is pretty hard to hit even with a good gun. Sawed off shotguns are weak and very short range, AKSU's shoot all over the place in full auto. Guns exhibit realistic bullet trajectory, they exhibit accuracy that in reality is pretty realistic for guns operating on cheap ammo in rough conditions. Sometimes guns jam, especially if they begin to wear out (in this game there is no repairing or upgrading guns, however Clear Sky & Call of Pripyat have it). You have to really think about the way you shoot, not a lot of running and gunning, more tactics, strategy, and aim. Especially in the beginning. Later as you get better armor and firepower, you can go a little more headfirst into combat.
Sometimes you can sneak around, but it is hard to hide. AI can be hit or miss, sometimes it's too easy to outsmart an enemy, sometimes they come looking for you but they walk in the other direction, sometimes they find you too easily and seem to know where you've gone even if they clearly don't have line of sight on you. Yet most of the time I felt that the AI was pretty good, sometimes it was quite clever, with guys flanking far and sneaking up behind me (always watch your back). Mutants usually run around doing their thing until you get close and they decide to attack, then they usually charge. Some you can unload a mag into them as they charge, others are too fast or too smart for that. Some are really hard to see even when they are right in front of you. One of the most memorable moments was when I first ventured into an underground facility (there are quite a few to deal with), walked into a room and got rushed by, something. It briefly attacked and then ran off, unseen, but I could hear it moving around, I saw something, it was still there, waiting for me. I inched into the room, hugging the wall, trying to find something higher to stand on and observe from, I could see something moving, but couldn't make out anything for sure. Now that part is easy, I know what it is and how to kill it, but it never does the same thing each playthrough, it's always in the same area but never behaves quite the same. That first time, it genuinely scared me and I was totally immersed in the fear and anxiety of creeping through those underground passages.
If you can get past the repetitive sounds in the background, repetitive lines, songs, and the guys in the bar that always say the same damn thing (I love the relaxing music in the bar though, and the sad song that you hear playing here and there), the environment really draws you in. Sometimes it's nice and sunny, the grassy hills and trees are beautiful, and then clouds roll in and it's raining, wet and cold and dreary. Maybe even a loud, disturbing thunderstorm. Then it's dark, really dark. Stumbling around, you can see flashlights here and there, good guys? Bad guys? What's rustling around behind me in the pitch black? The atmosphere is really great, even without any of the mods that improve on it even further. You see animals running around fighting, dragging corpses, roving in packs that will attack you. Groups of STALKER's running past on some mission, groups of bandits looking for an easy target, zombified stalkers (think more mind melted than undead) stumbling around mumbling gibberish, clumsily shooting at whoever they see. It's really an impressive world, despite the flaws you find.
The story itself is pretty cool in my opinion. You gotta play the game right though, there's a set of "correct" endings that you can choose between, and a set of "wrong" endings that you will automatically get depending on how you've played and if you did not take the time to explore everything and find the "right" endings. You'll know it when you get there, if you did it right or not, the "wrong" endings are not fulfilling. All I can say is take your time to explore, look for items and clues everywhere, especially when you get to Pripyat.
As I said before, the game requires patience, you will do a lot of running around, some backtracking, & you will have to take time exploring, figuring stuff out, & working your way through difficult sections. Think very wisely about what you bring with you. Artifacts can provide boosts in protection or strength, but often at a cost of low levels of radiation that slowly drain your health. So you need to balance the artifacts. You need to pack supplies carefully in your inventory; your carrying capcity is limited, so you need to make sure you've packed enough food, medical supplies, ammo, & a variety of guns. Armor/suits are assumed ruined when you kill an enemy, thus you can never pick it up, you have to either buy it, or find it stashed somewhere. You can't carry one main gun because sometimes you run out and the only ammo you find is for something else. You may have to run back to pick up a gun from a body and collect ammo for it.
The game forces you to think & work hard to get through. I personally had my frustating moments but nothing that drove me to quit. It has it's flaws & bugs but when you get past that, the game is so immersive & fantastic. The rush of just squeezing through a battle, crawling out of an underground complex alive, or watching an enemy slip up & get themselves killed, it's amazing for a game to create that.

Game #6 - S.T.A.L.K.E.R. Shadow of Chernobyl (PC)
November 7, 2014
When someone suggests a game to me that deals with an Apocalypse, I usually am interested enough to dive right into the title. Although, S.T.A.L.K.E.R. Shadow of Chernobyl isn't necessarily a "End of the World" scenario, it comes very close. The setting is the region of the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant in Ukraine, which on April 26th, 1986 saw the world's worst catastrophic nuclear accident in history. This real-world tragedy is delivered as an RPG style game in the flavor of a First Person Shooter. It's mostly compared to Fallout 3, terms of the subject matter and game design. This comparison would only be correct at a very high-level, since both game begin to divert away from each other quickly.
The game mechanics of S.T.A.L.K.E.R. are similar to that of a PC shooter with Keyboard and Mouse being the only option. Inventory management is handled with a Grid style storage box that has a finite amount of space. Additionally, players must be concerned with carry wait, since this will hinder how fast your character burns stamina and moves. The movement is far more complex than one would expect from a shooter. The Character can strafe, lean, walk, run, crouch, crouch lower...attempt to jump; all of these moves involve multiple button combinations and feel awkward in close combat. There are plenty of weapons to take into combat from Handguns to Automatic rifles; all are real world weapons and they tend to be readily available within the game world.
Playing S.T.A.L.K.E.R. takes patience and constant saving to progress through the somewhat linear mission lineup. Unlike Fallout 3, where missions are very story driven, the missions in S.T.A.L.K.E.R. are very point A to point B. You can talk to many NPCs that will offer additional information, but this seems to be less fun and more of a chore. Although, the graphics are decent for a game that launched in 2007, the story tends to be far less interesting then others of that time period. Being a PC game helped this title gain popularity since it was capable of modding, and some followers of the title have updated many aspects of the game design. In most cases the mods have been for the better and have served to improve on the initial experience.
As with all PC games, consumers can purchase this game at a fairly decent price in today's market of Steam Key Re-sellers like Amazon and Green Man Gaming. It's possible to find it under $10 a few times a year, and even more likely during the Steam annual sales. At the original launch price, I would have been hesitant to purchase this game. Although it received a Metacritic score of 82, there are too many factors that lead me to a score of 6-7. If you are looking for a game that has a decent game mechanic in an RPG design, then you have something to look forward to during the next big sale.

I have followed for this project for quite some time, years before it was listed on Steam. I have gotten several hours ingame with this Steam release despite the login problems, so hopefully I can give some good information on this. This review is clear of any "I can't play" rage. This is an indie game by the way.
What is this game? What do you do?
It seems like a beautiful 3d version of OGAME. You have a big open universe, where you go and claim yourself (and build up) several planets. You build up your troops/ships, find an alliance, then go to war for other peoples planets and try to defend your own.
The Bad:
- The game was designed and tested with only a handful of players in mind, leading to several problems.
- Current state: Unplayable - 2 much people broke everything. Not a 1-2 day fix.
- Current ingame content is scaled back from previous versions. No ingame combat, and limited to one planet is NOT how it has always been. This does mean that certain aspcts can be expected to be brought back fairly quickly, however. "Not much to do" describes this perfectly.
- Chat system is a joke (and has been for several years). This us a priority issue.
- Unclear/bad tutorial with people asking the same questions over and over and over again.
- Various building problems
The good
- Beautiful yet simple universe
- Lots of the systems that are missing have been ingame in the past, even if in a very simplistic way, so the Dev has a good idea of how to actually add good content fairly quickly.
- Despite a lack of user freindlyness, and problems with the new building system, there is actually a noticeable LACK of bugs. The main issues seem to be the login and building issues, and the building issues are only a big deal because it's one of the only things to acutally do right now!
- Smooth, competitive game when actually working (Handful of players, back when combat was a simple numbers game, was fun!)
- Limbo system. Your troops >> space >> stream them to planet of your choice. Attack or defend anywhere in the universe, in a battle that can last hours or days, giving time for both sides to play works really well

I played Just Cause 2 for countless hours and had lots of fun, even managed to get 99% completion. It is impossible to get 100% in JC2 because of a map bug that was never patched. This problem should have raised warning flags, but i decided to trust Avalanche one more time with my money. So I bought this game during a sale for around 19€, a few days later I applied for a refund. Why? If you are interested, read on, what I found after a few minutes:
- Unskippable stupid intro videos
- Nagging for online account
- Limited graphics options
- No option for setting FOV
- After playing for a few minutes, i noticed that even on max settings the game doesn't seem to look as good as the screenshots or even as JC2 (on my i7-6800K with 64GB RAM and a MSI 1080). The controls feel unresponsive, the default keyboard layout is terrible (can be remapped).
- The game is nearly uncontrollable due to an extremely narrow FOV (especially bad on my monitor in 3440x1440)
- The camera is so close to the avatar/car/helicopter that aiming or steering properly is made impossible.

I was unable to finish the tutorial missions because I got stuck on a bridge where I was supposed to plant explosives - whatever I did, the game didn't let me place them.
In conclusion: To me the game feels like a late beta version, not ready for release. I also learned to NEVER AGAIN trust Avalanche. IMHO in its current state this game is NOT worth money (or maybe 0,99€ during a sale for those masochistic enough to put up with the problems...). If the game is ever patched (see JC2 - they never did bother to!), my opinion may change, of course.

I wasn't really a Tropico fan until this one. The original Tropico had a lot of good ideas in its individual citizens and its banana republic politics, but it was held back by technical limitations and short-sighted designs. After an odd detour with Tropico 2, the developers returned to the original concept and polished it up in a brand-new 3D engine, and the results speak for themselves.
Tropico 3 places you into the spit-shined spats of a Caribbean dictator, charged with helping his hapless little island flourish. Each individual citizen is modeled with needs, jobs, opinions, and motivations, so the key to success is keeping enough of them happy (or suppressed) to achieve your own agenda. This is mostly done by building homes and services they want, and making sure they have enough money to enjoy them. You'll be building churches, clinics, restaurants, casinos, and more, in addition to the farms and factories needed to fund them.
The big stumbling block of the first Tropico was that your little Tropicans couldn't be trusted to actually get♥♥♥♥♥♥done when it needed to be done. That's not a problem here, as your citizens spend far more of their time on their tasks and only go astray if their needs are very conspicuously not being met. And as it turns out, when your island is running like it should, the money just pours in. Even the most basic exports like excess food or meat will earn you everything you need to outfit your island. And once you get more complex industries up and running, money will never be an issue again.
As a result, Tropico 3 is way, way easier than its predecessors and a lot of its contemporaries, but this is by no means a bad thing. Economic prosperity allows you a lot more freedom to build your island the way you want, with all the services and luxuries you can stuff into your borders. You'll need them too, because your citizens are noticeably pickier than in previous games and won't hesitate to turn to armed rebellion. Some scenarios lean heavier on this aspect but managing the different factions and quelling uprisings are a larger part of the game, as they should be.
One very welcome feature added for this outing is the opportunity to customize your dictator. Tropico 1 let you choose his or her traits but 3 lets you give them backstories, change their outfits, and then watch them walk around and interact with the people. You can actually use your little avatar to inspire workers to work harder or give rousing speeches to the commoners. The traits also seem much more powerful this time around, and honestly work as a sort of difficulty system. Taking traits that help with scenario goals can make a huge difference, but you can also choose flaws that add a greater challenge.
In the end, Tropico 3 is the game the first one should have been. The core mechanics are not very far removed; most of the buildings and edicts are the same, and the politics are virtually unchanged. But everything works the way it's supposed to, is balanced to not be so frustrating, and is presented in some charming, picturesque 3D. There's no reason to go any further back in the series than this, so if you've ever wanted to lord over your own tropical island, start here.

Game #6 - S.T.A.L.K.E.R. Shadow of Chernobyl (PC)
November 7, 2014
When someone suggests a game to me that deals with an Apocalypse, I usually am interested enough to dive right into the title. Although, S.T.A.L.K.E.R. Shadow of Chernobyl isn't necessarily a "End of the World" scenario, it comes very close. The setting is the region of the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant in Ukraine, which on April 26th, 1986 saw the world's worst catastrophic nuclear accident in history. This real-world tragedy is delivered as an RPG style game in the flavor of a First Person Shooter. It's mostly compared to Fallout 3, terms of the subject matter and game design. This comparison would only be correct at a very high-level, since both game begin to divert away from each other quickly.
The game mechanics of S.T.A.L.K.E.R. are similar to that of a PC shooter with Keyboard and Mouse being the only option. Inventory management is handled with a Grid style storage box that has a finite amount of space. Additionally, players must be concerned with carry wait, since this will hinder how fast your character burns stamina and moves. The movement is far more complex than one would expect from a shooter. The Character can strafe, lean, walk, run, crouch, crouch lower...attempt to jump; all of these moves involve multiple button combinations and feel awkward in close combat. There are plenty of weapons to take into combat from Handguns to Automatic rifles; all are real world weapons and they tend to be readily available within the game world.
Playing S.T.A.L.K.E.R. takes patience and constant saving to progress through the somewhat linear mission lineup. Unlike Fallout 3, where missions are very story driven, the missions in S.T.A.L.K.E.R. are very point A to point B. You can talk to many NPCs that will offer additional information, but this seems to be less fun and more of a chore. Although, the graphics are decent for a game that launched in 2007, the story tends to be far less interesting then others of that time period. Being a PC game helped this title gain popularity since it was capable of modding, and some followers of the title have updated many aspects of the game design. In most cases the mods have been for the better and have served to improve on the initial experience.
As with all PC games, consumers can purchase this game at a fairly decent price in today's market of Steam Key Re-sellers like Amazon and Green Man Gaming. It's possible to find it under $10 a few times a year, and even more likely during the Steam annual sales. At the original launch price, I would have been hesitant to purchase this game. Although it received a Metacritic score of 82, there are too many factors that lead me to a score of 6-7. If you are looking for a game that has a decent game mechanic in an RPG design, then you have something to look forward to during the next big sale.

Pros:
- Great soundtrack
- Large variety of classes
- Creative class themes and skillsets
- Beautiful sprites
- Great monster design
- Great visual feedback (monsters explode on death, the screen shakes, lots of pretty colors, etc. which is extremely significant in a grind-centric game)
Cons:
- Every single player is funneled through the same maps, in the same order, killing the same bosses, doing the same quests. The world map is set up like a giant flowchart. This really hurts the immersion of the game, and in my opinion, is one of its largest flaws. The maps are made specifically to get the player from level x to level y, rather than being an explorable part of the game's world. Every time you outlevel a map, that part of the world becomes useless to you. All of these beautiful areas that you explore become void after you "complete" them because the developers only created them for the express purpose of leveling you through a certain range. This makes the game just seem like a series of rooms rather than a virtual world.

- They seem cool at first, until you realize that they re-use the same formula for every single boss in the entire game: "traps" (that don't thematically fit the boss at all) randomly spawn around the area, the boss has a distastefully large amount of HP, and it has maybe one attack that requires the player to actually react. The fights are never challenging, and the devs knew this, which is why they gave them tons of HP to compensate (so now we have painfully long, boring fights). The bosses also spend a lot of time just sitting there staring at you, doing absolutely nothing while you whale on them. All of those awesome boss entrances you see in the steam trailers couldn't be more any more misleading to how lifeless the bosses actually are.

- They'll hit you once, and then idle in place for about 3 seconds before they decide to continue chasing you. It makes every monster feel like a training dummy or a ragdoll, which is unfortunate because the combat system itself is pretty fun. They are lifeless, and barely move around on their own. If you've played a Dynasty Warriors game, it's pretty much like that. You have all of these amazing, flashy abilities, but monsters just kind of loaf around and wait for you to blast them all to bits. Cool for a few hours, but doing this for 250+ levels worth of content just isn't acceptable. There are other MMOs that do this, but they have other features that make the effortless slaughter more acceptable. Games like Maplestory and Latale, for example, can at least get away with this type of gameplay because they have immersive worlds that are actually explorable (and even their monsters are more responsive than the ones in ToS).
- It sounds great on paper, but it turns out to be a pretty lackluster feature once you actually play. It's meant to create more distinction between players of the same base-class, but everyone ends up using the same skills. There are classes and skills that are very interesting, but pointless to pick due to poor class balance. It tends to feel like you're simply the product of the strongest class you have specced into. Even if you aren't technically a carbon copy of another player, the differences will be so miniscule that you feel the same.
- Additionally, the devs have now made it so that you can "go back" through the class tree at any time, which totally ruins the branching sub-jobs. Before, each time you ranked up, you had to choose between one of two classes that had vastly different playstyles (such as a supportive ice magic kit vs. a destructive fire magic kit), or choose to rank up your current class instead. The classes you didn't choose would no longer be available for your character. They removed this restriction, and now you can rank up any class that you've reached the level requirement for. While this technically gives the player more freedom, it makes for much less thematic characters that end up seeming like a mish-mash of the strongest skills from every class. The original system created unique strengths and weaknesses for the player depending on what they chose (more Crowd Control and party-oriented play as cryomancer, or more DPS and solo oriented play as pyromancer?), but now everyone can just do everything, and frankly, that's pretty lame.

- They don't flow with the rest of the game, the bosses are no different from the bland story quest fights, and they don't introduce any new mechanics. I don't feel like there's a point to them. The monsters inside are often re-used models with inflated hp bars. They're not any more difficult than the rest of the game's content. It doesn't even feel rewarding to complete them; it's just a huge timesink. This is another example of the devs caring less about the soul of their game and more about what is currently popular in korean mmos.

Made by the Devs of RO, TOS is the true 'spiritual successor' of RO; you will enjoy the game more or less depending on how many of the following points you agree with below:
1. You loved RO's 2D sprite/3D world art and general art style
2. Enjoy top-down camera view action RPGs (D3)
3. Love deep customization for RPG classes and/or love deep class and subclassing trees
4. Are ok with the typical grind associated to most Korean MMORPGs and typical slew of fetch quests
5. Like anime
6. Hated RO2
7. Are looking for an MMO with interesting and unique game mechanics in the rpg classes (most of the cool ideas are in the deeper, advanced classes obtained later in the game)
Impressions from CBT:
Overview:
This rpg is like Ragnarok Online, 2D sprites with a 3D world; camera is top-down angled view centered on your character similar to other action RPGs (Diablo 2/3, Dragon Age).
Combat:
Tab targeting system for PvP/PvE with a few aoe/ground-targeting abilities. Bonus % modifiers to exp when partying; Party up to 5. Loot options available while in party. Death penalty is item durability loss for both weapons and armor. (eventually up to zero durability (items cannot break imo)). Durability can be repaired via NPC or other players with the right economy class skills. Quests can be shared/completed with party. Raids/Dungeons exist.
Social:
Typical social features including emotes, chat, party creation, whispering, announcements via megaphone item to scrolling marqee at the top of the UI.
World:
Not seamless world; hybrid combination of party-instanced areas and server-instanced areas connected by portals. Upon entering a portal, there the next area will load with a splash screen during loading. There are dynamically instanced channels depending on server capacity and population per each instanced area in the RPG world.
Classes and Persistent States:
All classes have an associated skill tree and branch from 4 base classes: Swordsman, Cleric, Mage, Archer. Leveling gives you stat points and skill points. Upon reaching key milestone levels, you have the option to either:
1. Unlock new skill trees/subclasses related to the initial base class you chose to be.
2. Choose to 'upgrade' a skill tree you have previously unlocked, in order to put more skill points into existing skills; thus making those skills stronger/more potent.
In short; having chosen a base class, you can either become a jack of all trades/swiss army knife, or a master in a particular specialization. 6 primary stats govern several other derived stats; not too simple nor complex and more info can be found on their wiki.
Pets/Mounts:
There are a few classes that can mount; 3? Pets (as of CBT) can be used to assist you in your adventures. Pets gain levels and need to be maintained (fed, taken care of) and have a relationship rating per created character.
Account:
Multiple characters are allowed per account. Pets are shared at the account level between characters. To my knowledge, accounts are tied to the server in which they are created on, unless some real currency server transfer option is released.
Economy:
Microtransactions for avatar looks and customization; Global market exists for posting items for selling/buying. One on one trading is allowed.

What IS important is the gameplay. The gameplay itself just feels very wonky where the challenge is not in the obsticles and layout, but trying to fight with the physics which for some unknown reason beyond any justification is not analog (there are steps: slow, medium, fast, and nothing in between to smooth out the transitions between speeds). They've made three games already where Sonic's physics were exactly the same and nobody complained, yet they decided to change them for the worst. Maybe you can get used to it? The game has pretty much the exact same controls as the previous three boost games, but the physics in the other three boost games are inarguably better yet absent in this game. Totally not the case I bet, but as I was playing, the gameplay seemed to be more of an afterthought than the graphics.
I ignored the reviews and gave this game a chance; was very excited and was expecting to like it, but it really isn't fun to play. I think I should've waited for a sale.

Alright in the past two weeks I've played a lot across a range of servers, nearly 100 hours.
I have to say I love the game, I hate, asuming from experience, 10% of the community and I chose to reccomend this only because I hope that the developers will fix some issues I will talk about in a minute.
First off The game is gorgeous and every moment you're out theres a constant alertness that you wont get in most other games because when you die it's full loot. Don't get caught gazing across a peaceful pond or else you might end up being whipped in another players stockade!
The survival system is pretty much what you would expect, harvest food and water in order to survive, or well don't... It's pretty easy to pick it up and start playing in the first 5 minutes without your hand being held.
The damage system is pretty unique giving five sections of the body individual hp bars.Sometimes you'll get hit by a club 8 times and not die because the damage is spread out, other times you'll take 2 to the dome and be laid out.
The combat could use some work, the blocking isn't super responsive now, three types of attacks, you can cleave which is nice.  Two days ago I was in a base that got the wall blown out and about 10 poorly geared tribe members jumped in with clubs.  Three of my friends and myself  took down about 5 of them in our first swing because of all the cleave. It was a hell of a fight.    Basically in 1v1 you want to  block swing, rinse repeat twitch fighting. Think early Chiv.

Base combat... Is awesome!!! Nothing like cracking through a wall to crush those hiding behind it and claiming whatever isn't destroyed as your own.  However the trebuchet is highly overpowered at the moment. It takes some serious farming to get but If I stick it ontop of a sky platform I make,  I can literrally hit anywhere on the map long as I have a spooter. I personally think they need to make this item an 'on solid ground' only  placement and drastically decrease the range per stone of counterweight, perhaps even make it exponential. As it is currently these Trebs can shoot what seems to be miles  with under 100 stone ( mined in a minute seconds from one node) So it definately needs balance.
The political system is pretty fun and interesting, makes for some good RP if you're into that.
Now for the bad....  Hackers... I would say around 5% of the community is currently using exploits or hacking. It's terrible and as of this morning has actually run me out of the game until they are dealt with. In the past two days I've seen multiple people duping or downright hacking in items, speed hackers, invisible players killing me, fly hacks, etc...    This morning a pair of them came onto the server me and my buddies spent days building on ( so did a bunch of other groups of players).  I s@#$ you not these guys were running around at 500 miles per hour dropping hundreds of fire bombs  blowing up everything.  Within thirty minutes these two guys destroyed everyones work on the server. It's disapointing  to say the least.
But, I've definately gotten my money out of this game and as I said before I hope the hacks and exploits are fixed in the future.  So, while I reccomend the game, I warn you that everything you do on a server can and most likely will be gone the next day. With all the attention this game is getting from the hacker community, it's a tough tough world for legit players gamers unless you get access to a secure server.   I have heard that the hackers avoid offical servers, but at this time I cannot confirm that because I tried to play on those servers at first but it was way to laggy so I went to community servers.

I've heard a lot of good things about this game, and had some high hopes that it would be a pretty good horror game. I'm sad to say I was a little disappointed. While Alien: Isolation delivers on being an excelent port, having a pretty great story, and a great atmosphere, it was overall a letdown, mainly because it failed at being scary.
**Minor Spoilers**
PROS
I think it nailed the atmosphere. Everything feels like it's going to♥♥♥♥♥♥and you can't trust anyone or anything. The technology is very interesting, and stayed true to the film.
The port is absolutely fantastic. By default it ran on ultra at 4k(!!!) with all the effects on, and rarely dropped below 60fps. I have a pretty powerful computer, but it's by no means top of the line.
The story was great, and that and the atmosphere was really all that kept me going to completion.
I have 13.9 hours in the game. About 12 of those were for the main story, which is great. It didn't feel arbitralily padded for time. The other 1.9 was for Crew Expendable and Last Survivor DLC, which were very short but decent enough.
CONS
The game can be very frustrating at times, especially with the stealth, and especially in the first half of the game. This is the reason for my negative review, the game was just too frustrating. The humans are very OP. The can see you crouched across the room and shoot you, hear you while crouching (albeit somewhat closely), and definitely hear you walking or running. This is strange, considering the Alien is supposed to be the one to spot you the easiest. You can crouch behind Alien and he won't notice unless you get very close, and walk fairly close without it noticing. He can see you if you stand, but often won't see you if you're crouched like the humans do. The deciding factor is that you can kill humans, but only scare off Alien. Take note that I was playing on Hard, which is the recommended difficulty. At one point the stealth was frustrating enough where I set the difficult to Easy. This didn't change the difficulty of the stealth, it just seemed to make guns do less damage to me.
This ties into the other reason why the other main con: the game just wasn't that scary. Frustration was a big cause of this. When you die towards the end of the level because of something spotting you, often unfairly, you just want to sprint though and ignore everything, If you're frustrated and annoyed, you're not worried about getting killed. This takes away all the fear of being hunted. I found myself many times just trying to find the shortest route possible where I wouldn't get caught, not hiding at all. And it usually worked. If I get caught, just hit escape and load the save. To be fair, I am a horror game veteran. The last horror game I played was SOMA. SOMA wasn't super scary, but I think it has Alien beat by quite a bit. To someone who isn't used to horror games or gets scared easily by horror games, you might have a different opinion.
I will also give the game credit for not relying heavily on cheap jumpscares. There definitely are some, and a lot of them don't work, but most of the fear comes from the feeling of being hunted and isolation (hey, name drop!) It just didn't work as well as I would like.
Working Joes were a weird NPC. If you dislike uncanny valley, mannequins, dolls, etc. then you might be afraid of them. They certainly are creepy. They just aren't threatening. You can easily outwalk them, unless you get cornered. Once you have guns and bombs, they're fairly easy to take down. Otherwise they're just annoying to deal with because they patrol important areas. You know that trope in games where you see a dead guy, but when you get close they're not actually dead and they attack you? Alien: Isolation uses that so many times with the Working Joes. Except in this game you can't do much to stop them when you know they're going to grab you. You can shoot them, but that's going alert everyone nearby. You can't melee them, no matter how hard you try. They use this cheap tactic so often that it stops being startling and starts being a nuisance.
My last gripe is the save system. There are checkpoint you have to manually save at placed sporadically through the station. This is a huge pain point because during very lengthy stealth sections there will be few save points. You will be listening to the same dialogue many times, pulling the same levers, pressing the same buttons, hoping to just get to the next save point. If there were just a few more it wouldn't be as annoying.
I got the game on sale for $15 including all DLC, and for that price I would say it's a worthwhile experience. At the current price of $49.99, $59.99 to get all the DLC, I would say give it a pass. Wait for it to be $15 or less.

I don't normally buy into early access, but I heard good things, and am glad I picked it up.  This is easily the best early access game I've played, and I think it's going to end up in my top 10 list of all games I've ever played.
I usually prefer games with a detailed story and and an actual ending/goal to hit (even if it's a Skyrim style ending where you can continue playing, at least it has a milestone to reach where you can say you're done).
Well this game doesn't really have a story, and the end goal (to build a rocket defense) isn't very interesting to me either.  But in attempting to reach that goal, you find that you end up making more goals - your own goals.  And that's infinitely more interesting than anything a static story can provide.
Your factory is a giant feedback loop of problems and solutions.  Solving one problem creates another.  And the fact that *you* created that problem provides a sense of duty unlike any quest I've seen in a game:  Not delivering enough iron gears to that factory?  Make more iron gear assembly machines.  Oh hey why is electronic circut production so low?  Uh oh, you've increased iron gear assembly but now you're starving your electronic ciruit assembly machines of iron plates, which are now going to the increased iron gear production.  We'll have to fix that by increasing our iron ore resource gathering.  But we'll need more furnaces to turn that raw ore into iron plates... and it goes on.
In addition to this feedback loop of problems and solutions, the game uses scientific research to throw a wrench into things.  As your factory grows, you'll end up researching new technologies that make you rethink how you solved previous problems.  Transport belts are no longer the only or best way to move items from one place to another - you'll need to consider designing rail systems and logistic networks to scale your factory; for some problems, these solutions are far superior, but you don't have access to all that tech at first, so you need to design with the future in mind.  Perhaps your design won't support certain things without a huge ovehaul.  You could just upgrade transport belts in place, but how long will that band-aid last?
This game has huge parallels to software development.  Problem solving, discovering and embracing design patterns, creating and testing proof-of-concept implementations, refactoring existing implementations, recovering from technical debt, designing with the future in mind, managing cost vs performance, etc.  If you're a programmer, you'll probably love this game.  And if you're not, you'll at least understand why programmers love to code.

I bought this outside of Steam shortly after it came out. It's a fascinating, frustrating, ultimately disappointing quasi-open-world shooting game with RPG elements. Rather like Deus Ex, the individual components are mostly rotten but they work well together and overall the game feels more than the sum of its parts. The visuals have aged well although mods can make it look even nicer. The storyline is simplistic and boils down to a lot of fetch quests. The shooting action feels unsatisfying - it strives for realism but suffers from poor enemy AI, which is either uncannily accurate or dumb. On the other hand the atmosphere and sense of being trapped in hell comes through strongly. It has a distinctive and very influential post-Soviet, post-apocalyptic rainscape mileu that must surely have influenced the zombie survival game DayZ.
The biggest problem is that the developers ran out of time. The opening levels are detailed, packed with story elements, *almost* large enough to work as an open-air sandbox although you do eventually run out of things to do. At a certain point (specifically beyond the Red Forest level) all of that drops away, and the last few levels are just on-rails shooters. Literally so in the case of the Chernobyl section, 'cause there's a bit where you run along some elevated rails. It's heartbreaking because the Pripyat and Chernobyl sections have detailed recreations of the real locations that look fantastic, and are incredibly atmospheric, but there's just nothing to do except run through them tossing grenades. In contrast the opening sections have lots of little quests but the landscape is mostly muddy fields.
Overall I remember the game fondly for its unsettling, grim atmosphere and fascinating world. It's not technically a survival horror game but there are several nervy moments, including SPOILER the underground chap who sucks out your brain SPOILER and the dog things in the spooky, radioactive forest. As a game it plays better if you add some of the copious mods that were released for it. STALKER was famously stuck in development hell for years, and in the end the developers had to chop out tonnes of content and make the remaining levels much smaller, and in the end SoC feels unfinished. It's a shame they couldn't somehow merge this and DayZ, the resulting game would be the best ever.
NB The Steam version seems to have a couple of small differences with the boxed copy - there's a lot more head bob and the mouse seems floaty.

I understand the people in the community who wrote this game off back when it first launched but from what I have experienced after playing it for about a year now is the fact that the devs at zenimax actually care about this game and work constantly to improve it for its playerbase and that alone speaks volumes.
Pros & Cons
Pros: There are a lot of things this game gets right, character creation for one was great because it offers more in depth customizing like adjusting height, weight and  build, as well as applying lore friendly tattoos and face paints and even choosing from a selection of voices to have for battle grunts in combat.On the topic of customization the smithing in the game allows for cultural variants of every weapon type which is something i simply adore, one of my personal gripes with skyrim was how nearly everyone wielded a nordic style weapon regardless of race, place of origin etc. The biggest positive this game offers in my opinion is the exploration of multiple provinces, which gives it a lot of replay value as well as providing lore on areas that bethesda either refuses to revisit for an upcoming tes or has yet to cover.
Cons: I want to preface this by saying my gripes are completely subjective. The easiest negative this game has is its grind, which are the MMO elements in this mmorpg, to some this is a plus but for me it's simply tedious, and by the grind I mean the sole driving force behind progression in any form of combat in this game, smithing. I personally hate the fact I have to either search for raw materials or buy them from guilds, it doesn't make sense as to why a smith wouldn't have ore/ingots laying around for sale. That grind somehow extends to even magicka, as even mages have to grind out woodcrafting for staves.
Verdict: I can't speak for the PvP experience in this game but the PvE and main quest in short borrow a lot from oblivion, you can tell the devs drew inspiration from the narrative in that game, if you enjoyed that, you'll enjoy this and if you are tired of exploring the same old provinces of skyrim, cyrodiil and morrowind, I highly recommend giving zones like hammerfell, summerset high rock and black marsh a shot as they contain plenty of new interesting lore all while providing a different landscape to explore.

I'm going to say the Homeworld games themselves garner a RECOMMEND, but I have some issues with these remastered versions.  These remasters, at least with Homeworld 1, have some really annoying bugs.  I've run into several that have hindered playing the game, especially in an RTS where response time is a factor.
I've had the "auto launch" and "stay docked" boxes randomly flip during a level, so I'd have to select auto launch to keep the fighters in the mothership.  Very often the groups and individual ships will change their tactics on their own, aggressive to passive, etc, between levels which is a problem when you notice half your fleet is taking fire and not engaging enemies.  Assigned groups are forgotten between levels, or all the ships in the group will not respond, and rapid reassignment is needed in the middle of fights.  Oh, and spacebar out to the long-range tactical map randomly stops working.  Often.  It's ridiculous since you need the wide shot of the battle pretty much the whole time.
Overall, I think the gameplay and controls were better with the originals.  The new overlays/graphical updates are ok, but nothing earth-shattering.  The bugs are aggravating enough for me to bounce off these games and just go play the old ones.  Still the original games themselves are fantastic.  I just don't like the update.

Otherwise known as the patience simulator, this open world hunting game is all other kinds of beauty. It has its bad points and good points, mostly good, but I think it's definitely a one-of-a-kind. At first, it is a free-to-play game, but the options are scarce, and what you can do vastly outweighs the actual point of playing.
They give you the ability to kill mule deer (males are hard to come by) and cottontail rabbits (which you can't even kill due to the caliber of the gun you are given to begin with. I upgraded to the "Wayfarer" membership and was rewarded with a shotgun (complete with basic ammo) and a revolver, both very useful weapons as now I can practically hunt anything that I want to.
The gun sounds and mechanics are beefy and feel realistic, the tracking is awesome and finally getting a kill is quite rewarding. The animals behaviours are quite accurate also, being an individual who is thoroughly intrigued by animal behaviour, I definitely felt aware of their naturalistic tendencies.
Overall, if you're looking to play a game that you have to invest a little bit of cash in to play properly, then go ahead. You won't find anything like this anywhere else.

I'll preface this by saying that I am a long-time member, with about two years of membership behind me, and another two years already paid for going ahead, the additional time coming after a hiatus and due in large part to its arrival on Steam.
I came to this game two years ago or so out of curiosity, and stayed because of how enjoyable it was.  Starting as a Free Player, I too was frustrated by the "lack" of content - whcih was even more acute back then, with only a .243 and Mule Deer on offer - no GM$ shotgun (or GM$ at all for that matter!) or cottontail as something different.  I've seen new content come over those years... Red Deer, Roe, three new reserves, countless additional weapons, equipment, and clothing options.  And I'll say this: it is totally worth it, in every way.
Buying an annual pass for about $50 as part of the Trailrunner package you get everyhthing you need to hunt, plus a year's time to hunt it in.  Compared to countless other games, it's a steal!  Sure, you have to pay an additional $35 a year to keep the bonuses you get by being a member, but remember: in a lot of other games...they update with truly new and revolutionary things once a year anyways, and they charge you full price!  For $50 you get the game...then every year thereafter, you renew your access to this game, whcih over the course of the previous year, has changed significantly and for the better!  All at reduced cost.  Where other games woudl have you pay again and again full price, the Hunter rewards you, essentially, for loyalty to it, and instead of updating just once a year and charging you for it...the game updates regularly.
Remember where I mentioned how they came out with three reserves, at least 9 rifles, 3 hand guns, 6 shotguns, 3 bows, and 2 black powder weapons? Along with 6 animals?  All this over two years.  Well they weren't dumped into the game as part of 'annual updates' that they forced you to pay for.  No, they were fed piecemeal throughout the year.  And while for the weapons, you did have to buy them, the three reserevs and all six animals were usable by mambers from the beginning, and in NOT ONE of those situations were any of the 23 new weapons they added REQUIRED to hunt these animals.  Sure, they may have made things easier or more interesting, but not once were existing weapons locked out of new animals just for sake of a cash grab.
Now, look at yoru other favorite game that comes out with a new version each and every year.  What have they added?  Probably not much. And for every 'new' feature they have added, they've probably taken out a feature - and not only that, but some of the new features are probably not even new!  Just reimaginings of existing features that in years past were also introduced them removed!    I could go on about the pricing model here, but I'll just say this as well.  While you DO have a certain degree of pay-to-play in the game itself once you get into it...it's only for expanding your options.  Whenever a new animal is released, as a member, should you buy into it, you are never locked out of a species.  it's automatically given to you.  Likewise with new areas to hunt in.  Because of this, the game is constantly changing, and indeed, updates in some fashion come once every 2-4 weeks once averaged out in my experienced play schedule
The devs themselves are also incredibly open and active, moreso on their official forum, but Alena (their PR person) certainly does her part over on the Steam areas, addressing concerns and the like.  Certainly, they are more active and engaged with teh community at large than most other devs I have played games from.
Now, after having addressed teh negative commentary from others, I'll talk about the game itself.
It realyl is a nice game, a relaxing one and one that is so different than many others that I come back to it again and again over the years, even after taking months away from here.  The environments are immersive and active, with not just the huntable wildlife but also little things like insects, rodents, birds, also ambiently adding to teh world.  ENvironmental sounds are wonderful, the graphics are nice, and indeed while in many games graphics are a nice thing to have... In here, the graphics are central to teh gameplay.  Stalking through bushes, crawling through grass, hiding behind trees and rocks to get into position to take the perfect shot...that's all key here, and it feels so very engaging because of the environment you are put into and how it looks.  Sure there are issues with the graphics (floating rocks here and there, the grass and bushes often being one-way impediments that hinder you...while the wildlife can see through them just fine) but that's not exactly an unreasonable issue, it is one I have heard they are addressing, in due time.
The tracking, stalking, and other aspects of the actual hunt are engagng and fun, and the equipment they give you access to lets you do many things...whether you buy a ghilly suit and decide to hunker down in a tree stand or in a ground blind, or use your camouflaged outfits to stalk your quarry through the dense forests...there's always a tension that you can feel while on the search.
The ballistics model of the game was always quite good, but has only gotten better with the latest patch to the game, with birdshot, bows, and crossbows soon to be overhauled as well to the new model.  There are quirks to it, but this is a game after all, and none of them are unreasonable or game-breaking by any stretch!
The animals themselves react realistically and are appropriately bold or skittish, with some animals (often higher scoring/older ones) being more skittish or unresponsive to calls or other lures...thus requiring more patience or actual stalking, while the younger, smaller, lower-scoring creatures are more likely to react, simply by virtue of their inexperience.  With their procedurally-generated trophy parts, no two animals are the same and one can tell just by looking what the score might be... Unlike some other games where the antlers are generic, with teh numbers randomized only after harvesting...this game lets you pick your target to harvest for the highest scores.
And of course, with optional contests, leaderboards and the like, there is a healthy, competitive environment to keep you always looking for that larger trophy to get yourself on the leaderboards.  And even shoudl you fail in that, the animal will be recorded into your hunter's logbook, so you can review for yourself, and see personal bests and more in your statistics.
All in all, this is a good game, and while certainly not for everyone, it is somethnig for the serious hunter, the enthusiast, or someone else who may be unable, for whatever reasons, to actualyl get into the woods and seek out game.

After playing on the founder server I decided to edit this, first of all: I did hit the recommend button for lack of a better option, but read it more as a "maybe" than a "yes".
Graphics and OST reminiscent of RO but everything else is different, gameplay is more action-based, job system is more complex and the game felt way more like a theme-park mmo with quest lines, instanced dungeons and such (it does seem to get a bit more open as you progress in the game, but don't go expecting anything like the openess of RO). Servers are under heavy load right now and lag is rampant, like every online-only game at launch.
The downside (or why I'm not sure on giving it a "yes") is seeing how IMC is treating the F2P aspect of the game. Right now the free user limitations are ridiculous and seen to do more harm than good for the game; Here are some of the things that non-premium users can't do for example: they can't use trade, can't do dungeons more than 2 times a day, can't share items between their own characters nor put more than one item on the game market besides paying 30% of their selling price as taxes while premium users pay 10%. Seems pretty bad, right? So in order to make it more "fair" to non-premiums, IMC made premium tokens tradeable and put a "free tp" system where you can earn tp (cash shop currency) by staying logged for a certain time, but the limit for this free tp is so small that it only helps gold sellers buy megaphones and spam everyone's chat, while the premium tokens can only be bought with in-game currency after tons of grinding, leaving new players without basic mmo functions such as being able to trade.
I really hope IMC sees how much being greedy can hurt this MMO and stop before it's too late, because it's a fun game with a lot of potential and I'd hate to see it ruined because of greed.

It is hardly worth reviewing this game, given the hype around it is so high that people couldn't care less about listening to other's views on it. There are many videos on youtube covering this game, guides, wikis and many other material, so if you haven't already clearly decided that this is the best game ever, you probably haven't seen enough of internet latelly, or maybe you aren't yet convinced that it is that great of a game.
If you meet any of the last cases, then maybe my review will see an use in your screen.
First of all I do not recommend this game, based on my own personal reasons, expectations, and experience with playing in two betas, and open release.
(1). Obligatory Linear Questing.
Be not swayed by the similarity and countless links to Ragnarok Online, which is the main reason of the hype surrounding this game. Tree of Savior's experience is hardly anything similar to it.
Instead of keeping it's "Soul Predecessor"'s legacy of open and free to explore world and lore, Tree of Savior falls to the exhaustively explored style of Obligatory Linear Questing, in which the player is forced to go through a linear story quest from the beginning to the end, being carried through a linear path along the maps to see the end of the story and the entire content.
Disappointing isn't enough to start describing the feeling of having to do the questing line for every character I made, which, on itself, is hardly entertaining or interesting even once. To skip dialogues is the most trivial if not natural reflex in this game, given how obvious the story is:

"Darkness was sealed by the goddesses."
"But now Darkness returned and the goddesses are nowhere"
"The chosen one (you) will find them and save the world"
That's it.
And of course, since the story is shoved in your face, that makes it even less appealing. Tree of Savior's lore isn't good enough to make a movie out of it, or cinematics, or cut scenes, or animations, ANYTHING. It is worthless. Who cares?
Instead of learning from Ragnarok Online that had a open world with lore scattered through it, and you had to, individually, find them, IF YOU WANTED TO, that made the discoveries a lot more appealing. That also led to Ragnarok Online creating individual places in the world with extremelly interesting, and sometimes creepy, stories. Some of them needed quests to be unlocked.
But no. Shove the extremelly boring and clichê story in our faces through a "Must Be Done" story quest line, like any other MMORPG in the market, because that's "just how it is done".
Bad choice developers. Bad choice.
(2). Class System Wastes It's Own Diversity Potential.
Since the game has around 80 classes, the game developers decided that they had enough classes to use and throw away. In this game, classes have linear skill power. Which means that the first classes are weaker, and the later ones stronger, turning skills and classes in the beginning of the game almost completelly useless later on.
Nevermind if you enjoyed playing one of the first classes, it will be completelly useless in the late game.
(3). Class System is Too Diverse for no Resets.
Despite having 80 classes and even many more class combinations, the game doesn't offer a class reset system.
Which is absurd. So far it seems players can only have about 22 characters, given they buy the right "Barracks" for so. Even with 22 character slots, it isn't enough to explore all the game's classes and combinations, which tells how limited the player's experience of the game is going to be.
Why not allow players to switch between classes they've unlocked, like in Final Fantasy 14, or Eden Eternal? It makes absolutelly no sense for such a design choice, given the absurd ammount of classes, and how many class choices and combinations end up breaking your character into something so useless that it gets stuck. Yes...
(4). Some Class Choices and Combinations are Useless.
If you have tried Wizard III in Tree of Savior, directly, you have discovered through the most painful way that you will have to delete your character, because it is useless. Given the diversity of class combinations, and the linear grindy questing, there are many ways to get stuck in this game with a frustrating character that doesn't work. And you can't fix that.
(5). Lack of Item Transfer Between One's Own Characters.
But hey, you can at least transfer your stuff to a new character right? If you've found yourself wanting to delete a character given how useless it is, remember that you cannot transfer all your spoils to another of your characters, unless you have help from someone else, or buy a token with real money. Way to waste someone's time!
(6). Fails to MMO.
Do you enjoy waiting for that specific mob to respawn so a high level player appears and instantly kills it? Do you enjoy competing with 8 players for 4 Tree Saps that respawn each in 5 minutes? Do you enjoy the fact that your high level character cannot play with low level characters, because the level of them will not synchronize?
Kill Steal, Resource and Mob Competition, and lack of Level Synchronization. Failures of old times, design consequences that were constant in old MMOs and tended to disappear in the last few years are back, reminding people how MMOs weren't about playing with other people, but annoying the hell of each other.
(7). Wasted Potential.
This game's design point towards the possibility of an extremelly fun dungeon-crawler, focused on the flexibility and diversity of builds, focused on killing monsters, trying different builds, and different party combinations, you know, just like Ragnarok Online.
That is almost how this game is already, except that everything is wasted on it's own limitations. Killing monsters randomly is hardly worth experience (unless you have a party that is alone in a specific juicy hunting spot, that is extremelly rare btw). Trying new builds is limited, because there is no class resets, and dungeons are extremelly hard, rare and stupid. Plus, there is no level syncronization, finding new party members becomes harder, and playing with your friends even harder.
Most of the content is focused on questing, which gives you a fractioned experience between useless and meaningless walls of texts and dumb annoying objectives, that instead of working as unique content, like in its "Soul Predecessor", Ragnarok Online, in which questing was mainly used to unlock places and obtain rare and unique equipment, in this game, and like almost any other MMORPG in the market, quests are just more of the same, they are just means to obtain XP. A completelly wasted effort to create content just for the sake of obtaining the same reward: Experience. Something that could be obtained by just killing hordes of monsters. Wasted content.
Conclusion:
As a Veteran Ragnarok Online player, and a player of over 180 hours of Tree of Savior divided in two betas I was extremelly disappointed with the way they carried the development of this game. There are many nonsensical design choices that just, clearly, remove fun from this game, turning it more inconvenient and extremelly grindy, with no respect whatsoever to the player, to the community, and to the game itself. They learned absolutelly nothing from Ragnarok Online (including the mistakes), the mechanics are mostly old fashioned, and many decisions, mostly made as a way to explore the Free to Play model, end up destroying this game's experience.
You WILL be swayed by the graphics.
You WILL be swayed by the soundtrack.
You WILL be swayed by the class options.
But eventually you will find that the game had no substance, and you will be morbidly disappointed, for the horrible failure this game is.
I'm sorry to tell, but this game isn't worth that much time, even less any coin.

I bought this outside of Steam shortly after it came out. It's a fascinating, frustrating, ultimately disappointing quasi-open-world shooting game with RPG elements. Rather like Deus Ex, the individual components are mostly rotten but they work well together and overall the game feels more than the sum of its parts. The visuals have aged well although mods can make it look even nicer. The storyline is simplistic and boils down to a lot of fetch quests. The shooting action feels unsatisfying - it strives for realism but suffers from poor enemy AI, which is either uncannily accurate or dumb. On the other hand the atmosphere and sense of being trapped in hell comes through strongly. It has a distinctive and very influential post-Soviet, post-apocalyptic rainscape mileu that must surely have influenced the zombie survival game DayZ.
The biggest problem is that the developers ran out of time. The opening levels are detailed, packed with story elements, *almost* large enough to work as an open-air sandbox although you do eventually run out of things to do. At a certain point (specifically beyond the Red Forest level) all of that drops away, and the last few levels are just on-rails shooters. Literally so in the case of the Chernobyl section, 'cause there's a bit where you run along some elevated rails. It's heartbreaking because the Pripyat and Chernobyl sections have detailed recreations of the real locations that look fantastic, and are incredibly atmospheric, but there's just nothing to do except run through them tossing grenades. In contrast the opening sections have lots of little quests but the landscape is mostly muddy fields.
Overall I remember the game fondly for its unsettling, grim atmosphere and fascinating world. It's not technically a survival horror game but there are several nervy moments, including SPOILER the underground chap who sucks out your brain SPOILER and the dog things in the spooky, radioactive forest. As a game it plays better if you add some of the copious mods that were released for it. STALKER was famously stuck in development hell for years, and in the end the developers had to chop out tonnes of content and make the remaining levels much smaller, and in the end SoC feels unfinished. It's a shame they couldn't somehow merge this and DayZ, the resulting game would be the best ever.
NB The Steam version seems to have a couple of small differences with the boxed copy - there's a lot more head bob and the mouse seems floaty.

Before I get started I’d like to say that when I first played the game it crashed after I finished the second avatar mission, then consistently crashed every time I tried to continue playing my save. They managed to patch this issue quickly, so I’ll give them credit, but I am aware that this problem was not just affecting me but everyone who was playing the game while connected to the internet. There are also performance issues in the game that seem to come out of nowhere considering I was playing the game on max setting above 60fps for most of my playtime, specifically two levels seem to make my fps drop to 30-45 for seemingly no reason. Besides, I would just like to go over my three main problems with the game in this review.
I had thoughts while playing the game like ‘this is okay’ and ‘that’s alright’ and it did not take long for those thoughts to apply to every level I played, none of them offered anything unique or fun when it comes to platforming. The optional secret levels are more interesting than the main levels since they have a gimmicks/mechanics that you must work around to beat them, rather than the main levels which just seem to be ‘get to the end’ with a lot of boring filler between the start and finish. The only positive I can think about the levels is that the environments looked nice. Forces is similar Generations/Colours but offers less alternate paths, controls even more floaty than past Modern Sonic games and is a lot more on-rails than those games too. It’s a big disappointment considering that Generations/Colours were some of the best Sonic games in my opinion and Forces seems be a watered-down version of them.

If you removed Classic Sonic from the game it would make Forces better, he feels like he has been included to just make the game a little longer and for a bit of nostalgia (which feels completely pointless with how bad the execution is). Nothing wrong with nostalgia in my opinion but his inclusion in Forces seems like a big slap in the face after playing a fantastic game like Sonic Mania. Classic Sonic somehow controls even worse than he did in Generations and at many points it felt like I was fighting with the controls to make it through the level.
Even in some of the worst games in the series, there is one thing that Sonic games have always been good at: the music. The only song I like in Forces is the cheesy main theme, almost every other song just borders on annoying. I was not expecting Forces to be an amazing game, but I was genuinely surprised with how bad the music is and it is nowhere near as catchy as other Sonic games.
I was almost at the end of the game (which takes about two hours) but I was so bored and just stopped playing, it has been refunded. If you haven’t played a Sonic game before, you won’t like this game. If you are a Sonic fan, you’ll just be disappointed again

I was extremely excited to play this game due to it getting a LOT of love on the internet among hardcore gamers.
Unfortunately, this is easily the laziest port that I have ever touched in twenty years of gaming. The control displays (when you find actions to interact with the environment) are built for an Xbox 360 controller. The PC controls are designed poorly, so poorly in fact that I found myself looking online for better options for re-binding them that were designed by a human being rather than whatever twenty fingered alien completed this port in a bar on Tatooine.
Incredibly, the PC controls are so badly designed and overly complex that re-binding it becomes a kind of sudoku/puzzle game, because any change to one key inevitably overrides another action key that was already used for. Even the options menu to change key bindings uses the same dastardly Xbox 360 button displays - this goes beyond ridiculous, and would not have been excusable ten years ago, let alone in 2014.
While I appreciate that buying an Xbox 360 controller fixes many of these issues, the one way you can guarantee you will anger your consumers is by selling a product that requires a peripheral and not advertising how important this peripheral is to being able to genuinely play the game. There are more than enough third person action games that you can play perfectly well on a keyboard and mouse, and this port was more than lazy, it was an insult to its consumers. Fans who defend the game on the basis that "you should have a 360 controller anyway for other games", actually: no. A good consumer would never support a bad port no matter how much you like the game at its core, if you do, you are nothing but a slave doing a company's PR work for it.
The atmosphere and story of this game seem good and the graphics, though looking a bit dated, can be fixed with modding, but there is absolutely no gain in value for these traits if the control aspect is so badly designed. Dark Souls II remains nothing more than a pretty picture until I go pay MicroSoft for their (in my opinion) crappy controller.
I have also seen from recent remarks on the reviews page that a new, Direct X 11 version of this game is coming out which will not be a free update for those who own this version of the game plus DLC. This, alongside an already terrible port which has been given zero care or love by its developers, is an abhorrent practice and I will be avoiding buying games made by this company in future if I see this ever again and strongly recommend doing the same.

Here are some tips for prospective new players:
- Get past the med labs. I got stuck there and it was no fun. Just get past that point and you should have the skills you need to survive the rest of the game.
- Try not to hide in lockers too much; hide under desks or behind objects if it's safe to do so!
- If you can see its face, it can probably see yours and it'll probably start snacking on it real soon.
- If you do use lockers, be warned that there are QTEs to hold your breath and lean back. You may die once or twice just learning the ropes.
- If you hold your breath while in a locker, it also drains your health. If you're at low health, you can't hold your breath for long and the xeno will rip the locker open and kill you.
- If you get stuck, try a new approach. Maybe you're playing it too safe? Sometimes you can get away with very risky moves if you're lucky.
- Use your gadgets. It's easy to get stuck if you don't have anything to help you survive. Sometimes you just need to leave a room that has no hiding places. A momentary distraction might be what you need.
It's a good game, but you can be very unlucky with the Alien's random AI. Keep your wits about you, don't be too afraid of dying, and keep persevering!

Before I start this review, I should say that I suffered from crashing once. I think it's rather childish to review bomb this game for crashing, considering Fallout 4 suffered from the same at launch (and pretty much any Bethesda game) and people don't review bomb those games. Steam reviews aren't Sega's customer support or Sega's twitter, take it up with Sega, not Steam's review service.
I ran this game with everything at the highest settings, blur turned off, 1080p resolution with an unlocked framerate (a welcomed change from Lost World's locked 60fps). My PC specs are on my profile, for those interested.
Sonic Forces is a good game that I enjoy whole heartedly. I've played a total of 3.2 hours as of writing this review and have gotten through the 14 out of the 30 stages and 2 of the 14 side missions, not including the three Episode Shadow missions.
The controls, if you've played Generations, is a bit weird to get used to at first and while it is very scripted, it's also very fun to play through.
S ranks may be easy for some (especially if you're a Sonic vet) however I'd argue they're not AS easy as Generations, however that's up for debate right now. I know that there's some stages I just haven't gotten S ranks in through normal play, however that may account for dying in the stage (I'm not sure if that effects S ranks or not, however I doubt it since you're also deducted points on how often you die).
The custom character is okay in terms of customising the base avatar with no cosmettics on, it's enough to get the job done but I wish there were more options for voices, ears, colours, and even how the mouth portion looks (including the shape and nose). It's when we get to putting items on them where everything gets better and makes your OC- I mean... avatar, look unique! If you have a Sonic OC, like myself, it'll put a gleeful smile to have your fanfics come true at last (minus the smut, this is a kids game).
The wispons seem fun to use with them being very situational at times, meaning the most useful ones (from what I can tell) are the Burst and the Lightning wispon, however I have only tried these two so I can't really comment on it just yet.
The tone of the story starts off dark (for a kids game), but it lightens up after 3-4 missions in (although the over-looming threat of Eggman and Infinite still there). While I don't remember much of SatAm, if I were to compare this game to it, I'd say it matches that tone (though, again, I don't remember it quite well).
Level design may appear bland at first sight, it can have some alternate pathways with a bit of exploring and good reaction times. I want to comment on Classic Sonic's physics and say it's better than it is in Generations, however I'll need more time to play around with him to make an official statement.
I feel that while the level design is alright in this game (considering the fact that two out of the three level designers are new people), Sega shouldn't of made this game their first project (or at least not alone, there should of been more experienced talent to assist them).
Levels are also short, like Colours, which is a pitty considering how much everyone defended every footage of gameplay with "It's the first level! Calm down!" despite Lost Valley (Modern Green Hill), Space Port, and Ghost Town (Classic Park Avenue) being the first three levels and while it is annoying that levels are so short, it's also a blessing for people who plan on picking the game up on the Nintendo Switch (like myself) for a quick rush of gameplay for a few minutes or so.
While levels are disappointingly short, they're also replayable thanks to the red rings, SOS missions, and many missions to play! After progressing somewhat in the game, you'll have access to a missions tab that'll ask you to perform certain actions in certain stages. For example, missions in this game ask you to perform Sonic's advanced movies during stages, such as: "quick step as Modern Sonic", "slide as Modern Sonic", etc. These are basic missions but they do help get unlockable customisations for the special character. However, there are daily missions too.
SOS messages are randomly occuring events where you're asked to perform one of three tasks in a stage you've previously done. These varients include: playing as a rental avatar exclusively (with no access to your avatar), completing a stage with a rental avatar (with the ability to play as your avatar), or to find a citizen in a locked box somewhere in the level and to free them before completing the stage.
You can't die in these stages or else you'll fail the mission, giving you an Unleashed-like moment of failure (remember getting a E rank and hearing a poorly orcistrated version of the main theme? Yeah, it's like that, but with Fist Bump).
Overall, I say this game will be fun for those who are already quite familiar with the Sonic series and enjoyed Colours or Generations; however if you aren't a fan then I can only say your enjoyment may vary.
