For these first 1 or 2 paragraphs, it will be a copy/pasted response explaining my lack of game time on Steam. This will be pasted to my other reviews for S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Clear Sky, and S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Call of Pripyat, only changing the games listed here. Starting from the 3rd paragraph and onwards, it will be the actual review.
I originally bought the "S.T.A.L.K.E.R. Collection" bundle for about $7.50 on Gamersgate, and back then they only gave me the DRM free(ish) versions of the game. On October 27th 2014, I was going to re-download the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. Series, as I had uninstalled it when I went on a massive uninstall spree. Only this time I noticed that GamersGate gave me Steam Keys for the entire collection! So my "XXX hrs on record" will be misleading, as I play
of S.T.A.L.K.E.R..
Now to the actual review. S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl is my favorite S.T.A.L.K.E.R.. I love the entire series, which is set in Ukraine, around the Chernobyl area a few years after the incident with the power plant. I even like Clear Sky, but Shadow of Chernobyl will always be my favorite. You start out in Cordon, an area located inside what's called "The Zone",  talking to Sidorovich. The reason you're talking to him is because near the wreckage of a crashed truck, with only amnesia and a PDA saying "Kill Strelok" to your name. You, known only as the Marked One at this point, ask Sidorovich for help in locating this Strelok, hoping that doing so will help you remember who you are. However, in return, you will need to do a few things for him, though he compensates you in return with information and some sort of good in most cases.
However, once you get that first mission from Sidorovich, you're free to do whatever you wish. You can completely ignore his task and go forth to explore the Zone. Granted, there will be a few areas you can't reach without doing the Main Missions, but a good portion of the game is available to you right off the bat.
Outside of the main quest line, which is fun and interesting, there are side quests you can find. Now, you won't find as many side quests as you would find in a quality RPG, but there's still a decent amount to find. But other than that, the Zone is a large world for you to explore, finding hidden stashes containing powerful artifacts which give passive boosts, and unique weapons. Hunting mutants and humans alike if you wish.
Also, S.T.A.L.K.E.R. has a very active mod community. Not as large as some other AAA titles communities, but still very active.
Personally, I think this game is a bit dated in the graphics department, and there are some annoying mechanics, like the fast weapon durability loss. I like to use the COMPLETE 2009 Mod, which greatly enhances the graphics and balances the game quite a bit, but still preserves the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. experience nearly perfectly. I say 'nearly' because the Complete mod is the center of many heated neckbeard arguments. The "veterans", which are just a very loud group of people both old and new to the series, claim it makes the game way too easy, and the opposite side arguing the opposite. I've seen this fight so many times with morons on both sides of the argument. The Complete mod DOES give a bit more health to just about everything, but it's not the ultra-mega game changer some make it out to be. It certainly brings the highest difficulty down from "Masochistic" to "Very Difficult", so if you want a Masochistic time, play without the mod. I'd only recommend the mod for Shadow of Chernobyl though. The Clear Sky version isn't very good and absolutely
The Call of Pripyat version, other than doing little for graphics, puts a save corrupting bug near the end of the game, I'll provide a link to the Complete 2009 ModDB page at the end of this review.

This game is an atmospheric and spooky game that takes place in an alternate universe after the chernobyl incident. In this universe, the chernobyl incident created an ever expanding zone which produces deadly anomalies and horrifying creatures whose prey consist of you.
You play as a STALKER, which basically is just a person who traverses the zone, who has suffered from some sort of amnesia. You only have one clear goal which is noted on your PDA: Kill Strelok.
Who strelok is or why you need to kill him is unknown, but you pursue this goal in hopes of finding out why you are trying kill him and what happened to you.
The game starts you in a small village with a simple goal of assisting nearby mecenaries in raiding a bandit camp, in hopes of retrieving a prisoner and a thumbdrive.
It sets the tone of the game very well. You can choose to experience the more stealthy lethal approach or the loud and proud route by talking to the head merc and choosing either option.
You get a quick feel for the tense gunplay (which I significantly recommend playing on max difficulty, it increases lethality for both sides during fights) and how the AI acts.
The game in essence is great. Sorry if the review isnt in depth, but the game is rock solid 10/10.
Though if you buy it know that you are supporting a person who practically tortured the dev team (who recieve no money from your purchase) and made them work in inhumane conditions.
No matter what way you choose to get it, this game is worth your time.

Get the community patch which upgrades graphics, enables quicker keys to save, breakable lights fixtures and more! Takes the game from good to great! STALKER is my favorite gaming style! (I got the file patch from gamefront. Its 703.1MB and an exe.
)
Sneak around and attempt to take out any force with stealth attacks. The more silent you are, the more deadly you become. When you kill an enemy, pick their body up and hide it. Enemies see only whats in their vision, and while an enemy is in-sight they appear on your mini-map. If you don't crouch, they will hear you even easier! Turn on night vision and pull out your silenced weapon to become the ultimate STALKER! (still challenging!)
Each NPC has a unique name, and they will remember if they like you. They can die from enemies too, though. The killed NPCs are replaced with half as many fresh new NPCs, most of the time, which helps the game still feel alive, and progresses. If you shoot your friend once, they will forgive you. If you shoot them twice, then its war...
There are different groups/factions. Military, Bandits, Loners, Duty, Freedom, etc. Everything is at war. If you pis-off the Military, they will attack your base. If you don't ball-up, they will all die. Game changing! Although, you can save anytime you want. Which makes winning a serious battle, actually possible. Making you the most badass in the zone! Although, no one truly knows how cool you are, due to saves! ;D  (I wish there was a video replay, where it shows you how [through saving] your character is elite.)
Mutated animals run around constantly. Sometimes you can take a souvenier from them. The types of mutated creatures become really sneaky and different than you can imagine. They will solo attack armed soldier squads too. Sometimes wiping them out. You get no rewards for helping NPC communities survive, but it is rewarding to know you just saved a friendly base.
Better equipment comes much faster from helping NPCs with a task. But you will probably gain access to much of the same guns much later on, from fallen enemies, except armor never drops from enemies. Bullets fall with gravity. You can watch a bullet fall towards a distant target. If you choose to use a sniper weapon, you will have to adjust your manual aim to compensate for this new thing called gravity. Also, the distance between you and your target feels real!
What else... there are... artifacts, which give bonuses. They are supposed to be found in anomalies, which are dangerous ghost like traps. If you hear your radiation meter going off, throw a metal bolt by pressing 6, to see if you are about to get zapped by stepping on a trap. Also, if you hear radiation, you are probably getting pummeled with radiation poisoning. Might want to step back. Suit up to get less exposure! (This seems bigger in the game Pripyat.)
Lastly, the atmosphere is really in depth. Everyone speaks with a Russian accent, and when the wind blows the bushes wave. Day/Night cycles and eating let you feel like you are really camping in the zone. Its cold and a loner's friend.

Smite is a MOBA game but with a twist. Instead of the classic MOBA style gameplay where you have to click where you want to go and the usual top down view, you play the game in third-person and use WASD to control your character and your mouse to move the camera and use auto attacks.
The game is all about the gods of different pantheons, which are constantly being updated with new gods and new skins for the existing gods. Most of the gods are also ver consistent with their lore, with *some* freedom applied to certain design choices.
The game offers different game modes, such as Conquest (classic MOBA map with 3 lanes, towers and jungle), Arena (mindless brawl with minion waves), Assault (get a random God and either re-roll or trade with teammates, only one lane with towers, can't return to fountain etc.) and more. The game is being updated at least every 2 weeks, with every 4 weeks being "major" patches which includes a new god.
For 24 euro you can buy the Ultimate God Pack, which includes ALL the gods in the game INCLUDING all future gods. That is way more generous than any of the other MOBA games, such as HOTS, where you can for the same price get 1 hero, 2 skins and a mount ... IMO, it makes Hi-Rez seem much more generous about their game than their competitors.
On top of that, there is often events/quests where you can earn gems (the currency used to buy voice packs, skins and chests) and even get a chest which can give you wards, skins and voicepacks. Every year there is a "season ticket" where you can vote for which Smite Pro team will win in a fight and earn points that also grants you items. Every year there is also the "Oddyssey" where you can buy skins and get awesome rewards.
With that said, there is sadly also some bad sides about the game...
The chests that I have mentioned before is an easy way for Hi-Rez to get their money out of people. I don't mind them persay, but lots of people have critized them for putting a lot of the skins behind these money-sucking chests, instead of making the skins available for people to buy outside these chests. (I.e. most skins cost 600 gems, while a chest cast between 200~400 gems) Others have complained that the chests are rigged and only give you the best skin(s) in the chest as the very last thing. Hi-Rez have stated they have adjusted the rolls, but that is still up for debate.
On the technical side, Smite has had its fair share of problems, some which they still havent fixed since I started playing the game. Some people had problems with the launcher not working properly, not updating or comes with errors out of nowhere. Sometimes the game ha crashed, slow at loading, at times so slow at loading you into the match lobby that you couldn't even choose a god and therefore terminate the match and get punished with 0% goodwill and unable to queue up for a new match for 5 minutes (it adds up the often this happens). In fact, most of these problems aren't your own fault, but due to bad coding/programming and servers that has been too unstable.
With that said, the game is fun to play and I've had a great time playing it (sometimes not so much when you get teammates who are dumber than a door and when you enemy team counter you so hard that you have to surrender at 10). The game offers a different take on the MOBA genre and makes the game much more fun and interesting to play than many other MOBA games. But the game also lacks many of the things that other MOBA games has that makes them better on some points, but I guess that is always the case with games in the same genre. Some has things others don't have and vice versa.

This is a pretty great MMO; the game has a unique art style and implements a sort of hack-and-slash battle system, rather than the typical DPS system that most MMOs use. I often found myself underleved in areas while still being able to conquer bosses, there is a level limit for areas though which hinders progression.    Grinding in this game is tedious as hell considering the low exp gain from monsters, your primary source of exp will be from quests where you are rewarded with the exp boosting scrolls. This, of course, is a very monotonous task that gets old really fast and almost deters you from wanting to put in the effort to progress. Some quests had glitches that also hindered progression, however, I would imagine those bugs have been fixed by now. Overall this is a pretty unique MMO and the true successor to Ragnarok Online(for those familiar with Ragnarok). I would definitely give it a shot if you are looking for a new free-to-play MMO. When I was in the Beta there was no use of currency  to purchase in-game items, but I do not think it is unfathomable that some form of "pay-to-win" method has been implemented.

This game seems to be dividing the indie community. Some call it a bland 'data checking' simulation, and they'd be right. Some call it a fantastic insight into 'eastern block' mentality and they'd be right.
In brief, in this game you play a border visa inspector, you perform well and do your duty, the state will reward you. You made mistakes, get sloppy, even get sympathetic to the resistance... then you better watch out.
In a very discreet way, this game probes your good and bad from your right and wrong. Very often you'll have someone who comes to the border that you know you SHOULD grant entry to, as all the paperwork is correct, but you know it may have negative results. Then again, you have someone who has no legitimate paperwork and yet you know the right thing to do morally is to let them in.
Overall, it is rather a bland, mundane game... but that's exactly the point, the subject matter ISN'T exciting or stimulating, if you were an actual border guard, your job simple IS to check the details are all proper and correct, but the scenarios and moral questions this game poses is quite unique and well worth playing.
As above, you will either love it or find it boring, personally, I love it.

Many reviews here seem to take have the perspective of the nostalgic, so I'd like to add that of the new(ish) player:
I hadn't played HW1 before, I had played part two in the 'classic' version.
Overall, it's a good game
I'd only buy it for the second part, not the first, which doesn't hold up that well in comparison. Hence I'd warmly recommend waiting for a steep discount before buying.
It's a fun game (/ set of games). The space setting is very well done for an RTS game, although the terrain, such as it is, tends to be rather empty. In other games, terrain use is a huge factor. Here it's more a question of fleet composition and how you use your assets.
In the remastered versions both games look very similar. Nonetheless, there are some refinements to the gameplay in HW2 which, in my mind, vastly improve it over HW1.* The main feature of each game is, of course, the campaign, but there are also custom battles if you simply want to scrap some ships. The HW1 campaign is slow and rather bland.** The HW2 campaign, on the other hand, has a similar story-line but does a lot better in setting it up.
The gameplay is very well adapted for a space-based RTS:
- No fixed base: It's a starship, so you can move it around, albeit slowly. Carriers add construction facilities and mobility.
- In lieu of terrain (e.g. high ground) it becomes very important to maintain a good overview of the battlefield
- Since it's a 3D map, attacks can come from any direction; there is little in the way of fixed base defences
- There are lots of different ship-types with varying strengths and weaknesses
- Fairly standard resource harvesting mechanic: Mine asteroids or collect debris from destroyed capital ships
- In HW2, capital ships are upgradeable with different modules, e.g. sensors, weapons buff for nearby ships or a jump module
- Modules are also targetable, e.g. you can destroy a mothership's production facilities or a cruiser's main weapons array.
- Small ships can land on some capital ships and be redeployed (e.g. after a jump)
Campaign only:
- You keep your current fleet and resources from one mission to the next
- All resources are harvested at mission end so you don't have to worry about moving on too quickly
- A downside: If your fleet was wiped out you may find you have to restart from the
mission to have chance at the next one. This is only really a problem in HW1, which has some time-critical missions that are practically impossible if you don't have the correct ships ready to go. This isn’t much of an issue in HW2.
The graphics may seem outdated, but not terribly so. It looks good in general, and the firefights and battles are very watchable, indeed. (It reminds me of the Battlestar Galactica remake, with some energy beams thrown in. Nifty!)
Overall, very good fun. Just not something to sink a lot of money into.
*Some examples:
- Everything in HW1 moves dreadfully slowly. I have spent a lot of time waiting for ships to get somewhere.
- In HW1 you can build single fighters. Naturally fragile, they need constant replacement. In HW2, small ships are built in groups of five. Individual ships may be destroyed, reducing the group's effectiveness, but are replaced when you repair (dock) that group.
- The HW1 campaign does not pause during narrated sequences (but you have no control). In extreme cases a mission can be all but lost by the time the narration has finished. It's not always skippable, either.
**I know HW1 has a soundtrack because you can buy it on steam. Otherwise I wouldn't have noticed it. The same goes for the atmosphere in HW1 in general: barely noticeable. HW2 does much better there, too.

Get the community patch which upgrades graphics, enables quicker keys to save, breakable lights fixtures and more! Takes the game from good to great! STALKER is my favorite gaming style! (I got the file patch from gamefront. Its 703.1MB and an exe.
)
Sneak around and attempt to take out any force with stealth attacks. The more silent you are, the more deadly you become. When you kill an enemy, pick their body up and hide it. Enemies see only whats in their vision, and while an enemy is in-sight they appear on your mini-map. If you don't crouch, they will hear you even easier! Turn on night vision and pull out your silenced weapon to become the ultimate STALKER! (still challenging!)
Each NPC has a unique name, and they will remember if they like you. They can die from enemies too, though. The killed NPCs are replaced with half as many fresh new NPCs, most of the time, which helps the game still feel alive, and progresses. If you shoot your friend once, they will forgive you. If you shoot them twice, then its war...
There are different groups/factions. Military, Bandits, Loners, Duty, Freedom, etc. Everything is at war. If you pis-off the Military, they will attack your base. If you don't ball-up, they will all die. Game changing! Although, you can save anytime you want. Which makes winning a serious battle, actually possible. Making you the most badass in the zone! Although, no one truly knows how cool you are, due to saves! ;D  (I wish there was a video replay, where it shows you how [through saving] your character is elite.)
Mutated animals run around constantly. Sometimes you can take a souvenier from them. The types of mutated creatures become really sneaky and different than you can imagine. They will solo attack armed soldier squads too. Sometimes wiping them out. You get no rewards for helping NPC communities survive, but it is rewarding to know you just saved a friendly base.
Better equipment comes much faster from helping NPCs with a task. But you will probably gain access to much of the same guns much later on, from fallen enemies, except armor never drops from enemies. Bullets fall with gravity. You can watch a bullet fall towards a distant target. If you choose to use a sniper weapon, you will have to adjust your manual aim to compensate for this new thing called gravity. Also, the distance between you and your target feels real!
What else... there are... artifacts, which give bonuses. They are supposed to be found in anomalies, which are dangerous ghost like traps. If you hear your radiation meter going off, throw a metal bolt by pressing 6, to see if you are about to get zapped by stepping on a trap. Also, if you hear radiation, you are probably getting pummeled with radiation poisoning. Might want to step back. Suit up to get less exposure! (This seems bigger in the game Pripyat.)
Lastly, the atmosphere is really in depth. Everyone speaks with a Russian accent, and when the wind blows the bushes wave. Day/Night cycles and eating let you feel like you are really camping in the zone. Its cold and a loner's friend.

I have around 450 hours into this game, mostly in older versions before the Steam release. It absolutely deserves the 99.9% positive rating it currently enjoys.
Sure the end game is a little weak at this time (March 2016). But each sandbox playthrough can easily take 50-200 hours, even longer if you just keep on playing. Factorio isn't really about the end game at this point, it's about the fun of getting there. It always has been. Over the last two or more years I've been playing, all of the content has improved consistently and regularly. I don't doubt this will continue. But even if the developers never touched this game again it would absolutely be worth $20. Don't let "Early access" fool you. This is a highly detailed, full-featured game that is ready to go.

Disclaimer: At the time of this writing I haven't completed the "win condition" yet. Yet.
Factorio is a game for which I have been waiting a long time. It can be a bit confusing to get started but if you can get past the somewhat bumpy start (the tutorial helps with this but I still had to do some outside research on some mechanics) there is a very addicting game waiting for you.
The premise is that you are crashlanded on an alien planet and you have to build a rocket to get off. The start certainly sounds simple. "I'll get some coal and some drills and some smelters and smelt iron ore into iron plates!" Things are going great. And then the game expands on that concept and expands on it again and what you end up with is somewhat of a logistic puzzle game involving transport of materials, designing assembly lines, and trying to balance all of your resources between everything you are using them for. Then the iron vein you were mining will run dry and you'll have to find a new patch and figure out either how to hook it in to your existing factory or tear down what you have and rethink how you were doing some things.
And all of this is made much more interesting by the research tree which, while a little too fast if you automate it correctly, consistently unlocks new technologies that make some things easier but also adds new problems to consider. So far I am most impressed by the train system in this game which made getting distant resources a lot easier, but also made me have to redesign how my resources were being transported because I, of course, didn't plan for having a train run into my factory.
And all of that without mentioning the multiplayer; so far I'm having a lot of fun with it. The multiplayer is just like the single player but everyone is building on the same factory. Currently there is no support for pvp or anything like that; well, you can certainly shoot at each other, but there aren't rival factories or anything (which I personally am ok with but some might be disappointed). No, most of the time, you are simply fighting your design, wondering WHY you put that conveyor belt THERE or the natives of the planet. See, as you burn coal and give off pollution, the lifeforms on the planet will become enraged and try to get rid of whatever is causing the pollution, so you also have means to defend yourself such as turrets and guns that you can craft.
Finally, I just want to touch on the graphics. They remind me of an updated version of the graphics I grew up with in Starcraft, Deadlock, and other PC games in the late 90s and that's one of the things I love about this game.
I highly recommend this game, but I also recognize that it may not be for everyone. If you are on the fence, be sure and try the demo!

SMITE was my introduction to the MOBA genre and I would not have it any other way. The gameplay is a great combination between a third person shooter and the strategies of a MOBA blended in the mythical blender of the gods. Ever since I started playing SMITE 8 months ago I only now begin to grasp the complex gameplay that allows for outplay more than other MOBAS like DOTA2. Although the sheer number of playable gods makes the game near unbalanceable if the player is good enough he(she) will be able to contribute to their team by utilizing the outplayability that is integrated into the game by its design.
If you have no idea what a MOBA is pick up this game. It is a great introduction and well worth devoting several hundred hours of your life into it.
Notes:

If you like MOBAs, but dislike the isometric camera, this is your game. It brings the action to you, and unlike the other MOBAs, this has 3rd Person Camera, which gives you more action without losing a bit of strategies. Teamplay is essential to win Conquest mode, but if you want, you can play Joust (3vs3) in which teamplay is less relevant, but important; or Duel (1vs1) where it doesn't exists because is only you against him.
The balancing of the game is a disaster, it goes from one side to another, which makes it funny because you have to adapt with some of the patches. The bad thing is that some gods are just too OP you can't do nothing if you don't play so much better. i.e: Susano can crush whatever is in front of him if the player knows how to use him.
And the worst thing about the game isn't any feature of the game, but the launcher. It gives so much people so many problems they just leave the game and wait until it's fixed (which is likely to be a lot of time, unless someone finds a solution, but not Hi-Rez).

Homeworld is one of my favorite games, when i heard it was coming to steam, i immediately bought it (and it was the reason i got into steam) and when i got my first game, i couldn't be more excited.
By playing both remastered and classic versions, i can see all the improvements they have done, and unlike many remasters out there in popular games, this one actually improves some gameplay mechanics rather than just giving some crispy new graphics.
Homeworld classic can be described as a gorgeous game, the universe backgrounds always give a sensation of awe and even an insight on how small we are in the universe. The gameplay is definitely a new turn on RTS games, where adding the element of 3d makes it more interesting (yet not frustrating) where most RTS games tend to be on one plane.
The movement is simple, selecting ships (by changing the focus of the camera) definitely makes it better to select groups of ships, movement and even strategy towards surprising your enemy.
The difficulty can be challenging yet by replaying levels you learn how to advance better. Some levels are hard, some are easy, and by recollecting al resources, you can build a strong fleet.
The game is fairly long and it can take a while to complete from beginning to end. With 16 levels, every single level provides a new challenge and different objectives that bring a small variety to the game.
Multiplayer is where i spend most of the time, the wide variety of maps and different forms of gameplay can abroslf oneself in, where survival and strategy (and even trying different AI's) can be very interesting.
The remastered version brings new challenges and missions for the ones trying to reach hiigara once again, adding even better graphics and new gameplay mechanics not present on the classic version.
The graphics are the first impression on the remastered version, shadows are better, textures are of higher quality, and the backgrounds by far are the best aspect of it. Being in awe of this graphical upgrade, these can be the best remasters i have ever seen.
Gameplay adds new elements not present on the classic version, such as adding cost to researching new technologies and separating formations in 2 (or more) groups in case the ship group is too big. The UI gets a whole new redesign, such as seeing the gameplay as the same time as you build ships/research/manage launching ships instead of the previous version, which you had to enter another screen to do so. Now the UI adds which group ships are active and status of ships, such as defending, attacking, harvesting, etc.
Harvester ships can now collect more rubble lying in space, which on the previous version they only harvested asteroids. Which also now in the remastered version, ships show their path trajectory, delimited by a line, these show where ships are supposed to go, these "lines" now even show which ships to attack, where will they dock, and where will the ship go to harvest.
The difficulty seems to be toned up, where now ships take more shots to be destroyed and formations take more effect into how to destroy an enemy ship. One aspect that i didn't like is the lack of consistency in tactics, where in the classical version, one could see the difference between evasive and agressive, now here both seem to be the same and asking a ship to be defensive - evasive, they still seem to hold unto the same tactic.
Multiplayer adds new elements of gameplay, for those even wanting to play with the new graphics in a classic multiplayer environment, options for "classic multiplayer match" can go on. Multiplayer even brings new races besides the Kushan and the Taiidan, the Vaygr and the Hiigarans where more variety comes into play.
Even though the cons seem to be more detailed than the pros, the pros by far outweigh the cons, making this game have a few cons amongst many many pros.
As an add-on, a mission previously cut from the original missions, and being brought back in the remastered version, we embark on an unseen adventure where our mission is to stop the Turanic raiders from reaching their homeworld. This mission was originally cut from the story due to the developers considering the mission too hard (Just like Super mario bros 2 returned in the lost levels) and also it was inconsistent for the fleet command to be chasing pirates instead of focusing on returning to their beloved planet.
What can i say about this mission? We see a new background element present to our left, which is the Turanic homeworld, an element not present anywhere else in the game. With nice detail and sharp graphics, we get to even know a little bit more about these space pirates.
The mission is very simple and straightforward, the Turanic raiders have emerged from hyperspace a few kilometers off their planet and we must destroy them before they reach safety on their planet. Armed with some frigates and scouts, we're quickly introduced towards 2 enemy carriers and many beam laser frigates (or however those enemy ships are called). When approached, the carriers will let out a swarm of fighters which slowed considerably my computer and will retaliate at any cost.
The mission itself can be easy and destroying the 2 carriers will complete the objective, the enemy didn't managed to destroy any of my frigates and focusing full firepower towards the carriers will destroy them easily. However, i won't deny that the mission was fun, playing it for the first time and finishing it left me wanting more. Fortunately, there's Homeworld 2.

Want to play a Tower Defence game in Space? Then this is the game for you. I’m not a big fan of TD games, but I can see who it can appeal to other players that do. It has a firm playability, where each planet you visit will be progressively harder than the last. There is an upgrade system for your ship and ability to unlock special weapons. There is also a plot, shown with you interacting with characters in the cut-scenes, so you are well-endowed with info about the missions and side quests.
However, the downside to this game is the lack of tutorial. All the controls needed are stated in the dialogue pop ups, but once they’re gone they’re gone. You won’t have the opportunity to view them again, nor is it available on the menu screen. Another error is misinforming the players on how to shoot – The instructions state to fire using the right mouse button, when it is actually the left.
The graphics are all right. The overall colours, environment and effects presented in the background suited that of a space themed atmosphere. There’s the occasional gradient changes, fog and asteroids, though the latter can be obstructing at times when there are multiple enemies on screen. Some overlap the moving asteroids too. In the later levels, I find much FPS drops and lag whenever there is an overload of spawning of enemies and/or effects on screen.
The BGM is fairly calm and simplistic, with most of the audio being the sound effects of your ship firing and the occasional special skills. Everything seems okay-ish, apart from the failure to establish proper controls and instructions on how to play. The graphics could also be improved for better stability.
Cosmic Dust & Rust is worth trying out, but it is not a game that I would recommend buying. I am only fortunate to have received this game from a giveaway.

I'd like to call this game the child of Fallout 3 and Metro: 2033, but that implies that it's more epic than it is.
I never played the vanilla version.  The word was the graphics were horrible and the bugs were rampant.  I went straight for the user-end patch that offered a complete graphical upgrade, bugfixes, that sort of thing.
Stalkers are basically looters inside a series of zones polluted by Chernobyl's alternate timeline fallout.  Your character was discovered amongst a pile of bodies outside a military truck, and you are nursed back to health.  The only thing you know about yourself is that you have a PDA with a single message:  kill Strelok.
SoC isn't actually that big of a game.  Each zone has your assortment of bandits, mutants, and factions that you can ally with or open fire upon.  Some encounters are random, dynamic, but some are pre-scripted.  The group of loners (your starting faction) that are defending themselves against bandits in the west end of a zone called Garbage will always be doing so no matter how many times you visit, and should any friendlies fall, they'll have randomized replacements next time.
I'll be up front with you - the story is gibberish.  I'm not even sure how much of the actual information was missing, but all of it was presented very, very badly.  Nonsensical flashbacks appear sometimes, but it's clear they had a sequel in mind to explain everything.  That may be the case, but having seen that mechanic plenty of times before, they still half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥its implementation.
The combat is challenging.  There are multiple types of ammunition, some armor piercing and others not.  Ironsights, even patched are essentially useless.  Bullets go wherever the ♥♥♥♥ they want, and you will waste entire clips trying to get ONE headshot that is EXACTLY within your sights.  Scoped headshots on the other hand are right on the money, but it'll be a little while before you can get either a scope or a weapon that already has one.  Part of the unofficial patch is supposed to improve the enemy AI.  Since I haven't heard anything about it failing to do so, I don't even want to think of how bad it must have been because it's STILL broken.  Enemies are obnoxiously perfect shots (you take extra damage from headshots) and yet somehow you can crouch and flank them and they will be completely oblivious - sometimes even ignoring you after you start shooting.  Should you sneak around and flank, frequently they'll pour whole clips into concrete walls in the direction of where you USED to be.  In any case, get used to reloading previous saves - it will happen many, many times.  Especially on the last mission where the enemies are downright CHEAP.
I'm not sure if sleep actually matters, but it's a way to pass the night.  Food matters, but there's so much of it that it isn't an intrusive mechanic.  Weapons deteriorate in condition but it happens so slowly that it doesn't matter.   Storage is a bit of an issue - always store your stuff in blue boxes (never store stuff in "stashes").  The inventory system in the game has strict encumberance, so if you're a loot ♥♥♥♥♥ it will drive you bonkers.  Take my advice and only sell artifacts after you've gotten some starter cash.
The weapon system is broad, with some degree of customization, but the truth is it's kind of wasted on the game.  It's just too short.  That's not to say there aren't things to do, but if you do minimal sidequesting, the whole game takes you about 20 hours, and it's hard to say how much of that time included reloads.  Being that there are two sequels, I see no reason to explore.  Most of the side missions have terrible rewards.
The game has great atmosphere.  It's nothing like Metro's polish, but it does the job, especially in the underground areas.  Mutants are creepy as **** and you'll always have some anticipation about what new kind you'll discover.  I feel inclined to point out that only one reload was from a mutant death.  The other several dozen reloads were from human enemies, so make of that what you will.

The Stalker series is easily some of the most fun I've had playing a video game in recent memory, surpassing even AAA titles. This is the first, Shadow of Chernobyl, and it's a very enjoyable experience.
Now that that's out of the way, I'll move on to the important stuff.
When you fire up a STALKER game for the first time, one of two things will happen; either it will load without incident, or the game will crash. It's a fact of life; the sun shines, it's currenty 8:00 AM as I write this, and STALKER games like to crash for no particular reason. Disabling the Steam overlay in-game and fiddling with the graphics options, or disabling whatever mods you may have active seems to fix most problems, but sometimes you'll get a bug that, no matter what you do, will not go away. In that case, it's time to hit the Internet and hope that someone has a fix, which, more often than not, they do.
When you do get the game to work, start it on a higher difficulty than normal. Sounds stupid, but there's a reason for that. STALKER does a lot of weird things to the guns on lower difficulties, including making a certain amount of shots (both your's and the enemy's) fade completely out of existence before hitting the target. If you're wondering why your gun isn't hitting anything even thought you've got the crosshairs on your scope lined up right on the target's head, that's why. Also, everything on the low difficulties is a bullet sponge. You are too, but only until the end, where the enemies kill you by so much as staring in your general direction. You still die fast on the higher difficulties, but now the enemies will, too. Just remember to save often to prevent crashes from erasing the last hour of progress.
If you've gathered one things from that last paragraph, it's probably that the game is pretty hard. It is, although it's also fair. You die after a few hits, but so do most enemies that aren't armored or bigger than you. In addition, every human enemy can be instantly killed by shooting them in the head with any weapon in the game (although you will need armor piercing ammo to do the same for the guys in the late-game). If you can deal with the iron sights and semi-automatic fire rate on your assault rifle, you can get through the game without much issue, although it's still a good idea to invest in better guns and optics; the iron sights on all guns tend to be a little bit hard to find. By that, I mean that the sights are off, and the bullets like to go everywhere. On the starting Makarov handgun, for example, the sights resemble a brick set between two other, differently colored bricks (although, to be fair, this is how Makarov sights look in real life). The bullets also go a little higher than you would expect. The rifles have the same problems, but they can be fixed by grabbing a scope and slapping the two together. And hey, you can take the scope off when it's time to upgrade your equipment, so you're not stuck buying another one!
Speaking of equipment, there's weapon degradation in STALKER. The good news is that, unlike the other games, you can sell your stuff no matter how broken it is. The bad news is that there's no way to fix the stuff you like. So, if you found that Desert Eagle chambered for 9x39 rounds, you might want to be careful how you use it, because that gun absolutely wrecks everything and there's only one in the entire game.
Oh yes, there's also load times. They're not that bad, but there's a lot of them. Whenever you go into a new area, it takes a few seconds to load, so get used to that.
The good news is, that's pretty much the extent of the bad. Now, let's talk about the good.
STALKER has managed to blend elements of RPG games and FPS games in a good way. It's still a FPS game, mind you, and it doesn't have experience points or any way of leveling up, but it does have a healthy amount of inventory management. During my playthrough of this game, I spent more time messing about with my guns and ammo than I did in Resident Evil 4. Be warned that bringing up your inventory does not pause the game; you can still move while rearranging things, and enemies can still attack you. If you want to pause, hit the ESC key.
The Zone is an excellent setting full of whimsy and terror. I spent just as much time frolicking over hills while drinking enough vodka to give a troubled Soviet general alcohol poisoning as I did crawling through decrepit buildings with my flashlight on, hoping a Bloodsucker wasn't waiting around the next corner, ready to tear my throat out. It really captures what it feels like living in modern-day Russia, except Russia in real life has more mutants than in STALKER.
The guns are a bit finicky, but the shooting feels fun and rewarding. The recoil is harsher than in most games, which is all the more reason why you should use semi auto.
Disregarding the crashes, the game runs pretty well. I only saw it start to sputter in a few cases, and it actually didn't crash on me that much. I believe I had an issue where it crashed whenever I tried to start a new game, and after that, it crashed two or three more times, but both of those were fixed by just firing the game up again. It wasn't as bad as New Vegas, that's for sure.
So, should you buy STALKER: Shadow of Chernobyl? That depends. If you're a fan of open-world games like New Vegas, then you will enjoy this game. I highly recommend it.

I played this during one of the betas a few months ago. Maybe I'm just too old and jaded for nostalgic video games now, but I didn't really enjoy it. I made it to about level 100 (which admittedly isn't very far in this game) and all I ever did was get shuffled around from area to area doing quests, then stop and do an instance for a couple of days to load up on exp from that. It got boring VERY quickly. The instances are fun at first, as they don't really use the "trinity" system from normal MMOs. You can go with the standard tank/healer/3dps setup or you could have 5 dps classes and as long as one or two of them has a few ranks in a heal skill normally your party would be okay.
There isn't really much point to player interaction outside of instances which is kind of sad as this is supposed to be a multiplayer game. Most MMOs seem to be going down this road though.
The class selection is vast and I think that will be the draw to this game for a lot of people. There are I think 50+ classes and HUNDREDS of combinations you can go with as each class is a "tier" and as you climb the ladder so to speak to the upper tiers you can take any class you want. If a class is really good you can choose to take that class again to make its abilities better and even get access to new abilities in some cases. There are classes even focused on non-combat stuff such as potion makers, scroll sellers (you can take any ability you have and sell a single use of it to other players, really useful for buffs and stuff) and even a class that can repair gear and give out buffs with a meal table wherever you are in the world. This is probably the high point of the game. There is so much variety between players that even if two people are the same class they could be completely different due to taking a completely different path to get to that class.
In closing this game will probably be a lot of fun for people but it definatly isn't for me. Wouldn't reccomend unless you're into min-maxing, or creating the perfect character in a game with a ton of choice.

I have a pretty good gaming computer, above the recommended specs, that has so far played every game I own on max settings. GeForce Experience automatically optimizes games' graphics settings for the best quality without losing too much performance. In the past, this auto optimization has put some settings lower than I do and am still able to play games on max settings without any noticeable performance drop. Meaning, if I had to guess, I would say GeForce Experience leans towards the lower side of graphics settings when optimizing. GF Experience recommended the optimization be max everything for this game, because, according to my hardware, my pc should handle it no problem, but on the recommended settings the game lags so much it is unplayable. Therefore, I have turned most of the settings way down and still whenever I am moving quickly, fighting, or in open areas the game lags, which is a huge negative considering how action packed this game is supposed to be. It may be a great game but it is a terrible port. I strongly discourage anyone without a super computer from buying this game. It pains me to say, but if the game means that much to you, try to play it on a console.

SMITE was my introduction to the MOBA genre and I would not have it any other way. The gameplay is a great combination between a third person shooter and the strategies of a MOBA blended in the mythical blender of the gods. Ever since I started playing SMITE 8 months ago I only now begin to grasp the complex gameplay that allows for outplay more than other MOBAS like DOTA2. Although the sheer number of playable gods makes the game near unbalanceable if the player is good enough he(she) will be able to contribute to their team by utilizing the outplayability that is integrated into the game by its design.
If you have no idea what a MOBA is pick up this game. It is a great introduction and well worth devoting several hundred hours of your life into it.
Notes:

If you like MOBAs, but dislike the isometric camera, this is your game. It brings the action to you, and unlike the other MOBAs, this has 3rd Person Camera, which gives you more action without losing a bit of strategies. Teamplay is essential to win Conquest mode, but if you want, you can play Joust (3vs3) in which teamplay is less relevant, but important; or Duel (1vs1) where it doesn't exists because is only you against him.
The balancing of the game is a disaster, it goes from one side to another, which makes it funny because you have to adapt with some of the patches. The bad thing is that some gods are just too OP you can't do nothing if you don't play so much better. i.e: Susano can crush whatever is in front of him if the player knows how to use him.
And the worst thing about the game isn't any feature of the game, but the launcher. It gives so much people so many problems they just leave the game and wait until it's fixed (which is likely to be a lot of time, unless someone finds a solution, but not Hi-Rez).

I downloaded theHunter with very little idea what to expect. I loaded the singleplayer mission, chose the default starting area, and set out. I was pleasantly surprised to have a gun range to test the beginner rifle I was given, and after getting used to the aiming set out with a cool PDA and deer call. After tracking down some deer I landed a shot, then followed the trail of the fleeing deer to the carcass. Having no experience with hunting, either virtual or in real life, I have to say hunting the deer was pretty fun.
I quit the hunt, then loaded back in, intent on hunting the other animal I was told my guest membership allowed me to kill, cottontail rabbits. After tracking one down, I shot it, only to be informed that the rifle I was using was not the proper caliber.
I looked my inventory and confirmed that I had only the single rifle.
With trepidation, I checked the store, and confirmed my fears; this game is absolutely rife with microtransactions that stain the entire genre. I'm shocked they didn't include an energy system, because they charge for just about every item or action you might want to do.
Want to hunt anything more than deer with anything other than the default rife?
Everything, from weapons to a box of ammo to equipment to hunting liscenses costs real money, at least $5 a pop.
It's a shame the developers felt gouging their customers was the only way to make money, because there's a legitimately interesting game underneath the "free to play" filth.

The game is simple. You're a bordercontrol officer (chosen from a work-lottery, no less) and you have to control that the people crossing the border has valid papers, the right papers, that they're not on the run from the law etc etc, and at the same time pay your bills and keep your family warm, fed and attended if sick. To do so you need money, and the more people you pass through the border successfully, the more money you make.
8/10.
(I lost my dear in-game son to illness btw so nobody's perfect)

How much fun can it be to check people's passports?  Well, it depends on you, but I like challenges that make me look for detail, work under pressure, etc.  Maybe because I'm a software engineer.  But in any case, depending on the type of challenge one finds "fun" one will like this game a lot or hate it.
In this game you man a checkpoint, checking people's passports and papers to see if they should be allowed through.  You also get a new set of directives each round from your fine bosses in the government: work papers required this time, no citizens from a particular country allowed, etc.  And since it's a parody of an Eastern-Bloc country under iron fist rule, you are offered bribes and such - which you can take or not, as you see fit.  You are also time-constrained because you're paid per-checkpoint person, and if you don't move fast enough you don't have enough money to feed your family, and that's one way to lose the game - your family starves or dies of illness because you couldn't buy medicine.
What makes a game fun is if one finds doing the same thing over and over fun: be it shooting monsters, hack/slash/loot, etc.  So if you find this kind of visual challenge fun, you will love the game.  If you don't, you will hate it because that's all this game is - checking passports, papers, keeping up with the politbureau dictates, etc.

-sparse and often questionable balance patches from the developers
-some game mechanics (such as invulnerability frames) are tied to framerate, and this is a pc game
-obscenely obscure lore
-broken pvp matchmaking system (lvl 150 players fighting lvl 350 players)
-the contols are more loose than its predecessor
-annoying anti-farming measures (enemies stop respawning after 10 to 15 kills or so)

-This game comes recommended.

-The main story is fun to complete the first time, but somehow manages to not be annoying the 10+ times you run through the game again to build new characters.
-Most playstyles are viable, even the more niche/creative/gimmicky ones
-Bosses are learnable, but it could still be said that they employ artificial difficulty sometimes

So, I chose to watch a bit of the anime (first 4 episodes), and I think I know what my problem with the VN is. It seems the point at which you branch onto each of the girls' routes is staggered along the common route. Michruru seems to be first, Amane, Makina, Sachi, with Yumiko being last. I chose the LAST route first, which made for a gruling grind through the common route with little action and foreshadowing. The anime also provides several in-the-moment scenes and foreshadowing scenes which hook you far more, and actually make you interested in continuing the journey through the story. It also cuts out several of the scenes from the VN that add no value to plot progression and character development, which made me not want to continue the VN more and more as I progressed. I recommend looking through a guide to see the best way to approach the routes. I'm gonna try out a route that branches earlier, then I will see if this VN deserves an upvote.

Allow me to begin by saying that this VN is certainly not bad, but not particularly high on my VNs-to-go-down-in-history list. This is where a "Neutral" button for Steam would come into play, but that is fundementally useless. However, I am leaning toward a downvote.
I played down one girl's route, Yumiko's, both good and bad endings, and it wasn't what I expected, in a bad way. For one, the bad ending just abruptly ended. I didn't even know whether I had finished the game or not. Given its rating and some of the clips from the anime that I had seen, I wasn't entirely sure what I expected, but certainly not how it actually played out. How I see it, it's a slice-of-life VN that roles into a more "loose-cannon" type of narrative that gradually tugs at your heart-strings.
Frankly, about the first 25-30 hours, it is just slice-of-life, with very occasional dabblings with some more action-packed scenes. As many have said, it gets more dramatic and emotional once you end up on one of the girls' routes at about the 30-hour mark. However, leading up to that divergence in narrative, there is so much drivel, idle chatter, romantic jokes, and attempts at humor that it gets tiresome extremely quickly. All the while, you are wondering when something of more substance will occur. I get character development, there is plenty of it, but hell they talk for the sake of talking in so many of the early scenes that it seems as if the writers didn't give a lick of consideration for the time-sink and attention readers need to give to these almost meaningless exhalations of air.
The MC, Yuuji, also came off to me as one of those characters who lost everything and ends up developing some sort of dark-humor, sarcastic facade that attempts to cast his past in shadow with an aura of mystery, when all it does is make him look like a juvenile who has yet to find out who he is and what he wants out of life. However, as you get to know him he does become somewhat likeable and endearing, while he also introduces many quotes about life, time, and society that are noteworthy, which I greatly appreciated.
The other characters exhibit your traditional tropes: kuudere, "tsundere," younger-sister figure, older-sister figure, class-rep figure. The roles were carried out flawlessly, but damn the shear amount of annoying interaction between Yuuji and the others was astronomical. Not surprising given the reason why all of them are at Mihama Academy, but it still remains a fact. Michiruru's utterances are faithly annoying throughout the entirety of the common route, aside for one particularly interesting scene. Makina is initially a bit mysterious and intriguing, which quickly falls flat on its face to expose a perturbed being that genuinely becomes somewhat charming with the unique way she talks. But this novelty eventually wears off and becomes more of a nuisance whenever Yuuji interacts with her. Amane, holy hell, the amount of romantic approaches she performs on the Yuuji goes from tantalizing to "Would you give it a break," fairly quickly. Not much to complain about with Sachi. Her devotion is admirable, but once you get familiar with her, the outcome of any interaction with her becomes fairly predictable. Now, Yumiko, my girl of choice, as it were. She is just a mysterious character for the majority of the common route. Interactions with her get extremely predictable after the first two meetings, and again with its equal dose of annoyance with how she tries to circumvent problems. However, things really take a 180 once you reach her route. A turn for the better? Eh, perhaps, but she just really needed to be honest with herself. The shear amount of time she spent denying and apologizing for things amounted to most likely 1/5 of her lines in the entire VN. Got old fast.
The artwork was perfectly acceptable, albeit with a tad low of resolution. A point of note is that some of the scenes had animated background sprites, which were very effective at adding value to the scenes. No complaints on the H-scene front, aside from the requisite comment about censorship, but that is just beating a dead horse. The voices were nothing to write home about. Entirely acceptable.
Overall, really disappointed. From what I have seen from the later VNs in the series it gets pretty interesting, and there looks to be quite a bit more action with the new introductions to the series: Phantom Trigger. However, this first installment of the series has left a sour taste in my mouth, which is a crying shame, because I went into this VN really looking to be whole-heartedly satisfied when I came out on the other side. Suffice it to say that I don't plan on
playing any of the next games in the series anytime soon.

Seems to do a rather good impression of a Kinetic Novel, as the first choice only actually comes up after about 10 hours of reading, and it comes up in a rather underwhelming situation compared to some earlier scenes where having a choice would make a pretty big difference. Almost like it started off as a Kinetic Novel and when they realized they had to have choices in it they just threw one in at the next point they could.
Overall, I'm not a huge fan of the way choices work throughout the game, will spoiler tag the explanation because it's probably better to experience it without knowing how it works when you read it yourself.
I do find the story a pretty strong point though, throughout reading this, I went through pretty much every possible feeling (unfortunately that does include the feeling of boredom, but that only happened 2-3 times throughout, and for over 60 hours, that's pretty good as far as I'm concerned). That's pretty much all I can say about the story without going on a very detailed and spoiler-filled rambling session.
The translation is okay, it does the job, there are some typos throughout, but not a lot to be concerned about. There are some times the translators very clearly took creative liberties as opposed to an actual translation, usually with the result of it varying from being kind of awkward to being utterly cringe inducing.
I'm going to sum up a couple of my problems with this in one paragraph to end this review off because they sort of mesh together for me. One of them being that the protagonist is unvoiced, it's kind of a common trope that I don't really get, it just seems to make things awkward to me, all kinds of no-name characters get voices, but for the protagonist we're just supposed to use our imagination or something? The other problem is that this release doesn't support Japanese at all. The reason I say these go together is because with the protagonist being unvoiced, and there not being any options to view anything in Japanese, you can't really follow along with a lot of the humor that's lost in translation, and a lot of it gets lost because naturally the protagonist is pretty heavily involved in a lot of the conversations.
Overall, not without its flaws, but I still very much recommend this, I was pretty much hooked on it from the time I started until I had finished every possible scene, cursing the times I had to work or sleep when caught in the middle of something particularly fascinating.

Well, what can one say about Homeworld? The first entry in the series was groundbraking in every sense of the world, and deserves its place alongside timless classics like Deus Ex and Starcraft. The second entry, cataclism has unfortunatley been lost to time, but the third entry, along with the first are parts of this collection. The third game, homeworld two, while not managing to reach the olympian hights of its predecessor, is still a solid game, with an unbelivibley well polished controlscheme, and a catalog of wonderful mods rarley found attached to any other game.
And then there is the remaster.
Finishing that aforementioned polish to a mirror sheen, whilest keeping the excellent atmosphere intact, it is one of the few remastered editions that I can wholeheartedly recommend.
Now some of you may be turned off by the legitimatley high pricetag, but keep one thing in mind.
You are buying two excellent games, with a combined singleplayer runtime of possibly above twenty hours, and their remaster, and a platform for mods ranging from Star Trek and Mass Effect to Macross and Halo, not to mention the complete recretion of the cataclysm storyline in the remstered engine.
Wait for a sale if you have to, but buy this game.

I will be 100 % honest in my review of Tropico 3.
The game itself has you be a leader of a big or small island nation, You have a lot of options in the way you want to run your country and this is one of the strongest aspects of this game. I started to really get immersed in my little island nation which was just at the brink of debt. The game is set around the Caribbean in the early 60s during the cold war tension.
Another strong aspect of this game is the political system. The two main factions of the game are the American government and the russian soviet union. Depending on the way you treat your citizens will give you an increase or a decrease in respect -  lean too much to one side however and the other goverment may decide to pay a visit to your island. You also have the people of your island's opinions to take care of and they way you deal with them is up  to you.
That's not to say the game doesn't have its problems - the game does show its age sometimes, for example in the ai path finding, I have seen people walk through one another and sometimes straight up walk through buildings. I love this game and I am happy for there to be more dlc availabale after purchase. The game's music, although repetitive, is great to listen to. Any fans of the genre of these games I highly recommend you buy this game despite it age.
It is easily a 8/10 must own for strategy fans.

This game is quite difficult, sometimes really unfair, but its still great to get through. You always get a great feeling after you finally beat a perticullarly hard part in the game. This game is defineatly not for everyone because you need to be able to stick with it and keep trying to be able to fully enjoy this game, but if you enjoy yourself a good challenge, playing through this game is fantastic.
The co-op is great, you can usually find some people to help you with most of the bosses and the harder areas. If you want to start co-op, you just have to look for a summon sign and you will be able to bring the person that put their sign down into your world. You can have up to two summons but the more people you have the harder the game gets so its not 3x easier with 3 people, but for the most part it helps you out because you can get people to do more damage, distract the enemies, and tank for you.
PvP is a pretty good part of the game as well, It has its ups and downs. under certain circumstances people can invade your world and kill you (or you kill them). if someone invades you you will be unable to leave your current map unless its to go through the boss door, one of you has to die for the PvP to end. You can summon in people to help you fight invaders, but the monsters in the map will be hostile to only you and your summons, not the invader (under most circumstances). There are a few other ways PvP can be initiated but that is the main one.
Overall this game is really enjoyable to play through and it defineatly has its moments of glory, dispair, and hilarity. As i've already said you will absolutely enjoy this game if you love yourself a challenge. If your not into really difficult games, then I would be hard pressed to find you a reason to play this game, I would only recomment this to people who are gonna keep trying even after they lose multiple times. That said though I would still say this game is worth picking up if what you've heard so far interests you at all.

My opinion: Papers, Please was a game I really enjoyed, but is definitely not for everyone.
These types of games really captivate me, and when it was announced I was really intrigued. I love games that go beyond today's formula, game's that seek to push and explore new boundaries, even if they might fail. This game is certainly one of them.
But that same thing also hurts it, and some people might find this incredibly boring. You play as an immigration officer at a checkpoint in a fictional communist state, and you process people entering the country. As you can imagine, immigration officers don't have the most exciting job. It consists of checking to make sure their passports and papers are authentic, and if so, admitting them into the country. The gameplay is virtually the same throughout the game, but somehow it manages to captivate me, and clearly tons of others as well.
The gameplay, as I said before, is largely the same. In fact, it's almost entirely scripted for the most part. On day three a certain event happens, on day eleven another does, and there's no changing it. Despite that, however, there is still an incredible chance for a diverse experience. In fact, Papers, Please has 20 endings, each occurs as a result of you doing things a certain way, and there are still a lot of choices in this linear story. One thing I really enjoyed is how the game allows you to explore all those options. The game is set to have 31 days of work (there is an endless mode for those who complete the story) and once complete a day, you are allowed to start a semi-new game from that day and make a different decision. When each day takes around 15 minutes to complete, this was a brilliant addition that removed monotonous repeats that would've made me lose interest in a flash.

TL;DR This is, by far and wide, the best Alien game ever made, on any platform. Do not miss it even if the Alien franchise is not really your thing - it's that good.
UPDATE: Finished the game. Absolutely loved it.
Some reviewers have complained about "too much backtracking" during the second half of the game. I do not understand this criticism at all - at most it takes you 5 minutes to travel across already visited places to reach a mission area.
(Note: early-game review, will most likely be expanded over time)
So far, I have no qualms saying this is by far the best Alien game I have ever played. The amount of effort (and. I dare say, love) that has been invested in it stands out at pretty much every turn.
Pros:
+ The atmosphere, no words. You simply have to experience it.
+ The environment. The attention to detail and coherence with the Alien universe is astonishing. Not a single inch of Sevastopol feels bland or uninspired.
+ The graphics. Fantastic work on item detail, lighting, and character animations (especially faces).
+ The audio. Everything from the soundtrack down to the creaking of closing lockers is near perfection, and adds an enormous sense of immersion (especially when played with headphones).
+ The voice acting. These are proper actors, and their line deliveries feel on point and authentic.
+ This game is LONG (about 20 hours on hard).
Cons:
- The AI, sometimes. Frankly, there are points where the Aliens AI just acts dumb to the point where it takes you out of the game. Even playing on hard, I have had it chase me to lockers it CLEARLY saw me enter, only to suddenly wander off in another direction once I closed the door.
- Arbitrary barriers. It does take me out of the game when a bunch of half-meter boxes effectively force me to crawl through the vents to get around them.
- Lip synch. This is just bad - none of it feels natural, and it does break immersion a bit when a character shoots of a full sentence when barely moving his/her lips. With all the amazing work that was done on the graphics, it's truly a shame this was neglected.
- The trailers. Writing this review and having the trailers playing in the background, I just realised they give away a ton of plot. Stay clear of them.
All in all, this is a great game. You owe it to yourself to give it a try.

This is one of the best visual novels I have ever experienced. In fact, one of the best reads out there. Second only to Katawa Shoujo, but as in that VN, this has me wishing I could have met the girls when I was in high school. Not sure I would have been as helpful to them as Yuuji, but... I kind of identify with them somewhat.
As you can see by the time I've spent on the game, it took me a while to get through all the routes. Now, the game centers around Kazami Yuuji, a young man with quite the past. One that is barely touched on in most routes, but the broad strokes are that he has been trained from youth an agent for some spy group (which appears to be multinational), and is agent 9029 (which based on how some of the routes mention makes him basically 007 for this organization). He simply wants a normal school experience, and this school, which has five other students, is basically the best choice. He is a second-year student.
As for the girls... I'll mention them in order of my playthrough.
Matsushima Michiru is a second-year student, sporting bleached blond twin-tails, and trying to be a tsundere (though her concept of it is a bit... odd). She is a bit of an idiot, but a well-meaning one. And frankly... she is likely much smarter than she acts. Her route was interesting, and the end of her good route may be the earliest of all of them timewise.
Sakaki Yumiko is a second-year student, and the prodigal daughter of Sakaki Michiaki, who is the President of perhaps the most powerful corporation in Japan. And since she is apparently the only daughter, her route's main issue is Daddy Dearest... Her route was also interesting, and was the first to delve slightly into Yuuji's backstory. The good route, I would say, ends at the second-longest point in time.
Suou Amane is a reddish-haired... well-developed third-year student. She is the most flirtateous with Yuuji, though that is partly due to her backstory. If you go her route, she has (in the words of Lilly from Katawa Shoujo) a "healthy adolescent sex drive".  Her route... man, her route is a tear-jerker. There are many parts of that route that can make you cry, especialy her history... and the end of the good route. Her good route ends at the latest point, by far.
Irisu Makina is an innocent and carefree first-year student. She has a bit of a lisp due to events in her past, and is the former successor of the Irisu Clan, which is a very powerful financial clique with holdings worldwide. In fact, they may well rival the Sakaki's East Beach Railway Express Group. She acts as the immature fool. Thing is, she picks up concepts very quickly, so... there may be some of that prodigy she was before the major incident in her past. She calls Yuuji "Onii-chan" at the start, and unless you go into her route, will continue to do so. Considering she technically buys you as her "Papa" if you do go into her route, she is a bit naive at times. Her route is action-packed, and while I'm not sure how I feel about the ending, seems to work. Her bad ending ends six months later, while the good ends a year later.
Komine Sachi is a pink-haired (because we need one in any VN, right?) first-year student, who... well, she acts as the maid for the school. Mostly because she cannot turn down a request, and tries to be a "good girl" at all times. While she is safe in the school, this is not so much an issue, but outside of it... this could lead to problems (one of which may have lead to her getting put in the school). She realizes early on that she has history with Yuuji. Her route has the most tear-jerker moments. And the roller-coaster of feeling is a trip, but a cathartic one. Her good ending is probably the second earliest in time period (there might be a few days difference between Michiru's and hers).
This is a phenominal story, and deserves to be read. Thing is, I'm not sure how one could continue afterwards. This alone makes me wonder if Fruit was supposed to be a standalone title, but it became so popular they put out two sequels. At least two of the routes are ill-suited for sequels simply because of how far into the future they go. Anyway, just a slight issue.
Side note: This VN, like Katawa Shoujo does not have a "True" Route. So, whichever you like most, can be the "True" route for you... at least unless the sequels change that...

Homeworld 1 is a classic for its well done story and deep mechanics, and it's inclusion to this pack alone makes it a good buy. The remasters on the other hand are dogged by problems found in Homeworld 2 as they use the same engine, and are ok but still inferior games to the first.
The reasons are complex, but boil down to the tactical depth you could achieve in HW1 thanks to the mechanics and physics system they employed to model ship to ship combat. For example, fighters have a impressive amount of maneuverability due to their speed and size, so any ship such as a frigate built to shoot at larger ships will have a hard time hitting them when the figher is at full speed. However when stationary they're sitting ducks and ANY weapon can easily hit them, which is more often than nought when they require refueling after some time in combat, or docking to get across the larger maps.
HW2 and the remakes dump this for a simpler probability and RNG based system when calculating if a shot hits, so that the same frigate would find it difficult to hit a fighter even if it was completely stationary, simply because it's classified as a fighter. Couple this with the removal of refueling, higher damage weapons that'll see your fleet destroyed and remade multiple times per mission, as well as sometime broken trigers and mechanics in singleplayer (due to being ported), and it becomes clearer why Homeworld 1 is considered a classic and it's sequels (and remasters) haven't earned nearly as much praise from players.
Buy it if you're really keen for a great (if old looking) RTS that set the standard back in 1999, otherwise wait for a sale.

As one who grew up playing the original Homeworld, I was severely disappointed by HW Remastered.
Pros: Shiny.
Cons: Too shiny, at times. The visuals are of course way better, but some maps have so much glare you can't see. On top of that, there's a massive reduction in functionality from the original game.
To name a few: projectiles still use HW2's disappointing percentage to hit based system, instead of the original's wonderful yet fair physics system. Do you want to see a single fighter flying in a straight line not be hit by literally dozens of frigates? The dumbing down of physics, of ballistics, and of ship roles is in some ways even worse than Homeworld 2. In Homeworld 2, the system may have been a step backwards, but it was *balanced*. Homeworld Remastered is an extremely unhappy marriage of Homeworld 2's inferior gameplay engine with Homeworld 1's ship statistics.
The campaign is poorly balanced to cover up the limitations of the new engine. Missile destroyers don't wipe out fighters anymore due to Hw2 engine's terrible missile physics? Add 30 assault frigates that can't hit them either! Capturing the frigates in mission 3 results in them being recycled instead of sent into your service? Send less enemy frigates! Salvage corvettes disable enemy ships before fully docking with them due to the hijack of Marine frigate code from Hw2? Popcap them low!
Trust me people, stick with your original disks, copies, whatever. Don't pay for this minimum effort pallet swap. (Yes, the models are clearly copied from the free work of modders for Hw2). And don't buy it because it has the original game, that's just sad. Homeworld 1 deserved a new engine, that could deliver a more beautiful experience of the original masterpiece, not this 3/4 finished hackjob.

I'm late to the show. I first tried STALKER when it came out half a gaming century ago, but my rig sucked. I was pleased to see, that it runs like a charm on my relatively modern machine.
First of all: The game is old. Do not expect up to date visuals, do not expect to find a modern UI. Expect to move your hand a lot over the keyboard, because those hotkeys are scattered like they were in the day. Expect to push your mouse over buttons in menus.
You should also refrain from expecting a fast paced shooter. STALKER will kick your♥♥♥♥♥ Do not expect to land a head shot with a pistol over long distances. STALKER features some pseudo realistic mechanics, which are not 1:1 real physics but give you a rough feeling about what it means to fire an old worn out gun during a rainy day at a moving target.
When I first launched the game and started moving around, I got a little dizzy, because the head bobbing is a little more than I can digest. It's an old but famous game, so naturally I looked for mods. The first hit brought me to a mod package, that tries to fix some bugs and combat annoyances, while trying to retain as much of the vanilla state as possible. Have a look at the "Zone Reclamation Project".
The difficulty is good. I play on "Veteran", the second hardest of four settings. I expected to die a lot, being punished for being careless and exactly that happens. One dog, one soldier, one mutant no problem, but as soon as I rush in and overlook one of them, the surround me and I'm dead.
I like how this game can do without pseudo RPG crap. While there is an inventory system and everything has multiple stats, there is no EXP, no skill tree and no character stat farming. Jobs (quests, missions) give you money and equipment and allow you to progress in the story.
Let's see if this turns out to be more than run around and shoot bad guys. The scenario is promising.
