Stalker is a series that is somehow both ahead of its time and dated simultaneously.
Graphically the game isn't, and never was, the hottest thing on the market. However, the world that they dev. team have created is one of the most genuinely sinister and oppressive that I have ever experienced in a game. The creatures are disturbing and dangerous, and the lighting (particularly in the darkness) effectively creates a creeping, relentless tension. The moment in the tunnels when you look back and see the silhouette of the Controller emerge for the first time (seasoned players will know what I mean) is one of the most unnerving experiences I can recall having.
Like all the games in the series, Stalker doesn't coddle its players. Starting the game is quite brutal as it can take a new player some time to come to grips to the realism of the gunplay and the initially unforgiving difficulty of the enemies. The bullet physics are realistic in that your weapons aren't perfectly accurate, nor are they entirely reliable, and misfires can be common with weapons of a low condition, so you must use your brain and know your weapons and their limitations before initiating a firefight. In saying that, the game rewards the player by lightening the load as you progress and get better weapons and armour, and by the mid-point the difficulty can lessen considerably.
The sound is here and there in terms of quality, with the voice acting being average and flat a lot of the time, however, the atmospheric sound, weapon sounds, and THAT droning voice towards the end (seasoned players will understand), really plant a disturbing and terrifying chill in your spine the whole way through. Voice acting aside, the sound in these games are one of my favourite parts.
Stalker: SoC is a game I keep coming back to replay again and again, not in the least because of the quality of the mods out there. In saying that, the world that the devs have created and the emotions that that world inspires in me remains with me for long after every play session, and I think that, once one gets past the initial hurdles that the game places in front of you, this is one of the best post-apocalyptic games I've ever played. I feel that, whereas classics like Bioshock (for a random example) are fantastic games that appeal to everyone, cult classics are fantastic games that are an acquired taste. This is very much, in my mind, the absolute definition of cult classic. I highly recommend it (with a good mod like COMPLETE if you wish to smooth the creases out) to anyone looking for a deep, memorable and unsettling FPS experience.

As of only an hour into the game it's still pretty early to fully review it, but so far it's pretty easy and capturing.
There's some issues with trying to get into the game, logging in, loading the T&C's - but keep trying and you'll get in.
First off I had a little difficulting beginning by finding an asteroid belt - You've just got to fly into a star directly and it'll open up the system. Navigating is pretty easy and straight forward - and it looks amazing just flying around in space.
Once you select your asteroid belt and begin forming your planet you'll be inundated with asteroids flying at your planet. You'll have to choose which ones you want to impact your planet, some will be good and some will be bad. Some will be a mixture of both, it's up to you to decide what is going to best. This can be pretty intense with 10 asteroids coming at you at once - so you've got to be quick. Once you've created the planet through the tutorial, you pretty much have to find your way from there trying to build.
Starting off building may take some time to get used to, knowing which buildings require what resources - but hovering over images will give you a lot of help. So far there seems to be texturing issues. I.e My planet is still a rock with two icy poles North and South, and none of the buildings showing up. But this is apparently being worked on. It took a little while for me to work out how to place a building since I couldn't actually see it - nor could I figure out why I couldn't place it. You've just go to zoom in close to the planet.
Your workforce is divided into Male and Female workers, each have their own bonus' for production - something that impacts your resource gathering speed and efficiency. Depending on which one you have more vagrant, you'll have more of them recreating. More men vagrant > higher men produced and the same for women. (Vagrants are the people you don't have assigned to a job.)
The game will run even if you're not on it, so you could either play constantly or come back now and again to check your planet hasn't starved to death.
So far you can only inhabit ONE planet, but you can create more, and so far there's only the building aspect unlocked, Ship building, government and quests are all locked until future updates. You cannot rename your planet as of yet. And it takes a while for you to build up enough population to build quickly. There are also difficulties figuring out the UI - there are no check boxes to close windows, but if you click the top-right corner you can close them. I found myself stuck on a window unable to do anything for 5 minutes clicking left right and centre trying to close it.
All in all, this is can either be a hands-on resource management, 'World building' game where you constantly re-assign your work force to speed up your building, or you can come-and-go every now and again to continue building a better world for your citizens.
I would recommend this game but it most definitely is not anywhere near being complete, and if you like staring at a rotating sphere constantly then get it. But when some of the teething problems have been solved it'll definitely be worth playing - especially since it's free. I will stress that it is only teething problems so far I've encountered and not any game-breaking bugs. I'll update this review as things continue.

Grisaia no Kajitsu is an expansive virtual novel which took around 70 hours to complete all its routes and good/bad endings. Appealing art as well as amazing narration by the main character (and occasionally heroines) with god-tier voice actors makes for pretty comfy viewing. Balancing between the drama and comedy that the series is known for Grisaia no Kajitsu doesn’t become tedious even after a lengthy playtime.
Fans and critics of the anime adaptation will enjoy this because the depth of each character’s story and background are immensely expanded upon. The plot and emotions from this VN simply could not be condensed into 13 episodes with a total runtime of approximately 4.5 hours.
It's not without its failures. A slow start during the "common route" and some generous interpretation of mental health for the sake of the story (eg
) could turn some people away if they do not progress far enough into the main storylines or onto another route.
The steam release gave us the potential to collect valuable market items and I was able to recoup the cost of the game on sale after crafting cards and getting lucky with drops. However, a steam release also meant the removal of R18 content along with some of the more risqué humour leaving fans of the series with the choice of playing the game with some content cut, purchasing the unrated version directly from Denpasoft, or installing unofficial patches.
An amazing VN and entry into the Grisaia franchise.

I won't comment on the payment system since other reviewers have done so at length. Trust me, I agree with them about 90% (the other 10% is understanding the hours I put into this game ended up being well worth the price. Still begrudgingly, though).
I'll focus on a brief recommendation for gameplay:
This is a game for those who love stealth and being rewarded for patience and diligence. This isn't an arcade in which you'll recieve constant gratification: you have to earn your satisfaction here. There is nothing like spending hours on a game and finally, FINALLY bagging the most beautiful and rare animal you've ever spotted. If you are interested in the semi-realistic hunting genre, but are sick of arcade-style Cabela games, this is absolutely the game for you. Try it out, hunt some Mule Deer, and if you like it, try picking up a subscription. The game is not free-to-play by any but the most technical of means, but I've found so much enjoyment out of it that I believe it is worth some amount of money. Decide for yourself which animals you are interested in hunting and just how much you might be willing to spend. The pay wall is indeed horrific and I won't defend it, but I still feel the need to encourage people who might be genuinely interested in such a unique and satisfying game.

Full :
Welp, this game came a long way since it's release, not a performace wise mind you, but with amount of content and a cool stuff you get from XL edition. New storylines, new guns, new vehicles, new missions, new islands, jetpack, it's all good fun, especially if you get it on sale ( which i do recommend ).
While it's all well and good, this game runs abysmal on budgets gaming systems ( and sometimes on real gaming pc's ). It took me a substantial upgrade to finally and truly enjoy this game. I had this game on day one ( and then got a refund ), and apart from initial graphical glitches it ran absolutely horrible, stuttered every 2 seconds, slowed down time, skipped frames.
My old sytem was :
AMD Athlon x4 860k @3.8Ghz
r9 380 2gb
8gb of DDR3 Ram at 1866Mhz.
Whatever system specs page says is a bull, you cannot run this game smoothly at 8gb of ram. After relatively short amount of time game will get well over 8gb of ram, for me it's ~9.1gb of ram ( with nothing but steam running on background ) after 10 minutes of play. Here's some data from MSI Afterburner ( RivaTuner ) :
You can see that game chews up almost 9gb of ram after just a few minutes of playtime, and it will get worse, ~10gb after few hours if you travel a lot. Not only that, but CPU load is 100% on all 4 cores at relatively empty area with nothing going on.
Same goes for VRAM, i've tested this game on my old r9 380, it plays well, but again, after some time game will chew up more than 2gb of vram even at 768p.
Next one is CPU requirement. This game is brutal when it comes to CPU, i own no game that loads up CPU to 100% at most of the times ( even gta 5 doesn't do that ), except Cities : Skylines, which is a huge city simulator. But i can see why that is. There's a lot of going on in this game, a lot of realtime physics simulations, AI, huge detailed explosions and other particle effects, physics based destruction, all of that is really hard to pull off. So make sure you have decent CPU to handle it all. I might suggest that my CPU ( i5 4570s ) might be a little bit too weak in super complex exploding action situations, consider it as a minimum when you pick up this game.
As for GPU, well, it's hard to tell, just make sure you have something decent and have over 2gb of vram, it doesn't matter AMD or Nvidia, though Nvidia cards run this game better.
Oh, yeah, game is very fun too, if you liked previous game you'll like this one too quite a bit. Even though unlocking upgrades system will drive you mad at first.

I understand the people in the community who wrote this game off back when it first launched but from what I have experienced after playing it for about a year now is the fact that the devs at zenimax actually care about this game and work constantly to improve it for its playerbase and that alone speaks volumes.
Pros & Cons
Pros: There are a lot of things this game gets right, character creation for one was great because it offers more in depth customizing like adjusting height, weight and  build, as well as applying lore friendly tattoos and face paints and even choosing from a selection of voices to have for battle grunts in combat.On the topic of customization the smithing in the game allows for cultural variants of every weapon type which is something i simply adore, one of my personal gripes with skyrim was how nearly everyone wielded a nordic style weapon regardless of race, place of origin etc. The biggest positive this game offers in my opinion is the exploration of multiple provinces, which gives it a lot of replay value as well as providing lore on areas that bethesda either refuses to revisit for an upcoming tes or has yet to cover.
Cons: I want to preface this by saying my gripes are completely subjective. The easiest negative this game has is its grind, which are the MMO elements in this mmorpg, to some this is a plus but for me it's simply tedious, and by the grind I mean the sole driving force behind progression in any form of combat in this game, smithing. I personally hate the fact I have to either search for raw materials or buy them from guilds, it doesn't make sense as to why a smith wouldn't have ore/ingots laying around for sale. That grind somehow extends to even magicka, as even mages have to grind out woodcrafting for staves.
Verdict: I can't speak for the PvP experience in this game but the PvE and main quest in short borrow a lot from oblivion, you can tell the devs drew inspiration from the narrative in that game, if you enjoyed that, you'll enjoy this and if you are tired of exploring the same old provinces of skyrim, cyrodiil and morrowind, I highly recommend giving zones like hammerfell, summerset high rock and black marsh a shot as they contain plenty of new interesting lore all while providing a different landscape to explore.
4 out of 5

My opinion: Papers, Please was a game I really enjoyed, but is definitely not for everyone.
These types of games really captivate me, and when it was announced I was really intrigued. I love games that go beyond today's formula, game's that seek to push and explore new boundaries, even if they might fail. This game is certainly one of them.
But that same thing also hurts it, and some people might find this incredibly boring. You play as an immigration officer at a checkpoint in a fictional communist state, and you process people entering the country. As you can imagine, immigration officers don't have the most exciting job. It consists of checking to make sure their passports and papers are authentic, and if so, admitting them into the country. The gameplay is virtually the same throughout the game, but somehow it manages to captivate me, and clearly tons of others as well.
The gameplay, as I said before, is largely the same. In fact, it's almost entirely scripted for the most part. On day three a certain event happens, on day eleven another does, and there's no changing it. Despite that, however, there is still an incredible chance for a diverse experience. In fact, Papers, Please has 20 endings, each occurs as a result of you doing things a certain way, and there are still a lot of choices in this linear story. One thing I really enjoyed is how the game allows you to explore all those options. The game is set to have 31 days of work (there is an endless mode for those who complete the story) and once complete a day, you are allowed to start a semi-new game from that day and make a different decision. When each day takes around 15 minutes to complete, this was a brilliant addition that removed monotonous repeats that would've made me lose interest in a flash.

This game is basically an FPS RPG set in an alternate reality after a second Chernobyl event, that creates a highly irradiated area known as THE ZONE filled with artifacts (loot), anomalies (radioactive traps), and mutants (MUTANTS).  I have been playing this game since 2007, on again, off again, and I am finally ready to say I can not rightfully recommend this game, even though I've logged 98 (semi)enjoyable hours playing it.  This game is the kind of game that reminded me why I love games, and why I hate some of them.
For the longest time, I couldn't really tell what I was playing.  It seems like an FPS with a run-of-the-mill post apocalypse amnesia story, and I began to play it as an FPS shooter, hoarding everything, and taking every mission I can, like I was playing RAGE or something.  This is not how you play S.T.A.L.K.E.R. games.  It is an RPG that you have to take your time with in order to immerse yourself in the game's story.  You must understand different social influences, environmental threats, and simple survival needs the zone might present to you in order to react to your situations properly.  Most importantly, you can not hoard loot. If you like Infinity Engine inventories (e.g. Baldur's Gate) where inventory management is an entirely different game, you will LOVE the inventory management in S.T.A.L.K.E.R.
The environments are beautiful for a 2007 engine, and surprisingly great even today, especially with mods like S.T.A.L.K.E.R. complete.  The loot is good, the story is fascinating, and the monsters are scary.  The game blends between open-world exploration and survival horror corridors pretty fantastically.  You tell yourself one more mission, and then the sun is up.  This game will suck you in completely.  This is good, because stalker has a very intense pretty learning curve (as I discussed earlier) and basically requires that you play it in "hardcore" mode.  You are constantly negotiating between different environmental threats, and sudden mutant/bandit attacks.  Not only are there bandits that might attack you, but there are different factions with different goals for The Zone - the missions you accept and many of the actions you take will affect their attitudes towards you, potentially creating other threats.  The most mundane actions are life threatening in the brutal world of S.T.A.L.K.E.R.
Why don't I love this game?  Well, remember how I said I've been playing since 2007 and I've logged 98 hours?  That's because this game is insanely glitchy.  I have run into numerous game breaking bugs that have forced me to start over.  It has a really good save menu, so if you don't use quicksave for days at a time (like I do) you'll be fine.  You can reload to a save point before when a friendly faction suddenly decides to shoot you in the face instead of paying for a mission for NO REASON AT ALL.  You won't have to accept the fact that your character is stuck in the wall now, and the game is anti-climatically over.
It's a shame, I can not get through this fantastically designed but poorly executed buggy game. It's one of the most refreshing games I've played in a long time.  It appeals to my old school PC Gamer side, and I love every bit of it - the game allows you to pick missions freely, explore the world an in open-fashion, and progress to the end at your own pace in an environment that is constantly engaging - I've just had that experience unplugged on me too many times.

So, after beating the entire game i can say that:
The game is good. Some people are still however complaining about the crash problem which... got patched in 30 minutes - 1 hour after the game got released.
Pros:
+Awesome graphics
+Incredible story, one of the best in the franchise
+Gameplay is good
+Huge customization options, it's a plus itself that you can create your own character.
+You can play as Shadow on some of the speedrun levels of Modern Sonic (only a model change)
+Free DLCs
+Didn't notice any FPS problems during Gameplay
+Music
Cons:
-Low FPS in cutscenes (May be fixed later on)
-Controls of Modern Sonic in 2D sections are... Just, come on...
-Game is unfortunately short
-Classic Sonic got way too low amount of screen time
-Weapons doesn't matter too much because flamethrower is S+ Tier
Overall - 8/10
-Is it worth 40 Euros?
I would personally say, it matters if you like Sonic.
Sonic franchise never had many good (3D) games, and this one is good. I would personally buy this one over, for example, Lost World.

I'm sad however weapons cannot be painted.
-Does the game really have that big customization?
Hell yes. You have plenty of cosmetic items, each for head, glasses, face, body etc.
You can choose a gender, race, almost everything.
This game has really incredible customization, considering it's Sonic game - a game about speed, not a dress up game.
-What can you do after beating the story?
Easy, 100% the game. This will take you plenty of time, believe me.
-What about (SPOILERS) Super Sonic?
It's not in the game yet. It's gonna be added as a (probably) DLC in the future, stay calm.
-What is the biggest disappointment for you?
Length of the story. It's incredibly short.
Also, screw the final boss' second phase.
That's everything from me. I liked it, sadly i completed the story in 4-5 hours.

This is the first time I've played a "remastered" game, but after finishing the Homeworld 1 Remastered campaign tonight, I have to say that this most definitely isn't just Homeworld Classic with spruced up graphics and modelling. There is no doubt in my mind that Remastered is the version to get for someone new to the Homeworld franchise, but at the same time, for players that grew up with and loved the original, some aspects of the Remastered version can be jarring.
Homeworld is the first significant RTS that let you use all 3 dimensions, and it's known for its strong story and interesting units. Remastered remains true to these roots, but it also takes lessons learned from later Homeworld games to try to make the original game more accessible and playable. The updated interface and units look fantastic, but Remastered is not without controversy because it tries to recreate Classic game mecahnics using lots of Homeworld 2 DNA, and while the results were generally good, not everything translated well. In the end, while Remastered is /similar/ to Homeworld Classic, there are plenty of subtle and not so subtle differences that make Remastered play like a strangely different game.
Below is an incomplete list of the differences I noticed during my playthrough:
1) Fighters are Corvettes are totally different. Fighteres seem to do less damage and are less durable overall, and you can no longer put them in a single gigantic formation. Corvettes don't seem to work as well against fighters anymore, but they seem to hurt frigates more.
2) Formation size is no longer determined by the player...the game breaks your large selection into supposedly "optimal" sub-formations. Gone are the days where you can put 40 Ion frigates into a single imposing wall of death.
3) Units tend to break formation, even frigates and capital ships. This bothered me quite a bit because my fleet didn't feel like a cohesive fighting machine as before.
4) You can no longer re-arrange your units back into Military Parade formation.
5) Depending on how you play, there are some scripting errors in missions. For example, I never got the option to research Multigun Corvettes in Gardens of Kadesh, and I had to finish the game without them.
6) You need more Salvage Corvettes to grab capital ships...4 for a Destroyer, 6 for a Carrier or Heavy Cruiser
7) The final mission seems to be buggy in terms of difficulty scaling. I started the Hiigara mission with 42 Ion frigates and something like 16 Destroyers and 5 Heavy Cruisers (salvaged from previous missions), and Remastered basically threw, on my doorstep, at least 60 frigates, 6 destroyers, and a heavy cruiser within 60 seconds of mission start. I'd lose my mothership in less than a minute because my ships with heavy guns start too far away to make it back to the mothership in time. The only way I beat the game was to retire 16 ion frigates at the end of Chapel Perilous.
8) Probes don't spin in flight and the fully completed research ship is stationary too.
9) Either the Assault Frigate or the Destroyer (I haven't figured out which one) will sometimes announce "Flak Frigate heavily damaged"
10) You get a lot more RU's in Remastered...In Classic, I never felt like I had a real RU surplus until near the end, but in Remastered, I had more than 20K by the 5th mission and I never gave a second thought to resourcing after that. The auto-harvest mechanic is also kind of funky...I didn't even bother sending resource collectors out in Supernova Station, but ended up getting 25K+ resources anyway.
11) The firing animations are quite different in a bad way. There used to be a recoil effect on guns that weren't ions that even corvettes had...but in Remastered, the guns seem to go pew pew instead of boom. Watching ship combat up close just isn't as cool without the recoil effect.
12) Frigates and Capital ships don't "burn" anymore...you do see some pretty cool looking hull damage but they don't vent plasma-like stuff anymore.
13) The sensor manager view is prettier and more usable, but it's not as clear as the original...dust clouds are practically invisible in Homeworld Remastered but they were very much discernable in Classic.
14) While you have the option to order strikecraft to kamikaze, the mechanic seems buggy at best. I sent 60 fighters to their glorious deaths but the enemy destroyer I targeted just shrugged it off.

Since the release of the Homeworld Remastered 2.0 patch, a lot of the initial problems that plagued this game have now been fixed, including formations and ballistic trajectories--two of the most important aspects of Homeworld 1. Now, in both Homeworld 1 and Homeworld 2 Remastered, the iron grip of the RNG has relaxed, and the game functions a lot more like it did in the original Homeworld 1.
When I first bought this game, I was greatly disappointed by how Homeworld 1 Remastered was essentially broken. With the patch, however, I can safely say that the Remastered edition does justice to both Homeworld 1 and Homeworld 2. It's incredibly fun to play, blending the playstyles of both games beautifully. The only thing that's still lacking is tactics, as it still seems that it's optimal for all ships to be on aggressive tactics at all times, due to the damage boost.
I look forward to playing through the campaigns again, now that the fixes have been made. It's been incredibly relieving to finally feel as though this game does justice to the games I loved growing up, and I can't wait to play more of it.

More open and easy to learn than the last souls game, although lacking in a few areas. The main games environments are fairly nice to look at, though don't often feel too creative (then again, none of the souls games have had "creative" levels, only atmospheric). However, that is addressed within the DLC available for the game with each carrying some interesting level design, and clever shortcuts. Mechanically, it is almost the same as Dark Souls save for a few changes: poise, and a i-frames on dodges. Poise seems to work mainly while still or swinging weapons, where as in DKS1 it was a constant. The i-frames in all dodges are affected by a stat called adaptability, where 25 is a solid soft cap for average i-frames, and 38(sometimes 39) is the best for dodging overall. Coming from DKS1 to 2, it feels slightly unfair, however when recognizing that the game was designed around these changes leaves one more at ease. With i-frames being a variable, they allow you to purchase life gems, or over time healing items, in a limitless supply. With the changes to poise being reflected in armor providing better defense as you level, as well as poise and poise-break bolstering rings. If one takes the time to practice rolling, it becomes roughly as easy as in dks1, however it is not anywhere near as forgiving without a higher level ADP, to balance that demand, the game has lower costs for leveling compared to previous souls games, and to balance that, limited spawns for enemies but can be replenished with in game, farmable items which essentially bring it back to a limitless spawn(these items do however raise the area difficulty by a NG cycle, so keep that in mind).
If you can get this game with the DLC intact, then do it, if you've been wanting to try the game. Otherwise, wait till it goes on sale, the same as with any other game. I still enjoyed this installment despite it being relatively unloved by past Souls fans, even as I too was one to disapprove of it; so take it from a once hater to now lover, it isn't as awful as you may have heard, it is quite the opposite.

I really wanted to this game to be great. I've been a fan of Sonic since the original game. I did kind of fall out of the series before 06, as I didn't really have the consoles to play it, and once I did, it already was old news. Sonic Mania really grabed my attention, and before it came out I went on a Sonic spree, experiancing many of the games I missed out on. While there many games I have yet to try, I was having a blast experiancing Sonic again, particularly Sonic Generations and Mania.
Peoples opinions on Sonic seemed to be a conviluted mess though. There were a lot of people hating of Sonic for one reason or another. I mean I understand if you don't like a game, but this level of hate just seemed so unpresidented. For me this made the reviews and opionions of the fans unreliable, and I knew I would have to play the game for myself.
Unfortunately, with great dismay, I have to say that I find this game to be pretty bad.
The stages are extremly short; with the ones I tried being only about a minute each. Short levels are not always a bad thing, but you comple it and there is no satisfaction. I know a big concern online was that it was too linear, well forget about that, the real problem is that this game feels so one dimensional with no real dynamics to the gameplay. This goes for all characters, Modern Sonic, Classic Sonic, and the avatar.
From what I've seen from the story, it is a little corney, but ultimately feels really bland. Most of the character interactions feel really lifeless, and you don't really get the sense of impending doom. Now this is a Sonic game, the story if supposed to be simple, but this just feels like really lazy writting and it doesn't give you any overhead sense that everyone is in danger.
In the end, I just can't recomend this game. I realize that Sega is in a weird spot with how there is so many conflicting opinions among Sonic fans, but this was really below the bar.

The only game I have ever seen that actually includes 'Moral Choices'. Not the kind in Mass Effect or the likes where you click a button and get a different ending where someone wears a slightly different hat or something, but as you play through the game you discover just how easier it is to slip into corruption when your family's lives are at stake.
It really is quite that simple. You work at the Border Checkpoint and have to check through people's paperwork as they try to get into the country, however many of them will try to use fake documents to sneak through. You have to pay attention to their birthdates, issuing country, expiry date and, letter on, things like there reason for coming to the country or quite simply their height. If you get one wrong, you get a beating from your boss and, if it happens too much, you start having your pay docked. Seeing as you get paid a measly amount, the fine you recieve can quite often be the difference between feeding your family, or watching them starve.
You soon realise how rare money is and how hard it is to come by, until eventually you find your own principles going out the window as you accept bribes just to stay alive. It comes to the point where you have a woman begging to come in to see her son, that she hasn't seen for six years, but you know that if you accept you lose the ability for pay for the heating in the middle of winter.
Papers, Please is, to me, just about a perfect game. It may not be the prettiest or the most complex, but it intigrates choice superbly into the game play and manages to get across a complex narrative without having to ramble on through cutscenes. You are always in control. You are the one rejected a woman who will be put to death if she returns to her country. You are the one who lets a serial killer through because you lose pay if you don't. The choices and the consequences are always in your hands.

The game is very well made, attention to detail is stunning. I was really surprised that its creators are Creative Assembly that make Total War games. First (?) attempt at stealth horror and such terrific success.
Story, characters, acting, everything is top notch. It's too bad these developers aren't making System Shock 3 right now, they would make a masterpiece. This is basically a System Shock like game, but one of the enemies you encounter is unkillable. Remove this, and you'll get a perfect System Shock sequel, a 'thinking man's shooter' instead of a horror game, like 'Aliens' was an action movie after 'Alien' horror. Anyway, if you like System Shock classics, you'll enjoy this one - loads of hacking, engineering, system overrides, audio logs, androids, complex levels - but with a scary arch-enemy that is almost always on your toes so you have little time to enjoy all this stuff. Oh well.
It is scary, so be prepared. It is even more scary in Stereo 3D, but looks really great. If you have nVidia 3D Vision setup, install the patch from HelixMod website that improves the quality of stereo. And if you play on a passive 3D TV like me, make sure to install the monitor driver ovverride to play in proper 1920x1080x60 mode instead of 24 fps (google 'pasive 3dtv edid override').

Ok then - theHunter.
It's rivalling in terms of hours played my other big favourite of the moment, DayZ, and I'd like to tell you why.
Firstly I am a real life hunter and shooter, but living in the UK access to real weapons and hunting isn't always easy. So when I saw this game for free, I thought it's worth giving a go. I haven't seen another game in this niche for 10 years, so I was keen to see what it offers.
I'm going to deal with the free to play issue. This game can be played for free. You can access all areas of the reserves straight away, and beautiful they are. Yes you are given two weapons for ffree - a scoped .243 and a 12 bore shotgun, but these two weapons are good for all but one species on the many reserves you can hunt on, and have limitless ammo. In terms of what you can hunt, you are restricted to one species of deer to start with but can also hunt three variants of rabbits plus pheasants for free. Additionally you will get two extra species free to hunt every week on a rotating basis
Yes there is downloadable content to buy - if you want to - but it's not at all necessary for the enjoyment of the game. I compare it to a well known MMO tank game; you can do it all for free if you want and earn your way to stuff in game play or you can add real money and do it quicker and funner. TheHunter's the same - it gives you the option to use real money if you really want to.
Pricing if you want to use real cash? Well it's minimal. Yes there is the option to buy a membership which for me is 8 English pence a day giving me licenses for all animals on the reserves plus free reloads of ammo. In terms of £ spent to hours played, as I have bought some extras, I'm on about £40 for over 200 hours, and I can see the hours going up and the £ spent staying at about £40. Considering I was charged £1 to aprk for 30 minutes today in town, I don't find this bad value for money at all.
Game play and graphics are ok - I do find it very immersive with TrackIR and Dolby 7.1 headphones. 60fps at highest graphic settings doesn't strain my middle of the road desk top PC.
What makes this game a challenge is that stalking and fieldcraft are probably more important than the shooting element. This is not some sort of immersive shooting gallery. Game can be elusive, wary, spookable, and even dangerous. If all you require is a game to blast holes in things try Sniper Elite.
The only downside for me is that the designers have had to make some gameplay approximations and simplifications which make the game less realistic, and less of a challenge. The most notable one for me is that the rifle trajectories are effectively flat, and range finding isn't really part of the game as your encounter ranges tend to be well under 50 metres. There's no wind effect on the shot either, so real life skills of range finding, usind hold over for range, and allowing for the wind don't appear here which is a shame.
Game play summary: you will spend a lot of time walking slowly from cover to cover straining your ears and eyes for the signs of animals which you can then track and if you get it right you will eventually see them and get in a position to shoot. A critic called it a walking simulator - sounds like he was a poor hunter as stealth is the key.
So thinking of trying it? Well all you have to lose is the download time to your disc. If you like the first couple of hours you'll probably decide to splash a little cash for a basic membership to give you quicker access to hunting species other than the free mule deer.
I've seen a review below where someone makes out that if you want to play the game you need to buy this and buy that and the sums run into large amounts of $. It's not so. You do not need to buy every bit of kit in the game - one shotgun with its birdshot, buckshot and solid slug will let you take on every single species on the map.
So that's it for me. It is a good hunting simulator. There is Gucci gear available for real £ but you can do a lot with a very little £. You can do massive amounts with no £ at all as long as you accept:
a) you need to work your way up the game to earn in game currency
b) you need to use the right skills to do this - play like a CoD buffoon and you'll never succeed
c) that people with real £ can buy goodies if they want to without stopping the game being free to play
d) that there is no 'win' in this game other than the satisfaction you get from hunting with skill

Extremly atmospheric  game with a rich universe set in the aftermath of the Cherno disaster in Ukraine centering around the exlusion zone where strange anomlys and mutants has appeared.
Central points of the game is Scavenging, Collecting Artifacts and surviving mutants and Cheeki Breekis while advancing the plot of the game.
Gunplay is somewhat accurat with balistics and damage modules and is further improved trought Mods along with Gameplay and Grapichs.
Downside is that it might not appeal to some people.

This game takes place in 2011, after when supernatural events start occuring around Chernobyl, and outlaw treasure hunters called stalkers swarm the area, looking for valuble "artifacts" created by said events, battling mutants, radiation, said events, each other, bandits, and the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
It's a mostly FPS, with small RPG elements.
The game is split up into a couple open areas, seperated by hills with impassable radiation, and brought together with convienent paths with loading screens.
It has horror elements, with monsters that literally jump you from out of nowhere, and forboding dark underground laboratory.
The lowest difficulty isn't very forgiving. Guns are very inaccurate, Ammo is expensive, and headshots are one hit kills.
It captures a great atmosphere, done with simple things like surviving on two sasagues a day, coming to a trader with a 100 lbs of loot, stopping by a campfire to hear to the guitar tunes and Russian banter between stalkers, and trying to survive with torn-up armor, a gun that misses every shot and jams every other, and no medkits and a clip of ammo left.
Play on master difficulty. It's not too hard and brings a fun challenge with highly lethal weapons going both ways.
Certain artifact setups can make the game very easy.
There's a stealth feature, but it's unfortunately underused, and most areas make stealth impossible.
Suffers from some bugs. Nothing game-breaking for me at least, but breaks immersion when NPC bodies are littered around campfire because they spawned in the fire, or when the quest marker for one I already did/someone dead stays up.

All right. So I've just completed the main story, at what seems a little over three hours. It was honestly about as short as most Sonic games, but I did enjoy the ride.
The game combines elements of both Generations and Colors, and does it pretty well. The Classic Sonic levels aren't as fun as I had hoped, but present Sonic's stages were pretty similar to Generations, and played pretty much the same.
I didn't experience any issues with framerate, though it did crash after the third stage. After that I switched Steam to offline mode and jumped right back in.
I actually really enjoyed the story and the cutscenes more than I thought I would, and enjoyed seeing my custom character in the cutscenes, and also enjoyed his stages. It's pretty much sonic, if he had a weapon and couldn't roll.
The customization is alright, nothing groundbreaking or expansive. A couple options here, a couple options there, and the items you receive, though nice, are riddled with re-colors. It definitely would have been better if they just gave you a color wheel and used that room for more variety in accessories, but oh well.
All in all, I actually enjoyed the game and after a brief break I'll be jumping back in to S rank my missions and finish the challenges. I also need to complete Shadow's DLC as well, but I'm pretty glad with the game despite it's release hickups.
If you're a Sonic fan and just want some Sonic gameplay, you'll probably enjoy it. If you're expecting some groundbreaking game that's going to completely revitalize the franchise, this isn't it. However, I do feel like it may be a step in the right direction.

If Valhalla was heaven, this game would be its hell.  It is brutal and merciless for a new player, with very limited guidance on what to do or where to go.  What you are after becomes clear quickly, but how to achieve it not so much.  You are left to explore the world on your own and its story and lore develops as you meet characters within the game.  Even without being spoon fed the plot, this story is emotional and memorable, amplified by the challenges you go through to progress.
Game-play has a learning curve but is versatile and you can adapt your own style of play. The amount of armors, weapons and spells is crazy in part to how rewarding the game is.  There is virtually no level cap (hard to achieve), and you are able to re-distribute your attributes later in the game.
PvP is unique, and can be forced on if you are playing online. There are designated PvP zones, however in hostile areas you can be invaded by others no matter your level and tore to shreds in seconds. Getting killed isn’t overly punishing (except for your pride), and once you become familiar with the game these fights can be intense and fun.
I’ve never played any of the previous games in the series, so I am not comparing it to them in any way.

Dark Souls 2 is the sequel to the critically acclaimed rhythm game Dark Soul. In my opinion, it's selection of music is a little lackluster compared to it's predecessor, but varied opponent types keep the game entertaining as well as the variability of ways to approach these enemies.
If you're familiar with Dark Saul, it should take you just a little bit to get into the groove of it's sequel. Dark Souls 2 changes up the rhythm mechanics of the game by removing backstab invincibility and good rolls, so returning players may need some time to get used to this change. If you haven't played Dark Suol, the main objective of the game is this: you are presented with sets of enemies that you have to lock in your rhythm by dodging at the right times and rhythmicly attacking so that you get counter-hit bonuses. There are many bosses in Dark Souls 2, many of whom have unique attacks such as autotracking overheads and AOE splashes. But, if you find the rhythm of the boss, you can catch it and eventually outdo their damage output.

It's a nice little Tower Defense game. You have this big crimson ship with roughly 12 slots for turrets and 4 slots for power-ups. When it comes to turrets, there's 3 types: Rapid Fire Lasers, Beams, and Rockets. Then, you can upgrade each type from one of two of the next tier. So basically there's 3 Basic Tier-1  Turrets I mentioned earlier, then each Tier-1 Turret has to Tier-2 upgrades you can pick one of. I believe when you upgrade the Rocket, you can choose either the 'SAM Missile Launcher' or some kinda bazooka thing. In either case, it's a more powerful version.
One thing to keep in mind is the resources: Gold, Aluminium, and Energy. Turrets cost Gold to purchase and require Energy to work. Inside the ships Internal Bay are several things that can be upgraded with Aluminium:
There's Energy Node A and Energy Node B, which generate, you guessed it, Energy. The Energy Nodes can have their Energy Generation upgraded so you have more Energy to pull from when buying and upgrading Turrets, and all Internal Bay stuff has their energy requirements increased when upgraded. Also, Node A and Node B are seperate. For example, the first Energy Generation Upgrade costs 5 Aluminium, and gives a +50 Energy increase. So if you get the first upgrade for Node A for 5 Aluminium, you can get it again for Node B, getting an addition +50 Energy.
The Engine, which decreases time to finish levels.
The Main Cannon, which you can use to manually shoot stuff either not within range of your turrets, or for when you turrets are destroyed(more on this later). You can upgrade it's "Mark", but I'm not too sure what this dose yet. I think it increases rate of fire or projectile speed. I'll update this later when I figure it out.
The HQ, which kinda upgrades all things around the ship kinda. Like all turrets and Internal Bay stuff has shields around it, and upgrading the 'Shields' portion at the HQ upgrades all shields. There's also a 'Mouse Magnet' upgrade option. When you destroy some ships, they drop Gold and Aluminium, which are attracted by the mouse.
While all those Internal things have their own upgradable stuff, they ALL have a HP upgrade option, since all those Internal things can be targeted from the outside. At the far left side is the Engine, not too far ahead, in the center is the HQ, with Energy Node A & B above and below it, and the Main Cannon just right of HQ.
Going back to the Turrets, you buy the in the External Bay menu in the Main Menu, and during a mission they can be destroyed, but come back at the end of the mission.
This is a fun little Tower Defense game, especially for just $1, where I'd be willing to pay $5.

Papers, Please has to rank up there as one of my favorite gaming experiences of the year. You take on the role of border passport inspector for an impoverished East German-esque dystopia. Your job is to check each applicant's paperwork, verify their authenticity, and either approve or deny them entry. The graphics and gameplay are incredibly drab and monotonous, yet there are many well developed underlying story arcs, truly difficult moral choices, and an ever present sense of oppression that gives this game a unique and amazing feel all its own, and makes it hard to walk away from until you see it through to one of its many (usually grim, or at best, bittersweet) endings.
This is a tough game to describe and sell to friends, because at its core, it's a paper-pushing bureaucracy simulator with pixelated graphics and a depressing mood, but it is so, so much more than that (trust me!). If you like games, or you even like a really interesting (and not too time consuming) experience, you owe it to pick up this jem for its bargain bin price.

What kind of person am I?
I like to think I’m loyal to my friends, as honest I can possibly be, hardworking and generous. Everything I keep around in my life seems to point to those things to some degree. I’ve had the same friends since elementary school, I try to be as upfront as possible even when it can knock me down, I get consistent work from quite a few outlets, and I like to give my time, my love, and even gifts. There’s a beautiful joy in doing that. In fact I love giving people presents more than I get them.
So I must be a good person, right? …Right?
But what would I be if circumstances were different? What would I be if, say, I had a sick family that counted on me to get medicine, pay for food, make sure the amenities were paid for and running such as heat, or simply paying rent to keep a roof over our heads? Would I be as honest? Would I be as loyal? I like to think so, but given my time playing Papers, Please, I’m starting to wonder about myself.
This PC game is a self-described “Dystopian Document Thriller”. I prefer the term “Dystopian Emotional Rollercoaster That Rips Out Your Morals, Waves Them In Front of You and Laughs While You Pretend You’re Not What This Game Lets You Be”. But I can see why they went with that one. It’s a bit easier to roll off the tongue.
You start the game as a rookie Immigration Inspector working at the newly acquired border town of Grestin after a six-year war with the neighbouring country of Kolechia has finally ended. The game begins on a positive note – you’re given a job, an apartment, and a seemingly easy enough task. You check over immigrant documents – much like a border guard does – and make sure the person coming through is clean.
How is this done? Cross-referencing ID cards with passport numbers. Matching pictures, making sure no document has expired, questioning minor discrepancies, checking their permits, etc. Normal things most of us have experienced one time or another just on the other side of the screen.
When I played for the first 10 minutes nothing seemed odd to me. It was just a different kind of puzzle game with a unique outlook. Rather than find the right pieces to mash together, I looked over documents and cross-referenced them with my Immigration’s rulebook, just to be safe. All in all, a pretty uneventful first day. I turned away some people and let others through.
Day two was when I realized this game was, as Michael Caine would say about Batman, something more.
I started my morning off as usual: I walked over to my booth, checked over notes my government had left for me, and proceeded to call in the first person wishing to enter the country. This was when I noticed the atmosphere this game is just oozing out its pores. The colour pallet is somber: blacks, browns and dark blues cover just about everything. On the top half of the screen is a bird’s eye view of the border. There’s my booth, a few guards, and a massive line-up of immigrants waiting to cross. Here’s what caught my eye – each person has no identity in that line. They are just a black silhouette. Another cow in the herd. I can’t connect with a person who has no face, so I don’t. Given the depth of this game and the sheer brilliance in its questioning of humanity, I know this was an intentional design choice. Emotion can only tangle logic and affect your decision. Or perhaps it’s not my view of them, but the government’s? I’m still not sure.
When I called in my first person to inspect, a black silhouette slowly dragged themselves over inside my booth. In steps a small man, standing just about 5 ft. tall and he hands me nothing. He tells me about how proud he is of Arstotzka and he excitedly recounts his itinerary. I ask him for his passport and immediately the excited tone goes away. “I need one?” “Yes.”
He promises to return with a passport and apologizes for wasting my time.
I found it a bit odd, but oh well, I moved on and called for the next person. In comes this tall, skinny woman and she hands over her passport, work permit and even slips me a card for a nightclub she says she works for. She tells me to call and let her know if I’ll be stopping into town and her girls will take care of me. I left the card on the counter and started reading her documents. Her passport number seemed OK, the names on the permit and the passport matched, she said would be staying to work for two months. Everything seemed hunky dory. I stamped an approval on her papers and gave them back to her and told her not to cause any trouble.
She smiled and walked past me.
As I call in the next person to inspect I notice this woman’s black silhouette isn’t moving in the same direction the others did. Instead of taking a right and heading off screen, she turns left and walks towards the border guards. Suddenly, the game stops. This woman takes out a grenade and tosses it near her and the guards. Before anyone can do anything it explodes, killing her and the three men on patrol. The game fades to black.
Oh god, what did I do? I’m responsible for that? Was it game over?
No. Up pops a newspaper headline about a bombing from the Kolechian terrorist that I let through. The deaths. The terror. It’s all there. Then the game fades back in and guess what? It’s day three on the job. I failed, but the game isn’t over. That’s just part of it.
It turns out I made a mistake and had my paycheck docked some. So I couldn’t pay for medicine for my sick son and food for my family.
This is when I started to pay attention to the game a bit more. Each person in the line-up wouldn’t have a face until they were in the booth with me. When they were, I was so crazy about not having another terrorist come through I would detain anyone – anyone – who looked at me wrong. Work permit says you’re here for three months but you said 7 weeks? Search and detain. That way I’m cracking down on enough people to lower the odds of a psychopath getting through and getting a few extra dollars. I was fine with this procedure and thought I would be good doing this for the rest of the game.

Grisaia no Kajitsu has been an amazing game that I have thoroughly enjoyed reading over the past couple of months. From its appealing visuals and music, to its deep and emotionally-derailed storytelling, this has gone down in my book as one of, if not THE BEST VN I have read to date. Compared to KS and IMHHW, this game is extremely dark and gloomy, so I will reiterate that is NOT for those faint of heart or looking for something cheerful to read. However, if you are looking for a story very rich in character development, you won't be disappointed.
I do not recommend the all-ages version. One of the best things about this game is its very mature theme and humor. Very much of said humor is sexual, and I feel the reader would be missing out on those incredibly hilarious moments. Beyond that, for some of the characters, the sexual nature of the relationship is actually very important. The all-ages version attempts to make up for this with some bonus scenes and CGs, but it does not entirely make up the difference in my opinion.
I would without a doubt give this VN a solid 9/10. It has some minor drawbacks, but in my opinion, they are not enough to take away from the wonderful masterpiece that is this VN. It is incredibly long, so be prepared to devote some time into reading it, but you won't be disappointed.

Whether you're familiar with VNs or looking for something new, all I can really say is to give Fruit of Grisaia a look at the very least, 100% completion at most (barring Bad Ends). Not a single moment of reading/playing this has been boring for me, and whilst it is mildly disappointing that there are some scenes removed when compared to the Japanese or 18+ versions, I can't really say it detracted from the experience since what's left behind is so amazing (though googling Grisaia Steam Patch might turn up something useful for those who want the scenes). Whilst the Common Route is rather long, it's full of enough hijinks and comedy to make it worth reading through in its entirety, and since the routes are essentially sign-posted and all near the end you won't have any issues with dedicating yourself to the wrong waifu by mistake. Great story, great characters, great music and all are what this has to offer. So good luck buddy. And don't worry about those damn onion-cutting ninjas. It's worth it.

First and foremost, because I would like to point this out first, because most of the people reading this probably will not want to read the whole massive explanation as to why I like this game. So to summarize, first, this game is an incredibly excellent game that suffers from some bugs and semi-regular crashes, but you can get unoffical patches and mods that help fix that a little bit. I gotta point out though, this game can potentially be balls-to-the-wall hard. So... Expect to play this game methodically, and not rushing through Call of Duty style hoping you won't get hosed down will bullets or surrounded by mutants and mauled to death. Because, spoiler alert, you will. And now, on to the big explanation!
S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl is a game ahead of its time. Running off of a system where you need to conserve bullets, monitor your weapons' and armor's conditions, and be very conservative with materials. All of this is mostly thanks to the weight system. In most games that incorporate a weight system, like Elder Scrolls titles and Fallout games, ammunition (Usually) weighs nothing. Not in S.T.A.L.K.E.R., no, in S.T.A.L.K.E.R., bullets weigh a devent amount. So this brings an interesting system to the fore. In most games, I would have main firearms, one as my preferred gun, and the other as my backup, and load up on ammo for both of those. You can do that in S.T.A.L.K.E.R., but it's not optimal. Rather, you should probably just load up on ammo for your main weapons (Pistol and assault weapon), otherwise you'll be over-encumbered.
S.T.A.L.K.E.R. also has a bleeding system. If you get shot in a non-vital spot, you bleed, and you should bandage up or you're gonna slowly bleed out. If it's a lesser wound, you don't need to worry about it, it won't bleed much. It's color coded, if it's red, you'll bleed out if you don't treat it, if it's green, it'll most likely heal in a moment or two. If it's yellow, it'll heal, it will just take a while, and you're probably better off bandaging it. This is the first game (Regarding it's time of release, in 2007) that I have seen a game make the bleeding system pertain to enemy AI as well. You hit and enemy with a few shots to the chest, he'll probably either die in a few moments, or curl up on the ground and eventually die like that. It's still very impressive.
Everything about the weapons, armor, and gameplay, generally is extremely impressive. But that doesn't mean I don't have my gripes with the game. There are a few problems:
A: this game can be buggy as♥♥♥♥♥♥ F6 oddly is the default quick save button. I set it to F5, becuase that's what it is in most games. That button is your friend. Use it a lot.
B: I feel that a lot of the mutants take waaaaaaaay too mant rounds to put down. Unless you manage to hit them in the head, which is hard. Hell, even the blind dogs take like, at least a clip and a half from my Vintar BC to drop if I don't hit them in theh ead. There's a point where it starts to feel ridiculous, considering that this game pretty much forces you to ration off your ammo supplies.
C: This game has an INSANE difficulty jump at the end of the game. It would be fine, if it didn't break all the rules that this game makes you obey. It forces you to move fast, and to act fast, while not dying. Up until that point, you essentially have to take everything slow and planned out. This ending just... It threw me off.
---- Quick save is your friend. Remember this. ----
Anyway, altogether, this game is awesome. There's a whole lot to do in it, between the warring factions, Duty and Freedom, and the side missions, there's a surprising lot to do. I would strongly suggest picking this game up if you haven't yet, and pick upt the STALKER: Complete mod for Shadow of Chernobyl. Makes it look a lot better, and tends to fix a lot of the issues the game has.

Living in the Zone, life can be tough. No, life IS tough. Anomolies waiting to tear you apart, radiation sitting everywhere, freaks of the zone gaining territory by ripping apart anyone in their vicinity, factions battling for control, bandits causing chaos, and the military attempting to put a stop to everything permenantly. The zone is a painful, unforgiving place, in which one mistake could lead you to your end. Welcome to S.T.A.L.K.E.R..
S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl is one of the three games from the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series. In S.T.A.L.K.E.R., you are a man living inside of the zone. Following the explosion of the chernobyl reactor, the radiation and other unkown forces created the zone. Anomolies, mutants, radiation, and other hazards litter the zone. The anomolies within the zone have the power to create artificats, objects defying physics and producing astronomical results. Catching the worlds attention, these artificats quickly became sought after, with people like you heading into the zone to retrieve them. Normal men, looters, murderers, bandits, rapists, all types of men flocked over to the zone to become rich. These men would eventually be known as stalkers. In this game, you are one of these men, trying to uncover the mystery of the zone while also trying to uncover your memory and how an assasination order came into your hands.
So how's the gameplay? Extremely brutal. The game doesn't explain anything, it doesn't hold your hand, there is no guidance towards what you do. Things are out to get you, bandits wanting your stuff, military wanting to put a bullet between your eyes with a sniper. There is nothing safe in the zone. You become genuinly scared of the zone, and when the first night hits, you simply want to put yourself in some attic and wait out the night so the things making noises could go away.
Actual gameplay wise, it's a standard FPS with some RPG elements. Lots of focus has been put into the guns, the enviroment, and making it feel like a real shooter in a lawless land. This is not Doom styled gameplay of megasprinting everywhere, this is serious tactical gameplay of where you plan everything ahead, shoot good and shoot fast. Utilize the lean mechanics and the enviroment to stay alive the best you can. The weight limit is low and unforgiving, bleeding and radiation constantly nag at your health, and if you step into an anomoly you can consider yourself dead. Supplies are extremely scarce, and the game loves teasing you with it. One time I set out to scale a destroyed building, a task which proved to be immensly difficult. Upon finally scaling it, I found a single supply crate tucked away, which upon breaking, was empty. That's when the bandits begun their ambush from ground level.
This is the game if you want a serious, tactical shooter set in one of the most scariest enviroments I have ever played. This isn't a horror game, but it sure as hell felt like one later on in the game. This is Fallout for men. A serious dose of Russian, Vodka, AK-47s, bandits, and mutants.
One last thing. The base game itself while somewhat buggy, do not mod it until you finish the first run so you understand what is being changed. If you do set out to mod it for your first run, only try and get the bug fixing mods like the Zone Reclamation Project. There are tons of other graphical and gameplay mods you can choose from once you get to that point. And play on the highest difficulty(Master). In lower difficulties, a horrible system exists, of where a chunk of your bullets and the enemies bullets simply doesn't exist. You fire it, and even though the shot would hit, nothing would happen, and same with the enemy. On Master, such a thing does not exist.

Was this game made by the same devs of the newest Thief title?
The atmosphere is great. The plot is solid. And the retro touches in the UI, while cumbersome, really make you feel like you're in an 80's flick.
But the gameplay is laughably broken.
This game should never have made it out of beta in this state.
The controls are clunky and unresponsive. You can't climb over knee-high barriers. You'll get stuck on invisible corners all over the place.  There is NO direction or explanation to anything-- I don't want the devs to hold my hand, but I spent ten minutes trying to pick up a flashlight on the ground in front of me because it didn't LOOK like a flashlight and the contextual command to even acknowledge it's existence wouldn't kick in unless you were standing square over it and looking straight at it. You can't find things unless you already know exactly where they are?
Worst of all, the game mechanics and coding don't work. Enemies can see thorugh walls and will follow a path to you. Not a path that traces your trail, not to any noises you make, not to any distractions you leave (or any one of the thousand that happen on their own) but right to YOU. Incidentally, the enemies are totally silent when they move-- unlike you.
That's not stealth.
If you pitch a flare into a room ON THE OTHER SIDE OF THE MAP, where NO enemy nearby can possibly see or hear it in ANY way. They will all come running to it, and then straight at YOU, regardless of which way you went or which distractions you leave behind.
A great atmosphere and wonderful cinematic experience are not enough to make up for broken gameplay.

After completing the story mode in 4,5hours in Offline mode thanks to the nice Leaderboard bug that prevented one from even playing more then 2-4 levels here is my rant regarding this game:
Modern Sonic Levels:
Good:
- Soundtrack (There are some nice tracks)
- Visual Design(The Background and the graphic are looking really nice)
- Replayability (Red Stars to collect and different paths to take)
Bad:
- Sonic has the mobility in Speed Sections like a truck(F.e. In later Levels when you are boosting at the speed sections you won't be able to take the corner at high speed unless there are some walls that prevent you from certain death because you can not drift, also the game sometimes doesn't respong towards the xbox 360 inputs)
- No Drifting like in Sonic Generations ( This makes Speed sections in the game a pain in the butt and aren't fun at all)
- Levels have a lot off cheap death sections where you will certainly die 1 or 2 times because the game tricks you into thinking you can go fast
- Level has problems in keeping up with your inputs
- Some Levels can be easiliy beat under 1 Minute on the first try by just pressing boost and pressing forward
- Some Levels are more or less playing by themselfs
- The Plattforming sucks because off the slugish controll
Classic:
Good:
- Level Design(You have different paths)
- Visuals are nice
- Replayability (Red Stars to collect and different paths to take)
Bad:
- Soundtrack (It just sounds like bad MIDI converted songs that were propably in the original format good)
- Classic Sonic controlls like Modern Sonic in the 2D sections (It feels like it is just Modern Sonic but with classic Sonic texture)
- Few classic Levels
- Building momentum like in Mania is not possible (There are always sections were you will be by force slow downed)
Avatar Levels:
Good:
- Levels are giving an Sonic Adventure and Sonic Adventure 2 vipe (Mix off Sonic/Shadow and Tails/Eggmann level design)
- Almost all levels are good
- A very high Replayability thanks to the weapons the Avatar is using
- Has the best BGM going for the levels
Bad:
- Control is a little bit off
- The visuals in the 2D segments can get in the way (Game zooms to far out)
Overall at the current state off the game it is a 4/10. Luckly Atleast SEGA has released an Patch so that the game can be played in Online Mode and doesn't have to be started in Offline Mode. If they could now fix the stuff like slugish controlls then it might get an 5/10 from my side but as it currently stands I would not recommend this game.
Also it is a big downgrade from Sonic Generations which is really sad. I've seen fan levels created through Generations that are by far better then 90% off the Modern Sonic levels in this game.
I hope as a big Sonic fan since childhood that the next Sonic game from Sonic Team will be better. Maybe even use a complete new engine or develop a new one as Sonic Team seems to have trouble with the Hedgehog Engine that they have created in regardings towards the level design.
If you want to play an good modern Sonic game then please play Generations it is by far the better experience.

There will be large bases with turrets on the north/south side of my ship, just pummeling everything directly beside my craft. While I would have finished this game 35-40min, a fair length of enjoyable time for $1-2, because of this poor AI reaction I've been sitting on the last planet for 20-30min alone.  With a fully upgraded ship at this point I can just barely get to the end before I cannot keep up with the stations flying by without the help of the turrets to destroy the other stations turrets.  Frustrating to an otherwise fine game.

This game is very hard in a way that kinda reminds me of Super Meat Boy.  Super Meat Boy is really hard, but it's very accurate, fair (for the most part), and also very fun.  Dark Souls II is rewarding when you figure something out, but my goodness does it take a long time.  I didn't play the first Dark Souls and I haven't really played too many role-playing games, so this game seems like a very tall mountain to climb.  Dying will be a huge part of your experience.  The good news is, after a while, you just don't care.  Eventually, you sucumb to the fact that you can't really save or pause your game (the game saves when you quit the game).  You just kind of plunge in there and hope for the best.  It took me a long time to understand how the weapons rating system works.  I was using a shield my character couldn't effectively use since I didn't have enough strength (kept wondering why it kept giving me that message).  In many games, if you're not a high enough rank, you just can't use that weapon, but this is Dark Souls II and they let you figure out.  I'm not saying any of this is bad, but they do not hold your hand.  I still don't quite know what i'm doing, but it's been a blast.  The varied amount of weaponry and armor you can obtain in this game is fairly extensive from what I've seen so far.  You fight bosses that are bigger than the screen and they seem impossible until you figure it out (hours later after suffering many, many deaths).  Overall, excellent game if you have the patience and perserverance to hang with it.

Let me preface this review by stating that my dissatisfaction with this game has nothing to do with cut content or lack of 18+ material. I am against censorship, especially the double standard that exists where extreme violence is ok yet bare breasts lead to madness, but that's an argument for another time.
This VN has a massive amount of glowing reviews. As a result, I approached this game with the surety that I would absolutely adore it. I'm easy to please. Give me compelling characters with clever dialogue and even a dash of plot, I'll happily read for hours on end. You want to throw in some strife? Great, have at! I require a little drama in my VNs. In the case of The Fruits of Grisaia, I just have to possess the patience to click through 500+ screens worth of everyday, boring "life stuff", for lack of a better term, before hitting a patch of story progression. Then we're right back to hearing about what Amane is cooking for Makina today, or what Sachi is cleaning. Rinse and repeat.
The mistaken belief many writers seem to have is that quantity is better than quality.  The common path is ridiculously long and drawn out, adding little to the experience except to establish what these girls eat and watch on tv. I would have gladly skipped it all and started with one of the girl's paths--that's how little I feel the 6 hours I spent trudging through the common path actually added to the story. Did I mention I read fast? It's also annoying to have to click after each sentence, especially when everything is so drawn out and convoluted that it could have been said in 50 pages rather than 100. Forget about the slow auto text, I'll just have to live with the carpal tunnel.
Yes, I'm bitter. I feel like I'm the only person in the room that doesn't get the joke. I have trudged through 3 1/2 story lines, and I'm still not impressed. (I'm working on Amane now and saved Makina for last, at least she makes me chuckle fairly consistently.) On the positive side, I found the girls' backstories sympathetic and somewhat compelling, but that just isn't enough for me to recommend this game.
I'm going to add one final thought, one that only a few other kindred spirits might understand: I wasn't merely soured on this novel because of the protracted plot. I absolutely detest it now due to the simple phrase "That a fact." That phrase was uttered by every last character in this VN, but what's truly reprehensible is that the MC said it at least 100 times. I am not exaggerating.
TL,DR: Long, drawn out, repetitious plot; underwhelming twists; and I pity the next fool that I hear say "that a fact" irl.

Gameplay involves:
Weapons feel POWERFUL throughout most of the game. Some items you will have to play with to understand their capabilities. Luckily there are tips that tell you what affects what, but for the most part, you're on your own.

It's great. Super immersive, beautiful graphics, well optimized... uncomfortable as heck to play.
It actually produced a physical response in me: blood pumping, tensing up, palms sweating as I tightly gripped my mouse. Up until about half-way through, I was practically paralyzed with fear, not wanting to leave my hiding place for what seemed like 10 minute stretches - but as it got closer to the end, and I JUST WANTED TO GET IT OVER WITH, I began to get a little braver and started hustling. Go to the place and do the thing? Okay. Done. Beelining, not looking back. Monster goes off the tracker for a moment? Time to move! This is a cool aspect of horror games that feels almost like leveling up in real life: overcoming your fear, adjusting to your environment, and being able to function at a higher level despite the adversity.
Highly recommend for fans of Alien or the Sci-Fi/Horror genre. Highly recommend if you like horror games. As many have said, it does seem to stretch content and goes on a little too long, but it's a worthy experience. I'm glad I played it, but I never want to play it again.

It's taking me way too long to defeat it, but only because it's such an immersive game - it completely terrifies me to play most of the time.

The AI can be weird at times (like I'm pretty sure I made direct eye contact with the Alien on several occasions, but nothing happened), but overall, it's well thought out and the movements of the Alien are generally unpredicatable. Which causes me to stress myself out in a locker for a good while until I get the guts to just run out into the open.
I heard someone say the pacing is bad since it switches between intense and calm scenes (aka you can generally tell when you're safe), but I think it's nice. If I needed to consistently be on edge for the entire game, never knowing if I was in a safe area, I don't think I would be able to finish the game out of stress. The predicatable switch in pacing gives a nice break from the intensity of some missions.
Overall, one of the best horror games I've played.

I was actually very surprised by how immersed I was in this game. I bought it on a whim because it was in the autumn sale and I heard some things about it so I thought, "Why not?". You start the game off and listen to the really catchy music with the title going slowly upwards as it bobs to the rhythm of the music. I thought the music was also very thematic as well, telling me the kind of setting I would be playing in, so that's a plus.
Okay, then I started a new game and, at first, it starts up kind of slow, showing me what to do and how to use the certain controls in the game. I'll get back to that in a bit, though. But just as I as getting bored with the game, thinking that it was becoming repetitive, it started to add story elements. On any random day the border can be attacked by a terrorist bomber or a group of them kill all the guards around the border and its up to you to take them out. And then there is also a secret organization that tries to get you to help them with their cause.
It was all of these things that kept me interested in the game, more immersed. I really couldn't stop playing it because I wanted to see what happened next, if something even happened next. Well, I guess I also got a sense of satisfaction of being given the power to dictate whether a person can enter or not. Anyway, I thought it was a really good game, very creative because of its unique gameplay and style that it gave me. Plus, it also multiple endings! So you have tons of replayability if you're done with the first playthrough.
I do have a complaint though. I just kind of thought that one of the upgrades was kind of useless. Like the 'double click to use inspection mode'. There was already another upgrade to activate it with the spacebar so I didn't think there was any need for that upgrade. I'm not sure what could've been in place of that but I'm sure that the creator could've thought of something. I would say the same thing about the book shortcuts but I found those useful so I'll leave that one be.
Other than that, I had a great time playing the game. It required me to be real attentive and I think it actually helped increase my perception because sometimes there is just one tiny thing that you can overlook and you can get a citation for it. So you have to really pay attention to the dates, genders of the people, serial numbers, and even the cities in the passports that they're using. Sometimes they try to trick you with that so be careful. Also the dialogue with the characters can sometimes feel very natural so that is another aspect that can immerse you into the game.
Now, Papers, Please definitely won't be the most exciting game you would ever play but it will pull you in with its unpredictability, interesting setting, and very intuitive gameplay mechanics. So if you're in the market for a PC game I highly recommend Papers, Please. If you are on the edge of whether or not to buy this, do it. You won't be disappointed with it at all, and it's only 9.99 so it's a really good price for what you get with this game.
My rating for Papers, Please is a 9/10
