I put in alot of time in SoC, but I learned that I don't like this game. My problem isn't with what the game is trying to be, but the experience often ended up more annoying than fun.
Instead of a full review, I will highlight bullet points of things I like or don't like of this game.
+Atmosphere: The world is definitely dark and gritty, and exploration is haunting thanks to rabid mutant creatures, anomalies, and trigger happy factions. The overall sound design/ambience is pretty good for its time, but I was annoyed by some overly repeating sound effects.
+World Design: The world design feels pretty good as it feels like it could exist and assets weren't so over used that the world wasn't believable. I'm not running in and out of the same buildings in different spots. In comparison to Ubisoft style open games, you don't have a ton of unnecessary fluff such as find all the relics or chests, do the time challenge missions, or find a tower to scope out an area.
+Freedom:  While there are definitely story based "road blocks", but sections of the game world are seperated into relatively large open areas and most building complexes/towns that you need to "attack" may offer alernate ways to enter and provide a chance a stealth.
=Equipment based progression: I miss an RPG style system, but it works well here as you progressively get better gear through your adventures. Admittedly, I've had to default back to the lowest tier AR and SMG due to ammo consumption in this game.
-Looting: You have a large, Diablo-esque inventory, but you have limited space and little use for large amounts of cash a few hours into the game. You get clues from stashes regularly from corpses, but stashes often end up being a better place to store items since you have a limited weight.
-Difficulty: I like a challenging game, and SOC is definitely hard. My problem is a combination of features that eventually annoyed me. Veteran difficulty was interesting because enemies can be killed quickly, but enemies always seem to have high accuracy, high damage threshold, have weapons that don't jam, and almost always are in groups. Meanwhile, my gun shoots all over the place, bullets ping off enemy armor, my rifles jam at the worst of times, and in the rare times I have AI support for missions, they're either Godlike or brain dead. I lowered the difficulty and apparently, doing that actually makes some bullets dissappear - seriously, read up about it. Also, many times in the game i've been able to kill goons with ease, just to get killed quickly out of nowhere with a shotgun or a guy who decided to have perfect accuracy while my gun jammed.  I've quickloaded in this game at a higher rate than any other game i've played.
-AI Fail: In some cases, the AI is good and you can get in situations where you move around the map and confuse them. But in other cases, I've had them shoot through walls, know my exact location after evading them, or in one mission, not notice I shot a comrade with an unsilenced AK47 with in 10 fen of him. Escorts are a pain as they never sneak and will constantly run without stopping, unless there is a firefight, in which they will try to be the hero, even if they only have a weak pistol against an army of rifle wielders. Aren't I supposed to do the killing while you stay behind? And you can't give them commands either. The bad companion AI in Skyrim and New Vegas is better than this.
-Glitches and annother annoyances: Many populated areas have NPCs that utter the same line or two constantly. Escort missions are terrible, where your escort runs head first into battle even though they desperately requested your help. A faction asked for my help with mutants from far away, and then killed them so fast before I could help me and called my useless. There's a glitch with dropping items in your inventory, which is awful when trying to get ammo out of guns and manage inventory weight while some enemy creeps up on you.
My final straw was some mission where I had to retrieve something from a body. I spent so much ammo trying to kill zombies and wierd leaping enemies. These zombies have figured out to shoot, are nearly tanks, and have nearly as good accuracy as a normal person. I killed most of the enemies though, worked my self to a building corner to kill one more zombie. I turned the corner, worked my way to the zombie shooting at me and strafing behind cover. It met up with another zombie out of nowhere and both were clipping through each other, shooting me with perfect accuracy through solid cover, even though their guns weren't actually above said cover to hit me. They killed me, and the NPC I was working for was still greeting me with "Hello! Hello!", half a mile a way, through an enclosed building, that is shut with an airlock. I had enough, and funnily enough, that NPC was stuck saying is greeting the past 10 minutes while I was shooting and being shot at.
I'm not compelled to bother with the other games in the series. I've got too big of a backlog and better games to play. However, SoC has an atmosphere, world design and challenge that many gamers crave.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R Shadow of Chernobyl is a single player, survival horror, open world, RPG. It is set in the year 2012 six years after the second CNPP explosion in what is none as The Zone of Alienation. The 60 Kilometer Exclusionusion Zone established around the CNPP. You are one of the many S.T.A.L.K.E.Rs that roam The Zone in search of valuable artifacts spawned by strange anomalies that seem to defy science. The game is quite difficult when you start off but as you progress you're given access to more powerful gear like tactical hazmat suits and exoskeletons. The controls are like any other FPS and easy to get the hang of. The survival aspect of the game is the need to eat, scavenge for medical supplies like anti-rad meds and bandages to stop bleeding, and searching for ammo and weapons. The atmosphere in the game is amazing. The first time I encountered a Bloodsucker, I nearly jumped out of my seat. One mission had me explore an abandoned laboratory that was crawling with mutants and ghosts. I couldn't go more than 10 feet without freezing from fear. I stood in one room for about five minutes straight, afraid to move and face whatever horrors lay deep within. Like most RPGs, there are side missions. They're okay for the most part. But after a while it gets a little repetitive with most missions being, go and kill this bandit, or go destroy a pack of mutants. But the rewards make it worth your time. There's a large number of weapons available in the game but most of them won't become accessible till you're at least halfway through the game. The game, minus side missions, should last you about a good 40 hours. But I highly recommend doing the side missions for extra money. Seeing as how most weapons and armor are expensive and trust me, you are gonna need good armor and weapons. Especially towards the end of the game. Now, the game does have a fair number of bugs. Most of which you can fix by installing mods like the S.T.A.L.K.E.R Complete mod which not only fixes bugs, but improves the graphics as well. The default graphics in the game are pretty decent for their time, but I still highly recommend playing with mods like Absolute Nature and Sharers Max. Final verdict: 9.5/10 The game is amazing unless you come across one of the rare game breaking bugs. My only other complaint with is that there wasn't much pressure to go out and explore. The S.T.A.L.K.E.R series of games is my favorite series of games; Let me preface this review with that statement.
Do you like Atmosphere?
Do you like a challenging, rewarding experience?
Do you like the feeling of helplessness, that edge of adrenaline as something that can snap you like a twig without lifting a finger?
If the answer to any of these questions is yes, then this will be a very rewarding game in every aspect of the way. The S.T.A.L.K.E.R series, specifically, Shadow of Chernobyl, is iconic for it's atmosphere so thick it drips out of your screen. The distant sounds of assault rifle fire as you clutch your rusty Kalishnikov to your chest are always terrifying. Is it bandits? Is it a local militia trying to fight off some horrible mutant? You'll always feel vulnerable in the wide, gray fields that make up much of S.T.A.L.K.E.R's landscapes. But don't think running for cover inside will make you safer.. Buildings can be home to traps set by enemies, a bandit camp, or a vicious Bloodsucker's lair.
The game mechanics are solid, if abit stiff. You'll never feel cheated if you die; This game is much alike Dark Souls in that regard. However, if you play on any difficulty above Stalker, expect frequent deaths; I reccomend Master, but that's just me. Fortunately, the game features a fairly primitive, if not effective quicksave/load system.
Many weapons feel powerful and give feedback; The thunder as you unload a clip from the shiny gun you found on a corpse will always light up the darkness and make you feel alittle less vunerable. Don't take it as a sign of invincibility - Often, you'll be found a few bullets short, gun empty and useless as something with razor-sharp teeth and claws advances on you. However, unless you play a stealthy character, often your knife will be next to useless in combat; As will many of the game's sidearms, unless your primary's run dry.
The game also features enemies of the variety of the environment; Anamolies.
They're results of the radiation that envelopes the zone, and they're very dangerous; being anything from Static electricty that'll light you up like a christmas tree, to a minature vortex that pulls skin from the bone. All are usually dangerous, but the name of the game in S.T.A.L.K.E.R are the results of Anamolies; Artifacts. They're mysterious objects that grant mystical properties on the human body, from massively increased healing to bullet resistance.
Of course, the game isn't flawless. There's many glitches in A.I., but you can't fault a game made in 2007 from a third party company for having some weaknesses. The number one problem with the game is it's voice acting and it's graphics - Even for the time it was released, it wasn't a pretty game. The voice acting is generally pretty atrocious, when it's there - Two of the more famous memes from the game result from this; (Come eehn! Doan juss stah ther!) (GEET OUYT OFF HEER STALKHERR), but overall, that's not the game's strength.
Out of the three games, Shadow of Chernobyl, Clear Sky, and Call of Pripyat; I would hesitate in calling this one the best. The other two have far stronger mechanical changes, as well as generally improved voiceacting and graphics.. However, Shadow of Chernobyl will always be the strongest in terms of the feel it gives you. You feel helpless, weak, and scared. Your life is valuable, and the zone can snatch it in an instant. The game doesn't baby you, nor does it hold back. You will die, and you'll love every second if you're a junkie for the things I've mentioned.

Overall..[Starting score of 5 - An average game.]

A powerful way to improve your character via artifacts (+1)

-CONS-
Glitchy, sometimes outright broken A.I. (-1)
Horrendous Voice Acting (-1)
Often uninventive areas (-1)

This game definately had a rough launch however the Day one patch helped iron out most of the issues with this game.
The game itself is pretty short 30 stages with 7 of them being boss battles, 7 Classic Sonic stages (1 boss stage), 9 Modern sonic stages (2 bosses) , 8 Avatar Stages (1 boss), 5 Tag team stages (2 bosses), then theirs the final boss stage which has you paly as all classic sonic and the avatar seperately with all 3 characters present in the final phase. The game also contains 3 levels for shadow, and collecting all 120 red rings unlocks 120 numbered and moon rings to collect but it also unlocks 13 extra/secret stages (5 avatar 8 Modern sonic)  whitch have a similar feel to the missions from sonic genarations.
In terrms of gameplay the avatar felt a lot like modern sonic except with an op weapon and no boost. classic sonic wasn't as enjoyable as the tag-team, avatar, and modern sonic stages.
Pros:
•Most of The stages are fun
•Extra/secret stages provide an extra fun little challenge
•Devian art simulator is a ton of fun to mess around.
•completing challenge missions are how equipment and weapons for the avatar is unlocked  (no lote crats /cheer)
•lots of replayabillity; Challenge missions, SoS missions, Red rings, Numbered Rings, Moon Medals.
•tons of modding pontential
•Shadow is fully playable in almost all Modern Sonic stages.
•Amazing soundtrack
Cons:
•Game wasn't fully finished prior to launch; day 1 patch was nessary for all platforms.
•not all of the games content fully implemented; sonic and avatar can both wall jump and sonic can drit however these animations remain unused with the exception of the Avatar being able to wall jump in only 1 stage.
•The levels are short... really short if you were to play the game's main story; 30 stages and watch all the cutscenes you'd probly finish the game faster than if you were to listen to the entire soundrack from start to finish.
•The awesome soundtrack gets cut off in certein portions of the game due to the transitions of a boss/miniboss/quicktime event/section change which made me belive that originally the modern sonic, tag-team, and avatar stages were originally intended to be much longer but had portions of their stage cut off.
•Super Sonic was originally intended to be in the game as some sort of unlockable bonus (probably intended to be unlocked afher completing all the extra stages like how it was done in colors) however it was actually made unacessible however dataminers have found it linked behind some sort of dlc which is already in the game and can be modded back in.
Overall I really did Enjoy this game its a solid 7/10 although for the length of the game unless you really into completing the game, doing all the challenges, and collecting all the collectibles It's probably not worth the full $40 and you should definately check this game out if you can get it in a sale. 1,500+ HOURS I've played this game and it continues to evolving - Good & Bad.
IGNORE reviews from those who haven’t REALLY played this game.  Want to skip to TL;DR, go to the end...
GOOD NEWS:
#1 - Value.  You easily get your money's worth. It takes 100-150 hours to work thru the main story line plus your 1st Faction.  On the flip side if you dislike Lore and want to PvP. You can grind your way to the upper levels in 40-50 hours by watching YouTube videos.
#2 - PvE.  As a previous Elder Scrolls gamer, I love PvE and Solo campaigns. When ESO first launched, I felt it struggled in this area EXCEPT for the main story line and the 3 Faction stories.  If you love Role Playing, Lore, or reading Quest back stories, count on another 300 hours of enjoyment as you to work your way through the main game.
#3 - DLC.  Orsinium is large. I pushed hard to finish the Orc story line and get the 1st and "easiest" Achievement and it took me 30+ hours.  The Dark Brotherhood quest is fun, its "Blade of Woe" adds a new element with various Kill Cams and help the game feel more like a traditional Elder Scrolls game.
#4 - Subscription. You do not need to buy a subscription to enjoy this game. But the plentiful Crowns, extra XP, all the DLC, and maybe most importantly the Bag of Infinite Holding for crafting goodies hooked me into paying for a subscription.
#5 - Holiday Events. These are FREE to all.  Witches Festival, New Life Festival, etc., are a blast and nearly every player in the game participates as the giveaways and rewards are significant.
BAD NEWS:
#1 - PvP.  The game is split into PvE areas and PvP.  The PvP area while large, with its own story line, is nowhere near the size or scope of the main PvE story.
#2 - Lag.  In the PvP area, when hundreds of players are on the screen at the same time, players often complain of lag.  This is something Zenimax says they are working on but it is an ongoing issue.
#3 - Inventory.  Crafting is a fun and an extremely useful part of ESO, but inventory is a problem as you amass lots of ingredients and mats. You can continue to buy more inventory but it gets expensive with in-game gold or with real $.  The ESO subscription resolves this issue but without it you may will find yourself needing Alt's as mules or spending $ on inventory.
#4 - Sales & Auction House.  There is no Auction House.  Players join guilds and each guild bids on Traders which are open to the public throughout Tamriel.  You can join up to 5 guilds (which players create) and you have 30 slots in each one, in which to sell items to raise money.  If your Guild loses their weekly bid for a Trader your items may not sell.
#5 - Grouping - ESO has a grouping tool to help players find others who can help them fight in Delves (dungeons), Trials or as needed.  The Grouping tool has gotten better but often if you want to play as a DPS (vs Tank or Healer) you spend a lot of time waiting.
TL;DR --->
BOTTOM LINE:
I have found ESO to be a great game.  Plus, the ESO community friendly and very helpful to newbies. If you are looking for a game you can play for a long time whether it be Role Playing, Sole Questing, Toppling a Castle "zerg-style" with hundreds of players, or peacefully Fishing alone in the wilderness - this game might be for you.

After a few major updates, I came back to the game to give it a second chance. It has definitely improved a ton since I last played. I'll make this review much shorter so people will actually read it. I'll touch on the main points of the negative review and explain the old feeling, and the new feelign on each.
God balancing:
Old: Absolutely terrible, buffing OP gods and nerfing weak ones.
New: Besides a small handful of gods peppered around being OP, out of the 88 total playable gods, they do a pretty damn good job at balancing them. New gods are still OP at launch, but it's a MOBA, that's forgivable.
Team Matchups:
Old: Every round is a landslide victory one way or the other.
New: A few games here and there are landslides, but at least it still feels like you can fight back throughout the whole thing. Not nearly as bad as HOTS, but I still think LoL does it better.
Community Toxicity:
Old: Nice at first, but extremely toxic at max level.
New: Still nice at first with few smurfs, and most smurfs are there to genuinely help out newbies. Higher levels still have some toxicity, but it's not nearly as bad as LoL.
Prices
Old: Way too expensive, don't spend any money unless you KNOW you'll use it well.
New: I don't know how, but it got worse! $30 to get all gods unlocked permanently, future gods included, is a fair price for a MOBA if you ask me. However, if you don't spend this cash it'll take you at least a year of constant playing to get all the gods. Gems are still way overpriced. The new game mode however takes the cake for the horrible pricing. It costs 900 gems to unlock the city, the only place to spend the currency gained in the mode, and the only way to really get good gear for the mode. The cheapest gem pack that can buy you the city is the 1000 gem pack at $25 dollars. The cheapest combination of packs is the $15 800 gem pack and the $5 100 gem pack. So it costs $20 or $25 dollars to unlock the city to really get anything good for the mode. And the mode is absolutely atrocious with a small god pool, so you basically need the $30 god pack. All in all that's $50 to actually be able to play AND enjoy the new dungeon mode. That's ridiculous! I get that it's FTP so they need money, but $50 per person is just overpriced as hell.
TL;DR
Game definitely is a lot better, so is the company.
DO NOT SPEND A SINGLE CENT ON THIS GAME!!
The ultimate god pack is acceptable to buy only if you play a lot, but no more.

pros:
- unique art style
- instanced quest boss fights so you don't have to fight with other players to progress
- klaipeda has nice music
cons:
- extremely repetitive gameplay that involves auto attacking most of the time because you run out of MP so fast due to there being no mp usage balance for skills; skills have very long cooldowns and very high MP costs
- skills have a limited number of monsters it actually effects, so if you gather too many monsters your skills won't damage most of them even though they're within range
- some skills require items to use, so you're limited by how long your supplies last and how much you can afford rather than leaving whenever your mp gets low
- some classes use skills that effect the ground only, so there are times when their attacks are rendered useless because there are a number of flying monsters in various maps, forcing them to auto attack enemies instead or have to run around looking for monsters they can actually kill
- the game itself provides no insight as to where you're supposed to allocate your points so it's easy to screw up your build as early as the beginning of the game because you tried to experiment
- creature diversity is extremely poor in just about all the maps - you'll see dozens of the same monster in the same spot on many occasions, sometimes on top of each other
- too many weapon/skill types vs monster weaknesses to deal with which makes questing a pain; there are many forced boss fights, so you'll more than likely be faced with a boss that is strong against the majority of your attacks or ones you can't hit with your skills because they fly
- you have to repair your equipment frequently because you can't do much in the game besides auto attack monsters until they die (attacking multiple enemies at once degrades your equipment faster)
- the value of monster drops has been reduced when selling to npc shops since beta, making it even harder to pay for repairs, potions, attributes, and other items
- tanking in itself is completely flawed in the sense that you take almost no damage so you can gather large groups of monsters at once, but because of that, your equipment degrades at rates many times that of people who are able to kill monsters much more quickly
- bosses are boring at best - most of the time you're autoattacking them for ~5 minutes depending on your class while running in circles to avoid their extremely predictable attacks.
- their AI is poor and often they will pause in place for seconds at a time after using an attack.
- many of their attacks don't fit their design and are recycled (a tree boss and others randomly shoot bullet hell-type of pellets at you).
- many different bosses have the same attacks, even if they're an entirely different creature
- hitboxes are very poor, so you'll wonder how you even got hit half of the time, especially during boss fights
- quest boss progression is extremely unbalanced - in some cases you can fell a boss in a matter of seconds, but a boss one level higher may take minutes; some higher level bosses are actually weaker than lower level ones
- almost no character customization in the game, unless of course you're comfortable spending up to $30 for a permanent hairstyle. temporary ones are around $15. you can unlock some hair colors through gameplay (kill thousands of the same monster to unlock), but they're very dull colors that otherwise should have been added to character creation
- everyone has the same lifeless face - there are no facial options to choose from and there are no hair colors to choose from because the colors are locked to the styles
- aside from hair style, every class looks the same, so you'll always run into clones of your character (especially in towns)
- the only customization after character creation besides the very few unlockable hair colors are hats you can get from monsters that do a poor job of making your character feel unique
- player to player trading has been REMOVED...unless you buy premium membership that costs $15 a month that gives the following benefits:
* increased movement speed for your character - run around maps faster and hunt for world bosses much easier
* reduce the tax from the market from 30% (normal) to 10% (premium)
* increases the amount of items you can list on the marketplace simultaneously from 1 to 5
* allow training of 2 attributes at once, which has the potential to save hundreds of hours of time as there are hundreds of attributes to buy for all the skills combined
- founders get an entire month of head start got damn

A very forgettable and short experience.
This is my main problem: 1 to 2 minute stages, most of which are extremely linear with lots of straight/automated paths and QTEs. Really brings the input the player has to an insultingly low level. It was really difficult to get enthralled with the game when the levels are over in the snap of a finger, and when you did so little yourself besides boost and attack a chain of enemies. For Classic Sonic, it's just some mediocre platforming that really pale in comparison to Mania's level design.
My second major problem is the game is absurdly short. I beat the main campaign in just 2 and a half hours. Worth 40 dollars? Hell no, I got MUCH more time out of Sonic Mania which has much better replay value. Finding red rings isn't fun, and S ranks are very easy to obtain just like in Generations.
I also found the controls very strange and awkward. Both Sonics feel really floaty and their momentum feels like they stop to a screeching halt in midair the second you turn in the opposite direction. Modern Sonic controls terribly when in a 3D space so you pretty much just need to rely on quick steps to reliably move around. All the characters are just needlessly difficult to control in the air, and it really feels like momentum isn't taken into account which makes everything random and unpredictable, comparing it to something with actual good momentum like Super Mario Odyssey.
The Avatar just feels like a slower version of Modern Sonic stages with a weapon. They have exactly the same moves, besides the avatar not being able to boost. It makes the stages themselves feel incredibly samey, and the weapon/grappling hook doesn't justify enough differences to make this a "different" playstyle.
I really don't know what to say when the boss battle stages are the longest levels in the game. Those aren't hard either, just tedious. Forces didn't do too much wrong, but it was way too short and simple with little player input. Generations and Unleashed did the boost formula much better than this.

EDIT 100 Hours
OK, so now with over 100 hours in the game what are my final thoughts.
PRO's:

*a LOT of fun
*destructable physics
*variety of vehicles you can hijack, earn, drive, fly etc
*open world environment
*graphics - it looks amazing and plays great (for me)

CON's:
*dropouts due to connecting to square enix servers, happens a lot, really breaks your gameplay, especially during challenges, this needs to be patched or gotten rid of all together
*Vehicle handling.  Didn't bother me to start with with the car's, it's not great but ok.  The choppers fly pretty well.  Planes are, well planes and difficult.  But some of the cars, some of the boats and especially the motorbikes are ridiculous.  Seriously I played games with motorbikes that handled better on a x0386 platform in the early 90's.       In all vehicles crash detection is way off.  You might hit a lip in the road at the front of a bridge which depending on your speed may make you jump, or might wreck your vehicle all together.  This needs to be patched ASAP.
*inconsistency in the way grappling affects the wing suit.  This isn't a biggie but will mean you hit the ground sometimes doing something that in the same situation previously didn't make that happen.  But you don't die so not that big a deal.
*Finding that past settlement in a territory.  Some people have complained about finding the last object to destroy to clear a town/base, I haven't had that problem as I find the map identifies them readily enough however I've got a few provinces I can't clear simply because I cannot find the town/base I need to clear.
My final gripe.  WHEN you complete this thing.  Go and make a coffee as you'll HAVE to site through 9 plus minutes of credits before you can do anything with no way to skip.  The Developer's way of punishing you for finishing their game??
So in conclusion, overall for me it's a solid 7.5 out of 10.  Fun, as long as you don't take it too seriously with a few flaws that are annoying but not game breaking.  Definitely get it on sale.

! Disclaimer: Know that this is probably totally subjective and biased as I'm one of few who prefers Asian MMORPGs to Western ones and do not like the "best western MMORPGs" such as WoW. Also I'm a huge fan of TES.  !
TL;DR: Either you love this MMORPG or you don't. It's very unique compared to all other MMORPGs I've played and I'd highly recommend everyone to at least try it out and see what this game has to offer for themselves. No, this is not a Skyrim The MMORPG, rather it's The MMORPG about The Elder Scrolls and you'll get a lot more out of this game viewing it as such. You can play in any way you want, regardless of the class you choose and the world is HUGE. DLCs are completely justified imo and I can't wait for the housing update.
Now to the actual review... This will be super long so grab your favorite drink and a snack.
Honestly this is the best MMORPG I've played in a while.
Each and every quest NPC is voiced and their dialogue is very interesting. Not even once did I skip quest dialogue and every quest is worth doing. The voice actors are very well chosen and I'm so glad Sheogorath still has his iconic voice. The quests are all very unique, even if the quest objectives are not. Everything is lore-friendly every quest you accept actually makes sense, as in you won't just encounter and NPC that gives you a quest just because, most quests are even connected to other quests, even if you don't realize it at first.
Classes do not restrict you from creating the character you want. You can even totally ignore class skills and go for weapon and guild skills instead which every class has. Sure, class skills have their own benefits but really I'm very surprised how much freedom this game gives you in creating the character that you want. And whenever you feel like you messed up you can just reset your skill points for in-game money at a shrine.
The world (the continent Tamriel) is so full of things and it's worth exploring and looking in every nook and cranny. You get rewarded for being curious with Skyshards or a bit of story that is imo very interesting. Literally every container is worth looking into as there's a small chance you'll find a crafting motif you won't find in stores (except guild stores). Every province is unique as you'd expect from The Elder Scrolls so it gives you even more reasons to go literally everywhere and thanks to the One Tamriel update this is possible with one character, no matter from which faction.
I know this game has gotten a lot of negative things said about it when it first launched, and honestly it made me avoid this game, too. However after buying this game myself and playing it I can easily say it's really great. A lot of people were expecting this to be Skyrim the MMORPG but that mindset will only disappoint you. This game was never meant to be Skyrim the MMORPG, it's a great MMORPG about The Elder Scrolls, not the other way around.
The combat is a bit on the basic side, to be honest, but if you like basic, then that's totally fine! The combat system is a semi-action combat with an auto lock-on for long and mid-range skills, melee is completely action combat with lock-on, though. I haven't experimented with everything yet as I mainly play on my mage Breton, but so far the combat has been fun regardless. You can swap weapons mid-battle and each weapon set has its own skill set that you can customize, this is super great as it allows you to adapt to the combat situation rather easily. With the help of mods you can even create skill set presets, but I'll get to mods in more detail later. Also you can become a Werewolf or Vampire... That's super rad if you ask me.
I haven't really gotten into PVP so I can't really say much about it. Sorry about that.
Without DLCs, the Mages, Undaunted and Fighters Guild are available to you, with the DLCs you also have access to the Dark Brotherhood and Thieves Guild. Now I know what you may be thinking "What? Guilds locked behind a paywall? WTF??" but trust me, these two DLCs open up a big questline with their own locations and extras that I think more than enough justifies having to pay for them... After all this is a MMO, how else will they make enough money to uphold the costs for the servers? Next to having their own questlines and locations, the guilds give you access to guild skills and unlike other skills they do not progress by using them, you have to find special lorebooks (Mages Guild) or hunt certain enemies, complete dungeons, etc. etc. to increase the skill ranks.
The crafting in this game is so awesome. Make your own weapons and armor, upgrade them, dye them, enchant them... It's just really amazing. Make your own potions, your own enchantements and cook food and brew drinks... I haven't played any MMO that allowed you to do all that without failure rates or requiring you to use additional items other than the base materials. No bull****, just craft to your heart's content! Of course crafting has its own set of skills, so you can't be a master in all crafts. I'd say it's pretty similar to Skyrim; you either focus on being a smith, alchemist or enchanter, or be a jack of all trades but in the end never be good enough at anything.
Remember when I said classes won't restrict your character build? You can steal from NPCs or even kill them if you wish. Which gives you even more freedom in playing the way you want to. Want to be a "Dark Knight".. As in playing as a Templar that kills and steals? Why the hell not. Want to be a good guy even though you choose to be a Nightblade? Why. The. Hell. Not? Honestly I was very surprised when I found out you could steal from NPCs and even get punished for doing so if you get caught. Now I just wish the guards would also say "Stop right there you criminal scum!" when they hunt me down... *Sigh*
Also there will be a housing system pretty soon... I can imagine that this will only further enhance roleplaying and make the game even better. Let's just hope they don't put all of it behind a paywall.
I've been putting this off for a while as this can't be really put into the review as a criteria of why I believe this MMORPG is great, but this MMORPG actually supports the use of mods. They may only be UI mods and tiny "gameplay" mods, but the fact that you can use mods is super great on its own. There's a lot of mods out there already and they all tackle certain aspects of the game, like a grid view for your inventory to make it more PC-friendly, a Minimap to fill all your minimap needs, etc. etc..
Now to the most important thing: Is the cash shop P2W? Absolutely not, not in the slightest. There are costumes and so on and tiny convenience things, but other than that it's all in the green. Really.
There's so much more that can be said like the rest of the DLCs that are included in the Gold Edition and those that are not and the overall quality of the main quest and so on... But at this point I'll just say if you're not convinced yet, then wait for another Free Weekend to try this game or just buy it when it's on sale, you won't be disappointed, at least.

Stealth survival horror at its best. The Alien cannot be killed, don't even bother wasting your time, but that doesn't mean that you cannot manipulate the Alien. Their are other hostiles on the ship besides the Alien that will kill you on sight. So... having trouble getting past that group of pistol packing humans? Toss a noise maker right in the middle of them all and watch the Alien swoop in and shred them one by one. Just hide out until it leaves and loot their corpses and keep going.
Also, the sound in this game is AS nerve racking if not MORE, than avoiding the Alien. The constant thumps, hisses, Alien screetching sounds, keep you sneaking in the shadows because you simply do not KNOW where death is lurking. Once you get a feel for the game you can kinda get a feel for when something is about to happen and use that to your advantage.
The Alien's movements are totally random, but its introduction into certain areas and levels is very much scripted, so one trick I have exploited is, once you learn that the Alien has been showing up whenever I am sent to perform a task or pick up and shiny new toy, DON'T DO IT until absolutely necessary. If I know pushing this button brings the Alien into the map, then I will do everything else posible in the level before I can't advance without puching the button, that way I can usually complete the level safer and quicker because other objectives have been met without the Alien slowing my pace.
If you like horror, this game IS for you. It is without a doubt the single most tense game I have ever played.

A good addition to the storytelling game genre. While less obviously interactive than things like Gone Home or Homesick, the text-only approach is no less immersive for it. In a world filled with instant messaging mechanisms the interface gives a real sense of personality and emotion, and the messages are well written to give a sense of the characters involved.
I was initially dubious about the interface, having to tap away at the keyboard to make text appear after selecting an option, but watching deletions and changes occur gave a depth of personality to both characters. I think it may have added to the overall immersion.
While I'm not sure I will play it through again, and if I do probably not more than maybe once or twice over a longish period, that's because it is a story, and I don't usually re-read or re-watch ones that I have only just finished.
When you consider the price (free, at the time of writing) this is an interesting and touching little diversion.

Although the update for the game was released that fixed crashing issues on day 1 I still had problems with cutscenes running at only 20> FPS on my system where as the actual stages would run perfectly fine which is not a concern for me. All things considered I think that Sonic Forces provides an average experience for long time fans and it certainly won't be anything too unsual your first time playing however I do think that the game would benefit from probably some more difficulty and less linear paths as this becomes very apparent when levels become redundant in later levels. I played the original game way back in 2000. I played the two sequels when they came out, as well. I loved them to bits. But then I heard Gearbox was doing a remastering of the games. Say what you will about Gearbox, they hit it out of the park with this collection. I nearly cried when I started Homeworld up for the first time in a decade and a half.
The good: Basically everything. The audio was remastered based on the original recordings and it all sounds incredible. The graphics have been updated and look gorgeous. The UI now using the Homeworld 2 UI for both games, which is a massive improvement over the original Homeworld.
The bad: No one knows what happened to the source code for Homeworld: Cataclysm, which was a cool, albeit strange, spin off from Barking Dog Stuidios. Therefore, the Collection is, in my opinion, incomplete. Maybe we'll get lucky and the source code will turn up.
The takeaway: I had felt that Homeworld had held up pretty well, given it's age. I still think that, but the Remastered Collection brought the game to being as close to perfect as a game can get.

Stealth survival horror at its best. The Alien cannot be killed, don't even bother wasting your time, but that doesn't mean that you cannot manipulate the Alien. Their are other hostiles on the ship besides the Alien that will kill you on sight. So... having trouble getting past that group of pistol packing humans? Toss a noise maker right in the middle of them all and watch the Alien swoop in and shred them one by one. Just hide out until it leaves and loot their corpses and keep going.
Also, the sound in this game is AS nerve racking if not MORE, than avoiding the Alien. The constant thumps, hisses, Alien screetching sounds, keep you sneaking in the shadows because you simply do not KNOW where death is lurking. Once you get a feel for the game you can kinda get a feel for when something is about to happen and use that to your advantage.
The Alien's movements are totally random, but its introduction into certain areas and levels is very much scripted, so one trick I have exploited is, once you learn that the Alien has been showing up whenever I am sent to perform a task or pick up and shiny new toy, DON'T DO IT until absolutely necessary. If I know pushing this button brings the Alien into the map, then I will do everything else posible in the level before I can't advance without puching the button, that way I can usually complete the level safer and quicker because other objectives have been met without the Alien slowing my pace.
If you like horror, this game IS for you. It is without a doubt the single most tense game I have ever played.

A good addition to the storytelling game genre. While less obviously interactive than things like Gone Home or Homesick, the text-only approach is no less immersive for it. In a world filled with instant messaging mechanisms the interface gives a real sense of personality and emotion, and the messages are well written to give a sense of the characters involved.
I was initially dubious about the interface, having to tap away at the keyboard to make text appear after selecting an option, but watching deletions and changes occur gave a depth of personality to both characters. I think it may have added to the overall immersion.
While I'm not sure I will play it through again, and if I do probably not more than maybe once or twice over a longish period, that's because it is a story, and I don't usually re-read or re-watch ones that I have only just finished.
When you consider the price (free, at the time of writing) this is an interesting and touching little diversion.

So, after about 4 hours of playing, I’ve completed the main game plus some minor extra stuff. Yes, the game is that short. Even then, I watched all the cutscenes and stuff, which there are a lot of for some reason. I was overall just expecting Sonic Generations 2 from the trailers, but no, that is not what this game is at all. At times, it doesn’t even really feel like a Sonic game, but does that make it a bad game?
So, let’s start with the main “selling point” of the game, the custom character. This is probably the coolest thing about the game overall and can change the game a lot. Just selecting what type of animal you want to be changes stuff, for example, birds can double jump. Because of this though, the different abilities aren’t well used. Not even in the stages were your character is supposed to be used. You also never give your character a name, which I found odd. The thing that bothered me the most though about your custom character is that you can’t boost or even spindash. I mean, why not? Not having that just makes some platforming more difficult. I also found it very annoying that your character never talks and when people talk to your character, it’s just like only they can hear what you are saying. Just simple lines like “hi” and “thanks” wouldn’t hurt, specially not since you only get 3 different voices to choose from per gender.
There are also a lot of other things that just makes this game not feel like a Sonic game at all. Firstly, the story goes way deeper than it needs to, specially considering how bad it is overall. There are so many cutscenes and dialog, but it just seems like that’s there to make the game feel like it’s longer than what it really is. It doesn’t help that most stages are around 2 minutes or less, making the cutscenes feel even longer. The cutscenes also constantly switch between being pre-rendered and being rendered in-engine. This just makes it look weird, especially on higher resolution monitors. I guess this was made due to cutscenes having to be rendered in-engine when your custom character is in them, but why not just render them all in-engine in that case?
There are also a lot of other things that just makes this not feel like a Sonic game. There are for example no real zones anymore. Well, there are “areas”, but you jump between them all the time, so there are no acts, just one big set of levels to play.
There are also quick time events now, which I guess sort of fits. Kind of reminds me of the tricks you could do after going off a ramp in like Sonic Generations, which aren’t here.
In some stages, you also control 2 characters, Sonic and your own, using the abilities of both characters. So basically, your own character with boost, like it should be. This kind of reminds me of Sonic Heroes, though, the character switches automatically instead of you having to do anything, so it mostly just reminds me how awkward it is to play as your own character.
Lastly, there’s this weird medal system. After you complete a stage, your medal goes up in rank. What this does, I have no idea. It’s never explained in the game and my only guess is that the higher it goes, the more cosmetics you unlock, but I honestly have no idea. Seems like some sort of level system, but why that was even considered being added, I don’t know.
The controls are overall fine. Don’t know how they managed me make them feel worse than before, but somehow, they did. When you’re running straight forward for example, just slightly moving the joystick in makes your character fly off in that direction. Really makes it hard to try going specific paths, which is specially needed if you want to collect the red rings.
They also managed to make the homing attack very unreliable. Almost half of the time I had a circle around an enemy and tried to do a homing attack, I would just fall to my doom instead of attacking the enemy. I’ve never had this issue before in any other Sonic game, so why here?
The wall jumping is also very unreliable. Most of the time, I just drag my face across the wall instead of grabbing onto it. Eventually I grab to the wall, not really knowing what I did differently. Most of the time there are places you’re supposed to wall jump, the camera angles get so weird that I don’t see when I jump off and often jump way longer and fall instead.
This is honestly what disappointed me the most. The soundtrack overall is just average at best, with a few tracks standing out, like most of the classic Sonic stages, which has a nice 16-bit style to them. Too bad there aren’t a lot of those. The modern Sonic stages are now just filled with dubstep and lyrics, which just sounds out of place for a Sonic game. After playing the game, I can’t really remember any of the songs and don’t feel like listening to them outside of the game, like I would with most other Sonic games.
They finally figured out how to make a good PC port. Everything you would ever want in a port is here, good graphics options, unlocked framerate, everything. There are some odd things though, like “AA” and “AF” with no description what they mean, just assuming the user knows exactly what they are. Other than that though, I have no complaints here.
It might sound like I was negative about this game, but overall, I had a good time. It wasn’t what I expected or as good as I hoped, and I probably won’t come back to it for another playthrough or to try and complete it 100%, but I don’t feel like my money or time was wasted either.

What is Factorio? At the most basic level, Factorio is a sandbox game about gathering resources and crafting items. However, the gameplay itself is unique since much of it revolves around designing automations using various methods of logistics to craft things on their own. This means the majority of the fun in Factorio is more like a creative puzzle.
You generally start by gathering ores and stones with a pickaxe, then you build drills to gather them automatically. The ores need to be moved to a furnace to be smelted into something useful. You can have a drill deposit directly into a furnace, but its terribly inefficient since it will fill itself with ore twice as fast as it can smelt it. You then realize you have to design a basic system to move your ores to more than one furnace.
You are given every tool imaginable to create something similar to a factory, with conveyor belts, grabber arms, all sorts of things. Its within designing these systems that the game shines its true colors. There is seemingly no single best design for any particular objective, since unlike other sandbox crafting games, Factorio throws the concept of minimalism out of the furnace and onto the train heading a hundred sectors in the opposite direction. There is definitely a hidden emphasis on maximization since you will be finding yourself expanding at all times to support your booming industrial and scientific progress.
As far as Early Access goes- this game is sitting at 99% positive at the moment. It dodges all bullets fired by the early access stereotype and leaves only one thing remaining: the promise of additional content. Since a single free mode playthrough is supposed to be about 50 hours, I'd say the price/entertainment value is pretty solid. Speaking of solidity, Factorio has been in development for over four years, and the game is extremely well optimized and perfectly stable. I had thought I encountered a few minor bugs, but they turned out to be simple mistakes I was making while not understanding the mechanics.
If you like building and crafting games, you should certainly check out Factorio.
If you particularly like the design aspect of building and crafting games, you will fire up Factorio for the first time, and you will dream of conveyor belts and geometric formulas when you finally pass out from exhaustion 20 hours later.

This is definitely one of the best visual novels in my opinion. There are two versions of this game: the all-age version here on Steam and the unrated version on Denpasoft. There exists quite a few differences between these two.
First, let’s talk about the similarities:
- Same prices ($40).
- No fundamental change to storyline, albeit a few small changes here and there.

Then, about the differences, the following describe the all-age version on Steam:
- Removed H-scenes: This is the single biggest problem why people not recommended the all-age version. While the H-scenes can be skipped on a few routes, for Amane’s and Yumiko’s (especially Amane’s), the H-scenes contain a lot of character developments and internal monologues. And the skips also make the rhythm of the game felt abrupt.
- Modified and cropped images: This happens to more casual ecchi scenes (likes when Amane walking around half-naked, which changed by adding a brassiere; or when Makina try to temp Yuuji, which changed by cropping only the non-ecchi part of the image). This is alright but a few cropped images look a bit unnatural.
- Modified dialogues: Same reason above, a few ecchi jokes got modified.
There also exists a patch to convert the Steam version to unrated version, you can use it at your own risk.
In conclusion:
- If you want to enjoy this visual novel to the fullest or want the best value for $40, buy it on Denpasoft.
- If you don’t like H-content, or intend to give it to someone who doesn’t like H-content, or simply want to own this game on Steam, or want to get it on Steam sales, etc., then I recommend this because the story is fundamentally the same.

tl;dr The AI cheats. It's programmed to cheat. And boy does it cheat. Also RNG.
And that makes the otherwise outstanding game incredibly frustrating. If it wasn't for the AI cheating, I'd easly call this the best horror I've played since Amnesia: The Dark Descent, if not EVER.
edit: Changing my review to Positive. Why? Find the "Unpredictable Alien" mod. It removes the terrible AI leash. The Alien won't be forced to stay at close range to the player anymore.
The game is best when... the Alien doesn't come down to get you, but stalks you from the vents and you hear him running around.
Full:
Pros:
- it NAILED the aesthetic. It looks, it sounds, it works just like the original movie. It's fits the "Alien" franchise more than the movies that followed the original movie, it's THAT good. I was blown away by the UI, visual and audio design. I've never seen a game do such a great job at mimicking the aesthetic of it's source material. An incredible retro-futuristic piece of art
- character control - it's tight and it's good. You move swiftly, you can crouch, you can sneak, you can peak (useful). Weapons handle as expected
- story - better than Aliens (1986)
- crafting and items - you get a wide varierty of tools to use which will help you survive. From combat-oriented molotovs, flashbangs through medkit to distraction-related tools like flares and noisemakers. Great UI, too
- lighting and graphics - graphics are good, the game performs well, but the lighting is outstanding. It seems like every source of light was placed after deep thought about why and how it is there
- stealth - core of the game. It's fair, even too fair (as in: hard), I've never had a situation where I shouldn't have been detected but was. Numerous ways to hide and distract your enemies make for very tense and surpisingly strategic gameplay
- it's tense as hell - the alien is terrifying, and so are the androids
- nice level design
Cons:
- the last chapter (or two?) isn't that great
- rare checkpoints - in theory they are close by, but when you play the game for the first time, it feels like an eternity. It makes the game more tense, but in some areas it's only annoying
- buggy UI - I've had to restart the game mutliple times because I lost the ability to use and choose equipment, craft, or use my anything
- the main biggest complaint: The AI CHEATS. It blatantly cheats. Even in giant open areas it will always stick to less than 100 distance units away from you (game claims meters, but I refuse to believe that adjecent room is 40 meters away), which is always close enough so it can hear you. And that makes the game infuriating and probably unnecessarily lenghtens it
- when you hide, after being seen, the AI is designed to dance in front of you for a while. Sometimes it takes ages. Very quickly you'll go from being scared to impatiently annoyed
- the Alien teleports. Literally. It despawns and spawns out of thin air as you progress from one area to another - it's disguised as travelling through ventillation shafts, but often the process doesn't even trigger. You leave it behind in one area, you enter another, and it magically exits an air vent in front of you.
- the game loves to spawn enemies out of thin air - I've had a situation, multiple times, where I check the motion sensor before entering an area, just to have enemies spawn close as I enter it - for example, I checked before a large door if there's any movement - no movement. I go through the door, and immediatly see the Alien walking down the hallway 15 units away from me. What the♥♥♥♥♥♥
- Medical evac sequence - the Alien literally teleports from place to place, it has way too many spawn points
- equipment upgrades - you always need another upgrade to your torch or hacking device. And suddenly, when you get it, you use it once, and obstacles stop appearing in front of you, replaced by those that need higher upgrade. It's to get you to backtrack, I guess. But this isn't a Metroidvenia game. Too much backtracking.
- RNG - sometimes I've had the Alien come out of a vent, walk around for a minute or two, exit the area, and 5 seconds later repeat the process. It went on for a few times. I didn't even touch the controls in that time.
- random nature of the AI - in theory, on paper, this makes for a great game. In practice, it makes for a frustrating experience
If not for the cheating AI, this would be an unforgettable and incredible game. Unfortunetly, the AI makes it incredibly frustrating at times. Especially in areas where you have to go back and forth over and over again. Pick up only if you can handle that

I did play this in the free beta version and my first expression was extremely positive since it struck me as polished and inventive and very easy to get into. It uses a mockup of an instant messenger interface for five dialogue exchanges with your friend Emily (hence the title). These exchanges span a five-year period from senior year of high school to senior year of college, and plot out the course of your relationship. The game lets you to choosre from 3 options then you have to spam your keyboard to mime typing in your input. You may think this is stupid, but it isn't! You see what your character types and deletes and retypes before sending the final version of the message. And there are things where you can reset your profile picture and get Emily’s comments on it, or see the rest of your buddy list (even if there’s never any way to talk to anyone but Emily). The early stages of the game created a charming sense of connection for me.I should note that it is entirely possible to name the protagonist a female name, and the randomizer at the beginning of the game will suggest some female names as options, but the bulk of the story reads to me as heteronormative. We only see Emily date men and we only see the protagonist date women. It’s possible that you’re lesbian and Emily is bisexual, but nothing in the narrative actively supports this view.

Hunting games are usually no fun in my opinion, but I feel that 'theHunter' is much more than just a simply hunting game. Despite the game being extremely limited to nonpaying players as to what they may shoot, it does offer a good amount of activities to keep entertained. That being said, it does not limit its game world and what it contains, just bars one from registering harvests (term used by the game for collecting a kill). Regardless of the constraints, I find myself addicted to the gameplay, idyllic scenery and animated animals, which I continue going back to explore.
The game consists of exploring, tracking, harvesting and if one fails to down their quarry in the first shot, chasing. There are eighteen animals distributed around seven maps called reserves that anyone may explore. The maps are large enough to keep running into animals and not grow bored as one travels from one hunting spot to the other. Most of the fun is following tracks, spotting and then observing what you find. There are also missions one can complete to earn in-game currency (called Gm$ or 'gems'), and a good amount rewards just for tracking and spotting a listed animal or two.
As said before, the game is free-to-play, limiting nonpaying players to one gun and the ability to hunt all the mule deer they want. Although doing missions could land one with the in-game currency to afford a shotgun, allowing the hunting of cottontail rabbits. Sadly that is the extent of not paying for basic membership. The missions are also finite and some require weapons and hunting license bought with special in-game currency (Called Em$) which is different from money gained through missions.
Even with these restrictions, I recommend giving it a try.

This is hands down the best hunting game available. Nothing else comes close. I've been playing since it came out back in 2008, and it's the only game  that I still play after so many years.
It has to be said that calling this a "free-to-play" game is pushing the definition at best.   My advice is try the "free-to-play" for an hour or two to get a feel for the game, and see if it is something you'd like to play.  Then buy a membership bundle, or buy a retail CD-key, which you might have to use on the game's website and use the non-Steam client of the game.  The "free-to-play" experience is pretty poor.  In 2008, when there were few species of animals to hunt, and reserves to hunt at, the F2P wasn't so bad.   Now though, you'll see way more animals that you AREN'T allowed to hunt, than those that you are. Every time you spot, or aim at an animal you don't have a license for, the game will pop up with a nag dialog reminding you that you have to buy a license or membership to hunt that animal.  It's very annoying.  It's simply not worth it to play theHunter as a F2P game.  You NEED a membership to truly enjoy the game.
Another bit of advice is to avoid the "earn $ems" offers. These supposedly let you earn in-game money to purchase new weapons and equipment, without having to pay real money for them. While it is possible to earn a decent amount of $ems doing the offers, it's just not worth it. A disturbing amount of the offers don't actually pay out, or they redirect you to something that won't give you the $ems you were trying to earn. There's a serious risk of malware and being directed to attack sites. Most offers want you to purchase something in exchange for the $ems.  Obviously your email will be heavily spammed after participating in the offers too.  Save yourself the trouble and time, and just buy $ems.
Sounds like a lot of negative, but honestly this is the best hunting game experience around. It's constantly being updated with new weapons, animals and reserves.  It's fun to join the online competitions, but good luck competing against the stable of hardcore fans who seem to do nothing but play this game. A very intriguing and distinct polit-thriller set in an east european-like country in the 1980s. Main location is the border of Arstotzka, where the player takes the position as the border inspector. While the gameplay may look dull and simplystic since you do mostly paper work for 90% of the game, it becomes more challenging as you progress further. You have to watch out and point out every discrepancy in the documents of the immigrants, which becomes much harder since there always come more documents.
The Border is also the main focus point of the plot. Basically it all depends on you how the story will progress. Will you support the secret society who wants to bring change to the country or will you simply keep on doing your job and ignore them? Will you let the old woman who urgently need medical treatment pass or shoo her away because she hasn't brought the right documents? All of this and more depends solely on your actions.
There are a total of 20 endings and you'll have to replay the game a few times to see them all.
I'd really enjoyed Papers, Please and must say, it is one of these unique experiences that one must play by him/herself to appreciate.

When you look at the game and wonder wether or not stamping passports and checking visas can be exciting, let me tell you that "Papers, please" is an extraordinarily grasping and intense experience. The small stories that evolve around the people that come to your admission booth is one thing that keep you going. Keeping your family warm and your little son fed and healthy is the second. The pressure to reach the quota never lets you lose, and when the events around the oppressive regime of Arstotzka reach their peak I bet you will be as abdorbed as I was on my first play-though.
Fully recommended & Glory to Artstotzka!

Now that I completed all the 30 stages in the game as well as the Shadow DLC, I feel like I can give a proper opinion on the game. Long story short, its a fun game, even with it's short commings. If you enjoyed Generations, you will probably enjoy this.
So, first let's handle the elephant in the room, the Avatar. It's kay. For starters, the customisation options provided to you are pretty insane, with more being unlocked as you complete missions. The gameplay if the Avatar is closer to the Adventure games than the modern Sonic games. No boost, no double jump, no spindashing, just running around. The Wispons are where things get a little bit more interesting. You choose from a selection of base Wispons, each one having a variety of powered up versions, and they provide you with some useful powers to use. Whether it's dashing along a line of rings, turning enemies into cubes or hovering above ground I found them to be fun to use.
Modern Sonic is pretty much all you know, you boost, you avoid pits etc. Nothing much has changed since Generations here (other than the double jump coming back from Colours).
Classic Sonic is where my biggest issues with the game lie. He's just♥♥♥♥♥ He feels off, clunky and isn't nearly as fun as he was in generations. Luckily, he takes up the smallest part of the game but I would have really preferred it if they focused on finetuning the Avatar and Modern Sonic and left classic completely out of it.
Now, the game is short. REALLY SHORT. Can easily be completed in under 2 hours. Definitely the shortest Sonic game there is. That said, there is a decent amount of replayability, though as far as I can tell, the only incentive is more outfits for the Avatar which, at least in my opinion, isn't much of a reward.
Overall, it's a fun game. Is it as good as Mania? ♥♥♥♥ no. Is it worth the price? That's fully dependant on you. Personally, £34,99 is a bit much for what's on offer, but I had fun regardless.

Edit: Just to clarify, my PC is fairly decent and more than enough to run the game. It just crashed constantly and couldn't get past the third mission. I've heard that a patch has been pushed out and I commend SEGA for their timely response, however, I'm also still seeing people complain about performance issues.
So no, I'm not changing my review until I see the majority of those issues squashed. Chill out already, my negative review isn't going to stop you from enjoying your purchase, grow up.
Edit 2: As of 19th Nov I have played and completed Sonic Forces in it's entirety on my home console thanks to an insanely generous friend. However, my overall impression of the game is negative. A bland set of levels that became more of a chore to play through than a fun romp, at least they were nice and short...far too short.
Thanks to the push boost to win mechanic of the latest Sonic games, you can effectively one button smash your way through the modern missions in less than two minutes and the classic Sonic and avatar stages don't offer much of a difference. The story, what little there is - is total tripe and something I'd expect to find on a fanfiction website. I know that you should never go into a Sonic title expecting a good story, but this one was just lazy with entire chunks that could be removed without damaging the narrative such as the null space moment.
Characters are annoyingly cliche, music is obnoxious save for one or two tracks and honestly, the voice acting was probably the worst I've seen from the modern games with Sonic easily having the most obnoxious performance.
By this point you've probably disregarded my opinion thanks to how quickly I disregarded the Steam version and that's fine with me, you're entitled to do so.
For the rest of you, want my advice? Buy the game, but not for £34.99. If you can get this for £20 or cheaper then go for it, but £34.99 is far too much for the bland, repetitive and dull experience you'll get from this.

This is a game that just screams playing it safe.
Considering that this game is $40 from the start, my expectations were pretty low to begin with. Some aspects in the game are great, other aspects of the game are things that I don't ever want to revisit. The Avatar is one of the aspects that I don't see myself going back to because it doesn't really wow me enough to go and try out the stuff that I've unlocked. The other weapons that you unlock with the Avatar are inconspicuous and the game doesn't do a good job in telling you that you have them and how to use them. Another thing that I don't find myself revisiting is the Classic levels; I feel like that the level design of the Classic levels are mediocre, especially in comparison to Sonic Mania.
Modern Sonic to me personally is the only redeeming quality in terms of gameplay. Coming from a person who's spend over 100 hours on Sonic Generations, I can say that Modern Sonic's stages are fun, but it's definitely a step down from Unleashed and Generations. A lot of Modern Sonics levels are very linear and have very few open pathing to flesh out this gameplay style. This is not mentioning that I feel that his controls are a lot more clunky compared to the two previous games that I've mentioned. With the exception of the first stage, I like all of Modern Sonics levels, though I will admit that there are better levels than others without question.
The thing that defines Unleashed and Generations for me is that both games allow you to go fast while at the same time rewards you for exploring the enviornment. Good examples are Seaside Hill from Generations and Skyscraper Scamper from Unleashed. The pathing in both stages are fantastic; tons of alternative paths that lead to different areas instead of being a alternative route to the same area.
From a technical standpoint the game looks absolutely fantastic; I feel that the visuals are expertly crafted in this game, fully immersing you in its world. The soundtrack is also pretty good, a lot of tracks I can see myself listening to in the future. But honestly I'm a little dissapointed on how Sonic Forces turned out. If Sonic Generations is a B+ to me, then Sonic Forces is a C+. If they fleshed out the levels better and give me better reason to replay the Avatar stages then I have no doubt that this game would be better.
As it stands, it's one of the most mediocre Sonic games I've played in sometime. I love Sonic, but I cannot deny that this game is a bit of a let down.

Dark Souls is by far my favourite video game franchise. In techical aspects such as gameplay (combat, playability, interaction, online), audio and graphics, Dark Souls 2 is by far superior to the first game. Having said that, it´s always expected of a sequel to surmount to a higher techinical quality than its predecessor (otherwise any sequel could be regarded as something that is quite effective at blowing), in my opinion the tricky part to any game with a solid foundation is its narrative element, which encourages players to delve deeper into the heart of a game. In this sense, any of both Dark Souls titles are rich and hardcore, however it is my belief that the original game (Dark Souls 1, so to speak) aspires to a greater immersion into the narrative rich Dark Souls lore, as well as having a greater reward system in which motivation, emotion and ultimately satisfaction keep pushing the player to follow through the entire torturing and addicting game. Dark Souls 2 lives up to what it was supposed to be but is overall an "easier" more player friendly game (with a few exceptions, such as the death penalties) that takes away that addicting torture of the first one (not entirely of course, just to some degree). Therefore Dark Souls 2 is a great title that any Dark Souls fan should aqcuire right away, and to those who aren´t all in all excited about the first title (or didn´t know where to go or what to do after killing the Bellfry Gargoyles, the Capra Demon, or stepping into Blighttown), Dark Souls 2 is the game for you, and will introduce you with much more ease to a story rich world with incomparably "purist" gameplay.

For a free game, No More Room in Hell is pretty good. There's a saying that 'You get what you pay for,' but when it comes to this game, you can get some decent entertainment without having to pay for the work that went into its development.
That notwithstanding, I am giving this game a thumbs down because I'd much rather spend my time playing other games, even though there are expenses involved in obtaining them.
NMRIH plays like Left 4 Dead except that the vast majority of your adversaries move toward you by slowly shuffling forward rather than running like rabid psychopaths. The thought of playing a zombie apocalypse game in which the zombies behave like ones from a George Romero film rather than Return of the Living Dead or 28 Days Later really appealed to me. When I encounter one of NMRIH's few enemies who run, they tend to startle me and seem rather difficult to dispose of.
Sadly, even regular zombies can be difficult to take out, and that's due to one of the game's biggest flaws. Melee attacks are clunky and delayed, even when you're unarmed and at full health. Poor hit detection renders these attacks largely ineffective, yet zombies have no problem hitting you after you strike them and are backing away while they're stumbling backward. In other words, the unarmed melee attacks of your undead foes have greater reach than the sledgehammers and baseball bats that you can use against them.
The developers state that the game was intentionally designed so that combat would be awkward. The logic behind that decision is that the characters you control have been fending off the apocalypse and can't be expected to fight as well as fully rested soldiers. The fact of the matter is that you'll have an easier time using melee attacks to defend yourself in old school Silent Hill games than in NMRIH, and that really detracts from my enjoyment of the game.
You can find and use firearms, and although the hit detection for projectile attacks feels right, you won't be able to enjoy the thrill of taking too many zombies out that way because ammo is incredibly scarce. Of course, the lack of ammo was a deliberate design choice, and I respect that. What I don't appreciate, however, is the fact that you are prohibited from removing the ammo out of a duplicate firearm. For instance, if you are carrying a glock and find a live glock on the ground, you can't take the new one, nor can you take its ammo and feed it into the glock you were originally carrying.
Another thing that irks me about firearms in this game is what happens as soon as you reload a long-range rifle whose scope you were just looking through. As soon as the reloading animations conclude, your character automatically reverts back to looking through the scope of his or her rifle. This happens regardless of whether you stand in one spot or move around as your player goes through the process of reloading the rifle. This unstoppable behavior is annoying because you're very vulnerable to attacks from zombies that wander into point-blank range while you're reloading. Good luck successfully landing a headshot on a zombie that is right in front of you the moment you character compulsively resumes the act of peering through the scope of his or her long-range rifle!
There were times when I was wounded and/or infected, yet unable to consume the pills that I had in my possession. That makes no sense. There was not a single instance when I could apply the bandages I was carrying onto myself.
This game supports internet and LAN-based co-op. Those options are great, but the vast majority of people who play NMRIH online do not support each other, coordinate plans, or even communicate with each other. This is a criticism of the game's community rather than any faults inherent to the game, but it is yet another factor that soured my experience of playing it. Even starting a game of your own is unpleasant because it takes an unusually long time to stream data to the online server.
The things that this game has going in its favor are nice music, visuals, and atmosphere. Unlike Left 4 Dead, playing this game actually feels scary and tense. I really like the look of the game, although I did encounter some missing wall textures and zombie limbs clipping through fences. I also saw some zombie shadows clipping through walls, but that bug created a very freaky effect that unwittingly made the game feel tenser.
I'd recommend NMRIH if you can round up a group of friends to play with, but even then, you'd best lower your expectations when it comes to defense. I didn't really enjoy the experience of playing this game alone or with strangers over the internet. I did experience instances of fun, but those were overshadowed by instances of frustration (and waiting for the rest of the players to die or finish the map so I could participate in a game instead of viewing it in spectator mode).
It's not quite the same thing, but if you want a good free-to-play first person shooter, I'd recommend Shadow Warrior Classic. Better yet, get Aliens versus Predator Classic 2000 at regular cost (a mere $5) if you want a stellar game featuring terrifying single player campaigns and excellent co-operative and competitive netplay.

Homeworld. This game brings back memories. Both good and bad. The good you ask? Well it was one of the first narrative driven real time strategy games I'd ever played way back when. The music, the ship designs and the very look of Homeworld was captivating. After all this time, it still is.
The bad memories though? Well, I wouldn't call them bad memories, but a general memory of frustration. This is a very unforgiving game. Very. Through the course of the campaign you keep all the ships you build from mission to mission and are very limited on resources through out the game unless your very very patient. But of course, Homeworld has a rewarding quality to it, watching as your fleet slowly grows from it's mothership and but a handful of small frigates to guiding several capital class destroyers and carriers and an armada of frigates and the such through the cosmos in search of your true home.
The gameplay is a bit unusual at first unless you're familiar with Sins of a Solar Empire, even then the controls and abilities almost outweigh the more modern advances in real time strategy games. Homeworld was unique, giving you all six degrees of freedom to move your ships through the obstacles of space, hopping from one destination to another. Navigating through near endless behemoths of ancient debris, daring your way through dust clouds far to close to a star ready to go supernova and facing the very brunt of an intergalactic empire long forgotten to your peoples.
I had an immense amount of fun with this game, it's challenges, design and musical scores are it's major charms. The remastered version simply updates all the models and skyboxes in the game AND the original is available in the remastered collection as well. If you enjoy a good challenge and an excellent real time strategy game, Homeworld is the choice for you. But be warned, this is a truly difficult game that will test you one step after another. The second Homeworld continues this brutal trend as well as the challenges here aren't quite like other RTS games such as Starcraft, Empire Earth or Age of Emires. Homeworld sets itself apart in just about every way possible.
Is it worth a $35.99(USD) price tag? Yes, yes it is. If you see this on sale and have a hankering for a great real time strat to kick your teeth in, trust me, it won't be money wasted. Homeworld is a definitive experience of what most RTS games could only dream of living up to.
