Caveat Emptor! Steam's simple "Recommend/Don't recommend" rating system is too blunt an instrument to give a proper review for this game. I certainly wouldn't recommend this game + DLC at full price (and most of the DLC is really content that should have been in the base game rather than actual ehancement and expansion - Creative Assembly/Sega really need to re-examine their DLC programme - check out Paradox's approach to EUIV and Crusader Kings II to see how to run a proper DLC programme). Wait until it goes on sale for a significant discount and then consider it (but buy the earlier games first or Total War: Atilla). The Emperor Edition does finally bring the game up to what it should have been at initial release - at least from a technical and performance perspective. The initial release was frankly a disgrace - it taught me to never pre-order a game again, not to rely on a franchise "reputation", and too distrust many of the "professional" game reviewers and game review websites.
At best I would now rate it a 6/10 - it has too many design and aesthetic flaws from the clumsy agent and political faction system to a messy provincial system to some odd choices in functionality (inconsistent use of opening and closing windows - missing information in pop up panels and lack of proper linking through between event windows) to the poor choices over unit and building card designs - so while it is a not a "bad" (or appallingly disastrous!) game anymore and can be quite enjoyable it is by no means comparable to Shogun 2, Napoleon, MTW2, the original RTW or even Shogun 1. Even the patched up Total War Empire is IMO actually a better game than this one. Even at the hardest difficulty it is still far too easy at the strategic and tactical level (battles are still far too easy, too short and arcade like and naval battles are still pretty hopeless). If I really want a challenging game with depth and complexity then I still prefer the Europa Barbarorum II conversion/mod of Medieval Total War 2.

Okay, so here is my review about this game and my background. My first game of the franchise was Mideival 2 Total War, which was and is amazing and always will be especially with the Americas campaign and the other side campaigns. That set the standard for Total War games with me. So I think the people who have played the OG total war games like Shogun, Mideieval and the GOAT Rome 1, will automatically be overly critical of the later games. I know I was and still am to a certain extent. Its like people who play pokemon Gen 1 Fire red and Leaf green and they play the new ones and say it is trash because of the nastalgic tendancies. So I think everyone is being a little critical. However I also paid for the game after it is has been patched  a lot and for 11 bucks on sale, so I can understand if someone bought the DLC and the game at full price after seeing all the glitches the AI and gameplay on youtube from the past and even some now, that they would be frustrated because this was supposed to the be the biggest total war game. But for me it was worth 11 bucks actually more, so I would say wait for it to go on sale, its not worth 60 bucks, its good but not that good. Dont get me wrong Sega did a decent job, but I think they kind of swindled people who bought it at release. But the game is fun, the DLC just isnt worth it.
The gameplay is extremely different from the other games. For instance, the spies and champions are extremely powerful and can deal enough damage over time to basically annhialte a full stack. Also there are garison armies which can actually fend off a legit army if used properly. The biggest thing for me that is a downfall but cool as well is the fact that there are SOOO many factions, over 100, literally. Every turn for basically the first 100 turns you will discover a new faction, which is realistic I guess but its also very, well complicated. Declaring war on someone may result in an enemy tribal confederation or 4 factions declaring war on you. Oh the politcs thing is cool I dont have to send a politic to their gates to engage in politics. However, the politics system for you important characters such as inherators or faction leaders and their political rivals, makes NO sense. You can literally have a civil war which is a nightmare, out of NOWHERE. The civil war bar may not even be full at all and you will have a civil war or it could be up very high and it will never happen. It can happen at 90 percent of the gravitas or 40 percent, its confusing.
Finally the actual warfare. The warfare is waaaaay more involved. Flanking and using units special abilites affect the battle much more than in previous games. For instance a pike phalanx if its flanks are protected can literally take out an entire army no matter how strong(excluding missile units),  whereas in M2TW it was practically useless. The battles actually arent simply determined by troop quality(never was completely but it is less so in this game, in my opinion, feel free to comment, no harsh words though, just trying to give insight), now you can destroy an army with lesser soldiers if used properly, that was harder to do in M2TW(Please keep in mind I have only played and seen Rome 1 and M2Tw). I would say it is more involved. The amount of units a card can have is more so instead of 60 being in a stack now 120 can be which is cool!
Concerning the map, units automatically heal themselve in your own territory so you dont have to retrain them. Also you can set your forces in 3 stances which is forced march which forces them to march farther on the map but get ambushed, the forticifaction which is for an army that builds a defensive mini fortress to make it difficult to kill them all of and some other stance which makes them ambus other armies, I actually dont understand that one haha.  Also ship battles can be fought personally. The most ANNOYING but also cool addition to the map is the provinces, basically the map is split into many different provinces and if you share the province with a rival faction than it affects your settlments as well. This is EXTREMEMLY annoying if they have a seperate culture because the clashing cultures in the province will cause rebellion. If the whole province isnt under one culture one or both cultures suffer and it gives more incentive to conquer the whole province. Now this is realistic and causes you to have to manage the cities in more strategic way so it is more challenging. Instead of simply spreading out into a box or whatever way you want to, your empire will be shaped into the shape of the provinces.
Overall the game is more deep and I think TW players are to used to not getting this involved in the game, it is almost too involving. They are used to simply training high quality troops and sending them to clash and steam rolling. It requires more strategy. I do recommend this game, it is fun, maybe not at release but it is now.

Weirdly, this might be the best survival early access game there is at the moment. They just got it right with so many things.
Combat feels good, base defense and offense is just brilliant, you can have proper sieges in a very balanced way. It is addictively good. They added a lot of fun stuff, you can capture enemies instead of just killing them, and there is various ways of execution and humiliation. So one can finally deal appropriately with the cheeky american teenagers after they annoyed you in the chat.
Harvesting resources takes some time, but its quite reasonably quick. You can build a basic base that offers you some basic protection in less than an hour once you know how to, and you'll advance to medium-tier materials in a day which will already require enemies to set up serious siegeworks to get in.
The highest tier requires explosives and one can reach that level in 2-3 days of dedicated gameplay with 2-3 people.
Breaking into bases isn't terribly hard, on the easy ones a simple melee weapon and patience often will do. It seems mostly to be the fault of bad base design. A well designed base requires serious effort with good coordination, also the timing is usually quite tight. You can't spend hours on sieging a base without nobody noticing.
Overall, it feels they balanced the base building effort with the break-in effort. Something i didn't encounter at all in similar games like RUST yet.
Its the typical game you want to play with a bunch of friends in Teamspeak, playing alone can be a bit frustrating since you'll likely encounter larger groups all the time and kill on sight isn't always the case, but quite often.
The map is quite small, one find its way around after a few hours. You can run from one end of the map to the other in a couple of minutes, in contrast to say DayZ the map feels much smaller.
Gameplay, Features, Concept: Brilliant.
Now the ugly part.
No matter how good your PC is, this game will eat it. Performance doesn't really depend on your graphics card, but seems CPU or server limited. You simply won't see good FPS. ~24 FPS was the best i've seen. Sometimes the game freezes completely for several seconds. It is possible to have proper combat when the performance is good, but lagspikes and low-fps periods will happen, and you will be completely unable to block your enemies swings, turning the otherwise brilliant combat system into a joke.
The (official) servers restart frequently without warnings and often with a rollback.
I'm pretty sure they will be able to fix most of that, but i wouldn't count on smooth running 200 people servers anytime in the future, 20 people servers seem to run the smoothest atm.
Server wipes without any announcment ingame on new version releases. That means every week. Code base seems to be quite messy when thats needed, so say goodbye to your Hording Simulator 2015. Puts me off the game immediately to have my progress wiped every week.
Hacks: The game has been out for a couple days, and there is already plenty of hacks. I've actually had people proudly tell me how easy this game is to hack since its all client sided, and i believe it. I've seen hackers on servers myself already, and the recent announcement of the devs to "now look into hack proofing the game" tells me this is now the games main problem.
And will remain so. I am very certain that the hack issues this game has can't and won't be solved. It is always the same story with small dev teams throwing out a game like this: They didn't think about hack proofing the game from the start. They developed the game to work with normal players, behaving themselfes. Many things are client side, there are no server side checks at all, and the engine probably needs to be completely recoded to make the game harder to hack. That won't happen. Its an economic issue, there just isn't enough profit in doing that. So the game will get some patches here and there, but it will always be an ugly hackfest.
I've seen too many games suffer the same faith to think otherwise. Expecially when the devs write into their recent announcement that they're now "looking into options like VAC". They obviously didn't spend any thoughts on the issue until now, and that simple fact will ruin the game now. Very quickly.

This is a game that warrants a double take. When you first hear the concept it seems strange. A dystopian border patrol simulator. While at first the premiss of this game may disinterest many people browsing the large selection of games on steam. Trust me this game deserves your inspection. While its not your typical simulator it does a great job of putting you in the game's world. You are a citizen of a communist country called Arstotzka. Your name was pulled in a lottery for the job of the passport checker in the newly opened border of this imaginary country. The whole game is checking and double checking. The object is to either admit or dismiss as many people correctly in a limited amount of time. While this may seem repetitive at first its addictive. Whenever you start to feel bored of the gameplay they add a new twist or challenge to keep you busy. I have put a few hours and have only found one of the supposed twenty endings of this game. If you just want to play for the gameplay there is an endless mode for you to challenge yourself. For as simple as the story may seem it keeps you intrigued. The choices are everywhere. You are faced obvious options on such things as betraying the government, accepting bribes, or just helping people out. The atmosphere is immersive. After playing for a while you start to feel like a horrible dictator. The dark atmosphere and the things you have no control over provide surprising amounts of emotion. This is one of my favorite indie games of this year and am looking forward to more thing from the developer. I highly recommend buying it now or if you are a cheapskate nabbing it during a steam sale. GLORY TO ARSTOTZKA

On the face of it rymdkapsel looks like an isometric  type  tetris clone, but in reality it's a surprisingly good minimalistic  space  RTS come Tower Defense game where you have to build corridor like  capsules (that look like colored tetris  pieces) such as weapon rooms, living quarters, kitchens, gardens, reactors  and resource extractors.   The aim of the game is to complete  several tasks such as  researching  monoliths that once unlocked  gain you extra attributes such as  speedier minions, slower enemies, increases the range of your weapons or  makes for faster resource production. Other aims are to complete  all four monoliths  within 45 minutes and to survive the 28 waves of enemies that get steadily harder as you progress.   You race against time between  enemy attacks to build your various  modules.  The sensible thing is to  concentrate on aiming for one monolith at a time and  building   one each of   the modules  in turn till  the cycle begins again.   The sortest route to each monolith is  the optimum so use  the pieces  that appear at the top left of the  game field to decide  when to build a new corridor.  As your work force increases you can manage them via the  task bar at the bottom of the game field, swapping  minions between tasks as and when needed.
The game gets progressivley harder as your corridor like space capsule spead out like a spiders web,   reaching for the   four  monoliths.  Once you connect with  one of these you have to research it using a minimum of one   minion or a maximum of three.  The faster you   complete the research, the  sooner you can use it's attributes.   To ensure the survival of your minions you  need to place weapons capsules strategically throughout your maze of corridors as each  module only covers a small area no more than a couple of modules in any direction.    Enemies attack  minions which can only take a few hits   so   you're constantly having to create new minions at the end of each attack via  the habitat  module (but you need resources from the kitchen to create new minions).  Before an attack is imminent you get a brief red flashing warning.  At this point you  should    swap all  minions tasks to   weapons    to ensure that all of your weapon stations are manned by minions.  This is the safest location for a miniom during an attack.  Once the attack is over  you should then  retask your  minions  to return to their previous tasks ASAP.  This is done by dragging   them via a task bar at the bottom of the game field to where you want them to be.  There's an alternative method of returning to previous tasks,  which you're informed of in the tutorial, and which I didn't really take note of it at the time, as I found using the task bar  easier;   I think its done by  clicking on the appropriate modules that were being worked on previous to the attack but not 100% sure..
When you first start the game  there is a short tutotial that  holds your hand through the first few module builds until the first attack is imminent.  I failed miserably  at my first few  attempts trying to send out  corridors to each  of the  monoliths without  building the support services and because I ignored the tutorial.  You have to ensure you have a constant supply of living quarters  and food  to be able to increase the size of your colony and to sustain it as well as  build extractors, and reactors to ensure you have energy and resources to build.
If you are into strategic games and tower defense games coupled loosely with a space theme you'll love this game.  It looks  minimalistic, but it sure gave  me a buzz playing it.  It's one of those games   where you don't relaize  where the time has gone after looking away from the monitor.  I'll surely be playing this for a long time to come, or at least until i've managed to complete  a few rounds.
The    games name rymdkapsel is derived from the Swedish  name for space capsule.
it could use a little more variation between games and several new features but it is fun to create, manage, and defend your own base as you expand to collect the monoliths

You have a couple of minions that are responsible for everything that's happening on your space station. There are a couple of ressources that have to be transported and some building blocks that you can place and your minions have to build. All you can do, though, is assign minions to certain very broad tasks (or should I say task groups) like construction, base defense, food supply and so on. This is not inherently bad and clearly the idea of the game, but it just doesn't work at all with their AI. Example: one task group is construction. Let's say I put all my 10 minions into construction with 4 building jobs on the space station available, each one needs 2 kinds of ressources. Then all the minions will attempt to do the same thing, i.e., move to the "first" ressource, load up, and run to the first construction site. Of course, because they have the same speed, all of them will arrive there at approximately the same time at which point the 2nd to 10th minion will realize that that ressource is no longer needed because the first minion already supplied it. They will then look for another building that needs that ressource or go get another ressource. So basically there's no point assigning a lot of minions to one task because their AI doesn't realize which ressources are already being supplied. This pretty much breaks the game because time for movement is of essence in this game. The idea was good but the execution is terrible in my opinion. I assume this could have been patched to something more enjoyable in a matter of a few hours.
Even if it would work a little better there's not much to do. It's pretty much a waiting game. The strategy is not very deep. The game modes available are pretty much all the same, just with easier or harder waves of enemies or no enemies at all.

If you're into playing MMORPG's with deep character customizations through choosing a class, then doing stat building and skill choices then this game is for you. On the surface this game looks like a simple RPG game but it'll start to open up and seem more advanced and complex once you start to understand the game a lot more and get further into it.
There are many different kinds of classes, starting from the four basic ones. Such as melee, mage, ranged, and support. They all have class trees, meaning eventually down the line you evolve into stronger and diverse classes of your choice. Each class from the beginning to the end have each their own different skills.
Game is definitely more fun to play with friends in a party.
The only things I somewhat don't like in this game is your character's appearance customization. It's probably just me but sometimes everyone looks the same. This most likely probably doesn't matter if you just buy not game changing costumes with real money. The other one is that the game is a grind (For me at least.), of course I'm only saying that because I have a busy life so you can ignore what I said for that.
For answers if the game is pay to win, it really isn't. The optional thirty to sixty day subscription is just something I grabbed since I don't exactly have many hours per each day to play. Which I can explain for why the subscription is useful for me in that way and also why it doesn't really matter much anyway.
One of the subscription bonuses is a small 30% experience bonus in killing things. It actually is small since someone who doesn't have the subscription that plays 7-10 hours a day. Will still make more experience than someone who only plays 2-4 hours a day with the subscription bonus (Like me.). The other thing I needed from the subscription is to be able to upgrade two different skill attributes at the same time instead of one at a time. It's mainly just for convenience as it's not truly needed.

If you're a veteran MMORPG player from the golden age of MMORPG's, you've come to the right place. Tree of Savior is just about the only MMORPG to release in this decade that caters exactly to those that are fond of hardcore MMORPGs of an age long ago. The style, feel, input and feedback of the game pays much homage to MMORPG titles such as Ragnarok Online. In fact, the original director of Ragnarok Online is the director for this game. You can rest assured that this game will keep you busy with lots to do and much fun to be had.
Now let's get into the actual critic. This is actually my first review but I've played MMORPG's my entire life and have played this title for more than my actual listed play time.
PROS :
Alright. Let's put everything into context.
First and foremost is definitely the rustic feel of this game. The art style, atmosphere, music, everything just plays so well into constructing an amazing world for you to explore. The art style is extermely reminiscent of Ragnarok Online and some view Tree of Savior as the "true" sucessor to Ragnarok Online. You have all the amazing customizability and environment from Ragnarok Online put into a much more modern take on the same genre without losing it's original feel.
The biggest attraction of Tree of Savior would definitely have to be the class system. Tree of Saviors class system is very unique in that a player can custom tailor their class to fit their specific play style. Are you a "Swordsman" class but prefer to use many new active skills instead of basic attacks? Advance into "Highlander" or "Barbarian" to progress down those paths and gain access to a whole new branch of skills. But maybe you enjoy using basic attacks. If that's the case, you can choose to further hone your skills as a "Swordsman" and invest further into your original first class instead of advancing into a "Highlander" or "Barbarian". Tree of Savior gives players the opportunity to "Rank up" their current class instead of advancing to a new class and increase the maximum skill levels of their current class' abilities, giving them potential to be stronger than those that followed a different path if utilized correctly.
Tree of Savior also encourages players to diversify their class choices to fit their play style. Just because you chose the path of a Wizard and advanced into a Pyromancer doesn't mean you're stuck being a flame based magic user forever. You can easily advance into a Cryomancer at the next class advance and become both! Just because you chose the path of magic doesn't mean your only role is damage dealing. You can advance into other classes that compliment your current set of skills as well. A Pyromancer has the ability "Flame Ground" which sets an area ablaze dealing Damage over Time. Should a Pyromancer also advance into a "Linker", a class that specializes in monster manipulation, the "Pyro-Linker" could set ground abalaze, "link" together monsters, and drag them over the fire to be slow roasted. There are plenty of classes with complimenting skills such as this example. The greatest thing about Tree of Savior is finding them all and trying them.
Customizable stat distribution is a very big thing for me. It means that the game does not have a "preset" style of playing that the game has already defined for you. If you feel like being a warrior class that goes complete glass cannon and forsakes all durability put everything into Strength and have at it. If you feel like playing a Wizard up close and personal you can easily stat in some extra Vitality for some health. If you feel that you want to shoot arrows faster rather than harder, you can easily stat in Agility for some speed. Being able to customize your stat inputs helps you refine what your playstyle would be instead of just following along a guide.
Now onto the cons. A game without cons does not exist. But Tree of Savior has some debateable cons so let's get into them.
CONS:
Tree of Savior players on a linear leveling system of starting at level 1, to infinity. That is to say, there is no level cap. In concept, this is designed so that players play at their own pace because there is no race to a "end game" goal to do content. Players will just play at their own leisure finishing content as they progress into different worlds and areas. However players must be reminded that this was originally a Korea MMORPG. It takes alot.
. Of grinding to progress speedily. In my humble opinion this is actually a good way to gate players from speeding through the entire games' content in a single week. But in a game whoms biggest emphasis is replayability by creating multiple characters in different classes, it just slows down progress a ton and doesn't feel great. Grind is both a necessity but a gimp when it comes to MMORPG designing. In all honesty comparatively to other MMORPG's, the grind isn't so bad but it is there nonetheless.
This may be a smaller point but the map layout for Tree of Savior is a bit strange. You'll be progressing linearely through the game and maps and everything will be placed within your level zone, but should you decide to explore a bit the map directly underneath your level 20 map could be a level 100+ map. Now the monsters won't instantly agro and oneshot you or anything, infact they won't agro you at all if you're out of the level gap, but it's just a bit strange unless you're the explorative type. Because of the linear map progression based on current level, you'll never really re-visit older maps save for farming specific materials or major towns and adjacent fields.
My conclusion for this game is you should definitely try it. Whether you're an MMORPG Veteran or a newbie to the genre the experience playing it was amazing and you won't experience another game like it.

If you liked Metro 2033 atmosphere and gameplay (probably last light as well, but I won't add it here since I haven't played it), you will love STALKER even more. Above all,  it's important to note that some people who developped that game was formerly within STALKER dev team.
STALKER is somewhat an open-world game and a Survival horror FPS that will really get under your skin (the only thing that doesn't make it open-world is that it is divided by "loading zones"). You're free to go whereever you want, provided you got the skills for it, and the game also strongly encourages exploration. While not being mandatory, players who dig exploration (like me) will truly feel satisfied. Also, this game being a survival horror piece, ammo is scarce, and your capacity to carry stuff is VERY limited (and since ammo will be the bulk of your carrying capacity, you might have to do some tough decisions before leaving the main hub found later in the game). Sure, human mobs will drop ammo, but it's a thing that you can't plan on since you'll be visiting a lot of areas where humans won't be a threat. There's is also a weather system implemented in the game that can alter your experience (especially nighttime). Being an avid fan of horror, I would often travel during nights since the world will at times truly scare the hell out of you. But more importantly, this factor is truly shining in some particular indoor locations. If you have headphones, do yourself a favor, and use them! And play this game at night for god's sake.
Stalker is a game that really passed under the radar, most probably because it was overshadowed by its severe abundance of bugs and glitches upon its release that probably made it unplayable (or broken) for many. But thanks to the great community of modders, you can now not only experience the game with MUCH better visuals and textures, the Complete mod (2009-12) will fix most, if not all, bugs that plagued the original game.
This is my first ever written review in English, so bear in mind that it is flawed, and far from perfect.

It is a shame that I can't recommend the game.
Some parts of it are enjoyable, but there are just so many bugs etc. that I just end up frustrated more than anything while playing.
Lets start with the good:
-A game inspired by tabletop RPG's. Not as good as either VtM Bloodline nor VtM Redemption, but that most likely is because of the budget which is ok.
-The game tries to create a vampire society feel with different "clans".
The neutral stuff:
- The talent trees are randomized for every character. This can be either good or bad. I personally dislike it because I tried both a witch and a warrior and both had awkward skill trees. The witch got talents that improved fighting (+ dexterity every level, +axe damage), while the warrior had a few talents that were for spell casters.
- The dialogue is very hit and miss. Sometimes I like it a bit and at times I just cringe at how it is written.
Now for the bad things and the reason I won't play it anymore:
- Spell casting flat out doesn't work at times. While playing a witch I had a huge number of times there the animation for a spell started, but nothing happened after that. I also had the reverse where I was for instance knocked down, but the spell casting did continue through it.
- Mist form is a spell in the game that transforms you into a cloud of mist, but it doesn't function as it should (I think). At one point I transformed into mist, but a spike trap still damaged me (killed me even) and an enemy was just tracking me while I passed it.
- Your own spells are dependant on you hitting the enemy, but spells of quite a few enemies are either tracking you or instant hits. There are a few spells you can dodge, but those are only the spells you can learn aswell.
I will give 2 examples of what I mean with tracking/instant hitting.
The first is that when you fight a vampire golem or ice golem or similar and they hit the ground to knock you down, you can see the path of the shockwave bend quite far if you dodge around while the shockwave is approaching you.
The second example is that of spider webbings. If a spider decides to lock you in place with its webbing, it hits you instantly without the possibility of doding or responding.
- Enemies quite often spam their spells/attacks. In a fight with a golem it just knocked me down 4 times in a row without giving me a possibility to do a thing about it.
- At one point I ran into a bug that caused my stamina, health and energy to stop regenerating. At first I thought my character lacked blood, but that was at 83. So I thought of a debuff, but there was nothing indicating this. In the end I suicided to respawn in a safe area which fixed it, but needing to die to fix this is not that good to say the least.

This is a sequal worth mentioning after your friend tells you smugly that there is no such thing as a sequal that actually is a worthy succsessor to the original. Tell that friend to go away with their pesky elitism.
Every element of the game feels complete. There is no performance issues to note. I didn't witness any bugs while playing.
I admit, I don't like Hollywoods wash, rinse, repeat strategy. I don't like some certain game companies' likewise strategy. Until the sequal lives up to the hype. Until it is just as good as the original.
I can tell you what this game does to me. After paying the price of the game, I feel like I should get what my money is worth. I didn't feel compelled to finish the game and get over it. I took my time and inhaled in the whole experience the developers could offer and I enjoyed it very much.
The story is spot on and nothing feels forced in, no plotholes after the first games story. Gameplay is smooth and challenging. And I actually challenged myself to finish it on "Low Chaos" as the game is intended to be played. That was not my intention with the first game and I finished the first game on "High Chaos". Also, this game is a looker, I tell you. Art style is really good. Compelling story, solid and challenging gameplay, great visuals, no performance issues, no gamebreaking bugs. What else do you expect from a game?!
Right after the game came out, the players reported poor performance and the issue is somehow still reported. Not the case now. It runs smoothly with plenty to spare on my rather humble PC equipped with an i5-6500, 16 GB of RAM and a GTX1060 6GB.
This is a solid succsessor to the first Dishonored game offering pretty much the same premise but with different, fresh touches on the gameplay aspect. I nothing negative to say about this game, it is tremendous.
In conclusion, don't worry about the game not being as good as the first one,
. Play it, enjoy it, cherish it.

I really enjoy a game based on history.  The total war series as a whole is good, but Rome 2 has to be the best of them.  Good graphic and animations, and good sound effects. The battles themselves are fantastic.  Dependig on the settings u chose they can be massive, with several thousands of troops.  Each faction has units specific to it, althouh some can seem similar. but the different unit types can take away the old rock paper scissors feel. I bought this game on a black friday sale for 15 bucks; I would have kicked myself if I'd spent 50 bucks on it. For 15 bucks it is totally worth it. That being said...
PROS:
-Great graphics
+colors are not so vivid, giving a realistic appearance
-Battle cries are emtional and excellently done
+although random soldiers' mutters are repetitive, they are usually context-relevant and humanize the soldiers
+Roman Auxilary Cavalry voice is AWESOME
-Naval and land battle combination is cool, especially in siege battles
-Can command 40 units at a time
-Armies' unit cards are sorted intelligently (although this could be done manually in RTW 1)
-Grouping settlements into provinces allows for more fluid management, especially once you've expanded to an empire
-SPQR replaced by optional missions delineates gameplay allowing for a more sandbox campaign
-Imperium levels and corruption, although extremely annoying, reflect the instability and brutality of the politics of ancient societies (and modern, for that matter)

-Agents' passive actions (oxymoron?), such as Military Administration, Military Training, Spy Networks, etc., are cool.
CONS:
-Cannot play as Sparta without DLC (who pays 50 bucks and doesn't want to play as Sparta?)
-Most historic battles are DLC
-Units glitch on walls
+many times when you tell them to move left, they first move right, vice versa
+in a Rome city defense battle I commanded, units on walls wouldn't obey commands or act at all
-Naval battles are bugged
+ships sometimes will get locked into moving the direction they are facing; never stopping until they slide into a corner of the map
+naval artillery/missiles will lock onto a land target's last location within their firing range, continuing to fire after they've left that spot until you command the ship to turn around or move out of range (commanding the unit to stop does not stop their firing orders)
-Cinematic kill sequences disrupt the combat simulation
+Soldiers attempting to pull back from combat will stop and turn around to engage in a fight sequence instead of simply being chopped from behind
+There are no backstap kill sequences
+cavalry kill rate while chasing routing troops is frustratingly slow since cavalry MUST kill with cinematic kill sequence when not charging
+one sequence, in particular, may involve a soldier striking over and over again for more than 15 seconds, digging him deep behind enemy lines without being stopped by surrounding enemy soldiers
-AI has not been improved since I last played Rome: Total War Barbarian Invasion v 1.6
-Blood and Gore pack acted as an "on" switch for delimbing of soldiers; no new fight sequences were added.
-General's/agent's abilities do not reflect their actions
+you may now craft an agent to accomplish any sort of task; regardless of what actual experience they have
+generals essentially cannot remain idle without developing negative traits, unless they have already aquired their maximum of three traits
-Agents are not as specialized and can be more powerful than armies
+it's easy enough to develop a powerful agent; powerful agents can cripple armies into not being able to move for countless turns.
+all agents can perform all tasks with some differences in outcome (reminiscent of Dragon Age 2 and Diablo 3's overbalancing of classes, removing stark contrasts in capabilities)
-Extremely limited diversity of buildings in settlements
+settlements, even capitals, are not unique from each other; essentially only a few dozen mix/match possibilities with hum-drum differences
+no point in preserving old buildings from another faction since they get in the way of your 3-5 building slot limit
+cities' appearance in battle mode do not reflect your personal development of that city
-Encyclopedia is poorly organized and disruptive of the game
+Previous titles simply required a right-click to open a single unit/building information card

In Papers, Please you play an unnamed immigration control officer on the border of a dystopian soviet state called Arstotzka. The game consists of processing a line of proposed entrants to the country as they shuffle up to your booth, peer in with their 16bit faces and present you documents needed to enter. You then need to scrutinise these documents for discrepancies before either approving or denying entry. Firstly they need the right papers, then these papers need to be checked to make sure that they are factual (a passport with a different sex to the person for example). You can also choose to detain people if you so wish, at which point they are dragged off by the guards never to be seen again. The documents required change on a daily basis as political situations change in the country.
The consequences of letting through or denying someone incorrectly is a fine on your daily earnings. At the end of each work day you go home to your assigned apartment and depending on how the day went have to make decisions as to whether to heat or feed your family or if you can afford the medication required to keep your family from getting sick. The game never quite gives you enough money and when I played last night I never had enough money for rent, food, heating and medicine in one single day meaning you have to juggle with these most basic needs.
There is a larger story that unfolds across the game as you continue playing involving a terrorist faction from a neighbouring state that changes the way you have to process certain people, and a shadowy mysterious organisation that pass you cryptic messages. They are trying to bring down the government and attract attention from the ministry who turn up to your booth asking questions, you can choose who to help and who not to help and all your decisions have consequences.

The day to day stuff might seem mundane, but you get paid per process so you have to weigh running through people quickly against the possibility of missing something... its a game that can harshly punish you for cutting the wrong corner while constantly pressuring you to cut corners. Various events occur during the game, one event I had was after processing the first person in the line he told me that he was escaping persecution and would be killed if he returned and his wife was behind him. His wife didn't have the right papers and I had to decide whether to grant entry (and take the financial hit myself) or play by the book and deny entry. The pixelated people plead, bluff and beg to get their way - and honestly I've never felt like such a monster as playing this game.

Is it fun? Well sort of, certainly more than it sounds anyway. The document inspection part of the game is oddly compelling, the perfectionist in me wanting to get it right all the time but with so many variables making this incredibly difficult. The constant feedback of going back home with not quite enough money pressuring you into going quicker and inevitably making more mistakes. The small events added something new every day which made me feel very involved in the game - as if the fate of these people actually mattered. I didn't get far enough to see the overall story unfold to the end, after accepting a large bribe (without actually carrying out the deed) and moving to a better house I was reported by my neighbour and thrown in jail by the ministry of income pending a full investigation. Apparently there are multiple endings based on the decisions made throughout the game giving it a level of re-playability.

Papers, Please offers a unique experience playing the role of an immigration inspecter in a totalitarian state.  I never would have imagined before playing that I would get that one more turn feeling that I get from Civ games.  It requires extreme attention to detail in  which you inspect documents, compare people to their documents, and deal with every changing rules that are dictated by events that happen in the game.  I truly felt sympathy for border control inspectors after playing and will likely be a little less impatient on my next international trip.

In rymdkapsel, you direct small white rectangular minions to build a base, collect resources, and defend their territory against waves of enemies. As you can tell from the screenshots, it's highly abstract and pleasing to look at. What you might not be able to tell from the screenshots, though, is how attached you'll get to these little shapes. As they build new structures out of tetrominoes, as they research new monoliths, as they fend off the whirring attack shapes, you'll be rooting for them, not just because they're doing your bidding, but also because they have a right to build little lives for themselves outside of your goals as a game player.

Is your time of value to you? Do you seek to get the most out of every moment? Are you prepared to pay a few quid to make those moments special, if onl;y in your imagination?
If so, move on quickly. Don't waste your time on this game, or even this review.
There's about an hour's worth of "entertainment" in this game, most of which is the unrequited anticipation of the game expanding in ways you imagine it might. At first I did worry about those finite resources (the little pink flakes) and I was right to. Once they are exhausted the game is all but over.
You have weapons that are never upgraded, enemies that never change, base functions that are never enhanced.
The zen mode is particularly pointless. If it was a matter of building a functioning base, with resource management and exploration playing a part it would be fine, but there's none of that.
Your minions are born when you create "quarters" which implies that the quarters will be required to sustain the minions, but once the quarter has spawned it's allocated two minions you can reclaim it and the minions are retained, sleeping when idle wherever they fall!
Once you figure that out the main strategic aim of the game (to survive attack after attack) becomes much easier as you reclaim the resources of quarters after each spawning. Use those resources to build weapons. Get to the monoliths.
Yaaawwwn.
It's like the first level of a good strategy game.

Like the bizarre lovechild of tetris and dungeon keeper... in space.
Honestly, I had reservations with the puzzle game aspect before I started playing, but as soon as I dove in, I found that it does nothing to damage the simulation.
Very fun, and quickly pretty challenging.

...But it's a cautious recommendation. Just be forewarned that the game has limited replayability, though it wouldn't surprise me if Rymdkapsel is the kind of game that I'd play for a session of two every month for the next year.
This is the kind of game that one can write a reasoned review for after just a couple of hours. The minimalist art style is at once efficient and iconic--the kind of style that, if adopted by other games, one may remark: "Oh, yeah, that's very Rymdkapsel-ly." A bit awkward for the mouth, but like Rymdkapsel, efficient.
Rymdkapsel is a real-time, pausable strategy game in which you select from a series of 4-block segements to build a contiguous base--they call it a space station, but it would work for a variety of genres. You must manage three different resources--which, like the rest of the game, are represented by simple geometric shapes of differing colors--all of which have slightly different generation mechanics. The modules of the station are few, the minions relatively mindless, but the mechanic is tight: a stubborn completionist should get several hours out of the game before figuring out how to complete the last "mission goal".
There's not much of a tutorial to speak of, nor multiple play modes, nor much of anything outside of the primary mechanic: "given this limited toolset for this type of problem, how do you solve it?" Your first two-three playthroughs may seem a bit harried, especially toward the end--warning/spoiler: don't bother trying to build anything after wave 22--but as you warm to the mechanic it'll become an exciting quandary to tackle.
Much like Sudoku, this game is initially difficult to learn; one derives the most pleasure from solving it after the first 20-30 tries; but once you've got it down pat, it's much more of a lower-state-of-consciousness time sink. Not that that's bad.

I played WoW for years and decided to leave MMO's all together. I listened to the negative stuff about ESO for a while so avoided it.
Then I felt like just giving it a go. It was pretty good.
Here I am about three years later... the game is getting a little stale for me but I continue to play it here and there. I think deep down that MMO's are just not my thing anymore. They all seem to have the same inherant flaws and ESO is no different.
I currently feel the DLC are lack luster. The quests for them and the characters involved are very shallow. It's better than WoW's 'go fetch 10 of this' quest that hasn't changed for a decade though. Still, I feel there is a huge missed opportunity with storytelling and questing in this game. It just feels so bland compared to the other Elder Scrolls single player games.
So, is it worth it? Well, get it on sale for 20 bucks... or less if possible and don't subscribe - just use character slots as mules and play one class you like and forget about doing everything here... it just isn't worth it.
The Morrowind Expansion was sort of ho-hum. It looks nice and everything but the story was short. Some questlines were good, some not so much so. The Warden class, unless you really crave a bear or to be a frost mage, doesn't justify it for me. The land of Vvardenfell is detailed by a lot of land is just left unused which is a crying shame.
Thieves Guild / Dark Brotherhood DLCs - worth getting for the passives - storylines are OKish
Wrothgar (Orsinium) - worth one playthrough
Imperial City - pvp only, I could care less.
Those Dungeon DLCS - never tried them. if you subscribe, run them once for achievements and don't bother to waste the crowns to own them (crowns are the ingame currency)
Crown Store - mostly just visual things to buy. I get stuff every once in a while to support the game when not subscribed but the some of the items, usually mounts, seem very overpriced.
Crown Crates - A SCAM. Out to take your money. Avoid like the plague
In the end, the whole thing will feel like a job with daily quests with meager rewards that make you feel like a field slave and ask yourself why you're even playing it (then again, World of Warcraft felt the same for me towards the end). My recommendation is to never play an MMO again and save youreself the time and money for other games in different genres (normal rpg, strategy, survival... anything really).

In it's release state Rome 2 was a disaster. Since then the gama has been patched into a stable and playable state, and thanks to mods I have gotten my moneys worth out of this game.
However even considering the much improved emperor edition I cannot recommend this game. Battle AI is terrible and seige AI is downright laughable. Interesting mechanics and actual strategy are abandoned in favour of absurd arcady features (burning down metal gates with torches?), units have trouble keeping formation and most battles are over before you have a chance to flank or apply any real strategy.
Proper sieges are non-existant and most cities do not have and cannot build walls. Even cities with walls may be instantly taken the turn they are attacked due to the ridiculous torch throwing mechanic. This was supposedly an attempt to reduce the number of repetitive sige battles present in earlier games but it has the opposite affect of forcing the player through the same uninteresting garrison battle dozens of times every campaign.
The graphics are good (but not amazing) and the historical immersion is ok, but still with enough inconsistencies to make me cringe (why does Syracuse not have walls?).
Additionally Creative Assembly has joined the list of developers which dole out features which should have been in the base game in the form of overpriced DLC's. This is downright insulting considering the state of the game upon release.
Overall as much as I tried to enjoy vanilla Rome 2 It has too many flaws which ruin the experience, for every thing I enjoyed about Rome 2 there were 10 frustraing things I didn't. If you are looking to enjoy the total war experience I recommend Shogun 2 or Rome 1 with mods.

In Papers, Please you play an unnamed immigration control officer on the border of a dystopian soviet state called Arstotzka. The game consists of processing a line of proposed entrants to the country as they shuffle up to your booth, peer in with their 16bit faces and present you documents needed to enter. You then need to scrutinise these documents for discrepancies before either approving or denying entry. Firstly they need the right papers, then these papers need to be checked to make sure that they are factual (a passport with a different sex to the person for example). You can also choose to detain people if you so wish, at which point they are dragged off by the guards never to be seen again. The documents required change on a daily basis as political situations change in the country.
The consequences of letting through or denying someone incorrectly is a fine on your daily earnings. At the end of each work day you go home to your assigned apartment and depending on how the day went have to make decisions as to whether to heat or feed your family or if you can afford the medication required to keep your family from getting sick. The game never quite gives you enough money and when I played last night I never had enough money for rent, food, heating and medicine in one single day meaning you have to juggle with these most basic needs.
There is a larger story that unfolds across the game as you continue playing involving a terrorist faction from a neighbouring state that changes the way you have to process certain people, and a shadowy mysterious organisation that pass you cryptic messages. They are trying to bring down the government and attract attention from the ministry who turn up to your booth asking questions, you can choose who to help and who not to help and all your decisions have consequences.

The day to day stuff might seem mundane, but you get paid per process so you have to weigh running through people quickly against the possibility of missing something... its a game that can harshly punish you for cutting the wrong corner while constantly pressuring you to cut corners. Various events occur during the game, one event I had was after processing the first person in the line he told me that he was escaping persecution and would be killed if he returned and his wife was behind him. His wife didn't have the right papers and I had to decide whether to grant entry (and take the financial hit myself) or play by the book and deny entry. The pixelated people plead, bluff and beg to get their way - and honestly I've never felt like such a monster as playing this game.

Is it fun? Well sort of, certainly more than it sounds anyway. The document inspection part of the game is oddly compelling, the perfectionist in me wanting to get it right all the time but with so many variables making this incredibly difficult. The constant feedback of going back home with not quite enough money pressuring you into going quicker and inevitably making more mistakes. The small events added something new every day which made me feel very involved in the game - as if the fate of these people actually mattered. I didn't get far enough to see the overall story unfold to the end, after accepting a large bribe (without actually carrying out the deed) and moving to a better house I was reported by my neighbour and thrown in jail by the ministry of income pending a full investigation. Apparently there are multiple endings based on the decisions made throughout the game giving it a level of re-playability.

For a one man project, this title is by all means not only impressive, but could very well compare and hold itself high on a pedestal next to innovative RPGs from the late 90s and early millenium that defined the genre, such as morrowind, deus ex, Legacy of Kain and of course, Vampire The Masquerade : Bloodlines, wich I beleive this game could be called the late alternative successr of.
This game has everything: large array of items to make the ultimate vampire character, skills and abilities galore, intresting (VOICED!) dialogues, a great immersive soundtrack, a neat alluring network of underground places ranging from sewers to crypts to dungeons or just plain dark caves, characters (npcs), a sire system (make you own little coven of blood suckers), simple controls.
The graphics didn't seem to be a main focus here but considering what the game offers and the general world aesthetics to compensate this mild lack, I don't mind it.
Now the fighting and overall moving system is a bit clunky, but easy to overlook once you get sucked in. However, it is easy to get lost considering the procedural nature of some places, which is immersive, mind you, unless you have a map.
A few things I would have liked to see would have been a day/night system, larger cities and underworld cities (perhaps forests), the choice to play as a lycan, mortal witch/sorcerer, lych, ghoul or human, I also understand this world doesn't follow the World Of Darkness universe, which is a tad sad, but not so bad. Another thing I do mind greatly though is the poor customizability of the player character, between a few faces that all look alike and the choice between bald or one hair cut isn't what I would call customizability, but again, once you get into the game, it's easy to forget that.
With this said, for those of you looking for a game that brings back the freshness and inovation at the expense of mild clunkyness some of you may have felt from the good ol' days of rpg (1998 to 2004-ish) and for a game that satisfies that void feeling of wretched hunger left behind from finishing Vampire The Masquerade: Bloodlines one-to-many times and finding no appropriate successor, then look no further, this game is for you. Mind you it's a bit more of a dungeon crawler/rogue kinda game.

This game is like a roller coaster, alternating between scary, hard, annoying and beautiful. in your first encounter with it, the circumstances of your first contact are terrifying, thus creating a real fear of the
creature, leaving you immersed in the game as if your life were in real danger, however this is a very long game, with something around 20 hours of campaign, what isn't completely bad, but the constant exposition to threat starts to desensitize you to it, shifting the game from scary to very hard, verging the annoying, but, if you like a good challenge you may enjoy it, even though I do like challenges

I've been a member of theHunter since around 2011, when there were only around 2 maps and just a few animals to hunt.  This game has come a long way over the past few years, which is a great achievement for the small team (EW).  Even for a niche game, this one really stands out from the other (arcade) hunting games out there.  It doesn't take long to realize just how much detail the studio has tried to squeeze into this gem.  Just to list a few reasons why I love the game:
1) Great immersion, and the pace is just right to actually enjoy being in the wilderness.
2) The graphics are the best you will find in any hunting game, and still rival many newer engines/games of other genres.
3) Developers keep the community informed about new content/events with [mostly] weekly status updates.
4) Fair price for subscription-based gameplay, and the game keeps growing without waiting for a sequel like other one-offs.
5) They added waterfowl!
There are so many here complaining about the F2P tag and business model.  Whoever suggests that F2P means giving everything away just doesn't understand how a business works.  I understand F2P as a "modern" term for demo, where you get to decide how much you want to pay/play.  I'll agree that I've poured a good amount of cash into the game, but it's mostly because I want to support development of this game.  It doesn't take a genius to realize that there aren't a lot of hunter sims around.  As I said...this one is miles ahead of the competition, and I'd like it to stick around for a while.  While I invested a good bit of money, that certainly doesn't mean this game can't be played fully with even the most basic package.  The extras are mostly aesthetic, and in no way necessary to be successful.  I can imagine most newcomers will see all the extra (purchasable) weapons and be overwhelmed by the full cost of obtaining them all.  My purchases were spread over the course of about 3 years, so of course I'm not bothered by the fact.
The only thing negative I can really say about the game is bugs have a tendency to stay around for a while.  I understand this is probably the most difficult aspect of development, but it would be nice if the developers communicated more about what they're trying to fix rather than new competitions and addons.  Really hard to complain too much though, since this is extremely common with most publishers/developers.
Overall, it's a great game at a fair price, with a fantastic community.  I play in 3D, and it's easily the best I've exerienced, even against all the AAA titles.  Now...go play!

The mix of resource management, tower defense and "city builder" makes an interesting genre combination.  That is all rymdkapsel is: an interesting idea lacking any substance. It is like a good puzzle game, but rymdkapsel does not give you a variety of challenges you would expect to get in a puzzle game ("it is too short").
If you don't mind me oversimplifying - you choose rooms to construct which are randomly tetris-shaped - then your job is to assign tasks to your minions (to construct or defend). But you do not control your minions directly, you only assign tasks, and if lucky the AI will do exactly what you want. Periodically waves of enemies will invade randomly destroying your minions and resources. You need to be challenged but the way the enemy work feels like your success is more based on luck.
The graphics are simple pleasing geometric shapes. The soundtrack adds to the casual atmosphere and you never feel too threatened - until you suffer a major collapse of your minions and die the next wave.
If you are interested in playing a time sensitive puzzle game, then rymdkapsel is a worthy purchase if it is on sale.

☹ Limited replayability.
A game for fans of refining tactics and efficiency based challenges.
Rymdkapsel is a minimalist resource and time management game where efficiency is of utmost importance. Your goal is to expand your space station by placing down rooms as effectively as possible taking into account their shape which is somewhat random and inspired by Tetris as you stretch out through the void heading for your ultimate goal, the research of four mysterious Monoliths.
To do this, you command your minions to fulfil a specific task, such as construction or research and watch as they do their best to fulfil their roles while you oversee expansion and reassign positions as needed, like switching up an engineer who usually boosts resource production into a defencive role to thwart incoming enemies who periodically attack your minions.
The game uses a collection of known variables and tasks you with using them as best you can. As such, its the type of game that might appeal to those who enjoy refining a strategy or simply improving on a previous attempt. Don't expect a great deal of variation, you'll likely learn everything you need to during your first attempt and from then on, its a matter of using that knowledge efficiently to succeed.
Just like the resource you collect in game, there is enjoyment to be extracted from the game...I just feel it runs dry sooner than you'd expect, not helped by AI oddities such as your builders quite happily doubling up on resources for a construction or the lack of direct minion control can lead to mild frustration.
It's an interesting game and one that I'd like to recommend, but feels a little bit like a proof of concept rather than a fully fledged title. What's there is good but slightly limited and as such I'd strongly recommend waiting for a discount as even if you really enjoy it, it could prove to be very short lived.

In it's release state Rome 2 was a disaster. Since then the gama has been patched into a stable and playable state, and thanks to mods I have gotten my moneys worth out of this game.
However even considering the much improved emperor edition I cannot recommend this game. Battle AI is terrible and seige AI is downright laughable. Interesting mechanics and actual strategy are abandoned in favour of absurd arcady features (burning down metal gates with torches?), units have trouble keeping formation and most battles are over before you have a chance to flank or apply any real strategy.
Proper sieges are non-existant and most cities do not have and cannot build walls. Even cities with walls may be instantly taken the turn they are attacked due to the ridiculous torch throwing mechanic. This was supposedly an attempt to reduce the number of repetitive sige battles present in earlier games but it has the opposite affect of forcing the player through the same uninteresting garrison battle dozens of times every campaign.
The graphics are good (but not amazing) and the historical immersion is ok, but still with enough inconsistencies to make me cringe (why does Syracuse not have walls?).
Additionally Creative Assembly has joined the list of developers which dole out features which should have been in the base game in the form of overpriced DLC's. This is downright insulting considering the state of the game upon release.
Overall as much as I tried to enjoy vanilla Rome 2 It has too many flaws which ruin the experience, for every thing I enjoyed about Rome 2 there were 10 frustraing things I didn't. If you are looking to enjoy the total war experience I recommend Shogun 2 or Rome 1 with mods.

Players who've gone through Dishonored 1 will probably feel like there's something missing to really call it the second installment. With all the new additions of skills and maps, and even the opportunity to play either Corvo or Emily, it still felt like the game circled on what made D1 a success, but only took very safe (and promising) steps to stand out.
Despite this, the game was still a fun journey, and if you haven't played the first D1 ,D2 is a great starting point.
PROS:
-New skills opens up different play-style
-New locations and maps
-Does well in getting you to explore all the buildings
-Loved the experimental time travel device
-Some really beautiful location designs
Areas for Improvement:
-Story was too short and brief. It didn't make me feel as invested in the characters as the first one.
-Mission lore/ objectives menu can be more straight forward (I don't understand how the texts are so small when there's so much extra space available).
-Starting to get tired of the ultimate pacifist=good ending route. This discourages players from experimenting the "lethal" take downs.

Personal Rating: 8.5 of 10
This game is a worthy successor to Dishonored. It plays exactly like its predecessor safe for a few enhancement. So, Dishonored 2 is a first person tactical stealth action game that offers freedom to the players to play game as they like. The game also has upgrades, perks, skills and a selections of weapons at your disposal. These gives players to customize the character to suit their style.
It is worth noting that this single player only game is designed to be played with with an RPG mindset. Meaning, thorough exploration, character building and understading the story is recommended and it is easy and enjoyable because game is designed that way. The maps are created and designed for exploration and its quite rewarding as you may find collectibles, items or stories to shed light to the game settings. There are usually more than a route or solution to a destination or problem and players who loved the first game can easily immerse themselves to the characters.
Each level also has different settings and mood to it and some levels can really be enjoyable or bring a few surprises. Graphics art style is rather unique to its own and has sharper texture and colour compare to Dishonored. The music complements nicely to the game and it really helps with the mood without interrupting while sound effects are crisp and adequate.
Enemy A.I. has nothing to shout about and they behave in a rather expected manner with consistency. In other words, once you grasp hold of the behaviour, you can plan and execute your moves properly without any funny glitch or bugs that makes you question how or why. There are not many varieties or types of enemies so don't expect different strategy of puzzle solving skills. Either head on or stealth approach, these enemies, unfortunately, lack in providing some challenges but, on the other hand, less frustration.
Game is forgiving and just meant to be fun and enjoyable. You have a unique set of skills that isn't a huge skill tree but each make can a significant impact. Aside of that, there are also charms that works like perks that you can equipt and customize at anytime. The game does not have a wide array of weapons but each comes in different variety, upgrades or customization that may suit different play style.
Story is a continuation from the previous title. It is dark and has absolutely no space for humor so if the first is your cup of tea, this should fit right in. If you have not played the previous title, it is highly recommended to do so including the story DLCs since they are all related.
I've not encountered any game breaking bugs or performance issue or any problems significant enough to reduce gameplay experience such as clippings or enemies seeing through thin walls but playing the game 3 times to achieve different endings and chasing achievements, I can say if you cared not for the experience or achievements and go in gun blazing, the game can be really short and provide less challenge too. Also, at times when trying to navigate through crawlspace, its can prove to be a challenge due to unprecise texture over the actual polygon area.

No More Room in Hell is a fascinating, mind-boggling, mind-blowing, and miraculous video game. You get to pick one of the protagonists in a zombie survival plot. The main protagonists also known as survivors are Wally, Molotov, Bateman, Hunter, Jive, Butcher, Badass, and Roje. Wally is the oldest of the survivors. He is typically seen using the Colt National Match 1911. He  is based on Walter Sobchak, a character from the movie The Big Lebowski, as seen in his resemblance to the character, as well as his name being short for Walter. Molotov is an ex-firefighter wearing a beanie hat and his fireman's uniform. Bateman was working on the government in the White House. He is based on the character Patrick Bateman from the film American Psycho, as evidenced by his slothing, name, and use of the fireaxe in promotional images. Hunter is a younger man in NMRiH, who wears a baseball cap and dingy clothes. Jive is a survivor who seems to be a partygoer, based on his name and attire. he guy on the left is Butcher. Right now, he's not butching meat, he's butching zombie flesh. The guy on the right is Roje. He's a former soldier with a defective left eye. The girl in the middle is Badass. She's the first female survivor in NMRIH. National Guards are the ones who rescue the survivors, either in objective or in survival maps. They come in with a tank, or a truck or even a helicopter.They never appeared PHYSICALLY in earliest versions. They can only be heard through their radio messages. In the patch 1.08, they appeared PHYSICALLY, but as dead bodies.In the latest patch, which is 1.09, they appeared already as zombies. Also, if your wondering what NMRIH means it stands for the title of the game. There are two gamemodes. Survival mode is another mode in a map where you need to survive and protect the zones until the rescue arrives. Unlike objective mode, there's no objectives that you need to follow. The maps with survival modes are named with "nms" before the name of the map. Objective mode is a mode in a map where you need to accomplish all of the objectives given in the map in order for you to be extracted. Most of the official maps have objectives that needs you to get some IMPORTANT things around the map. The maps with objective modes are named with "nmo" before the name of the map. Items Welder Can be used to weld shut or cut through specific metal objects. Fire Extinguisher
Aside from being a heavy-hitting melee weapon, the extinguisher can be used to put out flames to clear paths to certain items or objectives. Flare Gun Not only a weapon for igniting zombies into flailing bags of flesh, but can be used to fire a signal flare for a helicopter to drop off a supply crate or even signal a rescue vehicle in some maps. Barricade Hammer A quick-hitting melee weapon that also allows the user to barricade doors, windows or other points (as chosen by the level designer) if they have wooden planks in their ammunition inventory. Maglite A crucially important tool used to illuminate the path for yourself and other players. Sometimes it flickers, but don't worry. It is an LED Maglite with batteries that essentially last forever. A future update might remove the infinite batteries in the Maglite. Zippo A lighter that can provide a small flame for the player to see with, but provides no other purpose (not even as a weapon). The flame produced by the zippo barely lights up the path in front of the player and only provides a false sense of security. Inventory Items These items can be carried in the player's inventory and can be used but opening the radial inventory and hovering the mouse over it. An exception can be made with the walkie talkie because the player uses it everytime they press the transmit voice button.
Walkie Talkie Survivors who want to be able to communicate with each other across large distances should seek out the walkie talkie. When picked up, it provides the user a passive and easy way to communicate with other walkie talkie users who are in a different area of the current level they're in. Phalanx This item is the Phalanx anti-infection drug. It is equipped from the Radial Inventory and consumed immediately. It will be removed from the inventory and will cure infection temporarily for 3 minutes, at which point it will slowly start to set back in and resume its deadly course. First-aid kit The first-aid kit, when used by the player will regain 40% of the player's health that has been lost. Note that the first-aid kit doesn't slow down infection if used after getting bit. It is advised to not use the first-aid kit unless the player's vision has turned completely black and white to avoid wastage. Bandages This item is used to stop bleeding inflicted by zombies occasionally. It is equipped from the Radial Inventory and consumed immediately. It will be removed and stop your bleeding, putting your health back to rights. It should be noted that if you do not use one in time you can in fact bleed out and die.

Rydmkapsel is like an isometric Tetris where you have to lay down blocks. But the twist here is that these blocks are populated by... well, I'm not sure what they are, but they look like rectangles. Each block has a function, so you have a block for defense, for harvesting, for gardens, for cooking and a few more. You have to combine all of these blocks together to create a living world where the main goal is to explore and survive. You can't build a straight road unless you're lucky because each time you construct something a random shape is generated so you have to work with what you get.
At the bottom of the screen you'll see a bar filling up. Once it's full enemies will attack. It starts with 2  enemies that can easily be defeated, but once the wave is over, the bar will refill and new enemies will arrive. The longer you survive the faster the bar fills up and the more enemies will appear. It can get very hectic, especially if your workers can't get to their battle station in time or if you have too few people left to defend it all.
And that's where the exploration part kicks in. There are monoliths to be discovered that can positively alter stuff. Like, for example, making your workers move faster. These seem essential the further you get and it's recommended that you discover and analyze them as soon as possible. There are also multiple objectives to complete, but at the moment for me it's not entirely clear why they're exactly there. Maybe to give you a goal, I don't know.
Graphically the game has a very minimalistic look. There are no bells and whistles, just the essential stuff. The music is also very soothing... until you get that battle alert at least.
So nothing fancy here but it does look sharp and colorful and has a style of its own which I can absolutely appreciate.
The game also feels very relaxing... until, well, things are about to fall apart. Just like how the real Tetris feels.
Anyway, I like Rymdkapsel. I like it a lot. You should too.
[Rating: 79/100]

I really want to recommend this; it's got a neat 'space minimalism' theme going for it, the tetris-RTS gameplay is kind of its own thing, and it is really fun ... for the first playthrough or two.
Unfortunately, this is the sort of strategy game where the first time you play, you realize all your mistakes five minutes after you make them.  The second time, you realize what's pretty much an optimal strategy for the game.  From there, all you can do is tweak that strategy a little bit.  Also, there's a pretty obvious and easy way to futz the tetris-block-placement part of the gameplay and once you start doing that, the game is more about how OCD you want to be with the building placement than anything else.
Fun for a couple of hours, but then the overall fun-to-work ratio gets much worse.  A pity, because like I said, there are some legitimately neat things about this game.
