Before I start I'll tell you in advance that the game has a few issues and actually took me 20-30 minutes to get running though after that it has worked more or less perfectly. The developer
personally help you out if you post your issue in the discussions and the nature of Steam refunds means it's worth trying out anyway. The game does come with a small readme too. I'll put what fixes worked for me at the bottom of this review.
Probably best described as third-person Diablo 2 set in an almost World of Darkness (i.e. VTM:B's setting) with the same lack of polish as STALKER but somehow it all works. I'm going to stress the ARPG/dungeon crawler link more as gameplay-wise it's towards the Diablo end. What it
take from VTM:B (and indeed improves on over it) is the use of non-combat skills in particular persuasion which gives you some fairly major benefits. Also blood drinking, of course.
The tutorial mode is essential for a first time player and even then you might have to check out the discussions for some things (in particular cracking safes and backstabbing) but I didn't have any major problems. Do note that you can conveniently zoom the camera in and out and change the mouse between a more traditional mode instead of having it control the direction the character is looking etc with hotkeys.
The graphics and sound are serviceable and there's plenty of voice acting which generally falls into the better end of VA quality, a (pleasant) surprise for a small budget game like this.
The ability to sire new members is fun but I'd have liked to be able to equip them with things or possibly use them to take things back and sell them for me like pets in Torchlight. In general inventory space is very limited until you grab the right talents.
All in all it's good fun and I'm not even the biggest fan of ARPGs. I can't speak for the class variety but I tried the Witch and there were a good few build options there.

TL;DR: That game is awesome but perhaps for a specific kind of gamers (fans of WoD, this game is for  you!).
I played a lot Vampire: The Masquerade, and the two video games (Redemption and Bloodlines) are one of my preferred. Still, since then, I have that itch of playing a vampire-related game (not a "Blade", or a "Twilight", mind you. "World of Darkness" related).  And since the disappointment of CCP games' abandonment of their World of Darkness MMORPG, I felt like that itch would remain.
Bloodlust: Shadowhunter scratches that itch. All in the right way.
I would not be surprised to learn the developers of this game had a similar itch, and went through the whole process or creating a game that was missing (at least, for me).
The cons:
- The graphics are 10 years-old quality
- The interface is sometimes clumsy
- Little or no documentation (what does "MM Knock Back" means, seriously?)
- 32-bits... Seriously, my game crashed once because it reached the "out of memory" limit. there must be a leak somewhere, but still... 32-bits?
The not-cons:
- No control over the save file: I'm a paranoid, so I wasn't  happy when I realized I would not have saves as I desire. The thing is, I realized that I don't really need them. I'm still surprised by that.
- The random dungeons: I  hate grinding for XPs or whatever, and the dungeons are a bit frightening... But increasing levels is fast enough, and as long as I don't need to do 100-levels dungeons just to make the story happen, I'll be happy (in fact, at the 4th level, my priority is to get out, because grinding gets boring)
- For me, the game crashes if you put high-quality graphics. Don't hesitate to lower them. Then, the game is stable as a rock (only crashed once after that)
The pros:
- The mood. Despite the primitive graphics, the developer nailed it down. I felt like playing a Kindred in a World of Darkness. The music, and ambient sounds. Everything helps you be part of the story
- The story. In spite of random dungeons, there is a story, a  background, and a setting. It's sometimes a bit surprise (every mortal seems to know about vampires?)
- Your bloodline. The childer you sire, fighting with you, or gathering loot or blood. Awesome.
What I want for Bloodlust 2:
- Keep "Bloodlust" as the name of your games. Drop "shadowhunter".
- A larger city
- More vampires
- More quests
- More character appearance customization
- A bit more sims-like behavior (mortals, other vampires, etc., and your childer should do things on their own... perhaps even including betraying you!)
- making it easy to add quests/characters/mods/(written) dialogs, even city blocks
- NOT better graphics. If I wanted graphics, I would be playing whatever current AAA game. I want that specific kind of game, and the graphics were good enough for me.
... because if there is a Bloodlust 2 in preparation, count me in, immediately!

I am a fan of the Horror-Survival genre. I have been a fan since the very first Resident Evil when the dogs jumped through the hallway windows and scared the living BA-JEEESus! outta me! In fact, I also love me some good horror movies to boot; Alien being one of my favorites. So I had to try this game when it came out. It promised scares like the first Alien movie and was a different kind of 'Alien' game. And what it promised, it delivered like a parasite bursting out of a morbidly obese paunch. This is by-far and bar-none the best horror-survival game I have ever played to date. It really is that good.
New AI was developed for the Alien, that makes it a formidable foe. You can't fight it to start, because it is just too powerful, so you must avoid it. So how do you avoid it? You must be patient and you must listen. This game is visually stunning and is complimented by its sound track . You'll live to hear the franchise musical queues that are scaterred through-out the game. And when you hear the Alien drop down in the room next to you, your blood will run cold. The atmosphere pulls you into this world and the interesting puzzles, and game play keep you interested.
This is the first review I've ever taken the time to write, so think about that.
If you see this game on sale, definitely buy it.
If you were thinking about getting it, DOEET NAO.
Gaming Tips /w Possible spoilers:
- Start out by just crawling to move around. This method of travel is slow, but it'll afford you a lot less aggro-problems. If the Alien doesn't hear you, he won't come looking for you.
- Be careful of what your walking on, as some surfaces make more noise than others.
- Keep your head up kid; look to the vents you may see drool dripping down O.o
- The robots (Working Joes) are really tuff and it makes more sense just to avoid them in the beginning.
- The most efficient way to kill a robot; stun it with either a flash-bang and then wack it in the head (5+ times) with your wrench. The gun is only meant for humans.
- Don't give up, because eventually you do get a weapon that affects the Alien (scares it away for a bit)

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding lemon bars recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1) 2 cups Flour
2) 1/2 cup Sugar
3) 1/4 teaspoon Salt
4) 2 sticks (1 Cup) Salted Butter, Cut Into Small Cubes
5) Filling
6) 1-1/2 cup Sugar
7) 1/4 cup Flour
8) 4 whole Large Eggs
9) Zest And Juice Of 4 Medium-sized Lemons
10) Powdered Sugar, For Sifting
Directions:
1. For the crust: Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F. Grease a 9-by-13-inch pan with butter.
2. Stir together the flour, sugar, and salt. Add the butter to the bowl and use a pastry cutter to cut it all together until the mixture resembles fine crumbs. Press into the prepared pan and bake until golden around the edges, about 20 minutes.
3. For the filling: Stir together the sugar and flour. Crack in the eggs and whisk to combine. Add the lemon zest and juice and mix until combined. Pour over the crust and bake about 20 minutes.
4. Allow to cool in the fridge for a minimum of 2 hours, then sift powdered sugar over the top before cutting into squares.
(Use an 8 x 10 pan if you'd like the layers to be a little thicker.)

This game quickly goes from "Ok, cool" to "I have not slept for 15 hours and I loved each and every one of them".
Some backstory: Factorio is a survival game with all of the bad parts cut out. You have no hunger bar, manual grinding is not encouraged, and automation actually makes things run faster. It's made to look (and, to an extent, play) like a mid-90s RTS, and even though I've never played one other than RCT2, I still think this aesthetic works in its favor. What does the game play like? Well, you know in Minecraft how once you get bored of digging 1:2 shafts in the ground you set up a crazy machine to do it for you? This is an ENTIRE GAME about that feeling. It's the type of game where you can make your own computer from chests and wires. It is the BEST feeling.
My only issue is the online. Creative/survival games often have online be a big focus: It's fun to collaborate to ease some of your own workload and help others with what they want to do. I don't think the devs had this in mind. Connections are Peer To Peer, meaning that servers are designed for LAN connections or only a handful of nearby connections. This means you have to manually enter in someone else's IP. This is REALLY a pain. Every time someone joins, everyone on the server has to wait for them to download the map. And downloading is SLOOOOOW. For some reason, it downloads about 1/5-1/8 slower than my usual download speed (server load? i don't know). And when someone on the server lags. EVERYONE lags. Sometimes I can hardly play because of the lag. I know this game has a mid-90s aesthetic, but I didn't want it come with mid-90s modem-speed. This is excusable, at least: Multiplayer only came out a few updates back, and after all the game is still in early access. But the sooner multiplayer is better optimized, the better.
Well, if you like your games single-player, just disregard that. And who cares about netcode when you have a fudging MASTERPIECE on your hands?
Buy it now.

I had initially left a preliminary review after finishing a single path. This is an update after having finished the entire game. All five paths, all ten endings.
Having done that, I've gotta say. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ that was an incredible experience. Maybe, my expectations (tempered by the likes of Sakura Swim Club...ugh) had an effect on this, but... I literally ended up dropping everything else I was playing on PC at the time just to consume more of these narratives. I know that the localization of The Labyrinth of Grisaia is in progress and I'm very much excited for when it will come out.
Pros:
-Since this is a VN, let's get the most important bit out of the way first. The writing in this game, while it takes it a bit to get started, is absolutely PHENOMENAL. Each of the character arcs is handled incredibly well. Each of the five characters are thought through and are very interesting character studies. Not to mention, the way the character personalities clash is often hilarious. It's to the extent that I've found myself contemplating some plot points or speculating about possible upcoming events while at work or on my commute.
-On the note of writing, I've gotta give major props to the writers that handled the translation. The amount of vocabulary that I've learned from this game exceeds most natively english titles. There were even times when I saw a word, thought it was a typo, looked it up, and learned that it was an actual word. Well done.
-This game doesn't fall into the pit trap of having copy/pasted narratives. Yes, there's some similar themes that happen on occasion, but I was pleased to see that each of the paths is basically unique and even each of the endings is distinctly different.
-The voice actors have done an excellent job. While I, no longer, speak Japanese, but the emotion, intonation, and delivery have left me often just letting the VA finish the particular line before advancing to the next bit....and, that doesn't happen often, as I'm usually speeding through dialogue, not bothering to wait on the VA.
-The music, while I feel that some of the loops could have been handled a bit better, otherwise, I have no complaints. Each individual track is fantastic, been pleasant enough to listen to, and I don't recall any of them having become grating, even after a multitude of repetitions.
-The art in the game is superb. I won't even deny that a handful of scenes have made their way into my wallpapers collection.
-Unexpectedly enough, there's also quite the collection of bonus material. I know that VNs commonly include their art and a few other things with them, but this is even more generous.
A couple of other comments, though they are not exactly cons:
-The way each of the routes is set up, once you branch off, what happened in the other route no longer exists. As a result of that, there were points where I couldn't help but feel a bit guilty choosing one option, knowing that I've avandoned the fate of a character in favor of another. That being said, I believe that this VN's character progressions would have suffered quite a bit if it was a "help everyone" type of story, so I'm not really complaining. Hell, it's not often that a narrative has left me to care this much for a character.
-I've gotta mention the censorship. I've gotta give credit to Frontwing to having included additional content in the M-rated version to make up for the cut scenes, but... It does (apparently) have an effect on one of the character arcs and it's the matter of personal principle to note this. I suppose, at least, that's easily enough remedied if you desire to do so.
TL;DR: All in all, though, it's been a marvelous and enjoyable experience (to the point of considering this to be the best VN I've consumed to date). I know that the $40 pricetag may seen intimidating, but if it'll help, I'll say this much. The first story arc I complete was Sachi's. In my opinion, even if the game had ended with just that, I'd still consider this to have been money well spent. I'm very much excited for the sequel to be released.

This game is the visual novel masterpiece you have been looking for.
The game blew me away, and I am not new to visual novels by any means.  If you are concerned about the removal of adult scenes, you can get this game legally from denpasoft and you should do so if this is a deal-breaker.  Personally, I enjoy them being removed so long as it is not done awkwardly because I think it actually improves the flow and pace of the story.  With this game we still got all of the build-up and even some racy images leading to these scenes, so I was really glad the game did not just skirt around the issue or totally ignore that aspect of the romances.
The characters in this game, and one girl in particular (Amane) will stick with me for a long time.  Some of their stories connected with me more than others, but the ones that did were absolutely riveting and unforgettable.  There were moments I laughed out loud and times I cried.  I was genuinely rooting for every character, including the protagonist, who has a face in many scenes although he is not voiced.  His character, however, was very interesting...just as interesting and intriguing as the heroines and that is a real accomplishment in this type of game!
If I had any criticisms of the game, it would be that the beginning (the common route) is on the lengthy side.  I went into this game knowing almost nothing about it (and I recommend not spoiling ANYTHING), and I was really starting to wonder where the author was going with this game.  However, I did enjoy it...it was amazing for short half-hour sessions as the common route is broken up into distinct scenes that take place during different times of day, creating many amusing vignettes.  Once I got into the main routes, I would read for hours, dying to know what happened next.  It's almost like this was 2 games in one, since the way this game made me feel was so different between the common route (very long, very amusing) and the main routes (suspenseful, heartrending).
If you are still reading this by now...buy the game!  Unless you are looking for fanservice only, you will not regret it.

BloodLust ShadowHunter is the game you never knew you needed. Part Vampires: The Masquerade and part Hellgate: London this game provides a solid story and great randomly generated dungeons. You can pick from multiple classes and multiple species of Vampires, and you'll fight creatures like mummies, wolfmen, and even Yetis.
Perhaps the most interesting feature is the ability to sire people. Almost any NPC you see walking the streets can be turned into a companion character. You literally get to build your own clan of vampires. Speaking of which, the game's gritty urban setting is ruled by different vampire clans. The skill system is tied to your reputation with said clan, meaning to unlock and level certain skills you have to get in good with their respective clans.
This is the only game I've ever seen that lets you pierce your nose and use it as another equipment slot.
I've put 21 hours into the main story so far and I'm having a blast! The game doesn't do very much in the way of hand holding though, and at the moment there are a lack of quality guides to help you through those tough spots you just can't figure out.
In short, this game is SO much fun, and worth your time. The graphics may be dated, and the acting cheesy, but this is a better RPG than Bioware has put out in years, and it was made by one guy with the help of some freelancers. There's  a lot of effort put into it, and as a result its endearing and memorable.
Highly recommended at full price.

You can turn Humans into vampires who will then fight at your side, which is good in theory, but the AI is dumb as a brick. Sometimes they just stand around and do nothing. Fortunately they can't die, at worst they get knocked out for a few seconds, so at least they still function as a distraction while you kill the monsters, but its still annoying.
The main content of the game involves dungeon crawling. There are several different dungeons, and the deeper you go, the better loot you find, but you also have to fight tougher monsters. There's an achievement for reaching the 200th floor, but I think these dungeons might just continue on forever. Every floor has a randomly generated layout and item/monster placement. Again, this all sounds good.
However, what I don't like is the number of quests that ask you to find a specific item within those random dungeons. Maybe you find it immediately, or maybe you wander around aimlessly for hours. It also doesn't help that when you leave a dungeon to complete a quest, everything resets, so when you get a new quest that sends you back to the same dungeon, you have to grind through everything all over again. It gets tedious pretty quickly. Maybe if the combat was more enjoyable it would be less of a problem, but I still think its poor design. The story, dialogue and voice acting are all terrible.
From reading the forums I understand the game is developed by one person, so I feel kinda bad for trashing his work. But at the end of the day it doesn't really matter to me how many people were involved or how much resources they had to work with. I just want to play good games, and a bad game developed by one person is still a bad game. I wouldn't even recommend picking up Bloodlust Shadowhunter on sale, because it would still be a waste of time that could be spent with better games.
On the bright side, this game was a great way for me to learn how to get a refund on Steam.

This game gets a ton of unwarranted hate just because people download the 60+ gigs and expect Skyrim online.  When they find out it isn't nearly as shallow, that there's actually a steep learning curve, they don't bother to give it a chance.  Most negative reviews have less than 10 hours played.  There's no way any of those people have gotten through a tenth of the content and overall the game suffers from these more casual players due to actual MMO fans getting the wrong impression.
If you like MMO's give this game a good chance to impress you.  If you're a fan of the elder scrolls lore, that shouldn't take long.  The combat from this game feels more "real time" with the need to actually click to amount to what would be more of an "auto attack" type of mechanic in, for instance, WoW, this gives the game a unique feel in the MMO realm and as a result combat ends up being a blast.
I log on ESO when none of my friends are on WoW, and it is definitely time well spent.  This has all the standard MMO elements you could expect with a crazy in depth crafting system that is worth a separate mention.  You will find it hard to resist running around the over world collecting mats and breaking down otherwise useless gear to be able to craft your own sets with properties and traits that you choose at the crafting table.
Finally I will say that the community is just as you would expect to find in an MMO, lots of people are willing to help and group up and explain the systems and mechanics to you, but some are toxic and reminiscent of my time playing LoL...  Just like any online community tends to be.  The difference is, this game feels very solo-able, and beyond story required dungeons, so far the sentiment has held to be true.
I haven't delved into PVP yet but with the combat system the way it is and a short duel against another player, it seems very promising.
Seriously, worth looking into this game if you're even slightly curious and a fan of MMOs and the Elder scrolls universe. Again, don't go into this expecting an experience similar to the stand alone games, you will be disappointed.

All in all though a single playthrough is estimated around 25-35 depending on the speed you read at and add 10 hours for each route. There is massive amounts of content here, all in all its one of my favourite visual novels so i can't recommend it enough. It does contain an insane 1million characters, that is a metric ton.

Looked forward to this game but it ended up being a disappointment.  They shouldn't have tried to fix things that weren't broken.
I've played TW games since the original Shogun, my favorite being Medieval II Total War, which improved greatly upon it's predecessors. Medieval II TW was intuitive.  Unfortunately Rome II was clunky and far from intuitive.
The interface seemed to be a random hunt and peck setup, scattered throughout the screen in a chaotic order.  Many details that added color to M2TW were removed from Rome 2 and then things that created nothing but tedium were added. The unit cards were larger than necessary yet gave no way to know the exact number of troops in a unit by looking at them; you have to guesstimate.  The creators also decided to use a mimicry of old Roman art instead of more appealing and identifiable pictures:  I feel that was an aesthetic, if not functional, mistake.   Management of settlements and provinces was limited and yet clunky.  Most everything is based off fighting penalties and not gaining bonuses.  Overall control leaves much to be desired, yet the AI factions, of course, flourish without fail or penalty.
Attilla looks like it made some improvements although it uses much of the same flawed system, so perhaps I would suggest playing that one over Rome 2, but honestly I have not had enough game time on Attilla to accurately commit to that suggestion.
All I can say is that Rome 2 has been painfully dissapointing to me, and I write that with sadness as a TW fan.

Emporer Edition fixes most of the problems with Rome 2 and actually makes it a solid strategy game. Never got all the bugfixing it needed though, and I can't go more than 2 hours or so without my game crashing. Save often is the only thing I can say.

Rome II is a disappointment for strategy fans and an omen for the series. The bugs are embarrassing. The wait time between turns is maddening. The battles (even on a massive scale) are brief and quickly become a raving, disorganized cluster flip. The unit cohesion and collision is the worst in any strategy game I've ever seen. The AI is so horrible that battles are easily won even when the odds are against the player ten-to-one. It's just a bad game. I'm embarrassed to have purchased it (preordered even).
What's unfortunate is that this is the path the Total War series is going down. They pushed a horrible product out the door before it was ready, and it took them a year of patches and updates to make the game slightly less horrible. Of course, it didn't matter to the developers. They created Attila Total War a little more than a year after Rome II was released, and Attila turned out to be what Rome II should have been originally. So they swiped $60 to $80 for one poor product then they swiped another $60 to $80 for yet another product that was essentially a glorified patch and DLC of Rome II. These developers have lost my admiration and my trust. I've stopped preordering Total War games, and if Warhammer Total War turns out to be the same load of garbage as Rome II and Attila then I'll refund it and not feel the slightest bit of remorse about it.

Short and sweet, “rymdkapsel” is quite a feat despite its simplicity.  I find that it has an addicting quality about it, almost begging me to find the perfect station layout even though the block shapes randomly generate in the que.  It’s simple enough to where the learning curve is light, but challenging enough that I feel compelled to do better the next time around.  While this game has been out for over a year now on other peripherals (Android, iOS, etc.), I’m very glad that it came to the PC as I probably wouldn’t have known that it existed…considering how much I enjoy playing “rymdkapsel”, that would have been a real shame.  My only gripe is the lack of game modes and options…after a game or two, you’ll see all there is to see.  Still, do yourself a favor and try “rymdkapsel”…you might not be able to pronounce it, but by gosh, you’ll more than likely have fun playing it.

Final Verdict: 9/10
You can check out the full review and video play sessions here:

Full review at:
The goal of video games as an interactive medium is to engage the user as much as possible through their interactions. Games are unique because of this and are enjoyed because of this interaction with the medium; this is where rymdkapsel separates itself from the competitors.  Its goal is to have minimal user input without souring the experience, macro problem solving would be a good way to describe it.
The objective of the game is very simple, survive. This is done by constructing a well-fortified station with the help of your minions. You are attacked at set intervals by an enemy and during the downtime you have to prepare and explore. The mode is quite simple and to be frank starts off very slow, and while it may pick up in pace later on it goes from one extreme to the next, due to the poor AI a lot of the time you can’t even perform an action during the break. There are some missions to help break the monotony but they’re very bland.
The minions are not controlled on an individual level, instead you’re given an overview and decide how many minions you want in a given field of work. This can cause some hilarities and frustrations as your minions walk around like sheep and try to build your masterpiece as they all focus in a singular area even though only one minion will be needed. The same can be said for their fighting as they only can work in groups of two, and if you get some unlucky RNG with the enemy grouping they can wipe you out even if you have overwhelming numbers.
The game has a pseudo 3D art style which uses vector based visuals which are quite a treat to look at, and for some this will probably be the biggest draw to the game. With the strong use of colour to help dictate certain areas of your station a colour blind mode has been added, which is greatly needed for those who suffer. Why more games don’t have colour blind modes, we’ll never know but it’s good to see it in rymdkapsel and they should be praised for noticing and rectifying this possible flaw in their game.
The soundtrack is quite ambient giving off a space feel while still being quite simple, sound effects on the overhand are a little lacking but nothing that will turn you off. The game was originally on PSVITA and as such we have to discuss the port. While it does run smoothly it really lacks a decent options menu, no audio sliders, UI is locked to 4 presets (though better than none at all) and there is a total lack of keyboard support.
rymdkapsel lacks a lot of things that would be considered micro, causing the player at times feel useless. This plays as a strength and a weakness to the game and may turn people off. For what it’s worth, rymdkapsel is very interesting and unique, while not perfect you should still be able to objectively view it and see some of the great ideas it has. How many strategy games can you play with one hand, while the other gets that itch which is always behind your left ear?

The best ALIEN game in years, Alien: Isolation might be too "realistic" for many or too frustratingly lacking in satisfactory gameplay for others. It's probably comparable to the movie Napoleon Dynamite in that people are likely to either love it or hate it with only a few in the middle. (What a strange comparison... but it might be appropriate for that one "love it or hate it" element.) For what it is, what it tries to be and what it doesn't try to be, I recommend it... but I wouldn't personally buy it at its full original retail price.
Some things I've Liked so far:
Aesthetic... it's just like the original ALIEN movie.
Atmosphere... excellent audio, tense music, fragility of your humanity: the immersion makes the game amazing. I've seen the Alien movies and played Alien games, so the shock value isn't what it was the first time witnessing those things, but that doesn't remove the tension created by the in-game audio or the music, which is the music from the original film and some extra (according to the credits).
Tension... the stressful qualities of this game would have me biting my fingernails too short if it were a movie or a book. However, because my hands are busy controlling the game, I have no time for that. That's a good thing!
What I've Disliked thus far:
Tension... the tension and stress is sure to cause an increase in my body's cortisol levels, removing melanin from my hair follicles and giving me gray hair sooner than I would otherwise have it.
Frailty of the protagonist's "weak human form" means a quick death if anyone or anything catches up to you
Elements About Which I'm Undecided:
The antiquated ideas of what technology would be in the future as seen through the eyes of the 1970s make some of the usability factors difficult to fathom. I love it and have a problem with it at the same time.
Alien: Isolation is more like a simulation in many ways than a video game. If you're looking for something to get your adrenaline pumping in a good way and have a great deal of fun doing it, this might not be the game for youl. If you're looking for horror with blood and dead bodies and survivors who are scared out of their minds who will shoot anything, even a friendly human like you, just because it moves, this might be just your cup of tea. If you get positive adrenaline boosts from tension and squealing violins and minor-key tunes, this might be just what you are looking for.
I have a 5.1-channel audio system around me and it's really great for producing atmospheric moods in games that do it right, as this one is so close to doing. However, the audio seems less precise than FPS games in which I can hear exactly where everything is around me and point directly at it by moving my mouse. Often audio in Alien: Isolation coming from an object in front of me will sound like it's coming from behind me; it's difficult to isolate the source using sound alone. That could be an attempt to cause confusion in players to increase atmosphere, but it seems more to me as if I have the speakers plugged into the wrong jacks. It reduces the effectiveness of the audio in my mind to some degree.
A thought: I'll probably improve this review's clarity at some point, because I'm sure it will require editing; I'm writing it while exhausted and typically produce strange text and/or a grammatical failure at times like this. Also, I'm only four hours into the game and might have a more comprehensive review to type after I've played it to completion and beyond.

Dark Souls II has a soft start, easing you into the game, and shortly after the character creation, a very good tutorial area.
After the tutorial area, you are introduced to what I can only word as a beautiful yet ravaged view. Majula. This hub is much more pleasant than in DS, and much more convenient. And this game is... Very different from the first one starting here. There are many ways to go, just like the first one, but you are given hints when talking to the Emerald Herald.
Something you are not quite as explained in DS is the paths you have to take. And DS2 wins points in comparison here. And also; the combat. It is much more fluid than it was in DS, even if DS had good combat, they polished it.
And most of all... The PVP and connectivity is a LOT better in DS2. I haven't personally had anywhere near as bad an experience with lag or unbalanced levels/gears in DS2 as I have on numerous occasions in DS.
Where DS2 loses points compared to the first one is in bosses.
DS had incredible fights, fights that you will remember years down the line. Be it the frustrating Big & Small duo or the savage DLC-induced old undead knight or the very last boss of the game.
DS2 has... A certain giant knight clad in thick armor who tends to surprise new players near the beginning and who is one of the better designed bosses in the entire game. A surprising swordswoman and a few others. But with about twice as many bosses as DS, that's kinda sad. Because I actually had to think for DS2. DS almost only had awesome boss fights.
And that's where I deduct points.
TL;DR
DS2, in my opinion, is just as good as DS was, but if difficulty and long-lasting boss fight memories is what you want, DS would be better suited.

I like to think of myself as a casual player in general. This means I play quite a lot of games, and spend an avarage of 20-40 hours in games per month. I played most of the RPG games from 2010 till now on hard or harder difficulties and had a blast. The fact that I learned something from each battle and was able to apply the newly formed knowledge to next battles was really rewarding even though I died countless times in many spots of the games.
Dark Souls is different. It is way harder than anything that I have played, but it doesn't teach me something that I can use at the next boss, or set of enemyes. It's mostly about luck, and spending tons of hours of your time walking the exact same corridor, fighting the exact same enemy and dieing at the same boss over and over again, untill you learn all the moves that that boss has, and how he uses it. This is not "respect" as pro dark souls players call it, it's a waste of time for me.
Most of those attacts that a boss has, if ussed by a player, would kill you instantly.So you basically learn the AI implementation of the boss and exploit it in order to beat it. I don't feel that good when killing a boss after attempting it 50 times, knowing that I actually beat him because I knew the AI  won't use the main attack if I stay to close or hit just once and then retreat. For example, the main attack of the Punisher boss, if used by the AI right after you hit him will hit you 90% of the time, but the AI doesn't hit with that move unless you hit more than once in a row. In ohter words, to win, you learn the moves of the AI, ignore what's generally possible to happen and always follow the same dodge/attack once/dogge repeat pattern, knowing that the AI won't use a spcial move on you if you do just that.
After you beat one boss, you get to the next set of enemies which will instakill you untill you learn their moves, and then the next boss will kill you as many times as the last one, because in the end, you don't earn anything from fighitng any previous mosnter or boss apart from a very accurate knowledge of how to beat that old boss. The new one is a complete new grind fest where you try again and again to beat him.
This game is not for me, or for people that like to have a sense of progression which is MEANINGFULL in a game. I like games where a challenge is better rewarded.

When looking for good Visual Novels, Steam is unfortunately often not the right place. Most of the VNs available there are rather geared towards heavy fan-service (not to say Grisaia has none) and usually aren't really good overall when compared to other ones - as can be seen from their score on VNDB (Visual Novel Database).
That being said Grisaia is one of the few exception, hopefully soon to be joined by Muv Luv as well. The story is entertaining, you easily get attached to the characters and for once the protagonist isn't your typical blank canvas - if anything he is very un-japanese in his behavior, which is a breath of fresh air in a Visual Novel.
For those who don't know what a Visual Novel is, it's fairly simple. Just imagine reading a book, with images and music to set the mood and atmosphere. On top of that, sprinkle a few choices you can make as a reader to turn the story towards what you want it to become. Note that in most Visual Novels, different routes are drastically different from one another (it isn't an "illusion of choice" like in The Walking Dead for instance).
Grisaia has no 'true ending' per se, and each route (5 of them) all have their own story attached to it. If one of the character doesn't interest you, there is no need to read her route. Just choose what you want to see, and enjoy the story.
Note: For those worried about the H-content being removed from the Steam version, I only played this version of Grisaia and didn't feel like anything was 'missing' - the story still flowed fairly naturally, and you still get plenty of lewd jokes (Amane, Sachi, please...). However, if you are really adamant about playing the original version, than Steam might not be the right place.
Have fun reading!

S.T.A.L.K.E.R remains to be the only game that I play which has FPS combat, for a multitude of reasons. S.T.A.L.K.E.R: Shadow of Chernobyl is an RPG set in the post-apocalyptic grounds of radiation-filled Chernobyl, where S.T.A.L.K.E.R's roam and reign in this wild west of mutants and Russians in gas masks. This oldie remains captivating to me because of this one, simple thing: It was crafted with care. Hell, the designers went INTO CHERNOBYL and modeled parts of the game after what they saw.
Shadow of Chernobyl is a game built on atmosphere. Ho-lee♥♥♥♥♥♥ atmosphere is extremely present. From the way the lighting is done, to the wind effects, to the echoes of mutated animals crying out in the fields, to the eerie trance of quiet music beneath the whoosh of wind blowing by you as you trek through a field, bleeding and tired from an encounter... It really feels like what the developpers intended, which is that you're struggling to survive in Chernobyl with what you can find. Without adding legitimate "horror aspects," S.T.A.L.K.E.R developped a tinge of scariness with the excessive ammount of eerie that drives home the point it was going for.
The combat engine is relatively simplistic, but it's satisfying. The damage frame makes cover actually necessary to outlast a longer fight, therefore making the lean function actually useful. The noise and visibility system added to the game also gives you the choice to go in stealthily or half-cocked, and also makes it that much more realistic; other people can HEAR YOU SNEAKING if you're sloppy, and wandering around with a flashlight will give away your position to anything that wants to kill you. Combine this system with angry russians, a gas mask, and some creepy torn up towns, and you've got S.T.A.L.K.E.R.
Honestly, I'd pick this over Fallout any day of the week. I'd recommend this game to ANYONE.

STALKER: Shadow of Chernobyl is, perhaps, one of the greatest video games I've ever played. Complete with role playing elements, fantastic action, extreme difficulty and terrifying moments, the game delivers in every way.
GRAPHICS:
First off all, I would highly suggest everyone download the STALKER Complete 2009 Mod on
, as it increases visuals and gameplay performance tenfold and makes the dated game look on par to Crysis. Without the mod, however, colors are bland, facial expressions are dull, shading is downright awful, and textures are muddy. It's not terrible, but I would highly suggest the mod be installed if your PC can handle it.
GAMEPLAY:
This is the iffy part of the game. While the controls aren't particularly difficult to comprehend, some movements feel clunky. Also, without the mod installed (let's face it, the mod improved everything), guns will jam frequently and bullets will go off course at point blank range. This is most of the time a reoccuring glitch, but is no less annoying. With the mod installed, you can have more role playing options available - joining groups and factions, repairing weapons and armor, and even getting more weapons and equipment not available in the original game, and the fact that this mod is free and easy to install just makes it better. However, the gameplay isn't perfect even with the installed mod. Enemies can shoot you through walls, the easiest difficulty is unbelieveably brutal to new players as enemies can kill you in just a few rifle shots or a few melee hits (if it's a mutant). The human AI isn't very smart, but hell they can kill easily. The truly impressive enemies are the mutants. Ranging from sickeningly deformed hounds to massive monstrosities that will haunt your nightmares for days, each mutant comes with its own abilities, attacks, and frightening appearances, making this just as much a survival horror experience as an RPG/Shooter. Glitches aside, the gameplay (though made better with the mod) is fun, easy to learn, and solid.
STORY:
This is where the game truly shines. The story is perhaps one of the most original that I've seen in any game in the past decade. You are a man known only as the 'Marked One,' due to the tatoo on your arm. You have no idea who you really are, what you're doing, or why you're in Chernobyl. All you know is that written on your PDA are the words: "KILL THE STRELOK." From there, you must fight through the horrors of the nuclear wasteland in the heart of Ukraine, uncovering the secrets of your past and the dark horrors that the government have tried so hard to cover up. The story is interactive, compelling, and interesting. The story alone makes the game a better experience.
MULTIPLAYER:
Nothing is more useless than the multiplayer. Not only is it completely broken, but the cooperative play just derives from the role playing experience offered in the main campaign. That, and you'll be incredibly hard-pressed just to find another person to play with, much less be able to connect to a lobby. This isn't an FPS made for multiplayer; I'd steer clear of it.
VERDICT:
STALKER: Shadow of Chernobyl is a fantastic game. Mods improve the experience and make the game more interesting than ever. With a fantastic story, solid gameplay and nice visuals from actual locations in the haunting Chernobyl landscape, this game, despite it's flaws, ranks in among the top best games I've ever played.

I just finished playing the game that was free for a weekend, I basically played it for 6 days because I didn't quit the game after free time ran out and my PC kept running.
Short review:
Game is better balanced than previous Total War games and I found no bugs and it runs smoothly on my mediocre PC, but has to be pointed out that this is with the latest patch.
6 days allowed me to start up various campaigns: Played Marcus Antonius' faction and Egypt itself in the civil war scenario, the Gauls and Seleucids in main campaign, and the tutorial itself (which in this game counts as a mini-campaign).
I was surprisingly pleased with the game as it in fact runs better on my PC than Shogun 2 did, but there were also negatives:
- Way fewer video scenes in the game than in previous ones, as example in the Roman Civil War scenario the intro is always that of RL future "Augustus", Octavius. There is no intro for Egypt and Antonius (hoped there would be some nice scenes for these) so I assume the victory video scene is generic or nonexistent as well.
- The various families in a faction are basically useless. Rome 1 had three Roman families who all had their own faction color, units, and directly controlled territories. While it is nicer to see all of Rome on map in a single color, I do think the many dev cuts on families end up a loss to the game. The centralized Roman (and also Carthagian in R2) gameplay with just 1 faction resulted in just "cosmetic" (as they all use the same faction color, symbol, and units it's not even that) difference between the families. How various player dynasties could work under one color (if loyal to a faction) or under their own if they break free, is easily visible if one plays a duke in Crusader Kings 2. This means it isn't impossible to have a proper and useful family system for a Total War game as well, if the developers take the time to implement it.
- There is something wrong with how quick save is handled, you are only allowed to use a single slot for a save file if you get into a battle which would be very needed as a backup for surprise and/or hard battles. This is especially bad if you play multiple campaigns at the same time as I did.
- Families and "dynasties" are not working as they should, unlike previous TW games you don't see marriages occur unless as a "political plot" you or AI instigates, and doesn't seem to influence anything more than what bonus or malus the "wife item" grants to the character. There is no birth of a heir neither, and all family members seem to be handled as parts of a political party who could swap between families in a faction if coerced.
As mentioned above, while in average I liked the game I really hate the generic feel and dynastic flavor lack of it. Antonius is ingame married to Cleopatra, but she seems to be just another generic "wife card" there, Egypt is not ruled by her but some random other "Ptolemy" males.
What about Alexander Helios and Cleopatra Selene II, children of Antonius?
Ptolemy Caesarion, son of Caesar?
The lack of children being born into a dynasty as in former games is disturbing, and an option where you can look up ancestors of a character (to see if it is actually a real blood-related member of it or just adopted) would improve the game immensely. Not to mention the historical background of Caesar's son being murdered on the order of Octavious woulkd be one great goal for the Octavian faction to succeed with and one for Egypt/Antonius to avoid.
Shogun 2 had proper families, children who grow up and take various positions. Why does Rome 2 lack this, when it would benefit from its existence much more than S2 had?
Developers should take a look at Crusader Kings 2 and improve the dynastic flavor instead of throwing out or watering down the dynasty system.

Papers, Please is a game where you play as a border inspector in the dystopian society of Arstotzka. To do so, you verify documents and pick up on potential discrepancies to determine when to approve their entry or deny it. This descritpion make Papers, Please sound like a boring monotonous grind.
Well it is not.
Papers, Please offers one of the most intense single player experiences in the indie gaming scene. As you get paid based on the number of people you screen, you are forced to work fast. Make too many mistakes, however, and you receive citations resulting in your salary getting docked. You become indoctrinated to dread the fax noise that comes with every citation. Your family lives on the edge of poverty and you are forced to budget accordingly.
As the government relaxes or strengthen their policies, your job changes with it, where the foreigner who was let in a day earlier may not be today, which allows for some essential variation to prevent the game from becoming stagnant. This comes in the form of detention of criminals, fingerprint and X-ray scanning and seal verification.
The game also does a good job questoining your morality. For instance, do you allow the guy with good documentation pimp in Arstotzka, or deny him and get reprimanded by your superiors? Do you buy food for your starving uncle or a present for your son's birthday?
Papers, Please is an indie game done right, in which it is not a pretentious, bland game that boasts of subtle depth while being♥♥♥♥♥♥to play, nor is it another "retro styled" hardcore platformer. It is a unique game that manages to tackle heavy morality issues while still being amusing to the player.
Two thumbs up!

Papers, Please is a game which shines through its tremendous writing. The story questions the morals of pride, nationalism, and humanity. Although the game's heart is at its story, it still has functional and enjoyable gameplay, which continues to refreshen itself on each progressive day. The lack of music within the work day is at times annoying, but overall adds to the dull, monotonous and monochrome environment the game tries to enforce. It also becomes fidgety at sometimes with certain instances, where I felt I was unfairly penalized for following the instructions as written. Nonetheless, it is still an exciting indie title that breaks the mold and gives off unique vibes.
Overall, the game is a truly one of a kind experience and should not be passed up by anyone who enjoys a compelling story.

To sum everything up, I enjoyed this game 100%, but before I go into detail about the game I should make a note that for the people playing a visual novel for the first time, you shouldn't expect much "gameplay" from this game. Yes, there are choices but they are very few compared to other choice-based storytelling games, you should expect to read a lot of throughout the game. Expecting otherwise will probably leave you disappointed, if you don't like reading you should turn back, because The Fruit of Grisaia has A LOT of reading. It's admittedly a different experience from reading a book (the BGM, voices, and illustrations help guide you on the atmosphere and the appearances/emotions of the characters rather than just leaving it up to your imagination), but you shouldn't buy this game if you hate reading.
* (If you don't want to read the long paragraphs of text you can skip to the short paragraph at the end for a summary)
____
Moving on, The Fruit of Grisaia is a standard visual novel, with choices that lead you to different routes that each focus on six different heroines. It's pretty lengthy and depending on your reading speed, it will probably take you somewhere around 60-85 hours to go through everything. Despite it's length however, there's a great attention to detail throughout Grisaia. An off-hand remark in one route becomes something the character actually does in another route, and the storywriters took great care in interwining each route indirectly with each other. The other thing is that all of the main heroines in Grisaia have background and purpose behind their characters. What might seem like a silly anime trope has a deeper and perhaps darker backstory behind it.
Even if the characters started out as simple archetypes, they sure don't now. Everything the characters do has some explained reasoning for it, and again you can see that the writers took a lot of careful detail in weaving the character's backstory with their personality and actions.  And again, despite the fact that there's thousands upon thousands of lines of text, the story for each route is quite diverse. I was surprised at how the seriousness and setting could change within each route, and it's nice to see that the routes for each heroine have their own little slice at all the different atmospheres and backgrounds a story can possess. The other thing I enjoyed was the fact that throughout learning each heroine's backstory, you also learn more about the past of the main character, Yuuji, and his personality as well.
It's something of an intricate puzzle piece, where all the different parts of Yuuji's past and personality connect across all routes, and over the course of the game you learn more and more about him. In addition to the diverse storytelling is that the writers of the story aren't afraid to pull their punches. Each route has a bad and a good ending, and even though you know that there's a better alternative ending, you can't help but be surprised, or even disturbed about the endings that just happened. Some of them can be absolutely brutal, and others can be lighter and less emotional.
____
* Short Version
To put it all succinctly, the Fruit of Grisaia is an absolutely enthralling and intersting visual novel with a diverse set of characters and storytelling and prose that is enrapturing in it's own way. The writing isn't afraid to hit you with a few punches, and the amount of detail that goes into crafting each route and character is amazing to say the least. This game is fantastic, and is worth every penny (for me at least).
If you're on the fence about whether or not you'll enjoy the game, you may want to watch a couple episodes of the anime adapation (I wouldn't watch more than 3, otherwise you'll be spoiled a bit) which will help you get a feel for the writing style of the game. It doesn't really showcase everything, but it should give you an idea of whether or not you'll enjoy the game (but don't judge the game solely by the anime, it doesn't really do the VN justice). If you have watched the anime before and enjoyed it, buy this as well. The anime doesn't really do the game complete justice, and although I watched the anime prior to playing the VN, I still found myself surprised at the turns the story took.

I dunno. I don't really want to give the game a bad review per se, but I just can't recommend it. If I were to go by the general rating systems used by mainstream gaming sites, it would be in the 6/10 range. It's really commendable one guy made it and all, but the game is essentially a mediocre rendition of several gameplay elements, and pretty lackluster visuals.
I don't really mean the poor textures either. Rather, the whole scale of the game, maps and field of vision just seem weirdly constructed relative to the player. Everything in the hub areas feel very claustrophobic and simply dumped there to tick a checklist of what needs to be in a game requiring objective locations. (oddly enough, Bloodlines had a similar feeling, but the gameworld was like 100 times more fleshed out, so it worked).
The combat is incredibly clunky and plays out in an awkward, third person hack and slash style. I'm sure attacks being halted if an enemy hits you is intentional, but it just plays out in a very sluggish and turgid way. Attacks don't even seem to connect when doing damage. The physics are as such, that you never feel in controls of combat. You may as well stand there and play it as if you were playing an MMO.
Character growth is just bizarre and stats seem to progress with the intention of minutely progressing a pretty selective path. Rather than making a 'build', you feel like your character isn't really going anywhere other than being able to utilize one of a few methods of play. When STR and DEX do almost nothing to help your damage/defense capabilities, you have a problem. The talent tree promises a nice random factor, but comes across as rather redundant as a whole.
The random dungeons are really well done and perhaps are the most worthy aspect of the game. The problem is everything around it; the questing, the story, leveling up, and general sense of accomplishment just didn't make me feel all that invested, or interested to keep going. The story is just stale, the characters around all feel like bad extras who turned up with no director to give them any degree of motivation or method. Characters running around idle in the hub area just so you can constantly bite them without any consequence is incredibly dumb too.
Also, I've no idea how this game is coded, but it EATS resources. My rig feels like it's going to explode as soon as you load the game up, and it's specs are way above being decent.
All in all, this is merely for old school RPG enthusiasts. If you liked some of the RPGs from yesteryear like VTM:BL and Arx Fatalis, there may be a very rough gem here for you. If you're selective about what RPGs you play, you'll probably not enjoy this, and will get rather frustrated early on.

Don't let the indie look and feel (and price) fool you.  This game is very deep first-person ARPG, filled with more randomly-generated items and dungeons than you can shake a cross at.  There's a thin main story (some nonsense about going after your vampiric sire) but the meat of the game is buried in vast roguelike dungeons where you'll use your own vampiric powers and weapons to mercilessly slaughter legions of the undead, monsters, and other trash.  The game is easy to pick up and play, and the ingame tutorials will get you up to speed quickly, although there's a few game systems that you'll need to puzzle out during your own play time.
It's not all just hack and slash, though.  Bloodlust also tosses in helping helpings of alchemy, crafting, and other activities to spice up the grind.  There's really nothing really new here -- BloodLust is, at its core, a very familiar ARPG grind -- but the unexpected level of polish by this one-man-band production is very surprising.  Highly recommended, and there are some major studios out there who could learn from this game!

Ignore my play time (0.5hrs as of 11/30/2016... it won't be that low for long), I just bought this on Steam during the Fall sale but I have been playing on the version I bought directly from Bethesda up until now. The Gold Edition during the Fall sale was the cheaper way to get all the DLC/expansions, rather than buying them individually from the crown store.
I originally played ESO during the open betas, and while I mostly enjoyed that, it ultimately didn't appeal to me. It still felt too much like an MMO, and not really like an Elder Scrolls game. I wasn't interested in playing another MMO, especially one with a monthly subscription fee.
Flash for about a year and they announce Tamriel Unlimited. To celebrate they were also having a sale so I went ahead and grabbed the game. I figured it was worth checking out after a year of updates and changes that I'd been hearing about since it launched, and now that there wasn't a subscription it wouldn't feel like I'd be wasting too much money if I ended up not liking it.
I ended up loving it! It actually felt more like an Elder Scrolls game with only minor MMO annoyances (races were segregated into factions (although you can buy something to change this), open exploration was gated by level and quests). It wasn't what we asked for (co-op Skyrim) but along with a few friends, it was close enough for me. Even the gated exploration wasn't much of a bother because every zone still had SO MUCH to explore, and so many quests to do. Each area is huge, even the smaller zones are still about 1/4 the size of Skyrim's entire map. So while I might not have been able to run from Morrowind to High Rock without completing a huge chunck of the game, the world still feels large enough to get lost in for a good long time.
Now flash forward again about a year, and we have One Tamriel which removes the gating and everyone is free to go wherever they want, whenever they want (after the introductory/tutorial area). This, along with a purchase of the Adventurer's Pack to remove race/faction restrictions finally makes this game truely feel like a proper Elder Scrolls game. And technically you don't need the Adventurer's Pack, because while you won't be able to start a Kahjiit in the Ebonheart Pact, you can still group up with anyone from any faction, or go and start questing in any faction that you want, right from the start. The only place your faction still matters is the PvP zone of Cyrodiil.
So, yeah. Definitely recommened. If you're an Elder Scrolls fan like myself, and even if you hate MMOs, I think you'll find this one will surprise you.

**Updated 5/14/17, Pre-Combat Changes**
With the rising popularity in Japan, IMC has been able to add on to their team and push out a lot of meaningful balance and changes for the better.  The Combat Rework will be the pinnaciale of their successes for this year (2017) alone.  As this will make the playability of the game much more interesting in the later stages as low Rank Skills do not fall off as hard as before.
The game, however, remains true to a Korean MMO.  Successes are based on increasing your RNG rather than Skill.  Skill is dimished more as certain class builds are both high damage and extremely simple, even with minimumal gearing and attribute points.
For example, a high level crafting material for the current high level crafted weapons, requires a character to finish multiple questlines from various stages of the game, to then unlock a daily quest that ONLY spawns at specific server times (server time is based on RL time not an accelerated in-game clock), once that is finished then you use the materials from the daily to craft a cube that can only be obtained from a high level guild raid.  Once you craft the cube you can open it and then it is up to RNG to get the high level crafting material, the cube itself has a 24hr CD, and on average gives you the item in about 15 to 20 days time.  Then once you get the material, then you have to farm the ores from a mission that randomly drops the ores from the mobs.
So a lot of time, for a fairly nice weapon/shield, but then there is the whole process of upgrading, transcending, etc. which are very large time sinks as well.  I would say it is on the more punishing end of the spectrum when it comes to the time sunk into the game.
tl;dr - It is worth a try since it is free to play.  The game certainly still has problem in terms of optimization, but it is a fairly unique MMO in terms of visual style and class system.

The best ALIEN game in years, Alien: Isolation might be too "realistic" for many or too frustratingly lacking in satisfactory gameplay for others. It's probably comparable to the movie Napoleon Dynamite in that people are likely to either love it or hate it with only a few in the middle. (What a strange comparison... but it might be appropriate for that one "love it or hate it" element.) For what it is, what it tries to be and what it doesn't try to be, I recommend it... but I wouldn't personally buy it at its full original retail price.
Some things I've Liked so far:
Aesthetic... it's just like the original ALIEN movie.
Atmosphere... excellent audio, tense music, fragility of your humanity: the immersion makes the game amazing. I've seen the Alien movies and played Alien games, so the shock value isn't what it was the first time witnessing those things, but that doesn't remove the tension created by the in-game audio or the music, which is the music from the original film and some extra (according to the credits).
Tension... the stressful qualities of this game would have me biting my fingernails too short if it were a movie or a book. However, because my hands are busy controlling the game, I have no time for that. That's a good thing!
What I've Disliked thus far:
Tension... the tension and stress is sure to cause an increase in my body's cortisol levels, removing melanin from my hair follicles and giving me gray hair sooner than I would otherwise have it.
Frailty of the protagonist's "weak human form" means a quick death if anyone or anything catches up to you
Elements About Which I'm Undecided:
The antiquated ideas of what technology would be in the future as seen through the eyes of the 1970s make some of the usability factors difficult to fathom. I love it and have a problem with it at the same time.
Alien: Isolation is more like a simulation in many ways than a video game. If you're looking for something to get your adrenaline pumping in a good way and have a great deal of fun doing it, this might not be the game for youl. If you're looking for horror with blood and dead bodies and survivors who are scared out of their minds who will shoot anything, even a friendly human like you, just because it moves, this might be just your cup of tea. If you get positive adrenaline boosts from tension and squealing violins and minor-key tunes, this might be just what you are looking for.
I have a 5.1-channel audio system around me and it's really great for producing atmospheric moods in games that do it right, as this one is so close to doing. However, the audio seems less precise than FPS games in which I can hear exactly where everything is around me and point directly at it by moving my mouse. Often audio in Alien: Isolation coming from an object in front of me will sound like it's coming from behind me; it's difficult to isolate the source using sound alone. That could be an attempt to cause confusion in players to increase atmosphere, but it seems more to me as if I have the speakers plugged into the wrong jacks. It reduces the effectiveness of the audio in my mind to some degree.
A thought: I'll probably improve this review's clarity at some point, because I'm sure it will require editing; I'm writing it while exhausted and typically produce strange text and/or a grammatical failure at times like this. The first game in the S.T.A.L.K.E.R series, Shadow of Chernobyl brings some great story and gameplay to boot.
There are some truly horrifying locales in this game, the feel of the game is very oppresive and gameplay can be down right damnably hostile even to the most careful of players. But, if you can get past that, the game has the potential to drag you through some truly memorable encounters, from the different mutants, anomolies, and even other humans.

STALKER: Shadow of Chernobyl is, perhaps, one of the greatest video games I've ever played. Complete with role playing elements, fantastic action, extreme difficulty and terrifying moments, the game delivers in every way.
GRAPHICS:
First off all, I would highly suggest everyone download the STALKER Complete 2009 Mod on
, as it increases visuals and gameplay performance tenfold and makes the dated game look on par to Crysis. Without the mod, however, colors are bland, facial expressions are dull, shading is downright awful, and textures are muddy. It's not terrible, but I would highly suggest the mod be installed if your PC can handle it.
GAMEPLAY:
This is the iffy part of the game. While the controls aren't particularly difficult to comprehend, some movements feel clunky. Also, without the mod installed (let's face it, the mod improved everything), guns will jam frequently and bullets will go off course at point blank range. This is most of the time a reoccuring glitch, but is no less annoying. With the mod installed, you can have more role playing options available - joining groups and factions, repairing weapons and armor, and even getting more weapons and equipment not available in the original game, and the fact that this mod is free and easy to install just makes it better. However, the gameplay isn't perfect even with the installed mod. Enemies can shoot you through walls, the easiest difficulty is unbelieveably brutal to new players as enemies can kill you in just a few rifle shots or a few melee hits (if it's a mutant). The human AI isn't very smart, but hell they can kill easily. The truly impressive enemies are the mutants. Ranging from sickeningly deformed hounds to massive monstrosities that will haunt your nightmares for days, each mutant comes with its own abilities, attacks, and frightening appearances, making this just as much a survival horror experience as an RPG/Shooter. Glitches aside, the gameplay (though made better with the mod) is fun, easy to learn, and solid.
STORY:
This is where the game truly shines. The story is perhaps one of the most original that I've seen in any game in the past decade. You are a man known only as the 'Marked One,' due to the tatoo on your arm. You have no idea who you really are, what you're doing, or why you're in Chernobyl. All you know is that written on your PDA are the words: "KILL THE STRELOK." From there, you must fight through the horrors of the nuclear wasteland in the heart of Ukraine, uncovering the secrets of your past and the dark horrors that the government have tried so hard to cover up. The story is interactive, compelling, and interesting. The story alone makes the game a better experience.
MULTIPLAYER:
Nothing is more useless than the multiplayer. Not only is it completely broken, but the cooperative play just derives from the role playing experience offered in the main campaign. That, and you'll be incredibly hard-pressed just to find another person to play with, much less be able to connect to a lobby. This isn't an FPS made for multiplayer; I'd steer clear of it.
VERDICT:
STALKER: Shadow of Chernobyl is a fantastic game. Mods improve the experience and make the game more interesting than ever. With a fantastic story, solid gameplay and nice visuals from actual locations in the haunting Chernobyl landscape, this game, despite it's flaws, ranks in among the top best games I've ever played.
RATING: 8/10

TLDR: This game is an unpolished diamond. It has many many tiny flaws, but a lot of great features. Not for everyone, but heartily recommend.
First of all, ignore the comparisons to diablo and V:TM. While some parts of Bloodlust certainly were inspired by those games, they are not anything alike. I would compare the "feel" of the gameplay more to the jedi knight series, with very little acrobatics. Instead, the game has a heavy focus of powering up your character and exploration. If you do not like taking your time to look under every nook and cranny, you will probably not like this game.
As an exclusively melee character, I feel I have experienced the worst of the game, and loved every minute of it. Here are the annoyances I've personnally met:
But despite all this, the drive to explore new areas, to try and be liked by the various vampire clans, and to unravel the main story keeps you hooked.
The game could be explained as 2 parts: exploring and puzzle solving, and adventure dungeon delving.
The exploration is incredibly organic. You are introduced to most "exploration" powers in the first area, and only have to be attentive to details to figure out the solutions. You will have to leave some things behind, but when you unlock new powers, a solution to an old puzzle will spark. You will often wonder if the people you meet are allies or foes, and, depending on your actions, they might be either. You will have to be carful not to trespass on an unfriendly clan's territory, or at least not get caught doing it.
When not exploring, you will be delving in a series of infinite randomized dungeons, fetching rare items npcs you want something from sent you to get, or simply getting better gear. The dungeons patterns are easy to recognize, although there are a few rarer rooms you might get that keeps things fresh. I only went to floor 16, which was deep enough for my purposes, and I am sure there are many things I did not see. There are 5 (to my knowledge) different dungeon tilesets, each with unique enemies and mini-bosses.
Perhaps the most refreshing feature of the game is that it barely cares about balance. You start off weak, and can very well stay weak. If you are well versed in RPGs, I am sure you will have no trouble finding a build that works, and that is enough to complete the game. There is a "power ceiling" that you can break through, a turning point where you suddenly start kicking some serious♥♥♥♥♥ There are various ways to attain this power, and no limits to the power you can attain. Powergamers can find a very satisfying experience in this game.
You have the option to persuade NPCs to advance the story, but you do not need much investment in the stat to fill the requirements for the whole game, especially with items that boost it. There is something of a stealth system, but no real rewards for it, nor much point to it. It's there, but it might as well be non-existent.
All in all, this is a very raw game experience that somehow manages to make me nostalgic despite being recently released. I can certainly see this game becoming a cult classic, and eagerly awaits whatever new projects WRF Studios work on.

I have always been reluctant to touch total war's latest game, largely because it would take days to write down and fully explore the myriad of affronts, not only to historical accuracy but to the laws of physics and biology themselves.
However, I decided, eventually, to give it a try on faith, since the total war franchise has at least been a series of high quality and highly enjoyable games so far. Well, when mixed with enough modded content and a healthy dose of suspension of disbelief that is...
Unfortunately, even with my overenthusiastic attitute to accuracy fully reigned in, I just could not enjoy this game. Firstly, the ui is an utter mess. It covers about 2/3 of the screen and only offers the option to minimise the, probably crucial, information it contains completely. The unit cards take up so much space but make it so hard to even differenciate between unit types because of the questionably bare unit cards, whilst they offer no meaningful information. Minimising the, totally unnessicary information tab also failed to free up the screen, as it turned my narrow band of view into a narrow L-shape of view. The ai, which tbh I barely expected to be competent anyway, blew me away with its stupidity, staying still until my units were in range, then running around in panic like ants whose nest has been stood on.
The camera was glitchy, or perhaps just designed badly; since the camera of Empire and Napoleon worked perfectly I fail to see why it was changed into this more juttering, uncomfortable mess. Which is a double shame as the environment, both its athetics and feel, was actually rather lovely.
The campaign suffers a lack of enjoyability too, amazing how so little depth of gameplay can create so long a loading time, and how convoluted yet totally uninteresting the character system is.
In short, even for a Total War veteran, Rome II offers a confusing interface, anarcronicistic and completely unrealistic battles and a dull, time wasting campaign.

The remastering of the original Homeworld is at heart a modification of Homeworld 2. The places where the second's engines places limitations on the translation of the original are seemingly minor, but have a considerable effect on the gameplay.
One example is the way HW1 smallcraft performance is affected. Some of you might recall that scouts and fighters in HW1 behaved in a semi-newtonian fashion, being able to change their orientation without affecting their current direction of travel. This meant that HW1 fighter formations could radically change direction very quickly; for instance fighters attacking a target in X formation would make their pass and then do the "Starfury Flip" a bit of a distance away from the target. This is no longer reflected in the Remaster.
The result is that fighter formations are more or less useless in Homeworld Remastered. Unlike larger ships, unmodded HW2 fighters generally have to bank and turn as if in atmosphere unlike their predecessors. This means that the entire formation must wheel around to affect a change in direction, which has the affect you might expect on their ability to fight effectively.
Small niggles such as these will affect your experience if you look for them. Thankfully you can compare the differences for yourself by trying out the original once again, as it is bundled with the altogether very affordable package. So long as you keep this in mind you really will not be affected, particularly due to Homeworld's gorgeous visuals.

This is easily my favorite RPG in years, it takes the souls formula and makes it better in almost every aspect. The gameplay is where the souls series really shines and dark souls II is no exeption to that. It is harder than it's predecessor  and sometimes it seems a little cheap with the amount of ennemies thrown at you(especially in the DLC), or attacks you clearly dodged still hitting you, but it is no big deal. The co-op is implemented much better this time around, you are able to summon up to 2 people to clear areas and help with boss fights. However summoning 2 people makes some of the bosses slightly too easy on a first playthrough in my opinion. The pvp is implemented better as well, there are quite a few more covenants and a lot of them are centered around pvp.
For me the biggest change from dark souls is being able to fast travel between bonfires from the start of the game. It saves you from the tedious back tracking that was present in the first one.
Also dark souls II is well optimized for pc unlike dark souls which pretty much needed a 3rd party patch in order to be playable. I run it maxed out on a 4 years old computer at a steady 60 fps.
Verdict: Highly recommended!
