So at this point if you haven't got the game already, what are y'all waiting for? It might look like another DOTA/League clone but it's totally not.
First of all, we should cover the gameplay. The goal is the same as most MOBA's: push past the enemy's defenses and take their base down. The main differences are the plethora of different game modes and the God's/Goddesses 'kits'. First, the gamemodes. The MOBA-esque mode is Conquest: three lanes and a sprawling jungle, but not the best for inexperienced players. You'll want to start off with either Assault or Arena: In Assault, you push one lane with a random God and rely on burst and sustain. In Arena, there are no lanes: instead you play in a Team Deathmatch (although you can push minions into their portal for points to). From those gamemodes, work up to Clash and Joust. Clash is the midway point from Arena to Conquest - pushing two lanes with a large opening in the middle of the map for fighting, whereas Joust is a 3v3 mode in contrast to the usual 5v5. There is also MOTD's and Siege mode, but although these modes are great fun they aren't the best for newer players.
As mentioned before, the kits of each god are slightly different from other MOBA's. They ALWAYS have 1 passive, 3 abilities, and an Ultimate Ability.The passive normally defines the playstyle of a God, so you should always check it if you aren't sure what you're doing. The 3 abilities range from healing to clearing minions to, well, almost anything. The Ultimate Ability is a souped-up ability that can change the flow of the game - at the cost of a longer cooldown (usually). Finding the right time to use abilities might take some learning but there is plenty of practice modes for you to take your time with.
Second of all, the third person viewpoint is more than enough to distinct it as its own MOBA. If you have already played any of the RTS-view MOBA's then it might seem a bit jarring at first but it doesn't take very long to become accustomed to. The more immersive viewpoint is supported by the game's host of recognizable characters, all with their own personality: Aphrodite, the Greek Goddess of Beauty, borders on narcissistic and is obsessed with the appearance of herself and others.
In addition to their own lore page explaining the legends of their respective gods, there are many different ways to play a single god. Using item purchased from the store (with in-game money that is gained over the course of the game, not microtransactions) you can change a damage mage to a tankier one or a tankier guardian to a one-shot mage. It's up to you to read guides on how to effectively 'build' a select God.
Now that that's out of the way, I'll cover some important points for new players:
*Communicate - Practice the VGS system or use Curse Voice to communicate quickly and effectively.
*Stay in Position - 99999% of deaths happen when the mage wanders too far and gets assassinated or when the guardian tries to chase a kill he can't confirm, leaving his team defenseless. If your struggling, just follow 'Tanks in the Front, Squishies in the back'.
*Prioritise targerts - Don't waste all your mana and abilities onto a guardian who'll just laugh right back; instead, focus on players with less health or who are out of position. It can be difficult to keep the above point and this one, but you'll get the hang of it in time.
*Don't be afraid to ask for help.
*DON'T RAGE QUIT FOR F*** SAKE (*^v^)*
*The last, and most important point for new players, is be aware of your surroundings. There is a class called assassins that specialise in getting kills. Avoidong death will take time and patience, and you will need to learn the warning signs. Loki, for example, can go invisble for a short time but his abilities are louder than most. Thanatos has an 'execute' ability, whice will kill you if your health is below a %threshold and provided he doesn't miss.The list goes on, and isn't limited to assassins, but being aware is the best way to stay alive (uwu).
TLDR; Game good, game free, game fun, game fresh, game kawaii (*^v^)*

Makers of Starforge, where some key features were not developed due to time constraints and lack of budget management. However, out of the many early access titles out there, Code Hatch is one of the only companies that actually completed a title, despite it being a bit lack luster. But important to note is that Starforge is 100% playable compared to other titles.
Reign of kings is the result of the learning experience that the developers have gone through with their past mistakes. It is incredibly difficult to make a amazing first game. As a company and team, you need a couple of attempts before you get into the groove of making video games.
Reign of Kings is still giving me a swell time despite spending more than 10 hours on the game. Thats already more time spent compared to $60 AAA titles.
If you like to build, survive, and fight as knights; this game is for you.
A large plus for this game (being set up in the medieval era), is no random headshots will kill your character, compared to other games of the genre. In addition to this fact, you are not forced to run around for hours on end with nothing to do, due to the fact that there is a crafting system available. Every player will be on even grounds after some time. Good weapons and pickups are not due to chance. The map may be smaller when compared to games like Dayz; however, this makes it easier to find friends and interact with other players. Thus the map is also more enjoyable to explore rather than walking for 3 hours without end.
The land claiming and Guild system makes the game even more enjoyable. Not to mention that players are able to govern entire servers. This causes some servers to be peaceful, while others are filled with war and bloodshed depending on the king of the server.
This game is an early access title, and if you decide to purchase it there is no guarantee that it will become complete. However, at its present state, I have already experienced abundant amounts of fun.

Cute game for the price.  Kind of a slow paced Diablo/Bloodlines cross.  Graphics arent great but they do the job.  Voice acting(what there is of it) isnt great but its not annoying, music is repetative but not really annoying either.   I guess the worst thing that can be said about this game is that it definately "feels" dated.  Not just the graphics either.  Combat is sluggish and charector movements are as well.  Oh and the landscape/backgrounds/surroundings are similar to that of much older 3D games.  Having said all that, I find the game fun to play in a relaxing sort of way.  If it had a bigger price tag, my advice would be to stay away from it for sure.  But at the price that I bought it for(6 bucks on sale), I definately recomend it.
Update:  After playing the game for a little while longer, I am actually enjoying it MORE and not less.  I cant say that about many of the games that Ive paid much more money for.  My previous observations about the game are still true(at least to me).  The game does seem "dated" in many ways.  On the other hand, its a game that has been done well and the further that you get into it the more you actually like it.  One of the cool things that Ive discovered about the game is that you really need to invest in ALL your stats to do well(not like some games where you just max out only the couple of stats which are important to the class that you play).  Similarly, you will find most of the skills on your skill tree actually USEFULL.  You will USE a majority of them on a regular basis to play the game well.  Is this game worth the $12-$13 asking price?  Now that Ive played it for awhile, my opinion is YES.  It is.  Im glad that I got it on sale but again, in my opinion, you wont go wrong by paying full price for this either.  Really good, solid game.

I loved Vampire: Bloodlines, but this is... "Meh"  Right from the get-go i was very uninspired by the story and just wanted to get the hell out of the begining dungen to explore the city. Once there, i was further unimpressed with lack of life, the city seemed dead. Then suddenly im attacked by some vampire hunter for no apparent reason, who seems to be such a high level that there really was no hope of winning while on a quest to go into a locked basment that the questgiver supposedly gave me the key to but really didnt.
All in all it was a very disappointing experiance. I understand this was made by like one guy, wich is impressive as hell, but unfortunatly it shows.

So the obvious paralell for this game is Vampire: The Masqeurade, acting as a barely affiliated sequel. Storywise it's garbage, you wake up in a tomb with several NPC's with lame dialogue and are essentially hinted at several timest hat the Emperor is bad and must be replaced. You are referred to as a Fledgeling, and despite quickly having access to secret-finding eyesight you will be relying on a dinky flashlight for all vision. The Dev's claim because they call you something in game we are supposed to accept that fresh vampires can't see in the dark as if that's not completely rediculous. Any creature that is created through magic and only able to live at night can be assumed to see in the dark. If you turn your brain off and realize the Dev's have no idea what vampires of fables can and cannot do, this game is enjoyable.
The game would be more impressive if there was ever a good Vampire: The Masquerade game. Bloodlines was okay in that it was too linear for my tastes but otherwise pretty entertaining. But let us be brutally honest in this respect: WoD won't have a good game title while the entire community is split between the new and old darkness settings. In a way this is where Bloodlust shines, it's generic brand vampire angst. There are a few different vampire families, your class decides which likes you the most.
The puzzles in the game are fantastic because they explain the rules of the puzzles very early on and make it clear that there are a ton of them. Other games rarely commit to avid puzzle use, but Bloodlust embraces it. You have several abilities right at the beginning that allow you to explore the environment, including a spiritual ball you can use to remotely trigger switches (YET YOU CAN'T SEE IN THE FRIKKIN DARK!) which allows you to open up side passages filled with goodies. While the puzzles are good, when they say this game is mixed with Diablo they DO NOT mean the good ones from the series, they mean 3. Prepare to mindlessly stack attributes while filling up several talent and skill tree's. You end up needing all of them to some degree, so it's not as bad, but it's still pretty lame pseudo-rpg development.
A "selling point" of the game is that it has a boring minion system that it pretends is an exciting family development mechanic. When you have a minion slot, if you bite a human they turn into a vampire and serve you. They can level up, do chores, and fight with you. Unfortunatly I don't know how to get rid of them, the tutorial entices you to turn an ugly bum when there are hot women on the surface to turn. Wading into combat didn't kill him, but it sure kills me. I wish the family mechanics were anywhere near as good as advertised, instead just being another generic mechanic with "vampire" written in permenant marker over it.
If you ignore everything but the general attitude and vibe of the game and love dungeon-crawling then you should be able to enjoy this game. Vampire fans of any kind will immediatly get frustrated at how badly the game portrays vampiric lore, especially World of Darkness fans. Everything vampiric in the game is a loose parody of a WoD concept down to them slipping up and referring to how vampires are made as the WoD term "The Embrace".
Is the game worth $13? Yes. It's something you can play for a few hours at a time and just build up your character without having a big story thrusted onto you. What Bloodlust isin't would be a good RPG; Making numbers get bigger isin't enticing character devlopment, nor is picking from talent tree's. Your "minions" are just that, they are emotionless lackies. It's a run and gun dungeon crawler with a bunch of gameplay mechanics carrying a very loose vampire theme. And I guess that's okay.
EDIT: Today the Dev added the ability to get rid of minions using cloves of garlic, so that is resolved. Be sure to upvote my truthful reveiws.

An amazing game that takes me back to old school dungeon crawling with some additional advantages. I know there are a few that can't recommend the game but I honestly don't think a good recommendation can come from less than an hour of gameplay. Now that it's finally been released out of EA; I want to say a few things about it.
The story is interesting although a bit non involved with the overall gameplay. I would say, it really doesn't need to be followed as closely to enjoy the game in its entirety.
Combat is a bit clunky but enjoyable once you get the hang of it. Reminds me a bit of the Gothic series.
Looting and dungeon delving is probably my favourite part of the game. There are tons of loot to find in the game with qualities from common to rare and unique. Dungeons are randomly generated each time you start one. There are random stairwells that appear every few floors to help with escape if needed.
Character progress is fun as well. Many skills and traits to choose from that increase your inventory size, allow mist transformation to save keys and move through gated doors, allow summoning of more minions, increase specific stats every level and even transform into a beast for brutal melee action. You can also increase the stats of your minions as you progress.
Overall, I would rate it an 8/10. I'm not one for considering graphics into my rating so please take into consideration for yourselves that it isn't top of the line. I think the developer did an amazing job and the game is enjoyable for what it is. I've played enough AAA titles to know looks and prices aren't everything.

A very unique and flavorful puzzle game where you play as a Cold War-esque border checkpoint immigration inspector. Each in-game day is timed and presents new challenges, such as new paperwork, denying access to immigrants from a specific country, or looking for an individual on a wanted poster. There is always a sense of urgency with your income and the livelihood of your family depending on you to make a quota while the immigrants are harassing you to work faster. With a branching story that changes based on your actions during the days (and your post-work "upkeep" choices) and multiple endings, there are many ways to play through this exceptional experience of a game. Papers, Please is a standout spin on life in the Cold War-era Soviet states that, while depressing and repetitive at times, is something that any puzzle game fan should pick up.

Quite a lot of fun.  I like the attention to detail you have to maintain, how frustratingly hurried you always feel, and the low-scale graphics are perfect to evoke the time period of the game!
For something that sounds so simple on the surface, this is very entertaining!

The first thing that I need to mention is the music in this game, it is a beautiful catchy 8-bit tune that will take quite awhile to get out of your head. The game is good, has multiple endings which are interesting, I've only gotten one, but it was interesting.  The main gameplay may seem repetitive after awhile, and you'd be right if that's what you called it, but it is catchy and you do need to focus really hard on getting everyone who needs to go through through and everyone else arrested, you can get a bonus for detaining more people. One last note is that you may want to turn nudity off in the settings right of the bat, it can be creepy sometimes.

Papers, Please lets you in the shoes of the Arstotzka's Immigration Inspector.
In a strange way, this game is not only about checking the entrants and see if everything matches: while doing your job, you will meet different people and you will have to face different situations, according to what you do during the gameplay. For instance, you can either decide to help criminal organisations, with the risk of getting yourself jailed, or either stay loyal to your leaders, with the risk of remaining without food for your family because of your underpaid job.
This unique Indie Game offers you a quite long and enjoyable gameplay, which is going to make you want to play it more and more, wondering what would have happened if you made different choices.

Welcome to the mind of the frontline bureaucrat!
Yes, you're repeatedly reviewing documents, but it's strangely addictive... and enlightening.
Do you callously do your job without regard for the person in front of you, or do you use what little power you have to show kindness to the poor disenfranchised soul? What will you do in the face of conflicting imperatives? Will you put your own safety and well-being above that of your countrymen… or even your family?
Sometimes depressing. Sometimes monotonous. Always thought provoking. Papers, Please is an impressive accomplishment in gameplay and storytelling.
Very unsusual. Not much of a game as such, more an unusual interactive story. Wonderful though, very much recommended.

I have always been reluctant to touch total war's latest game, largely because it would take days to write down and fully explore the myriad of affronts, not only to historical accuracy but to the laws of physics and biology themselves.
However, I decided, eventually, to give it a try on faith, since the total war franchise has at least been a series of high quality and highly enjoyable games so far. Well, when mixed with enough modded content and a healthy dose of suspension of disbelief that is...
Unfortunately, even with my overenthusiastic attitute to accuracy fully reigned in, I just could not enjoy this game. Firstly, the ui is an utter mess. It covers about 2/3 of the screen and only offers the option to minimise the, probably crucial, information it contains completely. The unit cards take up so much space but make it so hard to even differenciate between unit types because of the questionably bare unit cards, whilst they offer no meaningful information. Minimising the, totally unnessicary information tab also failed to free up the screen, as it turned my narrow band of view into a narrow L-shape of view. The ai, which tbh I barely expected to be competent anyway, blew me away with its stupidity, staying still until my units were in range, then running around in panic like ants whose nest has been stood on.
The camera was glitchy, or perhaps just designed badly; since the camera of Empire and Napoleon worked perfectly I fail to see why it was changed into this more juttering, uncomfortable mess. Which is a double shame as the environment, both its athetics and feel, was actually rather lovely.
The campaign suffers a lack of enjoyability too, amazing how so little depth of gameplay can create so long a loading time, and how convoluted yet totally uninteresting the character system is.
In short, even for a Total War veteran, Rome II offers a confusing interface, anarcronicistic and completely unrealistic battles and a dull, time wasting campaign.

After the great experiences and fun time with the marvelous Shogun 2, I've bought this installment almost on the day of its release, but I became dismayed quite quickly.
I don't know who wrote the system requirements (or coded the game engine), but still in 2017 I have trouble finding optimal settings to run the game fairly smoothly (50-60 FPS) without having fugly broken soldiers on the battlefield. When had an AMD Phenom II processor (supposedly okay according to the system requirements), the game was literally unplayable, no matter what videocards and settings I've used. After switching to a much beefy 4 core desktop 4+ GHz Core i5 processor, the situation got slightly (literally just slightly) better. Clearly the programmers have messed up something really bad. Usually the game never looks better in any scene than Shogun 2, but it can never achieve the butter-smooth framerates what Shogun 2 provided.
Anyway there are other problems as well. The official character skills and building tree displays are totally missing, even from the Encyclopaedia, so largely it remains on the player to google out a proper 3rd party skill/building tree.
The diplomacy A.I. is still not really working properly, or at least acts in a wildy weird way quite often.
Also the change of the region/town/legion system makes the game differ quite a bit from the earlier games of the series, defending a non-capital "town" is close to impossible, especially in the later game with the hard limit on the armies. That's a weird gameplay change, but I must admit it adds somewhat to the challenge, so I wouldn't count this towards the negatives.
My first and also my overall impression is quite negative about this game. The artificially impossible system requirements, the utterly buggy code (constant crashes in every imaginable situation in the early versions, about until the Emperor Edition release) just show how complicated to develop & release a fairly complicated game software on time in sufficiently high quality. With this release CA obviously failed to do so. :(
On the bright side TW: Attila & Warhammers are far better, so probably the CA crew learned the lesson the hard way.
You will never see nuclear reactors with the same eyes again.
SoC is harder to get into than Call of Pripyat, but that's only cause it is that much more complex. I definately recommend this game for those with a lot of time.

The only game of this trilogy, this franchise that I am happy to recommend to everybody out there who like post-apocalyptic FPS games. While post-apocalyptic reminds many of us of Fallout 3, Stalker's surroundings are different and instead of the barren lands full of debris you have to imagine a nuclear wasteland.
This wasteland is called the Zone and interestingly, the game follows the catastrophe of Chernobyl by adding a twist to the story: here the activities in the power plant did not stop after the incident, in fact, quite the opposite happened which was eventually followed by another explosion. Now, this huge radioactive area is fully of anomalies and mutants and of course stalkers, mercenaries who are obsessed with all this and aim to find all kinds of artifacts that are the results of the catastrophe.
While the game was released back in 2007 it should be noted that a mod called COMPLETE is available to enhance everything in the game: it ups the visuals, lowers the amount of bugs and glitches and even adds new features to make the gameplay easier and more exciting.
The game offers a free-roaming system: missions can be triggered after speaking with various individuals, other than that you are free to go wherever you want and whenever you want. There are many side missions, too, that lengthen an already long story and as the game offers at least half a dozen endings in the form of rendered cutscenes you have a high replayability value here.
One of the downsides for me was that I was not exactly notified that once I start a particular mission there will be no return. With the COMPLETE mod this is now corrected as after completing the story the game puts you back in the Zone and you are free to complete any pending missions you had. Another thing was the difficulty - I have played a lot of FPS games and these I usually complete on hard difficulty settings, too, so I consider myself a veteran but even Stalker was too difficult at times. I believe it is an AI issue as enemies can easily give you headshots from a far distance and there's no room for suprises attacks, either. They are just too good so quick-saving is recommended frequently.
Stalker is a classic. It may not be a beautiful game but its gameplay is certainly entertaining and unique. With the COMPLETE mod in place it is an even better experience.

Just finished up a rousing round of S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl the other day for the first time, and was thoroughly impressed. Story: The story follows Amanda Ripley, daughter of Ellen Ripley, lone survivor of the Nostromo. The plot picks up 15 years after Ellen Ripley’s disappearance, with the Nostromo’s flight recorder being found and taken to Sevastopol station. Amanda, an engineer working in a nearby system, is approached by Weyland-Yutani to accompany their retrieval of the recorder. In hopes of learning more about her mother, Amanda joins. Things go wrong from the start, as Sevastopol station is an absolute mess. Amanda, from the jump, is separated the WY reps and must explore and the station alone. This is a simple but effective setup for exploration and horror. The plot involves unraveling why the station is in disrepair and what is killing everyone aboard. Many of the subplots parallel segments of the original movie, exploring areas of the station, setting traps for the alien, etc. Even the fake endings, climax’s that do not lead to a resolution, are done in a similar fashion. The story does the franchise justice, while providing excellent context for the gameplay and atmospheric settings.
Gameplay: If you're looking for a more Aliens-type experience from Alien: Isolation maybe this game isn't for you. This is a stealth game through and through. Towards the end you can open your play style to be a bit more action oriented, but overall the environment and tools you have cater to a cautious and quiet player. For most of the chapters, gameplay revolves around avoiding the alien while completing tasks. The alien is what makes this game shine. Its actions are so varied and unpredictable that you’re constantly on your toes. You’re always strategizing about your next move, learning your environment so that you can trust you won’t come face to face with the alien. Especially in the early game, you have little to no defense against the imposing threat. Only flares and crafted tools for distraction can give you respite. This makes the first few levels with the alien so formidable and tense. Not knowing the levels layout and watching this enemy operate with such freedom and decisive finality can significantly intimidate a player. What you can learn to control is the sounds you and your surroundings make, this is paramount in these opening levels. Keeping quiet and making distractions are key to your success. As you progress you face off with Working Joes, an android enemy that provide a serious nuisance. While these encounters are not nearly as fatal, mishandling the situation can lead to a large loss of resources or the alien showing up. Towards the end of the game, you have a more impactful arsenal at your disposal. You will be equipped with certain weapons that significantly improve your chances of surviving both alien and Working joe encounters.
The stealth and survival mechanics work extremely well overall, all your movements and actions come off very fluid. However, the shooting mechanics are clunky and deter you from a run and gun approach. This isn’t a huge deal as shooting is rarely advantageous. The few scenarios where guns are effective are with the human enemies, but I found other ways of moving through the levels far more fun and safer. The other part of the gameplay is the mission objectives. Overall these tasks fit the environment, often asking to restore power, find a keycard, or fix something. Ripley is an engineer, so character asking your character to perform such nitty-gritty actions is logical and provides you many opportunities to cross paths with the alien. While there isn’t significant variety to the objectives, the context, environments, and alien will always keep things different.
To wrap up, the gameplay rests on the revolutionary alien and its exceptional unpredictability. The alien’s invincibility is a fantastic choice as your emotions begin to echo the terrifying state of mind of the original Nostromo crew. The crafting, mini-games, and stealth all compliment the games strengths. Lastly, I’ll mention the save system where you go from phone to phone to create a checkpoint. I enjoyed having no auto save or quick save. The phone checkpoints add to the tension the game builds. When you’ve traveled some distance, and have been successful in avoiding the alien for so long, there is a real reward to finding a phone at last.
Atmosphere: The atmosphere, graphics, sounds, and setting feel exactly like the original Alien movie. This game replicates that movie in many senses and does it well. The setting is Sevastopol station, a commercial port very reminiscent of the Nostromo in exterior and interior design. Everything looks wonderfully retro-futuristic in the same vein as the original movie. Homages to Alien are seen throughout, and if you’re as big of fan as myself you’ll love it! The Sevastopol is a deserted wreck by the time you arrive. Environmental story telling is evident as you can tell how the Sevastopol fell into its current state and what its past residents experienced. Graffiti, destruction, and logs add to the oppressive atmosphere with a dark backstory of a station in economic decline. This adds life to a primarily deserted station. The station was owned by Seegson, a Weyland-Yutani competitor that can’t quite manage to create quite as convincing androids. But with the alien involved you must know that WY have their reach extended here. Getting back to the atmosphere, the graphics are stunning and bring out the best in Sevastopol’s aesthetics. The lighting, steam effects, and metallic interiors all work together and contrast beautifully. The lighting especially creates some truly memorable moments. The red hues from the flare have a smoky, glowing haze, while yellow hues from a star can blow you away, illuminating a room through a window that provides a panoramic vista of deep space. The sound design is super effective in ramping up the tension of alien encounters. Thudding footsteps and saturated hisses announce its presence and instill fear. Ambient noises like moans and echoes add an empty feeling. The lack of sounds is huge too. Often there will be just the squeaking of your shoes and a clattering commotion somewhere far off in the station. The station provides a lot of sound effects. Vents, doors, monitors, and alarms all create this deep, extended sense of a large station in disrepair. Overall, the atmosphere is a strong suit for Alien: Isolation. There is so much to love about it, especially if you a fan of the original film.
Overall: I recommend this game to anyone looking for an atmospheric, horror, stealth game. If you first looked at this game when it was first released or it's been a long time, consider taking another look at it. A lot has been added since launch and it could be worth reconsidering.
Reasons I like this game:
- Large open world
- Good MMO experience
- No longer requires a subscription
- Huge amounts of content (I've played for over 100 hours and still feel like I'm just beginning)
- Fun with friends to do dungeons and quests together
- Many interesting and fairly balanced mechanics and abilities
- Addons bring many QoL fixes and changes to the UI and simplify micromanagement, with fairly easy installment (though difficult to transfer settings between characters)
- Many options and keybinds with support for up to 5 keys per bind.
Reasons I dislike this game:
- Poor performance. Even on an i7-4790k and GTX 970 I get horrendous (like sometimes down to 20ish) framerate drops in crowded areas and even when I'm in a solo instance where performance is better, framerate is hard capped at 100.
- Vanilla game feels lacking in graphics and UI. After playing with ReShade, the game without it just looks so bland and washed out. The UI (especially in guild stores) can be cumbersome and requires addons to have the capabilities one would expect (e.g. a search function).
- Many money-grabs in the form of timesavers, cosmetics, DLC, and extra account bonuses.
- Many real-world timers, e.g. daily dungeons, daily horse upgrades, research timers, daily crafting writs
- FOV goes up to "130" but feels about like 80, with the only way to increase it further being an extra game launcher (hook64)
- Requires a third-party launcher that complicates playing through Steam and using custom launchers like hook64
- Long load times
- Large install size (~65GB)
- Cannot activate a Steam version if you bought the standalone game
All in all, most negatives can be mitigated through the use of addons and extra programs, but your mileage may vary and the game becomes less stable by doing so.  However, a lot of these should be simple fixes for ZOS to implement in the vanilla game. That said, the positives do outweigh the negatives and when everything works, it's a very engaging and rewarding game to play that will satisfy you for hundreds of hours.

If you even think that you might appreciate spending time in a Elder Scrolls world, with Elder Scrolls lore, with other players, you should purchase this game. It is a fun, improving, MMORPG with great graphics. However, it is helpful to disregard any preconceived notions of what it is or how it plays. Here are the facts:
The game is not pay to win, the Crown store for paid items are all cosmetic or utilitarian. (there are different horses and other mounts, and there is a scroll that grants 50% higher XP gain for a couple of hours, for instance)
This is an MMORPG, complete with the 3 dungeon roles of Tank, DPS, Healer. There are 4 varied classes, that can each perform each role, with at least a moderate level of effectiveness. Grinding, simple, random quests exist, much like Skyrim's "Radiant" quests. Speaking of, this game will never be multiplayer or co-op Skyrim. This game began development around the same time as Skyrim, so likely was more influenced by Oblivion, at least aesthetically.
The combat is fun, but there is a learning curve, especially for high end DPS with animation cancelling and attack weaving. If you want to Tank or Heal, however, there is less of a combat learning curve and more of a dungeon mechanics learning curve. If you want to join random dungeon groups quickly, play and queue as a Tank or Healer, as there are far more DPS. If you want to play solo, which you can and there is alot of content tailored for that, play as DPS.
The hand-holding that is familiar to those who have played single-player Elder Scrolls simply does not exist in this game. If you wish to know something about a certain crafting mechanic, how to improve your combat effectiveness, etc, research it! There are guides, wikis, and subreddits, that have all of the information you need to be effective in all aspects of this game. My personal advice? Don't neglect anything, or have friends/guildies that don't neglect anything.
Configuration of your attributes, skills, gear and weapon sets, enchantments, food & drink buffs, and potions/poisons, can drastically improve how well you and the possibly random people that you encounter do at defeating that world boss or dungeon boss, or taking that keep in PvP.
Your fellow players that make up the (surprisingly large) community of this game are usually willing to be helpful and informative, although trolls and elitists will always exist. If you have a question, ask someone in zone chat or local /say chat. 9 times out of 10 you will get a helpful answer.
tl;dr
Graphics and Elder Scrolls lore alone is why I play this. I cannot stand the cartoonesque graphics of many MMORPGS, and I am already familiar with the lore, so I quickly fell in love with this game. Combining that with fun, fast paced combat and excellent community makes for an enduringly enjoyable experience.

I love this game, but it has some serious growing up to do in the genre of Sci-Fi.
One thing about this game that I love is the wide variety of ships we can choose from and also the ability to customize our ships to our liking. Now the one thing that saddens me the most is the fact the Frontier Developments basically stated that they player will never be able to pilot ships as big as Farragut which puts a dampers. One the greatest feelings in space theme games is piloting a capital class ship, commanding squadrons of fighters while laying massive firepower that turns the tide of a battle or defending the ship against ambush of fighters. Eve Online brought a never ending hunger for player driven wars between two player ran corporations or alliances over vast expansions of space in attempt to control the non-settled frontiers of space. There is also player built stations, player build fortifications, player held planets, player owned solar systems, and player owned shipyards that make it feels like the galaxy is alive. For such a vast open end game, it feels like there is very little purpose for the player except for tagging along for the ride, we barely shape the galaxy.
By limiting players ability to interact with your galaxy, you are faced with the outcome that players will not be able to do much in a vast open end world that you have created. The only thing that us players do have forward to look too is playing the vast variety of ships available in the game. When you deny two ships to the players who play, Frontier Developments are hurting their ability to be flexible in their approach. Basically you are putting a artificial block on the growth of ship variety by doing this, you can never build bigger than that single capital ship. Once players hit Corvette and Cutter, they can’t advance any further while NPC have Farragut and Majestic class ships that dwarf player owned ships. It isn’t because these ships are rare and limited in numbers, in-fact they are very common because you find them throughout all conflict zones regardless of where you are in the galaxy. We should be asking why capital ships are unobtainable when they are not unique or rare?
Groups are so important in massive multiplayer online games, it connects players together and helps them do things that they can’t normally do alone. Look at Eve Online that is built around players working together, they achieve amazing and epic accomplishments that are a envy of thousands of players while being big enough to be featured in national news articles. This advertises the game in a way that no other game has achieved because players want to be a part of this and willing to dedicate years to achieving something. By offering the ability to own solar systems, stations, shipyards, and factions; they are not only giving room for this game to grow, they are creating a environment that will advertise itself and help the game community to grow. By letting players be able to shape and expand the galaxy, Frontier Development are basically making it easier to establish the world around the players as things evolve and grow. Why must you limit the expansion of the bubble to your time schedule?
So basically what I am saying is, stop trying to force the galaxy to grow, let it grow on its own by giving the tools to the players. You can shape the basic story-line which players will follow without much of a issue, but once you are trying to micro-manage a galaxy of players, you will be limited severely to the point you will practically lose steam quicker. Players love the ability to shape, choose, and control their galaxy more than  tagging along for the ride with limited options to experience it. So do yourself a favor, be more flexible.

With a GTX 770, this really shouldn't be happening with these kind of visuals. Enemy design is blurry and unimaginative although some well placed monster spawns do give you a heartbeat spike while you're dungeon crawling. Animations are stiff at best while more than a few cases of figures clipping through walls.
The game has a small town area that you will be able to explore during the story as well as some prostitues/hobos to suck blood from or turn into your family. Past that is where the real juice of this game is. There is a well fleshed out randomly generated dungeon system in this game filled with traps, treasures, monsters, etc. It's actually quite charming to go into the depths and worry about being making the decision to go further or turn back while you still have the chance. When your hp goes to 0, you will get knocked out. During that time, you can either choose to wake up where you were or spawn in the last safe zone. The caveat is that your body may have been looted while you were down.
The class system is basic with 3 in total. There are skill and talent trees that will let you have some diversity in builds. I felt that weapons are extremely restricted to certain classes though as each weapon type usually requires you to heavily invest in one of the three main combat stats. Warriors usually invest in strength to get more dps, witch with charisma, etc. I got a gun early on that required 50 points in strenght and another sword that wanted 30 in agi. These are stats that I wouldn't ever invest in as I picked the witch class. Another odd deisgn choice was separating persuasion from charism. Persuation has its own stat while charisma increases your magic... Lastly is the game's family system. You can suck someone's blood and build your own family. You need to level up the blodo sucking skill to increase family size and your minions have their own stats and skills you can upgrade. As a result of this however, they feel like faceless npc's with no personality.
Overall, I highly recommend this game given its low price. While a one person developer certainly doesn't excuse its faults it does engender some sympathy for the lack of resources.

LIFE
The Dark Souls series returns with a meatier, deadlier, tougher offering of punishing gameplay, that attempts to rival the difficulty of previous installments, Demon's Souls (PS3 Exclusive) and Dark Souls (Multiple Platforms). A promise of Bigger environments, Better graphics, Beastly adversaries - this is a sequel worthy of the name. So say all the official reviews and gaming sites.. Question is: Have FromSoftware played it safe and churned out a second, similar reckoning? Or genuinely attempted to make a better, tougher game?
RECKONING
As you can tell from the title, I went with the former. The developers would be mad to deviate from the original winning formula of dungeon crawling/grind rpg... something or other.. What with the extreme success of their second incarnation of the souls series. That being said, when you stick to your guns instead of going all out, you better seriously deliver, again. Dying is no longer the trial and error 'Oh well, better luck next time' slap on the wrist but now a full on slap in the face as your feeble attempts will now be far more costly - depleting your health bar upon each death. No more cheap farming of souls from the weakest opponents - enemies no longer respawn in the same way, when they do, they are likened to a new game+. Your only saving grace is that of the new feature that allows stat management.
RESURRECTION
The Good - At first, the battle system is slightly alien compared to the first game, but in time becomes a quicker more stable reinvigoration. Weapons aren't insanely difficult to improve anymore and you're guided a little better in general improvement and boss soul use. The amount of bosses is staggering. The areas are still almost all connected. Weapons and Armour - all look better - new and old. Classy little touches like the plaque commemorating the number of deaths worldwide, the additional 2 slots to equipable rings and finally a real revamping of the dreaded 'New Game+' which pits previously unseen enemies against you amongst the originals.
The Bad - You are gifted the 'warp' ability from the beginning (something well earned in the 1st). Your humanity is restored at any time you wish (makes it too easy to summon help). As with every DS game, the PVP invasions are rarely as advertised - instead of being matched against true advicery within 10 levels of your own, you get pitted against someone who's blatantly completed the game, donning unknown armour sets and practically killing you in one hit - that or that just circle you in the vein attempt at trying to backstab you or wait for hours so they can parry you - BORING - easily the most vapid aspect of the game. There are also parts which require luck rather then skill, the 'memories of giants' come to mind... Recycled bosses - there's one who is an exact replica from the last game and another which is the same size and uses the same move set - CHEAP.
ETERNAL
Light is finally shed on the lore and story line - enter the land of Drangleic where the torrid curse is back and this time, taking your memories along with your humanity and sanity. The initial and only FMV of the whole game is long and well made, setting you up for the somewhat-story to follow. A chinsy tutorial area does not bode well to be honest and neither does the addition of elderly women in red robes cackling at your optimism. For me, someone who has spare weekends and the odd hour after work to seriously play a game, it took me near to the 50 hour mark to get through this one which is a satisfactory amount of time these days.
DEATH
I'll say now, - I prefer the first Dark Souls - it's environments were linked in a far more interesting fashion, the bosses were much more unique and it's general experience was far more other worldly - attributes of a proper escapist video game.
Expect even more frustratingly implausible bosses and patience pushing locations to delve into as FromSoftware take you down an all to familiar path of pain and suffering. Enjoy!

So at this point if you haven't got the game already, what are y'all waiting for? It might look like another DOTA/League clone but it's totally not.
First of all, we should cover the gameplay. The goal is the same as most MOBA's: push past the enemy's defenses and take their base down. The main differences are the plethora of different game modes and the God's/Goddesses 'kits'. First, the gamemodes. The MOBA-esque mode is Conquest: three lanes and a sprawling jungle, but not the best for inexperienced players. You'll want to start off with either Assault or Arena: In Assault, you push one lane with a random God and rely on burst and sustain. In Arena, there are no lanes: instead you play in a Team Deathmatch (although you can push minions into their portal for points to). From those gamemodes, work up to Clash and Joust. Clash is the midway point from Arena to Conquest - pushing two lanes with a large opening in the middle of the map for fighting, whereas Joust is a 3v3 mode in contrast to the usual 5v5. There is also MOTD's and Siege mode, but although these modes are great fun they aren't the best for newer players.
As mentioned before, the kits of each god are slightly different from other MOBA's. They ALWAYS have 1 passive, 3 abilities, and an Ultimate Ability.The passive normally defines the playstyle of a God, so you should always check it if you aren't sure what you're doing. The 3 abilities range from healing to clearing minions to, well, almost anything. The Ultimate Ability is a souped-up ability that can change the flow of the game - at the cost of a longer cooldown (usually). Finding the right time to use abilities might take some learning but there is plenty of practice modes for you to take your time with.
Second of all, the third person viewpoint is more than enough to distinct it as its own MOBA. If you have already played any of the RTS-view MOBA's then it might seem a bit jarring at first but it doesn't take very long to become accustomed to. The more immersive viewpoint is supported by the game's host of recognizable characters, all with their own personality: Aphrodite, the Greek Goddess of Beauty, borders on narcissistic and is obsessed with the appearance of herself and others.
In addition to their own lore page explaining the legends of their respective gods, there are many different ways to play a single god. Using item purchased from the store (with in-game money that is gained over the course of the game, not microtransactions) you can change a damage mage to a tankier one or a tankier guardian to a one-shot mage. It's up to you to read guides on how to effectively 'build' a select God.
Now that that's out of the way, I'll cover some important points for new players:
*Communicate - Practice the VGS system or use Curse Voice to communicate quickly and effectively.
*Stay in Position - 99999% of deaths happen when the mage wanders too far and gets assassinated or when the guardian tries to chase a kill he can't confirm, leaving his team defenseless. If your struggling, just follow 'Tanks in the Front, Squishies in the back'.
*Prioritise targerts - Don't waste all your mana and abilities onto a guardian who'll just laugh right back; instead, focus on players with less health or who are out of position. It can be difficult to keep the above point and this one, but you'll get the hang of it in time.
*Don't be afraid to ask for help.
*DON'T RAGE QUIT FOR F*** SAKE (*^v^)*
*The last, and most important point for new players, is be aware of your surroundings. There is a class called assassins that specialise in getting kills. Avoidong death will take time and patience, and you will need to learn the warning signs. Loki, for example, can go invisble for a short time but his abilities are louder than most. Thanatos has an 'execute' ability, whice will kill you if your health is below a %threshold and provided he doesn't miss.The list goes on, and isn't limited to assassins, but being aware is the best way to stay alive (uwu).
TLDR; Game good, game free, game fun, game fresh, game kawaii (*^v^)*

Wow...This was an absolutely amazing game. I was a big fan of the first and this was really just the perfect extension of it. The graphics were just gorgeous, the enviroments unique, the level design phenominal, the game play tons of fun. The adding of the bonecharm crafting and new powers for Emily was really cool, although it did take me a moment to adjust to. Learning the controls and crafting system in a new game is never my favorite part but this wasn't bad, especially since most of it is the same as the first game.
I just finished my first play through playing as Emily with Low Chaos.
When I first started I had just played the first game and it's DLC's 3 times through back to back so I had a few gripes as I adjusted to the new add on's. Namely Emily's Blink has a slight arch to it which for some reason bothered me, as well as Dark Vision having a slightly different color scheme that makes it a little more difficult to see items, which once into the game I think works better as it makes it a little less of a breeze to get through. I ended up waiting a month or two and finished some other games and once I picked this back up it just felt like Dishonored should.
The characters are all great, and the Dishonored trademark of rambling silly lines is still there which I love.  Emily kind of reminds me of the girl in Alien:Isolation. Tough clever woman looking to save her parent. I saw some hate in other reviews about her not having enough depth which I thought was silly considering in the first game you literally don't speak a word or ever even see your face until the end, you basically know you are an assisin, foreign and well respected...
I find with games the enviroment is more important for me to get into the world, the character is just a vessel for my own mind to experience this world and scenario, especially in first person games where your decisions have consequence.
That said Dishonored 2 really expands on the amazing world they have created. I love the juxtaposition of the metaphysical magical world interwoven with the heavily industrial sort of mechanical high/low tech world.
Bottom Line: If you loved the first ones you should love this one as well. I would recommend a decompression period so you don't get hyper judgemental of the slightest detail. It's a new game and a great successor to the last.

The Fruit Of Grisaia is a really long visual novel with 5 different routes with 1 common route
with 10 different ending ( 5 good ending and 5 bad ending ).
The Story : as always visual novels tends to have a great storyline ( unless its a fanservice game... ).
The fruit of grisaia is one of those visual novels with a great amout of detail to the story, the story follows one protagonist  his name is Kazami Yuuji, in which you pick a route ( in other words a girl from the 5 optional ) to follow her story and tragic past that might sometimes have connection to the player ( it can be related to the past of the protagonist or being related to his "job" ). In the end you must together with main heroine ( of your choosing ) overcome the hardships of traumatic pasts and find a solution.
All I can say that every route has a very detailed story and can be very emotional ( depends on which type of peson you are ). All of the characters are well developed and you will come to care for all of them ( of course there will be one special character which will be your favorite in which I would suggest to do her route last ).
Gameplay : Mostly you are gonna read... alot, no joke here I spent 100+ hours on reading every route and every ending ( of course I did a mistake with the common route so the time to actually be needed to read will be for 70+ ).
There will be only 5 choices in every route ( actually 3 of them are common route the other 2 are in which you chose a girl and which ending you will get ). So in other words only those who love visual novels will enjoy this.
Sound : Amazing simply amazing. from the voice acting to the soundtracks and even to the sound effects everything was simply perfect, indeed added the right atmosphere from funny,happy,amusing,sad,anger,horror everything was simply perfect in that retrospect.
Bugs : none to be had... seriously its hard to do those in those kind of games
Graphics : Those who like anime style will like the graphics here even though its just a couple of pictures and maybe a few animations.
Summary : This game is simply like a book, amazing characters, great atmosphere, brilliant storytelling, and of course a great deal of time will be spent so its well worth the money.
I can't spoil to much if you want to enjoy so I can't add to much detail to the plot ( and since the game is all about the plot I can't add anymore information ). But I will suggest to all of you do to the following routes in this order :
Michiru > Yumiko > Sachi > Makina > Amane ( this is how I did the routes ) of course as I wrote before I would suggest to do your favorite girl as the last route ( and since Amane was mine favorite I did her route last )
Overall I'll give this game a 9\10 ( Only because I didn't cried from every route )

I'm going to start off by saying that I have always hated Visual Novels. Keep this in mind as you read my review. This is going to be as spoiler free as I can make it.
The Fruit of Grisaia (Grisaia no Kajitsu) is more or less a picture book about a battle-hardened child soldier attempting to return to a normal life. I'm sure most people are thinking the same thing I was, "If I wanted to spend $30 on a book, I'd want a physical copy and it better be good." Well, while the former isn't possible, the latter is completely true. VN games always turned me off, before; lack of action, lack of many choices, pure focus on story, lots of reasons that I'm sure many people share. Despite all the reasons for not wanting this game, I found myself returning to the store page every now and then. I finally managed to grab it for around $12, and I feel like I ripped off the developer. This game is well worth the full price, and probably over. Just about every character, no matter how minor a part they play, has a personality. You either hate a character, like a character, or love a character - and not always for good reasons. The 5 classmates - Yumiko, Makina, Amane, Sachi, and Michiru - are all perfectly unique. There's almost no "copy/paste" idea present. The interactions between characters seem extremely natural, as well. I refrained from writing a review until I had finished every route the game had(other than the bad routes), and I found it harder and harder to do that as I progressed. Despite the circumstances of each of the characters, you can relate to every single one of them. I often found myself caught off guard when a character said "Yuuji", because I was so engrossed in the story that I had actually assumed the role of the main character. The replay value is pretty decent, as well. I'd love to travel through this story once more. The scenes often invoke emotions you can't imagine; I laughed at the most ridiculous things, I cried when things happened, I even felt myself worrying about the characters. By playing through the dating routes, I realized a common theme is that none of the bad stuff would've happened if Yuuji(you) hadn't showed up or made the choice to interfere. That caused a feeling of hopelessness and self-doubt in me, as well. That being said, I highly recommend playing through every girl's route. You learn more about not only the girls, but Yuuji as well. As you learn more about the circumstances for each girl being there, you learn about Yuuji's own past; a past he keeps hidden away. If you don't find the emotional aspect convincing enough, this game teaches practical knowledge, as well. I learned self-defense techniques, how to deal with women, and survival and cooking skills, to name a few. I can't remember the last time I learned something I could use in everyday life from a video game, aside from a profound lesson on human nature or a phylisophical idea. I'm currently letting my little brother play through himself, and he is the typical "COD AKSHUN POW POW GUN FIRE GIT GUD SKRUB" gamer. He loves it so much I had to threaten to take the computer away in order to write this review. I also plan on buying a couple copies for my close friends, and sharing this experience with them. I have fallen in love with this game, and it has sparked an interest within me for other VN's. If you see a Visual Novel in my library, it's because of Fruit of Grisaia.
TL;DR: 10/10 Would buy full price. Get this game. Even if you hate VN's.

Grisaia no Kajitsu is a well rounded, quality vn with good art, good ost and likable characters. The vn is the first of three popular visual novels in Japan that are planned to be brought to the west. My playthrough including every ending took me 60 hours with me reading at a fairly leisurely pace, so there is a fair amount of content to keep you satisfied. Unfortunately, as you can expect, sex scenes were cut for the steam release but there is an uncensored version and I'm sure you can figure out how to read the vn uncensored if you care about it enough to, I personally found it great even without them.
The main cast of girls have a good spread of personalities, each with a bit more depth than it might first appear.
In the most basic terms, there is a fun loving imouto type character, a caring if lecherous onee-san type, a maid who obeys any request, a borderline shut in who might be a bit on the paranoid side and a genius comperable to Cirno who tries her best to be a tsundere. The mc and side characters are also good, and help keep every hour you are reading enjoyable even during early segments that build atmosphere and character relationships through slice of life.
While Grisaia is mostly slice of life every main girl has a hefty load of problems that they will have to deal with in their route and some of it can get fairly dicey. The vn has a great balance of serious tone and enjoyable every day life to it that can make you very attached to the characters and involved in what happens to them later on in the vn.
TLDR: If you are looking for a vn on steam, you can be sure that Grisaia is probably some of the best steam has to offer. It is a little pricy for some, but if you can catch it on sale I would definately reccomend buying it if you are interested.

I bought this on a whim and it's worth it.  For those who are wanting to know if it's like Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines...I hesitate to say yes, but it might scratch that same itch.

There's also a surprising amount of voice acting in the game, every character is fully voiced.
The combat is a bit clunky and awkward, but still fun.  Besides a weapon and flashlight you will get some skills at the start, and can get quite a few more over time as you level up.  There are also skills used for things outside of combat, such as finding secrets (and there are a lot of secrets for those who enjoy hunting for that sort of thing).
As you encounter more NPCs and enemies, and do more quests, you can gain influence with various clans.  The dialogue with NPCs is pretty decent, and you'll get some different options if you spec into the right stats too.
The game is rough around the edges, but seems to be a hidden gem and I've enjoyed every minute of it so far.

Okay, I am going to change my review of this game after spending nearly 15 hours playing it so far.
Bloodlust Shodowhunter is the sort of game that took be back to my High School years of gathering around a Game Table with a Handful of 10 sided dice a few scraps of paper and a whole lot of Coke Cola. The Event was playing a Vampire themed Role Playing Game where you the player where the monster trying hard to either keep what was little left of their humanity or to simply watch the world burn around them.
My friends and I would spend hours at the Comic Book store rolling and debating as we strugled to keep each other from our final deaths while a mad but dethroned ruler was trying to start the god machine. A plot that had been in the works for at least a few hundred years if not thousands. Our storyteller (Game Master) was a really great creative writer in our school and had a fresh and lively story that spanned a couple of years of actual game play time twice a week.
Despite all the rough edges and some time janky audio and animations. I am transported back to those after school game sessions I had played in as a young man.
Anyone who knows me knows a certain saying I have about video games and the Indie Game movement.
"You could have the worst graphics and audio in the world but so long as you have a kick♥♥♥♥♥story, I love it..."
when I recently bought this game in early access, this saying I have was tested. Sadly I gave a knee jerk review after only an hour or so of game play. And shamefully I forgot my standing on what truly matters to me in a game.
This game is Early Access, it has a few flaws that are hard to miss at time. The Graphics are not Triple A quality, nor should they ever be expected to be.
The Story however, That is the real gem here. and I have to hand it to the guy, it is one awesome story.
The game starts with the player waking up after the embrace (Turned into a Vampire) with out the slightest idea what happened to them or why they are a vampire. Worse yet they don't even know how to be a vampire in this strange new world they find them selves in.
Quickly the story get rolling in the discover what going on as you move along sort of way. This includes discovering how to be a vampire alone with no Sire to guide you in you first steps into the night.
The Scenery and Locations are actually really interesting despite their repetitive issues. A lot of this game seems to be made up of a few key 3D mesh parts and a bit of texture work along with tweaked stock UDK parts every now and then. I could be wrong about the UDK stock parts however.
This game uses UDK (a stripped down version of Unreal Engine 3 for indie studios and students) as it's base engine. One I was once a very proud fanboy of until I recently migrated to Unity. I know a few of the challenges this guy must have had to account for. It's still a good engine to use and it can crank out some awesome games in the right hands. Hands like WRF Studio which is apparently Just one Guy with the Help of like two or three others in this games case.
The Diablo like dungeon crawling aspect is fun and while a bit repetitive, keeps my vampire always growing in power as I slowly build up my bloodline. This is the sort of Character level Metric as well as the state of my ever growing family of vampire minions. My pet Hobo and I are rocking these dungeon maps while the rest are out collecting loot for me to make use of in the game.
The interface is much like that of an MMO or again Diablo action bar with a few skills at my fingertips. This allows for me to quickly fire off power my vampire has discovered When he needs to use them.
Power as mentioned above are fairly strait forward. While there are clans in the game, You as a new vampire are actually not a member of any one clan and thus are not pigeon holed into a Clan set of skills and powers. As you progress and earn rep with the other clans int he game, certain power will open up to you that you can put a few points into. It's a lot more free form then a certain Vampire Themed computer game based on the table top game I loved as a young man.
All and all I really love this game and it the sort of love that had to be hard earned but now is never going to be let go.
I am still going to highly recommend this game to anyone who wants a great You are the Monster Vampire experience.
To people who are debating to give this game a try:
DO NOT PASS THIS ONE UP...
To the Developer:
DO NOT RUSH THE GAME TO RELEASE!
Keep crafting and polishing this gem for as long as it is needed.

It had a rough launch but I can say as it stands now it's a great achievement and a worthy addition to the Total War franchise. Sure, it has its problems, like any game with such grand scope, but choose to overlook the issues and be absorbed in to the broader experience and it's still one of the best strategy games money can buy.
As with any of the Total War games the attraction is in forging your empire through turn based strategy and watching battles come to life in real time tactical combat with thousands of units at your command. Follow objectives to loosely play out history or break the mold and make your own history, the beauty of any open world game is freedom to play how you want.
The Roman empire is a fasinating period and the world map will have you fighting naked barbarians in the frozen forests of northern Europe one day and chariots in the desserts of Egypt the next. Although I loved Shogun 2 (and it is the better of the two), I really enjoy the cultural and geographic variety that comes with Rome II.
My final note is that you will want a fairly powerful video card and system to run this game. If your video card is getting long in the tooth, then you will probably be better off with one of the earlier games in the series. I'm playing with a GTX 970 and it's great but many complaints are from people with older systems who expected the game to run better than it did on their PC's.

Good Game!

To sum it up in a single sentence: It's basically a stand-alone expansion for Dishonored 1.
Story beings with Emily all grown up and following in the footsteps of her mother. Of course, a new foe arises and you must pick either Corvo, the not-so-mute-anymore protagonist from Dishonored 1, or Emily, the new cat in town, to hunt down all the lieutenants before going for the top dog (or b!tch). It feels like a really short campaign, even thought it's roughly the same length as D1, that is packed with tons of lore for the diehard fans but leaves other wanting for more than random notes and texts that furter describe the lore. I personally wished the villains to be more entertaining and have more personality but that's just personal opinion.
Instead of roaming the streets of Dunwall, you now roam the streets of Serkonos, an island south of Dunwall. The name has changed but the scenery is the same most of the time. And don't get me wrong, that's not necessarily a bad thing, the world of Dishonored is a beautiful and grim place, I just wished that level design wasn't the same "go through this part of town to reach te actual area where the target is".  The areas where targets are found are usually unique and interesting in their own way (palaces, museums, bunkers, etc) but the march towards them are through the same streets we've seen in Dunwall as well. It's a beatufiul world but with slightly overused environments.

If you loved Dishonored 1, you're going to enjoy this one as well. If you haven't played Dishonored 1, why are you here? Go play the first one, then return!
Same mechanics, same skills (for Corvo), same level design that lets you approach a target from different angles. On the plus side, you get Emily (that has some very nice new skills) and some gameplay features that seemed like they were left out from the first installment. The new equipment blends well with the already existing stuff and the new bonecharm creation mechanic works well (albeit a bit overpowered at some times, I could choke an enemy in half a second with one of the crafted bonecharms).
Gameplay styles are the same as D1 but feel more flexible overal with more options for your specific needs. For example, you now have a crossbow bolt that makes NPCs run away in terror, then forget why and return to their post. Perfect for clearing out a path. As a bonus, your style now analyzed at the end of each mission (stealth, combat, lethal, non-lethal) for statistic junkies.
Basically it's the same as before, albeit slightly improved. Everything looks really good and runs good as well (after several patches). Dishonored has this unique style that does not require realism. You either love the art or you hate it.
Sound-wise, nothing changed as well. Soundtrack fits nicely into the atmosphere. It's nice to have a voiced Corvo, even though the actor is not the best choice in my opinion. Or maybe it's the dull lines he has.
As much as I liked the game, I can't shake the feeling that it's a bit too short and low-effort for a triple-A price tag. Sure, it has some degree of replayability (play with the other character, go full stealth or full berserk, etc) but after seeing loads of reused assets, barely no new enemies, so on, so forth, I just feel like there wasn't enough love put in this game like the first one. Coupled with a catastrophic PC launch, I'm going to give it a "Good" stamp.
Buy it when it's on sale, 20$ is a fair price for this small gem.
