Playing stealthy and low chaos (less lethal) in immersive sims is usually my bag, though you could argue you're missing out on a lot of fun if you stick to the stealthy powers.

What I like about this game: In terms of player freedom, this game is excellent; even better than the original Dishonored. The game offers a myriad of tools and potential strategies with which to overcome each obstacle. At the end of the game, you learn how several of your independent choices impact the world, as opposed to a binary good/bad ending. There are plenty of new, creative twists to the gameplay, ranging from simple things like non-lethal drop takedowns to complex things like time travel. The bonecharm crafting system is pretty cool too. The dialogue is also improved in my opinion; normally I prefer silent protagonists, but Dishonored 2 actually does a really good job with its voiced protagonists. This game is well-written. Overall, this game feels more creative than its predecessor.
What I don't like about this game: The graphics are too demanding. I don't have a beastly gaming rig, but my hardware is respectable nonetheless. This is the first game I've played on this PC that I can't get to run smoothly and still look good. At low-medium settings the max I can get is 45 fps. That's not such a big deal, though; the game is still playable. What I REALLY don't like is that the gameplay feels a lot less fluid than in the original game. Way too often, I get stuck trying to crouch under a desk or climb up a ledge. There are a lot of rooftops and ledges that LOOK like you can climb on them, but are actually out-of-bounds, which can be frustrating. Emily's Far Reach power (her equivalent of Blink) feels clunky and it's unreasonably difficult to aim sometimes, especially if you're trying to Reach through a doorway or between two obstacles. Overall, the physics feels a little wonky; for example, I once set down an oil tank at my feet, and then when I turned and started walking, the tank went FLYING into the wall and exploded. It's also worth mentioning that Dishonored 2 has more bugs than I would have expected from a AAA game. I had to replay the first half of Mission 8
because of a bug that would have prevented me from getting Clean Hands.
Final Verdict: Dishonored 2 is worth playing, but make sure you save and check your stats often if you want Ghost or Clean Hands. This game would have benefited greatly from a little more quality assurance. As it is, it's not quite as fun as its predecessor, mainly because the gameplay and physics don't feel as smooth.

When I started seeing screenshots of this game years ago, I knew I had to experience the entirety of The Fruit of Grisaia.
After that, I watched the anime hoping to grasp clearly what the fuss was about. I enjoyed what I saw, but I felt like too much was missing from the original novel. I wanted more.
I came to this visual novel expecting a funny, lighthearted at times experience complemented with jokes that could make anyone laugh, but also deathly serious in some situations. I expected each character to just come across as another archetype in different circumstances.
Two endings in (Michiru and Yumiko), and I have realized how gravely I had underscored this novel.
From tackling powerful topics, such as depression and suicide, and giving each character a truly memorable personality, Grisaia no Kajitsu is without a doubt an experience unlike any other. The ways that each character embrace their "unusual" circumstances are worthy of earnest praise and commendation, and every victory and defeat that affects them affects the player just as much.
Some people will equate this game as simply another eroge in the market and will lament that this is "the censored shell of the original", but perhaps it is because of the removal of the h-scenes that allows one to appreciate the story behind those acts of affection. To simply read through this game to alleviate one's desires would be a massive disrespect to the true nature of this novel, in my opinion.
The Fruit of Grisaia is an experience like no other. Time and again, I have been truly awed by the thoughtfulness of the plot behind each route, and the execution of the plot to make almost every action feel unquestionably real (even though sometimes the "actions" done are beyond reality. Michiru for example comes to mind.)
If you want a game that has been claimed by many who have experienced it as "life-changing", then this is pretty much as good as it gets.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl is a first-person shooter survival horror video game developed by GSC Game World and published by THQ.
The game is set in an alternative reality, where a second nuclear disaster occurs at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant Exclusion Zone in the near future and causes strange changes in the area around it. The game has a non-linear storyline and features gameplay elements such as trading and two-way communication with NPCs. The game includes role-playing and first person shooter elements.
The background and some terminology of the game  is borrowed from the popular science fiction novella Roadside Picnic by Boris and Arkady Strugatsky and the 1979 Andrei Tarkovsky film Stalker that was loosely based on it, as well as Stalker, the film's subsequent novelization by the original authors. The term "Stalkers" was later used for the scientists and engineers who explored the interior of Chernobyl's "sarcophagus" after its hasty construction in 1986.
In S.T.A.L.K.E.R, the player assumes the identity of an amnesiac "Stalker", an illegal explorer/artifact scavenger in "The Zone", dubbed "The Marked One". "The Zone" is the location of an alternate reality version of the Zone of alienation surrounding the Chernobyl Power Plant after a second, fictitious meltdown, which further contaminated the surrounding area with radiation and caused strange otherworldly changes in local fauna, flora and the laws of physics. "Stalker" in the context of the film refers to the older meaning of the word as a tracker and hunter of game or guide.
On July 11, 2007, GSC Game World announced a prequel, S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Clear Sky, which was released on September 15, 2008. On April 30, 2009, GSC Game World announced a sequel, S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Call of Pripyat, which was released worldwide in February 2010.

The performance still isn't amazing, so I just left it on auto graphics settings and kept a stable 1080p 60fps with a GTX 970 (other than one level which involved going between two versions of a house, but that was so cool that I didn't mind). Dynamic resolution was on by default though, which I thought was a bit weird for a PC game. With the auto settings (mostly between medium and high, with a couple very high) it still looked nicer than the first Dishonored, especially with the nicer art style and views.
The game itself is amazing. My first run was Corvo, non-lethal, no detections, with powers. It felt like everything from the first Dishonored was made even better. Level design was great, and two of them had really cool mechanics that required you to think and change up your gameplay (especially if you're ghosting it). The powers and combat are even better than the first as well. I've started a loud, fight-everyone playthrough as Emily, and using the new powers (especially Domino, which I love) is pretty awesome.
Even with the performance issues, this game is great. At the time of writing this, I have 31 hours in. I reckon about 27ish of those would have been from my first playthrough. That was about as long as I could have spent on it (non-lethal, no detections, and collecting every rune and bonecharm, and completely replaying a level because I thought of another way I wanted to finish it), but I'm still planning on immediately replaying it as Emily, and maybe doing a third no-powers run after that.
There's also a new game+ mode, which is cool but kind of feels overpowered. You get to keep all your runes from the previous game (about 55 for me), all bonecharm traits that you've unlocked (I think), and can use both Corvo and Emily's power sets. Bend Time + Domino makes combat pretty easy, but it's still fun (and you could just not use the extra powers).

I genuinely try to be less hard on free-to-play games, but it really says something when after 3 minutes I was already wishing for a button command to have my character wrap his lips around the barrel of his gun and pull the trigger, hopefully hitting a bird that happens to fly by.
I appreciate a game that tries to be realistic. But if I've learned one thing, too much much realism can have a nasty effect on fun. Ya know, that thing that games are supposed to be. I think it's cool that a game tries to give that slow, methodical approach to taking down animals. It takes skill and effort and I got nothing against that. But after about 15 minutes of very slowly skulking through the forest (your only other speed is so slow it feels like your character's legs are broken and they're still trying to walk on them) I finally find my first elk and I of course try to shoot it, only for the game to give a notification saying I don't have the license to hunt that animal. That's like having a driving game where you have to gas up every 200 miles and clean your windshields. I suppose some people may find that enduring. I find it sleep inducing.
If this is meant to be the most realistic hunting game ever, then that probably explains why I've always had the subconcious desire to never do it. If you're a stickler for realism then you'll probably like this, I suppose. Personally, I'll stick to fighting in giant mechs on the moon.
Edit: Okay, I didn't know that more of the game opens up when you pay actual money. Well, not to hop on the bandwagon, but that's even less incentive. I know free games have to make a little money from services, but you can't advertise as free and then lock out the majority of the content unless you pay. That's not a game, that's a demo.

Singleplayer review
Homeworld, first released in 1999 and developed by Relic Entertainment, is a science fiction real-time strategy game. This was their first breakout success and was met with critical acclaim and successful sales, which lead to a sequel. In 2015, Gearbox decided it was time Homeworld became accessible to a modern audience. Working with most of the original development team, they painstakingly remastered the two original games. Their time and effort really paid off with this beautiful and lovingly crafted remake.
Plot
For a Space RTS one would expect the story to be a bit one-note. Thankfully that isn’t the case with Homeworld, as the story is one of almost movie quality. It begins 100 years in the past. The world you live on is a harsh desert world, with its people split into warring tribes and factions. One day a crashed spaceship is discovered in the desert. Inside this spaceship, a stone table is found. The only two things on it are a map to a planet and the word "Hiigara" — home. The discovery of this tablet proves that the people are not as alone in the galaxy as they thought and this unites the factions. Jump forward 100 years and you start the game at the grand launch of the "Mothership". Thanks to what was learned from the crashed spaceship, this is the first ship capable of traveling at hyperspeed. What starts of as a routine test of the Mothership’s hyperspeed engine quickly turns into an ambush by an unknown enemy. To say any more about the story would lessen the impact it would have for new players. So the main mission is to overcome many perils and to guide your people to the lost homeworld of "Hiligara"
Gameplay
Homeworld doesn't really break the RTS mold, as the main focus is still on gathering resources, building a fleet and using it to destroy enemy ships to complete objectives. The one thing Homeworld does differently is the movement of ships. Because Homeworld is set in space, ships can move not only forwards, backwards, left and right, but can also travel upwards and downwards. This adds a whole extra dimension to fighting. You are not limited to a flat plain, but can use height for tactical advantage or even retreat to escape enemies. With this you have two view modes in which to control your fleet: Standard mode, which is the standard view mode with which you can select ships or watch battles or Tactical mode, which gives you extra details on where your ships are heading and gives a much easier representation and understanding on what height your ships are at compared to enemy ships. This mode is mainly used for precise movement of ships through the battlefield.
Level and game design
The campaign for Homeworld 1 is broken up into 16 levels, with Homeworld 2 being structured very much the same way. The player starts out with an objective and then must accomplish this objective before they can proceed to the next. In between each level is a voice acted black and white animated cutscene, which acts as narrative progression. While common today, it was a very unique way of telling a story back in the days before 3D rendered cutscenes. The look and feel of the game goes without saying. Anyone, who has played a Relic RTS in the past, can expect the same smooth and responsive unit control and well detailed vehicle models. The game is full of beautiful backdrops of various parts of space, from moons to bright and vibrant suns, they really set the mood and feel of the game. To also accompany that is the amazing soundtrack that just helps add so much atmosphere and wonder to the whole story. The use of orchestral instruments and choirs during the beginning of the game just gives such a sense wonder and vastness, which fits the fact that your people have to travel the vast void of space in search of a home. But as the game goes on the tranquil music turns to strange tense hunting music, drums and alarms to really put you on your toes, knowing that the enemy is everywhere trying to hunt you down. Sci Fis of the time, such as Battlestar Galactica, obviously had a huge influence over the soundtrack.
If any complaints have to be made, then it can be said that the movement system can be a bit tricky. Due to the 3D movement of ships, it can take a while to understand and get used to at first, as it isn’t very intuitive. That being said, there's a tutorial at the beginning of the game. Another minor gripe is the steep difficulty curve. Some missions are a walk in the park with others being extremely tough. It does help to make the levels very rewarding to beat though.
In conclusion, Homeworld Remastered is a very solid and complete package. This is a perfect example of what a remaster should be, not only including the original unedited non-remastered versions of the games, but also reworking everything from adding a new game engine, re-recording voice lines by the original voice actors and a fully remastered score. Relic has outdone themselves by putting so much love and care into this re-telling of an amazing story. With two games and multiplayer modes for each, Homeworld is sure to keep players occupied for hours on end!

Played the Non-Steam & Xbox versions, and I can say it's a good game to get away from LOL or DOTA with, fun with friends and isn't so uptight as either of the two. It's a slightly more streamlined experience, less complicated character/item stats, and simply easier and funner to enjoy in most cases. The all-too famous toxicity 80% of the players on both games becomes too much sometimes, and the SMITE community is 110% more friendly.
That being said, there's a downside to it being so noob/experience friendly. The game is simply filled with too much of a varying playerbase; "casuals", who take the game for what it is, a game, "gamer kids", the kids who simply play it cause it's FTP and neither have the capacity or just the interest in their performance than just having fun (There is no problem with that, just stating one of the majority groups), "League-ers/DOTA-ers", people who come from League and DOTA for a change of pace, with slightly more skill/ambition to do well in a game,  and finally, the "tryhards", the people who play SMITE to the best of their abilities and are far better in experience compared to the other groups of players.
I have no complaints to any of those cliches or player groups, the only problem is that there is little to no matchmaking criteria that seperates them, by current skill or experience, and at most times are just thrown together in a game of chance. It's purely a roll of the dice to get teamates you'll have synergy with or not. And considering that this game requires more cooperation/player interaction rather than someone carrying most of the game due to farming not being as impactful, all it takes is 1 player to be far from the average skill level on either side of the spectrum to impact the game/make it possible/impossible to win.
It's a fun game with friends, but hard on people who expect a balanced experience when paired with so many differing player skill levels.

As everyone has already said, the game is rough, outdated in both it's looks and controls, but ambitious.  As also stated, this is a game very much in the same feel as VtM Bloodlines though the story seems a bit fragmented in the early access version.  The controls are a bit awkward but can be gotten used to--and used well.  The general instructions are a bit vague in places but nothing you can't figure out with a bit of exploration.
As of the early access version, there are several instances of the story not making sense if you happen to meet certain characters during your free-roaming exploration as opposed to because someone told you to go there.  (Stuff like going into an area and finding someone who says they've been expecting you and to thank you for your help with a person you haven't actually met or helped yet...or stumbling across a character and begin with dialogue about how you need their help with something and you don't know who they are or why you need to go to them for help)  So, at this point, don't count on the story blowing your mind.
But all of this is minor and not even remotely worth counting against a really great game.  My only real negative on the game is the auto-save.  It saves after every little thing you do and you can't have multiple save spots.  I know this is to make the decisions mean more (as once you make it, you've made it), BUT here's the thing not considered.....
This game is also a dungeon crawler.  That means, if you screw up a decision and want to start a new character to fix the decision, it's not just a matter of playing some fun and enjoyable story over again....it's HOURS of wandering randomly generated dungeons to catch back up to where you were.

Bloodlust Shadowhunter is a surprisingly enjoyable gem of a game.  It can easily cater to Vampire masquerade, Diablo and Heretic/Hexen fans. The skill tree is extensive, the puzzles are fun, although not overly challenging, and the loot - ah, the loot is glorious. Finding that first purple item while crawling through the dungeon as a mere level (bloodline) 3 fledgling will  bring about an immense sense of satisfaction and will leave you wanting to find more, to delve deeper, to explore further.  I had not had a chance to fully explore the city, but the dungeon is rumored to have more than 200+ levels which can definitely take quite a few hours, if not days, to clear.
As this is still Early Access minor graphic glitches can be forgiven. So far I have not experienced any crashes, and reloading the game fixed any graphic stuttering that I encountered twice.
For the price of $12.99 I would highly recommend this game as it shows a lot of promise and with some polish can turn into a new cult classic.  It is not yet on par with VtMB, but it's closer to it than any other current vampire-themed games.

I've been having an actual blast with this of late, it's a thoroughly enjoyable - if rough around the edges - action RPG with some dark "World of Darkness" vampire leanings, but please don't expect something this is not; it ISN'T the next Vampire Bloodlines. It has more in common with Vampire Masquerade if anything, but at its heart it's very much a dungeon-crawler with some overworld questing, which leads to more dungeons :)
*The visuals are workable, they're not going to wow Crysis-lovers, but they're also not eye-gougingly bad, they're completely serviceable and they fit the atmosphere quite nicely.
*Audio is great, decent voice acting and suitably dark ambient audio.
*Loot. Loot. Loot and more LOOT! That is the crux of the game, the bread and butter, the alpha and omega.. you play this like any other aRPG; to get moar loot! Rings, gloves, boots, weapons, armour, helms, even facial attachments like masks, glasses and piercings. There are lots of quests to undertake, though a lot of them are "go here, collect this, come back" style, they're basically just reasons to reenter the dungeons and find more loot!
All in all, I've put 16 hours into this so far and I'm really enjoying it. The developers have been *fantastic* at responding to bug reports and fixing them. I have high hopes for this in Early Access :)

To start, if you like Bloodlines then you want to support this as it is by far the best spiritual successor to date.  That said... it has some issues that hopefully some funding will help fix.  Also, I've only played to just beyond the started area and the main street is rather empty, but seems like the start of a decent hub of activity.  There is a story, but I have yet to figure out if it's as detailed as Bloodlines.  I have yet to find out if/how many side stories there are, like the dozens that Bloodlines had.
Pros:
It has clan based vampires like Bloodlines
It has skill customization like Bloodlines
Randomized (?) dungeons, unlike Bloodlines
Massive amounts of loot, Diablo style, unlike Bloodlines
It has a very similar atmosphere to Bloodlines
Neutral:
The voice acting is decent, but not great.  Some good, some bad, like Bloodlines.
Combat is on par with Bloodlines and could use some work, but skills are interesting
Cons:
The graphics are on par (flat textures and dated models) with Bloodlines
The non-randomized level design is worse than Bloodlines
The "world" maps where you would interact with bystanders is far smaller than Bloodlines and so fewer to interact with
The UI could use some work and is worse than Bloodlines
The devs left in the default "Built with UDK" icon and task description, unlike Bloodlines
It's not even close to a finished product.  If you didn't like Bloodlines then you won't like this.  So much potential but failing so hard on the lack of polish.  It's still early access and I'm probably hoping for more than will be delivered, but it drives a stake through a fond spot in my heart.
The dungeon crawling aspect may or may not end up being core to whatever form this game takes, but it was one of the main things that drew me in.  The game is not balanced, the dungeon is tedious at points, but it is a great start and something Bloodlines didn't have.  (Yes, I had to fit that in.)  This game is not in beta.  It is most definitely still in alpha, but if you go in understanding that it's a good few hours diversion and I recommend it.

Great game.  Beautiful graphics, better combat than either predecessor, a larger world, and just an overall fun and at times very difficult experience.  I'm with the people that think Dark Souls 1 is better in many ways, especially the interlinking Metroidvainia style level design and overall atmosphere.  But this game has its strong points as well and is not to be missed.  Combat feels more true and the graphics are smoother especially when comparing each game's PC version.
If you've never played Demons Souls it is also better in certain ways than either Dark Souls game.  In fact it is still the most memorable experience I've had in a game in adulthood hands down and I will certainly play through it again which is something I cant say about Dark Souls 2 (I've played DKS2 for 195 hours so maybe thats why I'm over it). Factorio is a very clever look at the pro's and con's of logistics management, mass-production, industrialization, exploitation of natural resources, and Windowed Mode for games. You Factorio vets know what I'm talking about on that last one.
The reason why Factorio is so great as a strategy/puzzle game is that it's basically logistics engineering distilled to perfection and made into a game. While this means that your Factorio skill is only limited by your logic and visual thinking skills, there is one issue: The game has progression balanaced to a t, but there comes a time in every game (it's different for everyone for how many times it happens and how long it takes) when you are severely limited by your machines, or worse, your own sense of scope. These periods consist of listening to music and podcasts in another window while the game solves itself, with little else to do but build another assembly line. If you want to conserve your resources, you will get just a bit less out of the game, since it is really balanced for a perpetual "suicide burning" in terms of resource gathering. I am not a fast man when it comes to limited resources and a need to use them, and this left me with a lot to do, since taking more from the iron mines might leave me high and dry in a few hours time. So I spend most of my time waiting for research to finish so that I can build something else without being redundant, as I start another research project and find a new podcast.
Not to say that the game isn't still fun. Those "Eureka!" moments far make up for the "I'm not playing the game" realizations, and I know that my own underambition is the cause of most of my problems. There is still an infinite joy from setting out to perform an odd task and actually doing it, time and time again, wether it be creating a backup power supply off-site, or simply finding an excuse to use trains since you only need to transport massive resources long-distance if you've turned the "resource vein commonness" to minimum.
Factorio is possibly the best example of a management game in years, forwards or backwards. Progress is only limited to how much you're willing to do to get it, and unless you're a damn turtle (like me), the game never goes faster than you can handle, AND EVEN THEN, there is an option in world generation just for you slowpokes (mostly me)! The actual scope of the game is spot-on, with lots of actual game being locked off until you've done the right research, but never enough that you don't have something you could be doing already. You probably unlock Oil right before you run out of solid material to manage at home, and Trains right before you start needing to take resources from far away, and so on, with the only real issue being the amount of late-game filler tech, which serves only to build up to the actual prizes of technology without helping Jack off a horse.
Right now, the game is in Early Access, but if you think you'd enjoy a logistics-based engineering strategy/puzzler, you will fall in love with Factorio. The game is already basically a finished product, with more singleplayer story and some extra multiplayer features being the only addition I've even heard the devs say that they want in Factorio. The framework is already there, with polishes and outer walls done, too. The only thing needed is... whatever we get. If the game left Early Access any day since I wrote this, you probably wouldn't be able to tell, it's basically done already.
Fantastic way to burn all kinds of time. It's getting a bit stale now that I'm in late game, but considering the 40+ active hours of playtime, it's been a great purchase thus far.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R. SoC is a fantastic game, undoubtedly the most atmospheric game I've ever played, the level of immersion is absurd. You play as a Stalker, seeking wealth from the sale of artefacts found in the surrounding area of Chernobyl, however, the "Zone" is not a friendly place and danger throughout the game is constant.
The gameplay is great, although a little rough at first sight, you need to play at a more measured pace, as I said, the Zone is dangerous, there are many enemies, from bandits and mercenaries, through military and enemy factions of stalkers, plus mutants and environment traps known as anomalies which can kill you instantly. The AI is very good and challenging, which uses efficient combat tactics. There are a wide variety of items, artefacts, weapons and ammunition necessary for progression. The game is graphically outdated but there are mods that greatly improve the look, the setting in the game is a strong point, combined with great sound effects which contribute a lot to the immersion factor, tension is inevitable in some places as enemies camps and underground laboratories.
The plot is solid, despite being basically a shooter, there are RPG elements such as multiple endings which depend on your posture during the game, there are factions that you can be friendly, enemy or neutral, depending on your attitudes and choices. The game has a great replay value.
One negative point are the side missions, they are shallow and poorly drawn up, become repetitive with time, which discouraged me to continue making them. The base game is known to have some bugs, by recommendations I played with the Complete 2009 mod, which fixes those bugs, improves graphics, AI, sounds, among other things.
At the end, S.T.A.L.K.E.R. is a unique game, I couldn't recommend it more.

It's free. Freeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee. Completely and truly freeeeeeeeeee. That fact alone gives no excuse to not try this game out.
Realistic zombies (they look lonely, give one a hug :3). Realistic jumping (bunny hop). Realistic fatigue (nooo no no no nononono pick your arms up pickyourarmsup hit him hit him HIT HIM!). Not-so-realistic arrow flight paths (completely straight at any range? no drop? wut.)
Right off the bat, anyone will notice that this game has a particularly high difficulty curve. Pretty much gotta hit the ground running with this one. It's a good idea to look up all the controls, items, effects, and statuses BEFORE playing it. Check out the wiki while downloading it, but be prepared for a LOT of reading.
"But isn't there a tutorial?" Not an in-game one. In fact, what pops up these days is a link to the wiki! When I first started, I didn't know what the hell I was doing (didn't have the link back then). I got killed within 5-10 minutes EVERY FREAKIN' TIME! Then I got mad, looked up what I was doing wrong, said,"Ohhhh...", then I went and completed my first objective map. xD
This ain't Left 4 Dead. It's not fast paced, the zombies are VERY strong, you are VERY weak, and runners are your WORST nightmare. That said, it's still VERY fun, just like L4D. Just fun in a different way. :)
Pros:

+Plenty of adrenaline when you know you could die to pack of runners every time you turn a corner
+High difficulty curve keeps many of the "12 year olds" away (I run into one every now and again, though)
+Realistic gameplay
+FREE
+Head popping (fits in with realistic gameplay, but deserves a plus on its own :)
Cons:
-High difficulty curve (You gun git rekt.)
-ADS!!!!! It's a free game. The developers rely on ads and donations ( :( there's never enough) The ads can be VERY annoying
Q&A:
Q: Worth it?
A: Duh, it's free. I know what you mean, though. "Is it worth my time?" HELL YEAH, come on in, newcomer!
Q: Difficult? How difficult?
A: Refer to Con #1.
Q: Zombies, right? I can just shoot 'em, right?
A: Sure, if you have a gun, can find ammo for it, and are a good enough shot to pop 'em in the head.
Q: So you said I gotta look up everything about this before playing it... Ain't nobody got you know whatever.
A: Trust me, you're gonna be hurtin' if you don't. There's no real story or spoilers or anything like that, so it's a very good idea to run yourself through the basics.
Q: No story? What's the point, then? I mean, even L4D had some slight plot it followed.
A: True, but once again, this ain't L4D. The point is survival against very bad odds by yourself or with your fellow survivors. The high difficulty makes success feel oh so good.
Try this game out for about a week. Takes about 3 days to get used to it, I think. Still don't like it? Hey, it's free. No harm done. Purty sure it'll grow on y'all, though. :)
Good luck!
P.S.: In the event of infection, please refer to Wheaton's Law. Blatant teamkilling isn't funny when about 3 minutes later one realises they could've used the extra help.

No More Room In Hell is one of the greatest zombie games i have played. The fact that this game is also 100% free to play is simply amazing. The devs have somthing truly special here. I have over 100 hours put into this game, and im still not bored with it. So with that said lets get into the full fledged Review.
-=Gameplay=-
No More Room In Hell is a slow paced realistic zombie survival horror game. I see it as them taking, and i hate to compare it to, CoD zombies. But its more realistic, and slower paced. Theres two types of gamemodes here, Objective and Survival. Survival is your typical Wave mode. The first round you spend trying to find weapons and tools to help you out. But when the second wave hits and theres little fast kid zombies, look out. Thats when it really begins.
Objective mode is a nice objective based team mode. You must work with your team to solve simple tasks to help get to the end. Its my preifred mode of choice. The objectives also are not always in the same order and can be random, adding re-playability to it.
Both modes have their own unique maps, so dont expect to play Flooded with objectives.
Now as i mentioned earlier, NMRIH is realistic, hitting the body doesnt deal much of any damage. In order to kill the dead you must aim for the head. And NMRIH features plenty of weapons to get the job done. Ranging from your melee weapons like the classic baseball bat, to guns like M1911. Theres a great varity of weapons to find and each gun uses a specific set of ammo you must find. This game also is a great team game. Theres no way you will be able to go lone wolf and expect to do well. And even if you do your not gonna be all hot♥♥♥♥♥♥ This game is all about working with your team, and in Wave modes that the only way you will make it to the end.
Theres so much more i can cover but i must say, the gameplay is solid.
~5/5~
-=Graphics=-
I like to think graphics dont make a game, it complements it. And the graphics here arent anything amazing, and thats why i love it. The graphics may not be the greatest around but they look quite nice. NMRIH runs off the HL2 engine so if you can run HL2 you can run this, and thats one of the reasons i love it. Having lower graphics helps keep the system requirements low, allowing more people to play. And with myself not having a super hot rig, im very happy with things.
Everything looks quite nice here and theres not much more i can say about it.
~4/5~
-=Sound=-
Holy freaking cow the sound track is amazing. Like seriously, its really really good. It fits the game so well. Keeping a dark scary and somtimes downright depressing feel. It works so wel for a zombie game like this. I couldnt ask for a better soundtrack. Huge huge props for that.
Not only is the soundtrack great but the rest of the sound it pretty good too. Everything from guns being fired, to heads being blown apart.
~5/5~
-=Community=-
Being a online game i must cover the community, and it like many other games has its fair share of trolls and annoying kids that really are not mature enough to play this game. Theres also plenty of Modded lobbys that feature god mode, gun menus, etc. It can make finding a decent server hard at times, but once you do your pretty much set. Now while it might seem as tho i think the community is a bit, meh, thats far from the truth. In reality i have met alot of awesome people, and 95% of my friends on my friends list is from people that i met playing this game. And thats pretty great.
~4/5~
-=Achievements=-
I love achievements in games, and this game is racked full of them. Everything from completing maps, to getting a certain amount of kills with a gun. Being that there is no story mode,the only way to truly beat the game is to get all the achievements.
~4/5~
-=Pay To Win Or Nah?=-
Being that this is a free game we must address if its P2W or not. And the answer, its not. This game is 100% free. Theres nothing in-game for you to buy either. Making this a true gem you have no excuse to not give a go. Its pretty amazing and hard to believe a game like this will cost you nothing, considering this game in many ways is better then alot of 60-120$ AAA games on the market today. And thats somthing special indeed.
~5/5~
-=Final Verdict=-
This game is one of my fav PC games on steam. Its truly amazing what the devs have done here. And with there being talk of a sequel, im pretty excited to see what they cook up next. This game has so much thats amazing, the fact its 100% free is nothing short of amazing. If your reading this, stop and download this game. It cant hurt to give it a go. you dont have anything to lose, just one hell of a ride to gain.
~5/5~ -=Legendary!=-

While Dishonored 2 fails at some parts, it succeeds in what matters. And when it clicks, the immersion is surreal. I’m eager for my second playthrough since it deserves to be played more than once. Dishonored 2, as with the original game, offers a fairly broad toolset. It is an excellent elaboration on what was already a great game.
I strongly encourage you to not limit yourself to one playstyle and don't be afraid to try out interesting combinations. I am telling you this only because I was so close to giving this game thumbs down. I finished both, Dishonored 1 and 2, on low chaos and got the ending that felt like an ending. Yet, choking foes got tedious and my desire to murder them increased. So, I started a second playthrough specifically for high chaos and it is subjectively more entertaining.
The PC version of Dishonored 2 has had a rocky launch. My experience with the game hasn't been a flawless one either, but I seem to have dodged the worst of it. Most of the issues seem to have been ironed out. Yet I occasionally encounter framerate jitters.
The liveliness in Dishonored 2’s world encourages you to explore, which is both rewarding due to the way interesting things are spread around the maps and also helpful in the sense that it facilitates to every type of play. You are an assassin, but there are always at least two ways to dispense of your final marks in Dishonored 2 - and one of those can only be unlocked through careful examination of clues scattered around the area.
You have plenty of non-lethal options, with more variety than probably any other stealth game I’ve played. But this positive quickly transfers to a negative for me since common enemies are incredibly receptive to the slightest of movement. They have an excellent peripheral vision and see extremely goddamned far. For me, as a stealth player, this meant a lot more saving and reloading than in just about any stealth game I've played in recent memory, especially when I was going for a no-kill, ghost playthroughs of missions. And while the satisfaction of overcoming particularly challenging sections was more pronounced in some ways, it felt like a bit of a buzzkill constantly going to the pause menu to use the quicksave feature. Since loading can sometimes be a bit too long, this took away from the overall experience. However, I started a second playthrough right after I finished the game, something rare for me. This time, I am going for a high chaos, guns-blazing playthrough. And I can say that it's definitely more satisfying than my prior experience. After reconfiguring my bone charm setup, the combat just feels exquisite.
I can't figure out why, but it’s hard to care about the story. Nothing will surprise you here. Yet, I was able to accept it as is. It's sufficient. If you have played the first game, you are probably familiar with the same dialogue guards you pass by use. While the game has definitely seen an improvement in this department, it still gets repetitive near the end of the campaign. As I talked in the initial section (The World Design), you get useful insight if you are ready to hunt for them.
The world looks fantastic with a mix of Very High and Medium settings. The art style is breathtaking and the soundtrack, while not exceptional, is delightful. Sadly, the voice acting feels off. This might be a heavily personal issue but I preferred the voice of the Outsider in the first game. The main protagonist(s) don't contribute either. They sometimes try to narrate what is happening on screen and miserably fail. This makes them look monotonous.

TLDR:  this game sucks, just like the first one sucked.

Boring and annoying.  The entirety of this game seems to be trying to find obscurely hidden runes.  Why care about whatever the story was, when you're constantly being prompted to bring up the heart and find moar runes!
At least that's all I experienced in the short time I played this crap, before quitting.

I really like this game.
From a technical point of view, it's pretty terrible. The graphics are really dated, the writing/script is generally bad, the characters are awkward (the player character's totally goofy flashlight pose almost turned me off from getting the game altogether), you use a flashlight despite being a nocturnal predator, the voice acting is painful most of the time, combat is awkward, and the equipment system makes you look utterly ridiculous (my PC is running around in a metal vest, goggles and a tophat with a medieval spiked morning star. I'd feel awkward at a cosplay event in that costume, let alone as an immortal predator.. if I weren't Malkavian).
But someone has needed to make this game for a long time. Since Vampire the Masquerade: Bloodlines, in fact.
There are several things this game does which no other game has even attempted. The first is the lineage system. You can bite humans, turn them into your undead servants, and then have them act as your bodyguard or send them to check the pockets of your fallen enemies for you. You can even get them to bite other humans, creating a lineage of Vampires with you at the center. This is a very simple idea, but awesome. A Vampire game where you can actually have minions? Yes, please.
It has its own form of a politics system. There are a handful of Vampire clans and your standing with each one determines what kinds of supernatural powers you can develop (and other things).
The powers are well-thought out and enjoyable and, most importantly, very different. They're what carry the game, from a design standpoint. You have the mobility of a Vampire, able to jump great distances... past traps or upwards 15 feet to reach beyond human bounds. You can turn to mist and walk through gates and fences, you can summon a will o wisp to trip levers or scout around corners for you... and many other things.
Each of the three classes (warrior, thief, mage) has its own starting power options, but you can theoretically learn any 'class' during a single playthrough since it's only constrained by stats and your reputation with the clans.
And, since the powers are diverse, interesting (even game-changing in some cases), and broken up by the political system, you need to cultivate favor with certain clans to get access to the really good stuff.
While everything else about the game can be off-putting, it does include a number of innovative desgins which I'd really like to see more often, and which I have no problems supporting. Although there are a lot of things I don't like about the game, I've been waiting for a long time for a Vampire game where you can pick up some alcohol-sodden bum, give him a battle axe and a taste of blood, and send him at your enemies. Bloodlust lets you do that.
I really wish someone would have slapped whoever was responsible for the name and said 'Come on! Nobody thinks that sounds cool,' though.

Relatively spooky game. I highly suggest playing it vanilla or with the Stalker Complete 2009 mod, so you can get through the game atleast once and understand the central plot. Quests in the game aren't too 'diverse' usually ranging from item fetching, or murder boning random people. There are several factions to join, each with there own little perks. Replayability is iffy, there are multiple endings (which are actually determined by what you do in the game, instead of a choice at the end of the game) but I think honestly playing different mods is really the only way to get some solid replay value out of this title. There are some bugs (which sometimes are hilarious), and i only experienced a few crashes.
Overall, I would give it a 8/10. Definitely a cult classic. If you do get this game (or any other in the series) play it on Master difficulty. The game difficulty makes it so that you and your enemies bullets magically disappear out of existence. So the easier the difficulty the less likely the bullet is even going to register on you/ the enemy.

I am genuinely terrified by this game.  Visually, STALKER looks a little old and it's bugs and crashes are well known, which is perhaps a little off putting when travelling between lands (which you have to do on foot, no fast travel!).
I love how challenging SoC is - a balancing act of survival as you have to choose what to carry in a rather small backpack.  Guns, ammo, medikits and food are all vital on your journey through The Zone.  Like any game, you have your mission and the petty extras, which are quite fun at first, but become necessity as the cost of better armour, guns and ammo rises.
The game itself is quite back-and-forth, travelling by foot to other regions becomes a pain, but the main firefights in and around buildings are really good. No More Room In Hell is one of the greatest zombie games i have played. The fact that this game is also 100% free to play is simply amazing. The devs have somthing truly special here. I have over 100 hours put into this game, and im still not bored with it. So with that said lets get into the full fledged Review.
-=Gameplay=-
No More Room In Hell is a slow paced realistic zombie survival horror game. I see it as them taking, and i hate to compare it to, CoD zombies. But its more realistic, and slower paced. Theres two types of gamemodes here, Objective and Survival. Survival is your typical Wave mode. The first round you spend trying to find weapons and tools to help you out. But when the second wave hits and theres little fast kid zombies, look out. Thats when it really begins.
Objective mode is a nice objective based team mode. You must work with your team to solve simple tasks to help get to the end. Its my preifred mode of choice. The objectives also are not always in the same order and can be random, adding re-playability to it.
Both modes have their own unique maps, so dont expect to play Flooded with objectives.
Now as i mentioned earlier, NMRIH is realistic, hitting the body doesnt deal much of any damage. In order to kill the dead you must aim for the head. And NMRIH features plenty of weapons to get the job done. Ranging from your melee weapons like the classic baseball bat, to guns like M1911. Theres a great varity of weapons to find and each gun uses a specific set of ammo you must find. This game also is a great team game. Theres no way you will be able to go lone wolf and expect to do well. And even if you do your not gonna be all hot♥♥♥♥♥♥ This game is all about working with your team, and in Wave modes that the only way you will make it to the end.
Theres so much more i can cover but i must say, the gameplay is solid.
~5/5~
-=Graphics=-
I like to think graphics dont make a game, it complements it. And the graphics here arent anything amazing, and thats why i love it. The graphics may not be the greatest around but they look quite nice. NMRIH runs off the HL2 engine so if you can run HL2 you can run this, and thats one of the reasons i love it. Having lower graphics helps keep the system requirements low, allowing more people to play. And with myself not having a super hot rig, im very happy with things.
Everything looks quite nice here and theres not much more i can say about it.
~4/5~
-=Sound=-
Holy freaking cow the sound track is amazing. Like seriously, its really really good. It fits the game so well. Keeping a dark scary and somtimes downright depressing feel. It works so wel for a zombie game like this. I couldnt ask for a better soundtrack. Huge huge props for that.
Not only is the soundtrack great but the rest of the sound it pretty good too. Everything from guns being fired, to heads being blown apart.
~5/5~
-=Community=-
Being a online game i must cover the community, and it like many other games has its fair share of trolls and annoying kids that really are not mature enough to play this game. Theres also plenty of Modded lobbys that feature god mode, gun menus, etc. It can make finding a decent server hard at times, but once you do your pretty much set. Now while it might seem as tho i think the community is a bit, meh, thats far from the truth. In reality i have met alot of awesome people, and 95% of my friends on my friends list is from people that i met playing this game. And thats pretty great.
~4/5~
-=Achievements=-
I love achievements in games, and this game is racked full of them. Everything from completing maps, to getting a certain amount of kills with a gun. Being that there is no story mode,the only way to truly beat the game is to get all the achievements.
~4/5~
-=Pay To Win Or Nah?=-
Being that this is a free game we must address if its P2W or not. And the answer, its not. This game is 100% free. Theres nothing in-game for you to buy either. Making this a true gem you have no excuse to not give a go. Its pretty amazing and hard to believe a game like this will cost you nothing, considering this game in many ways is better then alot of 60-120$ AAA games on the market today. And thats somthing special indeed.
~5/5~
-=Final Verdict=-
This game is one of my fav PC games on steam. Its truly amazing what the devs have done here. And with there being talk of a sequel, im pretty excited to see what they cook up next. This game has so much thats amazing, the fact its 100% free is nothing short of amazing. If your reading this, stop and download this game. It cant hurt to give it a go. you dont have anything to lose, just one hell of a ride to gain.
~5/5~ -=Legendary!=-

But if you think too hard on it, you won't find it at all so keep thinking outside the box.
Mostly it's pretty intuitive, and there is room for the player to develop their own tricks to deceive or mislead enemies. There are often more than one ways to complete missions for any style so a large audience can find this gameplay enjoyable.
Generally I experienced good performance with exception to some small parts of the game, like when you hold the time-travel device and look into the glass, but understandable too as you are playing in a double-layered level, ingeniously designed, that part.
Certainly, whether you want to play the same character twice, it's worth replaying and seeking those leftover secrets, and enjoying the void powers of the other character on your chosen protagonist makes it worth playing a second time at least.
As a conclusion, I'd recommend buying this game if you're into this sort. Think Thief with a little more supernatural and perhaps killing if you so choose, and less stealing. As I said, killing is entirely optional which I really like in a stealth game because it adds to the challenge.

Played the Non-Steam & Xbox versions, and I can say it's a good game to get away from LOL or DOTA with, fun with friends and isn't so uptight as either of the two. It's a slightly more streamlined experience, less complicated character/item stats, and simply easier and funner to enjoy in most cases. The all-too famous toxicity 80% of the players on both games becomes too much sometimes, and the SMITE community is 110% more friendly.
That being said, there's a downside to it being so noob/experience friendly. The game is simply filled with too much of a varying playerbase; "casuals", who take the game for what it is, a game, "gamer kids", the kids who simply play it cause it's FTP and neither have the capacity or just the interest in their performance than just having fun (There is no problem with that, just stating one of the majority groups), "League-ers/DOTA-ers", people who come from League and DOTA for a change of pace, with slightly more skill/ambition to do well in a game,  and finally, the "tryhards", the people who play SMITE to the best of their abilities and are far better in experience compared to the other groups of players.
I have no complaints to any of those cliches or player groups, the only problem is that there is little to no matchmaking criteria that seperates them, by current skill or experience, and at most times are just thrown together in a game of chance. It's purely a roll of the dice to get teamates you'll have synergy with or not. And considering that this game requires more cooperation/player interaction rather than someone carrying most of the game due to farming not being as impactful, all it takes is 1 player to be far from the average skill level on either side of the spectrum to impact the game/make it possible/impossible to win.
It's a fun game with friends, but hard on people who expect a balanced experience when paired with so many differing player skill levels.

I just bought (for a mere $4.99, btw - another reason I absolutely *love* 'indy games') a game called 'Papers, Please'. Very original, innovative... 'different'. Very 'detective-esque'. I like it a lot.
You play as a border checkpoint guard in a cold-war era sovietesque fictional country called 'Arstozka' (surrounding countries are fictional, as well) to process immigrants and citizens entering the country. The reasons are numerous - allegedly for work, permanent move, visiting parents, children, marriage, passing through, etc. You are the sole decision-maker as to their 'Approval' or 'Denial' (of which you literally stamp one way or the other).
The game starts off simple enough... immigration controls are very loose to start, and you just need to ensure that their passports don't have any discrepancies. Over time terrorists start to attack the border, and other things happen throughout society / the economy that 'dictate' immigration reform, with immigration controls becoming more and more strict. This necessitates more and more paperwork (and other 'controls' and so-called 'random searches') needed to be approved for entering the country, and of course more potential for discrepancies...
But that's not just it. You get paid based on how many people you 'process' in a given time (or 'work day'). They allow a few 'violations' on your part to pass through as 'warnings', but after too many violations, you get penalized by losing part of your money.
The other issue is that your family relies on your salary to survive. They need food, heat, payment for rent, and sometimes medicine. There are also upgrades you can pay for to make your job more efficient or easier, potentially allowing you to 'process' more people at the checkpoint. You can accrue savings, for what purpose I'm not quite sure yet (it looks like maybe you can pay to have more of your family brought over and given passports for a 'better standard of living').
If you're not careful, and if you're not efficient enough, you may not have enough money to pay all your bills. You need to make choices as to what to pay for and what to forego. Family members can die, or with sufficient delinquency on your part, you get sent to the gulags and lose the game.
Moral and ethical dilemmas pop up frequently - with regards to your family, choices on who to save and who to let go cold or hungry or even die, and other ethical dilemmas surrounding the people trying to enter the country.
The music is very cold-war sovietesque, which is fitting as something akin to East Germany during the Soviet era. The graphics, in wonderful indy fashion, are delightfully retro and charming.
Very interesting, indeed. I definitely recommend it! For $5, the cost of a Starbucks Latte, it's totally worth it.

Now I feel obligated to actually write about it.
In short, its third person hacky slashy ouchy dodgy game, it’s unforgiving, but the difficulty curve is much easier than Dark Souls 1. While I do believe it took a few steps backwards from the previous game, it still is head and shoulders above most games.
For the Newcomers:
Welcome! The franchise is a very humbling experience for the newcomers; very quickly you'll learn that your top priority is keeping yourself alive. While this is common in video games as a whole, it’s especially true here. Everything in the game can kill you in a matter of seconds, and your health/life is a precious resource. Whenever you die, you drop all your currently held souls at your place of death, but also lose a bit of your maximum health bar, all the way down to half. There are ways to mitigate this of course, but it is always in your best interest to be safe.
All that being said, the game does reward exploration, and the world is very densely designed with plenty to be found. Be sure to take a good look around the skyboxes whenever you change areas, as you'll usually be able to see places you'll eventually go or have been before. This all helps the game build a great sense of atmosphere.
The combat is some of the most satisfying of any game I've played. Remember how a few sentences ago I was saying how enemies can kill you easily? Most of them are animated to look like it. Everything in the game feels powerful, the swings and sound with the moves give things a great sense of weight and power. Souls Games use a lock on system, where, with the push of a button, the camera will focus on a specific enemy, and your character will face them. This means your movements are relative to it, and while you have to fight multiple enemies at a time, the system is at home in 1v1-3 fights. With larger fights, it can spiral out of control and enemies can stun lock you to death if you miss your escape. The camera controls aren't perfect, and with some bosses, it’s easier to fight them without the being locked on, but they function fine for the most part.
For the Souls Franchise Veterans
Multiple design choices feel like a step backwards, the limited enemy respawns, many boss fights being large humanoids in armor, and lacking the world that Dark Souls 1 had. What I mean is that Dark Souls 1 had a world that was essentially continuous, when the map files are put together, everything is mostly to scale, with distances, like being able to see several late game areas from the first bonfire. Here, the world feels a bit less so, some blatant ones like the distance between Majula and The Tower of Flame are out of scale, but none as bad as the transition to Iron Keep. These can be forgiven though.
Something that I won't forgive nearly as easily is the boss design. While some are well done, Many of the later bosses, are multiple enemies or a boss with a few smaller helpers. This gets incredibly frustrating if you're playing solo, thankfully, there are npc summons for a few, but for some of these fights, the only challenge is patience as you run around looking for an opening between boring bosses.
Another thing of note is that the atmosphere feels much less dark than the previous game, and that NPCs will not leave Majula. One of the things I realize that I loved was the NPCs of the previous games had a lot more emphasis on the Character part of the acronym. While people would come and hang out at Firelink, they would eventually leave, and usually encountered later. It gave the sense that they had goals of their own, and by the end of the game, it’s empty and lonely, as you are the last one there. The Majula NPCs seem much more NPCs in a MMO sense, they're here to serve the player, and once they reach Majula, they won't evolve further. It comes to a head in one instance where a father and daughter are less than 10 meters from each other, but don't ever reunite. It doesn't so much build or develop their characters as it does make you want to drag one to the other. (Emit Force won't work).
In my opinion, especially so as a fan of the multiplayer (Sunbro by day, Bellfag by night), the most jarring change is soul memory (hereafter noted as SM). The SM system determines multiplayer matchmaking on a tier system, counting every soul that your current character has collected, ever. This means that there isn’t much incentive to stay at soul level range for PVP, and can make trying to connect with friends, especially those that have been replaying an area they've been having trouble with, a bit of a hassle.
None of these are really deal-breakers though, and more than anything who off how well designed the first game was.
We do get legal respecing though, finally.
A Final Note on Hardware
Something to note here is that the game was coded to be run in 30 frames/second. This means that with a PC running it faster, the change can be a bit drastic. While the game does look better, there are issues with some enemies being significantly faster, and some even able to land attacks as soon as their animation starts. There are also a few issues with hit detection/tracking of some bosses. But the most significant problems that arise are weapon durability and dodging. The game gives you a set amount of frames during your roll animation that you are invulnerable during, also known as iframes. With double the framerate and no compensation means that you're only invulnerable for half the time as on a console. This is annoying, but not too big an issue as most rolls are for spacing, but can be annoying. The other issue is weapon durability. Equipment in the game degrades with use, but is refreshed upon resting at a bonfire. With weapons, they take durability damage whenever they're used. If they hit a wall or the ground, they take a small flat amount, the same as with console versions. Against enemies though, they take damage based on the number of frames that they’re in the body, more so if the enemy is already dead. This isn't too bad for most areas, unless using a fragile weapon, but there are longer areas that you’d want a backup to fall back on.
As for controls, the Mouse and Keyboard controls aren't great, though a big step up from Dark Souls 1. I'm currently playing without a controller, but I would recommend trying one with it, it makes the attack input a bit more precise than the defaults, and was clearly made with a controller in mind.

Now, let's get this out of the way. I don't play Visual Novels, and I actively dislike most of Japanese entertainment offerings from games to anime and manga.  So this review is from someone who is not in to this whole scene. I have also read the fan translated version, so my hours in this one don't actually reflect the true hours I've spent on this story.
One note, this is the "no p0rn" version of the VN, and personally I think it only improves the story. The sex in the fan translated was mostly gratuitous and didn't really add anything useful to the story. I haven't played the story enough to say whether the censorship affected some of the jokes, however. Which would be a shame, because the adult jokes were often quite funny. But the sex scenes were useless. I'll have to get back to you about that.
For some reason, I just love this "book". It starts as a pure fluff comedy slice of life kind of thing, with slightly mysterious subtext. It helps to be aware of the Japanese stereotypes of "kuudere" and "tsundere", etc. for certain jokes. And make no mistake, there are a lot of jokes in this story.
You'll be laughing with tears in your eyes.
The game starts with a "common route" where you make some fairly insignificant choices, and then finally you choose the girl you will be pursuing. Yes, the whole game is basically a romance, with the twist of all characters (including protagonist) being emotionally unstable and having usually huge psychological problems.
The game also makes a huge genre shift about 6 hours in, once you're done with the common route. The common route is absolutely hilarious comedy, the story then starts to slowly turn more serious and with less humor. Until you will be crying, and this time not because of laughter.
However, if you make right choices, you will be graced with a good ending, so there is always light at the end of the tunnel. Just warning you that there will be a lot of drama and it all will look very bleak.
There's only two dark spots on the VN and the main one is the presence of a loli. That is to say, the Makina route, which (should) give the creeps for anyone who isn't in to little girls. Yes, technically she's not much younger than Yuuji (the protagonist) but the route even plays up her youthful appearance. So, yes, it's disturbing. My advice for those who find  lolis as disturbing phenomenon as I do, is to buy and play the VN but just... well, when Makina gives you money, refuse.
The second, but more of a minor problem, is the Michiru route. Because that sorely tests your suspension of disbelief. The premise of the whole route. The core of the issue... It's just pure and unadultered fantasy magic. But if you can swallow that, it's fine and often quite funny.
Among the best parts of the whole story is the protagonist Yuuji who is both a sarcastic badass, and hilariously unable to understand normal life.

10/10 Would watch Tunafish Man again.
but seriously, the emotional joy I experienced going through the game and reaching the "good" ending is possibly greater than a young me several years ago finding out that  Kraft Dinner exists.

Half of the visual novel is a telling of shenanigans, while the latter half splits to five heartbreaking stories where 'the fire really hits the fan'. The gist of it is about a protagonist being played the fool by students with abnormal personalities, having the most sane personality out of the rest of the students of the school. You are led to solving a trauma for one of the five students you decide on, the trauma that resulted in their abnormal personality..
The shenanigans portion of the game before the route splits off might seem like your normal everyday conversations, but there are a huge number of hints from every character's conversation about what their trauma can be behind their facades. Those hints are leading to 'the calm before the storm' before it actually happens; so if you are perceptive, you should find a few questions arising over your head why each character is acting the way they are. Well, just sit back and enjoy reading the slice-of-life humor, and look forward to the impending drama if you just want to read something fun instead of becoming a detective.
Enjoyment: 9/10
Characters: 10/10
Soundtrack: 8.5/10
Personal visual novel score: 8.9/10
{ note; I finished reading this visual novel outside steam release }

Follow through Juicy Yuuji's extraordinary school life while finding out why busty Amane prefers vegetables over meat, what moody Yumiko does on the internet, how Sachi is capable of nearly everything and why Mitcher is mostly irrelevant.
Check out this visual novel because its comedy is well played, the plot will pull you in (not to mention that some routes are quite hardcore) and voice acting is top-notch (damn guys, when Makina and Mitcher spoke engrish with each other). For those who are interested but never "played" a VN (visual novel) before, get the game when it's further discounted. Like 33%-50% discount.
I hope this visual novel gets the appreciation it deserves so the sequels have a chance to be translated as well.
Shota Yuuji and military drills cannot be missed.

Pros:
- Somewhat unique Art Style
- Somewhat unique gameply mechanics, more like older MMOs like RO and MU.
- Free.
Con:
- Lacking relevant pvp content.(Most of "major" Characteristics aren't in game)
- Uninteresting atributte system.(Nothing as good as RO's system that required alot of theorycraft)
- For some reason the game seens to be build with console in mind.(Feels better to play in a gamepad)
- 200 levels that SHOULD have been 50 levels. Seriously there's no reason for that amount of level when every level have minimal impact in your gameplay,
- Strange/Useless class system. Every 15 level you get a "class levelup" and every class has 4 skills that you put points where you want. But you will never put 2 points in skill A, 3 in skill B and 5 in skills C and D. You will always put 5 points in 3 skills. There's no tree and reason to split points between skills in the same "class".
- Free.(It may have problems with pay2win aspect in the future)
TL: DR Has some cons, but so far lacks pvp content. Has a grindy system of 200 level that could be made 50 to have the same results. And because of that will get some REAL powercreep later on.
Nowhere near the "RO2" some ppl are saying. But it's free, or eventually will be.

I dont know how they did it but they did, when you play this game you are no longer sitting in front of your computer you are hiding in a locker listening for the beep of the motion detector hoping the reading is accurate. 100% recommended for any true science fiction horror fan! THE ONLY THING is that I wish there had been a warning about possible eppilepsy issues because the intense flashing of lights in the medical bay could be dangerous for some people. 10/10 one of the best games I have ever played, total nerd-gasm.

This is honestly the first game since my childhood that I constantly waited for throughout the day, plotting an optimized factory.
Factorio is a very challenging game: not in the bullet hell sort of way, but in the sense of constant strategy and requiring your full attention at all times. That is the best way to make a game.
The crafting system is BEAUTIFUL, requiring only raw materials; even the most complicated buildings only need a few copper and iron plates in your inventory at once. (It creates everything you need out of raw material, and those materials make up the thing you want.)
The art style is akin to Dungeon Keeper and other mid-90s management games, which I was a fan of.

Homeworld is one of those exceedingly rare gems in gaming that seem to get everything just right.
The story is set in a rich universe with interesting races and characters.
The gameplay is fun and complex without being complicated.
The sound design is captivatingly immersive.
The visuals are absolutely stellar.
Its rare enough these days to find a game that looks, sounds and plays great all at once, but Homeworld's genius is in how well all those apects are so masterfully integrated... What does that mean? Well, without spoiling the game for you, imagine loading into a new stage:
...Your fleet just emerged from hyperspace. Judging from the earlier cutscene, you are heading to the outskirts of the system, a fact now illustrated by how distant the sun has become in the 3D space. You start to feel isolated, a feeling not eased by how haunting the in game music has become. Fleet command just issued an objective: Send a ship to investigate an anomaly. In response you open up your sensors manager to get your bearings. You find some resource asteroids and send your collectors to harvest them. The collectors reply with acknowledgments, you zoom in closer to marvel at how well detailed and utilitarian the design of the resource collector is. You hear fleet command reporting that they can research a new ship model. You glance at your resource unit indicator and calculate that you can do the research and build one new ship or forgo the research and build five more weaker but more manuverable ships. You decide to go for quality than quantity. You decide to split your fleet into two groups, one to go forth and investigate the anomaly and another to stand guard and protect the Mothership. As you monitor your fleets you notice that the music is changing, something bad is going to happen! you feel your palms getting sweaty as you issue commands to your ships, strikecraft to aggressive stance, set claw formation. You open your sensors manager, you see two large groups of red pings heading towards your fleets. Your uneasiness changes into fear as you realise how outnumbered you are and wonder if your fleet will make it...
Homeworld is filled with amazing moments like that, moments where you will be immersed in the game; its tension, its conflict and  in how real the stakes feel. As one tactical mistake can end in strategic failure and your losses will carry over as resources are finite and your fleet is persistent. If you lose a ship, its gone forever. This makes all the defeats all the more painful and all the victories you will achieve all the more cathartic and meaningful.
To sum up; get this game! you will not regret it !

There are 3 reasons as to why I bought Grisaia on steam.

I've read this VN once before with the unofficial translation, and absolutely fell in love with it to the point where I wanted to do whatever I could to support it when available. I ended up purchasing a Japanese psp version of the game, and now this one, and I plan to buy it again when DenpaSoft releases the unrated version(oh boy, h scenes!!). This VN stands as one of my favorite VNs and stories overall, only beaten out by Muv Luv Alternative.
The characters in this story are all really well done. They are extremely enjoyable, and if you don't like one of the characters, you're bound to like another.
Yuuji is a fantastic protagonist, who manages to be an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and a sweetheart all at the same time, in some manner.
Amane is the onee-san type role, and absolutely fantastic. Her route has a bit of a boring spot but quickly picks up and is one of my favorites in the game.
Michiru wants to be your run of the mill tsundere but manages to be a very interesting character.
Sachi is a maid who does what everyone says.
Makina's the loli/imouto type, and I'm not too interested in her but her route is fantastic, probably the best in the game.
And Yumiko is your violent kuudere, similar to Senjougahara from the monogatari series.
There is a lot more to each character, and a reason they act the way they do, but if I were to say more I'd spoil all the fun.
The story is absolutely fantastic, but if I were to go on about it, I'd probably end up spoiling it for you so I don't want to say anything, but there's plenty of good twists and events within the VN to really keep you interested.
There isn't a whole lot of choices to make in this vn. A few filler choices in shared route, and then 2 choices per route(One to get on each route, and one to decide the ending).
The one thing to keep in mind when reading this vn, is that it is extremely long(VNDB states about 50+ hours). The shared route goes on for quite some time.
This VN is definitely worth the cost, and I recommend it to anyone who enjoys VNs, or anime.
If you watched the Grisaia anime, the VN is a must, as the anime doesn't nearly compare to how good the VN is.
As I said earlier, if you'd rather wait for an uncensored version with more anime boob, DenpaSoft is also going to be releasing one at a later currently unannounced date.
