Released almost one year after the first title in the eponymous series, Drizzlepath: Genie is everything a worthy gaming sequel should be. It expands not just the narrative, but it features a visual overhaul coupled with freedom of choice and multiple endings. Developer Tonguç Bodur (has a cameo inside his own game), proves his skill once again while offering a new meditative journey for all open-minded players to enjoy. And again, far too many negative reviews for a title that doesn’t even have the performance issues of its predecessor.
Drizzlepath: Genie is most certainly less ambiguous than the previous title. Players must travel to and climb another Mountain of Fire, yet this journey is three times longer than Drizzlepath and definitely more eventful. If you played the first title in the Drizzle series, you know by now not to expect a lot of action, if any at all. Most walking simulators are non-violent and that is a fortunate thing and a true break from video gaming’s norm of nearly always killing or destroying something digital. And no, I’m not a hippie. In fact, the Postal series is among my many guilty pleasures. Just try playing those games in a non-violent manner and see for how long you can endure.
Once again, your constant travel companion is the drizzle itself. It turns to snow near the end of your journey and that is surely a metaphor for something. You see, even the Genie which represents the leitmotif of the entire game, should not be regarded literally. At least we now have a narrator protagonist in the form of Lula, a teenager living in a shamanistic society. She leaves her village in search of solace atop the Mountain of Fire, but along the way she will find more questions than answers. What starts as pure abstract poetry, begins to make sense as Lula shares stories from her past.
For someone who’s coping with constant loss, she sure seems very optimistic but that’s obviously a subjective point of view. The game offers each player a another perspective, based on how they perceive the journey along the path of their choosing. Yes, there are two paths you may travel upon and they seem to offer different experiences though the story’s conclusion is found in the same place. At least you can’t complain about lack of replay value.
2015’s Drizzlepath used CryEngine 3 assets which were pleasant enough yet the overall performance was mired by random frame rate drops. By 2016, Tonguç opted for the Unreal Engine 4 and its use in Drizzlepath: Genie is a notable step forward. Players have access to a lot of in-game settings and they may tweak them until performance is flawless. I still played in 4K resolution for the sake of superior screenshots, but in 2K res, the frame rate was close to 60 and with very few drops. Just as expected from the graphics engine, in the right hands. I played far too many UE4 titles that were messy to say the least. The Genie can be enjoyed on constant 60fps, maxed out and 1080p, no doubt about it.
I settled for 4K and stable 30fps (same compromise I took in The Vanishing of Ethan Carter) since walking simulators don’t require many sudden turns, haste is out of the question and they rarely feature the alert gameplay of many other gaming genres. Of course I would have wanted 4K@60fps, but we’re still years away from single GPUs pushing that kind of eye candy in recently released titles, at a reasonable price tag. I took nearly 100 screenshots just along the Red Path, so I can only imagine that Blue might yield several dozens more. One thing is certain: Drizzlepath: Genie has enough points of interest, to encourage players to stop and take in the sights from time to time. No one’s rushing you afterall.
A most pleasant soundtrack meets a convincing (if not always coherent) narration and offers few moments of silence. Even the sound effects are well simulated. The voice actress delivered her lines in a most professional manner so there’s not much to complain. You also have subtitles this time around, in case the initial poetry shall prove puzzling. I don’t see what more could have been done for the audio department.
If you played walking sims before, you know what to expect. No, not boredom. If you consider this adventure subgenre, boring, I don’t understand why would you play and expect something it never claimed to be. Drizzlepath: Genie looks the part and it can even compete with Ethan Carter and Dear Esther, in terms of scenery diversity and abstract themes. The journey splits in two paths after about 10 minutes from starting a new game. You can choose whichever you want and stick to it until reaching the Mountain. Or go back and attempt the other one, since there’s nothing stopping you from backtracking. I went for Red and never looked back. Might give Blue Path a chance to unravel its tale, in the unforeseeable future.
No matter what color you pick, you’re in for at least 4 hours of relaxing travel from point A to B. No threat to your unrelenting progress, no puzzle sections, no combat. Just taking a walk through the type of terrain that reminded me of Skyrim and the far too many hours I had sunk in its PS3 version until my save file refused to “talk” to me ever again. You even meet stone troll statues and flying dragons, which never seem to acknowledge your presence. The Red Path took me through both creepy and fascinating places and red triangle particles were floating near certain symbols you can observe. It’s the game’s way of drawing attention to players and proving that if you stray from the clearly visible path, you will find rewards in thinking outside the box. No collectibles though, just more abstract ideas which are materialized in either objects or floating text boxes.
One thing that bothered me about Dear Esther, was the slow pace and the lack of a sprinting option. Drizzlepath: Genie won’t torture you in this way and you even have a button for automated movement, in the forward direction. It’s convenient and you can just relax while changing the viewpoint and direction via mouse cursor without touching your keybvoard again. At least until there are several occasions during which you must jump across a gap or if you wish to toggle the “Gothic Vision”(film grain + Black&White filter) by pressing the default “G” key while in-game. Not sure how much it affects the gameplay or plot, but it does look cool. Really, the gameplay is pretty much the same as being advertised on the game’s Store Page. It’s not the developer’s fault if you didn’t read the “fine print” carefully enough.
I don’t even consider it overpriced. Just take a good look at it. The official screenshots appear the same as the ones I took. So you don’t fall victim to marketing ploys. This burger is just as juicy as the picture on the box. Or not. It’s up to you to decide, but I’ll definitely keep playing and reviewing the rest of the Drizzle series and its spin-offs. As far as walking simulators are concerned, Drizzlepath: Genie has accomplished its goal. Unlike the initial Drizzlepath, the sequel is fully tweakable (settings), stable, longer, more coherent and you can sprint most of the time. It’s up to informed buyers and potential players to enjoy it or not. Just don’t judge it from the wrong perspective of a gaming genre it does not belong to.

I began my review for the first Drizzlepath with a small complaint about the lack of a "walk" button, especially in a genre of gaming where taking things slow 'n' casual is pretty much of the essence. I'm pleased to say that Drizzlepath: Genie immediately rectifies this flaw, endowing your protagonist with a steady-but-calm walking pace more ideally suited to this style of "walking simulator". The narration even justifies the initial lack of a "run" button, explaining that an evil wizard has cursed you with the inability to make haste ('cause he's keen to get his hands on the same sacred relic that you seek).
As recompense, perhaps, the game offers you something I've never encountered in a walking simulator before: instead of continually holding down the "W" key, you can simply hit "Q" once and the game will auto-walk for you. That should shut up all the smart-arses who claim that "all you have to do in these games is hold down W"...'cause in this case, you don't even have to do that much! (Oh, and rest assured...you do get to use a "run" button in later parts of the game, so that slow-and-steady pace doesn't overstay its welcome.)
The graphics and scenery, again, are simply gorgeous (though I did kind of miss the sight of my own legs and shadow cast upon the ground, one of the first game's more impressive touches; a change of gaming engine, apparently). The music is wonderful, although the voice acting is again not among the game's stronger points (though at least our female narrator is a lot easier to understand this time around). The story and writing, I'm pleased to report, are certainly an improvement over the first game's obscure, meandering poetry, if still not anything to "write home about" exactly. There are moments, however, when the combination of music, voice and imagery harmonise quite beautifully...fleeting moments, perhaps, but they're definitely there.
Oh, and in case you're wondering about the ties between this and Drizzlepath the first, other than the same lead developer? Well, there's lots of drizzle (i.e. rain), and there's paths. A greater choice of paths, at that: while the first game was essentially linear, this one offers two very different paths which vary enough to qualify as two entirely different "games". So the monetary value, this time, is certainly more substantial (though the price is also a smidgen higher to compensate).
One new feature I wasn't entirely sold on were the pop-up illustrated images which superimpose over the screen every now and then, depecting moments of the narration and adding a bit more visual variety to the expected first-person POV. The boldness of the move is appreciated, and the images themselves are very nice, but I'm not sure I didn't find it a tad jarring and obtrusive at times (although it is infrequent enough to be no biggie, one way or another).
Overall, this game is a definite step forward from the first Drizzlepath's achievements, and shows enormous potential for the developer's future endeavours (all three of which I currently own, but have yet to play...I'm doing the chronological thang here). A definite recommendation to all "walking simulator" fans, though it's still hard to gauge how much conventional gamers might get out of such a leisurely, peaceful experience (with the occasionally dark 'n' spooky bit thrown in for good measure).
If you're a believer, like me, in the potential of games as an art form, then you'll probably find something to appreciate here. If, on the other hand, you just wanna frag 'n' brag 'til the zombies stumble home, you might want to look elsewhere for your interactive jollies.
Verdict: 7.5/10.

Factorio is a very clever look at the pro's and con's of logistics management, mass-production, industrialization, exploitation of natural resources, and Windowed Mode for games. You Factorio vets know what I'm talking about on that last one.
The reason why Factorio is so great as a strategy/puzzle game is that it's basically logistics engineering distilled to perfection and made into a game. While this means that your Factorio skill is only limited by your logic and visual thinking skills, there is one issue: The game has progression balanaced to a t, but there comes a time in every game (it's different for everyone for how many times it happens and how long it takes) when you are severely limited by your machines, or worse, your own sense of scope. These periods consist of listening to music and podcasts in another window while the game solves itself, with little else to do but build another assembly line. If you want to conserve your resources, you will get just a bit less out of the game, since it is really balanced for a perpetual "suicide burning" in terms of resource gathering. I am not a fast man when it comes to limited resources and a need to use them, and this left me with a lot to do, since taking more from the iron mines might leave me high and dry in a few hours time. So I spend most of my time waiting for research to finish so that I can build something else without being redundant, as I start another research project and find a new podcast.
Not to say that the game isn't still fun. Those "Eureka!" moments far make up for the "I'm not playing the game" realizations, and I know that my own underambition is the cause of most of my problems. There is still an infinite joy from setting out to perform an odd task and actually doing it, time and time again, wether it be creating a backup power supply off-site, or simply finding an excuse to use trains since you only need to transport massive resources long-distance if you've turned the "resource vein commonness" to minimum.
Factorio is possibly the best example of a management game in years, forwards or backwards. Progress is only limited to how much you're willing to do to get it, and unless you're a damn turtle (like me), the game never goes faster than you can handle, AND EVEN THEN, there is an option in world generation just for you slowpokes (mostly me)! The actual scope of the game is spot-on, with lots of actual game being locked off until you've done the right research, but never enough that you don't have something you could be doing already. You probably unlock Oil right before you run out of solid material to manage at home, and Trains right before you start needing to take resources from far away, and so on, with the only real issue being the amount of late-game filler tech, which serves only to build up to the actual prizes of technology without helping Jack off a horse.
Right now, the game is in Early Access, but if you think you'd enjoy a logistics-based engineering strategy/puzzler, you will fall in love with Factorio. The game is already basically a finished product, with more singleplayer story and some extra multiplayer features being the only addition I've even heard the devs say that they want in Factorio. The framework is already there, with polishes and outer walls done, too. The only thing needed is... whatever we get. If the game left Early Access any day since I wrote this, you probably wouldn't be able to tell, it's basically done already.
Fantastic way to burn all kinds of time. It's getting a bit stale now that I'm in late game, but considering the 40+ active hours of playtime, it's been a great purchase thus far.

Homeworld was damn near the very first PC game I ever played, probably the second RTS after Total Annihilation.  I loved the gameplay, I loved the story, I loved the music, I loved the lore, it's all phenomenal, and I still love it.
For that reason, I recommend that you play the Classic version of Homeworld 1, as the game has a LOT of differences that don't suit the HW2 engine.  Notably:
Weapons work completely differently.  They're projectiles in HW1, and can miss.  It's possible for a Heavy Cruiser to miss the Destroyer it targeted and vaporize a scout behind it on accident.  In HW2, it's a hitscan RNG, no projectiles about it.
Formations were VITAL in HW1.  Ion Frigates?  Wall of death lasers.  Interceptors?  Claw formation.  Multigun Corvettes guarding something?  Put them in sphere formation.  They flat out do not work in HW2.
HW2 is a good game, it fixed a lot of issues with HW1 and plays a lot differently.  I like them both, I just think that they shouldn't be packaged together.

Most real-time strategy games I've played are quite lacking in storytelling.  This is not one of those games.  The original creators of this game, Relic (known for the Company of Heroes and Dawn of War Series) are masters of blending storytelling with real-time strategy while not ignoring the importance of replayability through multiplayer.  Homeworld probably has the most poignant stories I've ever seen without the need for fully animated, fully voiced, lip synched characters.
Without revealing the plot, I can tell you that you will feel invested for the safety of the people you are commanding and fighting for.
On the more technical side, this game was way ahead of its time in 1999 and holds up well for being nearly 20 years old.  The graphical improvements are a welcome change and a more modern, post-dialup era multiplayer lobby is also welcome.  The voice acting of the narrator, the Mothership's computer, and all your units is outstanding and has not changed from the original.
The music also deserves an honorable mention for its ability to add to the feeling of every cutscene, every battle, and every dialogue you encounter.  Top notch stuff.  Especially if you like ambient electronic music.
The game is not perfect, however.  Like most RTS games from the 90's, it can be heavy in the micromanaging department.    I also have to dock the games for having somewhat clumsy default controls, a UI that leaves a lot to be desired, and a rather steep learning curve.
Another con for some may be the rock-paper-scissor formula that Relic is known for throughout their games.  In this game, there are units that are simply a hard counter to another unit.  In later Relic RTS games, you can see where they added in more unit versatility and soft counters through combined arms.  This leads to some rather spammy gameplay that might be a turn-off for some.

Been playing it for 14 hours now.
What I like about it:
- Pretty graphics
- Some nice ambient sounds --birds chirping, the ocean, thunder (think DayZ)
- Build castles
- Claim Territory by placing a banner in your building -- others cant build in your borders (nice so people can't hop your walls)
- Survival - forage for food, get water, hunt animals

- Proximity voicechat
- When you log out you turn into a "Sleeper", ie your avatar is replaced with a guy in a sleeping bag and people can kill you if they can reach you. So log out in the safety of your territory or find a really good hiding place.
- You can tie people up with rope and imprison them or send them to the gallows
- You can make crossbows, bows, siege equipment
- Weapons, armor, and blocks are all tiered (wood, leather, stone, iron, steel | dirt, grass, clay, wood, stone, stone slab)
What I don't like about it
- The combat is like Chivalry - good thing is you can block and there is a stamina bar. But many fights end up as run around the person hitting or kiting. You can choose which way you swing horizontally, but it's purpose is more so you don't hit a wall or tree while you swing. No directional blocking.
- Very little inventory space and the containers chests are quite small too.
Not many negatives. I've only had one game breaking bug occur in 14 hours. A couple smaller bugs. It's a fun game and for $20 bucks I've already got my moneys worth.

Grisaia no Kajitsu is a outstanding visual novel that have 5 route in the game, which means its will last you over 50 hours of gameplay (Just a rough estimation)
The start of the series, Grisaia no Kajitsu. In Kajitsu the story begins with the protagonist Kazumi Yuuji transferring into a certain school and meeting 5 other girls who attends it. There are only 6 students the school.
It gives off a very unique feel, unlike all other school-related VNs. The heroines are, unique, eccentric and weird in some way or another. To be precise, the entire school is full of weirdos, even Yuuji himself.
The common route is entertaining and really intresting, because the characters are all weirdos like with Michiru's stupidity, Sachi's lack of common sense, Makina's downright rude personality, Amane's horny big sister role player,Yumiko's "classic kuudere."  and Yuuji's tsundere personality.
It has good voice acting and all of the heroines and have nice soundtracks.
The art style is very pleasing to the eye and with vivid colours being used it makes a nice ambience around the visual novel itself.
The interface is very detailed and nicely designed.
To sum up i would definitely recommend this great title from Frontwing, The Fruit of Grisaia isn’t a game to be missed, and whether you’re a fan of visual novels, anime, or even just well-written stories, this is something that’ll be a deep, engaging experience.

Grisaia no Kajitsu. It's my favorite visual novel.
The interface is great and comfortable, there is a good selection of Extras, like CGI and even Windows soundpacks and even icons. On a technical standpoint, it's a great game.
I may not have many hours on this (Unless a R-18 patch is released, or created by the users) - but I have played it.
Now with the story, it has its fair share of funny moments, and its fair share of dramatic moments..as well as those moments that had me on the brink of tears, or just depressed for multiple days.
Amane's route is outstanding. One issue in this version is that you're missing out on the adult content, which is coincidentally a large focus of her route. Though, there is also a lot of humor and fun in this version without any adult content. I will not spoil Amane's route at all because it's something that you truly have to experience for yourself. When I first played through her route, I only got 2 hours of sleep for 2 nights in a row, just because of how interested I was. It's amazing.
Sachi's route is very good, it's interesting finding out exactly what drives her to act as she does, just make sure that you are ready for the reason. Try not to get the bad ending for her, though..truly horrifying. I don't know fully how to put how I feel about her route into words, but I assure you that it's great. The R-18 content here does not matter as much, I believe- though in general I do believe that not having it is a general issue.
Yumiko's route is nice, she's sort of like a tsundere/kuudere mix in personality, and her route is generally good, but not exceptionally remarkable overall. I enjoyed her route a lot, especially in seeing how she slowly becomes close to you, or Yuuji. Nearing the end a lot of unexpected things happen, and it is all played out pretty well, but once again, when you compare it to something like Amane's route, it's hard to stand out. However, I still enjoyed it a lot.
I have not yet completed Makina's route, though it is pretty good so far. Lots of humor, and a lot of dark stuff as well. Each route has two sides, and they are all generally played out well. R-18 content here as far as I have gone doesn't matter at all, but I can't say for sure since I have not yet completed it.
I have not started Michiru's route, but some people argue that it is the best route in the entire game. Others argue that Amane's route is the best. They're generally the two most acclaimed in this game.
Overall, there was not a single moment in which I wanted to just get through a certain part to get to the good stuff so to speak. The entire experience was perfect, from the comedy to the pure horror at some points in time, everything was great. I do not have a single complaint for this game, but it goes without saying that the R-18 version is the definitive version to get.
If you're looking for an outstanding visual novel that will last you over 50 hours of gameplay-
(Yes, even with quick reading)
look no further than Grisaia no Kajitsu, or "The Fruit of Grisaia"

A real treat for any "Alien" fan. And I mean "Alien." With no "s" at the end.
The game takes place between original Alien and its sequel. You play as Amanda Ripley, a daughter of Ellen Ripley who seeks answers regarding her mother's fate.
A:I biggest strength is its faithfulness to the source material. The Alien is done wonderfully, both visually and gameplay wise. It is a deadly and unpredictable beast, which will kill anyone in sight. You have no way of killing it but later in the game you do flamethrower which you can use to repel it for a moment. Strangely, it makes the game more stressful, as you need to manage your fuel carefully. The AI of Alien is great, making him fairly intelligent. He doesn't follow strict patrol patterns which makes evading him quite thrilling. That is quite impressing as it is Creative Assembly game who has established reputation of writing horrible AI.
The environments look fantastic. The original soundtrack by Jerry Goldsmith is back and it is tastefully expanded for the needs of the game. The new stuff added to the lore (mostly the addition of Wayland-Yutani's poor competitor Seegston Corp.) is really good and fitting. Overall, finally the game Alien deserved to get.
If I have any complaints it is the writing and the characters. It is not bad, but it is quite forgettable. People you meet are Alien Fodder and are not developed enough for you to care. Also while the 1st half of the game is brilliant it gets less interesting later on. Final two missions try to recreate the frantic finale of the film and to some extend it succeeds but as you need to switch from the heavily established by that point stealth focused gameplay to running&flamethrowing it becomes frustrating rather than tense.

I had a violent first outing with this game that ended with my giving up and quitting for about 5 months. I'm very lucky that I was convinced by a random internet commenter to give it a second chance, and that my white-knuckled, pontificating rage at a particular early level (the Medical Ward) was not an uncommon reaction to that questionably-designed section of the game. The dissatisfaction I felt when I realized your main antagonist, the eponymous alien, is designed to stay within a certain radius of you when you crawl a football field away from it in total silence made me feel smart and sophisticated as a long-time survival horror buff, but when I returned to see the game through, I came to the paradigm-shattering conclusion that sometimes current, and major, design studios can still get things extremely right.
On that first go, I quickly surmised that the plot is mostly phoned-in. And to a degree, I stand by that--the whole thing isn't much more than a sure-to-please rehash of the first Alien movie, but it does serve as a wealth of opportunity to internalize that film's impact by enabling you to live and breathe the carnivorous, soaring agony of having the odds stacked so high against you. Like Ellen Ripley, you might find yourself staring down the acid-drizzling xenomorph in the room, moving as slow as you can to your objective, humming quietly to keep yourself cool. It takes a lot of nerve and a fair bit of cunning to stay alive.
I don't want to get too psychoanalytical when talking about this game (though it does strike me as a powerful duplication of the Silent Hill 3 package--in which a woman has to navigate an openly hostile male-dominated environment and is hunted, relentlessly, by psychosexual terror and betrayed by just about everyone [there, I said it]), but the effort that went into generating this specific flavor of all-out dread is simply marvellous to see these days.
The atmosphere. My god, it's a thing of beauty. I never expected anyone to let me crawl around inside and rewire the hissing, crackling retrofuturist systems of a doomed space colony as envisioned in the late 1970s. Pipes are bursting, analogue computers are clacking and spinning reels of tape, and you can hear the station's skeleton moan as it falls from orbit around a looming gas giant. That vibe trickles all the way down to the oily, decaying, blue-collar details of the hellscape that you traverse, and you get a very tactile feel for these environments and the engineering obstacles you encounter--you click both mouse buttons to clamp onto a bolt with your maintenance jack, then hold down the corresponding WASD key to break the bolt loose. Your security tuner sings a little chiptune melody while it warms up, and you can damn-near
that the thing is a mostly-hollow hunk of low-memory plastic when you hear its buttons and notched dial click as you hack through a door. I goddamn -love- the attention given to the gadgetry.
The gameplay is like a linear Metroid Prime-via-Amnesia♥♥♥♥♥Bioshock, but the experience borders on exhaustingly tense most of that time thanks to its near-constant cat-and-mouse dynamic. You're being hunted, and you sure don't get a lot of down-time from this anarchic safari. Exploration is encouraged, but only if you've got the stomach to put up with something banging around inside the air ducts above and below nearly every step of the way. I was very happy bypassing most of the collectible lore, and closing those damn elevator doors behind me. Fast.
Despite my grown-up impatience with its overarching familiarity, with its too-rote tropes (psychotic panic-babble scribbled on walls does not interactive storytelling make) and manipulative scripted events, I was able to get absolutely lost in it the further I went. With luck, an emergent gameplay moment will occasionally surpise the♥♥♥♥♥♥right out of you. Once, while hiding from the alien as it dropped into a hallway outside an operating room, I looked over to find a random NPC crouched behind a turned-over table, shaking and thumbing his revolver, every bit as desperate as I was to stay out of sight. I had a chance to either knock him out and save his life, or keep him conscious to serve as a live distraction so I could slip away. That was when I really learned what this game is, and I felt extremely grateful I had reneged on writing it off.
The alien will kill you multiple times, no stealth or strategy involved to stay alive, only luck.

Alien: Isolation
Let me start off by saying that I am huge a fan of Horror games, horror movies & the Alien Series, despite the fact the last two Alien movies were quite bad I still enjoyed all of them. So when this game came out in 2014 I had to get it.
Environment: The first thing that I found to be amazing was the setting of the game, it was so authentic to the original Alien movie which gave an amazing nostalgia vibe and also made the game feel much more like an Alien game.
Graphics: So while in some areas of the game, mainly empty vent holes where you find just a black texture. The graphics in the game are really good, the best thing though is the light displacement in the game which is fantastic and really adds to the horror aspect of the game.
Sound: The sound in the game is great, with a great set of speakers or headphones you get fully immersed into the game and it just adds even more to the games horror and immersion.
Android & Humans: I must say playing it on its hardest difficulty really makes you fear both the Androids & Humans a lot more, it can also catch you off guard as well which really adds to the suspense.
Alien: Ah the alien, what more can I say here that hasn’t already been said. It. Is. AMAZING! Literally one of the best AI’s I have seen in a Video Game, the Alien is unpredictable, stubborn and is very aware of sound, movement & light. It is literally what the Alien is and it will find you and kill you.
A lot of people have criticised the game for not giving you the option to kill the alien or at least wound it. Well the setting of the game is between the first Alien movie and the second: Aliens. So in reality, on Sevastopol, there are no Colonial Marines and no Pulse Rifles. And while yes the shotgun should at least wound the alien, I am mighty glad they went the route of making the game more like the original, instead of giving you overpowered weapons.
Overall I recommend this game 1,000,000% to any who is: a) a fan of Horror games, and b) a fan of the Alien Series. This is the Alien games we needed, wanted and deserved, in the end it took an RTS developer to create one of the best Alien & Horror AAA video games.

I'm a pretty easy guy to please when it comes to games. A game does not have to be brilliantly written, beautifully textured, or flawlessly programmed to get me to recommend it. All it has to do is show me something I haven't seen before, give me an hour (or more) of a good time, or just be a little weird in one way or another.
So let's talk a bit about why I'm not recommending Drizzlepath: Genie.
I would heartily recommend Drizzlepath (the original). That game showed me something I've not seen before or since--an unintelligible South American woman rapping what I can only assume is the most pretentious poetry ever put to paper while you walk through a pretty environment in the Cry engine. It gave me about a solid hour of giggles. And it was plenty weird.
But the sequel is merely a slog. It's an American girl scooped right out of your local community theater just plain reading pretentiously written lines about the most basic philosophy concepts you've never had to think about because they're that obvious. And it takes HOURS of walking through the same environment with almost no landmarks and nothing to do or see or think about or enjoy. The only nice thing is the auto-walk button because otherwise your middle finger would hate you for the rest of your life.
So go play Drizzlepath or anything else instead of making yourself wish you had a sensory deprivation chamber for a little change of pace from the monotony of this game.

A bunch of pretentious drivel.  The game trys to be deep and phylosphical, but it just ends up been slow, boring, and cheesy.  The ending is terrible.  The pacing is slow and dull. I do appreciate that this game is trying to be something different, and for that it deserves praise.  It just fails to be interesting or engaging.  I found myself 2-3 times browing the web on my phone while my character was on walking cruise control.

Well...that was a deluding experience.
But that aside, let's just get to the point.
This game that promises multiple endings (as most 'walking simulators' do), is rather limited so far that goes, offering two endings that are all decided shortly after the start of the game.
The protagonist during the whole trip -which on the shortest path took a whole hour and half to complete- , will talk about her 'life and memories'...and bring up poorly written poetry and senseless koans. This for at least an hour. All narrated by a voice which -while not bad to hear- is extremely monotonous, making the poetry even worse than it is.
The only way I ended to get to at least one of the two endings was through sheer determination to get at least one ending, and attempting to ignore all the poetry brought up.
While the surroundings are indeed pretty to see, and the background music is pleasant, at the same time you could easily risk to get lost and walk back where you came due everything looking always the same.
So, let's get to a vote:
Plot: 4
Without spoiling what happens, the plot 'twist' so-to-call, is worth of a C-category film. It would had gotten an even worse vote, weren't it for the fluff about the protagonist's village and people which was one of the few highlights of this game. Loses a point for having obvious gaping plot holes.
Music: 7
Pleasant background music. But nothing else to bring up about it: nothing memorable.
Mechanics: 4
Poorly implemented. If you're needing the button to interact with items for exactly ONE lever in the whole game, and needing the ability to jump in only two locations (over the course of an hour and half) , for a grand total of 10/11 jumps on a line to win, why implement it at all? It's not a challenge, it's not a puzzle, and it barely gives anything to work with.

For the most part, fans of dishonored won't be disappointed with this installment. The gameplay in dishonored 2 kept all the stealth mechanics that we loved back in 1 (choking, drop assassination, etc.), and added more options for non-lethal approach as well as a new playable character, Emily, with more fun magical powers! The gadgets that are available stayed more or less the same, with some balances. What really takes the cake in gameplay is the map design. While there is nothing wrong with the design in dishonored 1, in dishonored 2 the non-linearity of area design is really taken to another level. Yes, I am talking about mission #4, The Clock Mansion and #7, A Crack in the Slab. Just like its prequel, one will have multiple ways to complete a mission. In one mission, I did not fight a single enemy, and spent 1 hour to solve a math riddle to get through the level instead :D
I can not give the same praise to the story portion of this installment, however. The reason dishonored 1's story is so powerful is not that it had a complicated story. It is because the narrative felt alive. Players can feel Corvo's emotions as he desperately try to save those he loved. The characters drove the story. Players will not find the same in this installment. Everything makes sense in the story, true, but there is also nothing compelling about it. Still, I don't blame the production team. It is hard, if not impossible, to come up with a story of the same intensity, considering how conclusively Dishonored 1 ended.
Overall, Dishonored 2 is a great game. One will find gameplay elements that are both familiar and novel, and easily do more than a couple playthroughs. Just don't expect it to be as great as Dishonored though.

Pros:
+ Superb soundtrack
+ Lots of content
+ CO-OP
+ Very replayable if you enjoy the gameplay
Neutral:
-+ The jokes present in this game are either random, references or memes. Personally I just find that type of humour annoying and obnoxious, but I know a lot of people do find enjoyment in it.
-+ The voice acting can be hit and miss, but it's mostly down to the meme-filled script being inconsistent.
-+ I personally was not a huge fan of the artstyle, as I hate low resolution textures, but again, it depends from person to person if you like this kinda style.
Cons:
- Collecting from cases/boxes could have been streamlined, A LOT. You'll find youself spamming E on hundreds of these things by the end of the game, and it's extremely tedious. Most of them take like 4 seconds to actually open and there are billions of them. If they had dumped the items into larger, less abundant crates this would have been a lot less painful.
- The quests do not scale whatsoever, and returning to earlier quests, overleveled, just makes it feel like a waste of time since it's so easy.
- Performance-whise, this game is extremely inconsistent. Even though I'm 3 generations above the reccomended specs according to the steam page, I still tanked to sub-40 fps during almost every large scale gunfight, even on the lowest settings possible. Pop-in and texture streaming are also way, way too prevelant here, and it really drags you out of the experience.

Okay I have had a blast with Reign of Kings.  I have played for a few hours now and I haven't ran into any game crashing bugs.  Outside a few clipping issues and some lag the game performs very nicely and is very pretty to boot.  Off the top of my head for this genre as far as other Early Access games the only other games that I can think of that look prettier are Subnatuica and Stranded Deep, and those two games are focused on Single Player so it is hard to really do a side by side comparison.
I did hit a few lag spots, but honestly my connect sucks from time to time so I have been happy over all with the netcode and latecy.  As far as over all community, it is pretty much what you would expect with this type of game.  If you have played RUST or DayZ you know exactly what I am talking about.  You will find two types of people, those that grief and those that are friendly.  There is very little middle ground.
The biggest thing the game has going for it is the true "King of the Hill" feeling.  Anyone techincally can become the king, but can you hold on to it, or can your guild?  The throne is litterally at the top of the hill and there is a long bridge and passage full of chock points that a strong force could hold fairly easy if they worked together. For those players like myself that enjoy this genre but not crazy about multiplayer generally, I still think the game is worth $20. If suffer she did, she decided thereafter to inflict those same platitudes on everyone else, or at least all the players of this game. Let me start this review off with saying, I've played my fair share of Walking Simulators, I've played a lot of the games that are very often referred  to as "Not really a game", I know what they consist of, I know what to expect, I accept the fact that they contain little to sometimes zero actual content or interaction. I enjoy most of them.
But this game? This game does not speak to me positively in
any way. It's so boring, there is literally 0 content. There is no interactivity, only automatically triggered events, it is literally a simulator where you walk through a path for 2 hours doing nothing but pressing W, A, S and D. There actually is a button to interact with things, E, but you use it once, you can only use it once in the entire game, you can only interact with 1 thing in the entire game, which is walking to a lever and pressing E.
The game is indeed beautiful, nice graphics as always with the Unreal Engine. But the performance of the game is horrid, I have a fairly strong computer, I had horrible FPS(jumping from 20 to 50) at all graphic sliders at medium or less, I even had Shadows at OFF. So to get the best FPS I had to put everything at the lowest setting and view distance at 20. I still had horrible FPS by the way.
That destroyed the experience for me in a great way, one of the things I heavily seek in games like this one is the beauty of the game, I enjoy the artwork. I couldn't with this game due to the bad performance.
I have no positive things to say about the voice acting, it was cringeworthy to listen to, it was to obvious that the voice actor was reading a script on a piece of paper, I didn't get a sense of any personality, it was blank, you can even hear the voice actor stumble in some sentences, you know, when you stop and start over again and delete that recording, but no, it was included in the game when the voice actor messed up a bit, when they stopped for half a second to start a word over again, it was all left in the game.
The game is relaxing though, if you experience ASMR you will most likely experience it here. The rain is nice to listen to, the thunder is nice to listen to, the talking is nice to listen to as white noise while you're reading something on your 2nd monitor while auto walking.
No key rebinding, so that's obviously a huge negative. The graphic sliders are not descriptive, it's just Low, Medium, High or, get ready, EPIC! Yea, um, I wan't to know what kind of Anti-Aliasing it is, High AA means nothing, tell me what kind of AA it is.
I have to say though, the first path I took(Red) did keep me interested for about an hour but then I dropped of after that, it was to repetitive, there was literally nothing to do other than pressing W, listening to horrible voice acting and a meaningless story while taking screenshots.
Pros:
Good looking world.
Easy game to get 100% achievements in.
Cons:
Bad voice acting, 0 character.
Bad story, you can't relate to anything.
Horrible performance, even at the worst possible settings.
Literally no content or interactivity.
Extremely repetitive, have fun doing both the paths, I hope you have 2 monitors to do something else while you auto-walk.
Not worth the price, this game should be free to play or one of those horrible games, which it is, that is priced at 20 cents.
I do not recommend this game to anyone, only reason to get this is if you're a person that likes to get 100% achievements in games, this one is an easy target. Other than that, don't buy it.
2/10. Giving it 2 due to the fact that it's a half decent world to look at.

is a nice casual walking simulator with a deeper story/philosophy which unfolds while you're walking. So far I've just chosen one of the paths, the shorter one, and the visuals are very nice indeed.
What I find most impressive is the involvement of its creator; he's a regular visitor/poster on the forums and takes the bugs and improvements of his game very serious and has already released some updates with new or reworked content!
That alone makes this Indy title a small gem.

First of all, Drizzlepath: Genie is a walking simulator in it's purest sense. All you do is walk while hearing a story.
The atmosphere is great! The game is created with the CryEngine which really shows. On your journey you'll see huge areas rich with detail. The rain, the grass moving in the wind, the various flowers - the all add to the beautiful scenery.
Through your jouney you'll visit different places such as flowery fields, snowy mountains, and caves.
If you like taking screenshots of beautiful places, this is a good game for it.
From time to time a narrator tells a story with a calm voice which adds to the whole experience. The story is quite poetic.
You walk very slow. I would really liked an option to walk faster. When I wanted to close a bit closer on the scenery I just stopped.
You follow a path on your journey but I still felt lost a few times. Some times there's a long period without any narration which can be a bit confusing (at least it was for me in the beginning). At one point the narrator said I was walking the wrong way but I'm pretty sure I didn't.
Very few times you'll find a small puzzle or some rocks you have to jump over - these seemed out of place compared to the rest of the experience.
Overall, if you are into walking simulators and looking at beautiful scenery, this is a good game. If you are looking for a bit more action or involvement, stay away from this game.
Disclaimer: a key was provided by the developer in return for an unbiased review.

So far, I absolutely love this game. It's intense and really captures the stark terror one might feel when stranded on a space station with a hostile xenomorph. The graphics and sound effects are superb and it's pretty much everything I could ever hope for in a sci-fi/stealth horror game. It's a very difficult game, too, and really challenges the player to pay attention to their surroundings and actions. There isn't much of a margin for error.
That said, my only gripe is the infrequent save points in the game. I suppose that's designed to increase the tension by adding a sense of urgency and danger but I felt it became more frustrating than anything. Certain parts of the game started to feel repetitive when you have to keep creeping down a series of passages in order to get past a specific, difficult part of the game only to die and have to "rinse and repeat" until finally succeeding and managing to find another save point. The repitition detracts from the sense of terror and immersion. More frequent save points or a 'quick save' option to use whenever would have significantly improved my overall experience so far while maintaining the tension.
That said, it's a great game if you like the survival/horror genre. I would recommend it to anyone that wants to be scared spitless while playing a video game.

Tropico 3 is a delight of a game. It features funny and charming music, atmosphere, and little details that continue to make me smile. The varieties of different approaches you can take to building an economy or satisfying your people are great, and the balance between diplomacy, economics, and and politics is very good. My major complaints with this game are that many game mechanics are not explained at all (very poor tutorial) and the ways things effect each other are not readily apparent in many situations. When first playing the game, youll often find your economy suddenly tanking, and youll have to dig through the economy hunting for clues as to why it is doing so. The constant effect of each building and policy should be more visible immediately within the UI, in order to avoid situations where the player doesn't understand the causes of an event. Also, the AI needs a lot of work, and the garage and combat systems are very flawed. Overall, I'm excited to see where they take it.

Drizzlepath: Genie does some things right though does have a few caveats that will deter some players. I'll start with a simple pros and cons list.
To expand on these a bit... the world itself is lovingly crafted and looks beautiful and can make for some fantastic screenshots.
The voice acting (one character, just the protagonist) is for the most part quite good. Sometimes the script gets a bit scholarly and it can feel a bit drab, but any lines with emotion come off well.
The story isn't perfect, and it took me two playthroughs (needed if you want to genuinely complete the game) to really appreciate it. I felt a bit underwhelmed by, and it can be a bit jarring at first, but that just may be that the hints along the way are very subtle and easy to miss. The vignettes and still images that help the story along are pleasant.
The game is tagged as a "Walking Simulator" and that's a pretty accurate description. There's not very much "game" here. There are a few jumping challenges, a few very basic puzzles, but it's for the most part just a lot of walking. I don't see this as necessarily a pro or con depending on who you are, but it's good to be aware of it going in.
The game encourages you to explore by making things off in the distance intriguing and piquing your curiosity. Unfortunately, the game can unintentionally penalize you by having a few areas where you can get stuck. There are invisible walls keeping you safe from most cliffs. This can be really frustrating, and if you've just recently loaded a save and don't have a checkpoint, you'll need to restart the whole game. I'm hoping the dev can fix this and include more frequent checkpoints and have them active even when loading a save.
The world can feel quite barren, though this feels deliberate in the sense that the plot relies on it. But I would have really loved to see some deer or squirrels or something other than trees or mountains in the distance.
I left thinking it was a bit of a mixed experience.
Full disclosure - I received a free copy of the game from the developer for review purposes.

Disclaimer: Key provided by developer for review purposes.

Drizzlepath: Genie is a walking simulator that takes you on a journey through beautiful scenery. The rain soaked atmosphere is very relaxing. It's not as dark as Dear Esther. The colours are quite muted, but that's appropriate for an overcast day. The landscape contains various locations and objects of interest and it's worth looking around to find things you might otherwise miss.
Occasional voice narration enhances the experience. It's extremely poetic and descriptive, painting pictures in words to further enhance the visuals. There's also relaxing music providing a soundtrack to your journey. It's pleasant enough to listen to but can get repetitive at times. I usually turn music off once that happens (which it does with all games), and often play without music or replace it with music of my own choice. It would be nice to have that option added. It's enjoyable enough just listening to the rain IMO.
There are many excellent opportunities for screenshots in this game, which can extend the gameplay time considerably. There's a control to zoom out to give a wider angle of view and another to crouch, which can provide you with a different viewpoint. You can even change to a grainy, monochrome view which gives a completely different look to the game, and is good for "arty" screenshots.
In spite of the overcast sky, sunlight does stream through gaps in the clouds. Unusually it shines from multiple directions. Perhaps this planet orbits multiple suns? This sunlight causes purple lens flare, which often looks appealing, but sometimes I felt there was a bit too much of it and I wished I could turn it off. UPDATE: If you set filter effects to medium or low the lens flare will be disabled.
It may be worth noting that I have not experienced any of the micro-stutters than mrorange mentioned in his review.
I don't understand what everything means in this game because I haven't completed it yet. In fact, I've only been exploring the green path so far (there are two different paths through the game), but after three hours I think I've experienced enough to write this review. I'll update it once I've played more. Unfortunately I suffer from motion sickness in first person games so I can't play them for too long without feeling ill. I also take loads of screenshots so it'll take me a lot longer to complete than if I simply walked through it all without stopping.
Overall this is a very pleasant visual and aural experience (rather than a game) which I recommend to anyone who enjoys simply walking around and looking at beautiful scenery. It's a treat to the senses and is ideal for relaxation when you feel like taking a break from more demanding games.
Disclaimer: a key was provided by the developer in return for an unbiased review, which is the only kind of review I'm willing to write.

Being a "walking simulator", Drizzlepath: Genie's gameplay is very simplistic. There is almost no action to be performed apart from some jumps, pulling a lever and stepping on a platform. However, the whole gaming experience comes from admiring the beauty of the scenery while walking down along a path in the mountains and listening to the narrator's voice. The visual and auditive stimuli are very well balanced in Drizzlepath: Genie, successfully inducing in the player a state of deep relaxation and introversion - which in my opinion is the essence of this genre.
Reminiscent of the symbolism of the red/blue pill of the movie The Matrix (like my boyfriend cleverly noticed), the protagonist Lula has to make a choice between journeying on the red path or the blue path. The red path, which is the shorter of the two, will lead her to embracing the painful truth of reality - of who she is and what the purpose of the journey was; on the other hand, the blue path, which is supposed to let the protagonist remain in her own fabricated reality will leave the end entirely to the player's interpretation.
While walking down the path, the narrator will provide various texts - ranging from words of wisdom, memories, little stories or anecdotes to abstract snippets rich in philosophical metaphors. While I largely enjoyed reading the texts from the first categories, the latter were almost incomprehensible for me and felt like random words glued together without conveying any palpable meaning. That's unsurprising, considering that I am not endowed with a poetic soul; though I am pretty sure that the fans of this aesthetic genre would enjoy them. The ability to toggle the subtitles on of course helps understanding the narration, however I found myself desperately wanting a button that allowed me to scroll up and read those abstract snippets again, in an effort of apprehending them.
However, what really "spoke" to me was the music that follows you almost all the time, a soothing, relaxing music, sometimes emotional, other times mysterious, always changing according to the scenery; the sound of the rain and thunder, the sound of the wind whooshing when you're on a high peak of a mountain.
The landscape is simply beautiful and stunning. You will often find yourself deviating from the straightforward path for the purpose of taking a screenshot of a valley from up above the mountain. The path is most of the times rather narrow and doesn't leave much space for exploration around it, but it will lead sooner or later to openings from which you can admire a breathtaking view of the entire world, triggering in you a very palpable feeling of expansion, just like a walk through the mountains in reality would do.
In comparison to the first Drizzlepath game, the graphics are considerably superior, the game now using the Unreal 4 engine (as compared to CryENGINE from the first game). There is a noticeable increased attention to the detail - the mountains are now covered with snow, the flowers and trees come in many shapes and forms, the drops of rain sparkle on the rocks in the light of the sun etc - in one word, the textures are much more complex.
On the other hand, both Drizzlepath: Genie or Drizzlepath could use some adjustments and improvements in configuring their engines. While Drizzlepath completely crashed my PC because of GPU overheating while playing on highest settings (my PC is not optimized for high-tier graphics but it's still a decent gaming PC), Drizzlepath: Genie was much more forgiving in that regard, resulting only in some frame drops and a blurred motion while turning the camera - nothing that I couldn't fix by lowering a bit the quality of the shadows which seem to be very resource-consuming.

In conclusion, Drizzlepath: Genie is a very relaxing experience and one of the good games of its genre. Would I recommend it? Yes! For the beauty of the scenery, for the boundless world, for the calming music combined with the narration, for the quite lengthy gameplay that it offers (2-4h for the red path, 3-5h for the blue path), I consider the price to be very affordable. Note though that in order to enjoy all of these, you must come equipped with quite a good gaming PC, since the graphic requirements are quite high (make sure to check the recommended specs before buying it).

The term 'walking simulator' was first tossed around to be an insult towards games that some deemed to be 'not really a game'. For some though, sitting down to a game that's relaxing and likely visually pleasing can be a tranquil experience, and no less of a 'game' than any other. Lately though, you see the term 'walking simulator' being applied to just about any first person game that doesn't let you shoot things. Even games heavy on platforming or difficult puzzle solving.
however, is your classic 'walking simulator' with soothing music, pretty scenery, and a story to tell.
You play as Lula, your goal is to find the Genie, and you have been cursed with the inability to run. That's right, this is quite literally a walking simulator. I'm not sure if that was meant as a joke (because if so, it was a really good one), as you usually can't run in games like this, with no explanation provided. At the beginning of the game, you are presented with two paths to take. Each will give you a different narrated tale along your journey. One path will lead you to what is technically the 'good ending' and the other the 'bad'. One path is also significantly longer than the other, so strap on your good hiking boots. The longer path does feel perhaps a bit
long. While it's broken up with things to see, most of it is the same environment and begins to wear you down with it's 'sameness'. It is worth it to replay the game for the alternate path however, as it is different, especially if you pick the longer path first.
The music is enjoyable, mixed with the sound of rain and occasional thunder (though the rain is more prevalent on one of the paths than the other) it makes for a nice ambiance. I played with the graphics cranked up to max and it looked quite nice, my only personal complaint being a lack of resolution that fit my monitor, but I know 21:9 is hardly standard, I only wish I could have had a nice full screen view of everything.
certainly isn't a game for everyone. The majority of it is much like a pleasant hike, minus the actual physical exertion. So if that isn't your kind of thing, then you probably won't enjoy this.  But if you're in the mood to sit back, relax, listen to a story, while meandering through nature, it's definitely worth a look.

Drizzlepath: Genie is a fun and relaxing "walking simulator" with a rich storyline and really amazing voiceover. Don't walk the Drizzlepath looking for challenging opponents or difficult puzzles. You won't find any of that here; in fact, there's only a couple of actual interactions with the environment in the whole game!
What you
find are incredible vistas, intriguing landscapes, and bunches of weird little "easter eggs" hidden here and there, all accompanied by lovely and literate poetry revealing the inner thoughts and memories of the game's main character, Lula, a village girl tasked with finding a mysterious "genie." There are two pathways to explore, each with its own ending, but venturing off of the path will yield some surprising and even seemingly incongruous finds: hidden objects, and even people! It's a virtual sightseeing tour, through the eyes of a young poet.
If you're in a hurry to get somewhere or to find answers, you may find the lengthy journey (five hours or so, if you walk the path at top speed and don't stop to smell the roses) a bit tedious. If, on the other hand, you like to see beautifully-rendered scenery and explore unusual and imaginative terrain at a relaxed pace--without anything jumping out to kill you--then Drizzlepath: Genie might just suit you.

Horror games put us in an environment where we constantly experience strong feelings of fear. “Alien Isolation” is not just another game in this style. It provides the player with the opportunity to enter into the fictional world of “Alien,” the franchise created by the incredible filmmaker Ridley Scott.
In this environment the player slowly discovers what is happening in a giant space ship. It is an incredible sensation to walk through the ship constantly afraid of what could happen; afraid of something we don’t know; afraid of something that we cannot see, but which could appear suddenly at any time, out of the darkness where it lurks.
This game is fantastic because it resembles “Alien,” the movie, in which the horror of the crew was felt walking through the dark corridors of their ship, knowing that something unexpected could happen at any moment.
Many games have been based on the movie’s universe. The majority are focused on the action of killing lots of monsters. In “Alien Isolation” however there is a mix of horror and action that refer to the first movie of the series. At last fans of this horrifying franchise can enjoy a game worthy of the universe created by one of the masters of science fiction.

TL:DR I'm of two minds with this one, but decided to not recommend this game, because the core gameplay just doesn't feel fun or exciting in any real way. Story is great, it's definitely my favorite part of this game. But the combat is uninspired, and pretty much the same thing you see in every other MMORPG. And the core gameplay is basically just number management, and nothing else.
Pros:
+ The Story: It carries the game big time, and is definitely it's biggest asset. This is one of the few times that i've consistently wanted to follow the story all the way through, and the voice acting on all the dialogue definitely helped that alot.
+ The Voice Acting: It not only makes the game alot more immersive, but it's also alot easier to follow the story, when you don't have to read 90% of it.
+ Graphics: The game looks great, and definitely does alot for the immersion of the game.
+ Player market: Players can form guilds, that can sell items from their own stall in several cities. The guild leaders takes a cut, which makes them want to have good traders and put up stalls in the right places. Everybody is profiting in this system, and i really like how they put it together. Also it's not a global market, where everybody's prices are listed on the same list. Each guild stall have individual prices, depending on whatever they have put for sale. Therefore the prices are not insanely low, and the insentive to sell stuff is still there.
+ The Thieving System: This is one of my favorite parts of the game, i spent alot of time stealing stuff and sneaking around. The guards are decent aslong as you don't fight more than 1 at a time, then they get incredibly frustrating as you're infinitely stunned/rooted. (Especially if you're on a horse, since you'll spent a good 3 seconds getting up after it throws you off it whilst they kill you.)
+ The Fist/rock throwing spell on the dragonknight class. (Throwing a rock into a guards face after he rooted you for a full 10 seconds is hillarious, i would go tea bag him if there wasn't a cooldown on the effect.)
+ Every single Khajit NPC (They just all seem like that friend who is about to get you into trouble, but will help you get out of it aswell.)
+ Dolmens: Those portals look really awesome when they appear, and the sound they make along with the storm is so incredibly immersive. I love standing in the city, and hearing that horn go off and just run to defend the city, very accelerating.
+ Pets and Mounts
+ First/Third person options (although first person feels useless when it comes to avoiding spells, since you can barely see the red casting markings on the ground.)
+ Freedom to explore: You can explore everything at any level now, which is wonderful. (But it certainly didn't change the importance of upgrading gear constantly to keep up.)
Cons:
- The Combat: This is my bigest gripe with the game, and really the main reason why i can't enjoy it. 90% of the time, i feel like i'm fighting a ghost. I'm pretty much just mashing a bunch of buttons, and the only reaction i'm getting it the health bar lowering.
- Number management gameplay: Playing a game like this honestly feels like working. I'm constantly getting loot with certain numbers, whilst leveling up and thereby making my old loot useless so i have to optimize to my new level all the way till max level. Whilst i do that i have to gather a billion weapons, armors, plants, hides, w/e to level up whatever skills i want to max out. And since this is pretty much all that this game is about, then that is pretty much what most of us are gonna do. Some might call this "progression" and say they enjoy it, i would personally call it "Wasting every single opportunity to increase the happiness in my life". I'm playing a video game, i wanna experience something, i wanna fight exciting bosses, i want to explore the world, i do NOT want to gather a million items to max out each and every skill, or do the same boring combat for weeks on end, that basically just consists of managing numbers, whilst just hoping that the next skill i unlock will make the game fun.
- Too much pointless loot, that only differs with numbers. (now you deal 5 more damage, yaaaay.)
- Too much Inventory management. (Also owned items, and stolen items of the same kind takes up 2 spaces even though they're the same item.)
- Item Laundering is only useful on rare items, since you can only launder a specific amount of items. So laundering 100 swords worth 200 gold each, is the same as laundering 100 potatos worth 1 gold each. (Let me launder my damn potatoes Zenimax!)
- And now that i'm getting to lvl 30, people are starting to kick me from dungeon raids. Proving that these games will only allow tryhards, and anyone playing casually will still have a bad time in these types of games.

So let's begin with a summary about the game, it takes place at the Second Era, one era before Morrowind, Daggerfall, Arena and Oblivion and two eras before the events in Skyrim. The game is set on Tamriel during the Interregnum, a period of time between the assassination of the Last Potentate, Savirien-Chorak, and the rise of Tiber Septim, where there was chaos, bloodshed, and no Emperor on the Ruby Throne. Varen Aquilarios attempted to turn into the Drangonborn for several years in order to legitimate the Throne, he formed a group of five people, named the "Five Companions". Their mission was to retrieve the Amulet of Kings to make Varen ascend into a Dragonborn, but at some point one of them, Mannimarco, betrayed the group, revealing his intentions, he was an agent of Molag Bal and it's plan was to merge Nirn and the Oblivion.
The Civil-War is based in three groups trying to take Cyrodill, Aldmeri Dominion, Ebonheart Pact and Daggerfall Covenant, depending on which side you pick you'll play at somewhere in the map, but after reaching some level you'll be able to explore the whole map, which is almost the whole Tamriel.

Normally, a video game is made for entertainment. In "Papers, Please", the entertainment is a side effect that comes from the engagement you have with the storyline.
"Papers, Please" challenges the very definition of a video game. Excluding open-ended games, most storyline-driven video games can be expressed in another media such as a written novel or a movie; even the most non-linear game with branching storylines and choices, which this game falls into that category.
However, "Papers, Please" can NOT be expressed in another media. It is a personal experience. Your emotion, your personality and your very own engagement with the story defines what the narrative is.
Don't let the graphics tip you off; if anything, if it does tip you off, then it's working on you, because the story is as cold as the visual suggests.
Gameplay-wise, it's a concept that would strangely be classified as "novelty" despite the very administrative nature of the gameplay. It takes a boring and tiring process that is, reading and checking documents, and turns it into a formidably executed source of entertainment. The green stamp and the red stamp, they don't look terrifying but you'll quickly realize the amount of power they hold, because "you" are the one stamping the documents.
Replayability will depend on your ability to ignore your emotions, if you do feel any. There are some branching paths in the story that I did not dare to explore because choosing the "other" option feels too wrong.

Dishonored 2 gives you the option to fight and kill your enemies, stealth your whole playthrough without killing a single person, or mix both. Going plain berserk probably won't work though--you
have to sneak a lot, or you'll find yourself fighting battles you can't possibly win... or will at least have to try dozens of times to pull it off... and you'll only manage if you set the game on Easy, so... don't try that, you're not really supposed to.
The game warns you, by the start of level 2, that killing will lead to a dark ending, whereas just leaving people unconscious will lead you to the good one, so if you wanna meet Jesus, live in heaven and all that crap one day, you
play this stealthly.
Ok, it's a stealth game. And since Dishonored 2 is a stealth game, it involves a lot of trial and error, or quicksaving-quickloading, which is rather annoying, but... well, I don't really see a way around that, and that's one of the reasons I'm personally not a big fan of stealth games. Thankfully, loading times here are really short, so it's ok. You do have a skill that reveals enemies in a certain radius around you (so you can plan your moves and try to get everything right) but said radius is so short that in the vast majority of times you end up being spotted on your first attempt to do anything. Often several times. So... F5-F9.
Nonetheless, Dishonored 2 is pretty good. You have Runes (to unlock skills, half of which are magic powers, the other half physical prowesses) and Bone Charms (equipable items that give you minor bonuses) that you must seek out in every map, money to upgrade your gear, interesting story and characters, and good level design (two maps are
interesting, and probably worth a look for anyone who works with this stuff... and simply cool for everyone else).
The game also gives you plenty of options for everything. You can play as the Empress Emily Kaldwin, or her father, the Royal Protector Corvo Atano. You can use magic, or not. If you do, you can teleport, turn into a shadow, possess animals, mesmerize enemies, chain them together to affect everyone with a single hit, ... Either way, you have a pistol, a crossbow with a variety of different darts, stun and shrapnel mines, grenades, ... There's also different paths to reach most places, and you can always choose wether to simply kill or somehow let live each level's "boss," which will, of course, impact the final outcome of the story.
Only one thing left me disappointed in Dishonored 2: the ending, sadly. I played the entire game without killing anyone nor ever being spotted, solved every level the "peaceful" (and hardest) way possible and all I got for it were 3 or 4 moving images along with small voice-over texts briefly summing up what happened after I... well, not to spoil anything: after I did what I was supposed to do and finished the game. But I had a good time anyway.

It is a very basic but good definition what to expect if you play a walking simulator. It is important to note that this genre is not for everyone. It is a mere niche in gaming. If you do not enjoy the fact of just walking around on a very linear way, this game might not be for you. But if you like very basic, but easy controls and to have a clear purpose, which means to get from point a to b. Why not to give this game a chance.
The game has some good atmosphere with a great soundtrack and a cute voice-acting which is comprehensible. It is though difficult to overall follow the story. To really understand what it is all about. This could have been done more clearly. I am also not very happy with the performance as I see even on my Titan X some weird stuttering when I turn for example around. Some gameplay glitches made me start the game twice – when leaving the prescribed path I was falling in a trench and could not get out of it.
You might get some nice screenshots out of this game. But can this be the only purpose of the whole game? I am not sure. Overall there could have been more landmarks and more events, some fauna, some animals. I am missing some more wow-effects. This was better in the previous Drizzlepath.
I like the genre and I am happy about every game that we get for it. I will recommend this game to gamer that like very slow paced games or look for some handy screenshot opportunities. Gamer that do not like to hassle too much. I will also recommend this game for everyone that is a hardcore walking simulator fan. That’s for sure.
For the casual gamer that looks for an interesting story and some more action orientated gaming experience, I can unfortunately not recommend this game.
The overall idea of the Drizzlepath series is great and I am happy to see more in the future. This time with a more captive storyline and more interaction. Why not implement some more little events during the long path to the top of the mountain?!
And my last point concerns Nvidia 3D Vision and VR gaming in general. This game could actually win a lot by implementing 3D vision in a native way – the engine allows it. And also with regards to VR gaming in the coming month, I see a lot of potential for games like Drizzlepath, in order to convince a whole new customer base - that might never have played PC games - which is looking for some simple virtual walking possibility.

Before I begin I want to note that I was provided with a key from the developer in exchange for reviewing this game. This did not in any way affect my interpretation of it and what follows is my honest unbiased opinion.
Drizzlepath: Genie is a first-person linear exploration game. You play as a girl named Lula, who must go on a journey to unravel some mysterious truth that will determine the destiny of herself and her loved ones. The gameplay is simple; you walk forward following a clearly defined pathway while listening to the storyline as it unfolds during your journey. A wonderful feature of this game is the auto-walk button, which prevents you from spending the entirety of the game holding down the W key to move forward. There are a few occasions where you have to jump to reach the next area, but there is no falling damage so failing to do so merely means taking a few extra seconds to try again. However, it is worth mentioning that correctly timing your jumps can be tricky and get to be slightly frustrating until you get the hang of it.
Soon after starting the game you will come to a fork in the road. Depending on which direction you choose you will end up with one of two different endings as well as a different narrative to accompany you on your journey. Because of this you can spend a decent amount of time in this game in order to unlock both of these paths and their end results. One path is considerably longer than the other and seems to drag on a bit too much at points as compared to the shorter path. There are some definite pacing issues with this path, and it could stand to be slightly shorter as I found myself wishing it could speed up a bit at times.
The landscape is gorgeous and well designed with clear attention to detail, causing you to really want to look around and take in your surroundings. Those who enjoy taking screenshots will be pleased to find plenty of opportunities for beautiful captures. The music that accompanies the game is serene and well matched with the environment. The sound effects, such as rain falling and thunder in the distance, are very well done and do quite a bit to set the atmosphere. The voice of Lula narrates throughout your journey and is one of my favorite aspects of the game, not so much for the voice acting but rather the content as the writing is beautiful and thoughtful, at times even poetic. There are also a fair amount easter eggs to be found if you look around a bit more carefully, something which makes exploring more interesting. All together these provide for a very aesthetically pleasing and calming environment that is very easy to get lost in.
This game is fairly demanding to run, and it seems that there is room for improvement as far as better optimizing it. While my PC is definitely not top of the line it can usually run new games on high/medium settings, but in order to run this properly I had to lower the settings a bit. This was not enough of an issue to prevent me from playing or enjoying the graphics it has to offer, but is worth noting for anyone with an outdated PC who is considering this purchase.
If you are not a fan of walking simulators you shouldn’t be surprised to hear that this is likely not a game for you. There is a certain level of patience required to appreciate this genre as it relies not on action and reflex but instead providing a nice atmosphere and a story to match. If you enjoy games in this vein and go into this knowing what you expect, you should find yourself pleased with the very calming and enriching experience which Drizzlepath: Genie has to offer.
