It’s been a while since my last review (apologies!), but I’m here now to tell you a little bit about Drizzlepath Genie, a new game in the genre known as ‘walking simulators’. It looks pretty, that’s for sure, but is there anything underneath all that beauty or is it just style-over-substance? Shall we take a closer look?
Drizzlepath Genie is one such game with a poetic story. For a walking simulator it has some very strong writing, with deep meaning. I enjoyed it, mostly, but sometimes the sentences seem a little too complex/convoluted making the story hard to understand at times.
Unlike other games in the genre the game offers two paths to take. Both will give you an entirely different experience, with different visuals and different stories. The bad/wrong path is the longest, the good/right path is the shortest. I’m not going to spoil it for you, you’ll have to make the decision yourself, but I (as well as the developer) encourage to play through both stories. I think that each path offers roughly 97% unique dialog, and one of the paths is about twice as long as the other.

While walking a female narrator (who is also your character) will tell you some stories. The stories start off a bit boring and at the start you have no idea what to expect so I guess this only makes sense. Later on the overarching story becomes more interesting and near the end of my first playthrough (bad path) I learned to appreciate it even more. But it’s a slow story, with a lot of padding, especially if you take the bad path. I later noticed that the good path is more evenly paced and for most people it will be the better and more enjoyable path to take, but in general it feels like there are a lot of unnecessary detours.
Also, it seemed odd to me that she would tell a short story only to tell it to me in parts, with minutes in between. I would’ve rather heard her tell the entire story, and then at a later time begin a completely new one. I consider this also a part of the pacing issues the game has.
The paths you take are rather linear and while you can explore a little, it’s not encouraged except for just a few times (if you see red/blue magic (fireflies?), for example, and floating verses/poems). But these distractions are hardly interesting for most people. They can’t be interacted with, you see. Plus, the fact that the game has some collision detection issues makes exploring rarely fun or worth your time.
As for the controls: these are quite simple, as expected. With the WASD keys you move around, with the mouse you control the camera, with E you interact and with Q you can auto-walk (which is brilliant if you’re lazy or, like me, have to take notes for your review). And there’s a zoom function that, to me, serves no real purpose.
The auto-walk button made me appreciate the environments more, though and I hope to see this function in more walking simulators from now on. But let’s face it; it will always remain a rather passive experience, even if you don’t use this specific button.
As for improvements… One thing that would make the game instantly more enjoyable would be to either implement a run button (which you’re already basically doing if I’m not mistaken, but it still feels like walking) or just increase the walking speed. Yes, it would decrease the game’s length but I think more people would enjoy it as most of us play the game for the story and not necessarily the walking part itself. It would definitely work for the bad path (considering the padding issues), but I’m not entirely sure how and if it would work for the good path. Despite that I think it’s still worth looking into.
I have absolutely no complaints about the audio. The voice acting is mostly solid, but I wish it sometimes had a tad more emotion.
The music itself is quite minimalist. Occasionally you’ll hear a few tracks, most of it piano music and/or string instruments, but other than that you’ll be listening to ambient sounds like thunder and rain falling down. It’s very calm and soothing and in this case it fits both the genre and the story.
Visually the game is pretty, but it has some pretty flat lighting. Fortunately, this can be solved by using ENB profiles (or other similar alternatives).
You’ll be walking across seemingly infinite forests, caves and mountains and while there’s little variety in the 4-5 hours you’ll be playing it it’s still nice to look at.
The performance is okay-ish, with framerates fluctuating between 40-60+FPS on my system (if you’re interested in my specs please visit my profile). I don’t think it will bother anyone since the game doesn’t rely on fast (action) scenes.
Overall it’s a very pleasing game to look at.

A playthrough can take anywhere between 1,5-3 hours and then you can play it again, taking a different path that tells you a different side of the same story and one that will also have some different art. Nothing major, though; if you’ve played through it once then you’ll have seen most of it. All in all it can take up to 4,5-6 hours before you’ll be completely done with it.
Drizzlepath Genie starts off rather slow, and has a lot of padding in it (specifically in the bad path), but it fortunately picks up near the end of the story, about 2/3th in. It might not be a game for anyone: there’s lot of complex, poetic writing in it and if you’re not a native English speaker you might have a little trouble understanding it all and making sense of it. You naturally also have to like or be interested in walking simulators.
Keep in mind that there’s very little interactivity – with this I mean that you might feel you’re not truly
a game - so you can expect a lot of listening/reading and walking (and a little bit of (frustrating) jumping).
If it was a little more concise this probably would’ve been a no-brainer. It will still be for fans of the genre I expect. For everyone else the game will probably be too slowly paced, which might make the entire experience feel unrewarding or dull at times. But if you ever have some spare money laying around it’s still worth a try, if only for the excellent writing and deeper-than-expected story.
Pros:
+ Strong writing with quite a decent story
+ Voice acting is also quite good
+ Could use some extra shading but overall it has pretty graphics
+ Two different paths to play
Mixed:
+/- Story starts off slow, but ultimately picks up
+/- The slow pacing in general might turn people off
+/- Repetitive environments, but fortunately, it mixes things up about halfway through
Cons:
- Might feel a little too poetic/cryptic for some
- The world feels and mostly is completely empty (although this might be intentional, I’m not quite sure yet)
- Can feel very passive at times
- Some performance and collision detection issues
(Ratings aren’t calculated based on a formula, but on my personal feelings)

Drizzlepath: Genie is about a girl who takes a journey down one of two possible paths to discover what the "Genie" is, and what it could mean for her village and her future. If you're expecting the game to be anything but a narrative of sorts, turn back now as that is what this basically is when you break it down. No puzzles, no enemies, no difficulty involved - this is why people tend to say it's a "relaxing" experience.
It took me just over 2 hours to complete the game. You choose one of two paths at the beginning of the game. You are encouraged to take the second path at the completion of the game as it will offer a "different" experience, however I opted to let the credits roll and call it a night.
The gameplay itself is effortless. There are a couple "parkour areas" that you have to complete, but again, this is about the journey being more important than the destination... or... gameplay.. Right?
So let's pick it apart a little, shall we? Not because I hated it, but because I think that it really wasn't all that good. There was so much room for improvement and so many little things that bothered me adding up as I played, that I just have to be honest about disliking those things. Again, I didn't hate the game and actually enjoyed the couple hours it took me to "beat" one of the paths, but I'm not about to rave about it to all those who might listen.
The description of the game here on Steam defines it as: "A captivating story and fantastic atmosphere combine with immersive graphics, natural environments, and a calming, ambient soundtrack to make it a journey you may not soon forget."
There's a problem with each individual element of that sentence.
1) The story wasn't captivating to me. I wasn't gripping the edge of my seat, straining to hear the next little tidbit of the narrative. To be captivated by it would be a very long stretch. I won't spoil what it's about, but the story asks several questions that either have no answer or can't be answered. These elements of the story discuss mortality, life itself, creation, greed, and so forth. Some of these stories were poetic, while others were along the lines of fairy tales. The questions asked should be the questions we've all asked ourselves before, and while I listened to the narritive, it was more like listening to some gradeschool journal of an inquiring child..... or was that the point? I mean the perspective is that of a young girl, so maybe that was entirely it, but I just couldn't be captivated by asking the cliche 'thoughtful digital novel' question of "what is life?"
2) The fantastic atmosphere and immersive graphics aren't fantastic or immersive. I played on the maximum settings with ease, and yet was unimpressed by it. The entire game seemed like a play-test for the Unreal engine. The collision detection was bad, the invisible barriers were bad, the constant lighting glitches were SO bad. I mean there were areas where small lights led the way to points of interest, and these lights would "ghost" across the screen when you move the mouse around. Even the in-game text had a shine so reflective, that it caused artifacting on the screen. The folliage and surface objects all looked last-generation, and store-bought with little to no customization. The terrain itself was completely contrived and unrealistic. There was nothing natural about it, really. I mean at least the description could be honest about the environments being something of fantasy rather than saying it's natural. There are even moments when character models make an appearance frozen in time along the path for no reason but to suggest the developer had models on hand from a demo that they put into the game "just because". It was weird. The lighting was what completely destroyed any and all immersion though... the fact that you could jump off a sheer rock face and survive didn't help either.
3) The soundtrack was well-suited, however with a distinct lack of volume control or the ability to disable the music altogether, I felt that it actually removed more of my attention from the surrounding elements and on-going narrative than it helped add to the experience. By the end of the game, I felt I was asking my own questions about life itself... for example: "What would life be like if I were to rip my ears out right now to avoid hearing this music play any longer?" Ok, that's a bit harsh I admit, but the music was overpowering, loud, and indeed atmospheric in a world without atmosphere which made it feel out of place. Softer music? No music? I was internally begging for both.
4) The voice acting is bad. There, I said it. I don't mean to offend anyone, but there's no real way for me to avoid that opinion. I've known a lot of voice actors, and I know how tough it can be, but I felt that the voice was about as far from what I would expect from the dialog as you can get. Maybe it was the accent, the tone, or the way that the sentences were read out with strange pauses and emphasis on what I felt were the wrong words.... but it all sounded like some nursery school teacher is reading a book to children. In a game that is supposed to tug at the meaning of life itself, it's weird to hear it from the perspective of a voice that doesn't sound like it's experienced professional voice acting before. Not to mention the audio quality was off-putting as well with full on lip smacking and that sound your lips make when you open your mouth, loud into the recording. If there was any immersion left to be had, it was removed by having this voice go on through the experience. I hope people can understand my meaning and that I'm not just trying to be rude about it. As I consider it, it would be like using Shrek's voice over Mel Gibson's in braveheart. The voice acting is kind of there, but totally not suited for the genre or outlet.
Lastly, was this a memorable game? Probably not for me... I played one of the two paths and nothing about it really makes me want to endure the other path option. Maybe I went into this game with my hopes up too high. I'll take my chances with saying it wasn't for me though I can see how some will probably really enjoy it. I certainly can't recommend to any of my friends that they play this though, and that's me being honest.

is a fascinating and very atmospheric game that offers exploration along two different paths and a well presented and narrated storyline for both of them. Both paths you can walk are exclusive to each other, so to experience the whole game you have to play it twice. That does not really get repetitive tough, because they are very different from each other, both in story and in presentation.
I don't want to spoil too much of the story, but it is about a young girl that takes a journey to find something mysterious, and the journey becomes more then just the path that she walks. She will either find or loose herself on the way, and with it, the whole world around her.  You also don't need to know anything about the first Drizzlepath game, or have played it. This is an evolution of its concept, and a great one at that, but not a continuation of the story.
The majority of the gameplay involves walking along one of both paths (with possibilities to explore alongside it), listening to beautifully delivered and voiced narration, and finding scenic views while you wander. Both paths together will take you about four hours to finish, but if you explore and take screenshots (and you should totally do that) it could take much longer. The ambiance and graphics are great and help you to immerse yourself in the game world, the world of Drizzlepath is a worthwhile experience in my opinion.
On gameplay elements there is not much in this game, but more then in the first Drizzlepath. There is a pressure plate on one path and a switch to activate on the other, and also a rock you have to break. There are also stones falling down on both paths, but you don't have to actively evade them. And there are also a handfull of jumping sections. There is also no falling damage, you can explore without fear of dying, you might get stuck sometimes eventually, but you can start over from your last checkpoint at all times, so thats not a problem. And there are a lot of hidden things to find while we are at that.
The best part is probably the beautiful female voice you get to listen to. The story that is told is not always easy to follow tough, it is very poetic and full of difficult concepts, life and death, loss and anger, faith and spirituality, there is something for everyone here. The optional subtitles that you can enable make it also easier to follow the story.
The good thing is, if the story is not your thing, you can just tune out and explore the scenery and still have a good time. But if you like that kind of narration, it will probably blow you away, leave you pondering and questioning. The music is fitting to the narrative, its very good most of the time, but can get a bit repetitive if you stay in one aerea of the game for a longer time.
Technically the game is demanding. If you have an older PC you might have to turn down resolutions and graphical options to get it running smoothly. I think there is still room for optimization for this game in that regard. The user interface and options menu is probably my biggest negative point. It is spartanic and there is no key rebinding sadly, and also no separate sound sliders for music and voice. Another thing i noticed is that the game does not like alt-tabbing at all, you want to avoid that while you play this game.
I personally had a great time with the game and liked most the many screenshot opportunities the game offers. With all that said, if you don't like slow-paced games without action, then this game might not be interesting for you. The walking is slow, you can not run. This is about relaxing and experiencing. If you can appreciate its beauty and accept it for what it is, you will probably enjoy Drizzlepath: Genie.
The game was provided for free and i am working currently on the German translation of this game. I also did Beta testing and provided technical and marketing advice to the Developer. This review is still as unbiased as possible with this involvement.

I waited until the game was at a good sale price before picking it up, however after completing it, I would say it would have been worth it at full price.
If you haven't seen the movie, or if it's been a while, I highly recommend watching it before playing. The audio and visual elements of the game are beautifully crafted, and pull directly from the film, with many subtle (and some not-so-subtle) tips of the hat to the original cinematic masterpiece.
The graphics are very pleasing, the engine is wonderfully optimized, and should run very well even without a top of the line PC.
My personal favorite part of this game is the audio. The musical score does a fantastic job of building tension, and seamlessly informs you when danger is lurking, not only without breaking immersion, but while adding to it. What could have been a boring 30 second wait for a tram, becomes an anxiety filled moment of "Please please get here faster" as the creepy string music continues to rise, while you can hear the Alien stomping around somewhere nearby. Which brings me to the next element this game uses excellently:
URGENCY. There are many "mini-puzzles" in this game that you will need to complete in order to activate a computer, open a door, etc. However, while you are completing these simple puzzles, the game does not pause. Need to read through a computer terminal to find a PIN number? The Alien is still hunting for you. Need to manually punch in that PIN number to open a door? You'll need quick fingers because the Alien could be stomping up right behind you. Even while using a save point, or crafting items, the Alien continues to hunt. Some people may not like these elements, but for me they worked perfectly as intended, building tension and a sense of urgency.
The Alien's AI is very smart, and worse (or better, depending on how you look at it): random. There will be no set path it will follow, so you will never feel like you're completely safe (and you're not). Even hiding in a locker, or under a desk, if the alien was nearby when you entered, it may have seen where you went.
Altogether I highly recommend this game for any fans of the Horror / Survival genre's, as well as any fans of the Alien movies.

I usually stay far away from horror games because the setting in them does not appeal to me enough to make me tempt the dryness in the seat of my pants. Alien Isolation was different. This was an Alien game. And it came with a reputation of being sincere to the original movie in plot, setting and feeling. I couldn't resist trying it out. I was not disappointed.
Gameplay-wise the game ranks with the best of them. The controls are simple and engaging. I felt like I was in full control of my character. The way that the game makes you use the controls (i.e. how to open a door) is fantastic and it made me feel more immersed.
There was a part of the game where the doorways that could open were not marked at all, which was a bit of a pain to realize, but otherwise I had very little issues with the way the game presented the environment. It also took me two thirds of the game to realize that the motion sensor actually shows the direction to go towards the next objective. This is not clearly stated anywhere in the game. Learning this sooner would have saved me a buttload of backtracking in the previously mentioned section of the game. I also didn't realize how to reload batteries to the flashlight until the last section of the game. But using the flashlight would have been dangerously revealing, so I didn't mind much.
The environment in the game was great for creating a hemmed-in atmosphere that you would expect from spacecraft. There were not many open spaces, but whenever there were, I felt even more threatened because of the lack of cover to hide behind. And I wanted to hide a lot. Most of my experiences in the game were from a crouched position. It was the only way to remain silent and therefore the only way to have a chance of staying undetected.
One of the best reasons this game was awesome were the characters that I encountered. They made the game interesting and motivated me to push onwards. Horror games where the protagonist is the only meaningful character make me lose interest quickly. The way that the plot played out was neatly done and it kept me interested all through the game. The pacing was spot-on. At times I had plenty of time to get worried all by myself and other times the Alien was such a menace that I had to take breaks to steady my nerves again.
Even though I was quite content with a dark (and sometimes very well lit) room and my normal display, I can't help thinking how nerve-wracking this game would be on Oculus Rift or other such device.
I played the game on the recommended difficulty setting and I recommend you do too. It is not too difficult, but it makes the Alien that much more menacing.

You are a border guard of Arstotzka, a fictional government that has forced you into your current job. Your job, I might add, is to get as many people processed through the border as quickly as you can. The more people you process correctly, the more money you earn for the day. However, the job is made difficult with forged documentation, lists of rules you must make sure everyone has adhered to and an ever-increasing pile of paperwork to sift through. As you make mistakes, it costs money and could potentially get yourself jailed if you’re that terrible at your job. Your family has demands as well and the cost of living will go up, demanding that you work harder at processing more people through the gate every passing day.
Papers, Please isn’t a pleasant stroll through the park. The work you’re doing is tedious and dull. Every new face a source of income and potential frustration. Inspections taking progressively longer as you become more paranoid of your fallibility. Let one guy through and he’s fine. Let the next woman through, whose paperwork seems legitimate, only to get instantly penalized as her documentation was expired. Then I begin checking documentation to make sure it isn’t expired only to get penalized for letting a criminal through. Curses! Then you deny the next person because something seems missing with his documentatio--oops, nope, he was completely fine. I just denied a man from seeing his wife. Now I have to be extra-careful with the next guy, which takes me over an hour of in-game time just to realize that his paperwork completely checks out.
I need to move faster. The Next person has concealed explosives but I forget to check his weight so he gets through and blows up the guards. The day is abruptly over. My income cut short, my family starves. I curse my inadequacy.
Papers Please is a constant balance of fact-checking, observation and being as quick as possible with some of the most intentionally-clunky tools a border guard could possess. Each tool taking their own portion of precious time to make sure the documentation is or isn’t correct. Even if you know that person’s paperwork is wrong, you have to verify it with the in-game data checker, interrogate the person to be sure you’re correct and then and only then, can you call for the guards. All the while, the clock ticks on insidiously. Waiting to instantly call you out on that inevitable mistake you’ll make.
There are two main game modes, story and endless. Story is a 31 day campaign with branching story paths based on the decisions you make. Whether it’s support for the rising rebellion against Arstotzka, support of the old government, getting caught doing illegal activities or adverse conditions affecting your family, ultimately remains up to you. The story is excellently paced and down to earth with each decision you make being personable. While some decisions may seem black and white at first, you may find out later that events didn’t play out as you expected. The story more or less gives reason for why you’re there and how your decisions affect what ultimately ends up happening. To you, the government or other factions at work. While many that try to cross the border are procedural generated, in the story mode there are some that aren’t. These crafted characters can be depressing, heart wrenching or sometimes amusing. This isn’t a simulation of a border guard’s job but it’s the closest game to being one while remaining entertaining for many.
Endless gives you three ways to play with four levels of difficulty. There’s a timed mode where you process as many travelers in 10 minutes as possible. Perfection which has you going as long as you can until you make a mistake. Finally, there’s Endurance which has you playing until the score balances out from your mistakes. These simply give you a way to enjoy the game after the story and are a nice, simple addition.
Unsurprisingly basic settings, but usable for a 2D game. You have fullscreen, windowed mode and software rendering in case your hardware isn’t good enough. There’s a nudity on/off switch as well as an “Easy Mode” which gives you 20 credits every day. Separate volume sliders exist as well. However, there’s only one very catchy song that’s played in the main menu. The graphic style is, what I would consider, an oppressive & depressing pixelart. It looks great despite it not being a very colorful title.
Papers Please is one of my favorite games of 2013. It keeps the dry experience of a border guard but still has depressing stories to tell. The pixelart and dreary atmosphere combine with the constant & insidious pressure to make for a very compelling experience. It’s a game that I shouldn’t find enjoyable but yet I do. Its an odd game that says something not only through words but through the game’s mechanics as well.

Also, the armor in this game lets you have a lot of freedom with how you want your character to look. I've personally seen many cosplays in-game, while making a few myself. I've seen characters ranging from Zero from the Mega Man franchise to The Miner from Risk of Rain. Personally, with the amount of hours I've put into this game, I find PvE not that difficult or interesting, what holds me to this this game it the PvP. Now the PvP is flawed, definitely. Laggy players end up one-shotting you with magic or a backstab, backstabphishers are everywhere, and hackers run rampant. Hackers in general are a major problem. Its very simple to do it, and you can really get screwed by them. Firsthand, I have seen plenty of hackers, I've seen infinite health hackers, casters that can cast huge AoE hacks impossibly fast, and, my personal favorite, a person who invaded me, backstabbed me into an area (since backstabs teleport you to where it connected on their end) where I couldn't kill myself, and proceeded to enter the safe haven Majula, which is not invade-able, and has the only merchant that sells you healing items and never runs out of stock and a merchant that sell you an infinite supply of most upgrade materials. Also,please use a controller when you play this game, the keyboard controllers really bad, in my opinion. Also, just want to say this at the end, make sure you can run this game. Just saying. Don't be like me, the player who doesn't have a good enough graphics card, and plays the game without being able to see particles, including, but not limited to, summon signs, bloodstains, and all casts, excluding crystal magic. A brilliantly made and masterfully designed take on an Alien video game is utterly ruined by a single flaw. Somehow a game released in 2014 doesn't have a checkpoint system. The only way to save progress is at the save stations, which are unbearably few and far in between, leading to situations where one will get trapped completing the same mission objectives and hearing the same dialogue over and over and over again.
The Alien's AI makes it brilliantly unpredictable, which unfortunately means it will sometimes show up and charge right towards you, or simply systematically check every nook and cranny until it finds your hiding spot, and there's realistically nothing you can do to escape either scenario. This isn't necessarily a gamebreaker in a survival horror context, but with the aforementioned save issues, this can happen utterly randomly mere feet from a save station, setting you back, once again, 10 or 15 minutes.
To add further insult, the save stations inexplicably lock you out of resaving your game after use for some time, meaning you can't even double back to a save point after making some progress towards the inevitably failed run for the next one.
I don't even know why this issue exists in a modern AAA title. I want to like this game, its in 99% of respects a fantastic game, but with this one, critical, baffling flaw breaks the entire experience, and leaves me unable to recommend it.

When I first heard of STALKER, it was the graphics and spooky atmosphere that impressed me. That was over 5 years ago. Since then it has undergone a convoluted and long development process, which left many to believe the game was dead. Well, the finished product is pretty good, despite some bugs and missing features.
You play the role of marked one, in a subtle and chilling story about genetics and radiation experiments in the Chernobyl disaster zone. The place is full of mutants and warring bandits, loners, and factions, and is one of the most atmospheric games I've played.
Graphics- The technical visuals are quite solid, as the engine was updated since they originally started development. Shadows cast during storms and by lights stand out in particular. The draw distance is decent enough to make you feel like you're actually in the world, and the animations and effects are quite good.
Sound- The sound design in this game is top notch, you can hear every clap of thunder or rustle in the grass, but the gunfire is what really stands out. You can hear every distant shot fired at you and the sound of bullets whizzing by inches from your head.
Gameplay- This game has some really incredible survival mechanics. You are forced to scavenge for ammo, food, water, and other survival essentials, or buy them at inflated prices from the few merchants in "The Zone". Your inventory allows you to carry a reasonable amount of supplies, but you will get tired quickly if carrying too much. The game does not rely on any traditional RPG stats, but you can improve your chances of survival by finding, stealing, or buying better armor, from simple kelvar-cloth hybrids to full military exoskeletons. You can also obtain a wide breadth of real world guns to fit your playstyle, and they fire a variety of ammunition types, adding another gameplay dynamic. Finally you can find "artifacts" out in the zone's many radiation anomalies which can reduce the damage you take from radtiation, boost your health, and increase your stamina, among other things. They also sell for a pretty penny, if you prefer not to be irradiated by artifacts.
The zone itself is an interesting and varied wasteland, with some interesting characters and fedgling game dynamics like random bandit attacks on stalker camps (which you have no obligation to assist) and faction alliances.
However, the game world is rather linear and segmented, it is a far cry from a true open game world like in the elder scrolls series. Also, the while the main quest and random encounters and factions battles are compelling enough, the minor quests given to you by traders and others feel really generic, like an after thought to the game. They are entirely random and never run out, unlike other games, in their defense. The factions feel like a remnant from alpha- they hardly ever leave their bases and go on raids (except the military) and they have very limited reactions to your actions beyond friend or enemy.
The game has been patched and is no longer the buggy release I was told about a while ago.
Value- The game can take anywhere from 25-40 hours to complete, but I would advise you to take your time, and explor to find the really rare weapons and gear, and meet all the interesting people. I probably spent closer to 65 hours playing it, which is not bad for a game i got for $5 on steam. It is a good deal even for the current going price of $20.
Overall, I would say try this game if a spooky survival shooter with some really original ideas sounds appealing to you. I am excited to see how clear sky plays in comparison, and what else GSC has up their sleeves.

Factorio started simple. Gather some resources, craft some tools to help you gather resources faster, build a wood crate to store more resources etc. Then using the newly gathered resources, you build a smelter to enhance the gathered resources. Using the refined resources, you build simple machines such as a drill that runs on coal to automate your resource gathering.
20+ hours later, you are 3/4 way in research to build a ♥♥♥♥ing spaceship.
The setting is at an alien planet, where you crashed your spaceship. There are peaceful natives that wont bother you if you distance your self them but you can easily kill them with your trustful gun. Too easy? Well when you are trying to build a new spaceship to get the ♥♥♥♥ outta that planet, you will generate pollutions along the way. This angers the natives and they will start coming after you consistently. Still too easy? They will mother♥♥♥♥ing evolve to kill you ♥♥♥♥♥. But dont worry. As history always goes, the inquisitor will always win against the natives.
The game is still in Early Access but it contain TONS of content. I repeat, TONS. There are multiplayer mode too where you and your friends can colonize the planet and pillage its resources together. YAY.
Don't worry about being bored. There are always things to do, research to make and the new things to try. As the game is about factory, you will always find ways to automate and optimize your production. All the tools that you need would be provided. You just need to understand how to use it.
Highly recommended for both singleplayer and multiplayer. One of the best in its genre.

Dishonored 2, the sequel to one of my most favorite video games of all time...I had been waiting for it since it was announced, pined for it when a friend gifted it to me months and months before its official release, pined some more when I did not possess a system that could run it without melting like a nuclear reactor, felt disappointment from reading the articles that the frame rates and such were choppy as all hell upon launch, and worried that its supposed mechanical and technical failures would plague an otherwise promising-looking game.
I finally sat down to play it, wiggled in my seat all the while, and dove in.
The story takes place almost two decades after the first game. Emily Kaldwin is now the Empress of Dunwall with her now-officially-150%-confirmed father, Corvo Attano, aka Lord Protector. He has taught her his skills, as much as could be learned without the Outsider's powers, and while the rat plague is gone, there is still the undercurrent of grumblings at the state of affairs the empire deals with. On the anniversary of her mother's, former Empress Jessamine Kaldwin, death, a face that we were introduced to in Daud's DLCs in Dishonored makes an appearance and proclaims herself to be the long lost sister of Jessamine and therefore the rightful ruler of Dunwall. Things seem to happen in fast forward as a coup is staged by this person, Delilah Copperspoon, with the backing of the new Duke of Serkonos--the current ruler of Corvo's homeland. Just as you're about to duke it out, you the player choose whether to continue this ordeal as Corvo or Emily. Whichever one you pick, the other is frozen in stone and you are branded an outlaw to be put down on sight.
Now, onto thoughts which will be summarized down below.
Leaping into Dishonored 2, it's like I never left Dishonored or the DLCs. The things that I loved most about Dishonored -- the art style and graphics, the basic mechanics, the profundity of lore and notes, the not-quite-steampunk time line, the multiple ways of traversing through the map and determining the fate of your targets - none of that has changed, thank God.
Serkonos feels like an authentic addition to the world of Dishonored that we thus far know. From what I learned about it in the first game, it gave off a vaguely Mediterranean feel, perhaps a bit Italian or Sicilian but the decor, architecture, and the like take very clear cues from the French Second Empire (1852-1870), much like how Dunwall was steeped in England's Industrial Revolution (1760 -1820/40). Being a History buff and amateur anthropologist, it is always thrilling and fun to see how people take certain time periods and adapt them to help fit a particular world that is somehow familiar yet clearly different. The creators of this game took the time and effort to not only plan out the history of this universe, but to make sure that the city felt *lived in* and made sense for those who walked its streets and lived in their houses. Much like Dunwall, it can be clearly seen within Serkonos the growing pains of rapid industrialization as buildings, technology, and machinery are slapped haphazardly into place to replace the old pre-technological means of daily life while social issues such as the welfare, job security and safety, law and order, and the health of the people are still dramatically flagging behind such manufactured progress. Dishonored 2 expands more upon the sentiment expressed by the first game - namely, the balancing act these Empires perform between human rights, the economy, and their civilization's development. In this way, the narratives are fictional but their sentiments remain true-to-life and perfectly parallel our own history.
I guess I can't really stress just how much I appreciate and dig how much time and effort went into this sort of planning. There is such a perfect blend of historical...accuracy and pointedness that could be applicable to both our world's timeline and its universe's timeline. Of course there will be anachronisms because magic and the quasi-nuclear properties of whale oil exist, but the stratification of the social classes, the clothing (with some fashion liberties taken), the treatment of the civilians, the struggle for power over the people between the Abbey and the government, all of this just echoes across the whole game, and always subtly reminds you of it from the notes and newspapers to the overheard conversations to the graffiti.
IN SUMMARY (which will probably be updated as I think more on it)
+Very similar mechanics as the previous game, plus some new ones that make it much more fun and challenging, including one that was (unfortunately!!) only used for one level
++++Lore-rich and world-building notes, documents, and papers to read. This is perhaps one of my most favorite aspects of the Dishonored games. I LIVE for this kind of thing. It's such an easy way to flesh out your world. Writing convincing and appropriate notes is a different challenge in its own right, so hats off to the writers and devs who helped with these fun and engaging paper trails.
+Stealth still remains fun as hell, and everything moves smoothly as a stealth game should. You even tuck and roll!
+Nice little touches that make the world feel lived-in and occupied, rather than as stages for NPCs to just navigate through.
+Lots of NPCs that do their programmed little song and dance that you can listen in on from a distance as they discuss the politics, gang activities, the economy, etc. Great world-building stuff.
+Everything you do, of course, changes the world, just like in the first game. There are quite a few things that make a difference and affect the rest of the game from there on out.
? - Not sure how I felt about the levels. I was intrigued and entertained, yes, but they felt a bit linear. Then again, the levels in Dishonored are linear as well so claiming that Dishonored was more expansive than this sequel is being a bit too maudlin, huh.

. Then there's also the fact that
.
-Not digging Corvo's voice. I don't know who would be a better voice for him than the man we got but I just...can't feel it. The addition of Corvo speaking makes me wonder why he didn't speak in the first game and why he *has* to speak now. It would have been interesting to continue this journey with him remaining mute. Quite a few of his quips are delivered a bit awkwardly or so monotonous that they seem to really toe the line between "jaded old man" and "really boring monotonous old man". I don't know if I would have preferred them to be "thought" instead of spoken, or cut out altogether, but I began to dread hearing him speak because it was just a boring grizzled father voice with nothing really else to going for it. The cut scenes before the beginning of each chapter, as you may guess, were kind of painful in that regard.
-Also didn't really how much Corvo gestured while he talked. It was always a point or a sweeping or a palm-out-give-me-a-break-here and that worked for Daud because he did it during moments where it would matter, such as driving a point home when speaking to Delilah's statue. Corvo gesturing is unnecessary and just kind of...it makes him seem like an overacting rag doll that I can't quite see.

A brilliantly made and masterfully designed take on an Alien video game is utterly ruined by a single flaw. Somehow a game released in 2014 doesn't have a checkpoint system. The only way to save progress is at the save stations, which are unbearably few and far in between, leading to situations where one will get trapped completing the same mission objectives and hearing the same dialogue over and over and over again.
The Alien's AI makes it brilliantly unpredictable, which unfortunately means it will sometimes show up and charge right towards you, or simply systematically check every nook and cranny until it finds your hiding spot, and there's realistically nothing you can do to escape either scenario. This isn't necessarily a gamebreaker in a survival horror context, but with the aforementioned save issues, this can happen utterly randomly mere feet from a save station, setting you back, once again, 10 or 15 minutes.
To add further insult, the save stations inexplicably lock you out of resaving your game after use for some time, meaning you can't even double back to a save point after making some progress towards the inevitably failed run for the next one.
I don't even know why this issue exists in a modern AAA title. I want to like this game, its in 99% of respects a fantastic game, but with this one, critical, baffling flaw breaks the entire experience, and leaves me unable to recommend it.

Review is separate for HW 1 and 2.
Edit: Homeworld Cataclysm is not part of this remastered edition, since it was developed by another studio and the source code got lost when that went out of business, though there is a mod that is trying to recreate it. At the time of this writing there are no campaign missions though, only skirmishes. Generally there are quite a few total conversions available for skirmish play.
Starting off with HW 1.
What is Homeworld? It's a space RTS game taking place on a 3 dimensional plane. The maps are always round and you can order your ships "up" and "down". You can either do that on the normal game screen, which is pretty beautiful in the Remastered edition, or you can bring up a tactical view, which makes it a bit easier. The camera can be freely rotated, but zooming on the other hand is pretty limited and finicky thanks to the 3D aspect. Basically you have to anchor yourself to a unit in order to make the most out of zoom. I guess pro players will mainly use the tac display anyway.
So far so good. The interface is pretty decent now (uses the HW 2 one I think). Since there aren't too many different combat units (variation of fighters, bombers, different corvettes, frigates and destroyers as well as a heavy cruiser class), there's not that much micro management, although letting your bombers attack into a multi attack corvette screen is generally considered to be a bad idea, which brings me to my first point of critique: The smaller strike craft feel almost useless later on in the game when destroyers and heavy cruisers are in play and you have some interceptors or stealth fighters or said multi attack corvettes...maybe even drone frigates; there's a lot of sturdier bigger craft that can fulfill the role of anti-fighter and anti-capital better than investing in easily destroyed strike craft. Maybe I'm just bad, definitely possible, but the game also never really explains what benefits certain "formations" have. I found out by accident that the "sphere" formation is a very bad idea for bombers or fighters, since then they remain stationary and surround the target. They work in conjunction and soak up a lot of the damage, but I found myself replacing them almost constantly, while my bigger craft were mostly untouched.
Next critique: The game's UI needs work, seriously. There is a button that displays what kind of craft you have and how many, but there is not button to select these craft. For example, try finding a particular craft, perhaps a resource collector, quickly and you're almost despairing. Speaking of resource collectors: Those buggers never seem to mine automatically, mining takes ages and then you need several resource controllers so they don't have to make the trek back home to your mothership every time, which takes, again, ages. And now we've moved on to the glacial pace this game can evolve to. In the later stages, trying to get your capital ships ANYWHERE can easily take 15 to 20 minutes. They turn and move really really slowly. Yes, that feels epic, but sitting there, waiting quarter of an hour for your ships to go SOMEWHERE is the antithesis of fun.
Graphics and sound are pretty decent, however, you are either going to dig or hate the music. It's very space epic-esque.
The campaign: Homeworld 1 consists of 16 missions (plus 1 bonus mission that can be found in the extra missions section of the main menu...no idea why they cut this one from the main game, because it fits right in there after mission 4 or so and is actually quite fun). Yes, fun, that's something that varies a lot in this campaign. To understand how the campaign works you need to realize that your goal is to reach your Homeworld (who would have thought) with your Mothership, which cannot move during a mission. Neither does it have any weapons...it just sits there and dies if you're not careful, but who cares, since you rarely get attacked anyway. In any case, your units are permanent, meaning, you take them with you to the next mission if they don't get destroyed. This bit is important, since that can either make the campaign really easy or pretty difficult. There is no difficulty setting, but even so I found myself challenged only a handful of times, but once your armada gets big enough, you should not have any problems at all. Some missions are gimicky, destroying asteroids in your way, moving in areas to avoid radiation. Those are pretty interesting, however, the main issue is that they are either over very quickly (mission 15 literally takes 3 minutes to complete...it's a timed defense mission...what!?!? That should have been part of a bigger mission), or take ages to complete, while you slowly crawl your way forward with your big capital ships of which you can only build so many before the supply limit stops you. Haha, BUT you can always capture more and just get a ridiculously large armada. I think I had 6 Heavy Cruisers, about 8 destroyers and 4 missile destroyers or so...while the game only allows you to have 3, 6 and 2 respectively. Add to that 21 frigates (mostly Ion), a full complement of multi attack corvettes as well as some 70 almost useless strike craft and the enemies did not stand a chance. This is the campaign in a nutshell...the story is pretty threadbare, neatly presented in kinda animtated, but still static images and moderately good voice over (all very downtrodden), but it barely makes sense and you're not even rooting for your own team, you don't feel resentment towards the enemies and there are no characters to identify with. Took me 9 hours to complete, but I had to repeat some stuff, and I guess at least 50% of that time was spent building stuff and waiting. By the way, all unmined resources will automatically transfer to your account after a mission ends, but that doesn't mean you should not replace any lost craft before you jump away, since the next mission can literally drop you in a terrible situation in which you need every ship you can get...Actually that happens quite often...
MP is well, I dunno, in HW 1 all races seem to have the same units, so...what's the point besides different designs?
All in all HW 1 is a good game, but by no means is it as good as people make it out to be. Unfortunately, if you're into this kind of genre, there's not much else, at least nothing contemporary. Sins of a Solar Empire comes to mind first, but that does not have a campaign either and is a 4x cross breed rather than a true RTS.
HW 2:
You can expect the same engine and gameplay, but in the campaign as well as the MP there are some serious changes. Also for some reason it just looks better to me. Weird.
- I find the campaign to be more engaging to be honest. It's also a bit more cohesive, but it's still space opera and in the end you have more questions than answers
- The backdrops are just GORGEOUS
- The music is more space nomady than space opera now. Better imho
- Small ships (anything not capital or special) are now built as a squad, which makes micro managing your ♥♥♥♥ing fighters and corvettes a lot easier now. Also these ships are now stronger in my opinion. They still die relatively quickly in large fights, but at least they do what they are supposed to do and you can rebuild them quicker.
- Resource collectors have taken over the job of the repair corvettes, because resource collection in the campaign doesn't matter anyway
- Salvage corvettes are now marine frigates and utterly useless (at least in campaign), since easily destroyed, have to remain stationary for ages to board a vessel and if you already have the max no of vessels you can't claim any more
- The game FINALLY auto saves
- Missions end automatically, which is bad, since you can no longer replenish your fleet after a big battle, which may mean instant failure of the next mission...stupid
All in all cool campaign, but some design decisions are questionable...

I am an avid Dark Souls fan. I have beaten the first game in the series over 5 times and have dumped a lot of time into the PVP into the game. The first Dark Souls probably has to be my favorite game of all time now because of how it gripped me with the difficulty, atmosphere, and world.
As soon as Dark Souls II was announced, I was ecstatic. it was my most anticipated game of all time and I immediately pre-ordered it. I avoided spoilers as hard as I could, and I waited for so long until the PC release still trying my hardest to avoid spoilers. I got the game and beat it. I kinda had fun...
I was a bit dissappointed at Dark Souls II in retrospect. My first playthrough was pretty fun because I got to explore this new environment while I was very aquanted with the controls and mechanics (mostly). The mapping makes no sense in a lot of areas (iron keep being above the windmill, the ocean below the ocean known as sinner's rise), most of the bosses are uninteresting and are just large humanoid bosses with a large weapon, with a few cool exceptions.
There was a lot of things I liked about this game, but honestly I didn't feel very challenged at all throughout my first playthrough. Multiple enemies in a small hallway does not account for difficulty either, I consider it to be extremely tedious and hard to take care of.
Soul memory, enemy despawning, and uninspired bosses is kind of what killed the hype of this game for me. Oh yeah, and don't forget about the DLCs which mostly sucked in my opinion.
My final thoughts on the game is that it's good. It's fun and challenging in its own respect, but it is NOT a good sequel to the first Dark Souls.
The game is good, but not as good as the fist game. I'll reccomend it still because I still managed to have a good time with the game (and beating it around 4 time for the sake of PVP) but I feel like there's little replayability and I think I'm done with it.
Give it a try, but play the first one before this one. That's a strong reccomendation.

Negatives include:

I will write this review in the context of the first
. If you have not played that game, I would recommend starting with that one. It is an absolute masterpiece, and if you are at all interested in first-person stealth I am certain you'll enjoy it.
is very similar, so if you can pick the first one up during a sale (it gets real cheap nowadays) you can use it to gauge your rough enjoyment of the sequel.
With that out of the way, if you played and enjoyed the first
,
It is, in my opinion, better than the original. I got it a bit more than a year after launch since the game was plauged by performance issues, but they seem to have been resolved (I didn't notice any problems at all). When I got the game, I played it through 4 times in a row, barely playing any other game in parallell (and this is coming from a devout
fan).
In
, you can choose between playing as either Corvo or Emily, and they play very differently from each other. Corvo is practically identical to his former self, same abilities and all. Arkane did change how you upgrade your abilities, which could have an impact on your playstyle, but they did not change the actual abilities themselves. You still have your Blink, you still have your Mind Control, you still have your favourite ability from the original
, but some abilities now have little twist that you can unlock.
I played as Corvo during my first playthrough, and it really felt like the original, but with better graphics, some new enemies, and a new villain. But the core gameplay is still the same: you get a target, you make your way to your target, and you eliminate your target, either by killing them or by some non-lethal means. Having the same abilities and all, it can really feel like the same game as the original; it's just more
. This might sound like a bad thing. But if you're like me, more
sounds like a dream come true!
But if more Corvo is not you cup of tea, you're in luck. Emily brings an entirely new set of abilities to the table. These new skills (combined with a new, different set of animations) give her an entirely different feel from Corvo. The two definitely play in different ways, and I really enjoyed both of them. If you're tired of Corvo, but still like what
had to offer, take Emily for a spin. The game even offers you the choice of not recieving the Outsider's mark, allowing you to play a run without any powers (whereas the first game forced you to get Blink).
Outside from the playable characters, the game has been improved at large. There is a greater balance between lethal and non-lethal gamplay than in the original. For example, if you parry your opponent's strike in combat you can choose to do a non-lethal counterattack instead of a lethal one. This allows for a non-lethal run that isn't focused on stealth. And even if you are playing a non-lethal stealth run, it means you can now fight back if you're detected, instead of having to run away. Bloodflies provide further to this balance by making incendiary bolts useful to non-lethal runs. Arkane also added a non-lethal mine that the pacifist player can add to their arsenal. There still is no non-lethal grenade, which is a bit strange in my opinion, although you can make your own by attaching a stun mine to a throwable object, and then treating that as a grenade.
Graphics are drastically improved, which is to be expected. The old art style is kept, which I personally like, but it's dependent on your taste. The villain is extremely hate-able, which makes completing the game so very satisfying. I played the game on Hard, which makes it challenging, but never impossible. Staying true to the original, there is almost always a way to get around or tackle potential problems. Enemies are deadly, and at Hard and higher you'll need to use all your tricks if you wish to play head-on lethally. Although your abilities may make you feel a bit overpowered (and to be honest,
), a single mistake can lead to your demise.
It took about 80 hours for me to finish the game 4 times. It divides evenly into 20 hours per run, but the lethal combat-focused run was definitely quicker than the others, and the never-detected run was a lot slower. Still, 10-15 hours is not unreasonable to expect from a single run, and since there are 2 playable characters there is a surprising amount of replay value to be found.
All in all, this game is a blast. If you want more
, you get more
. If you want to spice things up but keep the old formula, this game does that too. It's a masterpiece, and one of my favourite games of all time.

Tl&dr: whatever you expect from this game (M&B battle style, trading), search for it somewhere else, it is not difficult to find something better.
Mount & Blade engine, extended trading system, naval combat, main story... sounds perfect, what could go wrong? These were my thoughts when I bought this game and I got my answer very quick.. too quick. Everything can go wrong.
Honestly, it feels like someone took Mount & Blade, Sid Meier's Pirates and Port Royale, stripped all the good parts from all these games and then mashed them together.
I tried this game twice, first time when I bought it about a year and a half ago, second time this week when I saw a surprising "Very positive" recent ratings, thinking that the game was improved, bugs fixed and "fun implemented". If it could happen for Viking's Conquest, why not for this one?
Well... no! The frustrating problems that I found in my first eight hours were still there and I found some more. Some examples:
- during most of the combat scenarios (and by most I mean 75%+) I had no control over my troops. In all of the quests I got from governors, my troops were charging, holding position in predetermined places or following me, in the best case scenario. However, "someone" was always careful to give a dismount command to all my troops in the beginning of each combat for these quests (thank you). Boarding other ships... zero control over my own troops, just watch them going one by one to the other ship, landing in the middle of 5-10 enemies and get slaughtered instantly. The only type of combat when I had control over them was in random encounter on land.
- one more absolutely "lovely" aspect about troop management. At some point I noticed that, after each battle, my followers were automatically pushed at the top of the roster. First time I noticed this, I moved my doctor back at the end, thinking I made a mistake. After the next combat, he was in front line again. Basically I have to rearrange the roster after each battle. It was enough to forget to do this once and I could see my doctor, who could barely hold a sword, in the front line, getting his head smashed, instead of staying back and healing other people's smashed heads. Oh, did I mention I couldn't give him any orders during combat?
- trading. For me it is fun to study each city's production, think of the best trade routes, maximize profit, minimize expenses and so on. If you like it also, find another game, because here you have exactly zero information at global level about what is production of each city or min-max prices. Unless you are willing to take a pen and paper and note down what each city produces and what are prices for each product depending on supply, you can give up on the idea of having a trading empire in this game.
- naval combat: probably the only part of the game that is decent (except boarding). Not the best I've seen or most challenging, but it is definitely above average and can be fun, but, unfortunately, it is also just a small part of the game, too small to make up for everything else.
- (lack of) information. Take a quest from a governor. Complete the quest. Go back for reward, but the governor is not home anymore. In M&B you had the option to ask any lord of the same faction about his location and he gave you a general area where that moron is roaming. This option is absent here. Why? I have no idea. I can go around the map aimlessly, searching for some dude, or I can cheat and reveal the whole map.
Speaking of information, it is incredible how poorly documented this game is. Most of the other people's questions were answered with the sarcastic "read the manual, you will be surprised how useful it is". Ok, so I think to myself: maybe I was spoiled by the M&B style and the its major mods (like Perisno or PoP) which had/have a very active community and their own wikia pages. What's the harm in reading a pdf file? Download, open file... Chapter 1: Creating your character... Starting fleet for "Retired officer": Large Fluyt, Small Fluyt. Oh, how cute... it is outdated or wrong, or both.
Overall, the annoying parts outnumber by far the fun parts and I can easily declare it the worst game or mod, based on Mount & Blade engine, I have ever played.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R: Shadow of Chernobyl is a relatively unknown game made by Ukrainian developer GSC Game World and is set in the area around the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant, known as 'The Zone' and is one of the best FPS/RPG games I have ever played.
(Note: There is a summary at the bottom, if you dont wish to read the whole review.)
The atmosphere created within the STALKER world is very different to most games, you will find yourself really feeling alone in the world as you explore it, and the different areas you explore throughout the game each have there own seperate feel, whether its the dark abandoned military base infested with mutants forcing you to slowly pear around corners or the bareness of Pripyat with nothing but towering empty buildings above you and deadly anomalies around you the world that STALKER creates is one you wont find in any other game.
STALKER is also a fantastic survival game, whilst traveling through the zone you will need to monitor you hunger levels and dehydration and ensure you have an adequate supply for when you are exporing places with no access to food or water. When you are shot or mauled by a mutant you will have to bandage yourself to stop the bleeding or use a medical kit. To help you have a better chance of survival you can trade with traders or anyone you meet in the zone for both weapons and armour, with around 50 different weapons in the game, ranging from sniper rifles or rocket launchers. You will also have access to artifacts which both sell for a high price but also have influencial effects on your stats, these are found in lootable chest or within anomalies themselves. If you are looking for a multiplayer experience however, you may want to look elsewhere as there are only basic multiplayer P v P modes and there is no co-op within the game.
As a Role Playing Game Stalker offers many common elements, at the start of the game you will begin with nothing but a pistol and be forced to do a few odd side missions to generate some money and better weapons. There are numerous side quests avaliable throughout the world each giving unique rewards and artifacts to help you. Also when you kill another human character and loot there corpse there is a chance for you to be given coordinates to there stash of items somewhere in the world, which you can then go and loot. The story within Stalker will have your character attempting to work our who he is by trying to reach the center of the Zone to find 'The Wish Granter' which will be explained at the beginning of the game, your choices throughout the game will effect your overall ending as well.
In Summary:
Positives:
+ One of the greatest and most unique atmospheres seen in a game.
+ Fantastic survival mechanics.
+ Good Shooting Mechanics.
+ Good RPG Mechanics.
+ Great range of weapons.
+ Can become very creepy at times.
Negatives:
+ Below average multiplayer
+ Average Story
+ Stalker can seem a bit daunting at first
Overall: 9.5/10 'Fantastic Game!!!'

I've been waiting for something like this for a very, very long time.
I got the first Homeworld a month after it was released in '99 for my 12th birthday; besides being insanely happy that my parents had finally gotten me a present 'up my alley' without any prompting whatsoever, I was excited to have a new game that also pushed my boundaries a bit.  Up till then, I'd really only been a gamer because I was a *huge* Star Wars fan, and indulged that interest in whatever way I could, be it novels, comics, or games.  Tearing off the giftwrap and seeing a new PC game that wasn't a Star Wars title, but was still set in space, and was also an RTS (a genre I liked but decent titles in the Star Wars franchise being somewhat of a rarity), that for the time had amazing visuals if the screencaps on the back of the box were anything to go by, had me bouncing in my seat.
And I instantly fell in love.  The manual was basically a novel, not only did it have instructions, it was a primer on the backstory leading up to the events in game (I sorely miss those days, Mechwarrior was another title that had this type of thing going for it...*sigh*, nostalgia..). The first few missions had me dumbstruck by the 'in your face' factor-seeing your own home planet nuked to a crisp is enough to leave anyone a bit dumbfounded. The visuals didn't disappoint; skyboxes were gorgeous, explosions from dying ships were well done, seeing a fleet of Ion frigates all gang up on a Heavy Cruiser to make it pop like an overripe berry was amazing, the fact that you now had to strategize in three dimensions as opposed to two, as well as watch out for pesky Salvage Corvettes trying to steal your own ships to be turned against you was innovative...it was an *amazing* game, and after completing the story missions, I felt as if I really had led the remnants of my civilization on a grueling trek across the galaxy to their ancestral homeworld, battling pirates, the space faring equivalent of the Heaven's Gate cult, and the oppressive tyrannical empire that exiled you in the first place in millennia past along the way; I felt like I *accomplished* something, which was rare for a game even in those days, and is now even rarer.
Homeworld 2 took what was good about the first entry and made it better.  Fleets had even more versatility, graphics were improved even more, the 'underdog' feeling was back even though you'd now been an established power in the in game universe's lore for a few decades, the amazing soundtrack from the first game was improved upon, with tracks that would feel right at home in a cathedral.
The Remastered editions take the visuals from the second game, improve them slightly, and then apply that standard to both games, which is awesome.  What's not so awesome is the fact that some mechanics have been changed slightly, which actually results in certain campaign missions needing to be played in an entirely different, and often less enjoyable, way. For example, one mission near the end of the campaign in the first game consists of a sensor array surrounded by a giant sphere of enemy ships protecting it. Strategy for this mission dictated that you use cloaked Salvage corvettes to slowly steal a large number of these enemy ships, bolstering your fleet size to be able to both take on the rest, as well as destroy the sensor array, and leave you with a sizable force for the final mission, after completing the next two.  With the new mechanics, this is now nearly impossible; when your Salvage 'vettes latch on to an enemy ship, they no longer remain cloaked, which instantly alerts all nearby enemies, resulting in the loss of your corvettes and the loss of the stolen ship. Now you have a choice of either trying to lure small sections of the sphere away to pick off piecemeal, or engaging the entire enemy force, both of which result in significant losses to your own fleet, and at this point in the game resources for replacing your losses are scarce.  This makes the final 3 missions after this one next to impossible due to having such a reduced fleet of your own, and you do indeed need a rather large force to handle everything thrown at you in the final mission.
Overall, it's still a great game, and brings back a boatload of nostalgia for me personally, with stupendous visuals and an excellent soundtrack..I just wish the new developers had been content to simply improve graphics rather than try and tweak with game mechanics.

This game is an interesting speed game of trying to figure out if someone has the right papers and ID to cross the border.  You have to get enough people correctly through or stopped each day to afford food and heat for your family or they will get sick and die.  But make too many mistakes and you will pay for it. Paper, Please. is a boring, monotonous game where you do the same repetitive task for multiple hours with little to no reward. What little story the game does present to you is extremely basic and unfulfilling, definitely not worth the time investment, not to mention the premise for the game is heavily inspired (some might even say ripped off) from classic works such as Orewell's 1984. Obvious moral choices serve only to hinder you, and as a result the game can tend to leave you feeling lonely and depressed. On top of this, obvious quips in the game are more insulting than they are funny, such as the obviously Soviet Bloc world map using the United States of America instead of Eastern Europe, and the unfair treatment of transgendered people. This short, repetitive game is not worth anyone's time, let alone money. 3.4/10

I'm no critic so I'll start by venting some steam.
To Steam, please cut back on Pre-Releases, only allow a few games to go alpha because this has become a bane.  90% of all games are unplayable pre-releases and most stay that way forever.  There should be a punishment system for developers who take too much time to release a game, like paying back people who bought the game, at least 25% of what they paid.

Alphas, at least on steam, should be at least stable and playable because if the goal is only to test, know that there are companies out there who actually pay people to test their games, not the other way around, what's the point?

9/10 This Game Is My Favorite Round Of Space Station 13.
The Game Is Superb Looking Even In Mid-Quality Configuration, And Everything On The Screen Is Reminiscent Of The Movies, From The Machinery To The Walls And Views Of The Station, They Went A Long Way In Terms Of Object Design And Visual Effects To Go For The Nostalgia Angle, Which Works Perfectly For This Game And It Hooks You In.
The Gameplay Is A Very Good Take On The Amnesia "Hide From The Monster And Solve Puzzles" Paradigm, The Game Responds To Noises Your Character Makes, Learns Your Patterns Of Hiding And The Distractions You Use, And The Station Is Built In Such A Way That There're Alternate Paths And Multiple Ways To Approach Things. Its A First Person Metroid Game  Where It Pays To Revisit New Areas Later In The Game As You Unlock New Weapons And Abilities. The Crafting System Is Simple And Easy To Get A Hold Of, And None Of The Crafted Items Feels Either Broken Or Rebundant, There's One For Every Situation And Every Problem.
My Only Gripe Against This Game Is The Ending Of The Main Campaign. It Is Sudden And Out Of Nowhere, It Feels As Though They Ran Out Of Game And Simply Cut It Wherever They Got And Launched It.
Fans Of Horror, Fans Of Alien, And Even The Metroidvania Enthusiast Who Wants To Try Something New Yet Familiar Will All Enjoy This Game. It Is A Great, Almost Perfect Make.

After having been a member of Steam for over 5 years, this is my very first review. Though not important to the review itself, I am attempting to express how sure I am that I love this game, and to express to the developers how much I appreciate the tireless efforts they have made and will make to ensure that their product continues to grow and improve. Over more than a year, I put many hours into Factorio before it was released to Steam. Here are my thoughts.
The game is complexly simple. Start with nothing and, with as few boundaries as possible, build something. The style is up to you, but the game mechanics is factory-based automation. For those of you familiar with MineCraft’s factory-style mods, the concept will be familiar, but the execution vastly distinct.
As you build up and produce more pollution, the critters start trickling in. It is possible to lose to their attacks, but that will probably only happen if you aren’t watching and they find a fatal flaw in your design (or power grid). So, don’t worry about this being a combat-based game if you aren’t into that. 99.9% of the attacks are thwarted by automated defenses, anyway, with only the first couple or so requiring the use of your personal weapon.
As I said, complexly simple. The goal is simple at this point, but how you get there is up to you. Build a compact base or a sprawling megafactory. Build railways far and wide or just to a few key points. You will have to expand some and you will always have to keep new expansions in mind, maintaining power and defenses. When you get to where you can end it, it’s your choice. Keep playing all you want, or move on to starting over.
I easily sunk over 70 hours into each map I played, though I admit my play style is slow and steady.
As for the cons of purchasing, there are none for me. I consider it one of my best random finds. If you want the flashiest graphics, you will be a bit disappointed. If you want a deep story, that’s not here. But, if you want to sink some serious hours into building something that has your unique stamp on it, and you like maximizing production line efficiency (including your own layout) while throwing in a dash of base defense and exploration, you may enjoy this game, as I have.
The small development team is still adding content and improvements to this title. Some things may change, but it’s already got enough that it’s worth the money if you think this may be for you.

Its hard to review a game seriously that doesn't take itself so. But there's a solid and fun game here with a great presentation. Broforce is an intense patriotic (USA) fueled side scrolling shoot'em up with heavy influences and inspiration from over the top American action films. Each character or "bro" you get to play is a caricature of a hero of a film. RamBRO, BRO Dredd, BRO in Black, BROnan the BRObarian, etc etc. Each one is unique in their standard and special attacks and some even have some extra abilities. This variety keeps things interesting during this hectic shooter. You'll be fighting everything from terrorists to aliens to the undead. And all while dealing with the fully destructable tiled environment. Gaps, explosives, and falling stones will spell your doom just as much as the enemies firing at you. The campaign mode made for a great 5.4hrs of massacring fun. And there is other difficulties, arcade mode, and co-op/multiplayer compliments to all of it. Sprinkle in some level editing with Steam Workshop support and there's really something you can dive into here if you were so inclined.
Just with the fun of unlocking the bros and the campaign alone I think I got my money's worth. I'd still recommend a sale or bundle as its a safe game to place on the wait list. But while not a must play, its well worth it when you do. Fun and funny. Recommended BRO!

STALKER is not for the faint of heart. It's a survival game in many ways : you constantly end up being outgunned, outarmored, outlived. To defend yourself, all you have are crappy weapons with low damage, terrible range and even more terrible aim - and that's when the weapon doesn't end up being jammed when you shoot it, forcing you to reload at the wrong moment. The moment you receive a bullet right in the head, killing you instantly.
Inventory management is important, too : discarding everything you find will keep you poor for sure, but stockpiling or 12 similar rifles will increase your load, making your character constantly gasping for breath.

This game... oh man. This game is great. It's a shooter with a hilarious cast that very often makes fun of itself. The gun variety speaks to the scavenger in me, as you will never know what you'll get when you loot. Literally millions of combinations. The cel-style graphics also lend to the feel of the game, as it reminds you of a cartoon, in which you are the hero. The character customization isn't as varied as the guns, but is still great so you can brand your own hero. The class system is unique to the shooter world, and works very well.
The part that earns the top respect and enjoyment though, is co-op. The way this game does co-op is almost flawless. I am a huge fan of the drop in/drop out system of it, and the game accommodates by scaling enemies for 2, 3, or 4 people very easily. Stuff remains a challenge. It also lets you know on the main menu how close in story your friends are to your progress, and warns you if you are too far out of sync. My only complaint is ammo in co-op. It makes sense that when someone opens a chest, the ammo isn't shared, but when money is shared, and ammo is not? Kinda not balanced there. But it's only one tiny thing in an otherwise perfect system.
I love the characters too. There is no average. They are all over the top in some way or another; real individuals, albeit crazy. But who likes bland normalcy? Heh. If I had to pick a favorite player character, it'd be Gaige, or the Mechromancer. Just, awesome. "TO HELL WITH THE FIRST LAW"
Anyways, get this game. Even if you don't have friends to play it with, it's still gold. Hell, get 4 people together with a 4-pack and go nuts. It's worth every bit. I played the first for hundreds of hours on Xbox, and this one for like 30ish ours on there as well, but the computer plays much better. *and looks better too*... Happy Vault hunting, SLAB!
