Let me start by saying, and i cannot emphasise this enough:  DO NOT LOOK AT THIS GAME LIKE IT IS A MOUNT AND BLADE CARIBBEAN!.  In a lot of ways, it looks like it is, it is made with the same ol' engine, and from what I understand kind of in partnership with TaleWorlds;  but they couldn't be further apart if they were aspects in different dimensions.  My review for the original Caribbean apparently drew the ire of the fanboys or something (can't believe this game would have fans), so let me give this a more comprehensive review so you know exactly what you are getting.  The base game (the original Caribbean!) is the same, few real improvements were made, aside from a few "different" quests and a few contextual improvements.  This game is still incredibly bare, and so...  broken.  The hardest thing to do is to find the best place to start as there are so few pros to the cons of this game.  So let's begin:
Cons:
-This game is dead.  The previous employees of the studio that was working on this title were basically fired for inadequate production and the new team have pulled the plug on it.  Don't get this game and expect it to improve.  This is the complete package.
-The AI is garbage.  The difficulty of the game is increased by increased amounts of damage they do per hit vs better tactics.  I know, you're sitting there thinking, "So what?  That's normal".  Not to the extent I'm referring to though.  It is pathetic when a musketeer is a speck on the horizon and he is hitting you for half the 80 hit points of your health bar like it ain't no thing.  When you shoot in the game you'll see why it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
-Cannoneers do not operate cannons.  As a matter of fact, the ENTIRE siege portion of the game is so ridiculously broken and redundant, it will quickly become your least favorite aspect of the game.  For starters, there are 2 seige maps.  You're either gonna be on a sandy beach looking at a wooden palisade with cannon fire reigning down (attack from the corner) or you're gonna be looking at a stone fort way off in the distance overlooking the ocean, same scenario.  They are all the same based on those two maps.  Couple the no brain AI with an over-simplified command list.  you have 3 types of units in a siege;  infantry, musketeers and gunners(cannoneers).  The order list for the former two are charge, follow me and stand ground.  Gunners commands are simpler, fire at will or hold fire. Gunners in theory should be operating the cannons.  In practice, however, they group up with the musketeers.  You will be the only one working with the 5 possible cannons you can have in your army.
-Constant scripting errors and bugs in general rampage through the battle text.  I don't know what it's saying but it's probably why the AI is so broken, I don't know because I don't speak broken programming.
-Mount & Blade Warband was released in 2010.  It had better textures and character physics than this game that was released 5 years later does.
-The most ignorant placement of clickables I have ever seen in a game.  Attacking a trade caravan with my armada of 1st and 2nd rate ships and accidentally surrender because fast clicking to try to get through the redundant menus and it is there as an option.  My question to the devs is why is it even there.  There is absolutely ZERO benefit to surrendering.  EVER.  Question #2 is since the devs love their menus, why didn't they put one more behind that one, to confirm a stupid choice.  Laugh now, but let's see how you feel when you do it and hadn't saved in a few hours.  That's life you are never getting back and did not enjoy because of a dumbass mistake, buddy.  Same goes for when you accidentally click "replace one of your ships".  Once you do that, there is no backing out.  Get ready to sacrifice one of your first rates for that medium galleon.
-Campaign map pathing is a very annoying aspect of the game.  When you click on a destination, you would expect to travel to that destination.  until you get stuck on a coast line.  Most of the time its an easy fix by clicking somewhere away from what you are stuck on and you can continue reclick your destination to continue on your merry way.  Sometimes in certain places (northern coast of Cuba is where i have had it happen the most)  you will find yourself permanently stuck.  hopefully you had saved recently, because I couldn't find a fix for that one.  You'll know you're stuck too, because the nose of your ship will be jutting into the land a little bit, no matter where you click or what you do the game will not unpause.
-The governor portion of the game is pathetically bare.  Governors are the mount and blade equivalent of lords.  There is only two ways to get them to like you.  Do some work for them or give them settlements.  Unlike mount and blade, they don't care if you save them in a fight, and you can't hold "feasts".  When they lose a fight, no matter where they are, you lose 1 relationship point.  Give a different governor a settlement, and you stand to lose several relationship points.  This worked in mount and blade because there were ways to improve relationships simply by feasting, or helping them in combat.  It is broken in this game because after a while you're gonna have a bunch of disloyal governors and there's very little you can do about it.  Better off just to take on the world by yourself and your wife (if you decide to go that route), who's name seems to always be Louise...  but he usually escapes with his life after he has been defeated in battle.  Yeah, I said he.  Read the text pop up some time after HE gets beat in a battle.
-The information for this game is so limited.  If you encounter a problem you can post about it in the forums, but who wants to wait for someone to respond with  an "I don't know" answer.  then start taking about random stuff like computer specs and stuff?  Google your question and you're more likely to get sucked into buying Caribbean cruise than you are to find your answer if it's about much more than the followers in the game.
Look, I'm just gonna stop there.  This game has already taken up too much of my time.  If you're thinking about getting the game because you liked Mount & Blade Warband and also like pirates, don't say you weren't warned.  This game is a tragedy.  A tragic tragedy of immense ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and in no way other than the visuals should ever really be compared to it's predecessors.  Go play Assassin's Creed IV if you wanna do some pirate stuff.  Right now that's about as good as you're gonna get for a pirate game that I know of, and patiently await the release of Bannerlord just like everyone else.

After several hours I couldnt take the mediocrity anymore. Like so many other games before, its quantity over quality.
+ its pure action, if I had to describe a cliche action game, this is the game I would point to
+ the wingsuit is a great addition to the franchise
+ many vehicles
+ its quite a large map with different terrain and villages
+ a variety of weapons and gadgets
+ the graphics are nice
+ I never encountered any performance issues, it runs very smooth (60fps+) and is a great port
+ its fun to play around in the sandbox and with the grappling hooks
- the story is forgettable and not worth mentioning
- a lot of the missions are the same over and over again, its a chore to free all the villages just to progress in the story (it wasnt manditory in JC2) and after a while it doesnt feel satisfying to destroy things
- some of the story missions stand out and are great, but more often they are the same thing all over again....
- there is almost no point in vehicles, why bother driving to a place when you can parachute/wingsuit-fly there way faster
- almost all of the weapons feel the same, they all dont feel like weapons and more like pea shooter which maybe is because....
- all the enemies are bullet sponges

- the game always connects you online because of stupid leaderboards that nobody cares about, if that fails, the game will automatically try every 10 minutes to connect while stopping you completley from playing
- the intro at every start of the game is absolutley unnecessary and way too long
- after the Just Cause 2 multiplayer mod, everybody was hoping for a native coop support and they didnt deliver...
I honestly couldnt get myself to finish the game, yet play the DLCs I payed for. Its that boring. Its kinda fun for its stupid action, but that doesnt last long unfortunatley.
Just Cause 2 was way better in the memorable main missions and the overall fun factor. Just Cause 3 is trying to top that by adding more boring stuff to do, hence quantity over quality......I wouldnt recommend this at all.

Non-Spoiler Sypnosis
This game simulates an IM kind of setup, where you would pick 1 out of 3 choices to talk to a friend named Emily. Over the course of highschool and college, you talk to Emily, where you could either be a friend who wants to let Emily know you care about her, or a friend who is concerned but not enough to
, or a friend with a bad attitude.
Spoiler Infested Review
This game pits you through with conversations with Emily, gradually revealing that you have/had a crush on her and want to "hook up" with Emily. Although the game had a great execution with the IM layout that got me involved with the relatable setting, it poorly handled "branching choice development" which the game advertised and failed to deliver. The choices barely matter, because all they do is change dialouge. It still leads up to the same ending, which was a horrible ending at that, gave a horrible message (there are people who look at this from a different angle, calling it genius; the fact that you can never get your crush from highschool is not a good message you would want to spread from a game.) and leaves the reader quite unsatisfied that you cannot change anything and his/her choices MEANT NOTHING.
The personalities of the two characters in the game, and yes, two characters, aren't anything special. You can't even talk to someone else, although it presents the buddy list which does nothing but list edgy quotes and descriptions. Emily self-contradicts herself, especially at the end, saying she doesn't want to relive the past but still gets together with Brad again. The Main Character, no matter what you pick, still ends up revealing he had a crush on her indirectly anyways. The two never really show affection for each other except whenever you choose to go the party, which she says very blandly "why didnt you kiss me there", or her visiting you at college, saying "did you expect us to hook up?". The game just forcefully implements this to put it there. I personally could not see any form of love from the two, not even with the knowledge that the Protagonist likes her.
The game had an excellent use of its typing mechanic, though. Whenever you choose a sketchy choice, the protagonist is seen backspacing and deleting the message and typing something else, to rephrase the sentence. It follows usually with direct messages like "what are we anymore?", which I found an EXCELLENT use for the quite gimmicky typing thing you spam the keyboard for. It could've been exemplary had the dialouge been improved to flesh out the protagonist's character more effectively.
Overall, this game felt lackluster for its excellent execution and use of the typing mechanic but horrible handling of the plot, and I felt very unsatisified at the ending that repeats itself and gives a horrible message for a game that didn't seem too depressing at first. (Let me elobrate on the horrible message, you might argue that "oh, well sometimes something doesn't always end happy, but the plot and setting never really alluded to that, all it gave to me was two teenagers with normal relationship quirks.)
Visuals: 9/10 (for it's 2003 look, it's pretty good.)
Gameplay: 8/10 (you can't actually type messages of your own, its a choice with keyboard spamming, but its high score is due to the excellent use of the backspacing stuff)
Story: 3/10 (its relatable, but not good at all. horrible handling)
Overall: 5/10
Overall, the game is pretty short, so if you're just looking for a story, go ahead. But I didn't enjoy this.
The narrative is definitely worth the playthrough. However there is not much replay value to the game.

Alien:Isolation stands as only the third worthy entry in the Alien canon. I have held out faint hope that some day, somebody would give HR Giger's Alien, which gave me countless childhood nightmares, another treatment it richly deserves - who knew it would be a video game to wash away the taste of that abortion Alien 3, the WTF Alien 4, the vs. Predator nonsense, the mediocre video games...
Alien:Isolation is a first-person stealth survival horror game. You play as Amanda Ripley, Ellen's daughter, fifteen years after the Nostromo disappeared. But the Nostromo's flight recorder has been recovered and is held on a remote, decaying space station called Sevastopol. Amanda, a Company employee, makes the trip only to find the station suffering some kind of malady. What could it be? Hijinx ensues. Many laughs are had by all. Not.
Really the only criticism I can muster personally is that it's stressful to play. It's a real survival horror game. They didn't cheapen the fear of the Alien by letting you blow apart hundreds of them with overpowered weaponry, which has been an unfortunate trend in "survival horror" lately. The Alien hunts you. And it's going to get you, sooner or later. All you can do is outmaneuver it. But the production value and polish is out-of-this-world. Scariest game I've ever played. Best single-player game I've played in years. Every detail has been attended to. The graphics are outstanding. Story and plotting are great, you usually get a breather just when you need it. Getting to the next save point is an achievement and a huge relief. Still a better love story than Twilight.
So yeah. Want to run around in a first-person, ultra polished, ultra high-fidelity recreation of the environment, technology, and atmosphere of the first two, the only two movies, while scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, getting hunted by the most terrifying monster ever created, that you're powerless to fight? Get this. Please heap money on this development team. Here's hoping they're working on a sequel - as of October 2015 the studio director said they were disappointed with sales. Sega is still considering a sequel, but it may not be a sure thing.

Playing Homeworld is a great way to switch off and indulge in an evening of forgettable relaxation. The colourful space vistas, twisting neon engine trails, and soft explosions all come together to create a dreamy feel – which is just as well given how soporific the gameplay is.
Like other space RTS games, Homeworld removes the genre staple of terrain but provides nothing to replace it. Your activities will be managing bog standard rock/paper/scissors unit counters while gathering a single resource type. 3D movement is one of the USPs but it adds very little: in the vacuum it's just a slightly more fiddly movement direction, albeit one which grants your ships an arbitrary damage bonus to targets above or below their own plane.
The most you'll need to think about 3D movement is when positioning capital ships, most of which can only fire in front of them and all of which turn slowly. Unfortunately you can't explicitly set ship facing, making planning ahead a challenge, and during combat capital ships can veer off-target if their pathfinding AI decides that it needs to steer around an obstacle. With capital ship battles often decided by the direction in which each ship is pointing, this easily becomes a pain point.
Otherwise ships can either fire in all directions or turn quickly enough that their current facing doesn't matter. There is no apparent bonus for hitting ships from the rear unless you are specifically trying to disable their engines, a niche activity given how slowly ships large enough to have targetable sub-systems move. There really is vanishingly little else to discuss at a high level.
The automatic difficulty scaling of the campaign, in which the number of enemy opponents changes depending on how many ships you carry over from the previous mission, was ahead of its time. Unfortunately the AI will simply clump all its ships of the same type together and order them about as one unit, which actually makes the campaign
as it progresses due to the slower response times required by larger battles. You'll coast through the campaigns until their final missions, which both spike difficulty up to the same obscene level. They are disasters and I would suggest just watching the closing cut-scenes online instead of bothering with either.
I paid £9 for the game when it was on sale and am not unhappy with that. But I cannot recommend it for £27 nearly two years after release.

Figured I would review this game because I being easily scared do not know if I will ever finish Alien: Isolation. Trust me, I would love to finish this game just because I purchased it and should get my money’s worth, but hiding in a locker afraid to come out does not really facilitate this. All my own failings’ aside, this game is fantastic, it is gorgeous with a style that leans more towards the original Aliens movie, then any of the sequels. The moment I stepped foot on the space station I was instantly like “OH CRAP” because the music and surroundings convey the message, “Get out now it’s really bad in here.” In fact, though you do not even encounter the alien (even a bit)  during the initial portion of the game and I was still freaked out.
Other reviews like to mention that this game can be punishingly difficult at times, and I have to agree. The aliens sometimes will just keep patrolling in circles never really giving you a chance to duck out and continue on your mission, and when it does disappear into a vent it’s trolling you just to come right back out.
So the verdict, fantastic game that captures the spirit of the original film perfectly while really letting the horror of the situation sink into the player. Even if you aren’t a fan of the Aliens franchise you can probably enjoy this game, however if you have been hesitating on whether or not to buy this game I suggest picking it up when/if it goes on sale. Either for the asking price or on sale Alien: Isolation is a good purchase (even for someone to scared to leave a locker).

Arcade style game play. You're typically deployed into a hostile area where you shoot people/blow up things indiscriminately.
It's clear the game was heavily influenced by Metal Slug. You start out as Rambro (a play on Rambo and Broforce) and you progress through each mission, which simply involved killing everything and sometimes killing a boss. The coolest thing about this game is that, like Metal Slug, you also have to free POWs, but
Metal Slug, you unlock characters as you unlock said POWs.
So you start with Rambro, but then after one or a couple freed POWs, you unlock B.A. Broracus (they're all named like that). And as you progress through the "story," it takes more and more POWs to unlock a new character. Also, as you free POWs you get extra lives, and with the game increasing in difficulty as you go, you'll need those extra lives to make it through the levels.
The interesting thing about the gameplay is that you would think you should always unlock POWs, right? Well, as you progress, the characters you unlock have increasingly more interesting abilties/guns. So, sometimes you may want to hold onto Mr. Anderbro (it really should've been just "Nebro," ... come on, man) to finish the level for you, and then before you exit the level, go back and get the POWs so you aren't stuck with a less-preferred character. It's a neat little dynamic - should you risk not having extra lives to wreck shop for the rest of the level (but then get hit once or a few times and die earlier), or lose your character, get the extra life, but potentially be stuck with someone you don't particularly like? It's cool because it forces you to learn how to play with all characters and strategize for each one, which is an unexpected surprise for a game with such simple concepts.
Also, there are some missions that allow you to unlock new usuable items, and many of these levels require that you only have one life and use one character. It adds a little spice to a game that doesn't try to be anything more than it is: a shoot 'em up with very little story that's played for the pure enjoyment of the arcade-style play.
The boss fights are cool. Early boss fights are fairly easy, and later boss fights get kinda ridiculous, but what else can you expect?
While the score is average, honestly, this isn't the reason you play a game like this, and the devs knew that. I gave it that score because they didn't try to give it a story, but
. But it does get a little extra boost from a couple things - they did give you a reason for why you're doing what you're doing ...
And they made a comedic play on this. I guffawed pretty hard when I read for a particular country, the reason they gave for the mission was something to the effect of:
So this game ends up being a satire/sarcastic commentary on our own real-life American culture of generally not trying to understand other cultures but rather expecting other cultures to assimilate into ours. Way to go with the comedy, devs!
Other than that though, you just go to an area, shoot everything, and leave.
Also think it's neat that they didn't discriminate. You also have women "bros" to unlock too, and they made a great choice with "Ellen Ripbro."

A lot of readers to VNs have experienced significantly worse, for games made entirely for girls. At least I felt like a hero, I was resourceful, successful, romance not critical to my adventure, and I had eyes.

Paths are really short, SUPER short, but the art is wonderful. In most visual novels, the sample pictures may be the last cgs you get. Nearly every panel of this thing has new art, and more importantly fully drawn, romantic illustration backgrounds.
On sale, it's absolutely worth the price.

The story is short and relatively cohesive. If you're only going for one or two playthroughs, it's pretty solid. It's got a great art style, the sound scape is spot on, and the story telling is engaging.
I wouldn't recommend it, though, for the reasons below:
Unfortunately there isn't much of a 'choice' between falling in love with an elven stud and going on your own adventure. Most of the endings result in the two falling in love and herione blindly following Gavin's lead (there is only ONE time in the entire game where you have the option to be forward with him). Some endings the herione is pleased with the outcome and some she's like: uh, wait, hold up. Either way, it gets fairly boring and repetative. Can't we just be friends? Sword buddies? Teach me the elvish ways, not swoop me in your arms and drag me home to your mother.
Also the overarching story starts to fall apart the more you play through it. The passage of time is unclear, but the prisoners meet vastly different fates in some of the endings - but when you save them you always save the same dude. Why are the prisoners being moved around so much, why are the prisoners even there, why was the raiding party sent out in the first place? And then there are all these other questions: who is the REAL leader and decision-maker for our evil-doers, why are they even hanging out together, how did they come to set up camp there, WHY ARE THEY BUILDING THE THINGS THEY ARE BUILDING AND WHAT PURPOSE DO THEY EVEN SERVE?? Like?? I have so many more questions and playing more just made me more confused.
One last thing: the herione doesn't have much agency. She gets to make a few of the choices, but elf-stud talks more than she does, does all the cool stuff, and generally makes himself out to be an action hero while our herione gets herself into trouble. Like, okay, cool you can do that once or twice but eventually it just gets boring. We understand that our herione is naive and stubborn and a young warrior whose not that experienced in battle, we GET IT, but if our herione were a hero instead she'd get to do a lot more cool things.

About three years later I made a second attempt, this time with a new computer. I began running around waving a pistol around in a environment that looked like it was built by a map editor on a Sunday afternoon. It could have had a better start, but better starts nothing when I realized how much I enjoyed it while engaged in street-level fighting armed with a laser rifle while backed by some cheap knockoffs of the Brotherhoods of Steel from Fallout 3. All this in day long gaming sessions that would generally be considered 'unhealthy' by those who have successful social lives. But it's a testament for how addicitng and honest-to-god engaging this game was for me with its sense of realism, acute open-worldiness, and how I feel like I am treated like someone with brains if I want to win rather than the tiptoe-through-the-garden-markers-on-every-interactable that so many other games *cough Assassin's Creed cough* do.
I really don't know why I'm constantly comparing Stalker to other games, but let it be said that Stalker did come out in 2003, before all of them, so let's put a big medal for originality then eh?

So far I've played only the prologue campaign. I'm an old-school fan of TW, having played Shogun, Medieval, Rome, BI & Shogun 2 (not FotS). Normal version:
I was very skeptical about buying this game. I saw all the reviews saying how CA ♥♥♥♥ed rome 2 up and comments from other players saying that emperors edition is still bad. However, I decided to go against the odds and bought the game on summer sale and I must say I was suprised in a good way. Game is pretty much stable (sometimes it crashes on very big battles If you have high graphical settings), graphics look really good, AI sure is better( it tries to flank with cavalry or ships) and overall I like the experience but I must say some things sure could be better. Unit cards can be sometimes confusing and I found music to be rather made for historic movie not total war (rome: total war music mod fixes that, it is really worth it). If you have many units attacking only one they will pass through each other and create a blob (there are mods to remedy that) and speaking again about AI it sometimes does weird things (However, in every total war AI sometimes ♥♥♥♥ up). For example I trampled the AI to dust and he was left with 1 village and meager army and no he won't accept peace treaty unless I pay 12000 denarii/gold/etc or one time AI was trying to catch my cavalry with very heavy spear unit and by the end of the battle it was wiped out by my swordsmen not doing any serious damage.
All in all, in my opinion game is good now. Of course there are little things that may annoy but they can be easily fixed by mods.

Definitely worth the money if you like sandbox building and managing games.
Starting simple and manual, your factory grows as you produce more and more things in automated assembly lines. The end goal is (currently) to launch a rocket into space, however to get there you must automate the production of headache inducing assemblies to get science packs for researching, while fending off the local wildlife and all the while maintain enough energy to run your base and try to maintain an idea what the conveyor belt spaghetti you just made is doing exactly. Of course with careful planing and generous space allocations one can avoid the problem of having to cram another two assemblers into an already tight space, having a mess of belts or fluids mixing in the pipelines and instead you have straight forward assembly lines that are extendable and dependable with straight belts and a minimal use of logistics bots.
There is a ton of mods available for all kinds of purposes and it is decently simple to write them yourself or modify existing ones to suit your needs. The only drawback is that there is currently no automated updating feature for mods, such as steam workshop and that some game updates may change the way mods need to be implemented, invalidating a whole bunch of them.

While the graphics are fantastic, the story sort of bounces all over the place, with the endings feeling really shoehorned. The main character can't seem to settle on whether she is brave and independent or childish and vulnerable, making for a lot of awkward personality swapping. The relationship with the elf companion is seriously forced, and often ends with him trying to take the "Sword Daughter" back to his home to have children and tend the home.

Sword Daughter is the latest visual novel released by Hanako Games although the story is not a Hanako Games original. It was originally written by Rhondi Vilott, and it's representative of the 1980's "choose your own adventure" type of series. I bring this up now to keep things in perspective.
Although I'm giving this game a positive review, there were some aspects that did annoy me. So I'll comment on the negative things first and then highlight the positive things.
As anyone who's read my reviews of VNs by now, story is the most important aspect for me in determining if I will end up liking a VN. Although I do like the genre somewhat (I like some fantasy aspects although not all; I'm one of those people who isn't a LOTR fan), the writing did put me off at first. It's rare for a story to use the second person perspective, simply because it is difficult to pull off. But I think that the author used it to make the reader engaged more in the story. Most of the characters are either likeable or tolerable, and I thought that the main character Tyrna was in the middle. Now as for the potential love interest Gavin, I didn't like him from the start. He finds Tyrna and depending on the choices that the player makes, Gavin can either be helpful or an obstacle in helping to advance the plot. Aside from that, I really didn't like how in a lot of paths, Gavin would suddenly proclaim his love for Tyrna. I mean, really? No one falls in love that quickly unless they're extremely young and then I don't even think they would fall in love that fast. Gavin annoyed me so much that I wish there was the option to punch him in the face. That would have made me happy. lol
However, these are the only negative aspects I found. So moving on to the positive aspects. The art is extremely beautiful. It's different from the usual art found in VNs but I think that this is fine because of the genre. The music was great, too, and fit pretty well with the scenes. I liked that there were 22 different endings to get and there were enough CGs to make it worth replaying for them as well as the endings.
As I am aware that Sword Daughter is the first in the "Dragon Roads" series, I do hope that the next book in the series will be adapted to a VN format. I look forward to trying it out and have more hopefuly expectations for it. So yeah, I'm giving this game a thumbs up because I hope to see more.

I guess this is one where I wished steam had a number or star rating rather than a good/bad option. I bought it some time ago, didn't particularly like it so put it down for a while and picked it up again recently but found more of the same. Overall I'm coming down on the negative side of neutral with regards to it being a game book written in the 80's. It's not the worst thing I've ever seen but it has some significant problems with the story.
Firstly some of the graphics are nice. They're in a consistant style that suits the game book. I didn't find the music that intrusive (although I turned it right down after a while and it got repetative) and the sound effects are ok.
Onto the story and this is where it falls down. I realise this is based on an 80's game book and it has dated noticably. The characters are shallow, it's hard to feel anything much for them at all. The instant attachement to the elf who turns up is weird and creepy especially since her father has just been murdered. I mean don't you think you'd be too upset about your kin lying dead on the ground to repeatedly dreamily note how pretty the elf guy is?
***Spoiler's ahead***
What I really objected to was as far as I can tell, your character is constantly railroaded into a senario where she is rescued...falls in love with elf....gives up prior dreams of being a warrior to play housewife with elf (most common). Or gets captured...then enchanted and spends life with Loric as his wife. Or gets rescued then enchanted and spends life as the unthinking slave-queen of a dragon.
Seeing a pattern yet? Your female protagonist seems almost (or often completely) helpless the majority of the time, basically having to be rescued and ending up as someone's wife. You're meant to be a warrior type (look at the strong warrior chic yelling with sword in hand for the promotional picture!) but in reality you're anything but that. It gets old and is not a great message to be sending to kids either.
It's a shame the story couldn't have been tweaked a bit to give Tyrna a few better lines and involvement in the quests and battles. Especially in places where your rescuer-elf is physically abusing you by shaking you or shoving you on a horse against your wishes (which of course is just showing he cares) or forcing you to kiss him without warning (which of course is what you always wanted most in your whole life and you're instantly deeply in love!).... Anyway, can't recommend it. Sorry.

This is hands down, the best single player game I have played. The atmosphere is fantastic and unlike any other game out there. it was in development for years and even though they didn't manage to include everything they wanted, what they did is still incredible. this is no Console shooter or port, if you want a simple run and gun don't buy it and play for 20 minutes and complain when unlike Crysis you can't kill everything in 10 seconds with your hi tech gun and invincible **** suit.
First of all, don't play it without downloading the Complete mod for free first. This updates the textures, sounds, AI, fixes a load of bugs and errors and makes the game what it wanted to be. It doesn't change anything, just cleans it all up.
This game isn't like other FPS because it is actually hard. You don't start off with an amazing gun and squad and intel, you have a coat and a pistol and aside from that you are on your own. The Zone is an easy place to die even without having a host of powerful mutants and heavily armed humans roaming around. This game doesn't hold your hand like Western shooters do, or load you up with amazing gear under the guise of being some Spec Ops soldier. The atmosphere is incredible, part's of it are creepy as hell and scary and not like the Doom3 teen equivalent of having a monster jump out when you press the door button or a loud bang etc. It is hard to get into because it is so unforgiving, and the first few maps and missions you are constantly trying to find a decent weapon that doesnt force you to retreat when outnumbered etc. If you want a linear shooter like HL2 or CoD with no freeplay, dialogue or exploration and lots of cutscenes then look elsewhere. There are plenty of games liek that around. if you want a slow hard atmospheric adventure then give it a try, turn out all the lights and play it till the sun comes up; call in sick and keep on playing.

As someone who loves Dark Souls 1 and had high hopes for the sequel, I was very disappointed with what I ended up getting.
My main gripes are:
- Bad hit detection and hitboxes
- questionable changes to how rolling works
- the level design took a big step backwards from DS1, to the point where in some cases it does make no sense whatsoever
- uninteresting world in general
- shallow, forgettable characters
- lack of diversity in enemy/boss design (the majority of the former are generic humanoids, most bosses are big humanoids wielding a big weapon and having very similar movesets)
- enemies in general (including bosses) feel like they have infinite stamina
- way too many bonfires in some areas
These points go against everything that made the first game an unforgettable, suspense-filled and challenging experience. If you have never played a Souls game before, start with Dark Souls 1 - it has its own flaws, but they are very subtle in comparison. Should you like it as much as I did and still be interested in the sequel, hopefully you won't be as heavily disappointed as I was.

This game is largely overhyped. There's love to detail and excellent graphics (well-optimized, too!) and voice acting and authentic movies' features and allusions. But, there are a few aspects that ruin the experience for me (minor spoilers ahead!).
First, character body animation is past century, Quake I style. Seriously.
Then, game mechanics do not come up to what you'd expect from an AAA title. I'm playing the recommended Hard difficulty.
Androids sometimes wouldn't see you even if you are in plain sight. They wouldn't check the lockers in a room but would just stare and say they know you're there. Okay, let's assume the Apollo AI is just plain dumb.
Then, stupid enough, you can escape the alien by just running BUT you can't get past certain level locations that it "guards". No matter how silently you move and rely on your motion detector, that is. Maybe that's just a way to make an impression of variable game difficulty.
The puzzle mini-games  are so dead simple it's unclear why include them at all. Could be better off with some hacking/unlocking progress bar. On the other hand, it's takes some time to figure out when you try tacking the puzzle for the 1st time (and it's sometimes irritating, too).
As for crafting - it's very simple but I like it so far. Maybe it was wise not to make a more elaborate system. On the other hand, the game needs it. And here's why. It would be just unnatural to see certain useful stuff lying around when you know the station's been scavenged by its own staff for quite some time.
Bottomline, it's a mediocre gameplay with good graphics and voice acting and awful character animation (except the cutscenes).
As of yet, with 10 hrs on record, I'd only recommend buying this game when it's dirt cheap.

I think this is a good game. I have a lot of hours in it and I think I ll play it for a  good bit more. I dont think you ll be wasting your money for buying this, however there are a few catches:
- Bugs, glitches the fun stuff. Yeah there is nothing better than falling through your ship and dying in the sea. Or having enemies inside walls. Stuff like that. Not common, but happens.
- Silly option buttons. Here is an example; You have 6 ships of the line, the only thing that can happen is a swift defeat of the enemy right? You tear through 5 of the 6 ships of the enemy then board the last one and instead of clicking the "fight" option you mistakenly click "surrender" (will happen eventually, believe me). The game wont ask you if you are sure. Congrats! You are a slave now :P -Play with the no saves option at your own risk-
- Weird fps issues. This game definitely isnt a looker but it sure does drop to as low as 4-10 fps in crowded areas, especially if there is gunfire. It seems to happen even in powerful computers.
- Combat is somwehat random. A lucky hit to the head or a cannonball will happen eventually and you ll have a great view of the battlefield lying down. While I don't think this is a "con" of the game it can become frustrating at times.
- Skills. I mean a lot of them. Most are useless (By useless I include some skills that can work in your favor but have little to no impact on the game - e.g. Gambling, Looting). Some are only useful up to a point (Weapon master, Riding). The explanations are scarce and I found a lot of help in the community site, but still, if you are the "must know what it does" type, dont expect to find definitive explanations in-game.
On the bright side you have ships, pirates, swashbucklers (or weird full plate wearing medieval knights swinging on ropes - yeah, I did that, plate offers the best protection :P) are fun, and there is a lot of customization (ship upgrades, npcs, a lot of unit types) options available.If you can look past the aforementioned issues AND you like mount and blade, I think you ll definitely enjoy this game, otherwise, steer clear.

Good but (accurately) flawed Choose Your Own Adventure visual novel. If you grew up with those books you will probably love this game, but (as the creators point out in their patch notes) it has some faithful design elements that may seem incredibly odd or out of place to a more contemporary audience.
To cover the basic elements, this was a fairly generic story, set in the standard D&D/Tolkien setting (made unique and innovative because these elves are typically *shorter* than a human!). The art serves the settings and characters quite well, with some beautifully illustrated backgrounds and relatable portraits throughout. There are a few effects scattered throughout for animation (ranging from parallax levels of sandstorm particles to the much more common but basic screen shake) but the character visuals mostly rely on swapping a handful of expressions per pose over the course of conversation; it certainly gets the job done, and is about what you should expect from a VN. The music and sound effects were similarly adequate, setting the tone but rarely sticking out or being memorable mere hours after finishing the game. The play system (including merciful quick save/load and skip options right on the main screen) is setup nicely for your first playthrough but really shines if you decide to go the completion route, restoring every choice you're given and plumbing their depths as we did through elaborate series of bookmarks years ago.
But even as a veteran of CYOA, there were some rough edges that stood out to me. Looking at the story as a whole, let's say there are three main main plots to encounter; any given ending might resolve one (maybe two) of those while letting the rest dangle, as they were never introduced in that sequence to begin with. As a corollary, one major plot element is encountered no matter which path you pursue, ignoring the conflicts of logic if you were to fill out your routes to see how each path makes it fit. It's hard to call this a fault, knowing how a good DM may alter their campaign on the fly to make sure players hit the various setpiece moments, but learning the whole web of choices does make them all seem a bit arbitrary. You can attempt to roleplay, and if you stick to your guns you can have a complete and satisfying playthrough in about 15 minutes, but the outcome might still largely feel like it was never in your control. This game will frequently throw you for a loop, when you are suddenly placed in an unwinnable ambush several story beats after your last meaningful choice, which makes the entire exercise of cause and effect feel a bit unpredictable - but again, that's entirely accurate to the books it is emulating, so maybe not that isn't a fair complaint so much as it is something to be aware of.
My only real complaint with the story is how much it leans into traditional romantic tropes at the expense of the main character. For a game that (at least in my recommendations queue) bills itself around its strong female protagonist, something like 90% of the "good" endings revolve almost entirely around her forming an immediate relationship with the first man she meets. Maybe it's not for me to say, but that feels unfulfilling when the stated premise at the outset is her journey to complete the rites of adulthood and become a warrior in the Sword Games, and that plot thread is rarely heard from again after Love Interest McSavior is introduced. Again, not a bad story, if a bit heavy on cliche, but also not what I believe we were promised from the setup.
Overall I would happily recommend this game, even where it falls short of potential it's an enjoyable bit of generic fantasy action you can complete (and even 100% complete) in one sitting. It's got some elements that will be either baffling or nostalgic depending on your past experience with Choose Your Own Adventure novels, but as an old fan I feel it manages to modernize that format in a very successful way for the VN audience of today.

Whenever you choose an option where Tyrna goes off on her own, the elf dude ends up catching up with her and scolding her, and whenever she attempts to fight with her sword, she's ineffectual or nearly gets herself killed and then the elf dude saves her. Only one line in the description references romance, and it makes it sound like you have a choice in the matter, and the preview puts emphasis on the fantasy setting of the story. I don't think I've gotten the ending that included the title image of Tyrna charging ferociously with her blade, but she probably trips and falls on it on the following page, causing the elf to have to rescue her *** and bridal carry her off to the nearest clinic.
I ended up wandering when my choices would actually make a difference, or at least go somewhere I wanted.

Speaking of which, I kinda expected Tyrna to be a fierce warrior (since the game is called "Sword Daughter" and all), but she just ends up getting saved by her elven companion most of the time. This is hands down, the best single player game I have played. The atmosphere is fantastic and unlike any other game out there. it was in development for years and even though they didn't manage to include everything they wanted, what they did is still incredible. this is no Console shooter or port, if you want a simple run and gun don't buy it and play for 20 minutes and complain when unlike Crysis you can't kill everything in 10 seconds with your hi tech gun and invincible **** suit.
First of all, don't play it without downloading the Complete mod for free first. This updates the textures, sounds, AI, fixes a load of bugs and errors and makes the game what it wanted to be. It doesn't change anything, just cleans it all up.
This game isn't like other FPS because it is actually hard. You don't start off with an amazing gun and squad and intel, you have a coat and a pistol and aside from that you are on your own. The Zone is an easy place to die even without having a host of powerful mutants and heavily armed humans roaming around. This game doesn't hold your hand like Western shooters do, or load you up with amazing gear under the guise of being some Spec Ops soldier. The atmosphere is incredible, part's of it are creepy as hell and scary and not like the Doom3 teen equivalent of having a monster jump out when you press the door button or a loud bang etc. It is hard to get into because it is so unforgiving, and the first few maps and missions you are constantly trying to find a decent weapon that doesnt force you to retreat when outnumbered etc. If you want a linear shooter like HL2 or CoD with no freeplay, dialogue or exploration and lots of cutscenes then look elsewhere. There are plenty of games liek that around. if you want a slow hard atmospheric adventure then give it a try, turn out all the lights and play it till the sun comes up; call in sick and keep on playing.

Let´s start. Why is this my favorite game of all time? The answer is quite easy. It has everything I expect from a top notch shooter. It has unique compelling gameplay, the most immersive atmosphere I ever experienced in a videogame, it´s open world and it has addictive RPG elements. Even factions and a really great story. The reason this game flawed was that it had so many bugs. FREAKIN MANY. After years of patching and fanpatches it finally become stable and accessible for casuals. I don´t recommend to play it without thecommunity fixes which are called "Zone Reclamation Project" since I´m not sure if you would like purest vanilla of da stalker. Let´s go into the details and sort it out for you.
The original Stalker was really great looking but it already had its weaknesses. While textures and dynamic lighting were fantastic, the lighting in specific is even better than in some modenr games due to it being 100% real time but the animations and graphical bugs were bad though. Shadows were sometimes really ugly and unrealistic but it was rarer. S.T.A.L.K.E.R. Clear Sky though had some sick high shadow resolutions and realistic lighting! Beautiful landscapes setting the mood perfectly in all of the Stalker games. Back to SoC. Textures were really High Res for it´s time and everything else was top notch too. Animations were mostly robotic but they didn´t give you eye cancer. Guns were looking good and the skybox was incredible. The game was oozing with atmosphere and east european charm. It felt immersive and realistic. The complete mod even made the game looking sweet for today´s standards, adding bump mapping and steep parallax at buildings and streets. They worked and made the game even more immersive and realistic. With Complete Mod 2012 it looks polished and very good but it also overhauls the game balancing too much and make it too easy for the game´s survival aspect. There was also the single core focused engine and the sun shadow bug. The game loses it´s beautiful lighting if you turn off Sun Shadow since it´s turning off the sun. Dumb. It still looks amazing though. I don´t know if the Complete Mod fixed this graphic bug for everyone. It´s a shame that the engine creates this bug with newer graphic cards and drivers.
Like said, the landscapes were breathtaking and are still beautiful today if updated with the Complete Mod and even more so with Autumn Aurora 2.1. The atmosphere is already explained: It´s stunning and immersive, it won´t let you go away. It grabs you and whispers you in your ear: "I know you love me, I saw you fapping. Marry me!" Nuff said. The combination between the world, the free roaming AI, gripping atmosphere and RPG elements (which I will discuss later on in my review) are going hand in hand, creating one of the best gaming experiences I ever had. It builds Nostalgia like a chinese construction worker builds a skyscraper even if the game balancing was quite unbalanced at some points and had some quest breaking bugs. Side quests only though. Devs made sure the main missions work. Autumn Aurora though has a endgame bug where a save goies corrupt. So be aware with Autumn Aurora and save alot.
I have to tell you about the AI though. It was the problem many had with this game. It was bugged, unpredictable and just plain bad. Just quicksave often. Yes this game is so oldschool it still has the good old quicksave function and due to tough fights it´s necessary. I don´t know why it died. It´s a useful feature even for today´s times. Consoles.... And in this game it´s an elementary function to avoid frustration and anger. ^^´. Finished 3 dudes without having a scratch? Quicksave. Or don´t do it and make it extra hard for yourself. The locations are self explained. Eastern European places like industrial complexes and open places with borders, huge dumps of metallic garbage, discarded train stations, underground research labs with secret experiments, etc....and of course the highlights. PRIPYAT AND THE NUCLEAR POWER PLANT. Atmosphere overdose. Especially at night with all the terrifying mutants around you.
Even though the AI can be stupid as♥♥♥♥♥♥sometimes, as long as they don´t wallhack and annoy the crap out of you with their deadly accuracy and one hit headshot deaths, they are sometimes even very smart, taking cover, throwing grenades, luring you out of covers and sometimes even silently flanking you. It´s a very strange AI. Definitely better than this linear CoD campaign AI ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and a lot, A LOT more thrilling and challenging than in most games. Different enemy types from different factions, fighting each other and you of course. Establishing a great universe. The gunplay needs an overhaul with Autumn Aurora or Arsenal Overhaul though as it´s issue with more inaccurate weapons were that the bullets sprayed too randomly to have fake sprays in and out of ADS to simulate the weapon weathering as guns have health, as does armor,etc. It takes too long talking about every gameplay aspect here, watch a youtube vid. Because there are so many hella lot of aspects. I just told you the only big issue with gunplay, the rest is fine but can be improved with recommended mods really. It´s fun with vanilla already, but with mods it´s absolutely epic and godlike. Check out this as an example, not a recommendation as there are better ones outthere:
If you intend to mod make sure to inform yourself properly and backup your files.  Modding is worth it but can be difficult sometimes and generally wonky too if done not properly. Depends from mod to mod.
The atmosphere brings up a more unknown part of the game. Horror. At some parts this game freaked me out, even though after I played several horror games very often. Mutants like the bloodsuckers which can make themselves invisible, are giving you the creeps. A strong paranoia is common in quiet parts. Cry of fearish. Combined with the RPG elements it makes a great survival game too. You have an inventory you need to manage. Different ammunition types with different effects, many guns and a lot of different calibers, suppressors, scopes, modifications, PDA with quests and even an ingame encyclopedia. What I want to say is that this game has a lot of content and the game length is easily 20 hrs if you mod... it grow infinite. The dialogue in the game is good at most times and often even funny but you have to read, ok? There are voiced ones but mostly you have to read. So have patience or skip but then miss out on the most of the story. You can miss SO MUCH by skipping. And yes the dialogue isn´t much, loads of reading and it can be ome bad writing, but it non the less grips and entertains everytime.
There are several endings. The bad ending with the wishgranter and the true endings. In order to save your♥♥♥♥♥from getting the bad ending or the bad true ending follow these steps:
Do your side missions. Not the small quests, only major sidequests. Before going to the brainscorcher, meet with the guide in order to get to meet the doctor. The true true ending can only be achieved by not agreeing with a certain nature to join their program. The rest would be spoiling.
Shadow of Chernobyl is the best part for beginners and rookie stalkers to begin with. Don´t go into the other two since Call of Pripyat has a totally different story and Clear Sky needs some knowledge as it´s an prequel that connects storywise to Shadow of Chernobyl in its own way.

My GOTY and my GOTY x2 with the DLCs. I didn't review this earlier because it's too big. Instead I'll just say the good and bad points and be done with it.
When you make a sequel, you have make it bigger and better than its predecessor and Dark Souls 2 certainly is bigger and well, uh, better than Dark Souls 1. The scale is bigger, combat is more fluent, and the encounters (albeit unfair at times) are great. The PC port this time is vastly improved over the first game. Higher resolution textures, 60 FPS, 1080p, and robust online mechanic. Sadly there are some bugs that, as of this writing, weren't fixed like poor keyboard/mouse support, and while the overall graphical presentation is superior than the console versions, it is overall downgraded when you compare the final product to the demos you saw at E3, TGS, etc. This sort of false-advertisement should be stopped. Online is pretty okay, but 50% of the time you'll fight lagging people and gets you killed by a sudden teleporting back stab. The bosses are way too frequent and boss variety is poor. If you can dodge the Pursuer, you can use the same tactic to the rest of the bosses.
I didn't mention the other flaws in the game and other stuff because I may end up writing a very long review or simply I didn't care much for them.
Overall I love Dark Souls 2 and it's one of the best games I played all year. It's flawed, but the good outweighs the bad. I tell you, there are lots of good things about this game.
I do recommend you wait for a complete or GOTY edition because it's cheaper than buying the base game and the three DLCs separately.

This is a game you need to play to fully appreciate - screenshots do not do it justice.  Think 'hidden object game' crossed with 'time management game' in a depressing Soviet landscape.
It is a truly ingenious puzzle game at it's core and the dreary art style is a perfect fit.  You play as a border guard tasked with checking passports and visas and ultimately deciding who gets to enter the country.  It eases you into the game gently enough that anyone can play the first few rounds, but it quickly gets devilishly difficult as the rules and regulations for entering the country become more and more complex.  Accuracy and speed become factors if you care at all about feeding your family and protecting them from the bitter cold - you could always let them starve or freeze of course...
The game goes so far as to make you face moral dilemmas, it creates a sort of paranoia where you trust no one and even begin to question your own intentions.
Once I started playing, it was really difficult to stop and I would highly recommend trying this game if you like detail oriented puzzle games.  There's an overarching story that's actually quite interesting. It does get repetitive, but the variation between levels and the difficulty factor is enough to keep you entertained for a good while!

The first line of this story really should have been: Once Upon a Time.  Had it started this way I doubt there would have been so many comments/complaints about character development and short storylines.  Truthfully what fairy tale really does have in-depth character development or that much of a plot?
Storyline: Tyrna, a young woman (a maiden) has been trained by her father all her life to be a warrior.  On the way to the Warrior Games (a tournament to basically earn the right to be called a warrior) the caravan is attacked by orcs.  She is knocked unconscious fighting orcs and because of this is the only remaining survivor of the massacre her father dies in.  Gavin, a half-elf/half-human ranger (on patrol) comes upon the carnage and revives her before the orcs return or wild animals find her.  Of course it is love at first sight, what fairy tale does not have love at first sight.  The adventure and mild romance (mostly of the happily ever type) begins here.
Visually adapted story, though I would say illustrated would be more accurate, from an 80s Choose Your Own Adventure D&D (Dungeon and Dragon) book from the Dragon Roads series by Rhondi Vilott (Thanks Chudah for that information), this game "plays" in the same way the books "read".  Make a choice (or many choices) and follow the storyline to the end.  Unlike modern visual novels there are no "bad", "normal" or "good" endings.  There are no points to earn, algorithmic based choice lines to follow, no gimmicks to keep the reader's attention and no extra "hidden" finale ending.  There are only endings, a few that even lead to death (though most are the 'happily ever after' kind).  Each choice takes the player down a path, and through the quest based adventure of actually two people, Tyrna and Gavin.  Both have quests to fulfill and both have the will, tenacity, stubbornness, and skill to accomplish them.
The best feature of this game is Jump To A Section.  Here the player can see the endings that need to be found (as ??), and paths that have yet to be traveled (red x).  No need to make a flowchart or perpetually save the game at every question choice.  The player can click on the section and begin the adventure there at that choice, instead of all the tedium of skipping massive amounts of beginning dialogue or loading up a saved game.  There is also a feature called Controlled Skip which allows the player to skip all previous viewed dialogue and stops on new dialogue.  What a time saver that is.  Between both of those features the game plays very smoothly and very quickly.  There is even in-game achievement page called Have You Done This? with things to do like ride a dragon, become a queen or get stoned.
Though many comment on how short this game is, 22 endings that do not contradict or confuse is a fair feat of tight story telling.  I highly recommend this game for its simplistic approach and fairy tale overture.

is adapted from a choose your own adventure-type book from the '80s. As a story, it's meh. Although the title suggests an active warrior protagonist, Tyrna spends a whole lot of time having stuff happen to her and getting rescued by the main love interest, who's actually kind of a jerk. (Particularly in the bad endings, and when Tyrna kisses him first instead of just waiting for him to make the moves on her.) The fact that Gavin tags along with Tyrna for most of the story means there's lots of dialogue, which probably made this more suited to adapting into a visual novel than a solo dungeon crawl-type game book would be; but I was still disappointed by the lack of a good romance.
As an adaptation into a visual novel, however, I think
is quite good. There's plenty of save slots, as well as a section map that marks the scenes you haven't read yet and lets you easily jump to them. (It took me under two hours to reach all the scenes and endings.) I don't think the music is original, but it's fitting. The art is Western fantasy instead of anime-style. It's distinctive for a visual novel, and pretty, and there's a good amount of CGs. (And I kind of want to use Gavin's portrait for my next
character, because he's a nice-looking elf even if he is a dbag.)
If you like visual novels and don't mind the flawed story, I'd recommend
for the art alone. I certainly wouldn't mind seeing other game books adapted in a similar style.

Reign of Kings is an action adventure sandbox survival game developed by CodeHatch. We all know of CodeHatch from their past blunder that is known as StarForge. Broken promises and missed opportunities galore with StarForge. Took forever in early access, didn’t make real on half their promises and lets be honest. Their kickstart was a scam. That is highly unfortunate for anyone who backed them. Their game had a ton of potential but it fell hard on it’s face and left a lot of gamers, customers… Very, very, very… Unhappy.
So now we have Reign of Kings. Another early access title by CodeHatch. Should you be careful with your purchase? Absolutely. Since the start of their original Kickstarter for StarForge there has been a slew of survival game releases. So now they have an example to follow. Sure it seems fishy they put this title into early access the same time as Medieval Engineers by Keen House hits, but the two games aren’t really aimed to be all that similar. So lets go to it.
The main focus of Reign of Kings is to survive. To do so you must harvest materials such as hay, flax, wood, sticks, iron, stone, food, water, and other materials. At the core of the game is the crafting system as this is needed really to do anything. The goal is to survive. As most survival games you need to find food and water. We have to eat and drink right? That is after all a trope of all survival. Makes sense we find it in this game.  However look at most survival games crafting is a second hand thing. There is world loot in those games. Not in Reign of Kings. It is all about the crafting. Which really brings the game down in my opinion. I feel the game could benefit from having random generated world and having one or even two “kingdoms”. Having two castles. The two kingdoms could go to war. Then also have the whole civil war within.  The fact that there is one designed map with next to no points of interest aside from the castle and a “ghost town” really kills it for me. I don’t get a good sense of immersion because everything is player built. Honestly… I would just stick to Rust if I knew this was the case.
There is one really cool system to the game though. That is the King system for all intensive purposes. A player can sit on the throne and become the king. If there is already a king the king can be killed. To become king you can go to the castle and sit on the throne. Now there is player structures so a good solid group can fortify the castle pretty well. The design for the castle/island is fairly cool however It would be much more entertaining if the castle weren’t a citadel/throne room and was a tad more customizable. The person who becomes king can rename the kingdom and can also set taxes. I am not to sure what the cap on taxes is but it stands to reasoning if you want to stay king set the taxes high so that the other citizens are starved. It works even better if your community is willing to roleplay.  Still this is the one feature of the game that stands out above the other survival games.
The combat is similar to Chivalry, but it is the weakest point of the game at this point. Perhaps I am not a hardcore player in this sense but it feels clunky, it is very glitchy, and I have not played a survival game with worse combat. ''It's a solid game''. "It has its moments.''' ''It's competent''.  You see, I was searching to express the good parts of Rome 2 and I' can't quite reach the words ''It's awesome, get it now'' , like I would about most other Total War titles. That must mean that I'm mixed about Rome 2 and after some pondering, I don't think I'll recommend it to my friends.
Rome 2 is in itself a solidly designed strategy and if it weren't for the other titles in the series, I'd probably like it more. It certainly has a few things going for it:
It's different and modernised enough so that you don't feel like it's the same as its predecessors, the battles are mostly entertaining, modern graphics, and there are some nice design additions:
They've introduced a system where armies level up and gain traits, even though they need to stock up on new recruits they retain their "unit tradition". A good addition that mimics the way real life legions retained their own unit's traditions, stories, habits and in-jokes over time. Case in point: Legio IX Hispana, "The Ninth" , about which a few novels and films where made.
Agents and generals matter a lot now and you can level them up in different ways, which makes you pay much more attention to individuals.
Some design decisions are a bit wonky: they've done away with the family tree, which removes immersion from your lineage. The political system is good in theory but fairly annoying in practice, everyone hates you anyway. You now have a limit to the number of your armies which takes away a lot of the fun of managing your empire. The building system is convoluted and ultimately not engaging.
Ultimately, my biggest gripe with R2 is that I feel it lacks in flair and immersion.  The little things add up, from the interface, the music and the unit cards and limited rosters, to the fact that it all feels 'game-y', from the weird build&tech trees to the general abilities and the all-too-many unit stats. There's no real passion for the ancient era flowing from R2, it could just as easily be a Heroes title or some other decent strategy game.
It's not a bad game, it's just... the other Total Wars are better, so why play this one?

As someone who has neither experienced the horrendous Rome II launch or Total War games any older than Shogun 2, I may not be the most qualified to talk deeply about this venerably old series or this game in paticular, but a hundred hours into the game and a couple of wins under my belt i will try anyway, if for nothing else then for the hell of it. :)
Rome II is, for those of you who don't yet know, a grand strategy game revolving around the creation and manuvering of general centric armies with which you try to expand your kingdom in such a way that your win condition is met. There is no winning by expanding carelessly and no set victory prequisites like Shoguns Kyoto (The province of Rome is close to being that however since it almost always is part of the required victory-conquests, so as to make sure the player gets to bump heads with the titular faction).
Victory is acheived through war, but doplomacy and trade is both viable and arguably neccesary compliments to your strategies, and compared to Shogun 2 these play a much larger role due to the decreased mercurialness of the AI factions. If the player is clever he or she can most likely keep a few favoured allies for the entirity of the campaign without having to plan for the inevitable betrayal of Shoguns clans. Overall the diplomacy system feels manageable and I never felt like a declaration of war or alliance declination was impossible to understand the logic behind. Sure, the AI still has its kinks; like strange alliance preferences, and a lemming die hard attitude to making war on mammoth empires, but most of that probably has to do with the AI having been programmed to regard the player with increased suspicion so as to make sure you bump heads with the titular societal condition :)
---
As for war and combat, both is focused on the clever use of rock, paper scissor soldiers that counter each others within the boundries of up to five tiers of units. Swordmen kill spearmen, for example, but late game spearmen will destroy early game swordmen all the same. Flanking is also very important and in the real time battles, positioning units on the fly makes for complex and hectic gameplay both in small and large battles. The old battle types siege, ambush and ordinary battle are still there, with some variation between factions due to settlement type and size. New is the encampment battle that is fought when encamped armies is attacked. It is basically like fighting a very non vertical crowded fort and does not feel at all like it is supposed to be like that (there are also some bugs regarding the achievements one could get in such a battle due to some features being removed because they were deemed stupid by the devs). The battle type in itself is unremarkable, but it is part of a new system of stances armies can use to move around faster, raid or fortify, giving the game some extra depth that way. Ambushing is also done this way which is a nice improvement.
The AI is competent enough and will see through and counter low level plays on hard difficulty and upwards, forcing players to adapt alongside it. On normal the AI allows you leniency by not adapting as fast (or at all), leaving you to mop up their armies nicely provided your simian guile is up for the task.
Naval battles are somewhat depressing in comparison. Never really getting them in Shogun I never did here either, but watching both my own and the AI's fleets all jumble together in a large chaotic flotsam, occationally boarding one another with hillariously "not-thought-through-at-all-by-CA" bunny leaps of up to 20 metres, the naval combat dissapoints. Then again it might not if you are competent and interested enough to do something of it. If nothing else the disembarkation function, that allows fleets to partake in coastal land battles is great, givning fleets some landbound omph as well making controlling the sea about more than just  backdooring doomstack-prevention! So thats nice at least.
For those more interested in the empire management than the tactical combat an auto resolve is available at all times, but it should be used with caution as the stunt AI systematically will lose your siege weapons and cavalry and just curl up and die during ambushes. Its great for mop up battles and other less interesting affairs you dont want to watch the game laboriously load into (while on topic it is worth mentioning the loadtimes are markedly shorter here compared to Shogun). For some reason CA seems to want to punish people for using it by declaring never resulting to auto resolving is worthy of an achievement. You better love small settlements (often the same due to lack of map variety) because you will assume direct controll of hundreds of such battles to win such a badge. Also you mustn't loose once, so good luck! ;P
---
Like with most Total Wars of new (or so im told) much of the older complexities of the series has been either opted out of or for better and for worse been "dumbed down" as we are prone to call such adjustments, and even though I can still feel and appreciate that Rome II at heart is a coplex game to master, a lot of said streamlined features really fills me with estrangement.
A good example is the political system. Instead of having a family and a clan separately as in shogun (and some kind of even more fleshed out family tree in earlier titles I never played) you have in Rome II a system of two political factions vying for power in a kinda sorta republic voting kind of manner (kinda, and it is basically the same for all factions, which is a lost opportunity if you ask me). Having little power for your own -ruling- party is bad and will result in an unstable realm, but having too much angers people as well leaving you to either balance the politics 50/50 or scumming yourself to avoid civil wars as a result of you politicising too well. Bonuses for having a large political power base is huge, but always offset by the risk of civil war, an event similair to the realm divide of Shogun where everyone else would gang up on the upstart human trying to unite the land; here broken up into both the civil war (that can be avoided all together by just keeping the political factions in stable power relations), and a hostility increase to all known factions based on your amount of conquests. This system is better imho, and doesn't feel as much like a "boss battle style" game mechanic as much as a reality of imperialistic policies taking the toll on both internal and foreign relations. Overall though the sytem is clunky and feels like an afterthought. Random events that are supposed to shake things up happen only during the early parts of the game, and even then they do not allow for more strategizing than picking the one you think will work out the best. A wasted effort, sadly.
Other streamlined functions are the tech tree and level perks that have been overhauled to consist of pairs of threes where each part is separate from the rest. In the tech trees case this means that military and civilian tech is split into tactics, strategy and siege as well as economy, culture and construction respectively.
Personally I like that the tech tree is larger than the Shogun II one, but i dislike the "tech garden" as opposed to just having one or two large trees to work with. Oftentimes one or two branches is left almost unused since some are more pressing or neccesary to finish early or just plain better in the long run. What must have sounded like more options for the players during development ended up being a lot of dead space and a few preferable options.
The character perks also feel like a step in the wrong directionm having short lived specialized heroes that never reach their full potential due to the specialisation needed to be useful rendering them weak at everything but a chosen activity.

Dark Souls 2 is a continuation of the Souls franchise by From Software, a 3rd person action / RPG game with an emphasis on melee combat.  Its hard to review this game without comparing it to the original.  Overall I think a lot of the complaints I had have been addressed, although this game is not a strict improvement.
There's probably 3 main points to make when it comes to reviewing this game.  The gameplay mechanics, the environments + story, and the difficulty.  As a short aside, this applies to both the main game and the Crowns DLC trilogy, which is significant added playable content on top of the main game.
The gameplay mechanics are very much improved.  The game's upgrade system and statistics are mostly transparent and streamlined, although a few annoying exceptions persists where upgraded stats do not reveal their relevant number thresholds.   Although the possibility still existed enemies could not consistently attack though walls, although this perhaps is more due to the enemy variety than the game system itself.  Menus are much cleaner and acessible, and the game character and camera controls quite fluidly overall.  Attacks do not buffer so heavily, bows and spells can be more easily aimed for functionality, lock on range is much more graceful, and so forth.  Keyboard controls are even reasonably functional now  Overall, a great improvement.
Environments and story are what I feel are more lacking.  It is hard to describe, but the previous Dark Souls game (and from what I have seen of Demon's Souls), the environments feel less inspired.  Something about the other games felt much more unique, but uts not to say that they were without their bland environments (Darkroot Basin, for instance),  The reason may be that most of the environments in this iteration are broken up into many smaller chunks with more bonfires and is much more straightforward.  Blighttown in DkS1 had a total of 2 bonfires before the boss, while the similar location The Gutter DkS2 has four, and is much more straightforward.  DkS2 only has one exceptionally aesthetically pleasing location for me (Shrine of Amana), wheras DkS1 had quite a few (Anor Londo, Ash Lake, Painted World, Kiln).  Dark Souls 2 definately has better graphical fidelity, but this doesn't mean everything.
As for story, Dark Souls 2 initially doesn't impress much as its story seems to be much weaker, but given a bit more time with the game I see things I initially missed.  It is hard to give much description, but there is definitely enough subtelty and uncertainty to satisfy me, and I quite enjoyed that in original game.  It lacks the strength that comes with the origin story of the original game, but being different does not mean that it is much worse because of it.
Lastly, difficulty.  It is hard to form any accurate sense of difficulty between the two games as Dark Souls was my first game in the genre, and I do not get to have that initial learning experience a second time.  The game is more accessible and also easier to me personally, but this may simply be that I am a veteran.  I look around corners carefully, kite enemies to observe patterns, and tread with caution.  The game was not without its hard moments, but with the improved game mechanics there are definitely a lot less ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t ones.
Its hard to say all I could about the game because there is so much one could talk about!  It is a game I would recommend to a core (non-casual) gamer, especially to people intimidated by the reputation the original had.   More functional than the original, a little less charm, still worth it.
