Dark Souls II is a great sequal to Dark Souls I (you dont HAVE to play DS1 to play DS2, but I would recommend it).  This game reminds me of what many other games have forgotten over the years, its about playing a well concieved game.  There are many details that make this game great, each weapon (even of the same type) dont always fight the same, the bosses each have their strengths and weaknesses, there is no handholding the player through the entire game, the story is deep, but not shoved down your throat with long boring cut scenes.
As a whole this is a game that is so easy to come back, and play 2,3,4, or more times through and still find items you missed, or new stratagies to beat your foes.
Even with all of these good features there are some aspects that have turned away some  players, the game is ruthless, and unlike in DS1, DS2 will not let you farm till your overleveled for and area, forcing you to get better or suffer the consicences.  Some mechanics at times can still be a bit rough around the edges (like jumping, or shooting arrows around corners) but I have yet to find anything that breaks the game play.
TL;DR - DS2 is a good game that is a moderate to hard challenge for the average gamer with plenty of depth to demand multiple playthroughs.

The design of this game is so poor, I can't even begin to imagine where all the adoration for this game come from. Well, yes I can -- I will admit the environment is astounding. It's creepy and atmospheric. But the gameplay is beyond broken. It's supposedly going for a realistic feel. Part of that realistic feel is that you can miss your target even if your cross hairs are directly on him. Sounds good in theory. Unfortunately, the implementation is embarrassingly poor. I literally emptied three clips on a guy that was about 5-10 feet in front of me. So not only did several bullets somehow not hit the guy right in front of me (even though my cross hairs were on him), but the guy was also a bullet sponge.
If you're going to be realistic then be realistic. I get the idea that I could miss a guy 30 or 50 feet away from me even when my cross hairs are on him...but not 5-10 feet away. That should be a hit 99% of the time, especially if my character is supposedly military trained. And what's with the bullet sponge bad guys? You're going for realism? Then pretty much every guy should go down with one shot. Even if I shoot a guy in the leg or arm, they'll likely fall or flail around for a bit...not continue to shoot back as if nothing happened. But I would literally hit guys in the chest and they just kept firing back like it was all good. Unbelievable.
Ultimately, what you get is a VERY overrated game that's big on atmosphere, but is so fundamentally broken in the gameplay department that it's unplayable. Honestly, this is one of the worst purchases on Steam that I've made. I would love to get my $5 back.

This is probably one of the best games I've ever played. Keep in mind, I don't make that statement lightly. Factorio is one part real-time strategy game, one part management tycoon-esque game, and another part survival game. You start with some iron in your inventory and after about 10 hours in, you have an absolutely massive automated factory generally too big for you to see all on one screen yet for some reason you never forget what each part of the factory is doing. You'll go from coal powered machinery billowing out clouds of smog to electric furnaces buzzing with logistic robots. By the end you will see thousands of machine arms moving resources/goods to storage containers, furnaces or assembling machines and assuming you've done it right, it will all go off without a hitch. Trains delivering fresh ore to the main factory lines being unloaded in perfect unison onto conveyor belts to be refined into intermediate products which allow for research and more intense production. I don't even know where to start or end when discussing this game because it's just so damn well done and it's so much fun to play. If ever there was a game worth grabbing for 20 bucks and playing with friends, it was definitely Factorio. I promise you won't regret it.

Sword Daughter is a visual novel adaptation of the 1980's Choose Your Own Adventure-style game book in the "Dragon Roads" series by Rhondi Vilott.  As such, the writing and story direction is very similar to what one might expect from classic entries in the genre.  Unfortunately, the game has received somewhat of a bad reputation due to its lack of depth and shallow characters, but a fully fleshed out visual novel with intricate plotting and rounded characters isn't what the game is supposed to be.  For those who've spent countless hours as a child discovering your love for reading while devouring Choose Your Own Adventure books faster than your parents could buy them, you'll find Sword Daughter to be quite familiar.  The style hearkens back to these old stories with treasure, tragedy and monsters behind every page and the path to adventure entirely up to you.  Anyone expecting more of the game is going to be sorely disappointed.
You take on the role of Tyrna, a young woman trained and raised by her father as a sword daughter.  Competing in the Warrior Games was all she ever dreamed of, that is until everything forever changes when a group of raiding orcs ambushes her caravan and takes her companions prisoner.  With a mysterious elf by her side, will she seek vengeance, truth or love in this exciting adventure?
Although the story has elements that place it in the otome category, I do not feel it's a very good example of the genre.  Aside from one dimensional characters with barely any development at all, the romance has absolutely no build up and comes completely out of left field.  Oftentimes one of the characters will start talking about love and being "more than friends" when they've barely known each other a few hours.  This can be off putting and uncomfortable (not to mention kind of creepy), but if you can get past the love-at-first-sight awkwardness, it's bearable.  I enjoyed some of Tyrna's inner monologue as she works through strange new feelings at being accompanied by not only a man but a beautiful elf ranger, and there are a few lines of steamy yet innocent writing that will tease mild feels.  However, if you're expecting an amazing love story, this probably isn't the right place for you.
That said, while there is nothing here we haven't seen before, the setting and world building is really well done.  Although each route is rather short with a few of the endings popping before you've barely begun, it takes playing through the 3 main story branches and 22 endings to grasp the full scope of the overall plot.  Every character, object and location has a history,  and even though we don't get to read about it here, you know it's there because the small details given them hint at something more.  It's this attention to detail that gives fictional worlds life.  The lore behind the story is fascinating.  Granted, your standard fantasy tropes are all present, but the interesting twists on old ideas are refreshing.  I only wish we were able to further explore the back stories of the villains who were more compelling than the heroine and her companion.
Sword Daughter's presentation is phenomenal and possibly worth the price of the game alone.  There is real talent behind the images that accompany this story, and to express in meager words how beautiful the artwork is does a disservice to the artists, but try I must.  The hand painted character images and CG's have a slight impressionistic feel to them which conveys a story-book like quality to the game.  However, it's the breathtaking backgrounds that steal the show with their detail, subtleties and emotion.  Some of these images could serve as hanged canvases on their own!  The soundtrack is high quality as well, with some lovely ethnic-inspired selections that help transport the reader to a far away world filled with magic and dragons.
Although short (4 hours to complete all endings, and I'm a slow reader), this Choose Your Own Adventure story is worth it, especially for the price. You're not going to find a better representation of the genre in visual novel format.  I just hope the game sells well enough to allow for more adaptations in the Dragon Roads series, but only time will tell.  It's definitely worth a look if you're able to appreciate it for what it is and not for what many critics expect it to be.
Bottom Line: Recommended for those who appreciate classic "Choose Your Own Adventure" style writing as well as anyone who enjoys beautiful fantasy artwork.

I was bored and waiting for a train one day in August and saw an issue of PC Gamer, a "100 Greatest PC Games" special issue. Homeworld Remastered was at spot number 62. I tend to suck at RTS but I added it to my wishlist for later. I impulsively bought it the other day, after games higher in PC Gamer's list didn't quite click with me, and it's shaping up to be one of my best purchases on Steam ever.
You play as a race of peoples whose culture and history have been erased, but have managed to preserve a map to their ancestral homeworld. Your attempts to reach the homeworld are resisted by an Empire, with whom your people have had contact thousands of years prior. The story is wonderfully enigmatic, and poignant, and thrilling. There's a curious religious element several stages in, which I also won't spoil. Mission objectives are varied, with unexpected twists and emergency changes of plan when things often go awry. The interfaces are beautiful and clean, and the mechanics of the game are fairly easy to pick up, with a short tutorial that should cover everything you need to know.
So yeah.
TL;DR -- Doesn't matter if you're not a strategy or RTS buff. Unless you don't like space and are allergic to fun buy this now.
P.S. And if you're curious how this game looked in 1999, you have the option to play each of the games in classic mode.

A truly unique RTS (and the only one I know of that truly has 3d maps), HWR gives you the ability to move craft in literally any direction.  Don't know if the videos shown display this ability or not, I do apologise.  The remastered version is about as close to the original than any other game I have ever played that has been remastered to such an extent except for the 1st halo maybe. I have not played it, I will not buy a console for only 1 game (**** you square enix, for making FF15 exclusive to PS4).
All craft are very unique, in what craft they are intended to combat.  The story is very rich for what you can expect, ships communicating to each other with icon thumbnails that are usually not an actual face (outside of some cinematics between missions).  There are 4 different playable factions, each with their own unique strategies for multiplayer and skirmish mode.  Only 1 race is playable in both games during storymode.  There is only 1 type of currency for both games, mined from asteroids (or dust clouds as well in HW1).  Most missions require careful tactics, lest your currency dries up before the next mission (still possible with just resources that are in each map - but not likely.
The only critisism I have seen from the community, in the remastered versions, is that weapon projectiles function differently from HW1 classics.'  I personally didn't really care enough to get upset by it, I was just happy enough for the remastered versions to be as good as they are, but there are some players who are not too happy about that.
Be aware, however, most missions can take a substantial of time to complete.  Although, there are setable parameters to make multiplayer games go faster and during anytime you can save on singleplayer.
P.S.:  there is a third homeworld game that occurred between HM1 and HM2 named HW:Cataclysm.  I do not know why it wasn't remastered but the story of it not essential to the plot of HW2 (outside a near extinction event of a non-playable species).

If you liked the first game, you're probably going to like this one.
The plot is close to identical, the empress is usurped and you have to remove the tyrant from power, only that you now have a few more options in how you play. A lot of people were weary of having two playable characters, who are both voiced, no less, but the devs made the option so fluid that you don't feel like you "chose" the character you're playing as. You feel as if the game was made for that character. The whole game can be adapted to perfectly fit either Emily or Corvo with just some changes of dialogue, and the voice acting was so well done that it doesn't feel unnecessary or that it was added at the expense of everything else.
Combat is very much like the first game with a few different powers should you chose to play as Emily. New ways of movement and problem solving are found with each character and adds quite a bit of replayability. Whether you wish to cause a rampage, killing everyone, or methodically knock them out without ever being seen, any style feels accommodated for. You have tools you'll need for any way you want to play.
You'll need to play the game at least four times to get most of what it has to offer.
Karnaca has a lot of architectural and stylistic similarities to Dunwall, but being farther South it feels warmer with much more plant life and buildings having many more sun roofs, amongst other subtle differences that give it a very cool feel. So much detail is put into every environment, while it still manages to retain an actual narrative, much more than can be said for so many games of it's time.

Papers, Please is a very original game, but unfortunately it doesn't reward the time you spend with it. During the first hour or two of playtime it's easy to find yourself immersed in the dystopian fictional world and curious about what will happen next. However, after a while you realize that there is very little variety in terms of the scenarios that present themselves. Assuming you manage to stay on the good side of your superiors, this lack of variety leads to sessions that drag on and on and become extremely tedious.
After reaching the end of any given playthrough there's little point in playing again. The only changes you'll encounter are when you get to choose a slightly different path by allowing somebody's wife through (or not), confiscating a diplomat's passport (or not), and so on. The differences in outcome are minor at best and certainly not worth 30-60 minutes of drudgery as you click through endless piles of documents.
The game's presentation is bare bones, but I think the audio and visual style works well and accomplishes what it sets out to do. The interface is decent, although the small space you have to work with means papers get lost under other ones and lots of annoyance as you go digging for whatever it is you're looking for. The system for finding discrepancies is fairly opaque at first, which will lead to frustration as you wonder how to properly execute your instructions. Even later on this can be an issue at times as the demands you're placed under become more and more complex.
I think Papers, Please is an interesting experiment and worth at least playing around with for a few hours. I'd definitely wait for it to go on sale though. I just don't think most people will find enough enjoyment here to justify paying full price.

This is not acceptable.  Early Access does not mean you can push out software that simply does not run on your recommended system specifications.
Other reviews speak of poor performance, but this isn't just poor, it renders the game unplayable.

Since the game has come out, the performance has improved to the point where it is playable. Server logs would be incredibly helpful in this area as well as a teleport option to a given user rather than to a simple X,Y coordinate.

They've updated security!  I'll change it to recommendation for now since the hacking seems to be at a minimum for now.  At least until they find the next vulnerability.
Logs would still go a long way to determine who's doing what and who to ban.

This game is compelling in a way I can't even describe because it is so different from anything I've experienced before. Essentially, the gameplay boils down to being a TSA agent, but the setting, atmosphere, and music somehow manage to turn that into something so much more. You find yourself doing to people what you would hate having done to you if you were attempting to get through security at an airport or border all because of orders handed down to you and the family you are trying to protect. Do you deny someone you know is going to do something terrible despite him having all the correct documents? Do you turn away someone desperate to escape a terrible situation because his passport expired a day ago? Do you invade a person's privacy to determine their sex? It's a strange position to find yourself in and all of these scenarios add an interesting level of morality to your decisions. You keep wanting to play to see what happens next, what rules change, and what people show up at your gates. The endless mode and the multiple possible endings in the story mode add to the replayability of the title, and trust me, you will want to know what else can possibly happen based on the choices you made throughout the game. Overall, it's a fun and very interesting game. 8/10.

There are games that leave an impression for a lifetime and this is one of them. How else could I forget such a unique title as this? The world you explore and survive in feels alive unlike any other open-world game I've played to date or since. This is a game that has sent me through a whole range of emotions from fear to exultation at having succeeded at survived in the dark depths of the Labs....those labs...*shudder*. Good adventures always end bittersweet. It was constant anxiety with this one. I was never quite certain what was around the next corner. Always wondering if I would run into a pack of mutants ready to rip my face off or other more murderous STALKERs. This will be a spoiler-free review of the game and I'll do my best to cover what I can. S.T.A.L.K.E.R. Shadow of Chernobyl originally took over seven months for me to complete. Granted, I took a few breaks from the game which is why it took so long. According to Steam, I've logged over 41 hours with the game. Feels like the longest 41 hours of my life. The game made me as jumpy as a rabbit when playing it and some of the things in the game elicit such a fearful response that it made it difficult to play it. Is that silly? Maybe, but that's the fun of it as well. Even so, I still faced my fears down and finished the game. Only to begin jumping right into the sequel afterwards. I am a sucker for punishment.
Shadow of Chernobyl is such a unique game that it's hard to quantify all of what makes it so. When I had played this, I hadn't really been exposed to much of the horror genre and it's still not one of my favorite genres, except for psychological horror. Which I can only think it's because I want to overcome my fears. What better way to do it than in a world full of radiation, mutants and horrifying creatures. SoC is an FPS and RPG hybrid with lots of open world elements. There's a main quest to complete, lots of optional side missions that you're free to tackle and plenty of weapons to choose from. The big selling point for SoC (outside of its post-apocalyptic themes) is the A-Life engine. The A-Life engine allows creatures and NPCs to roam the wasteland with a set of guidelines and rules. They eat, sleep, move around, shoot enemies, talk to friends and generally act like human beings. In combat they avoid hazards, throw grenades and act tactically, sometimes sneaking up on you when you don't realize they're there. It isn't uncommon to see a skirmish between an important NPC and his vanguard against a random bunch of mutated dogs that were at one point on the other side of the field they were in. This world is unscripted which means that sometimes events such as a quest giver being attacked and killed can happen. And then you're completely unable to finish your quest. That's not intended to happen, but A-Life allows for it.
My first run through of Shadow of Chernobyl was with the Oblivion Lost mod. You'll want to run this game with at least one mod to fix a lot of the issues the original game has. Due to a rushed development timetable, a lot of content and original ideas had been cut from the game. But, the modding community took it upon themselves to fix up the numerous issues and open the game up to the developer's original vision. One of the more popular mods is Oblivion Lost, which was recommended by Moonshinefox as the most optimal and true experience of SoC. You can find a full list of changes
. Suffice it to say, it makes the game shine. As an overview, the mod adds Emission events which happen at random times. If you're standing outside, they can kill you with a big old dose of radiation. Worse, it causes the anomalies to move around in the world, kills off NPCs that are also outside (potentially screwing up your quest) and also causes an increase in the number of mutated creatures. Yay. Oh and what are anomalies? They are areas where the laws of nature and physics have been corrupted and are dangerous/lethal to passing entities. There are anomalies of fire, electricity and so on. The mod also adds factions that interact/shoot at each other, weapons, random weather, artifact transmutations, better realism, and a lot of other things.
Settings are fairly reasonable and include most of what you need. However, some settings don't work such as the AA slider, it doesn't actually do anything and V-sync is completely broken. Fixing these problems will require installing a mod. You can check out the issues and modding solutions on
. As for what settings do work, there's a reasonable selection of resolution options, gamma, contrast and brightness sliders. Advanced video options include vision distance, objects detail, grass density, textures detail, lighting, shadow quality and anisotropic filtering sliders. They don't give you any numbers to understand what you're changing though. Key rebinding and alternative keys are also available in the game. The only audio sliders are SFX and music though the game supports up to 7.0 surround sound.
This isn't a perfect game by any stretch. It has a lot of bugs and quirks that have been tackled by the modding community but it can still lead to some unfortunate situations while you're playing. Including but not limited to: being stuck in a level with no ammo and unable to move forward, wonky combat balance and NPCs behaving erratically. However, I think the Shadow of Chernobyl experience is worth the risk. It's steeped in atmosphere, the game engine makes the world feel truly alive even if it's heavily scripted and the richness of this Russian post-apocalyptic world is utterly unique. Sometimes the best games are the ones that are the messiest. It's a pity that there hasn't been any continuations in this genre but I hold out hope someday, someone will give it a go.

Borderlands 2 is an...okay game. If there's one game that rubbed me the wrong way at every turn, it'd be this one. It has improvements over its predecessor in story, but otherwise this game feels subpar to the original in nearly every way. And that's inexcusable.
For starters, Borderlands 2 tries to troll you incessantly, but sucks at it. Games that troll you with a point are kooky; games that troll you just to make you replay levels over and over and call it replay value aren't. You can probably guess which one I think BL2 falls under.
Most enemies in the game after about the first six hours in deal
too much DPS for players to handle solo, so you frequently get stuck in last-stand mode near-instantly when fighting. It doesnt help that BL2 did away with health kits, meaning the only way to heal yourself is with insta-health vials, which are only acquirable through killing enemies. Since these drops are random (though biased a bit if you're low on health) you'll frequently be on the verge of death and hoping to get a random vial if you can't regenerate health on your own, and even if you can, enemies usually deal too much DPS for regen to save you. This was probably done to make fighting more hectic, but it instead creates a vicious cycle of getting crippled, hobbling for a vial, getting shot once too many, crippled again, etc. Since you receive less time to save yourself (or for allies to help you) each subsequent time you get crippled, you'll eventually get stuck dying instantly and having to re-fight enemies again. Or you can sit around for 5+ minutes each time you revive to let your health regeneate.
The thing is, you can always respawn in Borderlands; death really doesn't make you lose anything but time. So, frequently I found myself slogging through waves of enemies trying to lame them out with sniper fire because it was easier than instantly dying only to re-do the entire fight, all because insta-health vials either didn't drop or were inaccesible. And again, you lose nothing but time. It's the same boring grindiness from the original Final Fantasy days, but without the good music.
I would say this is just a problem of playing the game solo, but I encountered the same issue when I was playing with one or two friends. In BL1 the enemies were actually scaled for the amount of players in game, so you didnt get stuck laming out firefights and boses. If BL2 has such scaling, it's quite ineffective. And since environments are way larger this time around but weren't given many New-U spawn points, you'll frequently be backtracking through giant chunks of empty level, even with vehicles (AKA: poor level design). This is worse in the DLC, with Hammerlock's big game hunt being the worst offender; it can legitimately take you 8 minutes of driving to get back to where you where.
It doesn't help that the game loves to intentionally make quests irritating by making you either not get a reward or pull a bad joke.The first time or two, this is fine; again, Borderlands is a series that likes to mess with players. Hell, bad jokes are part of the game's charm. But, after having almost every quest do this to you (more so side quests) after slogging through combat and dying multiple times from either walls of bullets or (more likely) no health drops, the gameplay becomes labored. The jokes dont come off as charming anymore, just bad writing. It all becomes a chore, unfun. Hell, Borderlands as a
is supposed to be
, not the opposite.
Borderlands 2 also ignored several of Borderlands 1 flaws, and I think the problem here was lazy development. Your map is still a useless set of lines on a blue background instead of having location markers (or topographical information of any kind), the UI still sucks because it's made for consoles, and skill trees have barely changed. Well, they have on the surface, but because the four base classes are nearly identical in function to the BL1 classes, the trees provide nearly identical bonuses. Everything
, but the sheer lack of attention put into the UI, inventory management, and skill trees can only be described as lazy.
BL2 has actually
in a couple of areas. For example, weapon balancing is worse in this game because some weapon brands (Jakobs, Torgue) were made overwhelmingly more powerful than others (Bandit, Dahl). This is because BL2 tried to give weapon brands more personality by making each brand do something special (every Jakobs weapon has a hair trigger, all Dahl firearms fire in bursts). However, some classes of weapons (snipers for dahl, pistols for torgue) become way weaker than other options, and some brand bonuses (like the hair triggers) make the entire brand insane. BL1 has weapon balancing issues too (Maliwan was a bit too powerful, Vladof was too weak), but never this extreme.
This artificially shortens the amount of variety in guns since so many are simply unusable against the gigantic meat puppets you have to shoot; if your weapon isn't caustic, a Jakobs, or explosive, it probably sucks. Hell, the whole draw of BL1 was that it had
of guns.
There are also far more glitches this time around, from clipping issues to AI scripting bugs. It doesnt help that the AI is essentially the same as BL1, meaning Gearbox didn't even improve that.
The story of BL2 is the best part of the game, which is good since BL1's weakest part was easily its story. Hell, BL2 made Handsome Jack, one of the most entertaining psychopaths in videogames. Unfortunately, the story itself is so predictable and focused on Jack that he's basically the only interesting aspect. I didn't even care about the story much by the end, just what Jack was going to say next; and trust me, so will you. While that's a sign of a great villain, it's also a sign of a story that never attempts to compete with its antagonist's shadow, and it definitely needs work.
It doesn't help that the writing and voice acting of many characters is intentionally obnoxious or annoying, which makes it hard to care for any of them, especially when the game
expects you to.
You're probably noticing a trend here. It's genuinely difficult to enjoy easter eggs and fourth wall breaks when the game is doing everything it can to be as annoying and drudgerous as it can.
The DLC, save the first one, is forgettable. I'd recommend Tiny Tina's Dungeons and Dragons DLC since it's easily the most entertaining storywise. Otherwise, don't bother. Captain Scarlet's Pirate Booty is meh (think a bunch of fetch quests and a garbage boss fight with more vehicle backtracking), and the Torgue Arena is entirely consistent of the same grindy fighting the rest of the game has (though, to its credit, Mr. Torgue's voice acting is great).
Hammerlock's big game hunt is easily the worst, mostly because of its annoying and hapless antagonist, Nakamura. Handsome Jack almost saved BL2's story on his own; conversely, Nakamura ruins Big Game Hunt entirely by himself.
glad I didn't buy the DLC individually.
Would I recommend this game? No, I don't think so. I hate being a broken record when I find sequels worse than their source material, but I can't call a game that made me this bored good; that's an insult to good games. Gearbox knows how to make a game laden with jokes and silly dialogue, but the heavy grinding, fickle gameplay, lack of improvements, intentionally annoying design, and bad bosses make BL2 fall flat.
TL;DR
A 5/10. This is a *technically* playable game with obvious, ubiquitous flaws that mar the experience from beginning to end, and many design changes from its predecessor have made it far less enjoyable, engaging, or stable. Gearbox can make great games, but this isn't one of them.

This is probably one of the best games I've ever played. Keep in mind, I don't make that statement lightly. Factorio is one part real-time strategy game, one part management tycoon-esque game, and another part survival game. You start with some iron in your inventory and after about 10 hours in, you have an absolutely massive automated factory generally too big for you to see all on one screen yet for some reason you never forget what each part of the factory is doing. You'll go from coal powered machinery billowing out clouds of smog to electric furnaces buzzing with logistic robots. By the end you will see thousands of machine arms moving resources/goods to storage containers, furnaces or assembling machines and assuming you've done it right, it will all go off without a hitch. Trains delivering fresh ore to the main factory lines being unloaded in perfect unison onto conveyor belts to be refined into intermediate products which allow for research and more intense production. I don't even know where to start or end when discussing this game because it's just so damn well done and it's so much fun to play. If ever there was a game worth grabbing for 20 bucks and playing with friends, it was definitely Factorio. I promise you won't regret it.

An outstanding first half makes the latter half of this game all the more disappointing. The building of tension leading up to your first encounter with the Xenomorph is perfectly paced, and when you are finally pitted against it, having to work yourself through the maze of the Sevastopol station while listening to the Alien stalk you through air ducts is the closest youll ever come to living the movie. Even checking email on terminals is nerve-racking as at any moment it can pounce up behind you and skewer you with its tail like a shish-kebab.
Yet still, it all falls apart in the latter half as you are tasked with the same rote "puzzles" over an over again. Get to Point B. To do so, unlock this keypad with the code that sits in the terminal right next to it. Pull this lever. Turn this crank. Flip this switch. Hack this terminal. I sh*t you not when I tell you that most "boss fights" in this game consist of pulling levers and turning cranks. Yes, Amanda is a mechanic, I get it, But so was Clark in Dead space and his tasks weren't nearly as mind gratingly repetitive.
This is a LONG game. On average a play through will take 20h and you will enjoy about 10 of them. In the last half the game is reduced to a poor man's action game, the threat of the Alien reduced to a nuisance thanks to flame throwers. Similarly, synths are quickly dispatched with head-shots by boltgun or shotgun and humans are more effectively dealt with by clobbering with a wrench than any other weapon. None of the combat is tuned enough to be actual fun, much like the instructions to flip the next switch. Perhaps by design, as this is meant to be a stealth game but in the final third act the game does not seem to know whether it wants you to stealth it or shoot it by shoving weapons and ammo into your hands.
Buy it in a sale or bundle, but know that this is really only recommendable for hardcore fans of the movies (which I am) and even so, its a stretch. More frustrating than fearsome, it feels too much like an opportunity wasted after such a great opening and initial half.

This Game is absolutly amazing in everyway. The voice acting, the music/sound, and by far the best lighting and use of lighting i have ever seen in a video game, Ever! I have so much to say about this game and the Pros deffinantly out way the cons by far so lets get started.
-Alien: Isolation is a game based around Ellen Ripley's daughter Amanda. This game takes place after the events of the first alien movie. Amanda is still on the hunt for her lost mother and is still finiding a way to find her thus the reason for the story to start here. A man samuels seeks out Amanda in aiding there trip to Sevastopol Station where the games story takes place. During the game of Alien: Isolation you will come in contact with various types of people and or enemies. Androids, Survivors and of course the Alien. This game is based completely off of stealth and if you try to treat this game as anything else other than that, it will punish you. Trust me.
Anyways lets get to the pros of this game.
-The Alien, By far one of the most unique enemies i have seen in any game. Not because of its looks or design but because of how unpredictable it is. From what i've seen and the developers say it has no scripted paths at all. It evolves and reacts to the players choices. Which means you try and treat this game as a FPS call of duty game you might be buying a new controller because it is now in your wall.
-Android, Survivors i love that the game isn't all about the Alien. As much as it is fun and scary with being hunted some missions later are just filled with other enemy types and lack the Alien. In my opinion this is good because it gives the player some breathing room and a sense of sanctuary, but that won't go on too long.
-Lighting and visuals are a huge thing in this game. It's beautiful and if you're a huge fan of the Alien movies it really puts you back into that universe and really makes you feel a part of it. At moments in the game it can get extremely scary especially with the games amazing soundtrack plus the Alien maybe in your stage. Have fun keep the crap from leaving you because there was various parts during my playthrough where i screamed, Pretty loud.
Now i could go on forever but lets talk about a few cons then mention a few things i've heard from other people.
-Cheap deaths, Now this barley happened to me at all but it has to other people so im going to mention it. The Alien tends to cheat in a way where he magically knows where you are even if you are hiding in a locker doing everything right for him not to see you but he just gets you anyways. Sometimes he'll teleport and kill you or just ignore every person in the room if there is a firefight and take a straigh B-Line for you. Now None of that really happened to me because i rarly got in to firefights and always out smarted the Alien so I was fine, It just varies on the player.
-Length, A lot of people complained about the game being too long and trust me it is. You backtrack a lot throughout the game to the point if you've been paying attention you might not have to use your map at all because you know everyplace on the Station. Eventually some of the maps are dynamic tho and will change due to the players choices and story progression and if you're a huge Alien fan like me the extra length is just an added bonus to play the game even longer.
Now to talk about some things people have complained about but from playing the game from start to finish can't be true at all. A lot of people complained about the save points in the game and there not being enough of them. I personally had no problem with the save points and actually thought they were placed rather in great locations. Now i admit there were moments where i was dying to get to a save point and maybe it was down the hall to the left but my objective was to the right but i just took the extra minute to detour and save my game so i dont loose the last half an hour. With a game like Isolation you have to be patient and smart about you're choices and even sometimes go out of your way to get back to a save point but in my opinion that doesn't take anything bad away from the game.
Another thing to mention that people thought were an issue was salvage, that supplies and ammo was scarce and was hard to find, in my opinion i say what ♥♥♥♥ing game were you playing haha. There was never really a moment where i came too low on supplies. By the end i actually was maxed on all of my varies traps and bombs and had 14 shotgun rounds, 66 revolver rounds and 6 boltshot rounds. And for the record o played on Normal. My only way for thinking that they had such a hard time with supplies is you guessed it, they treated the game as a FPS and didn't sneak a lot.
The last thing i wan't to mention is a few tips.
-When hiding in a locker or anywhere if the Alien is near you don't have you're tracker out, The Alien will hear the beeping.
-Try you're best to not fire you're weapon at all and if you do make sure you have an escape plan in mind or make use of you're traps to lure the Alien away from you're location.
-If you decide to trick or take the Alien head on try using different tactics the Alien will learn and maybe the last time you lure him away with a noise maker, maybe this next time it won't work.
-Never run, EEEEVVVEERRRR!!!!!
-You also don't need to crouch everywhere especially if you know the alien's not close but make sure you do sneak a lot.
And last but not least.
-Know if you take the Alien head on Using the FlameThrower or other weapon it will enrage the Alien and you may see him even more throughout the stage and he will try to hunt you even more so stay alert.
Anyways i hope this review gives you an idea of this great game and i hope you buy it and have as much fun as i did! So... go buy it, like now, go what are you doing? Buy it! :)

This game is compelling in a way I can't even describe because it is so different from anything I've experienced before. Essentially, the gameplay boils down to being a TSA agent, but the setting, atmosphere, and music somehow manage to turn that into something so much more. You find yourself doing to people what you would hate having done to you if you were attempting to get through security at an airport or border all because of orders handed down to you and the family you are trying to protect. Do you deny someone you know is going to do something terrible despite him having all the correct documents? Do you turn away someone desperate to escape a terrible situation because his passport expired a day ago? Do you invade a person's privacy to determine their sex? It's a strange position to find yourself in and all of these scenarios add an interesting level of morality to your decisions. You keep wanting to play to see what happens next, what rules change, and what people show up at your gates. The endless mode and the multiple possible endings in the story mode add to the replayability of the title, and trust me, you will want to know what else can possibly happen based on the choices you made throughout the game. Overall, it's a fun and very interesting game. 8/10.

Performance won't be a problem in this day and age, but the X-ray engine's poor optimization was killer back in '07, and the fact that the patches would erase your save game only added insult to injury (again, this won't affect the gamers of today). After I had finally tweaked the game into a playable state, I found an intriguing title with a fantastic premise, and a living, breathing world overflowing with atmosphere. However, exploring The Zone wasn't the beautiful experience that it should have been. The place was crawling with bugs, glitches and anomalies (and not just kind you are supposed to be exploring there!) The shooting physics were far from consistent, the translations were poor, and the game would still crawl along at a snail's pace. There is still much to love about the game, but playing through on vanilla left me feeling that the title just didn't live up to all that it could have been.
That all changed with I discovered the heavy modding scene for the series. I recommend reading up on the various fan overhauls for Stalker, and installing one before you even first step foot in The Zone. There are many to choose from, such as Complete 2009, Misery, or my personal favorite, Lurk. After playing through the game with fan enhancements, I found myself beyond taken by this title's bleak wonders. I would go as far as saying that Stalker with the Lurk mod is my favorite first person shooter experience of all time. I found myself so infatuated by the Zone and her mysteries, that I read  and enjoyed the book ('Roadside Picnic,' Arkady and Boris Strugatsky, 1971) and  watched and adored the film ('Stalker', by Andrei Tarkovsky, 1979). I also researched the fascinating tragedy of the real life Chernobyl disaster of 1986.
In conclusion, if you are a patient gamer who fancies a real challenge and getting lost in a bleak world in a devastated Ukrane, I simply can't recommend a modded version of S.T.A.L.K.E.R enough.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R can be best described as "That Russian game" because it just is every Russian fantasy period. Running through Chernobyl killing mutants. I mean there's more to it than that but everything, from the look to the amount of Kalashnikov porn lives and breathes Russian and to a greater extent Ukrainian culture.
The premise of SoC is that you are a S.T.A.L.K.E.R. A treasure seeker and one day you awake with amnesia with a single objective reading in your PDA. "Kill STRELOK". With no further purpose in mind you set off north to the power plant where mutants and other stalkers reside. What I love about the plot is it has this inherant mystery to it. You gradually uncover more clues about Strelok and his group, and about the Zone of Exclusion as a whole. Compared to the two other S.T.A.L.K.E.R games, this one sets the stage as both a horror game and as a mystery game.
Adding to that SoC has very challenging complex gameplay. The AI is very good and GSC intended the firefights to feel similar to multiplayer matches in games like Counter Strike. The AI waits for you, it ambushes you and ramboing in only seeks to get you killed. You have to be smart about your engagements.
One thing to note about this game and the other two is that there are mods that fix most of the bugs and improve the overall gameplay. The two I recommend are STALKER Complete 2009 and LURK.

Broforce is a pillar of unprecidented fun and action that is hard to find in modern couch co-op games. Currently in the world of PC gaming, not too many titles exist that offer this kind of instant action and variety in a local 1-4 player setting. Broforce in particular is unique, in that really anyone can jump in and figure out how to play instantly. Blow up bad guys and the landcapes they terrorize, with a huge variety of unique action heroes from all the classic action movies you grew up watching.
Broforce is well optimized. It looks and plays great on a decent tv in big picture mode.
The action is non stop. The blood and gore is over the top. The gameplay gets heavier and more difficult as you progress. The variety in gameplay changes on a whim as you blast through evil and rescue more Bros. Best of all, there is no story or narrative to skip through: just jump in and play over some hi-fives and a 12 pack with your friends. If you have no friends, you can still have fun playing single player, or join a session online.
I've played all the AAA titles, I've bought into the hype of overpriced games that never delivered. Broforce is one of the only games in my huge library that I expect to continue playing for the foreseeable future with my friends and family. The entertainment value you get here for $15.00 is just staggering.
Also worth noting, my wife never played video games in the six years we've been together. She probably has most of the over 100 hours already in this game at the time of writing. The fact that she is now obsessed with this game means that anyone can play this and have fun.
A must buy for anyone who considers themselves a gamer at any level of enthusiasm.

Первый Left 4 Dead был одним из лучших кооперативных шутеров с огромной потенциальной продолжительностью – ведь каждое прохождение отличалось от предыдущего. Особенно в Versus-режиме, где четверке героев противостояло четверо управляемых живыми игроками монстров. Все кампании L4D проходились за пяток часов, но переигрывать их можно было десятки и, без шуток, сотни раз, и всегда по-новому. Поэтому говорить что-то о неполноценности первой части было бы, право слово, кощунственно. А во второй взяли да улучшили практически все.
В геймплейном плане игра не претерпела существенных изменений в сравнении с предыдущей частью. Локации стали чуть просторнее, что дает больше свободы игрокам со снайперскими винтовками. Арсенал оружия стал обширнее – особенно это относится к оружию ближнего боя, где появились сковородки, катаны и рок-гитары. Видов зомби-боссов и обычных зомби стало больше: в различных кампаниях появляются редкие обычные зараженные, вроде зомби-клоунов или зомби-рабочих, а к известным по оригинальной игре охотнику, курильщику, танку, толстяку и ведьме присоединились плевальщица, жокей и громила.
Кроме увлекательного кооператива, в Left 4 Dead 2 присутствует также не менее увлекательный соревновательный мультиплеер. В режиме «Сражение» участники одной команды играют за выживших и проходят уровни кампании, в то время как члены второй команды, вжившись в роли зомби-боссов, пытаются им помешать. В режиме «Сбор» также наличествует разделение на команды выживших и зараженных, но теперь первые должны не проходить локации, а собирать разбросанные на карте канистры и заливать топливо в генератор. Кроме того, игра поддерживает систему «Мутаций» – модификаций режимов, вносящих новые правила и кардинально меняющих геймплей. Благодаря такому контентному разнообразию, Left 4 Dead 2 может стать отличным вариантом для поклонников захватывающих кооперативных развлечений.
Спустя столько лет, приятно возвращаться снова. Можно провести сотни или даже тысячи часов, в этом безумном мире и всё благодаря весёлым и разнообразным модам.

ESO has come a long way since it's release...
I'll be blunt, I, like most others hated the release. Buggy as hell, the game sellng itself out releasing a game far from ready on top a plethora of issues. During release I ran with the game for a month. Fuelled purely by nostalgia and it only got me that far...
Now that I've returned and had a good 80 hours or so clocked in, let's see to the feedback I could offer to give y'all some perspective.
A lot of the bugs and stuff had been sorted out, levelling is so much better now that you've got scaling throughout the game. Meaning there's basically no levels to each zone, it'd be not too smart to skip zones but at least you can do dungeons and stuff with higher level buddies so there is that!
The Dark brotherhood quest has been very interesting so far, as have the thieves guild but Orsinium is probably my favourite. There's a dragon age kind of a vibe when npcs tag around with your for some quests. I've not completed them all and I'm still doing them thus far. I ain't going to spoil anything but they are all pretty great.
As for the main game itself, it's vastly improved. You can attack almost anyone, steal stuff and the likes just like the Elder's scrolls we're all familiar with. All in all, there's still quite a bit of room for improvement, as is with all mmos! I'd still prefer an actual auction house over guilds bidding for the ability to auction in specific places.. Crafting and all that is awesome as it had been, nothing tedious at all.
Dungeons have their difficulties and varied stories interesting enough to keep things going, the various difficulties do put up quite the challenge to do them!
For those who are considering returning after the burn out from release, I say give the game a chance. For those of you who are afraid to try it, I'd say the same thing, especially those who are familiar or fans of the Elders Scrolls series!

Reign of Kings is gem among tons of terrible early access games. There's been a long while since last time I played a game for 8 hours straight, but this game finally made it happen again.
The game could be described as a mix between Life Is Feudal and Rust. It's a bit more casual than LiF, and brings the good parts of both games to the table, while adding cool mechanisms like ruling the kingdom, capturing people and even being able to torture them. There's also a huge amount of crafting recipes available to be in such a early state. You have much freedom in the way you create buildings, and there's several addon's and materials to be added - so creating a house will never be the same twice.
The negatives are few, but some people seem to experience low FPS in areas with alot of constructions. There are also some annoying server crashes/freezes each 2-3 hours'ish, and sometimes they might make your inventory disappear. These are issues that I'm sure will be fixed.
I'd recommend this game to anyone searching to a sandbox game with heavy focus on PvP.

First Spawn:
I find myself on a beautiful beach. I see a campfire and some dancing figures in the distance. I run towards them, hoping to make new friends and explore the world together.
I approach them, cautiously. My time in DayZ has left me a little gun-shy in these survival games. They spammed a few wave emotes, so I came in closer and thought I'd join them.
Queue Admiral Ackbar, "IT'S A TRAP!" One of them tossed several spears into my chest while the other clubbed me into submission.
Well played, you savages.
Spawn 2:
Decide to completely avoid the beach area, and attempt to find shelter with the high king. Surely, he would not deny shelter to a loyal citizen of his kingdom. I run to the bridge, not seeing a single soul on my way there.
I hop over their little hedge fence with little effort. It was cute though. So, +1 point for aesthetically-pleasing, but -1 point for lack of actual defensive-usefulness.
I was greeted by the king's loyal guards, fully decked out in metal armor and weapons. I un-equip my club-like-thing, and yell into my mic, "I am here to serve my king! Long may he reign!"
One was walking around me, judging me, and seeing if I would be a problem. The other one equipped this long, brown item into his hands. "My word, good sir, that is a fine rope you have there!"
Next thing I know, I am a ragdoll, completely left to the whim of my capturer. The laughter I brushed off early, should have been my early warning. He took me to their stockade, and locked me in. I was helpless. More laughter.
Then, the one guard equipped the largest axe I have seen in game yet. And proceeded to chop my head off, despite my pleas against such an idea. I then heard them say, "Leave his body, as a warning to the rest."
Before I respawned, I saw the king apologize for his guard's poor behavior, and said he was "new" and "still in training." Followed by a strange term that must be for the upper echelon's of royalty in game. He used "lol". Surely, he meant "Lots of Luck" in my future lives. God bless him. Long may he reign, indeed.
Spawn 3:
Spawn on beach. Run inland, not towards castle. I find a huge wooden shelter that must have taken hours to build. I find a stray block on one wall, and jump into their base. Nothing fancy inside. But wait...
A man in inside this base. He is sleeping. Had this been one of my first 2 spawns, I may have gone, "Oh, my word. This is your fort. My apologies." And then promptly left.

That is a hard review to write.  On the plus side, Alien: Isolation is a truly terrifying game.  I can't tell you how many times I jumped out of my seat while playing this in the dark.  If you want fear and heart racing, this game will do it.
BUT, it just keeps going.  I don't mean in a good way.  It isn't too long in time, but the 'end' just keep going and going and it feels so drawn out.  Also, the massive difficulty spike around mission 15 onwards ruined the game for me.  I honestly didn't enjoy finishing this game as the difficulty was out of this world.  I know people online say they didn't die, but I played hard all the way through and honestly wish I didn't.  I just didn't enjoy the last half of the game.
I'm going to give it a big thumbs up.  But, I would recommend that when you get to the first 'end', just stop there and pretend you finished,  You will have a better experience that way.  But if you really want to finish the game, once you get to mission 15, just drop the thing to easy and enjoy the story.

Alien: Isolation takes place 15 years after the events of Alien, and introduces us to Amanda Ripley, Ellen Ripley's daughter, as she goes on an expedition to investigate the disappearance of her Mother. Alien: Isolation feels more like a horror-survival game, rather than a FPS-Horror like Deadspace. Graphically speaking it is very detailed, the lighting is perfect and the sound effects all add to the ambience of suspense. I can't go into more of the story without giving something away, but  Alien: Isolation is a great playthrough and I recommend watching the original Alien prior to playing it, so you can put the game's storyline into context with the overall canon.

I have been a fan of the Alien franchise for many years now. In that time I, along with many others in the gaming community have been holding out for a game to fully embody the look and feel of the better half of the movies (Alien and Aliens). While the game meant to give us the latter movie's direct and nerd-faintingly awesome sequel (Aliens: Colonial Marines) turned out to be a bucket of xenomorph excrement not worthy of anything more than getting spaced, our hopes--or at least mine--were fulfilled with the release of Alien Isolation.
The game, with the exception of a few sets, looks like something straight from the 1979 classic. Creative Assembly has my utmost respect for their attention to detail in all aspects from environment, to sounds, the soundtrack, and in perhaps the greatest feat of all: they made the iconic xenomorph scary again. The creature has been in existence for more than 30 years now and we've all mowed through thousands of the buggers in the Aliens vs Predator games or simply become numb to their shock factor after seeing the films enough times.
To fully describe how I feel ruins the experience and words can't do the genuine fear I have felt while playing justice. While the game has some bugs and a few glitches, and at times you would swear the AI controlling the Alien is either blind and stupid or just plain cheating to find you it still turns out to be a decent game.
Grab your survival gear and venture into the Alien universe--but do so quietly because it WILL hear you.

Factorio is simply amazing, and it is only getting better.   Just look at the amount of time played by some of the reviewers, or of friends on your friend list who own it.  In terms of value - I could only dream of living in a world where developers put this amount of time, effort, community collaboration, and content into their work.  In this day and age where quality early access games are few and far between, and microtransactions filled free to play games domintate the market in terms of sheer numbers, drowing out smaller and newer developers, it is such an amazing refreshing feeling to see a game like Factorio.
Factorio is a sandbox openworld building game where your goal is to automate everything.  It shares a similar concept with many games, in such that each resource requires a combination of resources that come before it to create.  You start small, but believe you me, you get big!  Towards the end of the tech trees when your factory gets really big, it is truly astounding that it actually functions and that YOU actually made it!  It reminds me a lot of lego's in a sense, and also the human body, in that each little part does its function and as a whole they create this amazingly complex machine.  You actually learn a lot while playing it too, in an engineer'ish type way. Sometimes changing just one thing creates this huge butterfly effect, and rather than reverting it back, figuring out why and making it work is so much more fun.  With multiplayer (which I will talk about a little more down below) you can see in real time how people look at the same problem and solve it in different ways, which I find fascinating.
There are a million ways to play this game, but personally I (and I know so many others do too, as this is one of the core concepts that draws people like us to this genre) love figuring out how to make each little contraption work at the most efficient rate I can.  I also loved making my first factory as symmetrical as I could, because it just looked so cool.  Copper on the left, iron on the right in the exact pattern.  Oil up the middle with some green chips on each side just because it looked cool!
If you have even the slightest bit of OCD this game will turn it on overdrive, but in a bizzarly fun way...I can't really explain it, just trust me xD
The developer is constantly adding to the game, and listens to the community feedback, which is in my opinion neccesary in 2016.  There is so much more I could say about this game, but I will just add this one final and AWESOME end note....It already has *PERFECTLY* working multiplayer, which makes it just THAT much better.  These are my absolute favorite types of games, and I have always wanted a good open sandbox game to play with my friend(s), and now I have one.
If you are even considering buying this game for whatever reason, do yourself a favor buy it.    These are exactly the types of dev's we need in the gaming world today, our support means everything!
*An easier way to use muliplayer is being added in one of the next updates, but as of now just use the program "evolve" which allows your to share an IP address with whoever you party with, and just join a party with whoever you want to play with.

Amazingly good industrial sandbox game.
Take resources, refine them, build infrastructure. Do research, build more infrastructure. MORE INFRASTRUCTURE. Soon, you'll have 25 screens (at maximum zoom out) full of conveyor belts, refineries, pipes and whatnot - either an unholy mess or ordered industrial centers, depending on how you planned and how you built.
Gameplay-wise, this is the most fun sandbox I've ever played, tied with Kerbal Space Program. It has a problem that, in the single-player end game, there is little to do; still, multiplayer conflicts, self-defined goals, mods or just enemies attacking can provide dynamic goals (and consumption for the goods your infrastructure produces). The basic tech tree is immense, and it will take tens of hours to explore it.
Performance-wise, it runs very very well on most everything. Since it's a simple (and well-programmed) 2D sprite game, it can easily handle thousands (if not more) of objects in the game world. I played it multiple times from start to finish, the only 'stutter' I get is the disk write on save. Not a frame missed otherwise.
The game is also very, very moddable. There are plenty of huge (and small) mods out there, which can greatly increase the tech tree and add nifty components. I recommend the following mods: Speedbuttons (time acceleration), Bob's (huge techtree increase), Orbital Ion Cannon (as in Akira or C&C, very fun), Launch Control (auto-launch rockets during the endgame), Endless Resources (if you want), Warehouses (bigger storage) and Air Filtering (reduces pollution). The mods are coded in LUA, so it's easy to edit a mod or make one's own.
This is easily a 10/10. If you like industrial-style sandbox games, give it a shot.
My experience: I've played this game starting 3 years ago, and have been happy to see it grow and improve. With and without mods, I think I clocked around 600 hours in this game.
P.S.: Another nifty thing: do notice that this game doesn't cost $19.99 or something like that, but a flat $20.-- . I like that it doesn't try to skew my price estimation, as is generally the fashion.

Have you ever been stuck in line at customs, waiting with passport in hand to visit or return to the United States and watched as a uniformed TSA agent peers intently at your passport deciding if you get to enter or not? Did you ever think, ‘By golly! Somebody should make a video game about this!’ No? Neither have I, but Indy game maker, Lucas Pope has in his “dystopian document thriller,” Papers, Please available on Steam for $9.99.
In Papers, Please you have been selected by the clearly communist government of East Germany – I mean Arstotzka to be a border checkpoint inspector at the recently opened border crossing between there and some made other made up country. Seeing as how vital this job is to the national security of Arstotzka you are given a detailed training course and after a long six weeks of shadowing an expert border crossing agent you are finally on your own to prove yourself after learning all the tricks of the pros! Ha ha, just kidding. You are given a tiny handbook, a weird stamping gizmo, and off you go!
So you walk to work and start checking passports! How thrilling is that? Actually it’s not, it’s incredibly tedious as the game is overly complex. There are a million different reasons to deny entry and each day your job gets more and more complex as government edicts make your life a living hell. There are not just the obvious things either that could be wrong on the passports, sure there’s the obvious of the picture not matching or the wrong sex, or the id number on the passport doesn’t match the id number on a travel permit. But then really nitpicky things like the issuing city doesn’t match, since all the nations and city names are fictional, something you’d only know by flipping through your rule book for each and every passport.
So you spend usually a minute or two scouring and comparing all the papers. When you find a discrepancy you are supposed to interrogate the person. You do this by selecting the comparison icon in the bottom right corner and select the two mismatching items. If the name on the work permit doesn’t match the passport, click on both and then interrogate the person. You can even have them detained by your guards if you feel it necessary. But this system is incredibly clunky if someone does not present proper documents or the city does not match as you have to flip through your rule book and select the broken rule. Now that you’ve handled that person in line, time to do it all over again! If this all sounds like a lot of work, that is because it is! After eeking my way through the first couple days in game I felt like I had just paid $10 to work a second job and even a particularly exciting one!
Underneath all this work there are a few story lines which I guess are kinda interesting in the way you get weird customers at a boring retail job can spice up your day. But the payoff is just not worth the work required to get through the game. I think somebody forgot to tell the maker of Papers, Please that we PLAY games, not work at games. Just because a game is incredibly complex and intricate does not make it fun and actually can make it far far too tedious, cumbersome, and ultimately dull.
While it can be kinda satisfying to detain some idiot for trying to pass through your checkpoint with phony papers or even approve a lady entry who’s running for her life but doesn’t have all her required documents the game still drags. Work. Work. Work. Work. And eventually I’m sick of it. I want to give at least a kudos to the developer for trying a new idea of intertwining a story into a mundane every day experience but there is far too much work to get there. Even worse it feels like my job is pointless as somebody must be watching everything I do. Each time I make a mistake a computer printout reprimands me and after more than two mistakes each day starts hitting me with fines. Get too many fines and you can’t afford your rent and you’re fired and arrested for delinquency. Lovely.
Each day add up your pennies, pay rent, and then go broke. Just like real life! Apparently you are paid $5 per person who passes through your booth as long as you get them through before closing time. However good luck affording luxuries like heat or medicine when your family is sick, especially if you are hit with even one or two penalties during your work day.
In the end, I’d probably pass on Papers, Please even if it was half the price. Unless you are really into comparing documents or you ever really really wanted to be a TSA agent. Papers, Please is too much work and not enough actual fun for me.
Final Score:
Graphics: 5/10
Game Play: 3/10
Music / Ambiance: 8/10
Story: 5/10
Value: 5/10
Overall: 5.2/10

If you like retro-gaming and hidden-object games -- this is a great take on the genre. You play a "Check-point Charlie" -- a person who checks papers crossing the border of a progressively authoritarian regime. You must work as fast as possible (or your family will starve or worse) as well as thoroughly (not careful enough and not only will your pathetic pay be docked, but you may be sanctioned or let terrorists into the country!)
It's a very rich game narratively, and you have a great deal of freedom to act for somebody stuck in a box the whole game. You can support resistance or state oppression, grift or keep your nose clean, or just do your job and not stick your neck out. The game has 20 endings and only a couple I found were pleasant. Good fun -- I was surprised how sucked into the game I got!

This game is not 'fun' so much as it is 'interesting'. Check papers, deny or pass, repeat. Sounds boring, but really it is pretty gripping. You have to earn enough money to feed your family (without alerting the secret police) each day, which can be difficult at times. Some days you have to go hungry, others you have to go without heating because your son needs medicine and others you can afford all the luxury's your small proletariat family can think of because you managed to rake in enough money through corrupt practices at work, or shooting a terrorist before he kills your friend, the guard. So many choices are weaved into the game as subtle moral decisions. Do you feed your family or allow the wife of the man you just approved escape the tyranny of Obristan or some such place. Will you be a good patriotic citizen, devoted to the dear leader or will you attempt to subvert the regime that you work for, the very regime that has claimed to have liberated you from wage slavery and yet has put you into it itself.
The choices in this game are a mirror image of Fable, and by that I mean the evil opposite kind of mirror, the kind with parallel universes inside. Fable has you make yes or no decisions that are clearly laid out to you as decisions, one emblazened in fire, the other surrounded by angelic light. In Papers Please, everything is gray.
The game has a fine sense of humour about it, and thus it recieves my approval.

This may seem like a plain time management game, but ... wow, it is well crafted! This really lives up to its promise of simulating a communist immigration inspector job ... moral choices both overt and subtle, steadily piling up democracy, and a perverse (and fitting) sense of humour. If the concept appeals to you, this is a must play!

ESO has come a long way since it's release...
I'll be blunt, I, like most others hated the release. Buggy as hell, the game sellng itself out releasing a game far from ready on top a plethora of issues. During release I ran with the game for a month. Fuelled purely by nostalgia and it only got me that far...
Now that I've returned and had a good 80 hours or so clocked in, let's see to the feedback I could offer to give y'all some perspective.
A lot of the bugs and stuff had been sorted out, levelling is so much better now that you've got scaling throughout the game. Meaning there's basically no levels to each zone, it'd be not too smart to skip zones but at least you can do dungeons and stuff with higher level buddies so there is that!
The Dark brotherhood quest has been very interesting so far, as have the thieves guild but Orsinium is probably my favourite. There's a dragon age kind of a vibe when npcs tag around with your for some quests. I've not completed them all and I'm still doing them thus far. I ain't going to spoil anything but they are all pretty great.
As for the main game itself, it's vastly improved. You can attack almost anyone, steal stuff and the likes just like the Elder's scrolls we're all familiar with. All in all, there's still quite a bit of room for improvement, as is with all mmos! I'd still prefer an actual auction house over guilds bidding for the ability to auction in specific places.. Crafting and all that is awesome as it had been, nothing tedious at all.
Dungeons have their difficulties and varied stories interesting enough to keep things going, the various difficulties do put up quite the challenge to do them!
For those who are considering returning after the burn out from release, I say give the game a chance. For those of you who are afraid to try it, I'd say the same thing, especially those who are familiar or fans of the Elders Scrolls series!

I have been a fan of the Alien franchise for many years now. In that time I, along with many others in the gaming community have been holding out for a game to fully embody the look and feel of the better half of the movies (Alien and Aliens). While the game meant to give us the latter movie's direct and nerd-faintingly awesome sequel (Aliens: Colonial Marines) turned out to be a bucket of xenomorph excrement not worthy of anything more than getting spaced, our hopes--or at least mine--were fulfilled with the release of Alien Isolation.
The game, with the exception of a few sets, looks like something straight from the 1979 classic. Creative Assembly has my utmost respect for their attention to detail in all aspects from environment, to sounds, the soundtrack, and in perhaps the greatest feat of all: they made the iconic xenomorph scary again. The creature has been in existence for more than 30 years now and we've all mowed through thousands of the buggers in the Aliens vs Predator games or simply become numb to their shock factor after seeing the films enough times.
To fully describe how I feel ruins the experience and words can't do the genuine fear I have felt while playing justice. While the game has some bugs and a few glitches, and at times you would swear the AI controlling the Alien is either blind and stupid or just plain cheating to find you it still turns out to be a decent game.
Grab your survival gear and venture into the Alien universe--but do so quietly because it WILL hear you.
