DISCLAIMER(s):  I am not an avid consumer of the survival horror game.  I believe I can count the games from that genre I have played with fewer than two hands.  However, I play a hideously large number of games and there are many, many lessons of game design which apply across genre lines.  I played Alien: Isolation on the ‘Hard’ difficulty and at the recommended lighting level.  I did not try any of the DLC content.  I did not use external guides, nor any sort of modifications.  I did not attempt to use the save system to ‘re-roll’ my results - also known as ‘save scumming’ -, if such a thing is possible in Alien: Isolation.  I did die...many, many times.  If I misinterpreted any mechanics, I apologize in advance as again, I did absolutely zero external research during my play.
Alien: Isolation
One of the most remarkable things about Alien: Isolation is that it is essentially designed from the outset to provide you with an experience that perfectly captures the same feeling of the original Alien movies, but avoids every single pitfall that attempting to translate a film to our favorite interactive medium entails.  That is an incredible feat of design which some people have said is impossible.  You will find yourself in situations that are completely beyond your control, without actually taking away your sense of agency.  You, the player, will be palpably afraid of the things that hunt Amanda Ripley, the protagonist.  Her fears are your fears, her victories are your victories, even when those victories are made meaningless by what happens next - especially when they are made meaningless.
The world into which you immerse yourself is one completely of imagination.  It is a near-future of mankind, as imagined in the 1980’s.  While advanced technologies such as self-aware AI, fusion reactors and interstellar communications exist, so do extremely rudimentary computers, ancient space-flight technology and revolvers.  This is not Mass Effect, nor even Prometheus.  Every single detail is lovingly grungy and properly industrial.
As Amanda Ripley, you depart your humdrum, blue-collar engineer life to search for answers to your mother’s - Ellen Ripley’s - disappearance.  Amazingly, the flight data recorder from the Nostromo was recovered and has been brought to Sevastopol Station; A quiet, lonely backwater.  Well, we all know what happens to quiet, lonely backwaters.
Ripley arrives to find the place in a state of pandemonium.  There is moderate-to-severe damage to various parts of the station.  The inhabitants are running scared; Some are benign, while others shoot at anything that moves.  The ‘Working Joes’, the local synthetic humanoids, are no help at all.  And best of all, there appears to be no simple way to communicate with the ship Ripley arrived on; The only chance of evacuation.  Oh, and there just happens to be a killer lurking in the shadows, a seemingly unstoppable horror that is slowly but surely killing every human on the station.  Welcome to Sevastopol.
Throughout the game you will be able to save your progress.  There are no auto-saves.  Saving can only be accomplished by interacting with clunky, time-clock-like machines where you literally insert a big card and watch some lights blink.  Did I mention that at no point does the game care if you’re interacting with something?  Yup, if you decide Ripley should stop to poke a computer and dive into some good old lore, she may or may not be beaten about the head and shoulders or impaled by a giant spike for your carelessness.  That also goes for save points, cracking security, cutting through panels and all other manner of manual labors a survivor has to perform.  The one and only way to forestall imminent danger is to pause the game.  Also, bringing up the map or the crafting interface does not pause the game.
Did I mention immersion?  There are few ‘use’ actions in this game where you just click a button and Ripley does a thing. No, every part of that thing, you have to manually hold some buttons while pressing other buttons.  To aim and shoot a gun, you have to hold the right click and click the left click.  To cut through a panel with your torch, you have to use the movement keys to guide the cutting-beam.  To hack a computer, you have to complete a matching mini-game.  All the while, you must hurry so that the crazed android that just wandered off doesn’t come back to discover you.  Other things, like the fact that enemies can hear Ripley’s own motion detector if they are close enough, serve to reinforce the fact that this is a game where every tool you use has a downside and no game mechanic exists outside of the context of the game world.
Ripley’s life is perilous.  A bullet wound or two will kill her.  A fist-fight of any consequence will kill her.  The mere thought of engaging with an alien organism will result in instantaneous death.  You will learn to pick your fights with utmost caution and avoid all others.  And if you think sneaking will be easy, think again.  While androids and humans tend to be oblivious to the ventilation shafts you can traverse...Ripley is not the only thing sneaking around in them.  When you encounter the alien, you’d be wise to use the vents sparingly.  That doesn’t give you a shortage of places to hide though.  Throughout each level, you’ll find lockers, rolling cabinets and low desks which can serve to keep Ripley out of sight, at least for the moment.  But if the alien happens across your hiding place...let’s just say it isn’t simply a task of waiting for it to move on.
Ostensibly, the game is a linear, story-driven affair.  However, you often have the option of taking tram lines to other locations around Sevastopol, at least when they aren’t locked-down or out of power.  This is important, because there is only a finite amount of crafting material on the station, and you may find it useful to scavenge non-mission areas for them.  But beyond merely the ability to stray from the path, there’s simply the fact that, every part of Sevastopol makes sense as a true representation of a space station.  While many games try to emulate human habitation or vehicles, Sevastopol could really pass as a well-designed, real-world example.  There’s a power-plant, server farm, hospital, shopping mall, departures/arrivals section complete with luggage carousels, IT desk, comms station, marshal’s office and more.  It not only provides a theatre for this deadly game, but fully feels like a place that could exist as a small city in real life.  And like real-life, there are multiple routes from one location to another, some well-beaten paths, others involve some creative vent-crawling.
‘Isolation is one of those games that I will remember for the rest of my life.  There are all sorts of details I could go on and on about, gushing over shamelessly, but one simply must play this game.  Years down the road, I will get that itch, the irresistible need to boot it up again and once again feel my heart racing, imagining that a killing machine utterly beyond the limits of human control is right around the next corner, quietly sighing in anticipation of making me its next victim.  It is a triumph of design and hard work and the price of 59.99 USD buys you all of the game’s original and DLC content.  Get it on sale, sure, but get it you must.

Being captured is by far the worst thing that can happen in this game and while it is realistic in nature it is incredibly frustrating and tiresome. All of your gear, supplies and money are stripped from you and they will never be recovered. You must choose to either try to escape alone, wait and persuade others to join you, wait and hope, or try to ransom yourself. If you run and get caught again, you stand a chance of being "injured" somehow and losing stat point in intelligence or strength, further hindering you (this is especially frustrating at higher levels when it cost more to level up). Worse, even when you finally get away, you are still left with only the items that you managed to escape with. 0/10
Essentially, if you like Sid Meiers Pirates, but you also like the Mount and Blade fighting mechanics, this game is the best of both. I definitely recommend this game!

After playing for some hours I can say this:
The game is a M&B Fire and Steel combination with SId Meier's pirates. It lacks the depth of the former, and lacks the story of the latter - but it does have the feel of the former and the atmosphere of the latter. I like and will be playing it for more. However, it does feel like a total conversion mod of M&B fire and steel and I don't think the current pricetag of €19,99 is worth it. I will give it a thumbs up because I really want to play it more - but it really does feel like a rough, unpolished mod of M&B.
- It does have it's bugs and grievances that really should be patched.
* Taking over brothel protection is a silly battle you lag in and out of. Also, not a challenge.
* When sneaking into a city goes wrong you'll have to escape... but that's laughably easy since they've mispositioned   the character one step away from the exit.
* Finding places on the map from quests is not always easy (is it a region or a cove, for instance)
* Some quests don't make sense. Why would the Dutch authority send me to hunt robbers on a Spanish island while we're at war?
* Trading is not streamlined. You'll have to find out for yourself and it's far easier getting money from capturing ships and selling them.
* Fighting with bigger ships versus smaller ones is ridiculously costly in repairs and sailors and not worth doing.
* Commanding your fleet in battle doesn't work. I try to tell ships to engage the enemy and they instantly drop their anchor - no exceptions. Best have them just follow you.
* Civilians clip into buildings. Pushing R in fleet battles is stupid... speaking to people often does not have their face in the mugshot, sometimes your own lower jaw is clipping through.
* The nudity is just'... well, juvenile. Not complaining, but it's basically a money sink.

When you put RPG element into a FPS shooting game, this is what you get.
Borderlands 2 is an excellent FPS game with RPG element pinched in developed by Gearbox Software and published by 2K , this game is part of Borderlands Series and a direct sequel to a first game. You select one character from a handful of choice and drive into the world of craziness. Getting yourself some gears and equip your badass characters with some super duper weapons both cool and weird, so that you can continue to kill some more lives for even more gears and stuffs, repeat.
Just like all RPG game standard, the stories are driven and told through a series of story quest, it tells you to things and kill stuffs and then with voice dialogues playing in the background telling what's going on. You're playing as some badass calling themselves a Vault Hunter, they're not good person nor bad, they're people who do anything...for money and goods. You will be hired by several people in this world as they tell you to do stuffs for them, mainly has to do with some dirty work though.
There're handful characters to choose from, each has different skill tree and play style. Some characters can use specific type of gun better than other, while some gain benefit under required situation. Each characters also have mini class that they can gain benefit from, in the form of equipment called class mod, it can be used to further boost up your character into the way you prefer.
There're ton of stuffs to do, and all of them involving grinding (as act of doing same thing over and over until you get what you want or leveling up as desired) Several side quests are available for player to grind for better weapon and money and also yield some humorous scene here and there as bonus. All of these will be a lot funnier and loots/rewards will be better if you play a mission with your friends. Eventhough you have completed a game, there will be harder version (much like New Game+) for you if you want some more challenge and get even stronger weapons so there's replayability too. It took more than 100 hours+ to complete all achievements and you know what? it's not a truly 100% completed a game at all.
As for story, it's not go far from good guy vs bad guy, except you're playing as neither who only do it for money and stuffs (and maybe revenge) you will experience some standard but still fun enough plot, for me what's entertaining me is that there're a lot of things to do along the way to score some story mission, mainly with your friend so make sure you have some company. There's little lore about world of borderlands, so you don't actually need to find other source to get to know your game as everything are well-explained in the game itself. Although story seems like it would be too generic bland there are some moments in game that can bring you some emotion, much like angry, funny and nonesense, enough for you to feel relate to characters you've been interacting with. Despite it's retro graphics, Papers Please's art style is delightfully charming. It's gameplay is surprisingly challenging. It's setting is imaginatively grim. It seems to have all the hallmarks of an excellent game. So why did I stop playing it after only a couple of hours? Because it plays too much like real work! Not that I actually have a job like that, but at tedious paperwork that makes up the core of the gameplay is the sort of stuff I use video games to escape from! And then it makes me worry about my virtual-families finances on top of that? Honestly, I was starting to stress out more from the game than I ever actually did in real life. No thank you!
Amazing story. So many endings.

Papers, Please has no right to be as fun as it is. Papers, Please has no right to be as poignant as it is. Papers, Please has no right to be possibly the best PC game of 2013 I've played. Papers, Please is all of these things.
The gameplay of Papers, Please is more or less a tedium simulator. It's Paperwork: The Game. And yet, you know that you need to process as many of these poor people as you can so that your family won't starve. You know that the old lady who you just denied will probably never see her son again; you know the young man you just let through has less than glorious ambitions in your city. Will you support the rebels? Will you toe the party line? Will you let the young lady through, even though her passport is clearly fake, because her fiance was just before her and bribed you to do so? The choice in this game is staggering, and the simplicity of the game itself allows for complete assimilation of your mind into the mind of your character. You feel bad when your child gets sick, but you know that food is sometimes more important than heat.
Papers, Please is a work of video game brilliance - a work of art. I give it seven out of seven stars.

Features: Free building, sandbox, crafting, open world pvp, fps, full loot, medieval, "King of the hill".
Well my analysis:
The game is early, as always be careful, bugs are real.
Map and slots: is small (but not too). I think that the players limit will be  80 people no more. Currently 0/60 servers. Logically no mounts (yet). This very good for now.
Sandbox: trees, water, shrubs, minerals, animals in general. (Destructible objects).
Free building: You can build freely everywhere. It is simple and fast. As a note, there are domain objects (3x levels) that allow dominate an area and can not be built near by other players, more than 1 domain object by player. This closes pretty spiral sandbox. 6 levels of building blocks, the last one damaged by catapults. Can not modify field.
Crafting: About 3 lvl per station, not too big but not too small, it's ok for now.
Open world pvp: pvp exists wherever you go, no safe zones.
Pvp (combat): Ok, people this is FPS and three factors are determined: Ping + FPS + Hitbox. As pvp player, for me it's pretty ok but need fix better. Spears, bows, crossbows, stones, swords, axes, hammers, knives, 2h sword, 2h polearm 2h, 2h ax .... differents damage, attack speed and animatios (Please include shield when you can !!!). "Skills buttons (for example)": 6x differents attacks, parry 1x, 1x run / walk, jump 1x, 1x food, water 1x, 1x bandage, 1x range weapon, fast melee weapon 1x, 1x 2h weapon. Amputations are massive. In general is little buggy yet but funny.
Full loot and build destruction: Full loot is total and build destruction depend of the tier of voxels, defense / durability grow with level, last level only get damage with catapult damage (they are real expensive).
King of hill: This mode is funny and create a special role playing. Actually i am in court of king and the life is wonderfull :D, I go down to the valley to gank my vassals, tax system (1-20%), so funny.
Clans: Family system,it's ok but poor for the moment, nothing to worry.
Player Creation: I can only say is the Machine creator of trolls, laughing. It is very complete. (Please add Girls and more content in general to more laughter)
Enviroment: In general i like it. Dawn, day, afternoon, evening, night; Lighting is so good but I think they should make more long transition for example 2 hours, at the time is too short like 30 mins. Rain and fog very well implemented.
PVE village: Exist 1 npc village with monsters. Not experience yet, monsters are strong atm and need a special potion for go inside, the air is poisoned.
Capture system: I still have no experience preferred direct killing. But it sounds fun especially to maintain controlled enemy players that are good in pvp or simple trolls.
All this sounds very nice but there are things I do not like:
1. The general beach respawn should control more (cooldown??), and even put it further, (Currently exist respawn system in beds like rust and is perfect).
2. General optimization server: keep in mind this is a free building with "good graphics more or less", is a challenge for companies, but i hope that they can control and optimize the maximum. I think they could put a limit of voxels construction by player.
3. FPS combat, is ♥♥♥♥ing funny but need better fix the hitbox, and 2nd point influences this point. Animations and jumping movements should also improve.
4. Possible Upgrades: + large map + players per server + content + another king and create two regions.
In General sandbox is close and very funny but need optimization.

Warning: This is a long review there is a TL;DR at the bottom. Also I have dyslexia so prepare for spelling errors.
This is one game that I keep coming back to. I will go away and play something else (Usually M&B itself) but always return here to carry on my adventures. Blood & Gold: Caribbean is in essence a mount and blade game with added and altered features. A quick scan through the negative reviews reveals that this is often a complaint, that this should be a free mod rather than a seperate, paid, game. I disagree, primarily because many of the free mods out there for Warband would, if standalone, be worth paying for. This is a controversial opinion but I think it must be stated because if you think that this should be a free mod then you will never reccommend it. So is it worth it? I believe so, although I would still reccommend you get it on sale AND, this is essential, I highly reccommend playing with the 'Extra Starts MOD' availible on the workshop. This adds many new features and really adds to the experience. I always play with this mod activated.
There are many aspects of this game I really enjoy but I will not focus on these. Rather, below I explain what things could be improved in a sequel. With Bannerlord expected to be released soon perhaps a new game could be built on that engine. With the improvments I discuss below it'd be well worth it.
The 'Campaign' Map: The map is what really sets this appart from vanilla Mount & Blade. Not just in location but also in function. Instead of the mix of towns, villages and castles, there are city ports, missions, plantations, and mines. This has benefits in that it makes the focus of activity in the sea (which is important for the theme). However, the range of activities ashore is reduced making expeditions into the interior less enjoyable. A way to improve this would be to increase the diversity of settlements on land (such as towns, villages and/or cities) to give the player more freedom. I'd also recommend that the map be expanded to include more of the americas for that purpose.
battle/settlement maps: The battlefields and towns within B&G:C are all interesting and fun to explore, but they get repetative. More diversity here would be a major improvement. Furthermore the layout of settlments can be rather odd. It is hard to find certain buildings when walking around. Bannerlord's more in depth settlement mechanics, such as crime networks, would be a great addition and really bring the towns to life. [Some of the problems I have with the layout do stem from the fact I study Urban Design/Planning. So if you wanted I could go on for ages but I am being restrained here.]
Sea Battles: These are by far and away the best feature in the game. They could also do with massive improvment, but this probably comes down to limitations with the engine. As such I will not comment too much on this. Perhaps my biggest area of complaint is the boarding actions. Swinging form ship to ship and climbing the rigging are excellent features. But these actions get very repetative because of the limited number of ship models. Again more diversity would improve this.
setting: The timeframe is the golden age of Piracy with major factions battling it out for control of the seas. Which is all very well and good. Personally I'd perfer a game to focus on the early 18th century when piracy was on the decline but privateering on behalf of a faction remained strong. But that is just my personal opinion (Although if the devs were to do a sequel this might well be the most suitable time frame.) My main complaint and what could be improved here is the lack of factions. Other than the european empires (+ the Brotherhood of the coast) there are only native rebels. Giving the native tribes some settlements (hidden forest villages perhaps) as well as introducing other factions: Be they different native americans, runnaway slaves, Denmark (who somehow managed to get territory in the Caribbean) and other small groups with their own settlements (hide outs, villages etc.) would create more life and reduce the repetition which is the main issue with the game.
Graphics: My complaint here is not about quality but consistency. My main pet hate about this game is the fact the plate armour looks completely different to everything else. The quality is a lot lower and it looks really out of place. I think that the devs should really cross check the textures and designs they are using to make sure they match and are up to the same standard.
Miscellaneous: Night battles can be too dark. Too few banners/flags to choose from. not enough waky quests (come on I want to hunt for El Dorado). Needs more music (the music is excellent but there are too few tracks).....
TL;DR: The game suffers from a severe case of repetition. Repetative maps, models, quests etc. I have experienced no bugs unlike others. So it is a case (with a few exceptions) that everthing that is in the game is great! There just should be more. If you are curious about my opinion on X just ask. ;)
Overall rating 7.8/10

I have been a fan of the Alien franchise for many years now. In that time I, along with many others in the gaming community have been holding out for a game to fully embody the look and feel of the better half of the movies (Alien and Aliens). While the game meant to give us the latter movie's direct and nerd-faintingly awesome sequel (Aliens: Colonial Marines) turned out to be a bucket of xenomorph excrement not worthy of anything more than getting spaced, our hopes--or at least mine--were fulfilled with the release of Alien Isolation.
The game, with the exception of a few sets, looks like something straight from the 1979 classic. Creative Assembly has my utmost respect for their attention to detail in all aspects from environment, to sounds, the soundtrack, and in perhaps the greatest feat of all: they made the iconic xenomorph scary again. The creature has been in existence for more than 30 years now and we've all mowed through thousands of the buggers in the Aliens vs Predator games or simply become numb to their shock factor after seeing the films enough times.
To fully describe how I feel ruins the experience and words can't do the genuine fear I have felt while playing justice. While the game has some bugs and a few glitches, and at times you would swear the AI controlling the Alien is either blind and stupid or just plain cheating to find you it still turns out to be a decent game.
Grab your survival gear and venture into the Alien universe--but do so quietly because it WILL hear you.

DISCLAIMER(s):  I am not an avid consumer of the survival horror game.  I believe I can count the games from that genre I have played with fewer than two hands.  However, I play a hideously large number of games and there are many, many lessons of game design which apply across genre lines.  I played Alien: Isolation on the ‘Hard’ difficulty and at the recommended lighting level.  I did not try any of the DLC content.  I did not use external guides, nor any sort of modifications.  I did not attempt to use the save system to ‘re-roll’ my results - also known as ‘save scumming’ -, if such a thing is possible in Alien: Isolation.  I did die...many, many times.  If I misinterpreted any mechanics, I apologize in advance as again, I did absolutely zero external research during my play.
Alien: Isolation
One of the most remarkable things about Alien: Isolation is that it is essentially designed from the outset to provide you with an experience that perfectly captures the same feeling of the original Alien movies, but avoids every single pitfall that attempting to translate a film to our favorite interactive medium entails.  That is an incredible feat of design which some people have said is impossible.  You will find yourself in situations that are completely beyond your control, without actually taking away your sense of agency.  You, the player, will be palpably afraid of the things that hunt Amanda Ripley, the protagonist.  Her fears are your fears, her victories are your victories, even when those victories are made meaningless by what happens next - especially when they are made meaningless.
The world into which you immerse yourself is one completely of imagination.  It is a near-future of mankind, as imagined in the 1980’s.  While advanced technologies such as self-aware AI, fusion reactors and interstellar communications exist, so do extremely rudimentary computers, ancient space-flight technology and revolvers.  This is not Mass Effect, nor even Prometheus.  Every single detail is lovingly grungy and properly industrial.
As Amanda Ripley, you depart your humdrum, blue-collar engineer life to search for answers to your mother’s - Ellen Ripley’s - disappearance.  Amazingly, the flight data recorder from the Nostromo was recovered and has been brought to Sevastopol Station; A quiet, lonely backwater.  Well, we all know what happens to quiet, lonely backwaters.
Ripley arrives to find the place in a state of pandemonium.  There is moderate-to-severe damage to various parts of the station.  The inhabitants are running scared; Some are benign, while others shoot at anything that moves.  The ‘Working Joes’, the local synthetic humanoids, are no help at all.  And best of all, there appears to be no simple way to communicate with the ship Ripley arrived on; The only chance of evacuation.  Oh, and there just happens to be a killer lurking in the shadows, a seemingly unstoppable horror that is slowly but surely killing every human on the station.  Welcome to Sevastopol.
Throughout the game you will be able to save your progress.  There are no auto-saves.  Saving can only be accomplished by interacting with clunky, time-clock-like machines where you literally insert a big card and watch some lights blink.  Did I mention that at no point does the game care if you’re interacting with something?  Yup, if you decide Ripley should stop to poke a computer and dive into some good old lore, she may or may not be beaten about the head and shoulders or impaled by a giant spike for your carelessness.  That also goes for save points, cracking security, cutting through panels and all other manner of manual labors a survivor has to perform.  The one and only way to forestall imminent danger is to pause the game.  Also, bringing up the map or the crafting interface does not pause the game.
Did I mention immersion?  There are few ‘use’ actions in this game where you just click a button and Ripley does a thing. No, every part of that thing, you have to manually hold some buttons while pressing other buttons.  To aim and shoot a gun, you have to hold the right click and click the left click.  To cut through a panel with your torch, you have to use the movement keys to guide the cutting-beam.  To hack a computer, you have to complete a matching mini-game.  All the while, you must hurry so that the crazed android that just wandered off doesn’t come back to discover you.  Other things, like the fact that enemies can hear Ripley’s own motion detector if they are close enough, serve to reinforce the fact that this is a game where every tool you use has a downside and no game mechanic exists outside of the context of the game world.
Ripley’s life is perilous.  A bullet wound or two will kill her.  A fist-fight of any consequence will kill her.  The mere thought of engaging with an alien organism will result in instantaneous death.  You will learn to pick your fights with utmost caution and avoid all others.  And if you think sneaking will be easy, think again.  While androids and humans tend to be oblivious to the ventilation shafts you can traverse...Ripley is not the only thing sneaking around in them.  When you encounter the alien, you’d be wise to use the vents sparingly.  That doesn’t give you a shortage of places to hide though.  Throughout each level, you’ll find lockers, rolling cabinets and low desks which can serve to keep Ripley out of sight, at least for the moment.  But if the alien happens across your hiding place...let’s just say it isn’t simply a task of waiting for it to move on.
Ostensibly, the game is a linear, story-driven affair.  However, you often have the option of taking tram lines to other locations around Sevastopol, at least when they aren’t locked-down or out of power.  This is important, because there is only a finite amount of crafting material on the station, and you may find it useful to scavenge non-mission areas for them.  But beyond merely the ability to stray from the path, there’s simply the fact that, every part of Sevastopol makes sense as a true representation of a space station.  While many games try to emulate human habitation or vehicles, Sevastopol could really pass as a well-designed, real-world example.  There’s a power-plant, server farm, hospital, shopping mall, departures/arrivals section complete with luggage carousels, IT desk, comms station, marshal’s office and more.  It not only provides a theatre for this deadly game, but fully feels like a place that could exist as a small city in real life.  And like real-life, there are multiple routes from one location to another, some well-beaten paths, others involve some creative vent-crawling.
‘Isolation is one of those games that I will remember for the rest of my life.  There are all sorts of details I could go on and on about, gushing over shamelessly, but one simply must play this game.  Years down the road, I will get that itch, the irresistible need to boot it up again and once again feel my heart racing, imagining that a killing machine utterly beyond the limits of human control is right around the next corner, quietly sighing in anticipation of making me its next victim.  It is a triumph of design and hard work and the price of 59.99 USD buys you all of the game’s original and DLC content.  Get it on sale, sure, but get it you must.

If you enjoyed the first Dishonored, you will absolutely enjoy this one as well.  Or perhaps, like me, you will love it even more.  To me, Arkane Studios outdid themselves with this game even though it had a rough launch that consisted of performance issues.  Since launch, these issues have been resolved and is now flawless, atleast for me.
As an experienced gamer, it has become somewhat easy to analyze a game and determine the types of minds that were behind the development and publishing of it.  Which makes sense, because a game should be a relfection of the work that was put into it.  Some games are easily noticeable as being cash grabs, while others stick to what video games are supposed to be at their core - an artform.  That being said, this game reflects nothing but dedication, passion, love, and hard work that was put into it by the wonderful people at Arkane and Bethesda.  The art style is uniquely beautiful.  Level design is wonderfully creative (especially for the Clockwork Mansion).  The music provides plentiful ambience and adds another layer of immersion (R.I.P Daniel Licht).  The graphics, while not groundbreaking, are still very pretty and display an incredible amount of attention to detail.  Finally, game mechanics are executed with precision (part of which is reflected in the clever mechanics for the level: A Crack in the Slab).
This is a game where you play how you want, whether it be stealth or action, and the game will change parts of itself accordingly.  The games mechanics, weaponry, and supernatural abilites give you creative freedom to overcome your enemies.  Take your time and explore every level.  There are plently of discoverables as well as alternate pathways and methods to make your way throughout the level - there is almost always another way to overcome any situation.
There is so much to talk about for this game that I can't easily put it into words.  Instead, I encourage anyone reading this to buy the game for yourself to understand what I mean.  Things that I've missed are mostly likely covered in other reviews.  I just felt compelled to talk a little about this game from a passionate perspective and not in an in-depth analysis.  I consider it to be a masterpiece and would recommend it to anyone who is willing to view video games in a different way in order to recieve the full experience.  That's because this is one of those games that you don't just play - you experience it.
A great follow up to a great first installment.  So many ways to play and paths to choose from.  Lots of replay value.

I returned to this games after months of not playing it still wanting it to be good, but it's just not. I have plenty of minor gripes: how boarding parties size and composition are mysteriously determined, how my boarding parties shrink after capturing a ship while the AI's grow from doing the same, why I can't give orders to a boarding party, why do boarding actions start with the ships grappled together instead of having a change for musketeers to blast away as the two ships close in?
But my one big complaint, why I stopped playing months ago and again now, is the terrible path-finding. On the campaign map my ship will just run into some island and sit there grinding against the beach while the rest of the world keeps running around me. Sure, I can break out of this by issuing a new move order, but too often I was trying to chase down some fleet and the delay let them escape or, worse yet, the larger fleet I was fleeing took advantage of my misfortune to run me down.
If this were an early access game I'd tell you to keep an eye on it, but a year old game isn't going to suddenly see these problems fixed.

Like the many other piratey games out there, you play as a wanderer who must make their way in the Caribbean by building up an army and a naval fleet while plundering towns and ships at sea.  Eventually, you'll attract the attention of the colonial powers and may be recruited into their faction where you'll have the chance to rise through the ranks.
Naval combat aside, this just feels like yet another Mount and Blade mod, of which there are many.  Frankly there are others that are far better than this yet don't cost a penny. I payed $37.73 for Rome II with all the DLC last Feburary. Rome II was my first Total War game and I have no regrets on buying it.
Pros:
+ Campaign map and city management is well implemented and nice.
+ Diplomacy is slightly better then other Total Wars I've played.  (voice acting is cheesy though.)
+ Lots of different factions and campaigns (with DLC of course).
+ Politics and Civil Wars are interesting, but could of been better.
+ Sieges are awesome.
Cons:
- No family trees.
- Game seems unpolished in some respects, fast forward does next to nothing in battles, and units can be buggy.
- Turn Times are monsterous. I almost always doing something else on the side while playing this. Every turn takes a few minutes.
- While sieges are awesome, they ruined it by making hardly any the cities even have walls.
Rome II takes it's spot as my second favorite Total War behind Shogun 2. I wouldn't pay more than $40 for the game with all the DLCs, and would recommend the game, but I think you would be better off with buying older Total Wars until the price drops. I might of enjoyed this more then some other Total Wars, but not by much.

Set in a dystopian world. You have "won" a job at your country's border. You stamp passports, granting or denying entry to people trying to get into Arstotzka.
Sounds dull? Well, it's actually incredibly addictive. This game is innovative and surprisingly fun--albeit rather grim. The game is presented as a story that takes place over 31 playable days (there is also a endless mode that can be unlocked). As the story progresses, stamping passports becomes more and more complicated and there will be moral choices you must make. There's even a fair amount of replayability, as you can get different endings depending on what choices you make throughout the game.
The only thing I found irritating was how incredibly nitpicky the game can be sometimes. But it's still very fun and very addictive.
Highly recommended if you want to experience a game that is different.

Homeworld has three things that set it apart from most other strategy games:
1. Fully three dimensional gameplay. Your ships exist in 3D space, meaning an X, Y, and Z axis for them to fly and fight in.
This has a great affect on the strategies you use, and is remarkably controllable thanks to a great interface.
2. Your resources carry over from mission to mission in the main story.
That means every lost unit has an impact, so it's important to repair ships in battle and try to capture enemy ships when possible, something I generally ignore in other RTS in favor of building more things to blow up their things.
3. A genuinely good story.
Most war games bog their story down with the locations the war went to and who killed who. Homeworld has a very human story that quickly gets you invested in the lives of your crew, even if most of them don't have names. It's a remarkable thing and makes the campaign very rewarding and engaging.
Awesome classic, with outstanding plot and truly 3-dimentional fights.

If you like the Mount and Blade games and you like pirates, then I wholeheartedly recommend this game for you. It is exactly that: Mount and Blade with pirates and ships. The naval combat and ship upgrading system and addition of sea trade routes are all incredibly welcome and add some much needed variety and new game mechanics to the Mount and Blade formula. It's more than just being able to be a pirate and raid caravans and ships and rule the high seas that makes this game stand out. It's that it seems to have everything the Mount and Blade games have that i love, plus more. The same character building, faction reputation building, trading, economy-all that stuff is in here, plus more. It adds more depth and customization, but it also adds more that you have to manage/pay attention to or watch out for. Ships need money for repairs, their crew, upgrades, and ammo-all of which adds to your weekly budget and while it was a little overwhelming at first having all that to maintain in addition to all the land based expenses that i knew from Mount and Blade. After a few hours, though, I got used to it, and I love it now. It's all the same endless replayability of Mount and Blade with pirates and naval combat-just try it out!

This is everything i have always wanted in a game. Although it's still in Early Access state, it is ABSOLUTELY playable! It is a fully functioning game and so far i have yet to find any flaws other than the need for polishing up on cpu/gpu resource management and efficiency. The official servers are overwhelmingly packed but there are plenty of community servers and more show up everyday!
The games world rules are equivalent to what you would expect from a Hardcore PVP minecraft server. Absolutely EVERYTHING is raidable which means no items on the server are 100% safe from being stolen. Yes you can put up measure of protection for your items that will deter almsot anyone from stealing your stuff but if they try hard enough they can get them. When you log out your character starts sleeping on the ground on the spot you logged off leaving him and his inventory exposed to plundering unless you have either a good hiding spot or a nice house with a locked door. Claim the land your home is on and only you will be able to remove or place blocks on it and they will need to make a seige weapon to break in. Seige weapons are expensive and hard to use and leave the user vulnerable to other players sneaking up on them if they are not with a group so rest assured your items should be fairly safe behind locked doors.
Basically you gather supplies, and food which involves hunting animals, foraging berries, chopping down trees, gathering rocks, etc all to make your gear and your base, gather up friends and make allies on the server, join a guild or make a guild, group up and see if you can seize the throne for your own faction! Kind kings who give players guidance and have low taxes are usually supported by the playerbase of the server whereas most kings who come into power and raise the taxes to the roof are short lived when the furry of the whole server rallies up to get their vengence! Tax will literally tax everything you collect or harvest from the map, 50% tax? half the wood and stone you collect is instantly transported to the kings chest. Good kings never raise it above 10% and if your lucky 5%
You can build a bed as a spawn point otherwise you will land on a random location of the map when killed, if you join a different server you start from scratch with new players and a new map.

Set in a dystopian world. You have "won" a job at your country's border. You stamp passports, granting or denying entry to people trying to get into Arstotzka.
Sounds dull? Well, it's actually incredibly addictive. This game is innovative and surprisingly fun--albeit rather grim. The game is presented as a story that takes place over 31 playable days (there is also a endless mode that can be unlocked). As the story progresses, stamping passports becomes more and more complicated and there will be moral choices you must make. There's even a fair amount of replayability, as you can get different endings depending on what choices you make throughout the game.
The only thing I found irritating was how incredibly nitpicky the game can be sometimes. But it's still very fun and very addictive.
Highly recommended if you want to experience a game that is different.
